en: The Illumination of the Ornament of Clear Realization. Om, homage to the Omniscient One!
She who, through omniscience, leads the Śrāvakas seeking peace to tranquility;
That which, through the knowledge of the paths, accomplishes the welfare of the world for those who act for the benefit of living beings.
Homage to the Mother of the Buddha, endowed with whom the Munis speak of this entire universe in all its aspects, together with the assembly of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas. (1)
For those yogins who know that all states are equal to an illusory form, there is supreme liberation;
yet for embodied beings who are utterly stupefied by the mass of defects existing within the belly of saṃsāra, [there is bondage].
In order to lead [beings] himself in every way, the compassionate Lord Maitreya composed this commentary in verse-form (*kārikā*) which makes the method of the *Prajñāpāramitā* exceedingly clear. (2)
The one of radiant fame known as Ārya Asaṅga, the foremost among the wise, composed a commentary on the *Tattvaviniścaya* by virtue of his capacity as its author.

The master Vasubandhu, exalted by the pride of his expertise in the doctrines concerning the distinction between existence and non-existence, has established his authority in this commentary on the meaning [of the verses]. (3)
Through the friction of the reality of the objects of yogic practice, a great effort arose from his mental state for the noble and wise Vimuktisena, who possesses supramundane knowledge.

In the ocean of the treatise, he who understood how to pacify the views of opposing positions that had arisen in isolation is celebrated in the world as another [Vasubandhu] by the words of Vimuktisena in the *Vārttika*.
In that regard, those like me, whose intellects are wounded, are not at all capable of speaking about the unprecedented;
for who indeed is not crushed day after day by the best of the wise?
Or rather, there is no sequence of entities.
We have conceived a longing for the reality of the Dharma that brings about primordial wisdom; therefore, we are fully prepared to compose this supreme commentary concerning the true meaning. (5)
"Thus," and so forth.

For in every case, because there is doubt regarding the subject matter (*artha*), the engagement of all people is preceded by a determination of the connection (*sambandha*), the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the ultimate purpose (*prayojanaprayojana*); therefore, the connection and other such factors must be stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
For if its connection and subject matter were not explained, [no one would engage with it].

Fearing that, like the words of a madman or the like, it might be incoherent and purposeless, and thus no one would even be motivated to hear it, its connection (*sambandha*) and subject matter (*abhidheya*) must necessarily be stated here. Even when the connection and subject matter have been stated, [one might object] that this [treatise], by stating nothing new regarding an action already accomplished, falls under the logical principle of a "means" (*sādhana*) that expresses no distinction—according to the maxim that a means is redundant once the action is complete. Consequently, for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), the jewel-like *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra would appear to be devoid of a specific purpose (*prayojana*) that serves as a limb for engaging with it, since it is not subsumed within other sūtras.

In passages such as "they do not even care to listen," the uncommon fruit of the action must be stated as residing in that very [treatise] for the sake of engaging those desiring to act; it should not be something residing elsewhere, for otherwise there would be an irrelevant statement.
Indeed, a purpose is stated at the beginning of a treatise in order to incite others to action, not out of mere whim.
Furthermore, how is it that one is incited toward the sūtra by the instruction of a statement of purpose?
It is if the purpose residing therein alone is stated, and not one residing elsewhere;
for no one would be incited toward one thing by the statement of a purpose belonging to something else.

A *sūtra* is said to be a statement primarily intended for the communication of a specific meaning; it is not merely the subject matter, nor is it the mere sound devoid of the capacity to communicate meaning. Therefore, that which is to be expressed—residing within the subject matter and so forth—is what must be stated, but the purpose (*prayojana*) is not of the nature of an action. For indeed, the action characterized by the communication of its own subject matter is common to all sentences.
And since that [purpose] is already so well known, it does not deserve to be mentioned as the purpose [of the treatise],
because there is no deviation of the treatise from it.
If it is argued that it should nevertheless be pointed out for the sake of dispelling the doubt that it is not the subject matter [of the treatise]:
No, for that suspicion has already been dispelled by the mere statement of the subject matter (*abhidheya*).
Nor is it included with the desire to convey a particular feature of the subject matter,
because that [feature] has already been conveyed by the very presentation of the specific subject matter itself.
Furthermore, the purpose—the fruit of that fruit of the action—must be demonstrated;
for without it, it is impossible for one to engage with the sūtra based on the mere fruit of the action alone.
For indeed, a discerning person who desires a specific, principal fruit would apply themselves to its means.

Because an effect cannot occur without a cause, and because a known means, when practiced, bestows its intended fruit— just as the attainment of health results from the performance of complete and healthy remedies— one engages with the aphorism for the sake of understanding that means; therefore, the purpose itself must necessarily be shown, as it is primary among the factors that motivate engagement.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to demonstrate that [the ultimate purpose] by means of a text devoid of the relationship and other factors that serve as the means, the statement of the relationship and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating that the Sūtra is the means to the purpose of the purpose. And that is the purpose of the purpose.
Therefore, a statement that possesses a logical connection, employs appropriate means, and declares the goals of human endeavor is subject to critical examination;
any other is not so subject.
According to this principle, a means consistent with the relationship [between goal and method] must be demonstrated;
otherwise, no one would engage in the practice of its accomplishment, as it would be impossible—like seeking to adorn oneself with the crest-jewel of the serpent Takṣaka to cure a fever.
Nor does an infinite regress apply in this case.
For, since a person’s desire is severed by the complete attainment of the desired object, no further purpose beyond this need be sought; thus, what [need is there for] its connection and so forth?
To this, it is replied:
The relationship, for its part, need not be presented separately from the purpose,
because it would be fruitless;
for that alone deserves to be mentioned separately which, when stated, [remains unestablished].
Nor is it understood; for just as when one among the denotable objects and so forth is expressed, there is no comprehension of the others,
nor is such a possibility [of simultaneous expression] present.
When the purpose has been stated,
the relationship has not yet been stated.
For, as it is being demonstrated, the relationship between the treatise and its purpose— characterized by the nature of the means and the end— must be shown.
Nor is anything else—such as the ritual acts toward the lineage of gurus—a constituent part of that [activity], because it is not a factor for the engagement of the seeker;
and that relationship between the goal and the means is shown precisely by the statement of the purpose.
For, by one who shows that "this is its purpose," it is thereby shown that "this is its means.

Indeed, that which does not accomplish something cannot be its purpose, as this would lead to over-extension; therefore, since it is obtained through implication, it need not be mentioned separately from the statement of the purpose.
[The inclusion of all things] is for the sake of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).

One [teacher] says that only the subject matter (*abhidheya*) should be taught; another says that all counter-arguments (*pratipakṣa*) must be explained in order to abandon opposing positions (*vipakṣa*);
and yet another says that every aspect (*ākāra*) without exception must be described in order to achieve the complete knowledge of all that is to be known (*jñeya*).
This triad is untenable;
for instance, in the first position,
regarding the inclusion of all things:

For there is no class of things here in the *Prajñāpāramitā* that has not already been included in the Abhidharma Piṭaka and other works through the exposition of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*); thus, there is no fault of redundancy.

In the second [chapter], there is indeed a summary of all antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), because no object of opposition (*vipakṣa*) remains uncollected; for it is stated that the Śrāvaka path and so forth must be cultivated as antidotes.

Furthermore, it is not known against what specific counteragent [the definition is directed]; thus, because there is no comprehension of a specific counteragent for a specific opponent, there is the fault of non-comprehension (*apratipatti-doṣa*).
Regarding the third case as well—the inclusion of all aspects—there are two alternatives:
does it refer to the object (*vastu*)?
Is it a distinct form (*ākāra*) or is it non-distinct?
If the first alternative is taken, then the object itself is being grasped under the guise of a form; thus, the fault inherent in the grasping of the object follows.

If, however, the second alternative is taken, then because only a form devoid of reality—constructed by conceptualization—is grasped, there would be no engagement with any real object whatsoever, even indirectly, despite such a form being cultivated.

Furthermore, this [mere] form is not applicable to the goal of the person (*puruṣārtha*); thus, because it does not express matters conducive to the goal of the person, there is the fault of non-explanation.

Therefore, by way of summarizing the three aforementioned meanings, and because the faults arising from each individual position do not apply, there is the sequence of the eight realizations (*abhisamaya*) beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is comprised within the attainments of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, and is free from error.

The subject matter (*abhidheya*) is as follows: the entire path that brings about both mundane prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*naiḥśreyasa*), which was taught by the Blessed One—who consists of great compassion and instructs all beings through various miracles—in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

As it has been stated, the meaning of the noble *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras—consisting of the practice of the instruction on the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and so forth, distinguished by eight stages—is [taught here] for the sake of all those who delight in concise formulations.
Thinking, "May sentient beings practice [the path] easily and concisely," the Blessed One taught the *Bhagavatī Aṣṭasāhasrikā*.
Therefore, the purpose— the fruit of the action— is that there is an uncommon, concise awakening to the entire meaning within the mental continuum of those being instructed.

As it has been stated, the subject matter— the path beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)— which was not attained by Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others because their mental dispositions were corrupted by the poison of attachment to the existence of entities arising in beginningless saṃsāra and because they had not practiced the meditation on the selflessness of all things,
is now easily grasped through the ear and through wisdom upon hearing the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Having established it within the cognition of recollection produced by the latencies (*vāsanā*) deposited by that most intense experience, [one should meditate upon it].
Having ascertained it through that which consists of reflection,
and cultivating it through that which consists of meditative development— therefore, whatever is intensely visualized, whether real or unreal, [that very thing arises].
Upon the completion of cultivation, the result is a cognition that is clear and free from conceptual construction.

According to this principle, one who possesses the accumulation of merit such as generosity by relying on the conventional and ultimate truths should realize all aspects [of the path] through the sequence of attaining the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so forth—this being "beneficial" because it accomplishes the perfection of one's own and others' welfare. Thus, the purpose is the fruit of the fruit of the action, which is the appropriate means.
As it has been said in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*:
The wise should behold this path to omniscience which has been taught here as the instruction, for it has not been tasted by others. (2)

"Having established the meaning of the sūtra within mindfulness, they shall practice the ten-fold conduct of the Dharma with ease"— this is the purpose of the undertaking. Thus, by virtue of the section on the *Tathāgataguhyaka*, Vajrapāṇi has been entrusted with the teaching because he has fulfilled his duty in every way toward the protection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the true dharma-body (*saddharmakāya*) of all the Tathāgatas of the Fortunate Aeon (*bhadrakalpa*), and because [the teaching] has been handed over to him at the beginning of the empowerment and so forth, as it was for others.

The former masters [state]: "Because there is no specific statement [to the contrary], it was Mahāvajradhara, the Lord of the Ten Stages and resident of Aḍakavatī, who, for the sake of favoring all the worlds, spoke thus—beginning with 'So be it'—to the assembly of great Bodhisattvas headed by the noble Maitreya, who had requested the recitation of the jewel-like *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra. Others, however, maintain that because the *Prajñāpāramitā* was handed over in this very section on Entrustment (*parīndanā-parivarta*) with the words, "In this way, this *Prajñāpāramitā* shall circulate in Jambudvīpa," and so forth, the noble Ānanda is the compiler (*saṅgītikāra*).
Thus they think.

In this context, by the phrase "it is thus," which expresses a definitive determination and is intended to demonstrate the entire meaning of the sūtras as ascertained through a corresponding cognition, he declares its non-erroneousness with the words "it is exactly so. By the personal pronoun "by me," he indicates that he heard it directly from the Blessed One; and by the expression of experience, "it was heard," he shows that [the teaching] cannot be obtained from anyone other than the Tathāgata through the cognition of what has been heard.
Thus, due to the lack of capacity for the realization of all such phenomena (*dharma*), there is an absence of realization.
Furthermore, these three terms were indicated at the very beginning of the Sūtra by the words of the Blessed One himself.

For instance, after the Blessed One had passed into *parinirvāṇa*, since the stream of the Sugata’s words—which bring about the state of Buddhahood that is difficult to comprehend—is characterized by various meanings and diverse inclinations, how could a compilation (*saṅgīti*) be made by anyone in the absence of the realization of their meaning?

Regarding the statement "it is being performed": when the Blessed One was asked by Śrāvakas and others—who were empowered by the Tathāgata’s blessing and capable of dispelling the doubts of those to be trained—how the Dharma should be compiled in a future time, he spoke in the *Dharmasaṅgītisūtra* with the intention that there is no fault in performing the compilation of the Dharma even by one who has not personally realized the meaning, provided they have heard it directly and without error. He said:
"O monks, the Dharma should be compiled by you on the basis of 'Thus have I heard,' and it should be presented according to its proper connection and sequence," and so forth.

For this reason as well, there is the mention of place, time, and so forth. Furthermore, statements such as "Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One," were made by the compilers of the collection solely with the permission of the Blessed One; thus, there is no consequence of them being the words of one who is not a Buddha.
Consequently, the objection that the words of one who is not a Buddha might be interpolated into the words of a Buddha is rendered completely groundless from the outset.
And it is logical that it was recited exactly as it was heard.
And having established this, when some should have said, "It was taught to me thus," [they instead say,] "It was heard by me thus."

Having raised the objection as to why it was stated, "Thus have I heard," another argument was described—namely, that the teaching of the Blessed One would otherwise be untenable—but it has been demonstrated that this does not shine at all.
Now, one might ask: did not the Master Ānanda state, "In other places there are sūtras spoken by the Blessed One in my presence"?
"There are [teachings] spoken in the world of the gods;
there are those handed down through tradition which I have thus grasped by oral transmission.
With reference to all of these, he said: "Speak!"
O one of great wisdom, O son of the Sugata, please speak!

At the conclusion of Mahākāśyapa’s words, “Where was the *Dharmacakrapravartana-sūtra* spoken by the Blessed One?”— his mental continuum melted with the recollection of the Buddha’s virtues, his face clouded with tears, and with a resonant voice, Āryānanda said: “Thus have I heard.”
How then can it be said that there is direct hearing from [the Buddha] himself by means of the word "by me," which denotes the self?

This is not a fault, because in the case of a teaching through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata, even when one hears it from another by his power, it is just as if one were hearing it directly from the Blessed One himself.
Alternatively, having heard it from another source, because he is the foremost among those who uphold the Dharma, the Blessed One was questioned by him regarding the determination of the meaning;
thus, considering that the hearing [of the teaching] occurred directly from the Blessed One himself due to the determination of the meaning, he says "by me.
As for what was said—"What if I were to set forth the entire Śrutikā in this manner?"—that refers to the composition of the text, and thus there is no fault.

Having thus provided the introduction, he now provides the *nidāna* (the causal setting), answering the questions—"When, from where, where, and with whom was this jewel of a Sūtra heard by you?"—in order to establish his own authority;
for the assembly of place, time, retinue, and teacher constitutes the cause of the teaching.
"At one time" means it was heard at one time; this connects with what precedes.

By this, it is declared that this [sūtra] is difficult to encounter, because there is no perception of a sūtra equal to this King of Cintāmaṇi jewels at all times, and because it is shown to occur only occasionally.

Alternatively, by the indirect statement, "At one time I heard this jewel of a sūtra, and at another time that other," the compiler (saṅgītikāra) expresses his own great erudition for the sake of sentient beings, according to the analogy of a compassionate king of physicians.

Alternatively, the meaning is that everything was heard in a single moment. Just as in a dream, through the sovereign power of a deity or similar being, one may perceive a hundred years or more in a very short time, so too, through the sovereign power of the Blessed One, the auditory consciousness— which arises from the mental consciousness acting as its immediately preceding condition and which illumines the entire meaning of the Sūtras— manifests in a single moment.
By this, he declares his own status as an authoritative person (*pramāṇapuruṣa*):
"Whatever is to be heard by me, all that is heard by me in a single moment;
and because of having attained the gateway of the inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣamukha*), it is not forgotten."

Therefore, even though the compiler, during the subsequent teaching that proceeded in chronological order, might occasionally— due to the impossibility of constant concentration for the sake of favoring other groups of disciples— possess a mind that is indeterminate and directed toward another object,
this does not contradict the compilation of the Sūtra in its entirety at a later time.
Because, through the sovereign power of the Tathāgata, the condition characterized by a complete manifestation has arisen from the very beginning;
furthermore, he listens again with insatiability to the nectar-like flavor of hearing the Dharma.
If it is asked, "Did it not happen likewise for the remainder of the assembly of those to be trained? [the answer is as follows:]

This indeed occurs for a perfectly pure assembly of bodhisattvas according to the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā*, but not for all [beings], because of their lack of distinguished capacity and the consequent absence of such power of retention.
If it is asked, "How then is there a distinction within a single teaching?"—
this teaching, from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), consists essentially of the cognition that manifests as letters and words.
There is no fault in her being born either all at once or gradually according to her capacity. Alternatively,
it is for the sake of training those in other regions, for the gratification of those staying there,
for the purpose of having many disciples dwell together, and to demonstrate non-attachment.

"For the purpose of making the various lands into shrines, for the sake of the merit of embodied beings, and for the purpose of making such things known, the Buddha wanders on his journey. Thus [it is said].

The phrase "at one time he was dwelling on Vulture Peak" is connected with the subsequent clause by virtue of his mind being inclined toward the welfare of others, since at other times he dwelt elsewhere.
Afflictions, karma, and likewise birth, as well as the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable.
Because he has shattered all opposing forces, he is remembered here as the Blessed One (Bhagavān).

By stating this meaning, according to the method of etymologists (*nairuktavidhāna*), he is called *Bhagavān* because he has destroyed afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth. Alternatively, there is a scriptural tradition (*śruti*) which states: "The word *bhaga* refers to the six qualities: complete sovereignty, beauty, fame, glory, knowledge, and effort."
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "The Blessed One (Bhagavān)—one who possesses complete sovereignty and other such qualities—was dwelling there.

This refers to Rājagṛha, a well-known specific location whose name is significant in meaning. Therein lies Gṛdhrakūṭa, a mountain consisting of various jewels, which—as indicated by its etymological derivation—is called a "mountain" (*parvata*) because it extends a festival procession for those desiring merit, such as gods and others, on holy days like the eighth day of the lunar fortnight; and because it is desired by others as a place incapable of bearing the burden of great assemblies of Bodhisattvas and the like, unlike other locations that serve as sites for the Perfect Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) where the Tathāgatas teach the Mother of the Jinas.
There he dwelt,

[winning over beings] through the miracle of various kinds of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), through the miracle of teaching by means of a discourse on the Dharma that transcends the world and is exceedingly swift, and especially through the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsana-prātihārya*) for those beings to be trained in the three vehicles, by virtue of his thorough knowledge of their dispositions and latent tendencies (*āśaya-anuśaya-parijñāna*) and his bringing them to maturity.

By liberating those who perform recollection and other such acts, he accomplished his desired purpose; thus he dwelt by means of the four modes of conduct—locomotion, teaching, meditative attainment, and solitary retreat—which have as their nature the body, speech, and karma, and which take as their objects phenomena and sentient beings.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the present tense (*laṭ*) is prescribed in connection with the word *sma* when referring to a past time that is remote from the present? And yet, this is not so here.
The time of the compiler is remote; therefore, how can there be the grammatical usage "he was dwelling"?

True, but it is correct because of the subsequent mention of "and [what he did] while not remote" by another [author], or else because it is not a fault since it serves as an indication of what is remote in accordance with previous grammatical treatises or with reference to other people.
The phrase "thus he addressed" and so forth should be stated.
"By the great" means by virtue of possessing greatness corresponding to that number.

It refers to the assembly of monks who have attained full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the ritual of the three proclamations (*traivācika-karman*), the fourth motion (*jñapti-caturtha*), and the fifth consisting of those free from harm (*anāghāta-pañcama*), and who, as true monks (*ehibhikṣu*), have destroyed their afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because the Buddha, the Dharma, and likewise the Sangha cannot be divided even by hundreds of millions of Māras, it is therefore called "Sangha" (the indivisible).
The connection is that he "dwelt together with, accompanied by, and surrounded by the Saṅgha.
Regarding that, he expresses the greatness of its number with the words "half [of the bhikṣus]" and so forth.
The meaning of what is expressed is easy to understand.

The mention of a specific number, however, is for the purpose of defining the limit of those who are to be numbered, since the retinues of the Śrāvakas are infinite. It was previously employed to facilitate easy understanding by preventing the forgetting of the summary numbers of the extensive subject matter, to ensure the attentive listening of those who fear grasping what they have heard much, or to indicate the total magnitude. The greatness of his qualities is expressed by the words "by all," and so forth.
In this context, all [of them] are Arhats because they are worthy of honor due to the excellence of their qualities, such as worship and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

They have "exhausted the outflows" (*kṣīṇāśrava*); for while the outflows of desire, existence, and ignorance flow forth from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) throughout the cycle of saṃsāra, those who have attained the aggregates of the untainted (*anāśrava*), such as ethical discipline (*śīla*), which are the respective antidotes to those [outflows], are those whose outflows are exhausted.
They are "free from afflictions" (*niḥkleśa*) because the affliction known as the defilement of passion, karma, and birth has departed from them.

By means of the successive fulfillment of the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, and liberation—as they are attained respectively—through liberation from the bonds of misconduct, craving, wrong views, and existence; and by means of attaining the correct deportment, the play of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and the divine and noble abodes;
those whose minds have thus become self-mastered over the world are "those who have become self-mastered" (*vaśībhūta*).
Furthermore, because they have attained mastery through the independence of having abandoned all bonds, they are "those who have become self-mastered."

Because the abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) belonging to the side of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) constitutes liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*) through meditative concentrations and attainments, and liberation by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*) through the knowledge of the path of an Arhat, there is—due to the absence of those factors belonging to craving and ignorance—liberation of mind from passion (*rāga*) and liberation by wisdom from ignorance, respectively. Thus, by attaining that [knowledge], they are liberated in every way from both parts through liberation from the obscurations of the afflictions regarding attainments;
they are those whose minds are well-liberated and whose wisdom is well-liberated.

Because they are free from the fear of sorrow, lamentation, and so forth; the fear of self-reproach, reproach by others, miserable rebirths, lack of livelihood, punishment, ill repute, and death; the fear of being stained by the eight worldly dharmas, such as gain and loss;

and the fear of ignorance, doubt, and false knowledge which act as obstacles to their own realization—they have, respectively, transcended suffering, fear, the worldly dharmas, and uncertainty. Thus, by virtue of being fearless, they are the "Noble Ones" (*ājāneya*). Because they are endowed with the attainment of distinguished qualities such as the three types of higher knowledge (*traividyā*), they are "Great Elephants" (*mahānāga*) due to their state of supreme preeminence.

Those who have fulfilled their duties and accomplished what was to be done are those by whom the necessary task—namely, the liberation from all suffering and so forth—has been completed through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*); and by whom the incidental tasks—the ascetic qualities (*dhūtaguṇa*) and other practices performed according to one's own will—have been carried out. Through the realization of the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering, they have in every way removed and cast off the burdens of the aggregates (*skandha*), the afflictions (*kleśa*), their vows, and their exertions, because there is no longer anything to be fully known, abandoned, realized, or cultivated, each according to its nature.

They have laid down their burdens. They are those who, following after the Blessed One, have attained their own twofold purpose— characterized by the acquisition of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful— through the realization of knowledge and the abandonment of ignorance.
They have attained their own goal.

They are those for whom the nine fetters—beginning with resentment (*pratigha*)—have been completely exhausted along with existence (*bhava*) by means of the Noble Path as far as possible; thus they are "those whose fetters of existence are entirely destroyed.

They are those whose minds are perfectly liberated, being thoroughly freed and dissociated from all bonds through right knowledge (*ājñā*), which is non-erroneous, universal cognition, and the realization of reality; thus they are "those whose minds are well-liberated by right knowledge."

Because they possess mastery and sovereignty over every state of mind characterized by the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and because they have reached the supreme perfection of mind—the ultimate limit of the exultation of their own spiritual lineage—they are "those who have attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all states of mind.
Therefore, the word "by" (the third case ending) must be construed in every respect with the phrase "by these hundred monks" (*bhikṣuśataiḥ*) who are thus described.
All of them were Arhats.

Why? Because their outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāśrava*). They have exhausted outflows because they are free from afflictions (*niḥkleśa*); thus it continues up to "those whose minds are well-liberated through right knowledge" (*samyagājñāsuvimuktacitta*). Because they have attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all states of mind, each preceding term is the cause for each succeeding one. Therefore, some say that since the goal of all human endeavor is fully accomplished, no further qualification need be stated.
They are *arhats* because they have slain their enemies, due to having abandoned the obscuration of the afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Furthermore, they have "exhausted the outflows" (*kṣīṇāśrava*) because, through the absence of the afflictions consisting of the exertion for the exhaustion of the outflows, they are free from defilement (*niḥkleśa*).

Thus, having described the quality characterized by the absolute abandonment of faults through these terms, he now describes the quality characterized by the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) with the words beginning "by those who have attained mastery" (*vaśībhūtaiḥ*).

Through the accomplishment of extraordinary qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and through their union with the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they have become masters capable of benefiting the three worlds; thus the Blessed One appointed them to the task of working for the welfare of sentient beings.

Having been liberated from all forms of the bonds of craving and views, they are, respectively, those whose minds are well-liberated and whose wisdom is well-liberated. Because they travel as far as there is a destination by means of a straight, non-crooked path, they are "well-bred steeds" (*ājāneya*). Because they have conquered the battle against the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are "great elephants" (*mahānāga*); and because there is nothing further to be conquered, they have "done what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtya*).
Having accomplished their task by performing appropriate deeds;
having laid down their burden by no longer acquiring the suffering of renewed existence;
and having attained their own goal through the realization of Nirvana.
Because they have completely exhausted the fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*) through the eradication of the cause of existence;
because their minds are well-liberated through right knowledge by reaching the excellence of the culmination of the paths of seeing and cultivation;

and because they have attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states by proceeding to the excellence of their own lineage through the power of special qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*)—the syntactical connection is exactly as stated.
Each preceding term is the cause of each succeeding one.
Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika states: "When the denotation is established in the qualifier, the qualifier need not be mentioned again; therefore, there is no fault of non-termination."
He says that although one who is foremost among the upholders of the Dharma is included within the aforementioned number, he is not endowed with such qualities as these.

"Single," and so forth. Because it is impossible for that which is eternal to possess the relationship of receptacle and infused impression (*vāsyavāsakabhāva*) characterized as cause and effect, [the person] is "single" by way of continuity, according to the etymological rule that "a single individual (*pudgala*) is one who, filled with pure and impure impressions, takes up a rebirth corresponding to them. The indeclinable *yaduta* is used for the purpose of illustration.

"May his life-span be as desired"—thus [he is called] Āyuṣmat, because he expresses [the wish for] welfare, happiness, and honor. He is Ānanda because he has attained joy through the mastery of all the scriptures and his attendance upon the Buddha.

Regarding this, it has been said: "At the time of the teaching, this venerable noble Ānanda, due to a deficiency in the aforementioned qualities as a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), set aside and excluded this one individual."
Because their tasks are completed, because they desire their own welfare, because of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata, and because of all [their] perfections;
and because of the affliction caused by the five disadvantages, deficiency, lack of delight, and passion; and because of thirst for gain and so forth, and fondness [for them].
Through compassion, reverence, and respect.
Out of curiosity, for the sake of something special, due to an emergency, for the sake of jewels,
and for the purpose of worshipping at shrines and the like— a monk undertakes a journey.
Because they lack the fifteen causes for wandering, they do not go anywhere themselves; rather, out of gratitude and reverence for the Dharma, they always dwell in the presence of the Blessed One.
Because they are his own, this assembly of great śrāvakas is described as "his own.
[They remain] through their thirst to hear the jewels of the profound and immeasurable sūtras.
For from that [state], the accomplished ones wander through infinite world-systems.
Some say: "It is precisely because he spoke that vehicle that so many have gathered;
for that very reason, the sons of the Conqueror are not recited in the Āgama sūtras. [Others say:
"The *Ārya-śatasāhasrikā* was taught for the sake of favoring those beings who delight in the most extensive details of the words."

The *Ārya-pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā* was taught out of compassion for beings who delight in the intermediate [length] and who understand through detailed exposition, by means of a compendium of all topics.
And the *Ārya-aṣṭasāhasrikā* was spoken by way of condensing all those topics, for the benefit of beings who understand through what is unveiled and who delight in the concise.
Therefore, following that [latter], there was an assembly of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who delighted in the concise presentation of the Dharma seen in this life.

Others maintain that the immeasurable assembly of great bodhisattvas should also be understood as consisting of those with pure high resolve, those dwelling in the signless with effort, those dwelling in the signless without effort, those who have entered the certain course of conduct, and those correctly bound by only one more birth.
Thus spoke the master Diṅnāga:
"Thus, this *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* is [complete] with no fewer meanings than those stated;
here, a condensation of the text is intended, for those very meanings are exactly as they were stated."

Likewise, in accordance with that very [principle], for the sake of removing the dejection of those of little fortune who lack a retinue and the like, and for the sake of inspiring a devotion to fewness of desires, the Blessed One himself prepared the Dharma-throne. Demonstrating that this jewel of a sūtra is to be approached only by those who are concentrated, he sat down in the vajra-paryaṅka posture—free from defects such as excessive rigidity—and having first formed the mudrā of the Wheel of Dharma with an upright body, he established one-pointed mindfulness directed toward the object by fixing his gaze on the tip of the nose. Then, through the inclusion of all meditative absorptions, he entered the meditative absorption named Samādhirāja.

Having emerged from that meditative attainment, he beheld this world afflicted by suffering with eyes of loving-kindness and compassion; then, awakening the assembly of those to be trained, he taught this universal instruction— which culminates in the fruit of Buddhahood according to their respective capacities through its mild, medium, and intense divisions—

illuminating worlds as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the ten directions by manifesting sixty hundred thousand *koṭī-niyuta* rays of light from his major and minor limbs, from all his pores, and from his natural radiance, as appropriate.

Having established all sentient beings in the certainty of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, he pervaded this great trichiliocosm with his tongue-faculty. From that, amidst the many clusters of radiating rays of light, preceded by the empowerment of the Tathāgata Padmagarbha, he performed the welfare of beings as before through the teaching of the Dharma associated with the six perfections. For the sake of gathering those who seek that goal, he displayed the unimpeded sign of teaching the Mother [Prajñāpāramitā].

Thereafter, having likewise attained the samādhi called "The Lion’s Yawn" due to the disappearance of all fears such as timidity before the assembly, and in order to make the Dharma-preachers understand that the Mother of the Jinas is not to be spoken of to an impure listener— one unskilled in the distinction between the conventional and ultimate truths— he performed such a miraculous feat (*ṛddhy-abhisaṃskāra*) by which, preceded by eighteen great omens, all the eight untimely deaths (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*) contained within all world-systems were likewise destroyed.

Through the purification of their abodes, those beings there entered the assembly of gods and humans; having been reborn there, they remembered their past lives and, with joy and gladness, approached their respective Buddha-fields and paid homage to the Blessed Buddhas. Furthermore, all those beings were free from the defects of sensory deficiencies such as blindness, practiced the ten paths of wholesome action, delighted in the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), and, like those who have attained the third dhyāna, experienced happiness and became worthy of hearing the Mother of the Jinas.
Having thus become endowed with such wisdom, they uttered this inspired utterance:
"Excellent is self-control; excellent is tranquility; excellent is restraint; excellent is the dwelling in the holy life that has been practiced."
"Excellent is non-violence toward living beings"—this constitutes the twofold miracle of meditative concentration (*samādhiprātihārya*).

Thereafter, the Blessed One, declaring that this Perfection of Wisdom can be taught by one who has attained sovereignty over all that is knowable, acted—just as before—to inspire reverence in those to be trained; he surpassed all world-systems with his radiance, complexion, splendor, and majesty, respectively illuminating, heating, and shining upon their locations, just as Sumeru, the king of mountains, surpasses all other mountains.

In this very way, [the Buddha] manifested an ordinary physical body equal to the bodies of the beings of this world-system, so that disciples might not think, "This can be understood and taught only by those like him, and not by people such as we," and thus fail to exert effort; rather, it was to generate enthusiasm [in them] by showing that even human beings are capable of accomplishing everything.
Then, through the cultivation of the meditation on the true nature of reality by gods and humans whose exceptional faith had been born, [they attained realization].
Seeing that such an attainment of the Dharma would occur after some time, the Blessed One was worshipped with flowers and other offerings.

Just as gifts are enjoyed, so too, through the enjoyment of well-transformed objects and the clarity of mind resulting therefrom, merit increases; and by means of this increase in merit, the equipment of wisdom arises easily for those to be trained because their bodies and so forth are purified.

For the sake of such favor, those merits and so forth appeared upon his own head in the form of a gabled palace (kūṭāgāra), adorned with every ornament and equal in size to the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system, appearing as an exceedingly beautiful form for this world-system.
These were empowered by the Blessed One.

And having thus empowered them, [he perceived] that for those whose latent tendencies of the "I-conceit" (*ahammāna-vāsanā*) have been exhausted, there might be a deficiency in correct practice due to dejection and so forth during the teaching of the Dharma which has a single intended goal. Therefore, as before, for the sake of all beings residing in all world-systems grasping the meaning in its entirety, and likewise for the sake of proceeding with equality toward all beings, he subsequently—according to their respective capacities and through the distinction of being slow or quick—[proceeded] by first superimposing affection and so forth toward the prophecy of realization for some.
In order to demonstrate that no alteration of mind should be made toward us, he manifested an equal physical form (*ātmabhāva*) dedicated to the teaching of the Dharma in all its aspects.
The term "King of Sugatas" refers to two kinds of miraculous feats (*ṛddhiprātihārya*).

Subsequently, because he arises from a world-system that is subject to affliction (*saṃkliṣṭalokadhātu*) and because of the excellence of his wisdom (*prajñā*) and other qualities, he is not equal to all other Buddhas.

The Blessed One, thus dispelling the doubts of those of dull intellect in order to accomplish the welfare of the world in all its aspects, [spoke] because supreme, perfect enlightenment arises in every Buddha-field for Bodhisattvas who have fulfilled the equipment of equal practice and departure, and therefore by all the Buddhas...

The equality of all Buddhas consists in their commonality with respect to the body of accumulation (*saṃbhāra-kāya*), the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), and their activity for the benefit of the world; however, they are not equal in terms of the measure of their lifespan or caste. Thus, demonstrating his own equality [with them], he likewise [proceeds] by means of teaching the jewel-sūtras of the entire, unerring word (*pravacana-ratna-sūtra*) to the bodhisattvas who are his own disciples, born in various world-systems and who have made their respective vows.

In order to teach the means for fulfilling the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*), the Blessed One manifested a smile such that all sentient beings residing in every world-system—having completely uprooted the seeds of doubt regarding their mutual inequality—perceived the Blessed Buddhas together with their assemblies in each other’s world-systems and realized their equality. Likewise, preceded by the perception of signs such as the great radiance, it was not appropriate for them to arrive suddenly, as they were dependent upon their teacher; for that purpose, the sons of the Jinas from the world-systems of the ten directions approached their respective Tathāgatas.

Preceded by prostrations at his feet and having offered their greetings, saying, "How noble is your majesty," they were informed of the favorable disposition of their own sovereign after he had answered their questions. Upon hearing words of praise, they reflected, "O Blessed One, we shall go for the sake of beholding the Lord together with his retinue, so that we may know our own lord’s auspicious intentions. Having taken with them various jewel-lotuses as offerings sent out of reverence for their lord’s Dharma, along with messages, news, and inquiries regarding his health and well-being, [they departed] because of the decline of the five corruptions in this world.

Having received the instruction, "You shall dwell in heedfulness within the world-system," and performing worship to the Buddhas residing in the intermediate spaces, they arrived with immeasurable retinues. Having performed the preliminary worship consisting of prostrating at the feet [of the central Buddha], and having settled in their respective places, they delivered the news of their respective Tathāgatas and presented lotuses;
such is the twofold miracle of the illumination of the Dharma.

Thereupon, the Blessed One, considering that those lotuses had been sent for the purpose of honoring the True Dharma—thereby demonstrating that even in the arising of impure world-systems, one remains untainted by their defects—cast them back toward their respective directions. Within those lotuses, preceded by the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgatas and through the teaching of the Mother of the Victors, he established all sentient beings in the certainty of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Having dedicated them to the worship of the True Dharma and having perceived the assembled multitude of great Bodhisattvas and others according to their individual capacities, he [taught] the Perfection of Wisdom, which is endowed with excellence in the beginning, middle, and end.
One should understand that "he taught" refers to the introductory setting (*nidāna*).

However, it was not mentioned here because the present section concerns the teaching intended to benefit sentient beings who possess instantaneous comprehension (*udghaṭitajña*) and a preference for concise instruction.

As it has been said: when the Blessed One was dwelling in the great city of Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, surrounded by the aforementioned assembly while teaching the Dharma, then, from the presence of the Blessed One right there...

"It was in this place that I heard this jewel of a sūtra together with that assembly"— by thus mentioning the location and other details, the compiler, in accordance with worldly convention, establishes his own authority for the sake of the disciples,
thereby describing how they should listen to and reflect upon [the teaching] with reverence.
As the venerable Dignāga said:
For those possessed of faith, the Teacher and the assembly serve as the basis for engagement;
furthermore, the place and time are specified in order to establish his own authority.
"For the reciter in this world, speaking with witnesses while specifying the place and time, attains authority.
In that regard:

Those who explain the meaning of the Sūtras must state the purpose, the meaning of the compound, the meaning of the individual words, their mutual connection, as well as the objections and their refutations.
Thus, it has been determined in the *Vyākhyāyukti* that a sūtra should be explained by means of these five aspects. The purpose [of the treatise] has already been stated.

Therefore, for the sake of easy comprehension by the audience and so that the explanation of the treatise—whose subject matter has been divided—is easy for commentators to provide, the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) is first set forth by way of a concise indication.

In that context, for the bodhisattva seeking Buddhahood, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is taught by way of explaining the result, beginning with the thorough knowledge of all modes such as the generation of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

Since that [knowledge] cannot exist without the thorough knowledge of the path of the śrāvakas and so forth, the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) follows immediately after. Furthermore, since even that cannot exist without the thorough knowledge of all things (*sarvavastu*), the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) follows thereafter.

Then, for the sake of attaining mastery over the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*) in every respect, one must again realize the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*) through the cultivation of the three types of omniscience by way of summarizing the modes of knowledge regarding the objects of the path in all their forms. Having attained the Culminating Clear Realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*)—due to the acquisition of the ultimate limit of excellence through the path of distinction—and having refined the objects that were meditated upon according to their divisions as both individual and collective, [one proceeds].

Having understood that one realizes [the truths] for the sake of certainty, and having again cultivated them for the sake of thorough mastery, immediately after the realization in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbodha*), one correctly attains the realization of the *dharmakāya* in the second moment. In brief,
this is the summary meaning of the eight realizations (*aṣṭābhisamaya*) in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
And so it has been said:
"The Perfection of Wisdom is proclaimed by means of eight topics."
The knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of the paths, and then the omniscience. ||4||
Complete awakening in all its aspects, reaching the summit, the gradual [awakening],
awakening in a single moment, and the Dharma-body— these are your eight forms. (5) Thus it is said.
Because that which was indicated in brief is now explained in detail, it is called "well-expounded. Thus, the summary meaning is stated once again in detail:

therein, one who desires to attain perfect enlightenment must first generate the two kinds of bodhicitta—having the nature of aspiration and application—which contain within them emptiness and compassion; and for the sake of accomplishing the dharmas projected by that generation of the mind, [one should practice].

For the purpose of preserving the qualities already attained and for the purpose of their further increase, immediately after receiving instruction on practice and so forth, one determines that—following the roots of merit characterized by faith and the like which constitute the "aids to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*) attained through the excellence of hearing and so forth—there exists the fourfold "aids to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), consisting of mundane cultivation, which is conducive to the realization of the Four Truths; and furthermore, for one who possesses such practice, there exist other stages as well, such as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth, as previously described.

Practice proceeds by means of a basis—that is, by a Bodhisattva whose very nature is the *dharmadhātu*—preceded by taking all phenomena as its object, with reference to the greatness of mind that is supreme among all beings, the greatness of measure, and the greatness of realization. Thus, the threefold objective (*samuddeśa*), which serves as the focal point, should be meditated upon. Subsequently, for the sake of attaining that, there is—in the domain of the three types of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)—the practice based generally upon pure qualities (*śukladharma*) regarding the fourfold [stages] beginning with the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*).
At each realization and at every subsequent realization, there is the practice of application based upon the six perfections.

Thus, among the practices such as the "armor" and so forth—which possess the nature of the paths of preparation, seeing, meditation, and the special path according to their respective modes—one first dons the armor through the practice of armor.

Then, having mounted all the Mahāyāna dharmas by means of the practice of setting out, and having accumulated the provisions through the practice of accumulation, one must attain the practice of departure. It is in this manner that [the bodhisattva] proceeds.
Because it is revealed by the Tathāgatas through the sequence of realizing the qualities that bring about Buddhahood, omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is comprised within the first chapter.
And thus it has been said:
"The production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*)."
And the limb of penetration is fourfold;
the basis for practice has the nature of the dharmadhātu. ||6||
"The object, the aim, the acts of donning armor and setting out,
the provisions together with the departure— these constitute the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the Sage.

(7) Following this, since the realization of omniscience does not occur without the realization of all paths, [the author] demonstrates the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) by showing how he eclipses the ripened radiance of the gods and others with the natural light of his own body.

Because the pride of being a world-protector and so forth has been eliminated through indirect speech (*vakrokti*), the person whose continuum of pride has been destroyed is the one who should cultivate this realization upon attainment;
thus, after the description of the basis, the specific determination of its own object and so forth is stated, [followed by] the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).

In this section, the Blessed One has taught that all paths are to be fulfilled; thus, he first set forth the paths of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, followed by the Bodhisattvas’ path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is endowed with mundane and other qualities and possesses great benefits. Immediately thereafter, when the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is to be explained, because there is little to be said about it and because disciples proceed toward the fruit, its activity (*kāritra*) is indicated first, [and then it is explained] in its form as both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is twofold; thus, among the three types of impure paths of cultivation—distinguished by resolution (adhimukti), dedication (pariṇāmanā), and rejoicing (anumodanā)—the mental application of resolution has been explained in the passage beginning with "one constructs merit like a lump of gold from its elements.

To encourage the bodhisattvas who cultivate that [path], the Buddhas and others perform praise and so forth for such resolution; thus, praise (stuta), exaltation (stobhita), and celebration (śaṃsita) are described as having the nature of successive rejoicing.

Thereafter, just as a goldsmith transforms a piece of gold into an ornament, one makes that merit a tool for *samyaksaṃbodhi*. Having thus explained the mental application of rejoicing (*anumodanā-manaskāra*)—preceded by the mental application of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-manaskāra*)—for the sake of attaining equality between one’s own and others’ meritorious deeds, [the author] first establishes the characteristic of the accomplishment of the first [type of path], namely the two-fold untainted (*anāśrava*) path of cultivation distinguished by its application and purification; then, the second...
"It is taught as having the characteristic of ultimate purity. This refers to the section beginning from the second chapter up to the eighth chapter.
"O Blessed One, this realization of this bodhisattva mahāsattva is his perfection of wisdom."
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, because of its absolute purity. Up to this point, the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*) of the bodhisattvas has been explained.
And so it has been said:

The path of seeing (darśanamārga), which possesses great benefits through its worldly and otherworldly virtues, consists of the acts of darkening and so forth, as well as the paths of the disciple and the sword. 8.
Activity, resolute belief, and those [states] praised, lauded, and extolled;
the two mental orientations regarding dedication and sympathetic joy are unsurpassed. (9)
"Accomplishment and ultimate purity—this is the path of cultivation for wise Bodhisattvas; thus is the Knowledge of the Path (mārgajñatā) proclaimed.

(10) Thus, since the thorough knowledge of the Knowledge of the Path cannot be correctly attained without the thorough knowledge of all things, [the author] shows the Knowledge of All Aspects (sarvajñatā) by means of wisdom—which perceives the defects of cyclic existence—and by means of compassion—which entails a commitment to acting for the benefit of sentient beings.

Because Bodhisattvas do not abide in either existence or quiescence, and because this is taught through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)— just as it is for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— the *Jinajanani* first provides an exposition and then, for the sake of establishing that very point,

teaches the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*) by means of apprehension and non-apprehension through the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) and signlessness (*animitta*). Following the description of the Bodhisattvas’ application (*prayoga*) by way of positive concomitance alone for the purpose of cultivating those two, there follows the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is preceded by the demonstration of their equality and consists of the object of meditation.

It was stated thus in the eighth chapter. Beginning with the words "The Venerable Subhūti said," and continuing up to the end of the ninth chapter with the words, "In this way, Subhūti, this is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva; there is neither the proceeding nor the ceasing of any dharma"—this concludes the explanation of the omniscience of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
And so it has been said:
"Through wisdom there is no abiding in existence; through compassion there is no dwelling in peace.
Without skillful means there is distance [from enlightenment]; with skillful means there is no such distance. (11)
"The path of seeing of the Śrāvakas and others is held to consist of the discordant factors and their antidotes, the application, and its equality.

(12) Following that, for the sake of mastery over the three types of omniscience already fully understood, one again cultivates the three types of omniscience by way of a compendium of the modes of knowledge regarding all aspects, paths, and objects; this is the "clear realization of all aspects" (*sarvākārābhisambodha*).

Having explained the aspects (*ākāra*) and so forth— stating that they are to be cultivated through applications distinguished by their aspects, by means of the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) produced preceded by the knowledge of characteristics, and by the sequential adoption and rejection of qualities and defects— one then describes how, for the energetic practitioner who has increased the factors conducive to liberation, there is the attainment of the qualities of the irreversible Bodhisattva community of those in training (*śaikṣa*) through the gateway of the realization of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Subsequently, preceded by the cultivation of the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as the cause of Buddhahood,
and having accomplished the purification of one’s own Buddha-field through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), [the Bodhisattva acts] according to the capacity of beings.
In the ninth chapter, it is taught that the activities of a Buddha proceed without effort (*anābhoga*), starting from the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows,
beginning with the words "This is a great perfection" and continuing up to the twentieth chapter.

"Those various Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, are invincible by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras"—up to this point has been stated the complete awakening in all aspects (sarvākārābhisambodha) of the Buddhas and others, as applicable.
And so it has been said:
"The aspects (ākāra), the associations (saṃprayoga), the qualities (guṇa), the defects (doṣa), along with their characteristics (salakṣaṇa)..."
The group of those in training who have attained the aids to liberation and the aids to penetration is irreversible. ||13||
"Equanimity toward existence and peace, supreme purification of the field, and the realization of all aspects— this is [the path] together with skill in means.
(14) Thus, immediately following that, for one who has attained the realization of all aspects, there is the culmination of excellence by way of the special path (*viśeṣamārga*).

The term *dhigama* (attainment) is used to indicate the *mūrdhābhisamaya* (culminating clear realization). Following the sequence [of the stages], it first establishes the increase of the signs, the nature of the fourfold aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) beginning with "heat" (*uṣma*), and the stabilization of the mind through firmness;

subsequently, it presents the fourfold factors to be abandoned as the opposing side (*vipakṣa*)—namely, two pairs of subject-object conceptualizations (*grāhyagrāhakavikalpa*) based respectively on the side of engagement and withdrawal, and on the basis of substantial and nominal persons.

Having taught the fourfold counteragent (*pratipakṣa*)—each consisting of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—as that which is to be adopted in its specific state of abandonment, the "uninterrupted concentration" (*ānantarya-samādhi*) is taught along with the misconceptions (*vipratipatti*) to be eliminated by means of skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) based on both truths, immediately preceding the attainment of Buddhahood. Thus, beginning from the twentieth chapter with the words "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even while in a dream... up until the twenty-ninth chapter, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is shown through the immeasurability of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.
Up to the point "the measure is to be understood," the Culminating Clear Realization has been explained along with its causes; and thus it has been said:
The sign of that [practice] is its increase and its firm establishment; the stabilization of the mind is fourfold, and the antidote to conceptual construction is likewise fourfold. (15)
On each of the two paths known as seeing and cultivation, there is the uninterrupted concentration (ānantarya-samādhi), along with its opposing errors. (16)
Regarding the term “culminating clear realization” (*mūrdhābhisamaya*):

subsequently, one who has attained culminating clear realization brings the objects of knowledge—previously realized both individually and collectively—into a sequential order and contemplates them for the sake of stabilization. Thus, in the twenty-ninth chapter, by means of the roar of the lion, it is stated in a single word along with its cause that the resonance of the *prajñāpāramitā* is to be understood as being of thirteen types, beginning with generosity, which comprise all dharmas.
The sequential realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*) has likewise been described:
"It is threefold or tenfold in its sequence.

Immediately thereafter, for the sake of making those very realized factors well-practiced by one who has already cultivated the sequential realization, [the path consists] of a single moment alone, due to the fourfold distinction of those very attained factors—namely, the non-fruitional, the untainted, the single-moment nature of all phenomena, and so forth.

"Manifestation in a single moment" means that in that very chapter, by the phrase "the perfection of wisdom is to be understood as unshakeable because all phenomena are unshakeable," the awakening in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbodha*) is shown together with its cause through this single word.
And so it has been said:

"Awakening in a single moment (ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbodha) is fourfold by way of its characteristics" (17). Following that, having taught the threefold immediate awakening of Bodhisattvas— namely, the awakening in a single moment which has been meditated upon, and the awakening to the Dharma-body (dharmakāyābhisaṃbodha) in the second moment— he now proceeds to explain how the remaining three bodies are established as appearing through conventional truth (tathyasaṃvṛti), while being in their ultimate sense (paramārtha) the nature of reality (dharmatārūpa), manifested according to the inclinations (adhimukti) of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and others, and constituting their respective spheres of experience.
According to the principle that "since separation is considered to be non-different from that which is separated," even though it is not distinct from that [nature],

it is attained through the supramundane path and not produced; thus, in the sense of being uncreated, the *svābhāvikakāya* is realized through the realization of all phenomena as consisting of illusion-like consciousness.

Having explained that, one must necessarily accept— by means of the conventional truth of the yogins (*yogisaṃvṛtti*)— that non-dual mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which have undergone a transformation through the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) by way of generating the appearance of a distinguished object, perform purposeful actions such as the teaching of the Dharma. Immediately after the designation of the *dharmakāya* as the activity-endowed sphere of the Tathāgatas alone, born from the accumulation of gnosis (*jñānasaṃbhāra*) and possessing all aspects, [the text continues] for the sake of the great Bodhisattvas who have entered the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and who desire to hear the various jewels of the Sūtras.

In the twenty-ninth chapter, it is taught that after having attained the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogikakāya*)—whose limbs are adorned with the primary and secondary marks and which is produced by the accumulation of immeasurable stores of merit through the simultaneous enjoyment of the joy and bliss of partaking in the supreme, irreproachable Mahāyāna Dharma—the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) appears in the form of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and others. This body performs the welfare of the entire world according to the capacity of beings, its continuity never ceasing in any way until the peak of existence; it arises from a portion of the stores of merit and wisdom and is perceptible to those such as the śrāvakas.

For thus, Subhūti, beginning with "by a bodhisattva mahāsattva" and ending with the chapter's conclusion, "the fulfillment of the unsurpassed Buddha-qualities," the perfect awakening to the Dharma-body of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, has been described. And so it has been said:
"The essential body, the body of enjoyment, and likewise the other, the emanation body— the Dharma-body, together with its activity, is thus proclaimed to be fourfold. (18)

Immediately thereafter, in order to instruct those to be trained that one must practice just as the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita did, three chapters were taught by way of a conclusion. These chapters, through the medium of the story of his former life (*pūrvayoga*), demonstrate the benefits of the yoga of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) preceded by the propitiation of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). They establish the sequence of the aforementioned realizations (*abhisamaya*) by means of the middle way (*madhyamapratipatti*).

Furthermore, because that [meaning] is easily understood, it was not included in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-kārikā*. Since the collective meaning will now be stated by means of two other methods, this constitutes one collective meaning. Now, the meaning of the Sūtra is being explained through the exposition of the meanings of the words and so forth.
In this context, "tatra" (therein) is used as an introductory phrase;
the word "khalu" serves as an embellishment for the sentence;
and it refers to those who dwell in beautiful forest retreats.
Subhūti is one whose mind possesses excellence (*bhūti*) and perfection. He is called a *sthavira* because he has attained seniority through honors and other marks in the world including the gods.
In this context, in some instances, the teaching [of the Dharma] occurs through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the hands and other limbs, which consist of the physical activity of the Tathāgatas.
For example, there is the teaching of sūtras such as the *Daśabhūmika*;
in some cases, it occurs through the empowerment of speech, as in the *Ajātaśatruśokavinodana-sūtra* and others.

In some cases, it occurs through the empowerment of the mind (*manas*), as for instance in the *Samantabhadra-caryā-nirdeśa-sūtra* and others; for by means of favoring and entrusting those who have faith in the noble Subhūti, there is a gradual process of correct reception and so forth that leads them into the Mahāyāna. Thus, for the sake of ensuring the non-interruption of one’s own lineage, the inconceivable power of the Tathāgatas’ skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) is displayed, since [the teaching] is taught even by one who is otherwise entirely incapable. This is for the purpose of favoring those to be trained by the manifestation of such power, regarding the proclamation of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
In order to bring the noble Subhūti face-to-face while he was otherwise occupied by means of the gateway of speech, the Blessed One addressed him; that is, he called out to him.
To the question "How? he says: "May it occur to you," and so forth.

Because this concerns the teaching of the Dharma, although [these qualities] already exist, O Subhūti, may the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)— which consist of distinguished eloquence regarding the meaning and etymological definitions of the Dharma— be manifest to you in every respect.
Those whose being (*sattva*) or intention is directed toward awakening— that is, the non-attachment to all phenomena for the sake of the perfection of their own welfare— are *bodhisattvas*.
He says "Great Beings" (mahāsattvāḥ) so that it may not be thought that even the Śrāvakas are thus.
They are called Great Beings because they possess the essence (sattva) for the great accomplishment of the welfare of others.
Since greatness might otherwise belong even to non-Buddhist practitioners and virtuous people, the term "bodhisattva" is employed.
Therefore, it says, "of those bodhisattvas, the great beings, concerning the perfection of wisdom.
[This refers to one who] has emerged from the first incalculable eon.

Increasing his practice of resolute belief and having accumulated the equipment of merit, the bodhisattva, in a pure location, sits cross-legged and, preceded by the mental focus on the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, should first identify by name with the primary mind (*mūlacitta*) the method of the *Prajñāpāramitā* which illuminates the selflessness of all phenomena. Then, he should examine its various divisions of words and chapters with the following mind (*anucaracitta*). Likewise, he should grasp their number through counting, according to the distinctions of the eight stages of meditative equipoise.

Because it determines the essential nature at each moment of realization, because it is free from superimposition and denial through investigation, and because it is established by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) of direct perception and inference, *mīmāṃsā* is [the aspect of] thorough examination. Thus, one should investigate with a mind of discernment using these four aspects as the meaning of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), while investigating the syllables— both individually and collectively— in two aspects, namely, as being without meaning and as having true meaning, respectively.

Thereafter, having ascertained that object exactly as it was investigated by means of the mind of ascertainment (*avadhāraṇā-citta*), one should—having integrated that very object into the root mind which takes names as its focal point by means of the mind of synthesis (*saṅkalana-citta*)—perform cultivation with a mind of aspiration accompanied by zeal for that purpose for which one has been engaged. In this way, through the sequence of the arising of knowledge consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one reaches the further shore, the ultimate limit of excellence, by attaining the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñāna*).
Thus, having analyzed [the word *pāramitā*], when the suffix *kvip* is applied and there is elision of everything else, [the form *pāram* is established].

In the compound *nityam-āgama-śāsanam*, where the elision (*luṅ*) of the case ending has not occurred according to the rule *kṛti bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.14), and where the objective case ending (*karma-vibhakti*) has been applied, the term *pāramitā* is derived from *pāram-i-tā*, meaning "the state of having reached the further shore.

The primary (*mukhyā*) Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the Blessed Buddha himself, whose wisdom is characterized by the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and is non-dual knowledge (*jñāna*) comparable to an illusion (*māyopama*).

However, both the collection of words and sentences—that is, the scripture—and the path (*mārga*) characterized by vision and so forth, are the secondary (*gauṇī*) Perfection of Wisdom, insofar as they are conducive to the attainment of that [primary wisdom].
And thus the teacher Diṅnāga said:
"The Perfection of Wisdom is non-dual gnosis; that is the Tathāgata.
By virtue of being for that purpose, the name is applied to the treatise and the path as well."
Therefore, the restriction is made with reference primarily to the Perfection of Wisdom itself— which pertains to those three types [of enlightenment] and is devoid of any counterfeit teaching—
and not to those [three vehicles] alone, because this [Perfection of Wisdom] is necessarily involved within the three forms of awakening.

For it will be stated in this very same *Śrāvakabhūmi*: "One who desires to train [in the Mahāyāna] should listen to this very Perfection of Wisdom," and so forth. Since what is being demonstrated there is the realization applicable to the supreme human goal in all its aspects, and since—according to the instructions in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha* and other texts—the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is the seed of the son of good family, and that very thing is the fruit, the essence of all the Buddha-qualities; thus, by way of the twenty-twofold divisions of the realization of the thought of awakening, characterized by the desire for perfect enlightenment which has the welfare of others as its object:

In order to demonstrate that the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, shall set forth from, resolve upon, and attain even the threefold Prajñāpāramitā—that the arising of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) is distinguished by its own objective referent and essential nature, and that the meaning of the Sūtra is precisely that distinction—the Blessed One himself taught the Prajñāpāramitā in brief by way of an address. Thus, the condensed meaning of the passage is as follows: in whatever manner the various types of the thought of enlightenment are realized, the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, [should practice] the threefold Prajñāpāramitā according to their respective possibilities.

In order that they may correctly attain [the goal] through the sequence of the arising of knowledge from hearing and so forth, and for the sake of explaining in detail the very Perfection of Wisdom related to them, there are four kinds of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*),
Subhūti.
"May it manifest"— thus the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ārya Subhūti.
In detail, however,
it begins there with the awakening of the seed of compassion through the power of one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Through the perfection of application and intention, there is the embracing of the mind of awakening.

According to this principle, one should generate the bodhicitta that has emptiness and compassion as its essence through the power of one’s spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and so forth, by means of undertaking the bodhisattva vows and the like; having made the aspiration, "May I become a perfectly awakened Buddha and, according to the capacity of beings, exert myself for the sake of others through the teaching of the Dharma of the three vehicles and other means," one should fulfill it through practice.
This [aspiration] has the welfare of others as its object, is accompanied by cause and fruit, and is characterized by the desire to attain perfect awakening.
