Just as a distinction is perceived between one who desires to go and one who is actually going, so too should the distinction between these two be understood by the wise according to their respective order; thus, the generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicittotpāda*) is twofold, by way of its nature as aspiration (*praṇidhi*) and application (*prasthāna*). Now, [one might ask]:
"Great in enthusiasm, great in undertaking, and great in the success of its vast purpose—
the volition (cetanā) of Bodhisattvas is the arising of the mind (cittotpāda) for the sake of the two goals.
According to this statement, the arising of the mind is the mind associated with volition that arises as a manifestation of a distinguished object.

The desire for perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), the aspiration for it, and the wholesome zeal for the Dharma (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*) are mental factors (*caitasika*); how, then, can they constitute the "arising of the thought" (*cittotpāda*)?
This is true.

However, having perceived the world submerged in the ocean of suffering and without protection, one who intends to deliver it generates the thought of Buddhahood when there is an aspiration at the moment of wholesome zeal for the Dharma.

In this context, the effect is indicated by means of the cause; thus, this figurative usage (upacāra) is employed to make known that all wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*) of a bodhisattva who possesses aspiration and prayer increase.

Alternatively, "prayer" (*prārthanā*) refers to the resolve (*praṇidhāna*), which is the desire for perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). The arising of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), which accompanies that [desire], is extended [to the term] by means of the prayer.
For it is held that the stage of the production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) is primarily characterized by aspiration;
thus, it is logically established that the thought of the Bodhisattvas arises accompanied by such a vow (*praṇidhāna*).

Now, if one asks: what is this "perfectly complete enlightenment" (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), and what is the "benefit for others" (*parārtha*), which consist respectively in the desire for that [enlightenment] and the purpose for which the production of the thought occurs?
It is said that there is a summary exposition of perfect enlightenment in the *Ārya-pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-sūtra*, as it says:
"Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects should apply himself to the perfection of wisdom.
In this regard, the detailed exposition of it is as follows: [as it says].

"In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom by way of non-abiding, should fulfill the perfection of generosity by means of the non-apprehension of the gift, the giver, and the recipient," and so forth.
In that context, this is the summary exposition of the welfare of others, as it is said:

"A bodhisattva who desires to lead all those beings in each of the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, to final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder..."
"One should train in the perfection of wisdom.
In this regard, the detailed explanation of that [training] is as he said:

"A bodhisattva who wishes to establish beings who are stingy in generosity, those who are immoral in ethical discipline, and those who abound in malice in patience, should train in the perfection of wisdom," and so forth.
And thus it has been said:
"The production of the thought [of awakening] is the desire for perfect enlightenment for the sake of others;
and that [desire] is expressed both in brief and in detail according to the Sūtra. (19)
In this regard, its classification is as follows:

there, the first production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) is accompanied by aspiration (*chanda*) and is like the earth for the Bodhisattvas, because it serves as the foundation for the generation and establishment of the accumulations for the complete awakening to all phenomena in all their aspects. The second is accompanied by intention (*āśaya*) and is comparable to fine gold; it is called "intention" because the intention for welfare and happiness, which is comprised within the six perfections, does not undergo change in the future or at present, and because it is directed toward perfect awakening.
Having performed [this], the third is accompanied by resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), resembling the new moon of the bright fortnight;
it is a superior basis due to the progressive increase of all the dharmas of the bright side.
This is because it is called "resolute intention" (*adhyāśaya*).
Furthermore, these three, by way of being weak, medium, and intense, are subsumed within the stage of the beginner's equipment (*ādikarmika-sambhāra-bhūmi*).

The fourth is that which is accompanied by application (*prayoga-sahagata*), resembling a blazing fire; because it proceeds with ever-increasing excellence—just as a fire increases through the addition of different kinds of fuel—it is called "application" (*prayoga*) in the sense of being a preeminent yoga.
This is comprised within the path of application for entering the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) and is bound to the stage of conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
The fifth, accompanied by the perfection of generosity, is like a great treasure,
because it is never exhausted even when satisfying immeasurable sentient beings in every way with material enjoyments.

The sixth, accompanied by the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), is like a mine of jewels, because it serves as the basis for all the jewels of virtuous qualities, from which they are produced.
The seventh, accompanied by the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), is like a great ocean, because it is unshakeable by any unwanted calamities.
The eighth, accompanied by the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), is like a diamond (*vajra*), because it is indestructible due to the firmness of its conviction.

The ninth is accompanied by the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); it is like a mountain because it is unshakable by any distraction regarding its object of focus. The tenth is accompanied by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); it is like a great medicine because it pacifies the diseases of all afflictive and cognitive obscurations (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*).

The eleventh is accompanied by the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-kauśala-pāramitā*); it is like a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) because it never abandons the welfare of sentient beings in any circumstance.
The twelfth is accompanied by the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) and is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), because its fruits are fulfilled according to one's aspirations.
The thirteenth is accompanied by the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) and is comparable to the sun, because it brings to maturity those beings who are to be trained.
The fourteenth is accompanied by the perfection of gnosis (*jñāna-pāramitā*) and is like the sound of sweet music, because it teaches the Dharma that wins over those to be trained.
And these ten [perfections], taken in order, are comprised within the ten stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā), and they constitute the domain of the paths of seeing and cultivation.
The fifteenth [stage] is accompanied by the superknowledges (abhijñā) and is like a great king, because it accomplishes the welfare of others through its unimpeded power.
The sixteenth is accompanied by the equipment of merit and wisdom; it is like a storehouse, because it is the locus for the treasury of the vast equipment of merit and wisdom.

The seventeenth is accompanied by the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); it is like a great highway, because it is the path traveled and followed by all noble persons (*āryapudgala*).

The eighteenth is accompanied by calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*); it is like a vehicle, because it carries one comfortably without falling into either *saṃsāra* or *nirvāṇa*, proceeding by means of their union.

The nineteenth is accompanied by dhāraṇī and eloquence (*dhāraṇī-pratibhāna-sahagata*), resembling a spring (*prasravaṇopama*); because it possesses the common characteristic of holding water inexhaustibly and emerging in every way, it holds all dharmas—both heard and unheard—and emerges as boundless teaching.
These [first nineteen] are comprised within the path of distinction (*viśeṣa-mārga*) in the five bodhisattva stages.
The twentieth dharma is accompanied by generosity (*dāna-sahagata*), resembling the sound of joy (*ānanda-śabdopama*), because it is heard with pleasure by those disciples who desire liberation.
And this [path] is comprised within the preparatory path for entering the stage of Buddhahood and is bound to the stages of a bodhisattva.

It is the twenty-first [stage], accompanied by the path of the single vehicle, resembling the current of a river; because, through the realization of the equality of knowledge and the object of knowledge, and by means of vast compassion, wisdom, and skillful means, it performs the welfare of others without interruption.
And this [state] is comprised within the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*), having reached the fundamental state (*maulāvasthā*).

It is the twenty-second [state], accompanied by the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), resembling a great cloud, because all activities for the benefit of sentient beings—through the manifestation of dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven and so forth—are dependent upon it as the Emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

This too is comprised within the stage of a Buddha, having reached the subsequent state of pure mundane knowledge (*śuddhalaukikajñāna*) as conceived by those to be trained, since there is the perception of emanations and so forth proceeding through the sovereign power of the non-conceptual Tathāgata.

Thus, beginning from the stage of the beginner (*ityādikarmikabhūmi*) up until that which is comprised within the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), it is established that this very number of divisions— neither less, nor more, nor in any other order— must be presented according to the sequence of the realization of the meaning (*arthādhigama*) as stated above.

In this sequence, by means of the realization of the *bodhicitta* divided into twenty-two types, the connection is as before, starting with the words "just as the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, [attain] the threefold [nature]," and so forth.
And thus it has been said:
"By earth, gold, moon, and fire; by treasure, jewel-mine, and ocean."
By means of the Vajra, Acala, and medicinal herbs, as well as friends, the wish-fulfilling gem, the sun, and songs. ||20||
"By means of the king, the treasury, the great road, vehicles, and flowing waters;
and by means of rivers of joyful speech and clouds—it is twenty-two-fold. (21) Thus it is said.

This distinction, consisting of cause and fruit, must necessarily be understood as being divided according to the stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the bodhisattva, and the Tathāgata. To explain:
In the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, the generation of the mind is resolve.
Another is characterized by pure high resolve;
likewise, it is considered to be maturational on the stages and free from obscurations.
"Compassion is held to be its root; it always has the welfare of sentient beings as its intention.
Because of this statement, it is taught that the production of the thought of awakening (cittotpāda) must be generated as consisting precisely of cause, fruit, and object.

Some maintain that its classification must also be performed in that same manner; otherwise, because there would be a classification only of the cause, there would be no classification of it in every respect, and thus the classification would remain incomplete.

Others, however, describe these eight productions of the thought of awakening—beginning with those likened to a great king—as being comprised within the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*) on the bodhisattva stages.
The text that establishes all the various classifications of the production of the thought of awakening is not written here for fear of prolixity;
rather, it is omitted because this teaching was composed for the benefit of beings who delight in concise summaries and possess discerning wisdom.

The aforementioned distinctions regarding the welfare of sentient beings must necessarily be practiced, because it has already been established that this jewel of a sutra proceeds by way of summarizing the meaning of the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*.
Thus says the master Diṅnāga:
Thus, this work consists of eight thousand [verses], with no reduction in the subject matter as it was explained; here, a condensation of the text is intended,
for those very subjects remain exactly as they were explained.

Thus, considering that even the noble Subhūti was incapable— due to the non-abandonment of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)— just as he himself was incapable regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā* because it is accessible only through the wisdom of a Tathāgata in all its aspects, the noble Śāriputra,
having understood [Subhūti’s] mere request but not yet knowing the power of his spiritual empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), [proceeded].
He reflects with the words beginning with "thinking thus" (*tathetyādinā*).
"This" (*etad*) refers to the collection of reflections that is about to be described; he speaks of it with the words beginning with "in this way" (*tadevamityādinā*).
The word "what" (*kiṃ*) expresses a deliberation (*vitarke*).
"By one's own" means by that which functions in dependence upon oneself.
However, regarding its object, it is not by what is produced by another; rather, even though it is "one's own," it is by what is produced by oneself.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
*Pratibhāna* (eloquence) is the expression of what is logically consistent and appropriate.
By means of the "bestowal"—that is, the production—of the power of those two, which consists of unimpeded capacity;
he also states it in another way: here too, in the phrase "by one's own," it should be understood as "by that which belongs to oneself."
Will he teach by means of the empowerment and the performance of a distinction through the power of his wisdom and eloquence;
or rather, does the word "or" indicate an alternative, such that it is by the power of the Buddhas?
He thinks thus:

"Because the particularity of the skillful means is inconceivable, perhaps he has attained unprecedented knowledge, or brought about the excellence of that which was already established, or received the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata; otherwise, like me, the noble Subhūti would be incapable.
Nor can it be said that he speaks because of the existence of some distinction [in his status], such as being foremost among those who dwell in the meditative attainments (*araṇā-vihārin*)."
For even I, due to the existence of a specific excellence as the foremost among those possessed of wisdom, have attained the opportunity to speak;
yet, it is the intention of the noble Śāriputra that the *araṇā-samādhi* has no function in teaching.
This is because, owing to his dull faculties, he does not act impulsively.
Even when inconceivable means (*acintyopāya*) are present, it is possible to produce prior cognitions and so forth; thus,
demonstrating that very subsequent conceptualization (*vikalpa*), he says:

The passage beginning with "Then," etc., explains that the knowledge of others' minds [attained] by Śrāvakas occurs only when they apply their attention (*samanvāhṛtya*) and not otherwise; thus, by means of this statement regarding the power of the Buddhas, it is shown that [the Buddha's] knowledge does not require such application of attention.
This very form just mentioned has the nature of the three aforementioned types of conceptualization.
Whether based on volition (*cetanā*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), it is a mental discourse (*manojalpa*) consisting of seeking; and because it is a coarseness of the mind, it is *vitarka*.
Having understood with a mind that is restrained and conforms to that [state], he spoke this which is about to be described.
He states that very thing: "Whatever [there is]"—namely, the Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, and Avadāna.
The Itivṛttaka, the Nidāna, the Vaipulya together with the Jātaka,

the Upadeśa, and the two marvelous Dharmas— this is the twelvefold word. Regarding these, they speak for the purpose of planting the seed of enlightenment by generating the wisdom consisting of hearing, since they proclaim the textual teachings.
They "teach" for the sake of maturation by means of generating the knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmayajñāna*),

since they illuminate the meaning; they "instruct" for the sake of liberation by means of generating the knowledge consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayajñāna*), since they fully reveal it through the production of certainty regarding the words and their meaning.
Thus, the three phrases beginning with "uttering" (*udīrayanti*) are respectively explained as "speaking" (*bhāṣante*), and so forth.
Since human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is the basis and all such activities as speaking have that as their cause, they are metaphorically designated by the term "human effort."

Now, an objection might be raised: "Since even the Śrāvakas have directly realized the reality (dharmatā) of their own attainment, why do they not perform all activities such as teaching according to their own capacity? Anticipating this, he himself poses the question, "For what reason?
Some explain that if others were to pose this question, defects such as a lack of interest or insipidity would arise.

Others [hold] that this follows immediately after for the purpose of avoiding the fault of interrupting the discourse; for the sake of favoring those who are unable to ask due to timidity; for the sake of those whose minds have been made one-pointed; and for the purpose of avoiding the fault of distraction caused by a change in physical posture (*īryāpatha*) through speech.
"He who," and so forth, is the reply.

In that regard, when there is a teaching of the Dharma— the subject matter to be expressed— by means of the realization of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), those training therein directly realize that very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) through the realization of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
they maintain it through the realization of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

All that has as its object the meaning realized [by the Tathāgata] is not in contradiction with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) because it is the Dharma of the teachings, such as the sūtras, which accords with realization.
This is because it reveals that which is non-contradictory.

Therefore, this flow, this outflow, this corresponding fruit—which consists of the sūtras and so forth taught by those disciples—is similar to the very Dharma-teaching of the Tathāgata, whose nature is characterized by the metaphorical designation of "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*); for they teach that Dharma of scripture through the Dharma of realization.
They do not contradict [the Dharma].

Since "teaching" (*upadiśantaḥ*) is used as an illustration, it should also be understood to include "speaking" (*bhāṣamāṇāḥ*) and "expounding" (*deśayantaḥ*), as these are the subjects under discussion.

By this, he says the following: because they lack skillful means for constant meditative composure, they are unable to speak even on the subject of the Dharma regarding an object already realized in a way that does not contradict their own realization, let alone on the subject of an object not yet realized. Therefore...
This must be seen as the very power of the Buddha.
For how much can be inferred by one who follows his own reasoning? Indeed, it is difficult to explain that which is beyond perception—the goal and its cause.

Thus, according to this principle, it cannot even be inferred or taught [as being non-existent]. Having thus concluded this incidental discussion, the Bodhisattva who has now generated the first and subsequent stages of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) accumulates the equipment of merit through the practice of virtuous dharmas such as generosity.
By means of the accomplishment of the superknowledges (abhijñā) within meditative concentration (dhyāna), he travels to the various world-systems.
For the sake of worshipping immeasurable Buddhas and for the purpose of hearing [the Dharma].
Having attended upon immeasurable Buddhas for immeasurable eons,
he attains supreme pliancy of mind through that service.
Thus, established in meditative concentration through the power of mental flexibility,
he then receives instruction from the Buddhas within the stream of Dharma.
He [strives] for the sake of attaining the vastness of extensive tranquility and primordial wisdom.

Thus, by this very reasoning, for the sake of establishing the connection for the Bodhisattva who has so engaged, the noble Subhūti spoke the instruction beginning with "The Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva," preceded by the words spoken by the Blessed One.

In this sense, he is called a "Bodhisattva" because, through the power of wisdom, he takes awakening (*bodhi*) as his object, and because, through the disposition of great compassion, he takes sentient beings (*sattva*) as his object; thus he is both awakening and a being—a Bodhisattva—just as the meditative concentration that has impurity as its object is called "impurity."
The use of repetition (*vīpsā*) is for the purpose of including the Bodhisattva even though he has been mentioned in another section.

What is the designation (*adhivacana*)—the direct verbal expression—of that which consists of the imagined nature (*kalpita-rūpa*) and so forth? The meaning is that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), it is not the designation of anything at all. He says the same thing:
"O Blessed One, I do not conceive of that phenomenon as having a nature such as being imagined and so forth,
because in reality, that which is to be taught is unapprehendable."

He says, "In that case, there is an object for the instruction," beginning with the words "that too" and so forth. The *prajñāpāramitā* has as its intrinsic nature ten kinds of dharmas, such as practice and the rest.
For it is said in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*, with reference to the object of the instruction:
"How, O Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive that name," and so forth.
"Or the dharma of a bodhisattva" means that dharma for which "bodhisattva" is a designation; [he] did not find that dharma through hearing.
Not apprehending [it] through reflection,
and not perceiving it through cultivation;
or alternatively, not finding it by means of formless cognition due to the absence of a basis for proximity with a specific object.
Since [cognition] occurs even in the absence of an external object— as in dreams and the like— it is not perceived as possessing a form. Therefore,

not perceiving it through either [of these two ways], in which *prajñāpāramitā*— consisting of the tenfold practice and so forth— shall I instruct by means of training, for the sake of maintaining the qualities already attained and ensuring there is no falling away?
Thereafter, based on the attainment of qualities not yet attained, I shall provide instruction.

In every respect, this implies by implication that there is no instruction whatsoever from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), but rather it is an instruction according to the conventionality of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛtyā*).
And thus, immediately following this very point, he will say: "This is the instruction," and so forth.
Furthermore, that [instruction] should be known as tenfold due to the distinction of its objects.

In that regard, the instruction on practice (*pratipatty-avavāda*) consists in training in the practice of the aforementioned varieties of bodhicitta by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), acting without transgressing the conventional and ultimate truths, and being uncommon to the Śrāvakas and others. Furthermore,
because suffering and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)— which is the emptiness of form and so forth that constitutes the fruit— are of such a nature, they are of one essence (*aikātmya*).

Regarding origination (*samudaya*), because emptiness is not distinct from form and so forth which serve as its causes, form and so forth are characterized by the phenomena of origination, cessation, affliction (*saṃkleśa*), and purification (*vyavadāna*).

Regarding cessation (*nirodha*), within emptiness—which is devoid of arising, ceasing, affliction, purification, decrease, increase, and so on—there is no form, up to and including no arising of ignorance (*avidyā*), no cessation of ignorance, no Buddha, and no awakening (*bodhi*).
Regarding the path (*mārga*), through the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as giving and the rest, [one realizes] the self...

The instruction on the realization of truth (*satyāvavāda*) is as follows: it is the understanding that internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and so forth, external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) and so forth, and the prior and subsequent limits (*pūrvānta-aparānta*) are neither mutually joined nor disjoined.

Regarding the Buddha, it is the knowledge of the equality of the object and the subject (*ālambya-ālambaka-samatājñāna*), by way of the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) of the nature of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*)—which is characterized by the qualities that constitute a Buddha—as being of a single characteristic with the Buddha and his enlightenment.

Regarding the Dharma, it is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in all phenomena that are subsumed [within the path], through the inclusion of all aspects that serve as the antidotes to all entities subsumed within the three types of omniscience.

The instruction on the Three Jewels (*ratnatrayāvavāda*) is the teaching that one should proceed by way of non-arising (*anutpādatā*) toward the Noble irreversible Bodhisattvas in training, who are delimited by the number twenty— consisting of seven Great Beings (the four *phalastha* and three *pratipannaka*, excluding the *arhat*, within the Saṅgha as included in the Buddha-jewel) plus the Pratyekabuddha, and further distinguished by their dull faculties and so forth.

The instruction on non-attachment (*asakty-avavāda*) is the teaching that the body and so forth lack intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*), lest someone, through the practice of what has been taught, should become attached to the body and other things as being mere pleasures due to having initiated vigor (*ārabdhavīryatā*).

Since one who is prone to despondency might become weary if the desired goal were not accomplished even through practice over a very long period of time, there is the instruction and advice regarding non-exhaustion: namely, the non-conceptualization of everything from form up to perfect enlightenment.

Since the mind might become discouraged when receiving instructions on the path from the Buddhas and others situated in the ten directions for each respective purpose, there is the instruction and advice regarding the thorough grasping of the practice:
namely, training in the fact that all phenomena are by nature unborn.

The instruction on the five eyes consists of training in the realization of the five eyes—the flesh eye, the ripening divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye—as being one in their suchness; these eyes correspond respectively to the spheres of: (1) specific, determined objects; (2) the death and rebirth of all sentient beings; (3) non-conceptualization regarding all phenomena; (4) the realization of all noble persons; and (5) the complete awakening to all phenomena in all their aspects.

The instruction on the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) is the realization that the superknowledges— namely, the miraculous power (*ṛddhi*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the recollection of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), the divinely produced divine eye (*ābhisaṃskārikadivyacakṣus*), and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āśravakṣayajñāna*)— which have as their functions the shaking of the earth and so forth, the hearing of all sounds whether subtle or gross throughout all world-systems, the knowledge of the minds of others such as those possessed of passion, the recollection of one's own and others' many previous births, the vision of all forms, and the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, are primordially quiescent. This is the teaching on the superknowledges.

The instruction on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the teaching that the yogi cultivates [the path] as the antidote to the things to be abandoned; this path has the nature of the sixteen moments subsumed within the four truths, consisting of the receptivities (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) of dharma and subsequent cognition (*anvaya*). Through the realization that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, his form is unattached to anything, like a magician. Because the objects realized by the aforementioned path of seeing are not distinct from the object of focus, there is no separation between the paths of seeing and cultivation, just as the designation of "mutual distinction" is impossible between the conditioned and the unconditioned due to their single nature.

Thus, the establishment of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is not based on defining characteristics; nevertheless, it is cultivated as the antidote to the objects to be abandoned by way of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*). This is the instruction on the path of cultivation.
In this way, these ten kinds of instructions are expressed by the term "perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*), because brevity of text is desired here.

For instance, in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*, the text concerning the instruction (*pratyavavāda*) is clearly indicated as an authoritative source; however, it is not written here for fear of prolixity.
Thus, having explained the instruction, he states what kind of bodhisattva is to be instructed:
Furthermore, as for the passage beginning with "Moreover," the particle *sa cet* is used in the sense of "if.
"In this way" means by means of the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

When the tenfold subject matter of the instruction is being spoken, the mind does not shrink back nor does it contract; because it does not despond and does not become deluded, [it remains steadfast].

Therefore, by virtue of being faithful (*śrāddha*) and thus devoted to dharma, he does not tremble at the outset; when instruction is being given, he does not shrink back through groundless fear, nor does he become indolent.
Because he does not fall into despondency, he does not succumb to cowardice.
For this very reason, by virtue of being wise (*prājña*) and knowing reality, he does not become terrified among those who know the truth through constant dread.
When instruction is being given, his mind does not turn away nor does it become regretful; such is the nature of the mental faculty.
Because his back does not bend—that is, because his mind does not become broken—he does not fall into terror at the conclusion [of the teaching], owing to his union with faith and wisdom.
This is due to the fear of uncertainty in every respect.

Alternatively, at the time of speaking and so forth, because he has ascertained the text, its meaning, and both together in their proper order, he does not shrink back, does not cower, and does not despair.
Why? Because, through the means of valid cognition—direct perception, inference, and scripture—he determines his own subject matter without contradiction, and thus he does not fall into despondency.
His mind does not turn away, nor does it become dejected.
For this very reason, it should be understood that at the beginning, middle, and end, he is not afraid, he is not terrified, and he does not fall into terror.
"This very one" refers to [the bodhisattva].

The meaning is that the Bodhisattva who, through skill in distinguishing the conventional and the ultimate, is free from mental despondency and the like regarding the instruction as it has been explained—that one is indeed this very person.
If it is asked, "Since its defining characteristic has not been stated, how is the Perfection of Wisdom to be recognized?", it is replied:
it is that object concerning which one does not experience mental despondency and the like when speaking or otherwise engaging with it.
There is no fault here because it is understood by implication that the tenfold [perfections], beginning with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), have already been explained;
thus, while concluding, he says:
"If... and so forth.

If that bodhisattva becomes established in the subject matter as described through the instruction (avavāda) just mentioned, then this very teaching regarding the duty of attaining the sought-after goal should be understood as his instruction and admonition (avavādānuśāsanī).

Having done so, the practice within the perfection of wisdom— which has the nature of the bodhicitta and the dharmas projected by it— and which takes the form of non-apprehension (anupalambha), [is to be undertaken].
Its object is the four noble truths;
its basis is the three refuges;
and its cause for proceeding toward excellence is non-attachment.
The cause for proceeding toward transcendence is indefatigability;
the cause for not proceeding by other vehicles is the thorough mastery of the path;
and the cause for proceeding independently of others is the five eyes.

That which is the cause for the fulfillment of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) consists of the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); that which is the cause for reaching the ultimate goal consists of the paths of seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-mārgau*). All of this has been explained in the section on instruction (*avavāda-prakaraṇa*), and by this much alone the entire purpose is accomplished; thus, the tenfold instruction has been presented according to the sequence previously stated.
And so it has been said:
"In the practice regarding the truths and the three jewels beginning with the Buddha, in non-attachment, in tirelessness, and in the complete grasping of the path. (22)
"The instruction is tenfold, to be known in relation to the five eyes, the six qualities of superknowledge, the path of seeing, and that called the path of cultivation.
(23) However, regarding the Jewel of the Saṅgha, this distinction of bodhisattvas with dull faculties and so forth should be understood.
Relying upon the path of seeing consisting of sixteen moments, which is comprised within the *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths) to be explained hereafter:

during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing, there are two types of those practicing for the first fruit (*prathamaphalapratipannaka*), distinguished as the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the follower of dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Then, he who is free from passion regarding the desire realm becomes a stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*) at the sixteenth moment of mind of the path of seeing.

Then, on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), up until the abandonment of the fourth category of afflictions, that same [noble one] is of two types, distinguished as "those who go from family to family" (*kulaṅkula*) among gods or humans.

Thereafter, through the abandonment of the five categories of afflictions belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is the single type of one who has entered the second fruit (*dvitīyaphalapratipannaka*), namely, those who have attained [the state of] faith (*śraddhāprāpta*) or vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), according to whether their faculties are dull or sharp.
Then, through the abandonment of the six categories of afflictions belonging to the desire realm, one becomes a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*).
Then, because he has only one birth remaining, he is another type known as an "ekavīcika" (one-intervaller) among the gods.

Next, through the abandonment of seven or eight categories of afflictions belonging to the desire realm, he becomes a candidate for the third fruit, being either one who has attained through faith or one who has attained through vision, as previously described.
Then, he who is called an "anāgāmin" (non-returner) due to the abandonment of the ninth category of affliction of the desire realm should be understood to be of five types.

Therein, one who has abandoned the fetters of rebirth but not yet abandoned the fetters of manifestation, while in the process of manifesting the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), or having manifested the intermediate state, attains the end of suffering through the realization of the Path—such a person is one who attains *parinirvāṇa* in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*).

One who has not abandoned either of the two sets of fetters, but having been born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), attains the end of suffering—is one who attains *parinirvāṇa* upon birth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*).
Likewise, one who has been born [therein]...
One who attains the end of suffering through the manifestation of the path by means of exertion is one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (*abhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*).
By the opposite of that, one is one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*).
The fifth is the "one who flows upwards" (*ūrdhva-srotas*); furthermore, he is either one for whom the Akaniṣṭha heaven is the limit or one for whom the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is the limit.

In that regard, the one for whom Akaniṣṭha is the limit is of three types: the "Leaper," the "Half-Leaper," and the one who "Dissolves from All Stations" before entering Akaniṣṭha. The one for whom the Peak of Existence (bhāvāgra) is the limit is of two types: the "One Attaining Peace in the Present Life" and the "Body-Witness," both of whom are free from passion for the realm of form.
Following that, through the abandonment of the eight categories of afflictions belonging to the Peak of Existence, one becomes a candidate for the fruit of Arhatship.
Then, by relying solely on the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and realizing one’s own path, one becomes a Pratyekabuddha in the absence of a Buddha’s appearance; thus there are twenty [types].
Furthermore, this meaning is explained in detail in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*.

However, in the *Avaivartikacakra-sūtra*, the Blessed One has clearly stated the classification of individuals (*pudgala-vyavasthāna*), beginning from the Bodhisattva who follows through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) up to the Bodhisattva-Pratyekabuddha.
That very point should be examined; we have not set it forth here in detail, for why grind what is already ground?
Thus, the persons abiding in the first and second fruits, as well as the candidate for the fourth fruit, are not included because they are easy to understand.
[They are: those of dull and sharp faculties, those who have attained through faith and through vision, and those who go from family to family (*kulaṅkula*).
Those who go to the Single-Interval, the Intermediate, the Reborn, the Doer, the Non-doer, and the Akaniṣṭha [heavens]. ||24||
"The three leapers, the one who reaches the peak of existence, the one who abandons attachment to the form realm,
the one who attains peace in this very life, the body-witness, and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha]— these are the twenty.
Thus it is said for the beginner who has received the instruction.
Then the wise one, having completed the accumulation of merit and possessing firm resolve,
has his mental continuum thoroughly cultivated by wholesome qualities such as faith and the rest.
For the sake of accomplishing the equipment of gnosis, after the passage of incalculable eons,
one who possesses stable superknowledges proceeds upon the stage of conduct through instruction.

Having thus established this, for the sake of purifying the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), one must explain the four levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), which consist of mundane cultivation (*laukikabhāvanāmaya*) and are favorable to the realization of the Four Truths; these follow upon the roots of virtue characterized by faith and so forth that constitute the "aids to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*) attained through the excellence of hearing and other means.

The distinction [of these bodhisattvas] from the śrāvakas and others must be stated as follows: by virtue of the distinction of their objective support (ālambana), which consists of entities characterized by impermanence and so forth; by virtue of the distinction of their mental aspects (ākāra), such as non-attachment, because they serve as the antidote (pratipakṣa) to the vision of dharmas; by virtue of the distinction of their being causes for the realization of the three vehicles; and by virtue of the distinction of their complete embrace (saṃparigraha) characterized by skillful means (upāyakauśala) and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

Likewise, there are two types of conceptualization of the graspable (grāhyavikalpa): that which has the basis of afflicted entities (saṃkleśavastu) and that which has the basis of remedial entities (pratipakṣavastu).

The conceptualization of the grasper (*grāhakavikalpa*) is twofold: that which has a substantially existent person as its basis and that which has a nominally existent person as its basis. It should be stated that these aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are characterized by affliction through their association with the four types of conceptualization to be abandoned respectively on the paths of seeing and meditation, which will be explained in the section on the "Subsequent Clear Realization" (*mūrdhābhisamaya*). Furthermore, for those who possess these [aids] in conjunction with the aforementioned conceptualizations, their distinctiveness must be stated according to the division of each into weak, medium, and intense; thus, there are five kinds of distinctions.

The fourfold roots of merit, beginning with "heat" (*uṣmagata*), belonging to the Śrāvakas and others, have as their objective support the Four Truths—which consist of entities characterized by formability (*rūpaṇā*) and so forth—and serve as the cause for the realization of their own vehicle through aspects such as impermanence (*anitya*) as the antidote to the view of self (*ātmadarśana*).

Since they are devoid of grasping and do not involve the fourfold conceptualization that constitutes an obstacle to one's own enlightenment, it is established that even though they arise in association with that [conceptualization], they are "unassociated.
For it has been said accordingly:

For those beings who, according to their respective natures, possess the association with the fourfold conceptualization by way of objective support, aspect, causality, and thorough grasping, [the antidote is taught]. //26//

"The superiority of the [levels] beginning with *uṣman*— whether weak, middling, or intense— belonging to the Bodhisattva Protector, over those of the Śrāvakas who possess the [four] limbs, has been stated. (27) Regarding this,
he speaks of the object of focus (*ālambana*) for the weak root of merit belonging to the stage of *uṣmagata*:
"Furthermore," and so forth; "furthermore" (*punaraparam*) indicates the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of another method.

"In the *prajñāpāramitā*" means even though it is mentioned in general terms, its meaning is that it has as its objective support (*ālambana*) entities such as impermanence and so forth. For instance, in another passage:
The Blessed One has stated: "O monks, a sutra should be explained in accordance with other sutras.
And in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*, with reference to the focal object of the mild stage of heat (*mṛdu-uṣman*), it is said:
"In this regard, O Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva [contemplates] form as impermanent, form as suffering, form as empty, form as non-self," and so forth.

However, the distinction here is this: namely, that there is a concise exposition [here], whereas there is a detailed exposition concerning each truth individually; thus, no doubt should be entertained. "Practices" means with non-concentrated knowledge; "cultivates" means with concentrated knowledge.
This has been stated: the object of focus is the reality that serves as the basis for the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering, and which possesses the sixteen aspects beginning with impermanence.
To the question of "in what manner should that be taken as an object?
he says: "In this way," and so forth.

"Thus" means according to the sequence to be explained; "even by that" and so forth means that one should not conceive of an object not only because the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is absolutely beyond perception, but also by that aspect which consists of the negation of adherence and the like, and which takes the form of the cognition that brings about awakening—one should not conceive of it, that is, one should not form an attachment to it. This means [one should not adhere] by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) through such aspects as non-adherence and so on.
This is what is meant: the śrāvaka takes as his object a thing characterized by transformation and so forth;
its aspects, such as impermanence and so on, arise because they serve as the antidote to the view of a self.
The bodhisattva, however, takes as his object a thing characterized by impermanence and so forth.
Its aspects consist of non-attachment and so forth, because they serve as the antidote to the vision of phenomena (*dharmadarśana*).
Now, if non-attachment is simply the absence of attachment, then, being a mere non-existence, it would not logically function as an antidote.

If it is argued that if there were no adherence (*abhiniveśa*), then the same consequence would apply to the eyes and so forth as well, we reply: as there is an opposing side (*vipakṣa*), so there is adherence;
as there is a counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), so there is non-adherence.
And what is the adverse side?
It is the grasping at existence and non-existence arising from the conceptual construction of the unreal.
And what is the counteragent?
How is it that those two do not exist? And how is it that they do not exist?
It is if they are known to not exist in reality.

And so he will say immediately thereafter: "If, O Venerable Śāriputra, in that state of non-mind... and so forth. Now, one might ask: since the aspects such as non-attachment are established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why would a discerning person not have attachment?
To this he says: "For what reason?"—that is, for what cause?
Alternatively, the meaning is: for what purpose, for what cause, or for what motive is this absence of dogmatic adherence?
He states the subsequent point, beginning with "For it is thus," and so forth.

Because the nature (*prakṛti*) or essence (*svabhāva*) of the mind is non-arising and luminous due to its being devoid of a nature of being either one or many, and because it has dispelled the darkness of all false conceptualizations, the mind— which is not distinct from aspects such as non-apprehension— is in reality "no-mind" (*acitta*).

He thinks thus: since the mind is devoid of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), how could a mode such as non-attachment— which is not distinct from that [mind]— be, in reality, a basis for attachment?

Whether the negative particle (*nañ*) is used in the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) or in the sense of simple negation (*prasajya*), seeing that even when "non-mind" (*acitta*) is employed, there is no cessation of error because it is still associated with the mere conceptualization of existence and non-existence, he says: "That mind which is 'non-mind' does exist."
That mind which is not distinct from the aspect of non-attachment and so forth is, in reality, called "non-mind";
this should be connected with the question, "Does that non-mind exist?"
Since the object does not exist according to reason, the negative particle (*nañ*) is not employed in the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), but rather in the sense of simple negation (*prasajya*).

In that regard, even the mere designation of existence or non-existence does not exist; intending this, Subhūti, wishing to provide a rebuttal by means of that very point, addressed Śāriputra with a counter-question beginning with "What then," etc., [asking] whether it is merely the absence of mind (*acitta*)— that state which is "non-mindness" (*acittatā*).
In that state of non-mind, does existence as a real entity exist, or is it not reached by the conditions for perception?
Or rather, is it perceived, being reached by the conditions for perception?

In this way, it should be applied as "or non-existence"; it should be understood that the preceding word "or" (vā) is in relation to what follows, and the subsequent one is in relation to what precedes.
For that which is unborn by its own nature, how could there be permanence or annihilation?
For conceptualizations of the extremes regarding intrinsic nature are merely conceptual distinctions among phenomena;
can anyone ever arrange patterns such as inscriptions upon the sky?
Since such conceptualizations of distinctions in dharma cannot be established when [the object] has not arisen,
he, holding this intention, said "for this is not so," referring to the two points just mentioned; now, applying that very statement as a rebuttal, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "sa cet" and so forth:
the word "api tu" (but rather) has the sense of "only by way of censure.
"Paryanuyoga" means an objection; he states that very thing.
By the words "When the Venerable One," and so forth,
he thinks as follows:
"If, in the state of non-mind, neither existence nor non-existence is found or perceived, then how can you direct this inquiry at me?"
"There is that thought which is thought as 'non-thought'.
For even there, by "non-thought," only the mere absence of thought is intended; therefore, the superimposition of existence in the form of being either existent or non-existent is simply not tenable.
Since a negation cannot be employed without an object when the subject— the mind— is non-existent, he says that even "non-mind" does not exist.

Regarding the phrase "But what is this? and so forth, he speaks in order to respond by means of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) of the yogis, for it is said: "Without the ladder of conventional truth, the wise cannot ascend to the pinnacle of the palace of reality."
"Unchanging," and so forth; [it is] "non-mind-ness" precisely through a succession.
Because it is being cultivated as the cause for the non-alteration-perfection on the Buddha-stage, it is "unalterable" (*avikārā*);
and because it is the cause for the perfection of non-perversion, it is "non-conceptual" (*avikalpā*).
Thus, he says that what has been stated is not in contradiction with realization.
The phrase beginning with "atha" and so forth includes the exclamation "well done! well done! uttered twice out of excitement.
The word *yathā* means "in what manner.
The word *apināma* expresses honor.

By the power of that concentration (*samādhi*), the afflictions (*kleśa*)—which are called "conflicts" (*raṇa*) because they cause strife within the mental continuums of others for the sake of harming oneself and others—do not arise; this is the "conflict-free concentration" (*araṇā-samādhi*). It has been taught as the foremost among those who dwell in it.
The phrase "you have taught the state of non-mind" (*sannirdiśasyācittatām*) should be construed by changing the case ending [from accusative to dative].

But surely, since he was teaching the perfection of wisdom along with skillful means through the empowerment of the Buddha, what excellence was there such that even Śāriputra, who knew that [teaching], would offer his approval to Subhūti, saying, "Excellent"?
It is not anyone at all; rather, it is for the sake of favoring those disciples of theirs, by manifesting their greatness and removing the doubts of future disciples.
Or, it is simply through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata that there is this expression of approval (*sādhukāra*) preceded by a lack of dispute; thus, there is no fault.
By demonstrating the very greatness of non-thought (*acittatā*), [the text shows] that someone of indefinite lineage (*aniyata-gotra*)—
Furthermore, because of his sharp faculties, even while in the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), he is certain of non-retrogression due to a particular inconceivable skillful means;
thus [the author] says, "Therefore," and so forth, because by that very thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) he conceives [of it],
and therefore [it is characterized] by such modes as non-attachment and so on.
Because of the word "and" (ca), it means that one must examine and ascertain [the object] by taking as an objective support entities characterized by impermanence and so forth.
However, there is no fault [in our position], because on the eighth stage, all [bodhisattvas] are established as non-retrogressive due to their certainty.
And because there is no falling away, he should be understood as not being separated from the perfection of wisdom in its form as the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);
the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that he is not only to be examined as one who is irreversible.
Having thus explained the objective support (*ālambana*) and the mental aspect (*ākāra*), he speaks for the sake of specifying the causal nature of the weak stages of heat (*mṛdu-uṣman*).

"In the *Śrāvakabhūmi* as well," and so forth: knowledge that has attained a distinguished state is what constitutes a "ground" (*bhūmi*). This [work] is primarily intended to demonstrate the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) for one who desires to train in them—that is, for one who desires to practice them—by means of the very [stages] described here. It is to be heard because the text and its meaning are discerned by the auditory consciousness and the mental consciousness induced by it.
It should be grasped through mental attention consisting of reflection;
it should be maintained by means of practice consisting of cultivation;
and it should be recited by undertaking its study or reading from a book.
It should be mastered through the attainment of scripture and realization;
it should be propagated by revealing it to others through exposition and other such means.
In all cases, such as hearing [the Dharma] and so forth, one should train by accomplishing the mind that follows upon correct application (*samyakprayoga*).
However, through the fundamental mind (*maulacitta*), one should enter into yoga by means of effecting meditative concentration (*samādhāna*).
Because gender is dependent on worldly convention (*lokāśrayatva*), the word "yoga" is stated here in the neuter gender.
"Endowed with skill in means" refers to:
skill in fulfilling the qualities of a Buddha, in maturing sentient beings,
in swift attainment, in the accomplishment of activities, and in the non-interruption of the path.
Skillful means is the peerless [method] of Bodhisattvas throughout all the stages;
relying upon this skillfulness, they accomplish all aims.

Based on this statement, skill in means (*upāyakauśala*) is precisely a particular state of mind (*cetoviśe�ṣa*) that relies upon both the conventional and the ultimate truths, and which swiftly brings about the attainment of the aforementioned goal.

One who is endowed with and possessed of this must practice the yoga of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) for the sake of the full realization of all the qualities of a bodhisattva; that is, for the acquisition and attainment of all those qualities unique to bodhisattvas—distinct from those of the śrāvakas and others—which are characterized by the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
In some places, however, the reading is "for the sake of the complete attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha" (*sarvabuddhadharmasamudāgamāya*).
That, moreover, is incorrect,
as the author will state immediately thereafter.
"All the qualities of a bodhisattva," and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that "are not the qualities of a bodhisattva, such as generosity and so on, already taught even in the Śrāvaka vehicle? he says:
"For what reason?"—
the answer begins with "For right here," and so forth.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because."
"In which" means in those bodhisattva-dharmas. He thinks as follows:
"The dharmas of the śrāvakas and so forth are explained in detail in that Piṭaka, whereas the bodhisattva-dharmas are mentioned only incidentally."

Here, moreover, only the qualities of a bodhisattva are taught in detail, while the qualities of a śrāvaka are mentioned only incidentally. Regarding "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" (*anuttarā samyaksambodhi*): that which has nothing superior or more excellent is "unsurpassed. It is "perfect" (*samyak*) because it is non-erroneous; it is "complete awakening" (*abhisambodhi*) because it is the realization of all aspects. Thus, "perfect enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*) refers, in short, to the stage of a Buddha.
"For the full realization of all Buddha-dharmas" means for the attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha, which are characterized by the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
In the Śrāvaka vehicle...
Fearing that one might suspect that the Buddha-dharmas have also been taught [in this way], he asks,
"For what reason?
and provides the answer for that very purpose.
By the passage beginning with "In this very [life]" and starting from "even in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*," up until the end with "one should attain union (*yoga*)," this is what is stated:
that the wholesome state of the "mild heat" (*mṛdu-uṣmagata*) is the cause for attaining the realization of the three vehicles (*yāna*).
Furthermore, this causal nature should be understood to apply to all [the stages] beginning with heat.
He speaks for the purpose of providing an object of focus for the intermediate state:
"O Blessed One, I who... and so forth.
[This refers to] the designation "bodhisattva."

Previously, it was stated that there is no apprehension of that entity which was designated by the name "Bodhisattva," beginning with the words, "O Blessed One, I do not perceive that phenomenon. Now, however:
"All this is merely a name; it is established in mere conceptual designation.
The referent is not conceived as existing apart from its verbal expression."
Having established this, the remainder [of the meaning] is that the non-apprehension of that very nature of the name "Bodhisattva" which is to be taught has been shown.
The phrase "I do not know," and so forth, has already been explained. Alternatively, it means: "I do not know the past; I do not apprehend the present."
"One does not perceive the future because all dharmas are empty of the future"—this is how it should be applied.
To the objection that there must then be an object for the instruction, he says:
"even the perfection of wisdom."
The intended meaning is "mere name.
The nature of the name is "Bodhisattva," because that is the subject under discussion.
Regarding "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*): because the persistence of an object is not perceived due to its being grounded solely in cognition, this remorse is the state of mental regret.
He says that very thing: "That which..."
By the words "ham" and so forth;
regarding "income and expenditure":
injunction is income, and prohibition is expenditure.
Apart from affirmation and negation, there is no other word;
since all conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is comprised within these two terms alone, only this much has been stated.
This is said to mean that the object of perception, such as form and so forth, is characterized by being devoid of both coming and going in reality.
To the question, "In what manner is that to be taken as an object? he says:
"But rather," and so forth.
Even that name, which is the object, does not exist as a continuous stream.
Since there is an absence of anything to be negated, in reality there is clearly no negation;
nor does a correct usage of the negative particle exist without an object.
Alternatively, if it were based on conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it would be conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) and not ultimate (*tāttvika*).

According to this logic, it is "not established" (*anasthita*) and "not situated" (*aviṣṭhita*) because of its dissimilarity to the continuity (*prabandha*); likewise, it is "not persistently situated" (*tathaivāviṣṭhita*).
[The opponent asks: How can there be no inconsistency regarding the dissimilarity between the continuity and its name, given that the name appears through convention (*saṃvṛti*)?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because of its non-existence," and so forth;
the word "in reality" (tattvataḥ) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
The intention is that there is no fault from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). Concluding [the argument], he says:
"In this way, that... and so forth.
This has been stated by way of the gateway of *dharmatā* as the aspect (*ākāra*) of reality (*tattva*) which is free from continuity and its dissimilarity.
To explain the object of focus for the superior [level], he says:
"If," and so forth.

Thus, regarding that which is profound—being by its very name a mere designation and having as its intrinsic nature a mere conceptual construct—it is unfathomed by both non-Buddhist outsiders and by our own [followers] who fear the lack of a foundation.

This means that the object of focus (*ālambana*) is the Truth of Suffering and so forth, as distinguished by its being a mere conceptual construct. To the question, "In what aspect (*ākāra*) is it to be taken as an object? he says:
"Resolves," and so forth:
one resolves upon— that is, takes as an object— the fact that this designation cannot be expressed by any dharma, such as those that are wholesome and so on.
Far-reaching, vast, joyful, intent on helping others,
and great— such an intention, being superior in these qualities, is called *adhyāśaya* (resolute intention) by the virtuous.

Thus, that bodhisattva who is not devoid of such resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is primarily endowed with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) whose nature is the highest stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*).
Elsewhere as well, the meaning of the perfection of wisdom should be understood in this way by the force of the context.
He is "established" because he has attained the state of non-retrogression on the eighth bodhisattva stage, which is irreversible, due to his attainment of that specific task;
he is "well-established" because, through his fitness for its appropriation, he attains ever-higher distinctions, and thus does not fall away from what he has not yet attained.
And he says that these two are by way of non-attachment,
namely, "by way of the yoga of non-abiding.
This means that, from the perspective of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the aspect is inexpressible.
And in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*, with reference to the aspect of the object of the highest degree of heat (*adhimātra-uṣmagata*), it is said:
"O Blessed One, this conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṅketikī prajñapti*) which is 'bodhisattva'...
and so on in detail, up to "Buddha."
That too cannot be described by any dharma, whether wholesome or unwholesome,
up to and including existence or non-existence.
It is just as, for example, with a dream, and so forth.

Therefore, one should not entertain doubt; because it is the precursor to the fire of non-conceptual knowledge—which possesses both an object and a mental aspect—it is called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), being threefold like the stage of heat.
This is because, in the absence of obstacles, it becomes even closer to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The distinction of this [path] from the factors conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) should be understood.
And so it has been said:
"Its object is impermanence and so forth; its basis is the truths; its form is that [of those truths]."
The negation of dogmatic adherence and the like is the cause for attaining the three vehicles. ||28||
The arising and passing away of form and so forth, as well as their dispersion and persistence, are designated and inexpressible.
Thus, immediately following "Heat" (uṣman), he now speaks—"Furthermore," and so forth—in order to explain the object of the weak "Summit" (mūrdhan) stage of the wholesome roots.

It has been explained that one should practice—that is, cultivate—while coursing in the Perfection of Wisdom, which primarily has the nature of the Summits; alternatively, it should be construed as: one should practice with the mind of the preparatory stage (prayoga-pṛṣṭha-citta) and cultivate with the fundamental mind (maula-citta).
"One should not abide in form," and so forth.
In that regard, form is characterized by the absence of characteristics;
sensation is characterized by experience.
Perception has the grasping of signs as its essence;
mental formations have the characteristic of conditioning the mind;
consciousness has the characteristic of discernment.
Furthermore, that form is threefold:
imagined form (*kalpita-rūpa*), because it is imagined in the form of the grasped and the grasper;

and conceptually constructed form (*vikalpita-rūpa*), because it is conceptually constructed as consciousness itself appearing in such a way through the construction of the unreal (*asadbhūta-parikalpa*).
The form of the nature of phenomena (dharmatārūpa) is in reality formless, because it is perfected as the form of emptiness.
The same should be said for sensation and the other aggregates as well.

The sequence of form and the other [aggregates] is exactly as such according to the realms of objects, beginning with the vessel-world, in order of their coarseness and their degree of affliction. In that regard,
since one is unable to perceive a real entity because form and the others do not exist in reality, the mind should not abide— that is to say, no mental fixation should be established— upon them.

This is what is meant: because, through the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), form and the other aggregates are devoid of an intrinsic nature by virtue of their own nature as form and so forth; therefore, the objective support (*ālambana*) of form and the rest is characterized by its fitness for non-abiding. Anticipating the question, "Why is the objective support such?"—that is, for what reason?—he explains the mode [of cognition] (*ākāra*) by way of negation (*vyatireka*).
By the words "If [it were] in form," etc., he thinks as follows:

the mode of grasping the object is itself the aspect (ākāra), and the establishment of the object is grounded in consciousness; therefore, the object to be grasped must correspond precisely to its aspect.

Therefore, if one dwells upon form (*rūpa*) by means of aspects such as impermanence and so forth, then one courses in the formative activity of form and in the conceptualization of the engagement with form.

And in this way, one does not course in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which primarily has the nature of the "mild peak" (*mṛdu-mūrdha*). The same should be applied to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates as well.

This has been stated by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): the aspect (*ākāra*) is to be grasped in this manner, namely, that in the ultimate sense, form (*rūpa*) and the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all phenomena such as form are mutually one and the same essence.
In that regard, because impermanence and so forth do not exist within emptiness, no abiding should be established in form and so on by means of aspects such as permanence or impermanence.
For it has been explained in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* with reference to the aspect of the "mild peak" (*mṛdu-mūrdha*).
"Form itself is emptiness, emptiness itself is form; and so on, up to: 'O Blessed One, that which is the emptiness of impermanence is not [itself] impermanence,'" and so forth.
Since cultivation does not arise without volitional formation (*abhisaṃskāra*), how then is it that one who courses in volitional formation does not course?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?
he says, "Indeed not," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: conceptual construction...
The application of effort and the perfection of wisdom are both non-conceptual.
Therefore, how can one who courses by means of conceptualization while adhering to reality as real course in the perfection of wisdom?
One must course solely like an illusory person.

The three phrases—"does not grasp," "does not enter into yoga," and "does not fulfill"—should be understood respectively in the stages of preparation (*prayoga*), the main stage (*maula*), and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*).
Regarding the phrase "the perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*), it primarily refers to that which has the nature of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) at its lowest degree;
[this applies to the statement] "he will not go forth," and so on.

It should be understood that by grasping—that is, taking as one's own—an ungrasped formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) which is unfit for grasping, one will not emerge into omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).

And here, "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*) is used as a term for "omniscience in all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*) because of the commonality of the three types of omniscience; this should be applied similarly elsewhere as appropriate.
How is it that [formative activity] is unfit for grasping?
If it is argued that this is due to volitional effort (*abhisaṃskāra*),
then, raising the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For form," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:

Form and the other [objects] have the nature of being objects of volitional construction; since they are not grasped as existing according to reason, their object [is non-existent] in the Perfection of Wisdom.
Because it appears falsely, conceptual construction (*abhisaṃskāra*) is not to be grasped.
Demonstrating this very point, he says:
"That which is the non-appropriation of form is not that form," and so forth.
The meaning is that injunctions and prohibitions have distinct objects.
He says, "Even in the Prajñāpāramitā, one should not form an attachment to reality," because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of error;
he concludes by saying "That too," and so forth.
"Thus indeed," and so forth.
The word "hi" (indeed) is used for emphasis;
it means "in this very way."
Thus, he describes the concentration that has emerged from its object and aspect and which constitutes the "mild summit" (*mṛdu-mūrdha*) stage, beginning with the words "this... and so forth.
That concentration which is not grasped by any phenomena, such as form and the rest, and whose name corresponds to its actual nature, is described in that way.
"It is 'vast' because of the vastness of the *dharmadhātu*;
it is 'placed before' because it proceeds before the mind due to the two specific qualities of its object and its mode of activity as previously described," says the noble Vimuktisena.

Therefore, the reading "not placed foremost" (*apūrakṛta*) found in some places is not to be accepted; for it is restricted to non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa-niyata*) because of its specific determination toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),
or else due to its connection with vast compassion and wisdom (*karuṇā-prajñā*).
Because it is restricted to the performance of the welfare of beings through valid means, it is "restricted to valid means" (*apramāṇa-niyata*);
it is uncommon and inaccessible.
Because of the fivefold excellence of others, such as the aforementioned objects of focus and so forth;
he states the object for the intermediate [type] as:
"That too is omniscience."
By the word "also" (*api*), there is the inclusion of emptinesses such as impermanence and so forth.
[The question] "Why is it not included?
and so on, [is answered by] "For it is not... and so on.
The sign (*nimitta*) is the specific form; because they are of a single nature with one another in reality, it does not exist [as distinct], which means there is no apprehension of it.
This is stated by way of its being the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.

Because permanence and so forth, as well as the emptiness of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), are by their own nature devoid of intrinsic being (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), these are, through their mutual identity, an objective support (*ālambana*) such as form (*rūpa*) characterized by signlessness (*animitta*).
To the question, "What is the fault in grasping at signs? he says:
"If [it were so]," and so forth.

If it were to be grasped by way of signs (*nimitta*), then, seeing no liberation for a long time due to the grasping of signs within his own teaching and becoming despondent, the ascetic wanderer named Śreṇika would not have attained faith— namely, conviction— through the yoga of signlessness in this very teaching. The point is that the grasping of signs would be identical [in both cases].
Explaining that very point, he says:
"In this case," and so forth.

Here, regarding the signless state—the omniscient gnosis which brings about the state of a Tathāgata—one practices the mental application of resolute conviction by being resolutely convinced of its signs; because one follows the path through faith due to having dull faculties, one is a "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārī*).
Having entered by means of a limited knowledge of the selflessness of persons, he, having thus entered, subsequently does not attend to form and so forth as signs.
Nor, in that cultivation of the signless, does he perceive the knowledge that cultivates it as a sign, even though it is accompanied by the joy and bliss arisen therein.
In that context, joy (*prīti*) is mental well-being (*saumanasya*),
while bliss (*sukha*) is physical pliancy (*prasrabdhi*).
For he is one who, being free from worldly passion, has entered [the path] by relying on either the first or the second dhyāna.
Thus says the Venerable Vimuktisena.
By what aspect (*ākāra*) should it be taken as an object? He says:
"Not internally," and so forth.

One does not perceive, by way of signs—the remainder of the sentence being understood—that the knowledge which produces internal form (which consists of appropriated primary elements and their derivatives, the internal sense bases) exists as such through internal emptiness;
nor [does one perceive] external form (which consists of non-appropriated primary elements and their derivatives, the external sense bases) through external emptiness;
nor [does one perceive] internal-external form (the body consisting of both) through internal-external emptiness.
He says: "Then does one see apart from form?
and so on, "nor elsewhere," etc.
Thus, being attached to the cultivation of phenomena (*dharmabhāvanā*), how is such a person to be described? He says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "atra" and so forth: here, in this particular stage of yoga (*yogasthāna*), namely the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), Śreṇika is situated.
He should be called "one who has entered" (avimukta), not "one who has attained.
For this reason, Śreṇika is here called a "follower by faith" because he lacks the realization of reality regarding the omniscient knowledge that is entirely signless.

The intention is that one becomes a follower of the Dharma (dharmānusārī) through the attainment of reality by means of having sharp faculties. But how is it that even one with dull faculties can be thus resolved? To this he says:
"Regarding the phrase 'the nature of phenomena' (*dharmatā*) and so forth:
by the power of previous impetus, having taken the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* as authoritative through non-contradiction, he is thus resolved upon it as being signless (*animitta*).
Therefore, by him, no phenomenon whatsoever..."
He would not grasp any phenomenon as something to be adopted, nor would he take it up as existing, such that he might accept it;
nor would he relinquish it as something to be abandoned.
Let alone anything else—he does not even conceive of nirvāṇa.
In reality, it is not understood.
This means that by way of negating intrinsic nature, there is no acceptance [of things]; this is the "aspect" (ākāra) by way of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of form and so forth.
In this regard, there is the example of Śreṇika.

This is for the purpose of making known that, upon emerging from meditative absorption through his connection with the non-Buddhist teachers, he possesses the direct eyewitness-knowledge of that object by the power of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣabala*) alone.
To explain the object of focus for one of superior capacity, he says:
"This too," and so forth; "this" refers to...
The word "also" (*api*) indicates that it is not only what was previously stated, but also what will be stated hereafter.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "That form," and so forth.
The particle *yat* is used in the sense of "because";
the meaning is that it is due to not perceiving the causes of form and so forth.
[An objection is raised: "In that case, like a *śrāvaka*, the bodhisattva would enter nirvāṇa through non-apprehension when all things have ceased. To this, he says:
"And not," and so forth.
The word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis. "With the body not withdrawn, enduring sensation."
"Like the extinguishing of a lamp, there is the liberation of his mind"— thus [it is said].
Since *nirvāṇa* is rejected in the Mahāyāna,

by virtue of the authority of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and having adopted composure for the sake of sentient beings for that duration, he does not midway, like a Śrāvaka, realize signlessness through the power of great skillful means (*mahopāyakauśalya*).
He attains parinirvāṇa.
Since the parinirvāṇa of a Śrāvaka does not exist during the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), the word "gradually" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Regarding the phrase "not being complete," it should be construed with the words "by all aspects" and "by all Buddha-qualities," since others possess [these qualities] even to some small degree.
The powers of the Tathāgata and so forth will be explained later.
Therefore, the passage beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore) is the conclusion.

This means that, by virtue of the very absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the objective support (*ālambana*) of form and so forth is, in reality, characterized by the non-perception of signs such as blue and the like.
He asks, "In what manner should it be taken as an object?
and replies with the words "Furthermore," and so forth, [explaining] "in this way" means according to the sequence that is about to be described.
It is to be examined at the time of cultivation by means of reflecting upon the object as it has been determined;
