it is to be closely contemplated at the time of hearing and reflection by means of investigation through both reasoning and scripture.
"Which one is this? refers to which among the aggregates, such as form and so forth.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "What is it—a substance, a quality, an action, a generality, inherence, or a particularity? And "to whom does this belong? means: is it related to the self or to its attributes?
However, because [the causes such as] color and so forth have not yet arisen, the meaning is that it is neither anything at all nor belongs to anyone.
If that is so, then [the opponent] says:
"What is this phenomenon? and so forth.
[This refers to] the negation (*nañ*) which lacks an object.

The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), because of its non-existence through application (*prayoga*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) does not exist as a substantial entity (*bhāva*).
"If [he]... and so forth is the conclusion.
By means of the perfection of wisdom...
One should understand that [the practitioner] is not separated from the realization whose nature consists of the stages of *dhimātra* (mere mental attention) and *mūrdhan* (summit).
This is what was said:

Because one examines all things through wisdom (*prajñā*) by means of the correct discernment of phenomena (*samyag-dharmapravicaya*), and because they are not perceived as having any intrinsic nature, the aspect (*ākāra*) is the state of the non-existent nature of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by way of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Thus, because it possesses both the object of focus (*ālambana*) and the aspect, and because it is the summit of the unstable roots of virtue (*cala-kuśalamūla*), it is the "summit stage" (*mūrdhagata*), which is threefold.
And so it has been said:
Their abiding in form and so forth consists in their lack of intrinsic nature by virtue of being that [very state]. ||29||
The mutual nature of those two is the non-establishment of their impermanence and so forth;
the emptiness of those [qualities] of that [nature] is the mutual naturelessness of these two. (30)
"Non-apprehension of phenomena is the non-contemplation of their signs,
and it is the investigation by means of wisdom through the non-perception of everything.
(31) Thus, immediately after the "Summits," he now speaks, preceded by a question, regarding the object of the wholesome state belonging to the "Receptivities" (*kṣānti*) at its mild stage.
"What is the reason? and so forth.
The phrase "by way of the intrinsic nature of form" implies that it is "perceived as an object";
this is what has been stated.

When form and so forth are apprehended as being devoid of the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of form and so forth, for what reason should it be understood that [the practitioner] is primarily not devoid of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), which has the nature of weak receptivity (mṛdu-kṣānti)?
With the intention that this is the very nature of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā)— namely, "when this exists, that comes to be"— he provides the answer, saying, "form itself."
Otherwise, when the question "How is it that form itself is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form? is asked, the answer "Form itself is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form" would not be logical.

Furthermore, having raised the doubt, "In what way are form and the other aggregates devoid of intrinsic nature?", he says the following for the purpose of demonstrating that by establishing the very fact that the *Prajñāpāramitā* is devoid of intrinsic nature, the fact that all others are likewise devoid of intrinsic nature is established:

The Perfection of Wisdom is devoid of the characteristic of the Perfection of Wisdom in its general form; the word "also" implies it is likewise devoid of the characteristic in its specific form as well. Since the teaching has the fruit of eliminating cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*), one might ask: "Does the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) then exist? To this he says: "By way of the intrinsic nature of the characteristic. Here, "characteristic" refers to the general, while the "characterized" refers to the particular.
To this he says: "They possess an intrinsic nature by way of the characteristic of intrinsic nature. [It is] free from both the characterized and the characteristic, and devoid of verbal expression.
The reality that is established through designation consists of the arrangement of the characterized and the characteristics.
This is the intended meaning. This has been stated:
"The objective support, such as form and so forth, is characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature due to the identity of emptiness with both the object to be defined and its definition.
He explains the meaning of the aspect (*ākāra*) by way of the question: "In what manner is it to be taken as an objective support?"
"What then," and so forth.

The meaning here is: will he who trains in this objective support (ālambana) by way of conventional reality (saṃvṛti) emerge into omniscience (sarvajñatā) through the attainment of the wholesome qualities associated with the stage of weak patience (mṛdu-kṣānti) directed toward that [objective]?
He says this in order to accept that what has been stated is indeed not in contradiction with the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
"Thus it is," and so forth.

"He will go forth" means that the very absence of form and the other aggregates is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatā*); this refers to the cultivation of that aspect by way of both the conventional and the ultimate truth.
But how, while training in the wholesome qualities belonging to the stage of weak patience (*mṛdukṣānti*), will one proceed toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?", he says "Because they are unborn," and so forth, in order to provide a meditative object for one who stands in the middle.
The intention is that, through successive distinctions in the meditative objects and so on, one will certainly proceed toward a distinction in realization.
The first word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for emphasis;
the meaning is "they are indeed unborn.

Why? Because, due to momentary impermanence, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) have not emerged—that is, they have not gone to *nirvāṇa*—through the cessation of the characteristic of birth. Thus, the objective support (*ālambana*) consisting of form and so forth is characterized by non-arising and non-cessation by virtue of having no intrinsic nature (*prakṛtyasvabhāvatva*).
Up to this point, [the question was] "In what manner should it be taken as an object? To which he says:
"Practicing in this way," and so forth.

Thus, for one who practices and meditates according to the principle just explained—on the grounds that [these perfections] serve to realize the meaning of all destinies—it "becomes near," meaning it would be in close proximity to the attainment of swift realization. It is "for the sake of maturing sentient beings" because it joins them with wholesome qualities; such is the meaning of the phrase "for the sake of maturing sentient beings," and so forth.

Through the realization of the true nature of all phenomena, there is the purification of the body and so forth in all their aspects. Because this is the cause of purification, by practicing through the aspect of purification—that is, by way of the cause—the complete purification of the body occurs, as does the threefold bodily action that is completely purified.
The complete purification of the mind occurs, as does the threefold mental action that is completely purified.
The purification of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man results from their perfection through being established in their proper places, being radiant, and being complete.
The purification of the Buddha-field is the complete purity of both the sentient beings and the vessel-world. In the stage conducive to penetration, in every respect—
The meaning is: "to what extent [is it possible] because of its occurrence?
The passage beginning with "in this way" (*evam*) is the conclusion. He speaks for the purpose of providing an object of focus (*ālambana*) for one of superior capacity (*adhimātra*).
By the passage beginning with "If [he perceives] form," etc., he thinks as follows:

As long as one acts by grasping at signs through the application of dogmatic adherence, for that long one falls into the afflictions of cyclic existence rooted in apprehension, according to the statement: "Bodhisattvas are those who possess the afflictions of signs."
In this context, form is the effect;
the cause of form is the cooperative condition;
and form itself is the substantial cause.
Arising is birth;
cessation is through momentary impermanence;
destruction is through the impermanence of the continuum.
Emptiness is the non-existence of both.
One should understand that [the practitioner] is unskilled in means because of being engaged in perversions.
Having explained by way of negation (*vyatireka*), he speaks by way of affirmation (*anvaya*).
To the question "How so? he replies with the concluding statement beginning with "practicing thus," and so forth.

This means that because the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are untenable, the objective support consists of form and the other aggregates, characterized by their signlessness (*animitta*).
Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva practices in the perfection of wisdom whose nature is supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
To the question, "In what manner should it be taken as an object? he says:
"For while practicing," and so forth.
He does not understand injunction and prohibition as being joined together,
nor does he understand the negation of those two in any way whatsoever.
Such is the intended meaning. But how can there be cultivation (*bhāvanā*) when there is no comprehension?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason is that?", he says:
"For all phenomena," and so forth.

Because, by their very nature, the signs of form and so forth are devoid of a basis, there is a lack of full comprehension through both the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) and the mental application of reality (*tattva-manasikāra*). Thus, by way of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are not accepted as objects because they are not embraced by resolute conviction; and because they are not grasped by the mental application of reality, they are not appropriated. Therefore, since there is no falling away due to the presence of both the object and its aspect, there are three types of the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), characterized by the endurance of the supreme Dharma.
And so it has been said:
"The absence of intrinsic nature in form and the rest, the intrinsic nature of that absence, their non-arising, their non-departure, their purity, and their signlessness. (32)
"Non-apprehension of those signs, non-adherence, and lack of conviction constitute non-perception.
For this very reason:

Regarding what was stated by the venerable Master— that "Bodhisattvas do not produce [the patience of the path of seeing] because of the scriptural statement, 'One who has attained patience does not go to the miserable realms'"— that requires further consideration,
since there are statements concerning the Bodhisattvas' attainment of patience.
With the intention that [rebirth] is dependent upon karma, even the Sūtra stating that "one who has attained *kṣānti* does not go to the miserable realms" is not contradicted.
Furthermore, this must necessarily be understood;
for instance, by the command of the Blessed One, Śāriputra and others—
Elsewhere it is recited that [the Buddha], having taken Sundarananda with him, went on a tour of the hells.
Immediately following patience (*kṣānti*),
he now speaks for the purpose of the object of focus (*ālambana*) for the wholesome state of the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
"This," and so forth.

By means of that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through which no phenomena (*dharma*) are grasped, there is the meditative concentration named "Non-appropriation of All Phenomena" (*sarvadharmānupādāna*). In reality, the essential nature of this meditative concentration is such that its objects of focus (*ālambana*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so on, are not grasped—this is the connection. To the question, "In what manner are they to be taken as objects? he says:
"By this very [power]," and so forth.

Through the power of his own vows, merit, gnosis, and the *dharmadhātu*, the activity of meditative absorption proceeds effortlessly throughout all world-realms according to the capacity of beings. Thus, by way of its function, its aspect, and its object, he swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He speaks for the purpose of providing an object of focus for the intermediate [type of person],
beginning with "by the power of the Buddhas" and so forth;
this occurs in the context of the power of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, that statement was made either to illuminate a particular excellence of inspired eloquence (*pratibhāna*), or to strengthen the recollection of it among those to be trained (*vineya*).
Regarding the phrase "this one has been prophesied":

this is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that the Buddhas bestow a prophecy upon a yogin who has correctly attained meditative concentration; thus, it arises from taking as an object forms and so forth characterized by the cause of such a prophecy.
"By the Tathāgatas," and so forth.

They are called *tathāgatas* because they possess the perfection of the welfare of others by virtue of teaching the Dharma in all its aspects without error. They are called *arhats* because they possess the perfection of their own welfare through the abandonment of the afflictive obscurations and the obscurations to the knowable, together with their latent predispositions (*savāsanā*).

They are "Perfectly Awakened" (sambuddha) because they have realized the path that brings about the two kinds of perfect accomplishment. By what [means] does one reach this? By means of the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (madhyāgradharma).
To the question of in what aspect it is to be taken as an object, he says:
"He does not perceive even that," and so forth:
he does not perceive it with a non-conceptual mind,
nor does he conceive of it with a conceptual mind, because it is non-existent in reality.

"I am concentrated" refers to one who has attained meditative absorption (*samādhi*). "I shall attain [absorption]" and so forth refer to the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) occurring during the preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent stages, or those existing throughout the three times.
Regarding the phrase "by all" and so on:
"For these two 'all-nesses' (*sarvate*) consist of the all-ness of things (*vastu-sarvatā*)."

Because of the statement, "the totality of all," every object of conceptualization— such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth— is a thing characterized by all distinctions of past objects and the like.
This applies in every way, even in the most subtle manner.
"All" means every kind along with its latent predispositions (*savāsana*).

It does not exist because all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are untenable for a bodhisattva who has realized the true nature of meditative absorption (*samādhi*); since no cognition such as "I am absorbed" arises, it is impossible due to the cultivation [of the path] by way of the aspect of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
He speaks for the sake of the object of the superior [level]:
"By which concentration, O Venerable Subhūti," and so forth;
that is, by means of that which has reached the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) of the superior level.
"It is possible to demonstrate that samādhi"—the meaning is:
is it by way of the seclusion (*viveka*) of bodhisattvas and so forth?
In some places, the reading is "by which [means]? (*katamena*).
In this regard, it should be considered that the statement of the questioner himself—that "this samādhi can be demonstrated"—is inconsistent.
The reply beginning with "No, indeed" (no hīdam) follows.

The meaning is: "Not at all," because by the very nature of things (dharmatā), the triad consisting of the samādhi, the bodhisattva, and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) possesses a single, mutually identical form; thus, since they cannot be shown separately, there is no such thing as an object of focus characterized by distinct forms and so forth.
But how is it that, even while being cultivated, it cannot be shown?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?", he provides the answer by demonstrating its nature:
By the words "that too" and so forth:

since all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are non-existent, the non-conceptualization of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is the supreme means. Because it takes as its object the aspect of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one does not know that absorption; because there is no basis for proximity with a formless mind, one does not perceive it.
This is because [perception] occurs even in dreams and the like in the absence of a real entity, provided there is a mental aspect (*sākāra*).
The word "also" (api) implies that it is not only the mental aspect (ākāra); the sense is that perception as a specific "this-ness" (idantayā) is dependent upon conceptual construction (vikalpa).
When there is the non-perception of everything, the cultivation of the relationship between the object to be cultivated and the cultivator [ceases].
With the intention that [the thing] is not logically possible, Śāriputra said, "He does not know," and so forth.
Thinking that there is no fault from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), Subhūti said,
"He does not know," and so forth.
Regarding that very intention,
having raised the doubt, "For what reason?", he says:
"Because of its non-existence."
The word "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
However, the [application of] practice and so forth belongs to the illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*) due to the force of previous momentum (*pūrvāvedha*); such is the underlying intention.
He speaks for the sake of expressing approval because his statement does not contradict the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"Excellent," and so forth.
It appears to you because of the arising of a cognition in which that [object] manifests;
you teach it to others by describing that which is its objective support.
And the phrase "and thus here," etc., is the conclusion.
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
The meaning is that it is precisely in this way that [the stage] here is conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
But how, one might ask, should one train in this sequence?
Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason?", he says:
"For in this way," and so forth.

In the perfection of wisdom, which has the nature of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), there is that which is called the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*agradharma*). This is threefold, being the supreme among all mundane phenomena by virtue of its objects and aspects.
Thus it has been said:
His activity is meditative concentration; his prophecy is the non-exhaustion of mentation. ||33||
"The intrinsic nature of the threefold [perception] is the non-conceptuality of meditative concentration;
thus are the stages conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) categorized as weak, medium, and intense. This has been stated.

Thus, having performed the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and possessing a concentrated mind, while cultivating the selflessness of all phenomena, when—due to the absence of adherence to objects as being separate entities—one possesses a slightly clear light of knowledge...
When one perceives only the mind alone,
that is his stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata);
this very state is called the samādhi known as "Attainment of Light" (ālokālambha) in the Mahāyāna.

When, for the sake of increasing that very light of Dharma, there arises a medium-clear light of knowledge through the exertion of vigor in the cultivation of selflessness, that is the stage of the "Summits" (mūrdhan).
That itself is the meditative concentration called "Increased Light" (vṛddhāloka).
But when, through abiding in mind-only, there arises a clearer light of knowledge characterized by the absence of adherence to external objects,
that is the stage of *kṣānti* (receptivity).
Because one has entered into the absence of the aspect of the apprehended object, it is called the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) known as "having entered into one part of the reality-object."
When, moreover, the light of knowledge arises without the appearance of distractions that grasp at objects, that is the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
That itself is the concentration called "Uninterrupted" (*ānantarya-samādhi*).
All these stages, due to firm resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),
are called the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*).
And a bodhisattva abiding in this stage is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Ratnamegha* that [the Bodhisattva] has transcended all calamities of the foolish and is endowed with qualities such as incalculable samādhis, dhāraṇīs, liberations, and superknowledges. Having thus indicated the specific nature of the objects, aspects, and causes of the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), he now states the first conceptualization of the apprehended (*grāhyavikalpa*), which has all things as its basis, for the purpose of explaining the association with the four types of conceptualization.
"Training in this way," and so forth.
The sense is: "Why [is he training]?
With the intention that he trains by means of the conventional truth of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti*), he says:
"Training in this way," and so forth.
Not yet understanding the Blessed One’s intention, Śāriputra asks:
"In reality, in which dharma does one train?"

In that regard, because conceptualization based on the mere thing as its locus entails error, the Blessed One said from the perspective of ultimate reality that "one does not train in any dharma whatsoever.
To the question, "Even while training, how is it that one does not train?
and anticipating the inquiry, "For what reason?", he says:

"Not indeed," and so forth: they are called "fools" because of their association with defiled phenomena (*sāṃkleśika-dharma*), and "ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*) because of their lack of purified phenomena (*vaiyavadānika-dharma*).
Furthermore, because they are devoid of faith in such phenomena and of extensive learning (*bāhuśrutya*), they are "those who have not heard."
He thinks as follows: just as those who are attached perceive things as existing through the power of the conceptual construction of ignorance, so they do not truly exist;
therefore, those who train conventionally do not train in reality.
If they do not exist in that way,
then by implication they must exist otherwise; and since there is a fault due to the apprehension of them as real entities, he says this with that intention.
"How then," and so forth.
Because the error regarding active engagement has been eliminated, they do not exist in the manner in which they were adhered to.
Even though it was stated in that way, he says that nevertheless, they do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*).
"Yathā" and so forth:
just as they do not exist according to reasoning (*nyāya*), so too do they exist conventionally (*saṃvṛti*) by virtue of being delightful only when left unexamined.
"Existence itself is what is meant by 'being existent'—this is the meaning.
The phrase "in this way," and so forth, constitutes the conclusion.

Since [the object] is thus non-existent, for that reason, according to the etymological rule (*nairukta-vidhāna*), the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) cognition of the contrary is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*) because it is non-knowledge (*ajñāna*); by this, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of ignorance is expressed.
He says "those," and so forth, for the purpose of distinguishing the aggregates such as form; by means of taking the mere thing as their basis, all conceptual constructions are bound to them.
In order to indicate that they are connected, the connection with what precedes has been stated.
This should be understood in the same way for what follows as well.
To the question "How are they attached? he says:
"By them," and so forth.

All phenomena (*sarvadharma*), such as the aggregates (*skandha*) of form and the rest, do not exist in reality; they are superimposed through conceptual construction (*vikalpanā*) due to unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), and are thus "imagined" (*kalpita*).
For the purpose of explaining the conceptualization of attachment to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), he says:
"Having conceptualized those [things]," and so forth.

Those who are attached to the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism [conceptualize] those dharmas such as name-and-form and the conceptualizations of attachment to them; because an eternal thing lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), [they do so] conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*).
They do not know that [these things] are indeed eternal through worldly knowledge consisting of hearing and so forth.
Due to ignorance, they previously imagined [them to exist], but later, when the true nature of reality is determined,
if they do not find even existence, how then could there be non-existence?

Thus, by means of such cultivation, they do not perceive [them] through supramundane wisdom; therefore, although all phenomena such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) do not exist in reality, they conceptualize them through the power of their attachment to them.
To explain the conceptualization that consists in clinging to the two extremes, it is said: "Having conceptualized, they adhere to the two extremes."
The meaning is: "due to the conceptualization of attachment to that.
He says "having become attached," and so forth, for the purpose of explaining the conceptualization regarding affliction and purification through ignorance.

Relying upon the cause of dogmatic adherence— that is, the apprehension of signs— and having made them into signs, they conceptualize phenomena from the past up to the present through the power of conceptualization that is ignorant of the true nature of phenomena pertaining to both the defiled and the purified.
He speaks in order to clarify the meaning of the conceptualization that does not abide in the noble path.
"Having conceptualized name-and-form (nāmarūpa), they are attached"—
the meaning is that this is due to their attachment to not abiding in the path of vision and so forth.
In that context, "name" refers to the formless aggregates such as sensation and so forth,
while "form" refers to the aggregate of form.
He speaks for the purpose of [explaining] the conceptualization of apprehension:
"All phenomena are imagined by them as non-existent.
The meaning is: because of their attachment to that apprehension.
He speaks for the sake of refuting the conceptualization of a self and so forth:
"Those [things] being non-existent," and so on.
When there is a self, there is the notion of another.
From the distinction between self and other arise attachment and aversion;
all afflictions are produced when bound by these two.

Thus, due to their attachment to a self and so forth, they do not know and do not see, as previously described, the path— consisting of vision and the rest— which is non-erroneous and characterized by the selflessness of phenomena and persons;
he speaks [next] for the sake of [eliminating] conceptual constructions regarding purification, arising, and so forth.
"Not knowing the path as it truly is" means they do not depart, they do not go forth,
from the saṃsāra of the three realms.
Because they do not awaken, and so forth;
due to their adherence to [notions of] purity, arising, and so on, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the truth in the sense of being supreme.
For that reason, they receive and obtain the designation and number of "fools" (*bāla*).

The second conceptualization of the object of apprehension (*grāhyavikalpa*) is stated as being based on the entity that serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣavastvadhiṣṭhāna*), beginning with the words, "They do not have faith in the true Dharma. Because they lack the experience of its own nature due to a perverted practice— namely, through the application of conceptual adherence to that true Dharma which is the characteristic of the antidote and possesses the sense of being non-perverted— they do not have faith in it, nor would they resolve upon it.
By means of the method of negation (*vyatireka*), he explains precisely the contrary apprehension with the words "Furthermore, not... and so forth.
The phrase "some dharma pertaining to purification" implies [the absence of] the conceptual construction of an object of apprehension (*grāhya-vikalpa*).
And thus, due to the distinction of its objects, it becomes ninefold.
Namely: the conceptualization of the meaning of a heap, and the conceptualization of the meaning of a door of arrival.
The conceptualization of the meaning of the lineage;
the conceptualization of the meaning of arising;
the conceptualization of the meaning of emptiness.
The conceptualization of the meaning of the perfections;
the conceptualization of the path of seeing;
the conceptualization of the path of cultivation.
Regarding the conceptualization of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*):
it has been said as follows:
"The conceptualization of the object of apprehension (*grāhyakalpa*) is twofold, by way of the entity itself and its antidote."
"Each of these is ninefold, through the divisions of the mass of delusion (*moha-rāśi*) and so forth.

(35) Thus, in this context, the first conceptualization of the apprehended (*grāhya-vikalpa*) has all things as its object, while the second has only the objects of purification (*vyavadāna-vastu*) as its object; this is the distinction between these two conceptualizations of the apprehended.
And having established it thus, it is said:
"That which is the first conceptualization of the apprehended, the second is also that"— this is a *pūrvapādaka* (prior-member-based) [inference].
Whatever is the first, that indeed is the second.

For example, some maintain that the first conceptualization of the apprehended (*grāhya-vikalpa*) pertains to all things, whereas the second pertains only to the second [category] and not the first; that is, the first conceptualization of the apprehended has purification (*vyavadāna*) alone as its basis, while the second has defilement (*saṃkleśa*) as its basis. Others hold that the first has defiled things as its basis and the second has purified things as its basis, and that the distinction between these two arises from their being mutually exclusive in nature.

He states the first conceptualization of the object of apprehension (*grāhya-vikalpa*), which has the person as a substantial entity (*pudgala-dravya-adhiṣṭhāna*), with the words beginning "In this way" (*evam*). The meaning is:

by training in this manner according to the sequence just described, one does not engage in the two types of conceptualization of the object of apprehension; what, then, is the use of the first conceptualization?
"Because the obscuration of conceptual construction is equal," [the opponent says].
The Blessed One said, "He does not train";
the word "in reality" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
However, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), he says "training in this way" and so forth, because for a beginner,
such training would otherwise be impossible.
The three phrases beginning with "one trains in omniscience" (sarvajñatāyāṃ śikṣate) are to be understood as referring respectively to the stages of application (prayoga) and so forth.
Thus, due to the distinction of its objects, it becomes ninefold.
For example:
The conceptualization of a self as independent;
the conceptualization of a self as unitary;
the conceptualization of a self as a cause.
The conceptualization of a self as the seer and so forth;
the conceptualization of a self as the basis of affliction;
the conceptualization of a self as the basis of detachment.
The conceptualization of a self as the basis for the path of seeing;
the conceptualization of a self as the basis for the path of cultivation;
and the conceptualization of a self as the basis for one who has accomplished their purpose.
The second conceptualization of a grasper has as its basis a person who is a mere designation. Regarding that conceptualization, he speaks by way of raising an objection and providing a resolution,
beginning with the words, "O Blessed One," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: if one insists that the person (*puruṣa*) who is the grasper is merely a conceptual construct (*prājñaptika*), then because it consists of a false appearance, the person is of the nature of an illusion (*māyāsvabhāva*), and thus the "illusory person" is merely a conceptual construct. In that case, the training would apply to him as well; yet, since he is insentient, even if there is no full comprehension, liberation would be achieved without effort for everyone simply by virtue of the training applying to all. With this intention, how could one provide an answer to someone who says "he who... and so forth? That is the sense.
Since the nature of the false appearance of forms and so forth is common [to all], and since there is no other possible state, one should train like an illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*).
With the intention that liberation is not achieved without effort, he says:
"For by that," and so on.
Since you ask thus, I shall therefore question you in return regarding this very inquiry; I shall make a counter-question.
"Excellent," and so forth:
having accepted it by saying, "Excellent indeed, Blessed One," [the interlocutor continues].
Thus he heard from the presence of the Blessed One;
he had heard it.
To explain how he heard it in this way, he says:
"Bhagavān," and so forth;
he spoke while dismissing [the question],
saying "No," and so forth.
It is not at all different from that, Blessed One, because that illusion is not other than it;
nor is that form and so forth other than it.
Form and so forth are themselves illusion, and illusion itself is form and so forth.

The sense is that since these two are, in reality, devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) due to being destitute of a nature that is either one or many, they are identical in their form as false appearances.
Having established the identity between the form of an illusion and so forth, he says [the following] in order to demonstrate that one should train like an illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*).
"What do you think regarding this? and so forth.

"In this context, among these five aggregates of clinging which are like an illusion, the designation 'Bodhisattva' is the grasping of a sign (*nimitta*). The cognition that 'I am endowed with a real entity' is *samajñā* (conventional knowledge)."

Ārya Vimuktisena states: "Designation (*prajñapti*) is the manifestation of the adherence to the modes of the grasped and the grasper regarding the object of knowledge and the knowledge itself; conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) is the linguistic usage concerning various objects, whether appropriated or unappropriated by others."

In the stage of the lineage (*gotra*), the designation "bodhisattva" is merely a designation. In the stage of the generation of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*), one knows; thus, that which has a mind that is equal knowledge (*sama-jña*) as its cause for engagement is this very "equal designation" (*samajñā*). This is a designation based on the equal knowledge of all sentient beings, because in the seven stages of application, there is the penetration of the fact that all phenomena are mere designations (*prajñaptimātra*).

The Venerable Vimuktisena states: "Because on the eighth [ground] and onwards, one attains the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*) regarding signs, it is called 'conventional' (*vyavahāra*) merely as a conventional designation (*vyavahāramātra*) for that which is expressible.
This is because a bodhisattva distinct from form and so forth is logically untenable.
He says "evam etat" and so forth for the purpose of formal acceptance.
The repetition is used out of urgency.
The passage beginning with "Therefore, indeed" is the conclusion.

Since this is so, for that reason, because there is no other alternative, just as cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is produced by the illusion of karma, likewise even supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*) are produced by the illusion of gnosis (*jñāna-māyā*). Thus, through the yoga of non-attachment, it is established that one should train for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksambodhi*) like an illusory person (*māyā-puruṣa*).
Furthermore, liberation is not achieved without effort; for the point is that it is only when reality is known that it brings about liberation, not when it remains unknown.
[An objection is raised: "If there is only the illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*), how can there be the systematic distinction between affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*)?
Anticipating this question with "For what reason?", he says:
"Indeed, that very [thing], etc.
refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), namely,
the contaminated forms and so forth.
The phrase “the five aggregates” should be supplied [to complete the sense]: “for the sake of grasping the five uncontaminated aggregates.
The point is that the establishment of affliction and purification occurs exactly according to how things appear, even though they are like an illusory person.
But how is it that [all things] are like an illusion?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?", he says,
"For instance," and so forth.
Even when a matter has already been stated, if it is raised again under a different aspect, it is not a repetition;
thus, the fault of tautology should not be pointed out.
This should be understood to apply in all cases.
"It was said by the Blessed One.

Here, immediately following the statement that the designation "Bodhisattva" applies to these five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), the Blessed One stated that form and so forth are like an illusion.
The six faculties, beginning with the eye, are accompanied by consciousness and their respective objects; this is the remainder [of the sense].
Immediately following this, he will state: "Those are the five aggregates.
That which is consciousness is the six sense-faculties, because it is cognition itself that appears in their form.
And the six sense faculties are to be understood as before. Thus, the conceptualization of a grasper based on a person who is a mere designation has been explained.
And that, according to the distinctions of its objects, becomes ninefold; namely, the conceptualization of the designation of the aggregates (*skandha*).
The conceptual construction of the designation of the sense-bases; the conceptual construction of the designation of the elements;
the conceptual construction of the designation of dependent origination.
The conceptualization of the designation of purification;
the conceptualization of the designation of the path of seeing;
the conceptualization of the designation of the path of cultivation.
The conceptualization of the designation of the path of distinction;
the conceptualization of the designation of the path of no-more-learning.
And so it has been said:
"The grasper is considered to be twofold, having as its basis both substantial entities and designations;
[the former] in the form of an independent self and so forth, and [the latter] by way of reliance upon the aggregates and so forth.

(36) Having thus pointed out the combination of the four types of conceptual construction, he now speaks, while explaining "thorough acquisition" whose nature consists of skillful means and the spiritual friend:
"O Blessed One, not so," and so forth. "Those who have newly set out in the vehicle" means those who have recently entered the Mahāyāna.
"Imam" means distinguished by specific qualities such as profundity, magnificence, and the object of focus.
"They will be terrified," and so forth; therein, "unfounded fear" (*utrāsa*) is like taking a wrong path.
*Santrāsa* is terror (*trāsa*) occurring as a continuous stream;
it arises because the fear that has already emerged is not dispelled.
*Santrāsāpatti* is the arrival at a state of certain conviction regarding that terror.
"Fallen into the hands of evil friends" means:

one who, without making a distinction between the conventional and the ultimate, suddenly teaches non-arising and so forth by attempting to negate the perception [of phenomena] that has been practiced for an infinite time, is an "evil friend" because he is the cause of the sin of rejecting the true Dharma, which results in rebirth in the hells and other miserable states.
To have "fallen into his hands" means to have reached a state of being susceptible to his grasp.
He says that a matter stated by way of negation (vyatireka) becomes firmly established when it is further stated by way of affirmation (anvaya).

"Having come into the hands of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). This means, as before, that they have come into the hands of a spiritual friend— one who is free from qualities such as stinginess, who teaches the selflessness of all phenomena and so forth, and who leads one to the fruits of the happy realms and so on— by means of skillful methods (*upāyakauśalya*) such as ensuring the mind is neither dejected nor terrified, and by announcing the death of the beloved queen to the king according to the [disciple's] disposition.

With the words beginning with "Whom," there is a question concerning the nature of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). He states the answer with the words beginning with "Whoever [sees] him," and so forth.

Those individuals who, without transgressing either the conventional or the ultimate truth, instruct and advise this person—Devadatta and others—so that they may attain benefit through the perfections such as generosity, as previously described;
and those who teach Devadatta and others regarding the deeds of Māra so that they may avoid what is harmful—how do they do so? He says:
"Thus," and so forth.

In this way, the faults of Māra—the obstacles of Māra—consist in approaching in the guise of a Buddha and asking, "What do you have to do with unsurpassed enlightenment? thereby causing one to analyze matters that pertain to the future.

"These are the faults of Māra; why then do you engage in such practices as writing the *Prajñāpāramitā*?"—this is the discernment of the present situation. By the power of severing those [faults], he speaks for the purpose of the action of accepting and abandoning in due order, beginning with "In this way, regarding the works of Māra," and so forth, and then states what the task of a Buddha is.
The phrase "by you" and so forth [is the beginning];
"these" and so forth is the conclusion;
and [the phrase] "of one girt with the great armor."

For one who is endowed with the practice of armor (*sannāhapratipatti*) to be described below, who has set out in the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna-saṃprasthita*), and who is likewise possessed of the practice of setting forth (*prasthānapratipatti*), he is said to have "mounted" the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna-samārūḍha*).
By that very [practice], he has ascended the Great Vehicle;
for it is held that one first sets out by means of that [armor-practice] and subsequently mounts [the vehicle].
And so it has been said:
"The teaching on the lack of intrinsic nature and so forth, as well as the absence of mental despondency and so forth;
the abandonment of their opposites and the complete embracing [of these qualities]. (37)

Based on the Blessed One’s own statement that “a sūtra must be explained in accordance with other sūtras,” and following the method of exposition by the former masters such as Vasubandhu according to the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*, and in conformity with the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-kārikā*, one should supply implicit words (*bhāvādhyāhāra*) and so forth; and likewise, since even a general term functions in a specific sense through the force of context and other factors, and because words function in accordance with the intended meaning— which is not in contradiction with the teaching— therefore, in refuting [that unintended sense],...
And because it is based on the absence of an explicit statement [to the contrary], this has been explained strictly in accordance with the text.
Therefore, one should not think: "How can this explanation be something that does not follow the text?
Otherwise, if this principle were not adopted, there would be no such thing as an explanation of the teaching at all.
Because words are conventional, there arises doubt regarding the adoption of a specific meaning when they have multiple possible referents.
Furthermore, this commentary must be accepted as authoritative because it was written by Ārya-Asaṅga and others;
for it is so heard.

Although the noble Asaṅga had understood the entire meaning of the scriptures and attained realization, he was nonetheless unable to discern the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā*— due to the abundance of repetitions, the lack of clear demarcation between individual words even in non-repetitive sections, and its profound depth— and having fallen into despondency, the Blessed One Maitreya [addressed him] with reference to that.
The *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* has been explained and the treatise consisting of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-kārikās* has been composed.
Having heard that, it was further commented upon by Ārya Asaṅga, the Master Vasubandhu, and others; enough of this digression.

Immediately following the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), there is for one who possesses practice another [path], such as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) as previously described. Thus, indicating the basis of practice (*pratipatterādhāra*) which has the nature of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), he says:

"That which the Blessed One has said thus," and so forth— this is what has been stated. Namely, that which the Blessed One spoke beginning with "of the bodhisattva mahāsattva," and that which is called "mahāsattva" in other sūtras.

In that regard, since the Buddha-qualities have the *dharmadhātu* as their intrinsic nature within the preceding statement and those other sūtras, what is the meaning of "basis" (*pratiṣṭhārtha*) and what is the referent (*padārtha*) of the term "bodhisattva"?
To state the answer, he says:
"It has no referent," and so forth.
The referent of the term "Bodhisattva" regarding the Buddha-qualities is the referent of the term "Bodhisattva"; that, in reality, is a non-referent,
a referent of non-abiding.
This refers to the lineage (*gotra*).
Since liberation is impossible without realization, how can a Bodhisattva—who realizes the qualities of a Buddha—be something that is not a real entity? Anticipating this question, he says:
"Of all dharmas," and so forth.

Because, when there is non-attachment toward all dharmas through the absence of clinging to things and their signs, it is impossible to attain realization otherwise; therefore, for the sake of attaining the qualities of a Buddha, one trains as an illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*).
Therefore, the sense is: how can there be a basis for reality in an ultimate sense?

However, conventionally, the Bodhisattva—the very nature of the *dharmadhātu* who serves as the support for the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*)—is designated as the "lineage" (*gotra*) through the differentiation of the various stages of the practice of the Dharma;
therein, first of all, it is the basis for the arising of the four types of mundane aids to penetration (*laukikanirvedhabhāgīya*).

Then, through the power of the arising of those two—the supramundane paths of seeing and cultivation—just as one simultaneously ejects a thief and bolts the door, there occurs the simultaneous arising of all antidotes and the cessation of all discordant factors. Then, through the non-perception of those two, there occurs the departure from conceptual constructions regarding the cessation and arising of those discordant factors and their antidotes.

Then, through the power of former vows and skill in means such as generosity, there arise wisdom and compassion, characterized by non-abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; and through the arising of those two, there arises the quality that is uncommon to the śrāvakas and others.

Then, by means of the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) such as leading [beings] into the path according to their dispositions, there is the sequence of the benefit for others characterized by establishing them in the three vehicles.
Following that is the basis for the knowledge of effortless, signless activity for the sake of others that lasts as long as saṃsāra exists.
And thus, from this sequence of realization, this is the progressive order.
And by this [verse], the exposition of the very collection of all realized dharmas in the vehicle is neither deficient nor redundant;
likewise, because the state of being the conventional basis is implied, this entire meaning—
It should be understood that [the meaning] is indeed implied within the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, the text explained in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* with respect to each object and its basis is not written here for the sake of providing proof, for fear of prolixity.
And thus it has been said:
[The nature of the path consists of] the sixfold dharma of realization, the abandonment of the opposing factors, the full utilization of those two, and wisdom together with compassion. (38)

"The lineage (*gotra*) is said to be the foundation for the uniqueness of the disciple, the sequence of the welfare of others, and the effortless occurrence of knowledge. (39) Thus, since the *dharmadhātu* alone is the cause for the realization of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*), the Bodhisattva, whose essence is that [dharmadhātu], is the naturally abiding lineage (*prakṛtistha-gotra*) of the unsurpassed Buddha-qualities; it is designated as "the true nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*).

At that time, because the *dharmadhātu* exists universally, it would not be logical to distinguish between types of lineages (*gotra*) as follows: this lineage existing in its natural state (*prakṛtistha*), which has come down from beginningless time and is obtained through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); this acquired lineage (*samudānīta*), which is obtained through the practice of previous roots of merit;

this determinate lineage of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas, because it cannot be diverted even by great conditions; and this indeterminate lineage of Śrāvakas and so forth, because it can be diverted by conditions. Such a differentiation of lineages is untenable.

Just as one might apprehend [the object] through the sequence of realization of the Śrāvakayāna and so forth, it is designated as "lineage" (*gotra*) because the *dharmadhātu* is established as the cause for the realization of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*). Alternatively, this is the meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Or rather, just as there is a distinction among vessels—such as jars—which are produced from the same material substance and baked by the same fire, based on their being containers for different contents such as honey or sugar; in the same way, the diversity of the substratum (*ādhāra*) is taught according to the diversity of the qualities to be realized (*ādheya*) subsumed within the three vehicles. Thus, there is no fault.
And so it has been said:
"Since the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is without differentiation, a distinction of lineages (gotra) is not tenable;
however, that distinction is proclaimed on account of the distinction among the qualities to be supported. (40)

As for the etymological explanation (*nirukta*), it is by way of the sense of "elevating qualities" (*guṇottāraṇa*) that the *dharmadhātu* is the lineage (*gotra*); for from it those qualities grow and arise—this is the meaning.
And having established it thus, it is said: "All noble persons (*āryapudgala*) are characterized by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."

But surely, the lineage (*gotra*) should have been mentioned at the very beginning, since the arising of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), as well as the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), are preceded by it. Why, then, was it stated thus?
True, this is the sequence of the meaning;
however, this is the sequence of exposition, wherein the effect is explained first and the cause is pointed out afterwards—thus there is no fault.

Immediately following the basis, [the author] speaks regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*) for the sake of explaining what the object of focus is for the bodhisattva who possesses the aforementioned practice as his basis.

Because, by means of the realization of all phenomena that serve as the locus of the object of focus, and through an object of focus that correctly does not transcend the two truths, there is non-attachment; when that [non-attachment] exists, one fully awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment by proceeding toward the purification of the object of focus, and not otherwise.
One is called a *bodhisattva* because, by means of the objective and purpose of awakening, one accomplishes every aspect of one’s own welfare.

In that regard, first of all, one generally analyzes all phenomena—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—in their respective order as the ascetic life, non-killing, and indeterminate bodily actions, and so forth; thus, dividing them into three types, one contemplates them as being objects for acceptance, rejection, or equanimity.

Then, he reflects further: "The five aggregates of clinging and so forth, which are comprised within the mundane path, are mundane; whereas the four dhyānas and so forth, which are comprised within the correct noble path, are supramundane.
In that regard, the mundane five aggregates of clinging and so forth are with-outflows (*sāśrava*), because they do not serve as antidotes to the grasping at a self.

However, he defines the supramundane factors—such as the foundations of mindfulness—as untainted (*anāśrava*) because they serve as the antidotes to the view of a self; thus, he distinguishes them according to what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.

Then, taking those untainted factors as the basis, he explains that the conditioned factors such as the wings of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*), which are comprised within the realms of desire and so forth and depend upon causes and conditions, exist conventionally.

One contemplates in two ways: first, that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—such as *tathatā* (thusness) and so forth—which are not included within the three realms and are independent of causes, are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);

second, that the common dharmas (*sādhāraṇadharma*), such as the four meditative absorptions (*caturdhyāna*) and so forth, which arise from the mental continua of all noble beings, are manifested by the unconditioned.

One meditates in two ways on the uncommon qualities, such as the ten powers, which are the dharmas arising from the continuum of a perfectly enlightened Buddha; thus, through this sequence of realization, all phenomena are perceived exactly as they are in their illusory nature. This is to be known as the elevenfold object of focus (*ālambana*).
Since this is clearly established in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*—the treatise that sets forth the sequence of objects of focus as previously described—one should not entertain any misconception.
Thus it has been said:
"The objects of focus are all phenomena; furthermore, these are the wholesome and so forth."
And those known as mundane realizations, as well as those considered supramundane; ||41||
“Those phenomena which are with outflows and without outflows, those which are conditioned and unconditioned,
those phenomena shared with the disciples and those which are unique to the Sage. (42) However,

as for those who maintain that the object of focus (*ālambana*) is solely the *dharmadhātu*— which is eternally pure and non-dual— they must explain how there can be a progression toward ever-increasing excellence of purity, given its eternal purity.

If it is argued that "purity is maintained as being like the purity of the water element, gold, or space," then, in that case, by the very insistence on the thesis that "pure knowledge is ultimate reality," there is an implication of an adherence to its opposite.
Consequently, because there is no abandonment of the conceptualization of both the opposing side and its antidote, the undesirable consequence follows that purity would be merely partial.

But if it is asked: "In your position, Subhūti, since the non-existence of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the objective support (*ālambana*), how can there be a culmination of the objective support?"—
there is no fault here.
Since there is no entity that conforms to logical reasoning, non-existence is likewise called "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*).
And for this [conventional reality], whose true nature is concealed, its purification consists precisely in the gradual realization of its similarity to an illusion.
And having established it thus, the lineage (*gotra*) has the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as its primary element.

"The object of focus (*ālambana*) consists primarily of the transformation (*vikṛti*), whereas both [the basis and the object] are unprohibited in both cases; thus is the distinction between the characteristics of the basis (*ādhāra*) and the object.
Furthermore, the systematic determination of the object is a matter for much discussion, so enough of this digression," says Ārya Vimuktisena.
Immediately following the object of focus, what is the objective of the bodhisattva’s practice toward that object? To explain this objective, he says:
"Furthermore," and so forth; for what reason, for what purpose, is a bodhisattva called a "great being" (mahāsattva)?
He speaks in order to state the reply, beginning with "of the great," and so forth.
"Of the great" refers to a mass of sentient beings; that is, a general designation for an immeasurable multitude of living beings.
The term "mass" (*rāśi*) is used because even a single being becomes "great" due to the vastness of the activity of beginningless saṃsāra.

The phrase "of the multitude of beings" (*sattvanikāyasya*) is a specific designation for those comprised within the commonality of sentient beings (*sattvasabhāga*), which excludes heterogeneous entities by distinguishing between the various classes such as those who have entered the path (*pratipannaka*) and those who abide in the fruits (*phalastha*). [He] will cause them to attain preeminence.

The greatness of the mind consisting in being supreme among all beings: having realized that [greatness] because he has set out with that as his objective, he will subsequently bring about supremacy for those beings who desire to attain it by means of teaching the Dharma and so forth.
"In that sense" means: for that reason, a Bodhisattva is a Mahāsattva because he possesses such a great mind.
When there is greatness of mind, the abandonment is great.
To demonstrate the greatness of abandonment, Śāriputra says "It is mine too," and so forth, seeking permission by way of dependence on his teacher.
"O Blessed One, that meaning appears clearly to me;
by which meaning a bodhisattva is called a 'great being' (mahāsattva)—this is the sense of the sentence.
The word "also" (api) implies that this is not only [the view] of the Blessed One.
He states the meaning of the permission: "May it occur," and so forth. This refers to whatever matter you now consider to be appropriate, timely, or the right occasion for explanation.
"May that meaning shine forth clearly; may it become manifest. Having received permission from the Great One (Mahāmāyā), he spoke these words, beginning with "labdhānujñaḥ.
In this context, the term *ātman* refers to the sense of being the substratum of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*).
Because egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is established in this [basis], it is called "self" (*ātman*).

Because it has the nature of perishing, yet persists by the power of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) until the completion of its homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), it is called a "living being" (*sattva*).
Furthermore, because it repeatedly dissolves (*līyate*) into the realms of existence (*gati*), it is called a "person" (*pudgala*).
That which manifests is "existence" (bhava); that which disappears is "non-existence" (vibhava);
and the notion that "it does not exist now, though it existed previously" is "annihilation" (uccheda).
"That which exists by way of its own intrinsic nature does not not exist"—this is the eternalist view.
The perception of the five aggregates in the form of "self" and "mine" is one's own body;
such are the views beginning with these.

He will teach the Dharma for the sake of abandoning— and thereby relinquishing along with their latent tendencies— the views headed by those already mentioned, such as the adherence to false rules and observances (*mithyā-śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*), which have the nature of being an attachment to the mode of investigating phenomena such as a self;
the sense is that he will do so having attained the greatness of abandonment and realization.
Otherwise, for one whose reality to be attained is beyond perception, "its explanation is indeed difficult.
The word *iti* has the sense of "therefore"; [it refers to] one who is distinguished in the abandonment of all defects such as passion and so forth.
"Attainment" (*adhigama*) refers to the greatness of attainment; he states this in the same way.
Regarding the phrase "a Bodhisattva, a Mahāsattva," O Blessed One, the word "even" (*api*) implies that it is not only something else [that is so called].
"Bodhicitta" means the mind directed toward enlightenment; that is to say, the mind consisting of aspiration and application.

The "mind of omniscience" is the mind inclined toward omniscience, which is characterized by resolute conviction and is comprised within the stage of conduct through conviction (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*).

The "undefiled mind" is attained through the penetration of non-conceptual supramundane gnosis; it belongs to the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśayika*) on the seven stages of application (*prayogabhūmi*). The "unequaled mind," which flows effortlessly and without signs, is the "resultant mind" (*vaipākika*) on the eighth stage and beyond.
The mind that is equal and identical to the peerless Buddhas is the "unequaled-equal" (*asamasama*) mind; it is free from all obscurations and has reached the stage of a Buddha.
Alternatively, the mind that has become of the same nature as awakening (*bodhi*), whose form is non-arising (*anutpāda*), is the *bodhicitta*.

And that very same [mind] is designated in four ways according to the conventional perspective of yogis, in connection with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and so forth, through certain transformations: as the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatācitta*), and so on.
All of this is also uncommon and inaccessible to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
even toward such a mind, which is of great significance and worthy of partiality, he remains unattached.
By the statement "not adhering, not included, and not abiding," the greatness of realization is made known.
The word "also" (*api*) implies that this is even more so in other cases.
Having raised the doubt— "How can these two [non-attachment and non-abiding] exist, since cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is impossible without attachment and abiding?"—
he says, beginning with "For it is thus" (*tathāhi*), etc., to explain the reason for this.

Because that omniscient mind just mentioned—which is intended to characterize all previously mentioned minds, which serves as the antidote to attachment, which is untainted (*anāśrava*), which belongs to the side of stability, and which is non-included—is therefore a cultivation like that of an illusory person; such is the meaning. The conclusion beginning with "even that" [is stated] regarding its state of being untainted.
Since there is the actual existence of things, [the claim that] non-attachment and so forth are untenable is addressed by the question, "For what reason? and so on.
He states this for the sake of the subsequent response.
"Because it is without mind" means because it is unarisen in reality.
The passage beginning with "Śāriputra said" up to "you have explained what was taught as the foremost" has been explained.
Since this was introduced by way of a different subject matter, the fault of tautology does not apply.
And thus the Master Diṅnāga said:
"That very same object is repeated by relying on a different meaning.
Accordingly, it should be understood that the threefold objective of practice for a bodhisattva has been taught through its similarity to the objective of victory over the unconquered.
What is the difference between the object (*ālambana*) and the goal (*uddeśa*)? The object is immediate and proximate,
whereas the goal is pertaining to the future and remote.
Ārya Vimuktisena says: "By way of the analogy between the aiming of an arrow and the piercing of the target.
And so it has been said:

This objective of the Self-Existent Ones is to be understood through three greatnesses: [the greatness of] being supreme among all sentient beings, [the greatness of] not abandoning the mind [of awakening], and [the greatness of] the threefold attainment. (43) Thus.
Immediately following the enumeration, the practice for its accomplishment must now be explained.
And that [practice] has, in general, the pure dharmas as its basis within the threefold scope of omniscience,
beginning with the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*) and so forth, which are fourfold.
In each realization during the process of realization, practice (*pratipatti*) consists of activity based upon the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
It does not exist as an activity within the realization of the *dharmakāya*, because activity is impossible therein as it is the fruit itself.

In this context, the practice of armor (*sannāha-pratipatti*) and the practice of setting out (*prasthāna-pratipatti*) are, respectively, by way of succession and directly, of the nature of application (*prayoga*), and are comprised within the stages of equipment (*sambhāra*) and the stage of conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

The practice of the accumulations (*sambhārapratipatti*), beginning with compassion and ending with the *dhāraṇīs*, is comprised of the supreme mundane dharmas (*adhimātra-agradharma*) which constitute the nature of the direct path of application (*sākṣāt-prayogamārga*).
The practice of the accumulations that has the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), as its nature consists of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

And the practice of the accumulations that has the second stage and those following as its essence consists of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the nature of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*); thus, it pertains to both paths.
"Niryanapratipatti (the practice of departure) is based upon the path of cultivation," says Ārya Asaṅga.

Thus, among the practices characterized by the nature of the paths of preparation, seeing, and cultivation— namely, the equipment of armor, setting out, provisions, and departure— it is the practice of armor that is [discussed here] by way of its form as vigor.
To demonstrate the first [case], he says:
"Then indeed, the Venerable," and so forth.
"Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra" means either that Pūrṇa himself has "Maitrāyaṇīputra" as another name, or that he is the son of his mother Maitrāyaṇī; thus he is Maitrāyaṇīputra.
"Yadidam" means "this very thing" immediately following.
"Girded with the great armor" means endowed with the practice of donning the armor.
And this is the practice of armor implied by its meaning:
namely, for a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of generosity, there is the armor of the perfection of generosity through the giving of the gift of Dharma and so forth;
and for that same [bodhisattva], there is the armor of the perfection of ethical discipline through the complete avoidance of the mental orientations of the śrāvakas and others.

The armor of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā-sannāha*) consists of his endurance, delighting in, and investigating all phenomena through the lens of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), while enduring unpleasant speech from all people. The armor of the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā-sannāha*) consists of generating aspiration and so forth for the sake of the progressive increase of those very same roots of virtue.

The armor of the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā-sannāha*) consists of focusing the mind one-pointedly on the object of dedicating those roots of virtue toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment, with a mind unmixed with other vehicles.

Because, by maintaining the perception of that very [act] as an illusion, there is the non-apprehension of the gift, the giver, and the recipient, this is called the "armor of the perfection of wisdom. Thus, this is the first set of six perfections of the armor-like practice;
likewise, for one practicing that very same [path] in the perfection of ethical discipline, it is the second;
in the perfection of patience, the third.
The fourth [perfection] is in the perfection of vigor,
the fifth in the perfection of meditation,
and the sixth belongs to that very same one who courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, these constitute six groups of six.
Because of the sixfold commonality of the armors and because of their commonality with generosity and the other perfections, they are designated as the "six practices of armor."

Furthermore, in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*, within the exposition of the practice of armor (*sannāhapratipatti*), the six groups of six [perfections] beginning with generosity are clearly found; thus, one should not entertain any misconception.
Therein, at the outset, out of indifference toward enjoyments, one undertakes ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Being a protector of ethical discipline, one becomes patient (*kṣama*).

One who is unable to endure weariness applies energy; through the departure of indolence, one accomplishes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); having perfected meditative concentration, one attains supramundane wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, there is an exposition of generosity and the other perfections according to their sequential realization.
This very sequence is well-known.
And so it has been said:
"In each of their sixfold [perfections] beginning with generosity, that which consists in their summary..."
"That practice of armor is explained by six sets of six as previously stated" (44).
Having thus described the one who has donned the armor, he speaks of the second practice, the "practice of setting out," saying:
"one who has set out in the Mahāyāna and one who has mounted the Mahāyāna."

Since the word *yāna* (vehicle) functions as both an object (*karman*) and an instrument (*karaṇa*), one first sets out (*samprasthita*) by means of the practice of setting forth (*prasthānapratipatti*) toward the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, which consists of cause and fruit.

Subsequently, through the attainment of ever-higher distinctions, one has "mounted the Mahāyāna" (*mahāyānasamārūḍha*). These two terms [therefore] constitute the practice of setting forth, which is implied by the meaning [of the word *yāna*].

That is to say: first, by means of the signs and marks of one's own form through the stabilization of the mind, there is the establishment and commencement of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Then, for one whose mind has become stabilized, there is the practice of merit and knowledge;
that is, the commencement of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) through the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*), such as the gift, the giver, and the recipient.

Then, for one who has accumulated merit and wisdom, there is "resolute conviction in reality" (*tattvādhimokṣa*); this is the setting out upon the Noble Path (*āryamārgaprasthāna*), which consists of the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the special path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaviśeṣamārga*).

Following that, for one who is inclined toward the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is the "benefit of others according to their disposition"; this is the setting out upon the four immeasurables (*caturapramāṇa*), such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth.

Then, for one engaged in the welfare of others, apprehension is bondage; thus there is the practice of the yoga of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Then, for one possessing the yoga of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), how can there be activity? Thus there is the practice of the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-viśuddhi*) everywhere, through the non-apprehension of action, agent, and activity, like a magically created person (*māyā-puruṣa*). Therefore, for one whose conduct is thus purified, there is effort toward one's own goal; thus there is the practice of the threefold objective, such as the greatness of mind consisting in being foremost among all sentient beings.

Then, for one who has made the effort to designate [the objects], there is vigor regarding the full knowledge of the minds of others and so forth; this is the undertaking of the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*), such as the divine eye.

Then, for one who has attained the superknowledges, there is enthusiasm for Buddhahood; this constitutes the undertaking of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus, according to the sequence of realization, the practice of undertaking (*prasthānapratipatti*)—which has the nature of traversing the entire Mahāyāna Dharma characterized by its ninefold correct establishment—is established.
And in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*, the text that explains the practice as it has been described is not written here for the sake of providing proof, due to its great length.
Thus it has been said:
"In the meditative concentrations and the formless attainments, in generosity and so forth, and in the path, loving-kindness, and the rest..."
And in the yoga where perception has ceased, and in the purifications of the three spheres. ||45||

"In the summary [of the Perfection of Wisdom], in the six superknowledges, and in the method of the knowledge of all aspects, the practice of setting out (*prasthāna-pratipatti*) is to be known as that which mounts the Great Vehicle. (46) Thus it is said.
"Therefore" means because it is endowed with both the practice of armor (*sannāha-pratipatti*) and the practice of setting out.
The term "number" refers to a designation. This is what is meant:
"Because he is endowed with both the practice of armor and the practice of setting out, he receives the designation 'Great Being'."
Thus, for one who has set out, there is the equipment; this third practice of equipment, consisting of seventeen aspects, must be explained.
And so it has been said:
"The sixfold group beginning with compassion and giving, as well as calm abiding together with insight."
And that path which is the union [of method and wisdom], and that skillfulness in means; ||47||

"Knowledge, merit, the path, the dhāraṇīs, the ten stages, and the counteragent— this is to be known as the sequence of the practice of the accumulations. (48) Thus, in order to explain that, he speaks by way of introduction:
"Armed," and so forth.
To the word "how much" (*kiyatā*), one must supply the phrase: "endowed with another object, that is, a quality (*dharma*) delimited by a certain number.
For, being endowed with the undertaking of armor and the equipment of compassion and so forth, he is said to be "armed with the great armor."
This was explained by the Blessed One in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*.

Therein, it was stated immediately following [the description of the bodhisattva] that he is "armed with the great armor" because he is endowed with the practice of the armor implied by the meaning; now, [the author], dispelling the fault regarding the sense of the supplied word (*adhyāhāra*) by means of the equipment consisting of compassion and so forth, says:
"Here," and so forth.
"Here" is used as an introductory phrase for the statement.
"It is thus."
Thus this thought arises;
he states that very point with the words beginning "immeasurable" (aprameya).
They are "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) because they cannot be measured by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
They are "to be brought to final nirvana" (*parinirvāpayitavya*) because, according to their inclinations, they lead them to the attainment of nirvana through the three vehicles (*yāna-traya*).
They are "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) because they are devoid of numbers such as oneness and so forth.
This has been said:

for one who is devoid of compassion and lacks skillful means, it is implied by the sense of the argument that liberation is impossible because there is no establishing others anywhere [in the state of peace].

For one who is moved by compassion, having favored others through the six perfections—generosity and the rest—which serve as skillful means, [one acts] by providing immediate happiness through the perfection of generosity, and through the perfection of ethical discipline...

"By means of the introduction of ascetic happiness for one who is patient, energetic, and one-pointed in mind, I shall establish [beings] in that state— by means of the perfections of patience, vigor, and meditation through the introduction of absolute happiness, and by means of the perfection of wisdom through the introduction of ultimate happiness— just as I myself abide in the six perfections, through the acts of causing them to undertake, settling, and establishing them, so that they are no longer distracted. In this way, the seven accumulations are indicated.

Namely: the equipment of compassion, the equipment of generosity, the equipment of ethical discipline, the equipment of patience, the equipment of vigor, the equipment of meditative concentration, and the equipment of wisdom.
Regarding that, because of the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is no apprehension of an agent or an object;
thus he says, "And those do not exist," and so forth.
If that is so, then he says "non-apprehension," beginning with "he those... and so forth.
That Bodhisattva, endowed with the equipment of compassion and the like—
He brings those immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to final nirvana by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
If that is so, then [you might argue] that apprehension (*upalambha*) has been attained; to this he says:
"And not," etc.;
