the meaning is that [it does not exist] because it is not perceived from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
But how can there be both perception and non-perception of one and the same thing? Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"This is the very nature of things," and so forth.

Just as the nature of illusion is true according to how it appears, yet untrue because it is not established by logical reasoning, so too— taking as an example that universal worldly state of being a mere appearance which is untainted by the flow of conceptual reasoning— the nature of phenomena such as form and the rest is likewise.
The nature of perception and non-perception, which depends on the exclusion of different objects, would be non-contradictory because it is conceptually constructed.
The underlying sense is that there is a fault in the conceptualization of two properties based on the exclusion of a single object.

And these two have been stated for the purpose of mutually refuting misconceptions, not as being real in the way previously described; by this, the equipment for calm abiding (*śamatha*) has been indicated.
With the words "Just as... and so forth, he speaks of the equipment for insight (*vidarśanā*), namely, insight for one who has attained calm abiding.
Dakṣa means skillful.
Māyākārāntevāsī means a pupil of a magician, that is, his disciple.
The mention of the "four great crossroads" is primarily because it is the place for the manifestation of illusions.
A "body of people" refers to a multitude of beings.
"Manifests" means he creates an emanation.
"Disappears" means he withdraws [the emanation].
Having asked the general question, "What do you think? What do you understand? regarding the collection of matters just mentioned, he then says:
"If you think thus..."
Regarding the passage beginning with *api nv ityādi*:

the word *api* expresses possibility (*sambhāvanā*), and the word *evaṃ* has the sense of "thus" (*ittham*). *Tatra* means "in that [assembly]," namely, in the midst of that body of people (*janakāya*).
By someone such as a magician, a person such as Devadatta is "killed" through a weak application of life-force;
he is "dead" because of total annihilation;
he is "destroyed" through an application that causes the decay of the body.
If you think that "disappearance" means being rendered invisible,
this is not possible in reality because the subject (dharmin) itself does not exist.
The sense is that it indeed occurs according to how it is perceived. Having understood his intention, [the Blessed One] said: "Certainly not so."
The word "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Intending to apply the established meaning of the example to the point at issue,
he says "In this way," and so forth.
Having explained this in detail, he says the following as a conclusion, beginning with "If that... and so forth;
the word "this" (*imam*) refers to what follows immediately.

"Thus" means without transgressing the conventional and ultimate truths. Regarding what was asked—"to what extent?"—the response is the word "to this extent. This means that by being endowed with even this much equipment of compassion and so forth, one is designated as "armed with the great armor."
Because one might fall into the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and others by means of insight that takes emptiness as its object,
he next explains the equipment of the "yoked pair" (yuganaddha),
beginning with the words "Just as I... and so forth.
"Of what was spoken by the Blessed One" refers to the passage beginning with "This, Subhūti, is the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena.
The word *vata* is used here for emphasis.

He thinks as follows: "In whatever manner I understand the meaning of the passage beginning with 'this is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the Dharma spoken by the Blessed One as being pervasive like an illusion,' in that same manner, because the illusory nature of phenomena is non-arisen, this Bodhisattva is indeed one who is armored with the armor of non-existence.
He says this because he accepts it without error.
"Thus it is," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: even if he is equipped for the welfare of sentient beings through insight (*vidarśanā*) and through meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) such as the Gaganagañja and others, how can he be said to be "unprepared"?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because they are uncreated," and so forth.
They are uncreated because, according to logical reasoning, there is an absence of a causal agent (*kārakahetu*).
Because there is no cause for destruction, it is unmodified; because the conditions for the cooperation of both [causes] are impossible, it is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*).

Alternatively, the three terms refer respectively to the manifestation of what was previously non-existent, the attainment of its specific excellence, and the bringing about of the acquisition of the fruit.
He says this because it is accepted as being endowed with logical reasoning.
"Thus it is," and so forth.
Now, if bondage and liberation truly exist, how can this be the case—that [the world] is uncreated and so on?
For what reason is that?
Anticipating an objection from someone, he says:
"For it is thus," and so forth.
Otherwise, because investigation would be impossible if [the opponent's position] were accepted as it stands, this [critique] would be incoherent.
The same should be stated elsewhere as well:
form is unbound because there is no bondage through the conceptualization of the mind and mental factors of the three realms, which function by way of superimposed aspects;
and it is unliberated because there is no liberation apart from the discernment of the aforementioned conceptualization and non-conceptualization.
Because, in reality, form and the other aggregates do not exist, [the opponent] asks: "In that case, bondage and liberation must belong to the *dharma* itself. To this, he replies:
"Form-tathatā also," and so forth.
Since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is untenable in the absence of phenomena (*dharma*), the emptiness of form and so forth is neither bound nor liberated.
However, the point is that bondage and liberation occur for form and its suchness (*tathatā*) according to how they are perceived.
Because [the opponent] did not understand Subhūti’s intention, he spoke by way of an objection:
"Form," and so forth. The intention of the questioner is this:
[the suchness of form and so on].
"You say that [the self] is both bound and liberated;
this should not be said, because it would be contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition in a general sense."
Then, [the author], thinking that he must explain this specifically, says:
"Now, what is that? and so forth.

With the intention that the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, and others themselves are the illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*) because they cannot withstand the friction of analytical investigation, he speaks in general terms.
"Venerable Pūrṇa, as for [the statement] 'of a person created by illusion' and so forth—how is it that there is no occurrence of sublation by means of direct perception and the like?
For what reason? Having raised this doubt, he says:
"Because it is non-existent," and so forth.

Some say that because form and the like, which are conceptually constructed by logic, are non-existent and unreal, and because that which is mentally constructed is isolated and devoid of intrinsic nature, and because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-svabhāva*) is unarisen and unborn, [the Tathāgata] is neither bound nor liberated.

Another [teacher] maintains that the three terms beginning with "non-existent" (*asadbhūtatva*) are intended to refute the arising and other characteristics of reality (*tattva*) which do not appear through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception, inference, and scripture.
For a form that actually appears is certainly not negated;
it is not logical to negate anything that is being experienced.

The meaning is that, because bondage and liberation are established according to what is observed through such reasoning, how could there be sublation by perception and the other means of knowledge? The passage beginning with "this" is the conclusion.
[It refers to] the great armor.
"Armor" refers, in order, to the power of compassion and wisdom;
the remainder is "of the conventional and the ultimate.
He says that the unsurpassed one remained silent.
"Thus," and so forth.
Now, if it is asked: "Since calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vidarśanā*) are mutually contradictory, how can they coexist in one place?
It is not so; for when the mind has been made stable upon the object by means of calm abiding, [insight arises].
Then, for one who investigates with wisdom, because the light of right knowledge arises, the obscuration is abandoned—just as darkness is dispelled when light appears.
For this very reason, these two exist in mutual compatibility toward the arising of right knowledge, like the eye and light; thus, they do not stand in mutual opposition like light and darkness.
Indeed, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) does not have the nature of darkness.
Rather, it is characterized by one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).

And since it is said that "one who is concentrated knows things as they truly are" (*samāhito yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti*), it is not contradictory because it is exclusively conducive to wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, for one endowed with the equipment of the path of the "yoke-tied" (*yuganaddha*) practice, there is skillful means (*upāyakauśala*) and so forth. To demonstrate this equipment of skillful means and the rest, he speaks, introducing the discussion by posing a question:
"Thus it is, Blessed One," and so forth.
This means that by the previously mentioned sequence, one who is armored with the great armor becomes one who has set out upon the Mahāyāna.
Regarding this, it is said: "In that regard, since the Mahāyāna is not understood, there is the application of wisdom and compassion."

The noble Vimuktisena states that there are six questions, designated by such terms as "Which [is it]? and so forth, concerning these two: the non-deviation from one of them, the transcendence of the discordant side (vipakṣa), the certainty of remaining [in the path], the attainment of the tranquility of the application of the counteragent (pratipakṣa-prayoga-praśrabdhi), and the one who will go forth—[specifying] what, how, from where, by what means, where, and who shall go forth.
Therein, in order to set forth the equipment consisting of skillful means and so forth, he first addresses the initial question, saying:
"The Mahāyāna," and so on.
"The five dharmas, the [three] natures, and the eight consciousnesses."
The two kinds of selflessness constitute the entirety of the Mahāyāna's comprehensive grasp.

Thus, even in the words of the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*, by the force of the section on the equipment (*sambhāra*), the term "Mahāyāna" is primarily designated as a synonym for that which consists of the equipment of skillful means (*upāyakauśala*) and so forth, due to its immeasurability.
Furthermore, as to how the equipment of skillful means and so forth is immeasurable, he says:
"immeasurable," and so on.
Because it cannot be delimited by means of valid cognition such as direct perception and the like, the reality is indeed "immeasurable" (aprameya) as previously described.
This has been stated:

for one who possesses the equipment for the path of union, the equipment of skillful means arises from performing the welfare of sentient beings through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
The accumulation of knowledge (*jñāna-sambhāra*) is the practice of knowledge by one who has understood skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Furthermore, it should be understood as being twentyfold through the distinctions of the emptinesses, beginning with internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
In this regard, these are the twenty kinds of emptiness:
That is to say, internal emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā) is based upon the nature of the internal [faculties], such as the eye and so forth, which is neither immutable nor subject to destruction. (1)
Based on the suchness of the nature of external things, such as form and so forth, there is external emptiness. || 2 ||
Internal-external emptiness is based upon the suchness of the nature of the internal and external sense bases. (3)
Therein, the internal sense base is that which is comprised of the form of the faculties;
the external is that which is comprised of the form of the objects;
and the internal-external is that which is comprised of the physical bases of the faculties.
For that is internal because it is appropriated by the mind, and external because it is not comprised within the sense faculties.
And these three types of emptiness exist on the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

Because of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), even the emptiness whose nature is the knowledge that takes internal and other forms of emptiness as its object is itself empty; this is the "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Here, the "emptiness of all phenomena" refers to the knowledge of the emptiness of all phenomena.
And by that, emptiness is empty;
through the abandonment of the conceptualization that grasps it, this occurs on the path of preparation (prayogamārga). || 4 ||

The ten directions are the "great emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā) by virtue of being empty of directions; because they constitute a great configuration, this [emptiness] exists in the first stage (bhūmi) in the sense of being all-pervading.

Because the supreme *nirvāṇa* is empty of the nature of being an object for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, there is the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); since that [supreme *nirvāṇa*] is merely a state of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), this is the second [emptiness] in the sense of being "foremost" (*agra*). || 6 ||
The emptiness of the conditioned refers to the conditioned of the three realms, by virtue of the emptiness of the realms such as the desire realm;
this is because it possesses an unestablished intrinsic nature and is therefore capable of having an antidote.
This [emptiness] occurs in the third [stage] in the sense of being the supreme outflow.
Because the unconditioned—which is characterized by non-arising, non-cessation, and non-alteration—is empty of that [very nature], there is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
This is because there is an absence of any causal sign (*nimitta*) for designating arising and so forth as the opposites of non-arising and so forth.
This [emptiness] pertains to the fourth stage in the sense of being without appropriation (*niṣparigraha*).
Because an end is empty of an end, there is absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) by virtue of the end being past.

An "end" refers to a portion; in that regard, between the two ends of annihilation and permanence, there exists nothing whatsoever by which their nature could be established as the cause for delimiting those portions. This [emptiness] pertains to the fifth [stage], in the sense of the non-differentiation of the continuum (*santāna*).
The emptiness of that which is without beginning, middle, or end is the "emptiness of the beginningless and endless" (anavarāgra-śūnyatā).

Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) such as the beginning and so forth is continuously permeated [by emptiness], it is ultimate; thus, this [emptiness] pertains to the sixth [ground] in the sense of being neither defiled nor pure.

Non-dispersal (*anavakāra*) is the opposite of dispersal (*avakāra*), which is characterized by scattering, throwing away, and abandoning. Because it is empty of that [dispersal], it is the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*).

Since scattering and so forth, being of the nature of non-action, cannot serve as the basis for the designation of "non-abandonment," this [emptiness] exists in the seventh [stage] in the sense of non-differentiation.

It is the *prakṛti* (intrinsic nature) not created by any noble ones; it is the emptiness of that [nature] because of its being empty of itself. This is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), because that [nature] does not undergo modification or non-modification, whether conditioned or unconditioned. || 12 ||
The emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*) arises because a phenomenon is empty of being a phenomenon;
for all phenomena—whether the aggregates of the conditioned or the unconditioned—are not established by way of intrinsic nature due to their mutual dependence upon one another. (13)

And this is the eighth [stage], because it is the stage of the fruit by virtue of being the non-dual ground of emptiness in the sense of being neither deficient nor excessive, and because it is the basis for the non-duality of mastery over the purification of the field and non-conceptuality; and because of the distinction between penetration and cultivation, there is the "emptiness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) since form and so forth—characterized by being visible and so on—are empty of those very characteristics on the eighth stage, because the establishment of characteristics is merely a conventional designation of general and specific qualities. (14)

The emptiness of non-apprehension consists in the fact that past and other phenomena are not apprehended through the mutual non-perception of their opposites within the temporal periods of the past and so forth;
for these periods are merely designations for existence. (15)
And these two types of emptiness, by virtue of being the basis for mastery over gnosis (*jñānavaśitā*), exist likewise in the ninth [ground].

Because there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to a composite phenomenon due to its being dependently originated, it is empty of that [composite]; thus, there is the "emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence" (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*). Considering that existence is merely a collection (*sāmagrīmātra*), there is the "emptiness of existence" (*bhāva-śūnyatā*) because the existence characterized by the aggregates of appropriation (*upādānaskandha*) is empty of that [collection]. For the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the sense of a "heap" (*rāśi*); and since a heap is not a substantial entity (*apadārtha*), it is not the cause (*nimitta*) of existence characterized by appropriation.
This is because it ought to be so. || 17 ||
And these two types of emptiness, by virtue of being the basis for mastery over karma, are [attained] in the tenth stage as before.

Because the unconditioned non-existence, such as emptiness and so forth, is empty of that [non-existence], there is the "emptiness of non-existence" (abhāva-śūnyatā); this is because its designation occurs through the property of a thing, such as an obscuration and so forth. (18)
Because the intrinsic nature called emptiness is unconditioned by the noble ones' knowledge or vision, it is the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
for that knowledge and vision illuminate the object as it truly is. || 19 ||

Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains constant; because it is empty of any external agent, it is the emptiness of other-nature (parabhāva-śūnyatā). For human activity directed toward emptiness serves only to bring about exhaustion. Thus it is said. (20)

Furthermore, these three types of emptiness are to be understood on the level of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*) respectively as the basis for the abandonment of the afflictive obscurations along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanakleśāvaraṇa*), as the basis for the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanajñeyāvaraṇa*), and in the sense of self-existence (*svayambhūtvārtha*). By this method, the meaning of those treatises that lack a sequential order should be explained according to this direction.

"Arya Vimuktisena states: 'For those who describe emptiness exclusively by way of negating others, there is no sequential order of realization whatsoever; thus, for them, only the meaning of the specific context (*prakaraṇa*) must be stated, and not the primary meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*). Consequently, because these treatises on emptiness lack a sequential order of what has been traversed and what remains to be traversed, there is the possibility of a failure in the formal outline (*uddeśa*')."
Furthermore, regarding this non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), some maintain that it takes emptiness as its object;
others hold that its object is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) of all phenomena.
And this latter view alone is logical.
Whatever knowledge there is, each and every one of those has as its object the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena in reality;
just as, for example, in a dream,
knowledge has as its object the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of horses and so forth.
This cognition under dispute is the mind (*manas*), which is non-conceptual; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Since it has been said, "For one who does not perceive the apprehension itself, the perception of the object is not established," the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
It is not contradictory because it exists in similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the ultimate intrinsic nature (*tāttvika-svabhāva*) of all phenomena will be refuted later.
[Objection: But that which is apprehended does not exist.
It is, for example, like a double moon and so forth.

If it is argued that this emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), when itself taken as an object, likewise does not exist, and thus the existence of all phenomena would follow—this is not a fault.

Because there is no reappearance of the extreme of denial (*apavādānta*), which is like Devadatta, once it has been destroyed by its emptiness; nor is there the reappearance of the extreme of superimposition (*samāropānta*), which is like Yajñadatta, once its intrinsic nature has been destroyed.
Furthermore, that which is the object of cognition is not established in reality; thus,
faults such as the contradiction in the statement, "For the establishment of an object depends upon conventional consciousness," cannot be asserted.

However, in the case where emptiness is the object, it follows that knowledge has a lack of intrinsic nature as its domain, and it further follows that emptiness itself is conditioned. This is because, respectively, one might conceptually construct the mutual difference or non-difference between knowledge and its emptiness by treating them as existence and non-existence. Furthermore, regarding the distinctions among the various knowledges such as the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*) and so forth, there is much more to be said concerning the systematic arrangement of the equipment of knowledge; thus, these directions and subdivisions have been stated here as a digression, but the complete realization of the equipment of knowledge is not attained at this very moment.
This is because of the explanation of the sequence of the remaining realizations (*abhisamaya*).
It should be understood that the same applies elsewhere as well.

For one who possesses the practice of knowledge, merit arises from performing the welfare of sentient beings through right concentration and so forth, by means of the purification of wisdom (*prajñā*); this is the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*).

The equipment for the path (*mārgasaṃbhāra*) consists of the exertion in the path of examining phenomena and so forth by one who has already cultivated merit and knowledge. The equipment for retention (*dhāraṇīsaṃbhāra*) is the inexhaustible application of mindfulness (*smṛti*)— for the sake of teaching the Dharma over many eons through various diverse expressions such as "the aspect of that which is endowed with the path is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are primordially unarisen"— since mindfulness maintains [the teachings] by upholding both the text and its meaning.

Furthermore, these five—the equipment of skillful means (*upāyakauśala*) and so forth—are also taught in detail by the term "Mahāyāna" in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*; thus, no doubt should be entertained.

To explain the equipment of the stages (*bhūmi-sambhāra*), [the author] states that the stages are specific states of realization (*adhigama-avasthā-viśeṣa*), because they consist in the application of establishing ever-higher realizations for one who has attained the *dhāraṇī*, and in the application of maintaining those qualities.
Having uttered the introductory words of the objection, such as "Moreover, Subhūti, when you say 'How is he to be known as having set out in that? and so forth, he speaks the subsequent meaning.

"Set out by means of the perfections (pāramitās)" means that he has correctly set out in due order by means of the ten perfections, such as generosity and the rest, which are comprised within the ten stages (bhūmi) and are increasingly superior; thus, by way of indicating the result, the equipment for the stages (bhūmi-sambhāra) is described. This is what is meant.
In that regard, when all phenomena are realized as being without self through meditation— due to their partless nature—
there occurs a penetration of the *dharmadhātu* in its entirety.

Furthermore, by means of the universal sense, through the penetration [of reality] with a view toward generating certainty, there arises a clearer knowledge that directly realizes the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena.
At that time, the bodhisattva, by entering the state of rightness (*samyaktvanyāma*), attains the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

In this regard, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are forty [afflictions]—namely, attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, doubt, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—according to the distinction of the four truths; likewise, such [afflictions] exist in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*).

These same [afflictions], excluding the eight types of resistance (*pratigha*) to be abandoned by the vision of the Four Truths, amount to seventy-two. In total, one hundred and twelve afflictions are abandoned through the vision of the truths.
Because the truths are realized in a single moment of clear comprehension (*ekābhisamaya*), the first moment of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) constitutes the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).
Then, the other moments beginning with the second, up until the path of immediate succession known as "diamond-like" (*vajropama*), after which the Buddha-stage called *Samantaprabhā* is attained—
all of this is designated as the "path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*) because it consists in the penetration of the *dharmadhātu* in its sense of being supreme, and so forth.
And therein, sixteen afflictions are abandoned sequentially according to their occurrence;
namely, attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, the view of a self-identity, and the view of grasping at extremes— these six belonging to the realm of desire.

Those same ten [factors], excluding hatred, belong to the realms of form and formlessness; thus, the establishment of the ten stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā) is based on the differentiation of the qualities that serve as preparation for the paths of seeing and cultivation.
In this regard, as long as the qualities that constitute the preparation for a particular stage have not been fulfilled, one remains in that stage;
however, upon their fulfillment, it should be understood that another stage has been attained.
In this regard, these preparatory factors have been taught in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* as follows:
namely, the complete accumulation of all roots of virtue,
and the upholding of the Mahāyāna Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
The accomplishment of the four immeasurables;
the relinquishment of all one's possessions through non-conceptual application;
and the propitiation of spiritual friends.
The pursuit of all the true teachings as one's object of focus, without dependence on the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth;
and constant lack of delight in dwelling at home.
It is the non-separation from mental attention toward the unsurpassed Buddha-body in every respect;

the manifestation of the Dharma such as the sūtras and so forth according to reality; and the fulfillment of the promised goal. Because it is produced in every way by these ten factors—which serve as the purifications (*parikarma*) and specific causes—precisely through the purification of the specific characteristics by means of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*).
The stage called "The Joyous" (*pramuditā bhūmiḥ*) is attained because of the acquisition of joy through the realization of the true nature of phenomena as they were previously [explained].
And so it has been said:
"The first stage is attained through ten kinds of preparatory cultivation."
The disposition consists in the state of being a source of benefit and equanimity of mind toward all sentient beings. ||49||
Renunciation and service to friends by one who seeks the basis of the true Dharma;
always a mind inclined toward renunciation, and a longing directed toward the Buddha-body. ||50||
"The teaching of the Dharma is intended as the tenth statement, which is truth;
and their preparation is to be known through the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature.

(51) Thus, in every respect, the morality of undertaking the welfare of sentient beings consists in gathering wholesome qualities that are completely pure and free from the mental orientations of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Not letting the benefit conferred by others go to waste;
and having a mind free from ill-will and the like toward sentient beings.
Absence of regret regarding the ripening of sentient beings and similar activities;
enthusiasm for dwelling in the hells and other realms for a long time for the sake of even a single sentient being; and humility toward all people.
In the presence of the gurus, one should perceive them as the Teacher by carrying out their instructions;

and with no other activity, one should seek and apply oneself to the perfections such as generosity. Through such preparation, as previously described, and by means of the eightfold quality characterized by this specific preparation, the second stage, the *Vimalā* (Stainless), is attained through the removal of the stain of all immorality.
And so it has been said:
"Ethical discipline, gratitude, patience, great joy, great compassion, reverence, service to the teacher, and diligence in giving and the other perfections as the eighth. (52)
The intention to uphold the Dharma spoken by all Buddhas;
the proclamation of the true Dharma without regard for roots of merit and the like;
and the dedication of those dharmas that purify the Buddha-field toward that very same end.
Never experiencing weariness in acting for the benefit of sentient beings;

and possessing a sense of shame—both with respect to oneself and others—regarding mental orientations such as those of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas: through these five kinds of preparatory purification (*parikarma*), and as before, through the purification of the nature of awakening, one realizes the third stage, the *Prabhākari* (Luminous), because it produces the radiance of supramundane knowledge.
And so it has been said:
"Insatiability in hearing [the Dharma], giving that is free from worldly motives, the complete purification of the Buddha-field, and lack of weariness with cyclic existence. (53)
"Shame and dread of blame"—this consists of five kinds of mental reflection. This concludes the distinction regarding the mental attention of the Śrāvakas and others.
Through the mode of apprehension (*upalambha*), there is a lack of desire even for the attainment of enlightenment.
Non-conceit even when obtaining excellent things;
not abandoning the contemplation and so forth that constitute patience regarding the profound Dharma;
and not relinquishing any of the trainings.
The non-arising of thoughts of desire;
the lack of volitional construction regarding all phenomena;
and the non-appropriation of one's own body and so forth.

The fourth stage, the Radiant (*arciṣmatī*), is ascended through the aforementioned tenfold preparation, which consists of: the non-contraction of the mind when taking wholesome phenomena as its object, and the non-attention toward all [unwholesome] things. It is called "Radiant" because it is endowed with the flames that burn the fuel of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
And so it has been said:
"Forest-dwelling, fewness of desires, contentment, and the practice of the ascetic virtues and self-effacement. (54)
Not abandoning the training, revulsion toward sensual desires, world-weariness, the renunciation of all things, and freedom from dejection and dependence— thus [it is said]. (55)
Associating with householders and renunciants for the sake of gain and other benefits; visiting families of the faithful;
and [residing in] cities and such places crowded with people.
Self-praise and disparaging others;
the ten paths of unwholesome action;
conceit regarding one's learning and so forth; and failing to bow down to others.
Adherence to what is wholesome, unwholesome, or perverted;
the intellect characterized by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth;

and the manifestation of all afflictions such as passion—avoiding these ten factors, which are defined by such characteristics, because they act as bonds to enlightenment, one [proceeds] by means of the tenfold purification that implicitly entails the opposite qualities.
As before, the fifth stage is entered as the "Very Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*), because it is won with great difficulty.
Thus it has been said:
"Familiarity, family pride, envy, and places that lead to social distraction..."
Self-exaltation and contempt for others, and the ten unwholesome paths of action. (56)
"By abandoning pride, arrogance, error, doubt, and the endurance of afflictions, one attains these ten [qualities] on the fifth stage. (57) Thus,

by means of the fulfillment of the six perfections beginning with generosity, [one abandons] the longing for the state of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, the mind that is terrified by the non-perception of intrinsic nature, the mind that shrinks from the requests of supplicants, and the dejection regarding the spontaneous renunciation of all things for the sake of others.

By avoiding the thought of rejecting those who seek wealth due to one's own poverty—thus, through these twelve preparatory practices as previously described—the sixth stage, *sarvabuddhadharmābhimukhī*, is known.
And so it has been said:
"Because of the fulfillment of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom..."
He avoids those whose minds are possessed by a longing for disciples, a craving for fame, or fear. ||58||
One who is asked for alms yet remains undaunted, who is not dejected even when giving away everything,
and who does not reject supplicants even when impoverished— such a person attains the sixth stage. Thus it is said.
Through the knowledge of the three gates of liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— one sequentially abandons the grasping at a self, a sentient being, and a living soul.
Through the resolute conviction in the fulfillment of the ten paths of wholesome action purified in the three spheres, one avoids the grasping at a single person.
Because of the penetration of compassion that takes all beings afflicted by suffering as its object, there is no adherence to the view of annihilationism.
Based on the perfection of the Buddha-field, because of the non-apprehension of all things, there is the cessation of adherence to the view of eternalism.
From the realization of the equality of all phenomena, the apprehension of signs does not arise.
Through the realization of the single vehicle as the Mahāyāna, there is the relinquishing of grasping at causes.

Through the thorough knowledge of the non-arising of name-and-form and so forth, there is the dissociation from grasping at the aggregates. Through the comprehension of the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) that contemplates the profound Dharma, there is the eradication of grasping at the elements (*dhātu*).
Through the gateway of skillful means of the Mahāyāna, all phenomena are revealed; thus, there is the disjunction from grasping at the sense-bases (*āyatana*).

By cutting off all conceptual constructions, there is the severance of the grasping that establishes one in the triple world (*traidhātuka*). By abandoning the grasping of signs, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment, and other afflictions, there is freedom from the grasping of clinging.
Through the power of cultivating *śamatha*, there is the seclusion from grasping at a constricted mind;
through skill in wisdom (*prajñā*), there is the absence of nature in relying on the view of a Buddha;
and through the pacification of the mind by cultivating the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), there is the absence of intrinsic nature in relying on the view of phenomena (*dharma*).
Because the arising of non-obstructive knowledge regarding form and so forth, which relies upon both truths, there is no arising of reliance on the view of the Saṅgha.
Because of attaining the knowledge that there is no basis for dogmatic adherence, there is the non-occurrence of reliance on views concerning ethical discipline.
For the sake of correctly discerning the Dharma, because of traveling at will and simultaneously to all Buddha-fields, there is no production of grasping at disputes concerning emptiness.

In order to deliver the realm of sentient beings who are attached to objective apprehension, one manifests one’s own body everywhere in accordance with their needs; thus, by abandoning grasping through the revelation of non-contradiction with emptiness—by means of these twenty types of preparatory qualities (*parikarmadharma*), as previously described, having performed the specific refinement of characteristics and attained them—one reaches the seventh stage, the *Dūraṅgamā* (Far-Reaching). This is because, through the removal of the stains of the aforementioned twenty types of factors, it is well-distant from the obstacles of the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*). Thus, the seventh stage is attained.
And likewise, with reference to that which is to be abandoned, it has been said:

Grasping at a self and sentient beings, [the views of] a living being, a person, annihilationism, and eternalism; [grasping] at signs and causes, and [the views regarding] the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. (90)
Establishment in the three realms, attachment, and a mind that is cowed; adherence to views regarding the Three Jewels and the precepts. ||91||
"Disputes regarding emptiness and its contradictions— these twenty stains are severed by him who reaches the seventh stage.
Thus it has been said concerning that which is to be adopted.
The knowledge of the three gates of liberation, the purity of the three spheres, the contemplation of compassion, and the knowledge of the single principle of the equality of all phenomena. ||93||
The knowledge of receptivity to non-arising is the simultaneous comprehension of all phenomena;
it is the total eradication of conceptual construction and the abandonment of perceptions, views, and afflictions. ||94||
The settling of the mind in calm abiding, skill in insight, the taming of the mind, and knowledge that is unimpeded everywhere. (95)
The absence of attachment, moving at will and simultaneously to other realms,
and the perception of one's own self-nature everywhere— these are the twenty [qualities].
Thus is the knowledge of the mental conduct of all sentient beings as it truly is.
Sporting with the supernormal powers (*ṛddhyabhijñā*) for the sake of sentient beings in various world-systems;
transforming the supporting buddha-fields into states such as gold and so forth;
and honoring the Tathāgatas in order to examine all aspects of phenomena.
The accomplishment of the divine eye;
the purification of the buddha-field and its sentient beings to be supported therein;
and abiding everywhere in the state of being like an illusion.

And by taking up birth intentionally through the vision of the welfare of sentient beings—thus, by means of this eightfold preparatory cultivation of dharmas as before—the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā*), is experienced because of its unshakability due to the non-exertion toward the eight signs.
And so it has been said:
"The knowledge of the minds of all sentient beings, the supernormal powers, and the play in the auspicious."
The perfection of the buddha-field occurs through serving and examining the Buddhas. ||67||
Sensory cognition, the purification of the Buddha-fields, an illusion-like abiding,
and the intentional assumption of existence— this eightfold activity has thus been taught.
Infinite aspiration;
knowledge of the sounds of all sentient beings, such as gods and others;
and inexhaustible eloquence comparable to a river.
The descent into the womb praised by all people;
the station of kings and others;
and the lineage of the Sun and other [deities].
He is a kinsman related by blood to his mother and others;
he has a retinue under his own command;
his birth is celebrated by Śakra and the other gods; and his renunciation is prompted by the Buddhas and others.
The Bodhi tree, which is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), and so forth,

as well as the fulfillment of the qualities of the intrinsic nature of all Buddha-dharmas— thus, through these twelve preparatory practices characterized by such perfections, and having performed the specific preparations as before, the ninth stage, the Sādhumatī (Excellent Intelligence), is realized because it is irreproachable due to skill in teaching the Dharma.
And so it has been said:
"The infinite aspirations, the knowledge of the cries of gods and others, the river-like flow of inspired eloquence, and the supreme descent into the womb. (96)

Regarding lineage, birth, clan, retinue, and birth; regarding renunciation, the trees of awakening, the abundance of qualities, and one's own perfections— thus is the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi), which is the eighth stage for those of the lineage of the śrāvakas and others, and the stage of one who has entered upon the first fruit.
The stage of vision belongs to the stream-enterer;
the stage of attenuation belongs to the once-returner;
the stage of freedom from passion belongs to the non-returner.
The stage of one who has completed non-conceptualization belongs to the Arhat.
Due to the absence of specific terminology, the stage of the Śrāvaka belongs to the three types of practitioners who have entered the path.
The stage of the Pratyekabuddha belongs to the Pratyekabuddhas.
And having thus transcended the nine stages of the bodhisattvas as described—the ninefold *bodhisattvabhūmi*—a bodhisattva on the tenth stage should be called a Buddha, yet not a *samyaksaṃbuddha*.

This is because of the statement in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*: "In that Buddha-stage, by means of which knowledge he abides through such qualities as the basis of mastery over karma (*karmavaśitāśrayatva*)," and so forth.
That tenth stage, the Bodhisattva-stage called Dharmameghā (Cloud of Dharma), is to be attained by him through the raining down of the water of the Dharma.
Thus it has been said:
"Having transcended the nine stages, he is established in the Buddha-stage."
"By means of which knowledge that [stage] is to be known as the tenth Bodhisattva stage.

(71) Thus, the equipment for the stages (*bhūmi-sambhāra*) has been explained in detail in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*; however, because of the abundance of textual expansion there, I have not elaborated upon it here. Enough of this digression. Since the equipment for the stages consists precisely of the paths of seeing and cultivation, immediately following that, in order to demonstrate its nature as the equipment for the antidotes (*pratipakṣa-sambhāra*) through the distinctions of the states of abandoning the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*), he speaks by way of answering the third and subsequent questions:
"Regarding the three realms, the sun, and so forth":

therein, first, there are two types of conceptualization of the apprehended (*grāhya-vikalpa*) based on the mere thing (*vastu-mātra*), and two types of conceptualization of the apprehender (*grāhaka-vikalpa*) based on the person as a substantial entity (*dravya-pudgala*) and the person as a conceptual designation (*prajñapti-puruṣa*).

Because these are abandoned on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the state of their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa-avasthā*) is distinguished according to the division of the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*).

The fourfold set of statements beginning with "Fie on me! and "I shall depart from the three realms," which are dedicated to demonstrating the fourfold equipment of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa-sambhāra*) in their respective order, should be applied by relying upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Subsequently, on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), through the abandonment of the two types of conceptualization regarding the object—namely, the conceptualization of the object as having the nature of a mere thing (*vastu-mātra*) and the conceptualization of the subject—and through the abandonment of the two types of conceptualization regarding the subject—namely, the conceptualization of the subject as a substantial person (*dravya-pudgala*) and the conceptualization of the subject as a nominally designated person (*prajñapti-puruṣa*)—one realizes the states of those antidotes; thus, there is another fourfold equipment of the antidotes according to the distinctions of the factors to be abandoned (*vipakṣa*).
Demonstrating that what was stated regarding the reliance on ultimate truth is due to the negation of activity according to their respective order, he says,
"But rather," and so forth.
He clarifies precisely the negation of a locus.
Rather, one will abide in omniscience by way of non-abiding.
In this context, "abiding" is the apprehension of a real entity; it is the mental fixation [of the mind] through means such as instruments and so forth. "Non-abiding" is the negation of that.
Herein, the following is investigated:
If, first of all, "non-abiding" (asthāna) is simply the absence of abiding, then, being a non-entity, it is not logically tenable as an antidote.
Alternatively, if it is that which is not abiding, then there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to the eye and other sense faculties as well.
Just as non-attachment was explained, so too should the method be understood here; thus, it is not elaborated further.
The statement that "one does not set forth because of the negation of entities belonging to the three times," and so on, is addressed by the question:
"How can this be so, given that one sets forth through the cultivation of the true nature of reality?"
Anticipating the question "For what reason?",
he says "And whoever," and so forth.
"Both" refers to...
The Bodhisattva, bringing together both the path by which one departs and that [departure] itself in their true nature,
says "In this way," and so forth.
The intention is, however, that they exist conventionally.
And so it has been said:
"The counteragent is to be known as eightfold on the paths of seeing and cultivation."

"For the pacification of the eight conceptual constructions of the grasped and the grasper" (72)—thus, in the sequence already described, by practicing the entirety of the Mahāyāna without transgressing the conventional and ultimate truths, Great Enlightenment is gathered through these [perfections] beginning with compassion by way of its full realization; therefore, compassion and the others are the "provisions" (*sambhāra*). This is the seventeenfold practice of the provisions.

The fourth practice, the practice of departure (*niryāṇapratipatti*), must be explained as the departure resulting from the attainment of victory over the unconquered by one who has thus accumulated the necessary provisions.

Furthermore, that [practice] is eightfold according to its objects; among these, first is the departure through the summary statement (*uddeśaniryāṇa*) due to its predominance. That, in turn, is the departure through the greatness of mind consisting in being supreme among all sentient beings.

There are three kinds of departure [from saṃsāra]: the departure through the greatness of abandonment, and the departure through the greatness of realization. Therefore, with reference to these three kinds of departure as taught, he says:
"Mahāyāna," and so forth: the greatness of the object, as well as that of the two practices,
of knowledge, of the undertaking of vigor, and of skill in means.

"The greatness of realization and the greatness of the Buddha's activity—indeed, because of its connection with these [two] forms of greatness, it is designated as the 'Great Vehicle' (Mahāyāna). Thus, due to its connection with these seven kinds of greatness, the Mahāyāna is the bodhisattva path together with its fruit; the Mahāyāna has as its fruit the perfect awakening to reality, which is not merely that which is conventionally renowned in the world.
Because that alone constitutes bondage; otherwise, the cultivation of the antidotes in the Mahāyāna would be rendered purposeless.

Therefore, since the world—including gods, humans, and asuras—is merely an unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) and consists of a false appearance, one will certainly go to the state that is to be reached by means of the thorough knowledge of its own nature as being without true reality through its antidote.
Because one will thereby attain the greatness of being the foremost among all sentient beings and so forth, it is called the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*); such is the meaning of the passage.
Since it is impossible to achieve departure [from saṃsāra] without the realization of equality,
he says "space," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the departure through equality immediately following that.
Because it is like space in its equality, and because it possesses stainless gnosis that pervades the entire mandala of all objects of knowledge through its emptiness, that vehicle is "great.

Since there can be no accumulation of merit without the welfare of sentient beings, the realization of equality is not truly complete; therefore, following that, he speaks of the departure for the welfare of sentient beings, beginning with the words "Just as... and so forth.

Because of the statement that "there is room for sentient beings in the Mahāyāna," it is indicated that their welfare must be accomplished by means of that Mahāyāna; otherwise, since it would be devoid of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), the existence of such room would be untenable.
The phrase beginning with "by this" constitutes the conclusion.
By this alternative explanation and by this different meaning: because when there is mental application (*ābhoga*), the welfare of sentient beings is not accomplished in its entirety; therefore—
Immediately following, he says "naivāsya" and so forth in order to explain effortless departure (*anābhoganiryāṇa*):
"its arrival is from the past; its departure is into the future."
The meaning is that while [the cause] exists, there is no abiding; because of the absence of coming and so forth, liberation (*niryāṇa*) is established without effort.
This is without attaining a state free from eternalism and nihilism.

Immediately after stating that it is not the case that there is no effortless departure (*nābhoganiryāṇaṃ na bhavati*), he says "In this way for him," and so forth, in order to demonstrate ultimate departure (*atyantaniryāṇa*).
"In this way" means according to the sequence that will be explained.
"The prior limit" refers to eternalism (*śāśvata*). "Annihilation" refers to the posterior limit (*aparānta*). "Distinct from those" refers to something other than these two.
He says that it does not exist even in the middle. Explaining what was stated as "thus," he says:
"Empty of the three times," and so forth.

Since all phenomena are empty of the three times by virtue of being primordially extinguished (*prakṛti-parinirvṛta*), that vehicle is the Mahāyāna; therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that there is no such thing as a prior limit and so on.
Having expressed his approval because this explains a meaning that does not contradict the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), he says:
"Excellent," and so forth. Concluding [the discussion], he says:
"In this way," and so forth.

Since even ultimate departure (*atyantaniryāṇa*) is not accomplished without attaining the state distinguished by the three vehicles, he speaks immediately after this of "departure through attainment" (*prāptiniryāṇa*),
beginning with the words "having trained in this... and so forth.
"Here" means in this Mahāyāna.
"Omniscience," which consists of the three vehicles, is designated as "attained" in order to make known its status as the cause for the realization of all noble persons (*āryapudgala*).
Because of the confusion produced by a change in the word [from *anuprāpta* to *anuprāpya*], Ācārya Pūrṇa said, "This is the Noble One."

With the words "May it occur to you for the sake of the *prajñāpāramitā*," and so forth, [the Blessed One] requested [Subhūti] at the very outset. However, since the manifestation of knowledge and vision is impossible without constant mindfulness (*nityasamanvāhāra*), [Subhūti], thinking that it might otherwise be possible, said, "O Blessed One, I do not [see it]," and so forth.
Having transgressed—that is, having overstepped—[the request], he said "Certainly not" (*no hīdam*) and so forth, because it is impossible for one empowered by the Tathāgata to teach erroneously.
It conforms; the sense is that it is favorable because the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* has the Mahāyāna as its intrinsic nature.
[He perceives] his own capacity for teaching the profound Dharma in all its aspects...
Seeing this, he says: "O Blessed One, through the power of the Buddha.
And that departure by attainment is characterized by the negation of the relationship between the object to be attained, the attainer, and both of them.
Therefore, with reference to the negation of what is to be attained, he says:
"But rather," and so forth.
The word *api tu* (but rather) is used for the sake of indicating a sequence.

The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of "beginning with" (*ādyāditvena*), as seen in examples such as *pūrvāntataḥ*. The phrase "does not approach" (*nopaiti*) implies that he does not encounter any Bodhisattva who could be attained as having the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form (*rūpa*) and so forth; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The meaning is that the very Bodhisattva who is to be attained does not exist.
Now, one might object: "How can the Bodhisattva, who appears as form and so forth, be non-existent? Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason?", he says:
"Because of the boundlessness of form," and so on.

"Because no phenomenon exists apart from the dharmadhātu"—according to this principle, since form and the other aggregates, which have become identical in nature with the dharmadhātu, are infinite, there is an infinity of bodhisattvas; therefore, the sense is that one does not apprehend a bodhisattva.
With reference to the negation of the attainer, he says:
"Form," and so forth.

The meaning is that because form and the other aggregates are non-existent according to the correct principle, there is an absence of the perception of a bodhisattva who would be their substantial self.
If this is indeed non-perception, then [the author] says "this," and so forth, in order to state that it is reality.
"This too does not approach" means that even this [negation] does not exist;
for a negation (*nañ*) cannot be employed without an object, and therefore, in reality—
A sentient being is not apprehended.
Having thus indicated it in general terms, he speaks with reference to this self,
beginning with the words, "So it is, Blessed One," and so forth.

Thus, by the negation of both the object to be attained and the means of attainment, it is in accordance with the principle: "For these two kinds of totality regarding all things are indeed [the totality of the object] and the totality of the mental aspects."
In that context, "in every respect" means by way of the entities such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth;
"everything" means the intrinsic nature of all external and internal entities;
and "in every manner" means by way of the various modes and aspects such as internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, "all" refers to every mode, whether individual or collective.
Regarding "the dharma of a bodhisattva":
it is the very bodhisattva who, characterized as both the goal to be attained and the means of attainment, does not perceive that dharma which has form and so forth as its intrinsic nature.
He states the negation of the connection between both [subject and object] with the words beginning "prajñā" (wisdom).
By means of knowledge that possesses form and knowledge that is formless, respectively, I do not perceive nor do I apprehend them.
Or rather, for the purpose of establishing that very point through both perception and inference, he says:
"Omniscience. Concluding, he says:
"Such as I am," and so forth.

Which bodhisattva is the attainer? By what means of attainment? Through which gateway of non-attainment? In what connection—namely, that characterized by the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)? Since the word "which" (*katama*) here expresses a negation, the meaning is: not any [attainer] by any [means] in any [connection].
From what [source]? From the passage beginning with "Buddha" and so forth. Here, that which is to be attained (*prāpya*) is expressed by the word "Buddha.
Since the relationship between the means of attainment (*prāpaka*) and [the goal] is denoted by the two subsequent words, that very subject which was introduced is now concluded.
He says that by employing words according to the actual state of things, a real entity would exist merely through the presence of a name:
"And that," etc.
It is not maintained that there is a relationship of signifier and signified between a specific object and a specific word.

"Because it was previously seen, its generality (sāmānya) will indeed be taught"—according to this principle, its name corresponds to the actual state of things; yet, because it has not been brought into being, it is not produced. To the question "In what way?", he says:
"Just as 'self' [is a designation]"—
he explains that very point with the words beginning "self," and so forth.
Because it is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), like a donkey's horn, the self (*ātman*) does not exist at all, since it is not produced even conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*);
nevertheless, there is the designation "self."
If, according to this reasoning, all phenomena are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one might ask: "What then is that form (*rūpa*)? Anticipating this, he says "That which... and so forth.

Because it is unproduced (*anabhinirvṛtta*), it is therefore free from the state of apprehended object and apprehending subject in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvena*); yet, in terms of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtyā*), it is form, charming when left unanalyzed.
Thus, he says that the non-arising [of phenomena] by way of the state of grasped and grasper is the ultimate dharma: "In this way," and so forth.

By this reasoning, the very absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*) of all these phenomena is their non-arising; and that which is non-arising, because it lacks the maintenance of its own essential form (*svarūpa*), is not those phenomena. Concluding the point already established, he says:
"Regarding the passage beginning with *tad* (that): because the word *kim* (what) expresses negation, the meaning is "not at all.
[The opponent] then says: "In that case, the manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti*) is the phenomenon (*dharma*)."
And "not elsewhere," etc.: because all things have been refuted as being produced, they are not produced.
Even in nirvana, no dharma is apprehended at all.
All dharmas have the nature of the path of the perfection of wisdom;
the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharmas) have the characteristic of being that which is to be attained.

The dharmas of a bodhisattva are form and so forth, which serve as the basis for the designation of a "bodhisattva" who attains [enlightenment]. Or, whatever other general dharma might practice for the sake of enlightenment, that too is not apprehended; this is the connection [of the sentence] through a change in case-ending. Furthermore, he asks: "Who, then, is thus devoted to the perfection of wisdom? and says:
"If he," and so forth:
he practices with non-concentrated knowledge; he cultivates [the path] with concentrated [knowledge].
One examines by means of reasoning and establishes [the object];
one contemplates by way of establishing it within the condition of recollection.
[Objection: But how can one examine the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) through the perception of form and so forth?
[Question: For what reason? Having raised this doubt, he says: "In which... and so forth.

Because at whatever time one examines these phenomena, such as form and so forth, within the perfection of wisdom through their aspect of being without intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvabhāvya*), at that time one does not approach form, does not proceed toward it, and therefore does not go toward it nor take hold of it;
for one does not perceive either its arising or its cessation.
The meaning is that there is no other [entity] apart from that which is free from arising and passing away.
However, in the case of monism, the very perception of non-arising and non-cessation is itself the perception of form.
Anticipating the question, "How then does it not become form? and asking, "For what reason?", he says:
"For instance," and so forth.
Because as long as there is neither arising nor ceasing, those two are not form, since it is form alone that appears conventionally.
In that regard, existence itself is the moment; destruction is the dharma of passing away, and because it is the negation of that, it is non-destruction.
Since, from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), there is diversity, therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), both non-arising and non-destruction are form.
This non-duality of that which is neither produced nor destroyed is a single form consisting of non-arising and so forth;
for it is indivisible and free from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that produce dualization.
If this is so, he asks: how, then, can there be a designation of "form" (*rūpa*)? He replies:
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "yat punar... and so forth:

this manifestation—that the nature of non-duality, which by its very logic consists of non-arising and so forth, is "this form"—is a conventional enumeration, a designation, or a convention established through relative truth (*saṃvṛti*).
[It refers to] omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Since there is no departure through attainment without realization (*adhigama*), he says "Thus, O Blessed One," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the departure via the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) immediately following that.
The connection is: "In this way, [one departs] in every aspect.
The ellipsis is: "to depart into the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which is the knowledge of all aspects."
"Of all aspects" refers to aspects such as the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*); this is an adverbial modifier.

While thoroughly examining all phenomena—form and so forth—at that time, during the moment of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), he does not approach form; since this has been restated through another context beginning with "does not approach form," there is no fault of redundancy.
Intending to show that, this being the case, the practice of the conduct of suffering for the sake of sentient beings would be untenable, he says:
"Therefore, etc. This means:
because form and so forth are non-dual in their non-arising and non-ceasing, for that reason.
I understand the meaning of the statement beginning with "it does not conform to what has been spoken" as follows:
likewise, even a bodhisattva is non-arisen, because he too possesses the intrinsic nature of form and so forth.
In order to state the fault in the acceptance [of the opponent's view] expressed as "let it be so," he says "yadi ca" and so forth.
The word "kim" is used in the sense of censure.
The meaning is that because it is incompatible with non-arising (*anutpāda*), one does not practice at all.
Or rather, the meaning is: for what purpose would one not endure those sufferings of sentient beings for their sake? One would indeed endure them.
The meaning is that [the self] does not exist because of the absence of being (sattva) and so forth.
He provides the answer with the words "I am not," etc.
He thinks as follows:

If the Bodhisattva is non-arisen, then it follows that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, he does not practice the difficult conduct at all; in that case, since conduct is logically untenable in its true nature, you are merely proving what is already established.

Now, if there is no non-arising at that time from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), then since the Bodhisattva establishes its arising, how could this be contradictory to his conduct?
One should not think, "How can even conventional difficult practices (*duṣkaracaryā*) be performed?
To this, he says: "Nor... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "he practices with the perception of difficulty," the word "difficult practice" (*duṣkaracaryā*) is to be supplied as the object.

One might ask: "Since only Bodhisattvas perform difficult practices such as the giving of their heads and so forth, why does he not have the perception of difficulty? Anticipating this question, he says:
"Not so," and so forth.

Because it is not possible to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings by generating the notion that [the practice] is difficult, as long as the correct conduct (*samyakcaryā*) has not been perfected;

therefore, the meaning is that one who forms the notion of difficulty regarding the practices of giving and so forth does not become a bodhisattva by failing to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings.
How, then, is this possible? He says: "But rather," and so forth.

By means of the absence of stinginess and other such faults regarding generosity and the rest, one should cultivate the perception of ease—that is, the perception of it being easy to perform—and likewise, toward sentient beings, the general perception of them as mothers and so on, or specifically, the perception of women and men according to their age, whether they are older, younger, or of equal stature.
The sense is that if a bodhisattva practices the conduct after having formed the notion [of them] as mother and so forth according to their possibility, then the purpose can be accomplished.
Concluding that very point, he says:
"Therefore," and so forth.
By the word "up to" (yāvat), there is the inclusion of the notion of brother and sister toward women and men who are of equal age and stature.
To explain how the notion of self should be generated, he says:
"Just as," and so forth.
Due to the presence of the conceit of "I," the self is nothing other than one's own continuum;
it must be liberated from all sufferings— that is, removed from the sufferings of conditioned formations and so forth.
He states another alternative as well:
"And thus," and so forth.
They are not to be abandoned; rather, they are to be liberated through the application of the intention of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), by means of accomplishing such tasks.
One must not give rise to the lamp of the mind that is hatred.
When [does one do so]? It says:
"at least," and so forth.

Even at the very end, if one's own body were being cut into hundreds of pieces by those very same [beings]— this must be supplied as the ellipsis— an extraordinary degree of altruism would still be present.
Concluding that very point, he says:
"For thus," and so forth.
"Thus-minded" refers to the mind just mentioned immediately prior.
He will practice the conduct of giving and so forth;
he will dwell in all four modes of deportment.
Having thus established that there is no perception of difficulty regarding conduct when based on conventional truth, he speaks next while establishing it by means of ultimate truth:
"Furthermore," and so forth.

"Everything" refers to all forms, whether pervasive or otherwise, by means of all valid cognitions such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest. "In every way" refers to the modes of established existence, such as being a sentient being (*sattva*), a living soul (*jīva*), and so on. Furthermore, "everything" refers to the nature of agency (*kartṛtva*) and other such attributes.
Just as the self does not exist because it is devoid of the nature of being either one or many,
and for that very reason is not perceived,
so too are all phenomena.

Explaining that very point, he says: "In this way," and so forth. Regarding phenomena (*dharmas*), "in every respect" means by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so on; "everything" refers to speech and the like; "in all ways" means through modes such as being afflicted (*kliṣṭa*); and "all" means every variety.
Therefore, since there is no other alternative, one should act like an illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*).
And in that regard, the sense is: "How could there be difficult practice?
Having thus avoided the over-extension regarding non-arising, he states his own position.
By the words "yadapi" and so forth,
the intended meaning is that this is indeed exactly so from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
[This refers to] the Bodhisattva.
Because of the statement "non-arising," he says that emptiness is partial. He asks, "What then? and so forth.
The qualities that constitute a bodhisattva— the bodhisattva-dharmas whose intrinsic nature consists of the knowledge of the paths and so forth— are likewise non-arising,
because the underlying principle is the same.
He says this very thing:
By the words "O Bodhisattva," and so forth:
one must answer exactly what was asked; otherwise, the speech would fail to refine the listener.

Therefore, in order to avoid the notion of a limited emptiness, he states that emptiness has all things as its object by means of a series of questions and answers beginning with, "Is omniscience also [empty]?
In this context, "omniscience" (sarvajñatā) refers to Buddhahood;
"the qualities that constitute a Buddha" refers to those qualities characterized by the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
The fool, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), is one for whom the noble path has not arisen.
Phenomena such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth, which are based upon that [ignorance], are the phenomena of an ordinary person.
Having thus caused [the opponent] to accept the non-arising of all phenomena in this gradual manner, he states the following to expose the fault:
"O Venerable One, if... and so forth.
The word *nanu* expresses dissatisfaction. [The objection is: "Has omniscience not already been attained?"
The word "with effort" (*yatnena*) is to be supplied [as the remainder of the sentence].
In some places, the reading "without effort" (*ayatnena*) is found, which is indeed clear.
This has been stated.
"Buddhahood is to be attained through the realization of non-arising by means of reverent, uninterrupted, and long-term cultivation.
However, if all phenomena indeed..."
"In that case, omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) would have been attained effortlessly; consequently, all embodied beings would be liberated."
If, in the case of non-arising, there existed dharmas consisting of that which is to be attained and that which attains it,
then it would follow that attainment occurs without effort;
however, since this is not the case, he says [the following] with this intention.
By the words "I do not," and so forth:

by logical principle, I do not accept the attainment—that is, the grasping—of a dharma that has not arisen, whether it be that which is to be attained or that which causes attainment, during the stage of preparation; nor do I accept its clear realization—that is, its full comprehension—at the stage of the fundamental [meditative state].
He says that very thing with the words "nor indeed," and so forth:
an unarisen attainment, characterized by the state of being attained, is not attained by an unarisen attaining dharma.
Because both [the means and the goal] are devoid of intrinsic nature (*nīrūpa*).
To the objection that, "in that case, attainment might be achieved through the non-arising of either one," he says:
"But what, then? and so forth.
The word "utāho" indicates an alternative position.
He speaks, beginning with "But what, venerable Śāriputra," etc., for the purpose of providing an answer by means of a counter-question.
Because arising does not exist,
how can an unarisen phenomenon be designated as "arisen"?
If you say it is so, then let it be so designated.
For a thing does not undergo change merely by being given a different name; therefore, how can an unarisen acquisition (*prāpti*) be acquired by a dharma that has already arisen?
Or [if you argue that] the dharma itself remains unarisen...
Even though you designate it as "unproduced," there is nevertheless a logical fault;
for that dharma which is unproduced is indeed non-existent, being unproduced.
Therefore, how can an unarisen attainment (*prāpti*) be attained by means of an unarisen dharma?
This has been stated:
"In reality, since both the object to be attained and the attainer do not exist, how [could there be attainment]?"

[Objection: "Attainment is achieved through effort. Even conventionally, because one attains knowledge that flows effortlessly on the eighth stage and beyond through uninterrupted cultivation over a long period of time, how can there be attainment without effort by which all embodied beings might be liberated?"
With the intention of stating that this same objection applies to you as well when establishing production and non-production on the basis of the conventional and ultimate truths, he says:
"Is dharma itself production, or rather non-production?"
"The dharma of non-arising is 'non-arising'.
Thinking that even by way of conventional designation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti*), reality is devoid of verbal expression, he said this.
Regarding the passage beginning with "arising" (*utpāda*),
the intended meaning is that because both [arising and non-arising] are unreal, they do not appear as fit to be spoken of in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*).
With the intention that non-arising is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he says "non-arising also," and so forth.
Because it accords with the ultimate truth, this is called the "ultimate truth. He said: "Non-arising, O Venerable Śāriputra, is itself conceptual proliferation."
"Non-arising is also spoken of"—this is "discourse" (*jalpa*). This means that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is nothing other than conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
To the question, "What then appears at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*)?", he says:
"Non-arising alone," and so forth:
non-arising, which is indeed free from all conceptual constructions and is itself ungraspable, appears as the object of apprehension.
Manifestation is indeed a grasper that is itself without a grasped object.
But how can that which does not possess such a nature appear as having that nature? To this he says:
"Evam eva," and so forth.
In this very way, since it cannot be sublated by what is actually perceived, let it be as it is according to conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
Alternatively, it appears as something purely false in its very unexamined form.
Because it appears so intensely, it appears in a manner that is free from the forms of eternalism and nihilism.
He speaks thus for the sake of praise, because he has correctly explained the reality of dharmas.
"Of those who preach the Dharma," and so forth.
He should be established and maintained.
Now, one might object: in the absence of the realization of the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmiḥ*), how can he be a *śrāvaka*?
Thinking, "How is it so?
and "For what reason?",
he says, "For thus," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "from whichever" (*yato yataḥ*): by virtue of being included in the group beginning with *ādi*, the suffix *tasi* is applied to a word ending in the locative case; thus, there is also the form *tatastataḥ*.
Wherever one is questioned, from that very place one emerges by providing an answer.
It does not deviate from the establishment of the *dharmatā* characterized by its own realization;
and it does not contradict that *dharmatā*, which is of the nature of scripture, through its realization—
even in the absence of constant meditative concentration (*samāhita-jñāna*), this is the implied meaning.
Demonstrating the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata, he says:
"This is the true nature (*dharmatā*)" and so forth;
[referring to] the disciples of the Tathāgata who possess qualities that are non-reliant and qualities that are non-attached.
This is the nature of things: the necessity of dependent origination.
What is this nature of things? He says:
when there is the existence of the apprehension of entities characterized by form and so forth.
Furthermore, how can it be that the śrāvakas are those whose dharmas are non-reliant? Anticipating the question, "For what reason? he says: "Just as... and so forth.
Because they are non-reliant due to being devoid of the nature of being either one or many, and because they are worthy of non-reliance;
the Śrāvakas, whose dharmas are non-reliant regarding all dharmas, are indeed empowered for the proclamation of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
otherwise a correct teaching would be impossible.

Because they are characterized solely by the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), they lack such conviction in the Dharma; therefore, [the phrase] "through the empowerment of the Tathāgata" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

Furthermore, since even that departure toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) does not occur without the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*) and so forth, he says the following immediately after this to demonstrate the departure via the path (*mārganiryāṇa*).
“Excellent,” and so forth.
