Furthermore, since the conceptualization of the grasper arises from the awakening of latencies within one's own continuum— latencies projected by the beginningless, currently ceasing conceptual cognitions that grasp forms and so forth— this restriction does not apply that the arising [of the grasper] occurs only when there is a conceptualization of the grasped.

Therefore, because they are associated with the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that apprehends objects in the form of false appearances—being exactly like things produced through the nature of illusion (*māyā*)—they should be regarded as being non-apprehending, just like Pratyekabuddhas.
Now, one might ask: even if they apprehend an objective domain through such a conceptual construction, how can they be considered unreal?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For thus," and so forth.

In the states of meditative equipoise and non-equipoise, those Pratyekabuddhas will, respectively, neither hear nor directly realize [the teaching] in the form of the conceptualization of a grasper; this is the remainder of the sense.
The view is that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a cognitive affliction because it manifests as a non-existent object and is deceptive.
By this same reasoning, the nature of the path of the Pratyekabuddhas is also described through the non-abandonment of the conceptual construction of the subject (*grāhaka-vikalpa*).

Because it is stated that they are "similar to magical illusions" in some respect—this being a statement of similarity—the notion that sentient beings possess the nature of illusion is refuted; thus, for the sake of addressing the conceptualization that arises as a consequence, he says:
"What then," and so forth.
"Those sentient beings are like illusions."
Do you think that because these things have the nature of an illusory falsehood, they therefore do not illuminate the existence of ultimate reality, and thus your explanation is incorrect?
He provides the rebuttal with the words "They are like an illusion," etc.
He thinks as follows:

Just as an illusion in the form of an elephant and so forth is neither different nor non-different from the fragments of clay and the like— because it is not perceived as distinct from them— so too, it is because those who have eyes unclouded by mantras and other such factors do not perceive [the elephant] apart from the fragments of clay and the like.

Therefore, because it transcends the properties of a real entity by being indefinable as either identical to or different from [its parts], it cannot be said to exist in reality (*tattvataḥ*) like a person (*pudgala*) or other such things; yet,

because it has entered the path of experience through being established by the direct perception of even ordinary people, it cannot be said not to exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), like conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and the like.
Therefore, those things which are dependently originated have, from the perspective of ultimate reality,
forms that transcend the conventional discourse of existence and non-existence.

Just as an illusion is, so too are these entities such as sentient beings; thus, by means of a "reason of essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*) established through a well-known fact, a [previously] unestablished fact is proven. Therefore, they are compared to illusions. However, according to the correct reasoning (*nyāya*), they are furthermore...
Thus, sentient beings are indeed of the nature of illusion; therefore, no real existence of sentient beings has been demonstrated.
The two phrases "like an illusion" and "like a dream" are stated according to the distinction between the states of the awakened and the unawakened.
"Non-dual" means having a single intrinsic nature.
He asks, "Why is that so? and says:
"Without duality" (*advaidhīkāram*).
That which has no duality—that is, no manifoldness (*nānātva*)—is described as such.
The thought is that this proceeds from a pervasion through universal inclusion.

Thus, the meaning of the sentence is as follows: since these sentient beings are like an illusion (*māyā*) by virtue of having a false nature, therefore illusion and sentient beings are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
Likewise, since they are like a dream (*svapna*), therefore the dream and sentient beings are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
Demonstrating that very pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says:
"All phenomena as well," and so forth.
Explaining this statement of inclusion, he says:
"Even a stream-enterer," and so forth.

Since pervasion has been established in this manner, [the author] asks: how can the Blessed One, who is like an illusion, be the cause of the perfection of all qualities? He says: "The Perfectly Awakened One..."
"O Noble Subhūti," and so forth.
The Tathāgata is the *samyaksambuddha* in terms of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). Anticipating this [objection], he says:

"Even nirvāṇa," and so forth. For since I declare even nirvāṇa— which is the distinguished Dharmakāya, whose nature is non-dual gnosis, and which is like an illusion or a dream— to be such, why then would I not speak of any other phenomenon, namely the Rūpakāya?
The meaning is: "On the contrary, I do indeed say so.
This is because the double negation serves to establish the subject matter at hand.

The intention is that the Blessed One, when confronted as having the very nature described above, is the cause of the perfection of all qualities; otherwise, his nature would be contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and thus constitute a misconception.
Furthermore, he says "even nirvāṇa," and so forth, because the failure to realize the true dharma arises from an even greater degree of adherence to the existence of phenomena.

Intending to show that otherwise— due to the acceptance of the existence of phenomena through a partial emptiness like that of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas)— liberation would be impossible, he offers this rebuttal.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tadyadi" and so forth: the word "tat" (that) is used for the introduction of a statement; "yadi" (if) is used in the sense of an admission or concession.
As it has been said:
"No distinct dharma whatsoever exists that is superior to nirvāṇa;
nevertheless, it is spoken of even while accepting this [conventional designation]."
If there were any other phenomenon more distinguished than even nirvāṇa, then I would say that even that phenomenon is like an illusion and so forth.
Thus it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna:
"The arising of passion and hatred, the grasping of intense and evil views..."
When there is the acceptance of entities, disputes and those things arising from them occur.
That is the cause of all views; without it, the arising of afflictions does not occur.
Therefore, when that is thoroughly understood, there is the complete destruction of views and afflictions.
"By what means is it fully understood? Through the vision of dependent origination.
For the best among the knowers of reality has said that what is born dependently is unborn.
Thus, the concluding passage beginning with "iti hi" and so forth has not been written here, as its meaning has already been explained.
Having explained what arose incidentally, he now asks, "Who are these? and so forth, in order to state that the path of the pratyekabuddhas is distinguished even by way of its basis.

Regarding this Perfection of Wisdom, which consists of the path of the Pratyekabuddhas and is being described as characterized by the sequential abandonment and non-abandonment of the conceptualizations of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject— what kind of individuals belonging to which spiritual lineages (*gotra*) will be those who receive, uphold, and grasp it? Having understood the meaning through the majestic power of the Tathāgata, the noble Ānanda spoke as follows:
"Those indeed," and so forth.

"Irreversible" means that through the attainment of the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), they are non-retrogressive regarding *pratyekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment); yet, because of their aspiration for their own awakening, they are *bodhisattvas*.
[They act] by means of teaching the Dharma through physical gestures (*kāyikī dharmadeśanā*).
The great beings (mahāsattvas) are those who intend to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings in every Buddha-field;
or "those endowed with right view" means those who are possessed of middling wisdom and right view.
Or, "Arhats" refers to those whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāśrava*); they are worthy of worship because they have abandoned the obscurations of their own path of vision.

By these three terms, it is explained that, in relation to Pratyekabuddha awakening, there are respectively persons who possess a lineage acquired through effort (*samudānītagotra*), those who possess a lineage obtained through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatāpratilabdhagotra*), and those very same ones who possess a fixed lineage (*niyatagotra*).
In every instance, the word "or" (*vā*) should be understood as indicating a mutual alternative.
Furthermore, the noble Subhūti, explaining in another way, said:
"Of this [path], etc.
Now, is it not the case that they realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha preceded by instruction in their own path?
"How is it that even the Pratyekabuddhas are not at all those who rely [on others]?
Anticipating this question with "For what reason?", he says:
"Because," and so forth.

In this context, the meaning is that at the time of attaining the path of a *pratyekabuddha*, because instruction from others is unnecessary, they are "solitary buddhas" (*pratyekabuddha*) due to their self-awakening.
By means of a concise statement, no specific point is indicated, as it merely points toward the extensive meaning;
by means of an extensive statement, nothing is illuminated, as it merely elucidates what is already contained in the concise meaning.
Because its true nature is described as it actually exists, it cannot be conceptually designated.
For the purpose of summarizing, he says:
"Just as it is," and so forth.
Therefore, by the very same reason— that there is no purpose for which an indication and so forth would be made—
for that same reason there will be no one to accept it;
the sense is that because there is an absence of even that which is being pointed out.

Just as a magically created flower (*nirmitapuṣpa*), though lacking intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), appears in the form of specific locations and so forth, being delightful when not subjected to analytical investigation— in the same way, there is the attainment of the qualities of specific realization even without a real, substantial substratum. To indicate this, he speaks in the section on the "substratum" (*ādhāra*) for the purpose of presenting the example of the magically created flower.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then indeed Śakra," and the phrase "of this dharma-discourse":
it refers to this dharma-discourse of the path of the pratyekabuddhas, which has the nature of the ten wholesome actions and so forth.
The word *nu* is used for emphasis; the meaning is "only for the sake of worship.

Regarding the phrase "having manifested," it means that having produced [the form] through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), he acted exactly in that manner immediately after the arising of the thought (*cittotpāda*). Thus he said.
Then indeed, Śakra, and so forth.
"He scattered" means he threw [the flowers] directly and all around.

"Regarding 'indram anuvyāharāṇāya': the word *anu* has the sense of a marker (*lakṣaṇa*), and through its connection with that, the case ending of the object (*karma-vibhakti*) is applied to the word *indra*.
This is what is stated."
"Following Indra’s words, his mind became inclined toward explaining the true nature of the emanated flowers by way of a pretext, in order to demonstrate the essential character of the substratum.
The phrase "these" (*imāni*) refers to those being experienced at present.
The mention of "the thirty-three [gods]" is because that is their own abode, and it serves as an indication of a location suitable for their own perception.
"Seen before" means experienced before. Are all these flowers such that they have never been seen before? No; he says: [they have been seen before].
Regarding the passage beginning with "yāni" and so forth:
if this is so, then what is their intrinsic nature? To this he says: "These flowers are emanated."
This is what was said:

"These flowers do not exist and move about in places accessible to my perception, nor have they been brought from regions beyond the range of our vision, because they lack such [physical] capacities; therefore, these flowers are mind-made emanations."
Explaining that very point, he says:
"Not these," and so forth.
In this context, "trees" refers to those bearing flowers and fruits; "shrubs" refers to jasmine and the like.
Climbing plants such as the *atimuktaka* and others [are meant].
Because he has understood their discursive thoughts through the power of the Buddha, he speaks in order to avoid them,
saying "unproduced," and so forth.
One might ask: "Even though they appear from the mind, how can they be unarisen? Anticipating this question, he says:
"For not," and so forth.
Because, in reality, there are no flowers whatsoever produced from the mind—this being because the state of subject and object is unreal;
nor are they produced from trees and so forth, since that has already been refuted by you yourself.

By the statement "these flowers are unproduced," the intrinsic nature of the flowers is not denied; however, since their production is negated, one might then assume their permanence, which is incorrect. To this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yat tvam," the ellipsis is that one should not say "produced from creepers. He asks, "Why? and provides the answer.

"O Kauśika," and so forth. The thought is this: since that which is unarisen is not a flower, because for that which is eternal, its own nature is impossible due to the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—whether by way of succession or simultaneity.

In this context, by the abandonment of the conceptualization of the apprehended (*grāhya-vikalpa*), one distinguishes the realization of the Pratyekabuddhas from that of the Śrāvakas; and by the absence of the abandonment of the conceptualization of the apprehender (*grāhaka-vikalpa*), one distinguishes the unsurpassed realization of the Buddhas from that of the Pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, the realization is distinguished by its unique basis. Thus, the path of the Pratyekabuddhas is distinguished by the aforementioned cultivation of the non-perception of the aspects of the Four Truths of the Śrāvakas, which conforms to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) according to the actual state of things.
It must be thoroughly understood by the bodhisattva.
And so it has been said:
"Because of the abandonment of the conceptualization of the object to be grasped, but not the abandonment of the grasper..."
"The summary of the path of the Pratyekabuddha (khaḍgamārga) is to be understood according to its basis.

Thus, since there is the attainment of the levels conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), there is the aforementioned path of the Pratyekabuddha; therefore, he speaks of the meaning of the levels conducive to penetration, beginning with:
"O, how profound is his wisdom! and so forth.
Because he demonstrates the meaning of "heat" precisely by explaining the meaning of the reality that serves as its basis, he is one of profound wisdom.

He points out the designation of names and phrases and the designation of the aggregates such as consciousness for the sake of knowledge derived from hearing, by means of explaining the meaning of the texts.
Since this does not contradict the conventional acceptance [of phenomena], he does not contradict them in terms of their true nature (*dharmatā*).
He elucidates [the meaning] by means of reasoning in order to stabilize it for the sake of knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmayajñāna*).
He instructs by means of teaching the sequence of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) for the sake of knowledge consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayajñāna*).
This is what has been stated.
"The demonstration of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) without contradicting the conventional designation of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*)—
thus, when there is an objective support consisting of all phenomena, the stage of 'Heat' (*ūṣmagata*) arises.
Because this is demonstrated precisely through the description of the essential nature of a magically created flower, one is said to possess profound wisdom.
And so it has been said:
"The form of indicating the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without contradicting conventional designation is the stage of Heat (ūṣmagata)."

Having determined that this is indeed the appropriate form, he himself provides his own hand [of proof] regarding the conceptualization of self by means of the passage beginning with "It is thus. Furthermore, in this context, one should train in the path of the Pratyekabuddhas like a magically created person or a flower born of the sky.
He says "Evam etat, Kauśika," and so forth, in order to express his approval by stating that it has been well said.
He then asks, "What follows from that? and says:
"Training in this way," and so forth.
The collective meaning is that one does not train by means of apprehension (*upalambha*) anywhere.
"In the eight stages" (*aṣṭabhūmiṣu*).
Buddhahood or omniscience is said to be twofold, distinguished by the abandonment of the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations on the stages beginning with the eighth.
One trains therein through training in non-perversion, because it leads inevitably to the attainment of the state of a Tathāgata.
And since the training for Buddhahood and so forth is preceded by the thorough knowledge of all phenomena, he says:
"He who [seeks] Buddhahood," and so on.
Having explained what arose incidentally, he now says that one trains in the meaning of the "Summits" immediately after the "Heat" stage.
"Regarding 'he who [acts] toward the immeasurable,' and so forth:
increase (*vivṛddhi*) is augmentation (*upacaya*), and decrease (*parihāṇa*) is diminution (*apacaya*).
This is what has been stated."

"There is no training for the sake of the decrease or increase of form and so forth from the perspective of ultimate reality"—thus, the state of the "Summit" (*mūrdhagata*) arises with all phenomena as its object.
Therefore: "The Summit is characterized by the non-decrease and so forth of form and the rest. (9)
It is said that immediately after the Summits (mūrdhan), one trains for the sake of Receptivity (kṣānti).
"That which is not [the grasping] of form," and so forth, refers to grasping (parigraha), which is appropriation (svīkāra);
abandoning (tyajana) is relinquishment (utsarga).
The meaning is that for that purpose, one does not train by means of the power of the emptinesses, beginning with internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
And it is said in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*:

"By way of the non-appropriation [of anything], from the emptiness of form up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*)."
This has been stated:
"By means of the internal and external emptiness of form and so forth, there is non-appropriation and so on"; thus, patience arises with respect to all phenomena as its object.
And so it has been said:
"Patience [arises] because of the non-appropriation of form and so forth through the [meditations on] internal emptiness and the rest."
Thus, immediately after patience (*kṣānti*), one trains for the sake of the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
Thus he says:
"Nor of anything," and so forth.
Regarding the term *parigrahāya*: that by which something is grasped (*parigṛhyate*) is called *parigraha*.
There is both affirmation and negation.
Demonstrating that very point, he says:
"Neither for arising nor for disappearance."
Regarding the phrase "of no phenomenon whatsoever":

although this is a general statement, it might be apprehended as referring only to that which is of the nature of what is to be abandoned (*heya*). To prevent such a misconception among the dull-witted, he says:
"that which is not [the object] of any phenomenon whatsoever," and so forth.

"Even of omniscience" means that even regarding the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*), attachment everywhere is a bondage; this is the intended meaning. He asks: what is the benefit of the training as it has been described? He says:
"Thus," and so forth. This means:
"Training by way of the aspects of the non-arising, non-ceasing, and so on, of form and the other [aggregates]."
Thus, the state of supreme mundane dharma (*agradharmatā*) arises when all phenomena are taken as the object of focus.
And so it has been said:
"The state of the supreme dharma [is characterized] by the aspects of the non-arising of form and so forth.
(10) Thus, because all dharmas are non-apprehendable and possess a single flavor of reality, [the opponent], raising a doubt as to what omniscience might be for a bodhisattva, asks:
"O Venerable Subhūti, that which... and so forth.
At the conclusion of the sentence, the remainder is: "How [can one do so] without the perfections such as generosity?
For without the ladder of correct conventional reality, it is not possible for the wise to ascend to the pinnacle of the palace of ultimate truth.

Thinking that, according to this principle, the emptiness of all phenomena as described in the *Ratnacūḍa-sūtra*— along with its retinue of giving and the other perfections— is what should be practiced,
he says the following by way of providing a rebuttal:
"It is so, Venerable Śāriputra," and so forth.
Following the path of vision of the Pratyekabuddhas, the path of the Bodhisattvas—endowed with qualities pertaining to both this world and the next—must be explained; thus he says:
"O Noble Śāriputra, [the perfection of wisdom]," and so forth.
The perfection of wisdom is the meaning of the path of seeing for bodhisattvas.
Briefly stated, it is the non-apprehending samādhi immediately following the supreme mundane dharma;
and here, wisdom should be understood as being together with its associated mental factors.

Furthermore, by way of classification, it is likewise: with respect to suffering, there is the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*), and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
The same should be understood for origin, cessation, and the path. These sixteen moments of mind constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Moreover, a "moment of mind" (*cittakṣaṇa*) should be understood as the completion of the arising of the knowledge that cognizes the object to be known. Some...
They describe it thus: "The path of seeing consists of fifteen moments, because of the seeing of what was previously unseen. That is incorrect.

For instance, on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), taking as its dominant condition a prior investigation into whichever dharma presides over the truth of suffering, there arises within oneself an untainted cognition (*anāśravajñāna*) that experiences the truth of suffering; by means of this, one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
This is called "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*).
The knowledge by which one realizes liberation immediately after the acceptance (*kṣānti*) is called the "knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*).

Immediately following the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering, that untainted (*anāśrava*) knowledge which is personally and directly experienced— the realization that "this is the subsequent sequence of the noble dharmas" with respect to both the acceptance of the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering and the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering itself—
is called the "acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhānvayajñānakṣānti*).
The knowledge by which one ascertains that very receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding suffering is called "subsequent knowledge of suffering.

In this same way, the receptivities and knowledges regarding the remaining truths should be understood according to their respective applications; thus, it is logical that the path of seeing consists of exactly sixteen moments.
If, however, [the path] consisted of fifteen moments, there would be no determination of the subsequent-knowledge-acceptance (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) within the path;
for the final [moment] of the path would lack the vision of what was previously unseen.
If it is argued that the moment of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is not the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),

then, by the same logic, because the moment of subsequent knowledge lacks the vision of what was previously unseen regarding the three truths of suffering and so forth, it too would not be the path of seeing; consequently, the path of seeing would consist of only twelve moments.
And this is not an admission [of our position], so this is merely trivial.
And thus it has been said:
"By means of the moments of acceptance and knowledge, fourfold for each truth, [the truths are realized]."
"This is called the path of seeing with its benefits within the knowledge of the paths" (v.
11). In this context, through the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), there is the realization of the object to be grasped.
The realization of the subject occurs through the receptivity to subsequent knowledge and through subsequent knowledge itself.
It should be understood that in all instances of receptivity and knowledge, the yogi dwells in the signless.
Because that which has its causes complete cannot be abandoned, origination (*samudaya*) is abandoned at the time of abandoning [suffering] through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana*).

For this very reason, cessation (*nirodha*) is realized, and since that [realization] would otherwise be impossible, the path (*mārga*) is cultivated. Since it is the same regarding origination and the others, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the Mahāyāna should be understood as a single-moment realization (*ekakṣaṇābhisamaya*), due to the simultaneous realization of these effects.
Furthermore, with respect to each truth, there is clear realization through penetration by means of the elimination of misconceptions.
It is realized in exactly sixteen moments.
Therefore, some maintain that the formal establishment of the stages, such as "one who has entered the path" (*pratipannaka*) and so forth, is established on this basis.
The group of views such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the collection of afflictions such as attachment arise from the misconception that accepts a real ontological status.

Liberation, however, results from the vision of non-apprehension; thus, for the sake of that [liberation], the cultivation of the remaining aspects is intended as a means of preparing for it. Accordingly, when one cultivates all phenomena as being without intrinsic nature, without self, or empty—according to the method already described—the power of that cultivation reaches its fulfillment.
Since perception itself is a single entity devoid of parts, what other unseen portion could there be that might be examined by means of other instruments of knowledge?
According to this principle, a knowledge that effects the penetration of the intrinsic nature of all aspects arises, which is untainted (*anāśrava*) and has all phenomena as its object.

Therefore, others maintain that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the realization in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisamaya*), precisely because of this realization through penetration. [Objection: But since all aspects have been penetrated in just a single moment, and since no further cultivation by means of other aspects is possible within the path of seeing, how can the formal distinction between one who has "entered" (*pratipannaka*) and so forth be established? This is better [explained as follows]:...
The cognition of those who follow the path of liberation would be [erroneous] if another quality were joined with it by means of a cause of error,
just as the form of silver appears in mother-of-pearl due to the perception of a similarity in appearance.
To the extent that another aspect (ākāra) exists as something superimposed by some cause of error,

the establishment of the eight stages and so forth is well-founded, because it is possible to cultivate a different [corrective] aspect in order to uproot that misconception along with its originating afflictions and their companions.
And with this very intention, the realization in a single moment (ekakṣaṇābhisamaya) is established through the power of reasoning.
Thus, the path of seeing is described as the clear realization characterized by sixteen aspects.
Consequently, although consciousness grasps the nature of all aspects, in whichever portion...
Through proficiency in cultivation and so forth, there is the capacity to eliminate superimposed aspects;
its validity lies precisely therein because of the abandonment of the obscurations bound to those [aspects], and not elsewhere, as is the case with momentariness and the like.
Thus, one should not even ask: "What is the distinction of the Noble Ones from ordinary persons?"
To the extent that their knowledge eliminates the causes of error regarding the nature of objects, to that same extent they possess distinction; enough of this digression.
From where is it to be sought?
"By whose instruction should it be practiced?"—this means it should be cultivated.
Furthermore, although someone else might instruct it somewhere by way of defining [the path] and so forth through incidental speech, it is due solely to the power of the Tathāgata.
With the intention that, primarily, Subhūti alone was empowered by the Blessed One in the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he said:
"O Kauśika, the Perfection of Wisdom," and so forth; this is stated because of the teaching [contained] in the chapter.
He speaks thus because the empowerment of the Tathāgata has been forgotten.
"To whom does this belong? and so forth.
Not seeing any other capacity [for the answer] than that of the noble Subhūti, as before, he says:
"Of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
Manifesting his own freedom from pride through reverence for the Tathāgata, he says,
"O Kauśika," and so forth.
Now, in order to explain the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by means of describing its aspects (*ākāra*), he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yadapi" and so forth:
because of the statement, "The perfection of wisdom is non-dual gnosis; that is the Tathāgata," the perfection of wisdom here is the Tathāgata.

According to the principle that "whatever is dependently originated, that is itself considered by you to be emptiness," the suchness of form and so forth is expressed by the very words "form" and so forth;
this constitutes its status as the substratum.
Since it is dependent upon the speaker's intention,
[the term] "as a limit" (avadhibhāvena) is used; therefore, this is the meaning that results.

Since the Tathāgata exists in a state of being supported within the suchness of form and so forth— which serves as the support— he is not to be sought therein, nor elsewhere. Because this statement is intended as an illustration, it should also be understood that the suchness of form and so forth is not in the Tathāgata, nor elsewhere.
And this has been stated quite explicitly in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*:
"O Kauśika, the Tathāgata is not apprehended in the suchness of form;
nor is the suchness of form in the Tathāgata."
"The Tathāgata does not exist apart from the suchness of form,
nor does the suchness of form exist apart from the Tathāgata," and so forth.
Since there is no other dharma existing apart from those two, why should the perfection of wisdom not be sought in form and the rest, nor elsewhere?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For it is thus," and so forth.
This is the meaning of the sentence here.
The true, substantial basis consisting of form and so forth does not exist as the purity of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because it is perverted.
Therefore, the impure basis consisting of form and so forth cannot be the distinguished cause of the perfectly pure Tathāgata;
thus, the perfection of wisdom is not to be sought within form and the other aggregates.
If another property distinct from that [object] were real, there would likewise be a misconception; thus it is not the case elsewhere either.
Rather, it is precisely through the apprehension of form and so forth as being unreal that this occurs.
Therefore, what is meant is this:

Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there exists no relationship of container and contained between the suchness of form and so forth and the Buddha due to their oneness, there is no admission of these two as existing in alternation; thus, the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises with all phenomena as its object.

Having heard [the teaching] in a single aspect, he speaks of the aspects of the four moments beginning with the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*) by means of his ready intelligence (*udghaṭitajñatā*).
"This is the great perfection," and so forth. He says "It is so, Kauśika," and so forth, for the purpose of expressing approval through a correct exposition.
"Entities possessing such-and-such a nature are produced from causes possessing such-and-such a nature"—

according to this principle, since the largeness and other qualities of the causes, such as form and so forth, are untenable, how could the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) possess largeness and so on when it is produced with those very things as its objective support? Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because of the greatness of form," and so forth.
Form and the other [sensory objects] possess "greatness" because arising, abiding, and destruction do not exist in reality.
They possess "immeasurability" because, since form and the others lack the characteristics of transformation, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) capable of delimiting them is perceived.
For material things, dimension is their shape down to the level of the atom;
for immaterial things, dimension is their defining characteristic.
Because they are not perceived due to the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of form and so forth—just like space—they possess no dimension.
Because form and the other aggregates are like an illusion, they lack a prior limit and a subsequent limit, and thus possess infinity.

Having indicated that the greatness of the effect follows from the greatness of the cause and so forth, [the author] states that attachment to that [infinity] is bondage, beginning with the words "Thus, great... and so on.
The phrase "do not adhere" is to be connected everywhere.
To the question, "What follows from that?", he says:
"Therefore," and so forth.
This is what is meant:

"The greatness of form and the other [aggregates] consists in their having the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; likewise, they possess immeasurability. As before, they possess boundlessness because space is boundless; and they possess infinity because, due to the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) in form and the rest, there is an absence of extremes such as permanence or annihilation. Thus, with respect to all phenomena as objects, [the immeasurables are established] in relation to suffering in due order."
Dharma-knowledge;
receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding suffering;
subsequent knowledge regarding suffering.
"The receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination arises.
Thus, explaining the meaning of "endlessness" itself by way of the negation of the four aspects regarding origination, he says:
"By the endlessness of the object," and so forth.
Explaining this summary statement (*grahaṇakavākya*), he says:
"But how, moreover," and so forth.
The prior limit (*pūrvānta*) within [the cycle of existence] is the cause (*hetu*).
The time of existence is in the middle;
the end is the subsequent limit, which is destruction.
"From that" means because of the absence [of existence] at the prior limit and so forth.
He says, introducing [the topic],
"By this, O Kauśika," and so forth;
this is an exposition by way of synonyms.

Thus, having negated the aspect of the cause (*hetv-ākāra*) by means of the infinity of the first object of focus, he speaks of the infinity of the second object of focus in order to negate the aspect of the origin (*samudaya-ākāra*), saying:
"Furthermore," and so forth;
they are infinite because they are devoid of a prior limit (*pūrvānta*) and a posterior limit (*aparānta*).
The time of existence (*sattākāla*) is "bounded" (*paryanta*) because it is delimited on both sides by its two limits;
they are "unbounded" (*aparyanta*) because of the absence of such limits.
He states this very point with the words beginning "not for them," and so forth.

Now, it may be argued that the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) is observed through the certainty of those who perceive the final moment—that whatever effect conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of something is the cause of that thing; and the posterior limit (*aparānta*) is likewise observed.
As for the middle, whose existence is directly perceived, it is certainly established even more so.
How, then, are the beginning, middle, and end not apprehended?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"They are not apprehended."
"By means of cognitions with and without aspects," the word "logically" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"By this too" means not only by the previously mentioned formulation.
Having thus explained the infinity of objects in two ways, he says "sentient beings are infinite and limitless" in order to state the infinity of sentient beings.
Having raised the doubt, "Why is that so?",
he says, "For not," and so forth.
As before, there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) to be supplied here as well.
First, the negation of the mode of origination was established by means of the infinity of sentient beings.

Failing to understand the aforementioned infinity of sentient beings due to an attachment to existence nurtured since beginningless time, [the author] says "How... and so forth, in order to demonstrate a second kind of infinity of sentient beings.
"How so? is used in the sense of a challenge.
It is not so, because of the absence of a prior limit and so forth.
Due to the infinity of sentient beings, the perfection is infinite.
Rather, the thought is that [the designation occurs] due to a connection with number and so forth. Having understood this intention, he says:
"Not so, Kauśika," and so on.

Or, "by way of non-connection with calculation": *gaṇanā* refers to numbers such as oneness and so forth; *ayoga* means non-connection or lack of relation with that—this should be understood by resolving the compound (*gaṇanāyoga*) into *gaṇanā-as-yoga*.
The meaning is "by way of being beyond number," or "by way of a great multitude of counts," as for example the number situated in the sixty places [of the decimal system].
"Number" is said [in this context] to mean, as it were, an abundance of calculation through its connection with infinite numbers;
that is to say, even by these two appropriate modes, if the infinity of sentient beings is not established, then by what other mode could it be?
To this he says: "How then," and so forth.
In order to establish this by means of those words, he says:
"What do you think? and so forth.
Because he has realized the true nature of the reality of phenomena through the power of the Tathāgata, he speaks thus.
"‘Not this,’ and so forth: because a phenomenon (dharma) maintains its own intrinsic nature, ‘existence’ is not its designation.
Since, in reality, a phenomenon possessing a cause does not exist, and since a negation cannot occur without an object, ‘non-existence’ (adharma) is likewise not [its designation]."
How then is the conventional usage of the term "sentient being" so well-established?
To this he says: "This is adventitious," and so forth.
Because the aspects of cause (*hetu*), origin (*samudaya*), production (*prabhava*), and condition (*pratyaya*) are negated, it is said to be "adventitious" (*āgantuka*) and so forth.
These four terms are interpolated and superimposed; that is to say, they are merely conventional (*saṃvṛtimātra*).
Thus, when the cause and so forth are negated—
Questioning whether one might at some time establish the existence of a sentient being as having causes, he asks:
"What do you think? and so forth;
[namely,] is there eternal existence or non-existence?
Because a cause does not depend on anything else,
for it is by virtue of dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible;
according to this principle, he speaks because of the appearance of the existence of impermanent things.
"Not so, Noble Subhūti.
Now, applying those words to the meaning of "endlessness," he says:
"In which," and so forth. Wherein, by means of mere conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), some indication of a truly existent being has been made, therein what is the endlessness of beings?

The thought is that because of the connection with counting and so forth, there is no [such thing] at all, since that which is being counted is itself non-existent. Explaining this very point, he says: "If, Kauśika," and so forth.

"By means of an infinite sound of cognition" means by means of the sound that makes known the infinite realm of sentient beings. "By means of a profound resonance" means by that which persists for a long duration.
And these two words are qualifiers of "by means of sound" (*svareṇa*). Furthermore, "sound" should be understood as the activity of the palate and other [articulatory organs].
As for the phrase "even for eons" (*kalpān api*):
By the word "api" (also/even), it is meant that it is not only for a short time;
"therein" means in mere conventional reality, or rather, while speech exists— this is the sense.

"Since words are dependent upon the speaker's intention, they do not exist anywhere [independently]. If, however, the establishment of an object were to follow from their mere existence, then everything would be established for everyone. With this intention, he said:
"Not so, O noble Subhūti.

[The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that because the application of words follows the actual state of things, and because [the meaning] is dependent upon the speaker's intention, [your position] is not established?
How then can this not be so?"
Anticipating the question, "For what reason? he says:
"Because it is pure from the beginning," and so forth.
Its purity from the beginning means that from the very outset it is not corrupted by defects such as following after [defiled] causes.
Because it lacks the defect of maintaining a nature that is without cause, there is primordial purity (*ādipariśuddhatva*).
This is what was stated:

"If a being were both with cause and without cause, or if it were non-existent, how could there be the application of words according to the actual state of things (*yathāvastu*), by which the dependence on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣāparatantratva*) would not be established?"
Others, however, explain it otherwise:
a convention is established for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*), not out of mere habit.

And practical usage occurs because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is determined through the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), since the latter is not a real entity (*avastu*).

Therefore, since linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) is established with respect to a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no practical usage (*vyavahāra*) by means of that [characteristic], because it is not available at that time [of usage]. Thus, because its nature is unstained by the conceptualization of what is denoted by words, it is primordially pure (*ādi-viśuddhatva*). Furthermore, since convention is not established for that by which practical usage occurs—because that has been previously perceived—it is likewise primordially purified (*ādi-pariśuddhatva*) due to being untainted by defects.

Therefore, since it is impossible to employ words according to the actual state of things for the sake of conventional usage, it is not established that [the object] is dependent on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
Thus, while expressibility (*vācyatva*) has been refuted in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), its nature as a real entity (*vasturūpa*) has not.
Consequently, there is enumeration by way of conventional designation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛtyā*).
Others do not agree with the view that the intention of Śakra has been explained as merely illustrating the infinity of sentient beings through yoga and so forth.
They argue that [the text] says "by this as well," meaning not only by the previously mentioned mode of the infinity of sentient beings.
Ascertaining that no other alternative is possible, he states the following for the purpose of a conclusion:
"And thus again," and so forth.
The word "and" (ca) is used here in the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇa).
The negation of the aspect of conditions was established by means of the second [type of] infinity of sentient beings.
He states that the Dharma teaching of the Blessed Ones is not incomplete:
"Then indeed, those together with Indra," and so forth.

The leaders of the Sahā world-system of Brahmā, the lords of creatures, the world-protectors, and the sages such as Viśvāmitra and others— having realized the selflessness of both the grasped and the grasper through the teaching as it was spoken, however slight [their realization may have been]— approached and uttered words of exultation, praise, and the speech of rapture born of attainment. Thus they spoke.
He says that very thing with the words "Oh, what Dharma! and so forth,
[referring to] through the state of being a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
He says that Śakra and the others praised the Venerable Subhūti:
"He who [is the cause] of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
*Prādurbhāva* (manifestation) is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because by means of it, or from it, [the Tathāgata] becomes manifest.
By the phrase "with well-spoken words," it is indicated by way of connection as being intent upon faultless discourse;
it is taught by way of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
and it is elucidated by way of its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
That is elucidated from both perspectives.

He says, "The Tathāgata, that [suffering]," and so forth, meaning that by the very power of the Tathāgata, they have cultivated the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of the second moment regarding the origin (*samudaya*).
The thought is that [this is undertaken] for the sake of attaining the state of a Tathāgata with certainty.
"From today onwards" means starting from this very day.

"By this" means by that which consists of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). "Not separated" means because of not losing what has been attained. "He will dwell" means through the application of attaining meanings not yet attained.
This has been stated:

"For one established in the *prajñāpāramitā*, by virtue of the fact that form and so forth have the *dharmadhātu* as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there arises the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding the origin [of suffering] with all phenomena as its object, through the determination that they are the Tathāgata.
Thus, because this meaning was previously experienced during the stage of a bodhisattva, he says the following, placing it within his own hand:
"Thus it is," and so forth.
He states that very fact of having been previously experienced with the words beginning "When... and so on.
The king’s city is the royal capital.
A marketplace is a street of stalls.
"Young man" (māṇava) is a general term of address for a son of good family.
At that time, the Blessed One’s perception was thus:
"The future is time;
the future is the path."

"By incalculable eons" (*asaṃkhyeyaiḥ kalpaiḥ*) means by periods of time delimited by that number which is called "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyā*), situated at the sixty-fold place [in the decimal system]. This is the meaning.
Distinguishing him by means of his perfection as a Teacher, he says:
"Śākyamuni," and so forth;
because he took birth in the Śākya clan.

Śākyamuni is so called because his person is restrained through skill in all aspects and because he possesses the silence (*mauneya*) of body, speech, and mind. By means of this possession of silence, he demonstrates the defeat of the Māra, the son of a god, who was an obstacle to the perfection of his status as a Teacher (*śāstṛtva*).
This is because, by defeating him, he first attained the perfection of being a Teacher.
By these three terms—“Tathāgata,” “Arhat,” and “Samyaksambuddha”—he demonstrates the perfection of being a Teacher.
And that perfection of being a Teacher is twofold:
characterized by the quality of being a speaker and characterized by the quality of being a practitioner.
In this regard, because he speaks exactly as those dharmas are established and because he teaches the dharmas accordingly, his perfection of speech is described.
Furthermore, the perfection characterized by being a practitioner is twofold, distinguished by the perfections of knowledge and abandonment.
Therein, by the statement "the Arhat has slain the enemies," the perfection of abandonment is described.
And enemies are the afflictions such as passion and the like, in the sense that they destroy all wholesome qualities.
This perfection of abandonment was mentioned previously,
because the perfection of knowledge is preceded by it.
By the term "Samyaksambuddha" (Perfectly Awakened One), which refers to the complete and non-erroneous awakening to all phenomena, the perfection of knowledge is expressed;
for he is endowed with the attainment of the non-erroneous knowledge of an omniscient one.

Thus, by way of being the teacher of the non-erroneous Dharma, through the abandonment of all afflictions, and through the awakening to all aspects of phenomena, the unique and complete perfection of the Blessed One’s status as a Teacher has been described.
For instance, outsiders do not attain the status of teachers of the non-perverted Dharma,
because they have not abandoned all afflictions;
therefore, they are not true teachers.

Although the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are indeed teachers of reality (*bhūta-śāstṛ*) due to their abandonment of all afflictions, they are not teachers in every aspect (*sarvākāra-śāstṛ*), because they have not realized all phenomena in all their aspects.
However, it has been established that the Blessed One, by the reasoning already stated, is both a teacher of reality and a teacher in every aspect.
He now demonstrates that through which this perfection of being a teacher is obtained.
"Endowed with knowledge and conduct.
By this, he shows the cause for attaining the perfection of being a teacher. In that context, "knowledge" is right view.
The remaining factors, beginning with right resolve (*samyaksaṅkalpa*), constitute conduct (*caraṇa*).

The sense is that, having perceived reality through right view, one proceeds by means of those factors—right resolve and the rest—which constitute conduct; otherwise, seeing incorrectly and lacking conduct, one is unable to proceed.
Endowed and equipped with these two,
the training in higher wisdom is "knowledge," while the training in higher mind and higher morality is "conduct."

Since wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes the preliminary preparation (*pūrvaparikarma*), it is considered the "preliminary practice" (*puraścaraṇa*); however, the term "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is mentioned first because, through its purification, there is the purification of both ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For it is by means of wisdom that one sees as if with an eye, and by means of those two—ethical discipline and meditative concentration—that one proceeds as if with feet, thereby reaching the destination; thus, by the compound term *vidyācaraṇa*, the three trainings (*śikṣā*) are indicated.
And that twofold perfection of being a teacher is such as has been described; the Sugata expresses this by means of the term "Sugata.
For he has gone (gata) to an excellent (su) state of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment by means of the supramundane path.
The Sugata is like one who is handsome;
or, because he has gone [to liberation] without returning, he is the Sugata, like one whose fever has been completely cured;
or, because he has gone without remainder, he is the Sugata, like a jar that is perfectly full.
And these three meanings serve to distinguish [the Buddhas] from outsiders, those free from passion, and those in training (*śaikṣa*).
For, due to their perversion regarding a self (*ātmaviparyāsa*), outsiders who are free from passion have not gone to a beautiful state;
whereas those in training, because they still take up rebirth in saṃsāra, have not gone well.

Furthermore, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have not reached the state of being entirely free from all obscurations to knowledge regarding all objects of knowledge. And regarding this perfection of the status of a Teacher (*śāstṛtva*), there are two kinds of activity.
First, he demonstrates the activity of surveying the world to see who is capable and who is incapable [of liberation].
"He who knows the world" (lokavid): because of his thorough knowledge of the world of those capable [of liberation] and those incapable [of liberation], he is called "one who knows the world.

For in this way, the Blessed One surveys the world three times during the night and three times during the day with his Buddha-eye, in such modes as "Who is declining? Who is progressing? and so forth; thus he demonstrates the second activity, which is the training of those capable [of liberation].
"Unsurpassed charioteer of persons to be tamed":

having surveyed the worlds to see who is capable and who is incapable, the Blessed One disciplines those persons who are indeed to be tamed— those who are worthy, fit for taming, or capable of being tamed— because he has attained the state of their charioteer.
For "leading" (*vinayana*) is the state of being a charioteer;
it is like the charioteer of horses and so forth, because it removes [beings] from the wrong path and establishes them on the right path, and because it bestows specific virtues.
The inclusion of the term "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) is for the purpose of qualifying this state of being a charioteer.

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that he is the Guide even for certain individuals difficult to tame— those men to be disciplined who possess intense passion, hatred, delusion, and pride, such as Ārya Sundarānanda, Aṅgulimāla, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Mahārāja Kapphiṇa, and others. Furthermore, he shows where that activity of taming those capable of being tamed is situated.
"The Teacher of gods and humans.
Although the Blessed One is the teacher of all sentient beings without distinction by means of teaching the path to heaven and liberation,

nevertheless, it is primarily where the vision of the Noble Truths and the attainment of the fruits of asceticism are known that the Blessed One’s status as a teacher— his performance of the work of teaching— is established as being according to reality.
And gods and humans are his vessel;
therefore, he is called the Teacher of gods and humans.
"Wherein this greatness of qualities exists, that is the Buddha, the Blessed One"—this is the description of his essential nature.

In this context, he is called "Buddha" because his intellect (*buddhi*) is preeminent through its comprehension of all categories of existence (*padārtha*). Here, the suffix *a* (forming *buddha* from *buddhi*) is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *ārśas*, as that category is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
And his intellect is preeminent in nine ways: by means of the knowledge of an omniscient one,
by effortless knowledge,
and by untaught knowledge.
By means of the knowledge that abandons the obscurations of the afflictions along with their latent tendencies;
by means of the knowledge that abandons all obscurations to the knowable;
and by means of the power to accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings in every way.
Through the perfection of compassion, the perfection of inexhaustibility, and the perfection of the incomparable.
The Blessed One is so called because of his possession of complete sovereignty and other such qualities.
Furthermore, those sons of the gods, through the power of the Tathāgata, have again demonstrated the aspect of the third moment regarding the origin [of suffering];
thus he says, "It is wonderful," and so forth.

Although in reality it is of the nature of non-arising, the Perfection of Wisdom brings about the arising of omniscience through conventional truth; thus, because it transcends all foolish people, it is marvelous.
It is especially supremely marvelous compared to the Śrāvakas and others.

By the phrase "up to," there is the inclusion of the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth, as well as [the path] up to omniscience, and [the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena] regarding the origin [of suffering].

[This refers to] the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*). Regarding the term "producer" (*āhārikā*): it is that which brings about [the state] through the yoga of non-appropriation and non-abandonment.
Regarding the term "supportive" (*anuparigrāhikā*):
it means that which provides sustenance by way of not allowing any opportunity for those factors that create obstacles.
And so it is said in the *Madhyamā Prajñāpāramitā*:
“It is wonderful, Blessed One, how far the perfection of wisdom extends as the bringer and supporter of the knowledge of all aspects,
by means of the yoga of non-apprehension and non-abandonment,” and so forth.
This is what has been said:

"For a bodhisattva who abides in the perfection of wisdom by virtue of having the *dharmadhātu* as his intrinsic nature, there is no cultivation of grasping or abandoning with respect to all phenomena.
[This occurs] regarding the origin (*samudaya*) which has all phenomena as its object."
"Subsequently, the receptivity to subsequent knowledge arises."
The second chapter, titled "Śakra," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Third Chapter.

In order to establish the aspect of the fourth moment regarding the origin [of suffering], the Blessed One made certain sons of the gods belonging to the desire realm and other levels witnesses—since this is to be personally realized—and addressed others, saying:
"Whosoever," and so forth.
The terms "son of good family" (*kulaputra*) and "daughter of good family" (*kuladuhitṛ*) are words of honor.

The specific mention of "woman" and "man" is for the purpose of excluding those who are eunuchs, castrated, or otherwise lacking sexual organs. Furthermore, the non-acceptance of distinctions based on caste is for the purpose of making known the purity of all four castes.

The mention of "son" and "daughter" is for the purpose of making known that he possesses speech appropriate for those who have gone forth. The inclusion of the term "family" is for the purpose of making known that one endowed with noble lineage has the qualification for the True Dharma.

Ārya Vimuktisena states that the repetition of the word "again" (*punar*) is for the purpose of making known that even one of low birth who is capable (*bhavya*) has the qualification for this [path], due to the fault of their lot being destined to be experienced in a subsequent life (*upapadyāparaparyāyavedanīya*).
The phrase "this [knowledge]" refers to that which consists of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding the origin [of suffering].
In this context, Māra is the son of the gods (devaputra-māra), the deity of sensual desire (kāmadeva).
The sons of the gods belonging to his faction are the deities of Māra’s host (mārakāyika-devatā).
Because they perceive an opportunity for attack that has arisen, they are "those who look for an opening" (avatāraprekṣin).
Because they search for an entry point by investigating future opportunities, they seek an opening;
"opening" (avatāra) means a flaw, that is to say, a vulnerability.
"Nor even... The word "even" (api) serves as a conjunction in reference to what precedes it.
Beings comprised within the human realm of existence are humans.
Non-humans refer to yakṣas and the like.
Even when life remains, death occurs through some encounter with conditions— namely, the untimely passing away due to the failure to avoid dangers—
and none of this happens [for the noble one].
The thought is that this is because their mental continuum has been thoroughly cultivated by means of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
For it is said thus in the *Madhyamā Jinajananī*:

"By cultivating loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity through the yoga of non-apprehension, one attains immunity from interference by humans, non-humans, and so forth," and so on.
This has been stated:

"Preceded by the conviction that [phenomena] lack intrinsic nature, the four immeasurables are to be cultivated; in this way, the subsequent knowledge regarding the origin arises with all phenomena as its object."
Therefore, it was said by the noble Vimuktisena:

"For on the eighth moment of the path of seeing, there is a purpose for the Bodhisattva regarding the means of valid cognition; otherwise, he would strive for cessation in the ninth moment without regard for the realm of sentient beings.
He speaks now regarding the meaning of the aspect of the first moment of cessation.
"Furthermore," and so forth. "Set out" means having proceeded with the intention of their vows and so on.
"This" refers to that which sets forth the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
They will think— that is, they will know— that they must approach that son of good family for the purpose of hearing and so forth regarding the path of seeing, which has attained the ninth moment.
The thought is that he alone is capable [of teaching] through complete instruction, because he has realized the meaning of all the emptinesses due to having cultivated them thoroughly.
Regarding the phrase "one who grasps," and so forth:
the meaning is that he performs distinguished acts of grasping and so on, which serve as the cause for attaining progressively higher distinctions.
"They shall hear this *prajñāpāramitā*"—this is the connection with what precedes.
And "hearing" is the appearance in the form of teaching and listening, occurring through the conventional dominance of the realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Therefore, it should be understood as [hearing] from one who has arisen from the state of having been empowered by that realization.
Having indicated the aspect of cessation by means of describing one benefit, he speaks— strengthening that very same aspect by means of describing another benefit—
beginning with "And indeed, not...
The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), [implying] that there is not only the previously mentioned benefit.
The meaning is "another place. He has gone to, that is, reached, a location beyond five hundred bow-lengths from the village, which is a wilderness (*araṇya*).
Even a single tree is a cause of fear because it is inhabited by yakṣas and other spirits.
Therefore, "the root of that" refers to the root of a tree.
A house devoid of people and so forth is an empty dwelling (*śūnyāgāra*).
An uncovered place is an open space (*abhyavakāśa*).
The path is that which has been traveled by the great multitude; the wrong path is a route contrary to what has been said;
and beyond the forest is the wilderness (*aṭavī*).
Regarding the passage "as he approaches and goes to various places such as the forest," he speaks of that very thing while describing the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*),
beginning with "while walking" and so forth,
up to "seated" and "lying down."
Fear is the apprehension that an undesirable thing will befall one.
Stupefaction is the failure to take action to counteract it.
Because it comes into being where it previously did not exist, it will come to pass.
"It will arise through the continuity of the stream"—
this is connected with what precedes it [by the word "not"].
The thought is that this is because all forms of emptiness have been thoroughly cultivated.
It is also stated elsewhere:
"The bodhisattva who is embraced by emptiness becomes free from all fears," and so forth.
This is what was said:

"Because emptiness is the very intrinsic nature of form and so forth by their very nature, the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises with respect to cessation when all phenomena are taken as its object.
Regarding cessation, he speaks for the sake of the second moment:
"Then indeed, the four," and so forth.

The great kings, Virūḍhaka and the others, are marvelous in that they discipline beings within the three vehicles— such as the Śrāvaka vehicle— by means of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), even while lacking the perception of beings within the three vehicles from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tāttvika*).

By this, through the reliance on the two truths and the demonstration of the capacity to accomplish the welfare of beings in all its aspects, it is indicated by the explanation of the efficient cause (*samarthakāraṇa*) that the very fruit of the undertaking and so forth of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is Buddhahood itself.
This is what is to be grasped. Therefore, this has been stated:

"The fruit of roots of merit dedicated to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is the attainment of the state of a Tathāgata; thus, when all phenomena are focused upon, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) arises regarding cessation."
"Us," and so forth.
This was spoken in order to make known the majesty of the *Prajñāpāramitā*,
to make known [the author's] own service to the teaching, and to make known his gratitude toward the Blessed One.

"Unwholesome karma is of three kinds: to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*), and to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
Protection, defense, and guardianship have been explained respectively as the counteracting of the afflictions caused by that [karma].
Alternatively, when misfortune occurs through divine power, it is the operation of unwholesome [karma] alone.
It is not understood as belonging to another,
such as the occurrence of pestilence, famine, or the fall of thunderbolts and the like;
for in this human calamity, the activity of living beings is perceived as being present.
Nor is [the role] of fate understood,
because there is no fruit whatsoever without action, just as when a crop has already been produced, famine and the like may still occur due to the harassment of a foreign army.
In a misfortune where the operation of both the divine and the human is perceived, action consists of just this much: the divine and the human. As it has been said:

"For it is divine and human action that sustains the world"; thus, protection (*rakṣā*), defense (*āvaraṇa*), and guardianship (*gupti*) have been stated in their respective order as remedies for those two.
"We shall provide" means we shall do.
Establishing a connection for the sake of the third moment regarding cessation, he says:
"It is wonderful, O Blessed One," and so forth.

One obtains these aforementioned qualities and benefits—which are defined by the number of protections, shields, and guardians, and which pertain to the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmika*)—being comprised within the current birth, during the stage of application (*prayogāvasthā*).
He grasps [the object] during the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭhāvasthā*).
Having thus explained the connection, he speaks in order to produce the meaning of the mental aspect (*ākāra*), beginning with the words "But what... and so forth.

Furthermore, when it should have been stated that "when the perfection of wisdom is taken up, the five perfections beginning with generosity are included," why is the expression "six perfections" used?
This is said with the intention that even the perfection of wisdom which has a secondary nature is included within the primary perfection of wisdom;
for it is only through the non-erroneous realization of all phenomena that the primary perfection of wisdom arises.
Therefore, with the intention that all factors of purification are subsumed by that very [emptiness], the Blessed One said,
"It is so," and so forth.
This is what was stated.
"The perfection of wisdom is the synthesis of all modes of antidotes; thus, with respect to cessation as the object of all phenomena, the receptivity to subsequent knowledge arises.
Thus he speaks, indicating the aspect of the fourth moment regarding cessation.
"Furthermore," and so forth.
"Listen," and so forth, has already been explained.
Alternatively, since it is auspicious from the very beginning by virtue of being the cause of devotion, therefore listen well.
Since it is auspicious in the middle because it is a cause of nourishment, listen well to that;
and since it is auspicious at the conclusion by being a cause of liberation, attend to it with proper mental attention (*yoniso manasikāra*).
Alternatively, the words "well" and so forth are used respectively because they serve as the remedies for faults of weak, middling, and superior degrees.
Alternatively, there is the statement regarding the "virtuous" and so forth, which determines the phoneme, the meaning, or both, according to their respective order.

Regarding the phrase "the Dharma" and so on: one should grasp and take up the Dharma consisting of the Sūtras and other teachings; then, having grasped it with the mind, one should speak it in contradiction [to others] and dispute it verbally.
In these two ways, one should oppose and dismantle [the obstacles].

Alternatively, following the phrase "they will consider" (*maṃsyante*), the three terms beginning with "it should be analyzed" (*vigrahītavya*)—referring to the dismantling and reconstitution of both the phrasing and the meaning—should be supplied, starting from the point that the Bodhisattva who delights in the meditation on the Mother of the Jinas is the subject;
for it is the enumeration of his benefits alone that is the topic under discussion, as he will explain immediately thereafter.
"Those legal disputes of his, as they arise one after another, will disappear," and so forth.
They will disappear, meaning they will become invisible; for they will not remain, as they will find no standing through reasoning.

For this very reason, their intentions and desires will not reach fulfillment or completion. [One might ask: "But how can a thought that has arisen disappear without a counter-measure? Anticipating this question, he says:
"Thus indeed it is," and so forth.
By this, the following is stated:

this is the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), namely, that [the non-arising of the afflictions occurs] by virtue of the person who cultivates the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) being the basis.
"The resolution regarding them arises from themselves alone"—
this is explained by the passage beginning with "he will grasp," and so forth.
Alternatively, by hearing the summary, he will grasp it;
by mental attention, he will retain it;
and by reading the book, he will recite it.
By grasping the meaning of the text, he will master it;

by stating matters that are not contradicted by direct perception, inference, or scripture, he will respectively set it in motion, teach it, and instruct upon it— or rather, by teaching the non-arising of the three kinds of entities, beginning with the imagined (*parikalpita*).
One will master [the text] through the instruction of the mere recitation;
one will study it through practice during the first watch of the night and so forth.
These acts of grasping and so on should be correctly performed with a variety of intentions, such as the dedication toward awakening.
"Legal cases" (*adhikaraṇa*) refers to points of dispute.
Concluding [the discussion], he says:
"This too," and so forth.
The word "also" (api) indicates that it is not only the quality about to be described.
Having thus established that the perfection of wisdom possesses the power and majesty that pacifies all calamities, he says "Just as if," and so forth, to support this point through an illustration.
In some places, the reading is *parikalpam upādāya*, which refers to a specific effect arising from a specific possible cause;
by this, its rarity is indicated,
because it removes poisons from stationary objects and the like.
The phrase "the pacifier of all poisons" describes its essential nature.
"By a venomous serpent" means by a living creature possessing venom in its fangs.

Regarding the passage beginning with "by one who is hungry" (*bubhukṣitena*): even though someone might be tormented by hunger, they might act as if engaged in the propitiation of a deity, thinking that food is not the purpose [of their action]. To exclude such a possibility, he says:
The phrase "seeking food" is used; however,
since even one in such a state might seek food by resorting to fortitude, the term "searching for food" is stated in order to exclude that possibility.
"A creature born as a living being" means a being reckoned among sentient beings, such as a frog and so forth.
"By smell" means by the odor of raw meat and the like inherent in that [creature].
"One would bind [it]" means...
One should accept it as food with the understanding;
"one should follow" means one should go after or behind.
"Pratyudāvarteta" means that one should turn back.
Now, one might ask: "In a case where [the wind] does not turn back by the scent of living beings, how could it turn back by the scent of medicinal herbs?
Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason?", he says:
"Thus, for instance," and so forth.
This is the meaning of the sentence:

even within the conventional realm of cause and effect, that very medicinal plant possesses such a therapeutic quality that its potency overcomes the venom of that specific poisonous snake and no other; thus, indeed, powerful is that medicine.
"Even though there is diversity, some things are determined by their own nature, like the sense faculties and so forth.
This has been stated:
"By the perfection of wisdom alone is there the pacification of external and internal calamities; thus, when cessation occurs with all phenomena as its object..."
"Subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) arises.
To explain the aspect of the first moment regarding the Path, he says:
"In this way, in this way," and so forth.
The phrase *yāni tāni* is a collection of particles used in the sense of "whatever [they may be]. Regarding *tejasā* and so forth:

the very power (*sāmarthya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā* constitutes its brilliance (*tejas*), strength (*bala*), stamina (*sthāma*), and empowerment (*balādhāna*), which are designated respectively as the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), seeing (*darśana-mārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the special path (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
"From that very place" means: they will cease right where they were about to arise.
They will come to rest.
"They will be pacified;
they will not increase"— this should be understood respectively at the times of hearing, reflection, and cultivation,
or else as referring to the stages of preparation and so forth.
Explaining that very point, he says:
"From which," and so forth;
"from whichever," and so forth.
"In whatever place" means "in whatever location or basis.
The three words "will cease," "will disappear," and "will not remain" have the same meaning as the three words beginning with "will desist."
Now, one might ask: "How can a thought that has arisen not exist without another's response?
Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason?", he states the refutation as before, beginning with "Because of the perfection of wisdom," and so forth.

In the phrase "of passion and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes defects (doṣa) and the rest; by the word "as far as" (yāvat), there is the inclusion of attachment to the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and so on.
Regarding the phrase "of the grasping at nirvāṇa":
it refers to the adherence to both nirvāṇa with remainder (sopadhi) and nirvāṇa without remainder (nirupadhi).
It is "pacifying" because it uproots the persistent attachment to nirvana and so forth;
or alternatively, it is "not increasing" because it completely eradicates the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of passion and the like.
This is what has been stated.

"The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom itself is the pacification of the attachment to passion and so forth as being nirvāṇa; thus, the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñānakṣānti) arises regarding the path that takes all phenomena as its object.
To explain the second moment regarding the path, he says:
"And the four," and so forth.
Protection (*rakṣā*), defense (*āvaraṇa*), and guarding (*gupti*) have been explained.
Alternatively, protection, defense, and guarding should be understood respectively with reference to obstacles that are divine (*ādhidevika*), elemental (*ādhibhautika*), and personal (*ādhyātmika*).

Or else, misfortune (*āpad*) is threefold: that arising from one's own causes, that arising from causes reckoned as belonging to other beings, and that arising from causes reckoned as belonging to beings other than oneself.
The protection, defense, and guardianship resulting from its remedy are to be understood respectively as follows:

it has been stated that for one engaged in the undertaking of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and so forth, there arise from the Tathāgatas and others all forms of protection, defense, and guardianship; thus, by means of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, on the path which has all phenomena as its object—
"The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) arises.
Regarding the third moment on the path, he says:
"Furthermore, Kauśika," and so forth.

And [he is one] whose speech is authoritative because, out of compassion, having himself first abstained from taking life and so forth, he abides in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and establishes others therein;
and because he speaks in praise of those who have themselves set out [on that path] and approves of them, his speech is authoritative— this is the meaning.
It must be accepted otherwise, because it is impossible for his words to be anything other than authoritative;
this is also stated in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*.
