"He will himself abstain from taking life," beginning thus, up to—"he will speak in praise of others and approve of them"—in this way he will have speech that is acceptable; because it produces pleasure for the ear, his speech is gentle.
Because he speaks only as much as is necessary for the purpose, his speech is measured.
Because he is skilled in concise speech, his words are not diffuse;
he is neither overcome by anger nor overcome by pride when [an opponent] is present.
Anger (*krodha*) is a mental resentment directed toward a specific object that belongs to the category of aversion (*pratigha*).
Pride (*māna*) is the inflation of the mind based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
[Objection: But if there is no removal of faults without an antidote, how can such an arising of qualities occur for that very person?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?
he says, "For it is thus," and so forth.
The perfection of wisdom alone is the antidote to all faults.
And the thought is that it has been cultivated by him.
He tames [the mind] by establishing it in the abstention from taking life and so forth;
he transforms it by making it humble toward the sphere of all sentient beings through measured speech and other such means.
Regarding "enmity" (*upanāha*):
it is the non-abandonment of the latent tendency toward hostility.
Enmity is indeed a part of resentment (*pratigha*).
Regarding "ill-will" (vyāpāda): ill-will is malice toward sentient beings, toward sufferings, and toward those factors that are conducive to suffering.
Regarding "latent tendency" (anuśaya):
The latent tendency (*anuśaya*) is a continuous stream of enmity characterized by hatred.
This is what has been said:

"By the power of embracing the *prajñāpāramitā* alone, one who desires Buddhahood, having personally established themselves in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) preceded by the abstention from taking life and so forth, establishes others in that very same state."
"The path that has all phenomena as its object arises as the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*), [thinking] 'this is what must be done.
Thus he speaks in order to describe the aspect of the fourth moment regarding the path.
"Practicing in this way," and so forth; that is,
practicing in this manner while dwelling in the path through the subsequent-knowledge-acceptance (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Mindfulness is the non-forgetting of a familiar object by the mind.
Loving-kindness is the absence of hatred toward all sentient beings, characterized by the attitude of affection felt for an only son.

By means of these two, through the yoga of non-apprehension regarding all wholesome qualities such as generosity, and by way of not sharing them with any sentient beings, the dedication toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment is described as being twofold.
He speaks specifically of the activity of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "it occurs to him thus," the phrase "they will shatter" refers to causing a distortion of the eyes and other faculties through the manifestation of ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
The phrase "they will burn" means that [the body] will be consumed by fire through the loss of its own essential nature (*svarūpa-pracyuti*).
"Under one's control" (*vaśam*) means being dependent upon that.
This is what has been stated:

"By one who wishes to make acts such as giving inexhaustible, the dedication [of merit] must be performed through the power of mindfulness and so forth during the two correct compressions (*samyaksambādha*); thus, on the path which takes all phenomena as its object..."
"...the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) arises.
There is no disagreement here that the sixteen moments arise with exactly the aspects as previously stated, which were indicated by way of reference to others.
And so it has been said:
Because there is no relationship of container and contained between suchness and the Buddha, they are not admitted as being successive;
that is their greatness, their immeasurability. (12)
The non-existence of a limit to quantity is the definitive determination of form and so forth;
for one established in that, there is Buddhahood.
The non-grasping and non-abandoning of [the aggregates], and so forth. ||13||
The attainment of emptiness through loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] is the embracing of Buddhahood;
it is the purification of everything and the destruction of all mental anguish and disease. ||14||

The pacification of grasping at nirvāṇa, protection from the Buddhas and so forth, beginning with the non-killing of living beings, [are taught] in the manner of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). //15//
"Establishing beings who are themselves established [in the path],

and the dedication of generosity and so forth toward perfect enlightenment— these are the moments of the knowledge of the path (mārgajñatā). (16) Thus, for this path of seeing as well, the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) taught in the context of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) should be understood to apply here.

If it is asked: "If that is so, since the path of vision and so forth of the Bodhisattvas is already established there by the mention of the stages such as the Joyous (pramuditā) and others, for what purpose is it mentioned again? It is said in reply:

This is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that the path described for the Sons of the Conquerors (jinaputra) is not the same as that of the Tathāgatas, because the term "knowledge of all aspects" (sarvākārajñatā) is used for the Tathāgatas with reference to their attainment of the complete cause and fruit.

From that very [context], having extracted the mere cause, the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*)—consisting of the paths of vision and so forth for the sons of the Victors—is established separately.
However, the wise should investigate this:
whether the aspects (*ākāra*) have been formulated in accordance with the *Kārikās* and in conformity with the meaning of the text or not.
In this regard, having examined the commentaries of Ārya Vimuktisena and others, I have presented [this work] according to my own ability.

Some, however, maintain that by means of the aforementioned composition of the treatise, they did not state the meaning of the aspects (*ākāra*) with a different underlying intention, but merely imitated the sixteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). This should be understood as applying to those treatises which are intent upon explaining the meanings of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), both those already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned.
Others [object]: "Since they do not explain the sequence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, no specific order of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) has been presented.
Furthermore, how is the meaning of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-kārikā* to be explained?

For the host of afflictions such as attachment has its root in the adherence to the existence of things (*bhāvābhiniveśa*), and the practice of selflessness (*nairātmya*) is its opposite; therefore, without that [practice], how can there be the 'receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering' (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth?"

It is not so; for all these sixteen aspects, which are intended to indicate selflessness according to the method already described, have been taught in the various forms mentioned above out of a desire to establish the welfare of the disciples present.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that when practiced in this manner, they give rise to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) by virtue of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*); and the same applies elsewhere as well.

Since the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is to be explained immediately after the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and because the activity of the path of cultivation must first be described— given that there is little more to be said about it and because disciples are inclined toward its fruit—
the text says, "It is wonderful, O Blessed One," and so forth.
"Perfection of Wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*) refers to the path of cultivation that is about to be discussed.

"Present for the sake of complete subduing" means that it has become manifest as the cause for complete subduing in the sense of subduing [the mind] in every respect by bringing all types of afflictions under its own control; this is the first activity of subduing.
"For the sake of non-inflation" means...

The second activity of bowing (*namana-kāritra*) is for the purpose of bowing down in every respect; it consists in the prohibition of self-exaltation through the negation of pride (*ahaṃkāra*) regarding even a slight degree of realization that is distinguished by its immediate succession to *damanā*.
Immediately after that, there is the overcoming of all forms of afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, he speaks for the sake of the third activity, the conquest of afflictions (*kleśa-nirjaya-kāritra*).
"Furthermore, O Kauśika," and so forth. "Grasping it thus" means by way of the sequence of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) that is about to be described.
"Battle," and so forth.

This means that while engaged in a conflict with the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), he has ascended to the forefront of the battle by attaining the first type of antidote (*pratipakṣa*), which is the "weak-weak" level, as the counteragent to the first triad of adversaries, which is the "strong-strong" level. Thus, he is mounted upon the head of the battle.

The three phrases beginning with "avatarata" (descending) should be explained according to their respective order as the attainment of the remedies—namely, the moderate-weak and other types—which counteract the second triad of adversaries, such as the moderate-intense and others.
"Of one who has entered the midst of battle" refers to the acquisition of the intense-weak remedy for the weak-intense adversary.
"Of one who stands [in battle]" refers to the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the intense-moderate remedy for the moderate-weak adversary, for one who is stationed in the battle.
"Of one who is seated" refers to one who is seated for battle, because the extremely weak counter-factors have attained equality with the supreme antidotes.

By all of this—namely, the abandonment of the nine types of counter-factors and the acquisition of their antidotes—he declares that the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is no longer to be performed.
"No possibility" means impossibility.
He says that very thing [in the phrase] "there is no opportunity.
If it is asked for what purpose this synonymous expression is used, it is said:
it is for the sake of someone’s understanding of the meaning in some way, both at that time and in the future.

If that very [word] were used to express the meaning, only those who had not heard it before would experience confusion; therefore, to avoid that fault, [the word is repeated] so that those who were distracted at the earlier time and those who arrived later may hear its meaning,
and for those of dull intellect, so that they may repeatedly discern its meaning,
since a single word may have multiple meanings.
This is for the purpose of eliminating the conceptualization of [the word] as having a different referent;
for the purpose of ensuring the correct understanding of that meaning through those designations elsewhere, like a glossary;
and for the purpose of bringing about skill in the composition and delivery of meaningful discourse by those who preach the Dharma.

For the purpose of manifesting one's own analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), and for the purpose of planting the seeds of that [knowledge] in others—these eight purposes are what is meant by "teaching through synonyms" (*paryāyadeśanā*); this should be stated in the same way in all cases.
As for the phrase "that which belongs to him":
The particle *yat* functions in the sense of *yaḥ* (who/which). The meaning of the sentence is: "That which is an obstacle to life is [called] 'without opportunity' (*anavakāśa*)."
"Obstruction to life" means the severance of the continuity of consciousness.
"The subsiding of external calamities immediately following the disappearance of internal afflictions" means being invulnerable to the attacks of others.
He states the fourth activity with the words "by the assault of another," and so forth.
"Another" refers to a human being or the like; "assault" refers to the inflicting of blows with weapons such as swords and the like.
Explaining this heading (*uddeśapada*) by means of its detailed exposition (*nirdeśa*), he says: "If, however," and so forth.

If it is asked, "Since there is no subject matter distinct from the detailed exposition of the statements of the headings, for what purpose are the statements of the headings [formulated]?"—it is replied:
In brief, it is for the purpose of ascertaining the detailed meaning through a summary— just as one ascertains the meaning of a commentary by means of its root text—
and for the benefit of disciples who possess ready intelligence (*udghaṭitajña*),
as well as for the sake of accumulating the causes for others to attain ready intelligence in the future.

Master Vasubandhu states that this is for the purpose of demonstrating his own mastery in teaching both the concise and the detailed [explanations], and for the purpose of planting the seeds of such practice in others. Furthermore,

since the minds of yogins are concentrated on what is merely concise, the teaching of the detailed exposition is intended to show how their minds may become concentrated everywhere regarding its extensive meaning.

Likewise, since the minds of yogins are concentrated upon mere extensiveness, how could they be concentrated everywhere upon its condensed meaning? It is for this purpose that there is the teaching of the summary (uddeśa), according to the tradition.
This should be understood in the same way in all cases.
"Weapon" refers to the discus and so forth.
[This refers to] other things such as stones and the like.

Now, one might ask: "If a weapon or similar object is thrown by a person who lacks the power to hurl it to that specific location, why does it not fall upon the body in the interim, provided there is no intervening obstacle? Anticipating this question, he says:
"This is a great vidyā," and so forth.
This is the intended meaning:

by the power of the Mother herself, who possesses such a nature as that of a great vidyā and so on, while she is being recited, an arrow or the like does not reach her body because of the immediate onset of a contradiction with the quality of weight.

The three terms beginning with "Great Knowledge" (*mahāvidyā*) apply to the stages of practice and so forth due to its association with qualities such as greatness. It is "unsurpassed" (*anuttarā*) because there is no superior state through mental engagements such as resolute belief; it is "unequaled" (*asamā*) because there is no equal in terms of accomplishment;
and it is "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasamā*) because, through ultimate purity, it is equal to that which is unequal to other mental continua.
"How is it that this [perfection] is indeed the 'Great Knowledge' (mahāvidyā) and so forth?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For here, O Kauśika," and so on.
This is what is meant: "Because one training in the *prajñāpāramitā* preceded by loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth does not train for the sake of malice or the like toward anyone;
therefore, since it removes the causes of short life and so forth such as violence, it has the nature of great knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) and the rest."
"He does not intend for his own harm" means that he does not strive toward [actions] such as killing himself.
Immediately after the disappearance of all calamities, he states the fifth activity, which is the activity of attaining perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "atra hi," etc.:
"He will perfectly awaken to complete enlightenment" means that he will directly realize the realization of reality (*tattva*).
"And he will obtain the knowledge of the omniscient one" means that subsequent to the realization of reality, he will attain the knowledge whose object is all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
Explaining that very point, he says:
"By him, [the state of] unsurpassed... and so forth.
By the term "minds" (*cittāni*), there is an inclusion of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) by way of illustration.
"He will behold" means he will know.
But surely all yogic cognition is held to be without an object;
how then will he cognize all phenomena?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?
he says: "In this regard, Kauśika," and so forth.
He has attained [the goal] through the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), because of the abandonment of the two veils along with their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
It is "known" through the path of liberation by virtue of the attainment of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is "realized" through pure mundane knowledge (*śuddhalaukikajñāna*) by way of certainty.
This is what has been stated.

For just as the cognition of one who sees a true dream— though ultimately devoid of an object— arises by the power of a specific basis with the form of a particular object and independent of signs or scripture, yet remains non-contradictory because it leads to the attainment of the object displayed;

so too, through the power of practicing the yoga of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the cognition of a yogi [perceives] a past, present, or future entity exactly as it was, is, or will be, even if it is imagined by another.

In the same way, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it has arisen as non-contradictory, with a clear manifestation whose form appears as if external, displaying a manifold proliferation of various aspects and modes, and which is independent of inferential signs (*liṅga*) or scripture (*āgama*). Consequently,
since the Blessed One is thus admitted to have direct vision regarding everything, there is nothing that he has not attained, has not known, or has not directly realized.

The knowledge of the Omniscient One is said to consist in the absence of that [duality]; for even when error has ceased, the cessation of mental aspects is impossible due to the lack of a necessary connection— so say Ārya Nāgārjuna and others, following the Madhyamaka method.

Because of the connection with an excellence of faith and the greatness of merit, that place where the realization of the Tathāgatas and others has occurred is worthy of worship. Immediately following the function of awakening, he speaks of the sixth function—the worthiness of worship of the place that is the support for the perfection of wisdom—saying:
"Furthermore, Kauśika, in whatever place this... and so forth.
"At least" (*antaśaḥ*) refers, by way of general principle, to the ripening of prior karma— that is,
the ripening of karma that is certain to be experienced unless countered by the cultivation of its antidote.
Strengthening this very point regarding the reality of things by means of an illustration, he says:
"Namely, for example," and so forth.
The "seat of awakening" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) refers here to that specific location on the earth which is its essence (*sāra*).
The *bodhimaṇḍa* is that which is occupied by one seated in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*). Those who have gone there are those who rely upon its periphery.
The region of the ground situated within the four vajra-piles located at the intermediate corners around the vicinity of the *bodhimaṇḍa* is the *bodhimaṇḍa*;
thus the *bodhimaṇḍa* has been explained.
The interior of that is the central location.
Because it is understood by including the immediate vicinity of the root that has entered the ground, the portion of the tree extending outward from that is the "root of the tree.
"They cannot be [cut]" means:
The meaning is that these objects are not suitable for them;
[to] "viheṭhayitum" means to disturb or break apart;
"vyāpādayitum" means to cause harm or incite enmity.
"To cause possession" means to cause the entry of spirits, grahas, and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Since the location has no agency in preventing the arising of affliction and the like, how is it that one will not be able to inflict affliction and so forth there? Anticipating this question with the words "for what reason," he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra hi*),

the meaning of the sentence is as follows: those who, for the sake of all sentient beings, personally and respectfully cultivate for a long duration and without interruption the various forms of loving-kindness (*maitrī*)— which are free from fear, enmity, and terror— as the antidote to weak, medium, and intense malice (*vyāpāda*).
And they reveal it with reference to others.

Because those Buddhas of the three times arise there, that place has become truly distinguished; therefore, due to the inconceivability of the totality of causes and conditions, and by virtue of the majesty of the site, it is impossible to perform acts such as harassment there through the production of defective causes, owing to the power of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*).
Having thus presented the illustration, he says "In this very way," and so forth, in order to present the illustrated meaning,
with the same intention as before.
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?",
he speaks as follows, refuting it by means of demonstrating the greatness of the location:
"Indeed, by this very [means]," and so forth.
It is "caitya-like" because it serves as a cause for the accumulation of merit through acts such as prostration.

Some maintain that the phrase "that spot of earth is caitya-like" uses the word *bhūta* (become/like) as a term of comparison—meaning "like a father" (*pitṛbhūta*)—and thus it is "caitya-like" by virtue of being equal to other caityas.

For indeed, when a portion of ground is considered a stūpa because it is empowered by the verse beginning "Those phenomena which arise from causes," which illuminates the selflessness of persons, then [how much more so] a place empowered by the verse that reveals the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) in all things?
Because a stūpa is endowed with the mother’s [relics] through enshrining and so forth, it is all the more so;

thus Candragomin says that since it is the very nature of the witness, it is "the witness itself" (*sākṣibhūta*), and since it is the very nature of the shrine, it is "the shrine itself" (*caityabhūta*);
it is "to be venerated" because of being an object of homage.
He is to be honored through great respect by recollecting his virtues;
he is to be worshipped and venerated through soft, medium, and superior forms of worship, respectively.
He is worthy of being honored; he is worthy of being treated with respect by being established in a special position through the binding of the auspicious turban and other such rites;
and he is worthy of being revered as one who must not be transgressed in any way.
It is a protection (*trāṇa*) by way of warding off all calamities;
it is a refuge (*śaraṇa*) by way of being the basis for its application and the state of its non-futility;
it is a resting place (*layana*) by way of being an object of blameless delight.
It is the ultimate refuge because it is the state and station for attaining supreme nobility.
According to the principle already stated, its activity should be understood as being of exactly six kinds.
And so it has been said:
"Subduing in every respect," "victory over all afflictions," "incapability of being harmed by attacks," "awakening," and "the venerability of the support"—
after these functions, the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) must be explained. (17)

And that is twofold, distinguished by being with-outflows (sāsrava) or without-outflows (anāsrava). Among these, the one with-outflows is threefold, characterized by mental application (manaskāra) consisting of resolute belief (adhimukti), dedication (pariṇāmanā), and rejoicing (anumodanā).
Furthermore, the untainted realization (*anāsrava-abhinirhāra*), which has the nature of ultimate purity, is twofold.

Therefore, according to the [eight] liberations (*vimokṣa*), it is based upon the wholesome dharmas seen [in the preceding stage]; because it pertains to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it initially takes the form of non-direct realization (*asākṣātkriyā*).
Resolute belief (*adhimukti*) must be explained.

That too, being threefold by way of its fundamental divisions—as pertaining to one’s own welfare, to the welfare of both oneself and others, and to the welfare of others—becomes ninefold through the division of each into weak, medium, and intense.
That is to say: weak, medium, and intense resolute belief for one’s own welfare; likewise, resolute belief for the welfare of both oneself and others, and resolute belief for the welfare of others.

In this way, this ninefold [classification] of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), being divided each into nine types starting from "weak-weak" (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) and so forth, becomes twenty-sevenfold by means of these three sets of nine.
For example:
weak-weak.
Mild-middling;
mild-supreme; middling-mild.
The medium-medium;
the medium-intense;
the intense-weak.
The medium-strong,
and the strong-strong—
thus, nine types of resolute belief regarding one's own welfare are to be understood, as well as those regarding the welfare of both oneself and others, and the welfare of others.
In that regard, with reference to the weakest-weak degree of conviction regarding one's own welfare, he says:
"When this was said, Śakra... and so forth.
"With divine [songs]" means with those that are agreeable to the mind.
Muktakusuma is loose flower.
Dhūpa is incense such as sahaja, sāṃyojika, and so forth.
Gandha is fragrance originating from Malaya and other sources.
A garland fashioned from flowers of all seasons is *mālya*.
A method of rubbing the body with fragrant substances is *vilepana*. It is also the powder of gold dust and other such materials.
Vastra refers to the monastic robe (cīvara);
sitātapatra and so forth refer to the parasol;
and dhvaja refers to a banner marked with the emblem of Garuḍa or others.
The bell is marked with a vajra and so forth;
the banner is devoid of symbols.
"By various kinds" [is meant].
With various kinds of foods, edibles, and so forth;
some say that "bodies" refers to form-bodies (*rūpakāya*),
while others say they are the elements (*dhātu*).
"One should establish" means one should place [it].
"One should accept" means one should take possession of it as one's own.
"Should preserve" means he should cause them to endure for a long time.
"And those" refers to the stūpas; by the word "and," it is not only the physical remains that are meant.
In order to demonstrate that by means of those very words there is greater merit in the worship of the Mother, he asks Śakra a counter-question, beginning with "For that reason... and so forth:
"The embodiment of omniscience..."
"Brought forth" means that the nature of a body capable of attaining the knowledge of an omniscient one has been produced. "In which practice? refers to this.
The meaning is: "On which path?
Intending to show that liberation is impossible without the perfection of wisdom because the cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*) would not cease, he says:
"Right here, O Blessed One," and so forth.
By attaining the foremost state among those [states] like a diamond, which has the nature of fitness, it is realized;
immediately thereafter, it is fully awakened.
Alternatively, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is fully awakened.
Therefore, it should be understood that "omniscience is attained.
In this context, unsurpassed enlightenment is the perfection of one's own welfare,
while omniscience is the perfection of the welfare of others.
Now, refuting [the objection] by means of that very statement, he says:
"Therefore, then," and so forth.
"Self-existence" (*ātmabhāva*) is the body itself, or the body belonging to it, according to the logical principle: "the body of a stone statue."
Since that very [nature] is what is attained, it is called "attainment" (*pratilambha*); because of that, one does not enter into the category of being a "Tathāgata.
For there is the notion that all beings have already attained the state of a Tathāgata.
If so, how then is one a "Tathāgata"? To this he says:
"Regarding omniscience," and so forth;
he speaks of another quality as well:
"This which, Kauśika," and so forth.

"Being the basis for the knowledge of the omniscient one" means that it serves as the cause for the accomplishment of the knowledge of the omniscient one in others. Explaining this very point, he says:
"Enam," and so forth; "enam" refers to this acquisition of the physical body as a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
"Prabhāvanā" means manifestation.
The Buddha is characterized by the nature of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and so forth; the Dharma consists of the sūtras and other teachings;
and the Saṅgha is the assembly of bodhisattvas, such as those who are irreversible from the noble state.
"Even for one who has entered final nirvāṇa"— by the word "even," it is implied that this applies to one who is still living.
Having explained this in detail, he concludes by saying:
"Therefore, then, Kauśika," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: if the Tathāgata is superior to all others, how is it that even though he is the cause [of the teaching], there is greater merit in honoring his Mother?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?
he says, "Because of the omniscient gnosis," and so forth.
This is the meaning of the sentence.
According to the principle that "the perfection of wisdom is non-dual gnosis, and that is the Tathāgata," the Tathāgata as the *dharmakāya* is primarily the perfection of wisdom; therefore,
by worshipping the Mother who illuminates it, one generates far more merit than by worshipping the omniscient gnosis of the *dharmakāya*.
However, regarding worship of the Tathāgata as a reflection in a physical form (*rūpakāya*), there is no greater merit because it does not encompass the particularly distinguished *dharmakāya*.
Having taught that the merit is greater for one who worships after having written [the scripture], he explains the same principle even for the act of writing itself, saying:
"Whosoever, son of good family," and so forth.
As before, having raised the doubt as to the reason for this,
he provides the answer in the same manner, saying:
"For it is the knowledge of the Omniscient One," and so forth.
In order to demonstrate the second type, which is of a mild-moderate degree, he asks, beginning with "O Blessed One, those who... and so forth.
"They will not know" means that they do not comprehend the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*).
"Of great purpose" means that the accumulation of merit is the great purpose; she is "purposeful" because she brings that about.
"They will not understand" means...
Because of the lack of realization regarding the equipment of knowledge (*jñāna-sambhāra*).
The equipment of knowledge possesses great benefit; by virtue of being its cause, it is "of great benefit," "of great fruit," and "of great maturation."

The form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) are, respectively, the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of the accumulations of merit and wisdom; it is said thus because they are produced from them.
And [it is said] "they will not experience [them]," because there is no realization of the fruits of merit and wisdom.
Furthermore, they will not have faith because they lack conviction regarding the results of karma and so forth.
Having answered the question by means of that very statement, he asks a counter-question in order to demonstrate the mild and medium types [of beings], saying:
"What do you think, Kauśika, how many... and so on.
"By means of serene confidence through realization" (*avetyaprasāda*):
some say that serene confidence preceded by the recognition of qualities is "serene confidence through realization," because it arises from the abandonment of doubt.
For one who has seen the reality, faith in the Three Jewels and the fourth, the noble-loved ethical discipline (*āryakānta-śīla*), is what others call "clear confidence" (*avetyaprasāda*).
Considering that each subsequent [stage] possesses greater merit due to its connection with an excellence of superior vigor and so forth, he expresses his agreement by saying,
"It is so, Kauśika," and so on, as it has been rightly stated.
By this, the following meaning is stated:

just as those who have attained serene confidence (*prasāda*) through the deficiency of excellence in vigor (*vīrya*) and so forth, upon realizing the greatness of realization (*adhigama*), [do not attain it themselves].
It should be understood that by those words it is demonstrated that those who perform the worship of the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth are few;
otherwise, nothing at all would have been stated by the words of Śakra’s question.
Expanding upon the meaning of what immediately precedes by demonstrating the gradations of "slight," "more slight," and so forth, he says:
"O Kauśika, from those who are slight [in merit]," and so on.
"They increase the production of the thought of awakening" (cittotpādaṃ vṛṃhayanti).
From the simultaneous arising of the supreme mind of the wise one, his mind is well-restrained from infinite misdeeds;
he fears neither the afflictions nor suffering.
In times of prosperity as well as in times of adversity.
Having recollected such qualities as these, they support [the practice] through application.
The word "upavṛṃhayitvā" (having augmented) is a gerundial construction (*suv-anta*).
"Those who have initiated vigor" means:
They possess refined vigor.
Regarding "yoga":
they practice one-pointedness of mind through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and they abide therein by means of the realization of reality (*tattva*).
"In the irreversible [stage]" means in the Immovable [stage]. "Of those endowed with resolute intention" means...

"Far-reaching, vast, joyful, intent on helping others, great, and virtuous—through such excellence, the intention (*āśaya*) of the noble ones is indeed a superior intention (*adhyāśaya*). Thus, [the verse refers] to those who are endowed with such a distinguished superior intention; "and they" means...
The listeners: Furthermore, demonstrating their extreme scarcity, [the Blessed One] says, "There are indeed," and so forth.
But if all were to engage [in this teaching] with a common intention, how could there be only one or two?
"Let them remain [in this state]. Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because they are difficult to attain," and so forth.

"Difficult to realize and difficult to approach"—the meaning of these seven phrases, beginning with "by those of inferior vigor due to a deficiency in extraordinary effort regarding the four levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) distinguished by excellence," should be explained in their respective order.
This is what was stated: "..."

"Because an excellence of vigor is impossible, even if they initially proceed with an equal intention, not all become partakers of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Speaking thus, he explains the third type, which consists of the weak and the intense degrees.
"Therefore, then," and so forth.
"Quickly" means swiftly. "Easily" means without effort.
"Repeatedly" means again and again.
Now, one who desires the state of a Tathāgata ought to train in the conduct of a Bodhisattva;
how then is there training in the Perfection of Wisdom?
"It is said [to be] 'syāt' (it may be).
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For it is thus," and so forth.
This is the meaning of the sentence:

because formerly, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, the Blessed One trained in the perfection of wisdom through the yoga of non-apprehension for the sake of accomplishing that conduct; likewise, I too must rely upon the perfection of wisdom as the cause for attaining all the qualities of a Buddha.

"Because perception would otherwise be different, the conduct of a bodhisattva would not be accomplished, and thus there would be no attainment of awakening"—thinking this, that bodhisattva will come to know [the truth].
Explaining the fourth type, which is middling-mild, he says:
"Therefore then, Kauśika," and so forth.
"By the tens of millions" means ten million by ten million, [that is] by the tens of millions.
They were made of the seven precious substances:
*musāragalva*, lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*), silver (*rūpya*), crystal (*sphaṭika*), and gold (*hāṭaka*).
It is described as being together with red pearls and emeralds.
All seven kinds of jewels are preeminent, or else all other gems are merely varieties thereof,
distinguished only by slight differences in color and shape.
By this statement, these are the seven jewels; they consist of those [jewels] and have their nature. "Containing the relics of the Tathāgata" means:
"From within the relics of the Tathāgata.
"On that account" means having that as its cause.
In some places, the reading is "on account of that" (*tato nidānam*).

In this context, the meaning is as follows: from the worship of a reliquary (*dhātugarbha-stūpa*), one generates abundant merit (*bahupuṇya*)—the cause (*nidāna*) for attaining Buddhahood—from that very source.
Regarding the term "abundant merit," although a distinction in terminology is made in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, stating:
"Wholesome [action] associated with the desire realm is merit (*puṇya*)."
"It is the immovable [merit] associated with the realms of form and formlessness.
Nevertheless, here it should be understood as wholesome merit in a general sense, because this meaning is possible even in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
"Much, Blessed One! Much, Sugata!"
"Pūrṇabahu" is specified for the sake of establishing the vastness of his intellect; "Sugata," however, is to be understood through distinctions such as his composure and so forth;
and [the term] "abhiśraddadhat."
"Forming a firm conviction" means accepting it as true;
"conceiving it" means mentally superimposing it upon the mind.

"Having resolved" means having taken [the object] as an objective support through mental attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*). "With a serene mind" means having a mind directed toward it because of seeing its excellence (*bhadratā*).
"Having generated the mind for enlightenment" means...
Having formed a distinguished mind for the sake of unexcelled perfect enlightenment through the undertaking of the bodhisattva vows,
one should explain its meaning; that is,
having extracted the very meaning itself, one should speak of it alone.
"One should examine with the mind" means one should investigate [the factors] so that they do not contradict one another. "According to their predominance," and so forth.

In whatever manner— whether middling or weak— that wisdom is associated with superior resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), it too, according to that degree of superiority, should undergo thorough investigation and examination within this *prajñāpāramitā*;
it should perform this for the sake of, and as a cause for, the long endurance of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
He says that very thing:
"She is the guide of the Buddhas," and so forth.
She alone is the guide, the leader, and the mother of the Buddhas—namely, the Perfection of Wisdom.
Lest there be the total destruction [of the teaching] due to the impossibility of reading, recitation, and so forth because of the absence of this book;
and likewise, lest there be the disappearance of the arrival and realization of the true Dharma (*saddharma*) in the absence of a mother;

and so that, through the existence of the book which is the mother of the Bodhisattvas, the provision of assistance characterized by hearing and so forth will be accomplished by means of the non-deficiency of the guide (*netrī*).
The word "yataḥ" (since) is understood as a supplement; thus, the connection with the preceding clause is "therefore one should establish [it].
He says "tāñcainām" and so forth to show that one should not only establish it, but should also perform the consecration and other rites with the very intention already described.
By all of this— namely,
by hearing and so forth— the tenfold practice of the Dharma has been explained:
honoring, writing, giving, hearing, reciting, and mastering;
Proclaiming, self-study, reflection, and meditative cultivation—these constitute that [practice].
For that practice consisting of ten aspects possesses an immeasurable mass of merit,
due especially to its inexhaustibility and its incomparable benefit to others.
Thus it should be understood.
With reference to the fifth category, the medium-of-the-medium type, he says:
"Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone ten million," and so forth.
Regarding "Jambūdvīpa":
Jambūdvīpa is two thousand [yojanas] in extent, with three sides shaped like a cart;
one side, however, is three and a half yojanas.
To explain the sixth [grade], which is medium-medium-intense (*madhyamadhyādhimātra*), he says:
"Furthermore, Kausika, let alone this Jambudvīpa," and so forth;
"in a world-system of four great continents," and so forth.
The wind mandala is sixteen hundred thousand [yojanas] in depth and is immeasurable.
The depth of the waters is eleven thousand and twenty [yojanas];
thereafter, the remaining height of eight hundred thousand [yojanas] becomes golden.
Therein, Meru consists of four jewels, while the mountains are made of gold;
first among them are Yugandhara, Īṣādhāra, and Khadiraka.
Sudarśana, Aśvakarṇa, Vinataka, and Nimindhara—
these are the four continents situated in the directions beginning with the south.
Jambūdvīpa is two thousand [yojanas] in extent, triangular in shape, and resembles a wagon.
Pūrvavideha is one and a half yojanas [in width] and is shaped like a half-moon.
Three of its sides are likewise three hundred and fifty yojanas each,
while its circular [fourth] side, belonging to Godānīya, is seven thousand five hundred yojanas.
Kuru is eight thousand yojanas in extent and is square and level;
these [continents] are considered to be situated in the intervals between the islands in their respective order.
Deha, Videha, Kuru, Kaurava,
Cāmara, Avara, Śāṭha, and Uttaramantrin— these are the eight intermediate islands within it.
Then, for the purpose of enclosing the four continents, there arose the Cakravāḍa range;
like a boundary wall, that mountain of black iron was formed.
All these, together with the continents, are submerged eighty thousand yojanas in the water;
Mount Meru rises above the waters.
It consists of eighty thousand [verses].
These are joined by intervals of half-and-half reduction, and they are equal in height and thickness;
there are seven Sītās as their intervals, the first of which is eighty thousand [yojanas].
This is the inner ocean;
it is three times as large on its sides. The other Sītās are each half the size of the preceding one, and what remains is the outer great ocean.
"The celestial palaces are above Meru"—thus is the system of four continents (caturdvīpaka) traditionally taught.
The world-system consisting of these four continents is itself called the "four-continent world-system" (cāturdvīpaka).
He now describes the seventh [level], which is "intense-mild" (adhimātra-mṛdu).
"Furthermore, O Kauśika, let alone [the world-system of] four great continents," and so forth;
"in a thousandfold small world-system" means [the system consisting of] the four continents,
the moon, the sun, Mount Meru, and the gods of the desire realm.
And a thousand Brahma-worlds are considered a small chiliocosm (cūḍika-sāhasra).
In order to explain the eighth [level], which is the medium of the superior [degree], he says:
"Furthermore, let alone in a small thousand-fold world system," and so forth;
[this refers to] the second intermediate thousand-fold world system.
A thousand of those constitutes a second-order intermediate world-system (*dvisāhasro madhyamo lokadhātuḥ*).
Teaching the ninth category, which is the "superior-of-the-superior" (*adhimātrādhimātra*), he says:
"Furthermore, Kausika, let alone a second-order [world-system]," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm": a thousand of those [thousandfold world systems] constitutes the unsurpassed trichiliocosm world-system,
which is encircled by a great wheel and undergoes simultaneous destruction and formation.

Having first indicated the nine types of conviction regarding one’s own welfare through the state of having not yet cast off the latent tendencies of the conceit of "I," he now speaks for the sake of the first among the types of conviction regarding the welfare of both oneself and others—the "weak-weak" type:
"Furthermore, Kausika, let alone [the number of beings] in a trichiliocosm," and so forth.
"Without before or after" means:
The meaning is: "not before, not after, but simultaneously.

"By such meritorious action" means by the volition of merit consisting of the aforementioned acts, such as the honoring of stūpas containing the relics of the Tathāgata made of the seven precious gems.

"Buddhas are to be seen through the Dharma, for the Guides are the Dharma-body"—because of this statement, considering that worshipping the Perfection of Wisdom, which has the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) as its essence, generates far more merit than worshipping all the Buddhas, he spoke of his own realization for the sake of certain individuals:
"So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata."
Explaining this very point, he says:
"For [the perfection of wisdom]," and so forth.
By way of another method, he speaks while proclaiming the subdivision of the "mild-mild" [level] as it was previously described.
"Furthermore, O Blessed One, let it be so," and so forth.
"By way of a method" means by way of this exposition.
"By all instruments" [is the meaning].
"With ten thousand musical instruments such as lutes and flutes";
"with all songs" refers to songs in Sanskrit, Prakrit, and other languages;
"with all dances" refers to those characterized by the sentiments of love, heroism, disgust, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "with all kinds of musical instruments and percussion":
the sounds of conchs and the like are "all kinds of musical instruments" (*sarvatūrya*);
specific types of hand-clapping and percussion are "percussion" (*tāḍāvacara*).
He says "Evam etat, Kauśika," and so forth, in order to express his agreement with what has been well said.
The three words beginning with "bahutaram" refer to the stages of application and so forth.

The meaning of the three phrases beginning with "inconceivable" should be explained in their respective order as referring to the accomplishment of the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*.
Now, one might ask: if the Tathāgata is preeminent in every respect, how can there be greater merit in making offerings to his mother?
Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason?", he says:
"Born from the perfection of wisdom," and so forth.
Now, since this meaning has already been stated previously, nothing new remains to be said here. If it is asked, "In that case, for what purpose is this presented? [the answer follows].
It is said:
although this is so, nevertheless, in whatever manner the minds of other listeners might arise with doubt, the refutation of that is indeed carried out by means of the sequence previously stated;
for there is no such fixed rule.
Regarding this, it has been stated that for one [position], a certain objection and response are such that for another, that very same thing becomes neither an objection nor a response.
Therefore, one should not suspect redundancy.
The same should be understood in other cases as well.
"It does not approach even a fraction" means it does not attain any portion of its state; "a number" refers to a numerical measure.

"Beyond the number as specified" means a lesser number. "Even a fraction" (*kalām api*) refers again to a minute degree of influence. "Calculation" (*gaṇanām*) implies either a desire to express a genus or a specific enumeration.
"Upamām" means a similar state. "Aupamyam" means comparison.
For it is stated that "the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote that quality (*guṇa*) because of whose presence a word is applied to a substance.
Thus, "likeness" (*aupamya*) is the quality of comparison (*upamā*).
Regarding the term "proximity" (*upaniṣat*): [it refers to the cause].
"Excessive emaciation" refers to its state as a cause;
"is not fit" means it is not accepted.

By this statement regarding the non-perception of forms such as parts (*kalā*) and so forth, it is made known that there is a vast difference between the merit of worshipping a stūpa containing the essence of the Tathāgata and the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
This should be understood because only things such as wholes (*avayavin*), atoms (*aṇu*), and forms are established as being "parts" and so on.
He states the second [point] for the sake of the categories of weak and middling [faith]:
"Take up the *prajñāpāramitā*, O worthy one (*mārṣa*).

Because he is endowed with patience and other virtues due to his great majesty, Śakra is addressed as "O worthy one. Since that [address] was spoken correctly by the sons of the gods, the Blessed One himself said the same thing, beginning with "You should take it up," and so forth.
Now, one might wonder: "For what purpose is the *prajñāpāramitā* undertaken if there is no visible benefit? Anticipating this doubt with the question, "Why is that?", he says:
"When indeed... and so forth.
"Manifestations of such a kind" refers to the discursive thoughts (vitarka) that are about to be described. "We shall fight" explains this very point.
"We shall engage in battle"—
this is [the vow] mentally;
"we shall study our own Vedic texts"— this is [the vow] verbally.

Out of the faith born from perceiving the visible benefits, he speaks for the purpose of praise, beginning with "It is highly effective" and so forth. He speaks for the purpose of restating [the teaching] as something well-said.
"Thus it is," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "From what does the Blessed Lady's status as the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) and so on arise?
Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason?", he says:
"For this reason, Kauśika," and so forth.
Herein, the essential meaning is summarized as follows.
It is a *mahāvidyā* because it performs the purpose of the past Tathāgatas by pacifying the poison of all obscurations;
it is immeasurable (*apramāṇā*) because it is the cause for the future awakening of immeasurable Tathāgatas;
and it is boundless (*aparimāṇā*) because it is the sign for the present awakening of all Tathāgatas who are capable of performing immeasurable deeds.

It is unsurpassed because it serves as the cause for the realization of reality by the Sovereign of the Śākyas in order to deliver beings from *saṃsāra* during this defiled world-age characterized by the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*).
It is supreme because it is the most distinguished cause for the manifestation of the world, ranging from the ten wholesome paths of action up to inconceivable gnosis (*acintyajñāna*).
Through the power of the Dharma taught as the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the Mother, even when Tathāgatas do not appear, the Bodhisattvas...

Furthermore, because she causes the ten wholesome actions and so forth to flourish in the world through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), she is "unequaled" (*asamā*) due to her peerless nature.

Likewise, when the True Dharma (*saddharma*) of the Tathāgata has vanished, because she causes the practice of Dharma and so forth to proceed in the world through the power of the Mother of the Victors (*jinajananī*), she is "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*) by virtue of her equality with the unequaled Tathāgatas.

This very explanation is the appropriate one; otherwise, one might wonder for what reason the Blessed Lady possesses such qualities as being a "great spell" (*mahāvidyā*) and so forth, and thus he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "imāṃ hi," since no refutation is set forth by this text, nothing at all would have been said. Consequently,

those who first explained the passage beginning with "O Blessed One, this is the Great Vidyā, namely the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)," because it bestows the fruit of the great accomplishment of the purpose of defeating the great Asuras and others— by them [this objection remains unaddressed].
It is observed that the meaning of the section has not been characterized; therefore, it is now being characterized.
One should not think that the aforementioned explanation—which follows the text—is inconsistent, because the status of being a *mahāvidyā* and so forth is explained differently elsewhere.
Since words are conventional (*sāmayika*), enough of this digression.
The explanation of the words as they occur in the text is now stated:
"having approached knowledge" means having attained the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Regarding the phrase 'these indeed,' etc.: 'now' (sāmpratam) means at this present time.
'The ten wholesome paths of action' (daśa-kuśala-karmapathāḥ) [is the subject]."

The ten wholesome paths of action consist of abstaining from taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view.
Regarding the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*):
these are the four *dhyānas* born of meditative attainment, which have the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) as their intrinsic nature.
Therein, the first dhyāna has five factors: applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā).
The second has four factors: internal serenity (adhyātmasamprasāda), joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
The third has five factors: equanimity (upekṣā), mindfulness (smṛti), clear comprehension (samprajanya), bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
The fourth dhyāna has four factors: purity of equanimity, purity of mindfulness, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and one-pointedness of mind.
Regarding the phrase "associated with the factors of enlightenment," some say they are untainted (*anāsrava*) because of their predominance.

Others describe it thus: by the power of being embraced by wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*), even those factors associated with outflows (*sāśrava*) become the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)—that is, the causes—which are conjoined and function equally.
They are "manifested" (*prabhāvyante*) in the sense that they are made known.
These are the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).

Loving-kindness and compassion are, in every respect, of the nature of non-hatred; they are, respectively, the desire for sentient beings to be joined with happiness and to be separated from suffering.
Sympathetic joy is the gladness characterized by mental well-being toward sentient beings who are correctly practicing.

Equanimity (*upekṣā*), however, is the absence of both attachment and aversion toward friends and enemies; these [four] are called "immeasurables" (*apramāṇa*) because they have immeasurable sentient beings as their object.
Regarding the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*):
"space is infinite."
"Infinite consciousness," "nothing exists"— perception is a tumor, a thorn; non-perception is delusion.

"This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—through such mental attentions, there are four attainments (samāpatti) known as the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Because the perception of form has been eliminated, they are "formless" (arūpa) due to the absence of form; and because they bring about the equilibrium of body and mind, they are the formless [attainments].
Regarding the "six superknowledges" (ṣaḍabhijñā):

The six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are: psychic power, the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āśravakṣayajñāna*).
The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharmas*) will be explained in brief, and so forth.

In brief, a "dharma-aggregate" (*dharmaskandha*) is a mass of text, however large, that completes the remedy for each individual type of conduct among the eighty-four thousand types of conduct such as passion and so forth; thus, the eighty-four thousand dharma-aggregates are called the "Buddha-knowledge," and so on.

They are called "Buddhas" because they possess a preeminent intelligence through the realization of all that is knowable, and because they have attained awakening by themselves without the instruction of another.
Their knowledge is thus described as "self-arisen" (*svayambhuva*).
And because its nature consists of power that transcends the domain of all thought, it is "inconceivable knowledge.
[The passage beginning with] "by what was previously heard," and so forth.
This entire Dharma of teaching is the outflow of the dharmadhātu and the outflow of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). It was heard previously at the time before the appearance of a Buddha.
"Out of compassion" means out of pity.
"Imam" refers to the world-system named Sahā.
This is also an illustration representing both non-Buddha and Buddha-fields.
Regarding the phrase "dissociated from the factors of enlightenment":
some say this is because, in the absence of a Tathāgata's appearance, those residing there lack the capacity to attain enlightenment;
others say it is due to their deficiency in both wisdom and skillful means.
Because the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āśravakṣayajñāna*) is impossible at that time, the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) are mentioned here.
Furthermore, demonstrating the greatness of the Mother by means of an illustration, he says:
"Just as," and so forth.
"Oṣadhītārā" means medicinal herbs such as rice and the like, and stars such as Venus, Jupiter, and so forth;
thus it has been stated.
Or rather, certain medicinal herbs that shine like stars at night are spoken of in that manner.
Because they are nourished by the rays of the moon, the growth of the body and an excellence of power arise; thus he speaks in due order:
"according to their strength" and "according to their capacity."
The word *sthāman* ending in the vowel *a* should also be understood as derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes.
"Illuminating" means they reveal their own nature.
And "the stars" refers to Puṣya and the others.
He states the meaning of the illustration with the words "In this very way," and so forth.
"By means of passing away" means by means of final nirvāṇa.

Regarding the phrase "practice of the Dharma" (*dharmacaryā*) and so forth: the practice of the Dharma consists of application to such activities as writing down the Dharma, beginning with the *sūtras*.
It is the [realization of] the equality of self and others.
Practice is equanimous conduct.
Cultivating the antidotes in order to eliminate the afflictions of passion and so forth is non-equanimous conduct. Engaging in the four means of attraction and so forth is virtuous conduct.

"Is made known" means it is set in motion; "is manifested" means it is practiced. The three phrases beginning with "born of the Bodhisattva" refer to the distinctions between the stages of application and so forth.
"Skill in means" has been explained.
Alternatively, it is proficiency in emptiness, form, and compassion, as well as in the actions arising from them.
He speaks of the greatness of the mother by way of another method as well,
beginning with the words "Furthermore," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "for those who keep it in mind":
In brief, it is because of taking the aggregate form as the object;
"may they attend" is said because of directing [the mind] toward each individual constituent in detail;
that same meaning is repeated when it relies upon a different sense.
Because of this statement, one should not suspect that the subsequent statement—"they will not die without having avoided misfortune," and so forth—is redundant.

For there is a distinction: what was previously stated pertained to the section on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), whereas what is stated now pertains to the section on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Furthermore, "the king's great minister" (*rājamahāmantrita*) refers to a high minister who instructs in the path of correct policy (*nītimārga*).
Regarding the term "royal minister" (rājamahāmātra):
the chief elephant trainer, the mahāmātra, should approach;
that is, he should draw near.
The particle *yathāpi nāma* occurs in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
For it is said: "Who indeed is capable of defining the fixed meaning of verbal roots, prefixes, and particles?
By this, the following is stated.
"Because they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom, therefore, being so embraced, they will not find an opportunity [for harm].
This refers to the desire to converse.
By the expression "merely having arrived," there is the desire to address [the person];
by "the desire to speak," there is the desire to speak through a continuous succession of successive discourse.
"And they will think that he should be greeted with courtesy.
Kings and others will consider that one who is devoted to the Mother of the Victors should be made joyful by providing support such as robes, alms-food, and other necessities.
[One might ask: "But what is the cause for the desire to converse and so forth in those whose latent tendencies of the conceit 'I am' are undestroyed?"
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For this," and so forth;
[referring to] the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The Bodhisattva who cultivates that [state] is expressed by the term "perfection of wisdom" (prajñāpāramitā), because this section concerns the exposition of its very benefits.

Regarding the phrase "by means of bringing forth loving-kindness" (maitropasaṃhāreṇa): this is the activity of a friend (*mitra*), hence it is "loving" (*maitra*); the presentation of that [activity] is "bringing forth" (*upasaṃhāra*).
And since that [compassion] might also arise through means such as illusion, he says:
"by way of a mind of loving-kindness," which is to say, by way of a mind intent on the welfare [of others].

"By means of the application of compassion" (*karuṇopasaṃhāreṇa*): here, compassion is used figuratively for the effect of compassion; thus, the "application of compassion" is the bestowing [of that effect] upon them, by way of a mind intent on removing suffering.
This is stated in the *Āryaratnacūḍa*:
"The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), accompanied by a retinue of compassion and the other [immeasurables], is to be cultivated.
Because of this statement, one who cultivates it [the perfection of wisdom] possesses the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others, such that kings and others desire to converse with him.
And so it has been said:
"For all gods and humans become well-pleased toward a bodhisattva who is devoted to loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables]," and so forth.
Therefore, then...
The word *tarhi* is used for emphasis; it means "for that very reason," because the Perfection of Wisdom possesses many benefits.
[This refers to the passage beginning with] "Vyāḍa," and so forth.
"Vyāḍas" refers to cruel planets, yakṣas, and so forth;

"sarīsṛpas" refers to snakes. Having entered—that is, having reached—the midst of a wilderness or a difficult terrain dominated by those [beings], they were placed there by the ripening of their previous karma.

The connection with the preceding [phrase] is: "having set aside, that is, having abandoned, entry [into the path] by way of the maturation of karma to be experienced through an impossible counteragent.
Now, he says "Then indeed, of the other non-Buddhist teachers," and so forth, in order to produce conviction in those who harbor doubts regarding the teaching on the benefits for a later time.
The wandering mendicants who have gone forth by means of the renunciation of non-Buddhist sects; "with the intention of finding fault" means with the intention of causing harm.
"At that time" means at that moment. "Having observed their minds" [is the meaning].

It should be understood that it was only with the permission of the Blessed One that Śakra set forth the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the purpose of turning back those whose minds were intent on causing harm.
Accordingly, he will say immediately thereafter:
"And I have given my consent to Śakra, the lord of the gods."
"Of whatever extent" refers to the location;
"grasped" is the connection [with that];
"by that very door," and so forth.
The meaning is that they departed by the very same gate, path prepared with wood and other materials, and specific location on the ground through which they had come.
Not knowing that this was due to the Lord’s supernatural power, he asks:
"What is the cause here? and so forth.
"It is said that there is nothing unknown to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Then indeed the Blessed One [spoke] to the Venerable [Ānanda], and so forth.
"For the purpose of turning back," he says.
This is for the purpose of rebuttal.
In response to the doubt—“How could Śakra possess such a memory, given his lack of constant composure?”—he says:
“And by me,” and so forth.
In order to turn them back from this, the Blessed One gave his consent by authorizing Śakra to set forth the Perfection of Wisdom.
Now, one might ask: even though the Blessed One possesses great compassion, why does he not show favor to those whose minds are hostile?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"I am not," and so forth;
[and] "pure dharma."
Among them, I do not perceive even a single one who possesses wholesome karma conducive to hearing the true Dharma; therefore, I do not show favor [to any],
but this is not due to the influence of aversion— such is my thought.
"Those with hostile minds" means those with minds full of enmity.
Furthermore, in order to produce a further condition, he says:
"Then, indeed, of Māra," and so forth.
In that context, "Māra" refers to Devaputramāra.
The "four assemblies" are the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
"Ni yatam atra" means "necessarily in this assembly.
"Vicakṣuḥ-karaṇāya" means "for the purpose of making [them] discerning."
For the purpose of creating obstacles.
Regarding "the fourfold army":
a horse together with its four foot-guards constitutes this first division of the army.
An elephant together with eight [foot soldiers] and the preceding two makes this a two-limbed unit.
A chariot together with sixteen [foot soldiers] and the two preceding units makes this a three-limbed unit.
Sixteen foot soldiers together with the preceding units make this a four-limbed army.
He is the most inferior of all.
Furthermore, in this manner, one must understand that Māra possesses a vast host of forces.
"Array" (vyūha) means a collection.
"For a long night" (dīrgharātram) means for a long time.
He says that they, having gained conviction, performed worship and so forth.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "the Trayastriṃśa gods" and so forth: "through the vihāyas" means through the sky; "after a long time" (cirasya) means after a long duration (cireṇa);
"upāvṛtta" means having arrived.
"By a small amount" means by just that much.
"Those who have performed service for previous Victors" means those who have performed [service] toward previous Buddhas.
Those by whom the "office" (*adhikāra*)— the activity of the perfections (*pāramitā*) characterized by hearing [the Dharma] and so forth— has been undertaken are described as such;

or alternatively, those to whom the "office," that is, the commission (*niyoga*) consisting of the nature of hearing and so forth, was performed or bestowed by previous Buddhas, are likewise described.
"What need is there to say more?
means: what further doubt could there be?
The thought is that [the distinction] between apprehension and so forth is due to their reaching the range of the auditory faculty.
"Will train for suchness," and so forth.

"Suchness" (*tathatva*) means being thus (*tathābhāva*), because of the very definition [of *tathatā*] as non-alteration (*ananyathātva*); the short vowel [in *tathatva*] is due to this very [grammatical] rule.
The three phrases beginning with "will train for that cause" are to be understood as referring to the stages of application (*prayoga*) and so on.

"Those who have attended upon the Tathāgatas": those by whom the Tathāgatas were attended upon through the offering of a retinue, through hearing what was spoken by them, and through worship and so forth, are described as such.
[The compound is formed with] "niṣṭhā" (the past participle) placed first because it possesses the characteristic of being irregular [in its word order].
The word *paryupāsita* does not undergo the rule of prior placement [in a compound].

Now, one might object: "Since attending upon the Tathāgata and so forth are not perceived as being inherently connected to hearing [the Dharma] from the mother and so on, how can the latter be inferred from the former?
Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason?", he says:
"From this," and so forth.
From the *prajñāpāramitā*, omniscience—that is, Buddhahood—is manifested and produced.
For this very reason, it must be sought from that [source], because an effect cannot exist without its cause.
Explaining that very point by means of an illustration, he says:
"Just as, for example," and so forth. This is what is meant:

Since an effect cannot arise without a cause, and since the state of a Tathāgata must be sought as originating from the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), therefore the hearing and so forth of the Mother [the *Prajñāpāramitā*] necessarily lead to the attainment of the rank of a Tathāgata by way of nourishing the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) and serving as the receptacle for the seed.

Furthermore, such hearing and so forth—occurring only occasionally and in specific instances—necessarily leads to birth through a distinguished cause; thus, it allows one to infer its own specific cause, namely, the service and attendance upon a Tathāgata.
"Since this property is established for cause and effect— that [the effect] arises from a cause that has either that form or a different form—
it is well said [that the eye is the cause] by way of predominance. Thus he spoke, repeating Śakra’s words.
"Thus it is, Kauśika," and so forth.
Speaking of the third [level], the "mild-intense" (mṛdv-adhimātra), he says:
"The Blessed One [does not arise] from the perfection of giving," and so forth.
"Color" (varṇa) refers to praise (anuśaṃsa).
The connection is that he does not speak [of it] due to the distinction between concise and detailed exposition;
that is, he does not fully proclaim it.
It should be understood that this is due to the mere utterance of the name;
for he proclaims the designation by uttering the name in many ways.
Because it has the bodhicitta as its basis, it is supreme in terms of its basis;
because it engages with all things, it is supreme in terms of its object;
because it has the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings as its mission, it is supreme in terms of its mission.

The characteristic of each of the perfections, such as generosity and the rest, is defined by: (1) the supremacy of skillful means through the embrace of non-conceptual gnosis; (2) the supremacy of dedication through the transformation [of merit] toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and (3) the supremacy of purity through the realization that removes the obscurations of afflictions and the known.
Thus says the noble Ārya-Asaṅga.
To express his acceptance, he says:
"It is so, Ānanda," and so forth.
Since the six perfections alone are the cause for Buddhahood, why is there an instruction regarding the preeminence of only one of them?
Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason? he says:
"Because the perfection of wisdom," and so forth.

Since the perfections of giving and so forth are preceded by [the practice of] dedication toward omniscience through the purity of the three spheres, they are the "forerunners"; therefore, the connection with the preceding [verse] is: "For that reason, I shall speak in praise of them and proclaim their names.
By means of those words, he speaks in order to establish the meaning as it has been stated:

"What do you think? and so forth. "A gift not transformed into omniscience" means that, by way of non-apprehension, it has not been dedicated toward Buddhahood for the sake of all sentient beings through the perfection of wisdom; this is the remainder of the sense.
The meaning is understood from the question itself: that because a gift of such a kind is exhausted through the enjoyment of its fruit, it does not reach a state of excellence.
One whose intellect emulates the state of the Teacher said:
"Certainly not so."
Extending this principle to morality (*śīla*) and the other perfections, he says:
"What do you think? and so forth.

Having thus demonstrated, by way of negation (*vyatireka*), that giving and the other virtues possess the nature of *pāramitās* through the power of being embraced by wisdom (*prajñā*), he speaks in order to establish the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of wisdom as a *pāramitā*.
"What do you think, Ānanda, is that inconceivable? and so forth.
He says this because the fruit is inconceivable due to the non-apprehension of any real entity.
[Ānanda replies,] "So it is, Blessed One," and so forth.

Because it cannot be conceived by ordinary persons who rely on apprehension (*aupalambhika*), it is "inconceivable" (*acintya*); because it is not within the domain of the *śrāvakas* and others, it is "supremely inconceivable. Concluding the meaning of the Mother’s *pāramitā*, he says: "Therefore then, Ānanda, it is supreme," and so forth.
He speaks thus to summarize the meaning of the preliminary path (*pūrvaṅgamārtha*).
Therefore, Ānanda, it is because of the roots of merit dedicated toward omniscience, and so forth.
She is the *nāyikā* (leader) because she leads generosity and the other perfections to Buddhahood;
she is the *pariṇāyikā* (guide) because she eliminates all calamities.
"By this method," and so forth.

The meaning is that because giving and the other perfections are included within it according to the principle already stated, when the *prajñāpāramitā* is being proclaimed, the six perfections are all proclaimed; thus, it is not a teaching of the Mother of the Victors alone.
As for what was stated previously:
"I [speak] of the perfection of wisdom alone," and so forth;
there is no fault here because it is due to its preeminence.
To clarify this very point by means of an example, he says:
"Just as, for example, on this great earth," and so forth.
"They grow" means they undergo increase.
He states the meaning of the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*).
With the words "In this very way, Ānanda," and so forth,
he speaks concerning the fourth [level], the weak-middling.
He says, "Not yet, Blessed One," and so forth.

"Of the perfection of wisdom, all the qualities"—this means that these are not all the qualities of the Mother taken as a whole; rather, the intention is that they are mentioned because her qualities are exceedingly abundant. To the question, "To whom then do these qualities belong? he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "For indeed, by me," etc.:

the meaning is that this section which was received by me from the presence of the Blessed One has been set forth immediately thereafter for the purpose of refuting other non-Buddhist schools and the like, and these are its virtues.
He utters the word of approval (*sādhukāra*) because of the perfect exposition.
"Excellent, excellent, Kauśika! However, not only will these qualities belong to one who merely takes up even this much of the *prajñāpāramitā*— that is, merely recites it—
but also to whoever..."

He says, "Furthermore, Kauśika, I shall describe the immediate qualities even for one who, having written it down, should preserve the mere book preceded by worship," because [the listener] has conceived great respect upon hearing the benefits.
"O Blessed One, I too [will protect] that person," and so forth. "What need is there to mention" means:
for one who has written it down and performs the superior acts of memorization and so on, what doubt could there be that I shall provide protection and the like? This is the meaning.
Having likewise given his approval by saying, "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika," he spoke the fifth [section], the *madhyamadhya*, in order to state it:
"Furthermore, Kauśika... and so forth, ending with "...the inspired eloquence (*pratibhāna*) is to be brought forth."
One should produce speech that is both logical and well-articulated. "Zeal" (chanda) refers to the desire to speak.
He speaks again in another way for the sake of showing its benefits.
"Furthermore, O Kauśika," and so forth.
"Lack of a cowed mind" means the absence of a stiffened or paralyzed mind.
"May it not be," and so forth.
"May no one with a hostile intention question me or raise an objection"—thinking thus, there will be no state of mental dejection.
[Objection: But since it is possible for men to possess excellence in wisdom and other qualities, how is it that this does not occur when they fail to recognize the virtues of others' minds?
[Response: Anticipating the question "For what reason is that? he says:
For it is said, beginning with "of that," etc.:
"The fear of timidity before the assembly and so forth is produced by the apprehension of real entities."
"Because, through the power of being embraced by the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) alone, there is no apprehension of action, agent, or activity, it does not come to be.
In order to state the sixth [category], the medium-intense, he says:
"He will become beloved," and so forth.
In this context, a friend is one who brings about welfare and happiness;
a minister is a chief counselor;
and a kinsman is a person connected through a lineage of mothers and fathers.
Those born of the same mother and father, such as brothers and so forth, are *sālohita* (blood relations); these are the Śramaṇas who are sons of the Śākyas.
Pointing out the seventh [category], which is "intense-mild" (*adhimātra-mṛdu*), he says:
"And they are capable," and so forth.
He is capable through his endowment with extensive learning and other qualities;
he is competent due to his possession of the perfection of wisdom;
and he acts for the sake of subduing [opponents] in accordance with the Dharma.
One [view] holds that it is for the purpose of refuting them by means of their own words;
