another holds that it is for the purpose of eliminating them along with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by refuting the probative property (*sādhanadharma*) stated by them. *Pratyanuyoga* refers to an objection.
Its "explanation" (vyākaraṇa) is its correct avoidance;
in this context, "capable" means fit or suitable.
Explaining the eighth [level], which is the medium of the intense [degree], he says:
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "where," they will behold [the Buddha] from afar by means of seeing,
and they will pay homage by joining their palms in reverential salutation.
Having approached, they will pay homage with the five-point prostration (*pañcamaṇḍalaka*).
Lest there should arise the thought that these [beings] are limited because they are specifically designated as those who take up [the practice], he says:
"O Kauśika, let it not be so for you," and so forth.
"Pe-yā-la-mi-ti" means that those who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment will also think they must come there; such phrases are to be understood by extension (*atideśanīya*).
Among those, the three beginning with the Brahmakāyikas are comprised within the first dhyāna;
the three beginning with the Parīttābhas are likewise born of the second dhyāna.
Furthermore, the three types beginning with Parīttaśubha are situated in the third dhyāna;
the eight beginning with Anabhraka belong to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
The non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), however, are those who occupy a portion of the Great Fruit (*bṛhatphala*) heaven.
In order to teach skillful means for the sake of generating superior merit, [the Buddha] said:
"And thus, Kauśika, by that son of good family," and so forth.
The word *itaḥ* means "from this.
Likewise, anticipating the doubt of some person of dull intellect, he says:
"Let it not be so for you here, O Kauśika."
He explains that very point at the conclusion of the section on the "seizer" (hāraka):
"In this regard, Kauśika, it should not be viewed thus.

Among them, those whose latent tendencies of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*) have not been abandoned are born in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), belong to the sphere of desire (*kāmāvacara*), and possess the latent tendencies of sensual desire; those whose latent tendencies of sensual desire have been abandoned, yet are attached to the desire for form (*rūparāga*), are born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and belong to the sphere of form (*rūpāvacara*).
He states the ninth [level], which is the highest of the high (*adhimātrādhimātra*):
"Furthermore, for that son of good family... and so forth.
In this context, "the dwelling of ordinary people" refers to the house.
A *layana* is a dwelling place for monks. A *prāsāda* is a palace, a residence of a lord with a distinguished structure constructed from bricks and other materials.
It is well-protected due to the absence of disturbances from humans and other beings.
Anticipating the question, "Why is it so well-guarded as a house and so forth?
he says: "For where... and so on.
The word *nāma* expresses what is well-known.
They are of great splendor and great majesty.
As it has been said:
"Because they are thus renowned as being of great splendor, wherever they intend to come, such as to a house or other location," [they are honored].

"Therefore, by their power, that house and so forth will be well-protected. Then, in order to inspire confidence in the class of beings who are difficult to deceive, he asks, "How so, Blessed One? and so forth.
He states the sign according to their respective capacities with the words beginning "If, Kauśika... and so forth.
In that context, "one perceives a vast radiance" means:
One perceives—that is to say, sees—a great radiance of light there in the house and so forth;
"niṣṭhā" means certainty;
and "has come" is used figuratively.

"Having approached" means having entered inside from the house. "He will smell a superhuman odor" means he will experience with his olfactory consciousness a distinguished fragrance that transcends the human world.
"Never smelled before" means never experienced before. Because of the non-commission of all evils and through inner purity, one's conduct is clean.
Through the enjoyment of secluded clothing and other requisites, one’s external purity constitutes pure conduct.
The phrase "with uplifted minds" and so forth is to be understood as being associated with weak, medium, and intense states of mental well-being (*saumanasya*).
Joy itself is mental gladness; those in whom that has arisen are described as such. "Dwelt" means previously situated there.
"One must depart" means one must go away.
How can there be a withdrawal for those previously stationed there without effort? Anticipating this question, he says:

"Of those very [beings]," and so forth. The three terms beginning with "of prosperity" (*śriyaś ca*) are for the purpose of making known the mild, middling, and superior degrees of great power (*mahānubhāvatva*).
This is what was stated:
"Because those of great majesty depart by their own power, they do not require effort.
The word *abhīkṣṇam* means again and again.
"Abounding in serene confidence" means that one's faith increases through the vision of firm conviction.
Having previously indicated, in general terms, the state of pure and clean conduct in all respects, he now states the specific intended meaning.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tena khalu punar... and so forth:
"parisāmantake" means "from the vicinity of the assembly.
"Na kāyaklamatha" means "no physical exhaustion."
There is no physical exhaustion from traveling to other regions and so forth, nor is there mental fatigue; that is to say,
there is no mental distress due to a deficiency in alms-food.
Due to the absence of afflictions such as heat and other disturbances, he will rest in ease;
and during the time of walking meditation and so forth, because he is not troubled by thorns and the like, he will proceed with comfort.
"Being sung together" means through their mutual determination of the meaning of the texts.
Thus is omniscience;
Buddhahood consists in the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
Thus is the Buddha-field.
It is twofold, distinguished by way of the sentient beings and their environment, respectively, because of the absence of hunger, thirst, stones, thorns, and so forth.
And there is physical bliss infused with vital energy (*ojas*);
that which is strength in the body, brilliance in speech, and [clarity] in the intellect.
"Endurance"—these three qualities, when infused therein, constitute it;
thus it is so described.

As for the mention of "body" (*kāya*), it should be understood as referring to the primary body, as well as to speech and the intellect which depend upon the body, through a figurative attribution of the term.
"Light, indeed very light," and "bodily ease free from heaviness"— this is to be connected with what precedes. "By greed for food."
The phrase "endowed with a desire for food" is the ellipsis.

"Of the practitioner of yoga" refers to one devoted to the practice of specific meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). "By the movement of mental attention" means by that which is augmented by the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables].

Now, one might object: since a practitioner of yoga subsists on the food of meditation (*dhyānāhāra*), he would not have a powerful craving for solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); yet here [the Buddha] has his mother depicted and established after first performing worship. How is this so?
Anticipating this question, he says: "For what reason? and so forth.
"For it is thus, O Kauśika," and so forth.
The particle *yathāpi nāma* functions in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
As it has been said:

“Because he will be devoted to writing and other such activities for the sake of perfecting the meditative concentration on the *prajñāpāramitā*, non-human beings will think that they must infuse vitality (*ojas*) into his body.
Since this is the very nature of things, by virtue of having vitality infused into him, he will have performed the function of taking food, and his craving for food will become mild.

Having explained the nine types of conviction regarding the welfare of oneself and others through the equality of self and other, he speaks first regarding the "weak-weak" type of conviction concerning the welfare of others:
"Having written down this Perfection of Wisdom and made it into a book, one should set it out preceded by worship and honor it, but one should not [merely] take it up," and so forth.
"This very [act], O Kauśika, compared to that... [is superior].
The meaning is that the person who is about to be described is precisely this very one, as distinguished from the one previously mentioned who practices non-apprehension and so forth.
Summing it up, he said again:
"Therefore, O Kauśika, this very [mind]... and so forth, ending with "...the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) should be generated."
One should not ask what relevance this has to the section on the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
because the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*)— which has emptiness and compassion as its very essence— is primarily the perfection of wisdom itself.
It should be heard with reverence and a resolute intention.
Having removed one's veil or head-covering and sitting on a low seat, one should listen to the true Dharma with the intention of seeking liberation, while avoiding the fault of distraction.
One should even commit it to a book and preserve it.
One should not wonder why this point is mentioned here, since it was already stated at the very beginning in the *Svārthādhimukti-hāraka*.
For in that [previous] case, the establishment of one intent upon his own welfare was mentioned, whereas here it is one intent upon the welfare of others; this is the distinction.
And so he will state immediately thereafter:
"for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma," and so forth.

In the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, the commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this is the third chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Veneration of Stūpas Containing the Perfection of Immeasurable Qualities."
Regarding the second [category], which concerns the weak-middling [level], he says: "If, Kauśika, this Jambūdvīpa of yours... and so forth.
It is "complete" because it pervades all parts of the earth, and it is "tied in a topknot" because it extends up to the crest.
Regarding the phrase "of the Tathāgata’s relics":
the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent, meaning "by them.
Regarding the word "being urged": [it means being exhorted].
When it is said, "Take whichever portion you desire," one might ask:
why is it that, setting aside the distinguished form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Tathāgata, one should instead embrace the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Anticipating this question with "For what reason?", he says:
"Yathāpi nāma," and so forth.
Because there exists within the Prajñāpāramitā—the eye of the Tathāgata—a special regard characterized by exceptional devotion;
[the phrase] "I would embrace this alone" is to be connected with what precedes it.
He asks, "Why is there indeed this conceptualization regarding her?
and replies with the words beginning "For this...

Because this body, which consists of the ultimate reality (*bhūtārthika*) and the absolute truth (*pāramārthika*), is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and because it primarily illuminates that [body], the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is so designated.
Therefore, the thought arises that there is wonder precisely in this regard.
From what does the dharmakāya derive its very nature as the ultimate reality (*bhūtārthika*), such that through its manifestation there is wonder in the *Prajñāpāramitā*?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
For this has been stated by the Blessed One, and so forth.

Since it was stated by the Blessed One in another passage that "the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, whose nature is the non-dual gnosis resembling an illusion and who consist of the perfection of wisdom, are the Dharma-body," by this the analogy is indicated.

Now, if it is thought that through self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the cognition existing in the preceding moment determines itself, and likewise [determines] that which exists in the subsequent moment;
Having understood that "this follows immediately after that," one realizes that "this is the cause" and "this is the effect.

Otherwise, the rule of immediate succession would not be possible; or, if it were possible, it would lead to the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, since they are determined by way of the relationship between cause and effect, how can the Blessed Buddhas be of the nature of non-dual gnosis which is like an illusion?

Therefore, the claim that "this follows immediately after that" is untenable, because it is not established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), since the latter has only conceptualized objects as its domain; nor is it reasonable to assume its establishment by another cognition,
because such determination is impossible— whether by a cognition without an aspect (*nirākāra*) or with an aspect (*sākāra*).
Alternatively, if there is a delimitation,
it follows that something other than [the cognition itself] becomes the object of the cognition;
and that is not accepted by you, because it is impossible for such a thing to be apprehended.
Nor is the necessity of immediate succession determined by those two cognitions themselves, because both of them have already ceased.

It might be argued that when the preceding cognition is apprehended through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the cause-nature of the immediate succession with respect to the effect is apprehended; likewise, when the subsequent cognition is apprehended, the effect-nature [is apprehended].
"It is precisely the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) that is apprehended, because the nature of immediate succession—which consists of cause and effect—is non-different from those [two].
This is not so;

for the relation of cause and effect is ascertained through the apprehension of two entities by way of delineating the relationship of producer and produced, and not merely through the apprehension of immediate succession."
Otherwise, if there were a perception of a jar immediately after the perception of another jar, the causal relationship would be established merely by determining their immediate succession.

However, since self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), it lacks the apprehension that delineates the connection between preceding and succeeding entities. Therefore, in the absence of the determination that "this arises immediately after that," it is not logical for the causal relationship to be ascertained.
Because it would lead to an over-extension;
even the conceptual construction that "this arises immediately after that" is not tenable.
"Because there is no certainty regarding experience, it is like the conceptualization of momentariness and so forth.

Thus, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is stated: "O monks, do not indeed consider this beautiful body, radiant with the primary and secondary marks, to be a 'real body' (*satkāya*) whose nature is a mere accumulation of atoms.
By the statement, "Through the perfection of the *dharmakāya*, you shall see me as perfected through the realization of the non-dual illusion-like [nature]," the logical reason (*hetu*) is expressed.

And this body of the Tathāgata is manifested by the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and perfected through the fulfillment of the Dharma-body—that is to say, its intrinsic nature is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). By this, the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has been established.

This is what is meant: "That which is perfected through the fulfillment of the cultivation of non-dual gnosis that is like an illusion is the Dharma-body, just as were the Blessed Buddhas of the past."
"This body of the Tathāgata is perfected through the complete accomplishment of the cultivation of the aforementioned gnosis"—this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).

Because an object is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), it cannot be grasped by means of cognition with mental images (*sākārajñāna*) and so forth; therefore, non-dual gnosis is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*) as being colored by the aspect of the object, just like cognitions in dreams and the like.
It is established that [the mind] is to be cultivated.

Furthermore, by the method already explained, its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) in reality—due to being devoid of both a single and multiple nature—is ascertained through its resemblance to an illusion (*māyopama*).
Therefore, the fact that this mind manifests clearly through the power of cultivation is itself *tathāgatatva*; thus, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is not contradictory (*viruddha*). This is the illustration with respect to the previously accepted Buddha-dharmakāya;

however, for another [being] who lacks the dharmakāya, there would be the consequence of error—like that of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and so forth—due to the absence of being perfected through the completion of the cultivation of the aforementioned knowledge, which is uncontradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Since the Tathāgata is intended to be non-erroneous, this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary position.
Because atoms do not [combine], the reason is not inconclusive.

Therefore, this form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Tathāgata, which is radiant with the primary and secondary marks and is perceived by fortunate beings, is not the ultimate, real Dharmakāya Teacher; rather, it appears to them solely through the sovereign power of the Dharmakāya, which is a mass of supremely pure and infinite qualities.

One's own gnosis manifests in the form of the Tathāgata’s rūpakāya; because they do not recognize this manifestation of their own gnosis as the Tathāgata, they conceptualize it as "this external Blessed One" with the thought that he is the Teacher. By means of seeing, prostrating, and so forth, they come to partake in higher rebirth and the ultimate good in due course.

For even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that possesses a false appearance is indeed observed to be a cause of benefit through a traditional succession, just like the conceptualization of impermanence and so forth, because it is connected to the real entity; however, this is not immediate.

This is because as long as consciousness arises toward the object of knowledge through an adherence to the existence of things, that consciousness remains nothing but an error due to grasping at what is not that [entity] as being that; thus, it stays far removed from the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*).

Therefore, just as a magician does not adhere to the notion that "these are real" with respect to elephants and so forth— which he himself has created— even though they appear as if they were real entities; likewise, a beginner who desires to quickly attain the state of a Tathāgata, even if they have not practiced the nature of the Mahāyāna for a long time through many means in many ways, [should do so] toward the Form Body Tathāgata, which is a reflection of one's own gnosis arising through the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.
"One should practice faith that has practice as its essence through the application of resolute devotion toward the Teacher of the World.
Explaining this very point, he says:
"Furthermore, O Blessed One, it is not for me," and so forth.
Regarding the third [category], the weak-intense (mṛdv-adhimātra), he says: "But indeed, O Blessed One, from this... and so forth.
The word *api tu* is a particle (*nipāta*) used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
Now, one might ask: "If there is a distinction [between the mother and the Tathāgata], how can the worship of the mother be the worship of the Tathāgata?
Anticipating this question with the inquiry "For what reason?", he says:
"Because the bodies of the Tathāgatas are born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
This is the essential meaning here:

since such Buddhas, Blessed Ones, whose forms transcend all worlds, are produced from the Perfection of Wisdom, therefore, by virtue of its great majesty, this [Perfection] is to be honored. Thus, through its connection with the arising of the Tathāgatas, there is no distinction in honoring it.
"The Tathāgatas are also worshipped.
To clarify that when something is the basis upon which something else is worthy of worship, then by worshipping that [basis], the latter itself is worshipped, he says, with a preceding illustration:
"Just as, O Blessed One, in the Sudharmā hall," and so forth.
The divine assembly hall named Sudharmā is situated just outside the city of Sudarśana on Mount Sumeru, specifically to the southwest.
Seated therein, the gods deliberate upon what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
But how is it that one pays homage and so forth to another out of respect?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason is that? he says:
"For here, indeed, on the seat," and so forth.
The word *kila* is used in the sense of recollection.
Due to that connection, there is the understanding that even Śakra is worshipped during the worship of the seat; thus,
it serves as both the primary cause and the contributing condition for being designated as "Maheśa."

It is called "maheśākhyā" because it possesses great majesty by virtue of being designated as "mahānubhāva," and it is so described because it serves as a cause and condition through the respective distinctions of the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*).
It is called "āhārikā" in the sense of being that which produces.
In response to the possible doubt that the body of the Tathāgata alone is the producer of Buddhahood by virtue of being the cause of its persistence, he says:
"And of omniscience," and so forth.
This is what is meant:
it is precisely because they embrace omniscience that the relics of the Tathāgatas are so called.

Therefore, these [perfections] are not the causes or conditions for the arising of a previously non-existent omniscience; rather, they serve as the basis by acting as the causes for its persistence after it has been accomplished.

The phrase "having the knowledge of the Omniscient One as its cause" means that the Perfection of Wisdom is an object of worship because it has the knowledge of the Tathāgata as its cause; this is the implied sense.
For the purpose of concluding [the section], he says: "Therefore, then, O Blessed One, regarding these two," and so forth.
To speak of the fourth [level], which is medium-mild, he says:
"Let alone, O Blessed One, Jambūdvīpa," and so forth.

Furthermore, the statement beginning with "Moreover, however" (*api tu khalu punar*), although its meaning has already been explained, is not a mere repetition because it is stated in connection with a different context.
By the passage beginning with "For the relics of the Tathāgata," he explains precisely how they are manifested by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Therefore, then," and so forth, is the conclusion.
He states the fifth point, concerning the middle-middle meaning:
"But furthermore, O Blessed One, from this [point] onwards," and so forth.
The meaning is that because this Perfection of Wisdom, free from error, arises through the sequence of hearing and so forth, these physical remains are worthy of worship.
To the question of why they receive worship even through the arising of that [Wisdom], he says:
"namely, because they have been thoroughly permeated by the Perfection of Wisdom."
Because a fruit that arises from a perfectly pure cause is itself produced as perfectly pure;
since the Tathāgatas have been thoroughly permeated and perfumed in every way by the generation of great majesty through the *prajñāpāramitā*, they receive worship due to their arising from that.
Clarifying this very point by means of an illustration, he says:

In this context, "priceless" means that, by virtue of its excellence, it is not worth any price.
"By these of such a kind" refers to those very qualities.
"By those [qualities] of such a nature that will be described hereafter. "Being blown" means being filled. "One should restrain" means one should bring about a state of dullness.

because of the concentration on the intermediate space;

[This refers to] diseases such as colic and eye-diseases;
[and] *paṭala* is density.

He asks, "What is its own color? and replies, "If it is white," and so forth.

It should be understood that one should wrap it entirely with a cloth or tie it with a portion of it. There is no grammatical error in using the form "pariveṣṭayitvā" (having wrapped) with a gerund ending in *tvā*. One should also clarify—that is, bring down—the turbidity, which is the state of being filled with much dust.
To refute the opinion of someone who might argue that the example is unestablished because such jewels do not exist even for the renowned Śuddhodana in Jambūdvīpa, he says:
"But what then, Kauśika," and so forth.
He says this because [the Buddha] possesses exceptionally distinguished merit.
"Among the gods," and so forth.
The two terms "few" (*alpa*) and "limited" (*paritta*) are stated respectively in terms of number and power.
In the phrase "by those qualities of jewels and gems," the word "because they are permeated by them" (*paribhāvitattvāt*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Even when he has entered final nirvāṇa"— by the word "even," it is implied that this applies while he is still remaining [in the world].
Showing that veneration is due to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as a cause by way of another aspect, he says:
"And as for the phrase 'O Blessed One, [it is] thus,' etc.:

regarding the Dharma-teaching of the Buddhas—because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) proceeds by superimposing its own form onto an external object, it grasps that which is not [the object] as being that; therefore, while its own nature is ignorance (*avidyā*), it exists."
The abandonment of the remaining obscurations is not possible [for others];

therefore, for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are eternally in meditative equipoise, there arise—through the power of the wisdom of the perfection of insight (prajñāpāramitā)—appearances of unconfused teachings according to the inclinations and capacities of those to be trained, which serve as the conditions for their own realization. It is in accordance with such conditions that the teachings of the Blessed Ones are established.

Therefore, with the intention of benefiting those to be trained, the compilers [of the scriptures] have stated in certain places that the manifestation of pure mundane knowledge was thus revealed by the Sage.
Consequently, because it consists of the appearance of the sounds and cognitions of the trainees, the teaching is connected to the audience as well.
Just as the Dharma-teaching of the Buddhas is worthy of worship because it is produced through the sovereign power of the wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā*, so too is this teaching.

Likewise, the teaching of even contemporary Dharma-preachers is worthy of worship because it is derived from mutual reliance upon the Blessed One and is produced through the sovereign power of the wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
While indicating the sixth [category], the medium-intense, he says:
"Just as the Blessed One is a royal official," and so forth.
"Free from fear on all sides" (akutobhaya) means that he has no fear from any quarter; thus it is said.
"By the power of the Dharmakāya" means:
The meaning is: "by the power of the perfection of wisdom, which is the outflow of the *dharmadhātu*.
To explain the seventh [level], the highest-mild [degree of patience], he says:
"Let alone the trichiliocosm," and so forth.
Explaining the eighth [level], the medium-intense, he says:
"Furthermore, O Blessed One,
those who [live] among enemies," and so forth.
The three phrases beginning with "they abide" (*tiṣṭhanti*) should be explained according to their sequence as the distinctions of the fulfillment of the welfare of oneself, others, and both.
Alternatively, they "abide" because they remain for as long as saṃsāra lasts by means of the *dharmakāya*;
they "are sustained" because they maintain the welfare of bodhisattvas by means of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
They pass [their time] by remaining for a few days in an emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
"One should practice the perfection of wisdom" and so forth;
this was stated according to the distinctions between stages such as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

As before, having granted his own hand with the words, "So it is, Kauśika, so it is," he spoke to proclaim the majesty of the Mother, beginning with the words, "Even those, Kauśika... and so forth. He speaks thus while explaining the ninth stage, which is the highest of the high (adhimātrādhimātra).
“O Blessed One, this is a great perfection,” and so forth.
Demonstrating its very greatness, he says:
“Of all sentient beings,” and so forth.
This is what was said:

"Because, by the power of his mother, the Blessed One understands the mental activities of all sentient beings during the stage of preparation (prayogāvasthā) and perceives them clearly during the stage of completion (pṛṣṭhāvasthā),
therefore her greatness [is established]."
Establishing this very point, he says:
"For instance, O Kauśika," and so forth.
"For a long time" (*dīrgharātram*) means for a long duration.
Intending to show that the statement "he courses in the perfection of wisdom" implies an exclusion of others, he asks: "Why, Blessed One? and so forth.
"Not in others" means not in those consisting of giving and the other perfections.
He says "in all cases indeed," beginning with "in all [situations]," etc.:
giving by one who is free from expectation and devoid of craving for rebirth.
Morality and patience everywhere, and vigor in the arising of all that is wholesome.
Likewise, without the formless realm, there is meditative concentration joined with skillful means;
for this is the correct application of the wise in the six perfections.
By this statement, the meaning is that through this correct practice, the Bodhisattva courses in all [perfections].
He asks, "For what purpose is the mention of the perfection of wisdom?
and replies with the words beginning, "But moreover... (api tu khalu punar...).
And how it serves as a precursor has already been explained previously.
Explaining this very point, he says: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift," and so forth.
"Vipaśyati" means "one who cultivates.
To explain the meaning of accumulation, he says:
"And not these, O Kauśika," and so forth.
"Consecrated by the perfection of wisdom" means they have been thoroughly cultivated through the purity of the three spheres. "Consecrated for omniscience" means...
Regarding those things dedicated toward the state of a Tathāgata:
because there is no exclusion from being non-perfections, there is no distinction in terms of their form as perfections; this is the connection with what precedes.
Furthermore, by virtue of being denotable by the word "perfection," there is no differentiation.

They possess various colors due to distinctions such as blue, yellow, and so forth; they have various shapes by way of being even or uneven; and they are endowed with various heights and circumferences.
"Height" (āroha) refers to length.
Circumference is sphericity.
It is not a distinct shadow because it is excluded from what is not of that nature; likewise, because it is denoted by the same word, there is no differentiation.
He states this very point:
"Rather, it is a shadow," and so forth.
"Number" refers to a designation.
Having thus explained the nine types—beginning with the "weak-weak"—for each of the three kinds of mental engagement characterized by resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), he concludes by saying:
"Endowed with great qualities," and so forth.
She is "endowed with great qualities" because she brings to completion the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in one's own welfare, which possesses manifold benefits.
She is "endowed with immeasurable qualities" because she is joined with the resolute conviction in the welfare of both self and others, which transcends the sphere of number and measure.
Because there exists a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) directed toward the welfare of others for the sake of the infinite realm of sentient beings, she is endowed with infinite qualities.

One should not entertain any misconception regarding the fact that this very resolute conviction—distinguished by the three goals of self, others, and both, each of which has nine varieties—consists of twenty-seven types.
And so it has been said:

Resolve should be known as threefold: for one’s own benefit, for the benefit of both oneself and others, and for the benefit of others alone; and each of these is further understood to be threefold. (18)
It is weak, medium, and intense, and through the further divisions of weak-weak and so forth, it is considered to be of twenty-seven types. Thus,

by means of the aforementioned sequence of textual explanations— which are intent on demonstrating progressively superior benefits under various pretexts— all this mental engagement of resolute belief (*adhimukti-manaskāra*) has been fully elucidated.

In every case, within each mode of conviction regarding one's own welfare and so forth— beginning with the "weak-weak" and others— the counteragent itself consists of the "strong-strong" and other levels; thus, by implication, the adverse factors have been indicated.
What was taught regarding the conviction in one's own welfare becomes the welfare of others.
It should be understood that in the second [stage] the application is intermittent, while in the third it is uninterrupted.

The former masters maintain that if one were to accept merely the statement of the benefits as they are, then because all possible benefits would be expressed in a single instance, the expansion of the text would be rendered purposeless.
This is stated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārālokā*, the commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The fourth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of Qualities."

In order to encourage, respectively, the bodhisattva practitioner who has turned toward the perfection of wisdom characterized by the phenomena of the present life according to their resolve— during the first, second, third, and ninth stages of the mental application of resolve—

the Buddhas and others perform praise, laudation, and eulogy through nine successive modes for each stage. Thus, immediately after the mental application of resolve, [the author], explaining first the mere praise, says:
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then Śakra," etc.:
because it is not to be rejected due to an intention of renunciation and release, it is not to be abandoned;
because external dangers such as water and so forth are warded off, it is to be protected.
It should be protected by removing the faults of internal errors such as omissions and additions of syllables. One should "resolve" it by accepting it with the thought of not abandoning it.

"One should give" means giving away one's entire possession, together with its fruit, because it has the nature of the meaning of the text.
Showing this very [act] according to the sequence of the distinctions between the stages of preparation (*prayoga*), the main part (*maula*), and the conclusion (*pṛṣṭha*), he says:
One should offer it;
one should bestow it; one should relinquish it.
Alternatively, these three terms are stated according to the distinctions of the gift, the giver, and the recipient, all of whom are ultimately unapprehendable.
I shall explain this by means of his words.
"By that" and so forth; "the body" refers to images and the like.

"This very one [is superior] to those two" means that if someone were to give the relics of the Tathāgata to those two with honor and so forth, out of a superior intention to give preceded by compassion, this very person [is superior].
Now, refuting that by means of those very words, he says:
"In this very way, Kauśika," and so forth.
He states the second [objection]:
Furthermore, Kauśika, by the phrase "whichever son of good family or daughter of good family" and so forth:
because they have become worthy recipients (*pātrībhūta*) through their possession of the most acute faculty of faith and the rest, they are those who reside in regions such as Magadha;
"from there" means without having gone from the aforementioned person who is the donor.
He states the third [case]:
"Furthermore, Kauśika, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family, by means of the passage beginning 'those in Jambūdvīpa' and so forth,
would cause others to undertake [the practice] by making an effort for its acquisition."
One should cause [the teachings] to be established by stabilizing those that have been grasped. "From this" means from this person who performs the subsequent purpose;
"with indefatigability" means through one's own practice and application, free from laziness, one should bring it to completion.
Because he has generated enthusiasm, he is diligent;

thus, the connection with the preceding is that one should cause him—who has generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)—to grasp this *Prajñāpāramitā* by briefly teaching the meaning of the text.

One should encourage one who is negligent due to laziness, lack of aspiration, or attachment by instigating them toward what is wholesome. One should rouse one who is despondent due to low resolve, incapacity, self-conceit, or fear of regret by speaking of the benefits of superior vigor. One should gladden one who has correctly entered the path through the practice of unerring concentration, contentment, and vigor by praising their genuine qualities.
By thus bringing about obedience through the instruction of speech,
he will lead [them] and cause them to attain the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
And therein, by means of clear comprehension (*samprajanya*) and correct observation, he will respectively guide and follow them by removing the faults of lethargy and agitation.

In the *Prajñāpāramitā*,

the three terms "training," "practicing," and "striving" are stated respectively according to the distinctions of armor-like vigor (*sannāha-vīrya*), applied vigor (*prayoga-vīrya*), and non-retrogressive vigor (*anivartana-vīrya*).
[The term] "the destruction of the substrata" (*upadhi-saṃkṣaya*) refers to this.

Furthermore, Kausika, let alone all the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa; likewise, let alone those in the four great continents.

In the *Cūḍika-sāhasra* [chapter], it is said, "In the *Dvisāhasra-madhyama*," and so forth; thus, by means of these four *hāraka*s (sections), the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh measures of praise (*stuti-mātrā*) are indicated respectively.

However, after every instance where the words ending with "should cause to undertake" (*samādāpayet*) and "should establish" (*pratiṣṭhāpayet*) are indicated, one must supply from the previously mentioned *hāraka* the passage beginning with "What do you think? (*tat kiṃ manyase*) and continuing up to "would generate much more merit" (*bahutaraṃ puṇyaṃ prasavet*).
He speaks the eighth section of praise, beginning with:
"Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone [the merit of one who establishes] a trisāhasramahāsāhasra [world-system]," and so forth.

"Furthermore, Kauśika," and so forth,
by demonstrating the superior merit of one who establishes as many beings as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges within a trichiliocosm-megachiliocosm world-system in the four dhyānas.

The second, third, fourth, and fifth measures of praise (*stobhamātrā*) are indicated in their respective order.

In every case within the four sections (*hāraka*), following the word "one should establish," one should apply the sequence beginning from the previously mentioned section with "What do you think? up until the point "the manifestation of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
He now states the sixth measure of praise.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone [the merit of] a trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu," and so forth—by this, he states the seventh measure of praise (*stobhamātrā*).
Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "Moreover, Kauśika, whoever... and so forth, he states the eighth measure of praise.
Furthermore, by the words "Moreover, etc.":
one who is skilled in meaning (*arthakuśala*) is so because of proficiency in understanding the meaning.
That which is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), that very thing is considered by you to be emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Because no phenomenon exists that is separate from the dharmadhātu.
Based on this statement, one who intends to ask why the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is taught as the very object being perceived says:

"This too," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "If there is the comprehension of the referents of words, how can there be a non-comprehension of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) therein?"
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?", he says:
"For [he] will arise," and so forth.
This is what has been stated.

Because in a future time a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā* will arise in the sense of being similar [to the true one], a bodhisattva seeking unsurpassed enlightenment, having heard that [counterfeit], might fail to understand the correct *prajñāpāramitā*. Consequently, by practicing false treatises, he would fail to realize that the nature of perceived objects is like an illusion;
thus, through the loss of his intended goal, he might be ruined.
Therefore, it is said: "It is taught.
To address the questions of what its cause is and what its nature is—such that by abandoning its cause and its intrinsic nature it is avoided—the author says:
"How," and so forth.
Regarding "a counterfeit perfection of wisdom":
the rejection of the intended meaning and the conceptualization of another meaning— this,
it is said, is the counterfeit in the Perfection of Wisdom.

Explaining this very point, he says:
"those who have not cultivated ethical discipline," and so forth.

To support this, he says:
"those of poor wisdom," and so forth.
Because, through the application of ignorance, those of poor wisdom— being of a dull-witted nature due to doubt and the like, and having abandoned wisdom on account of false knowledge—
[hold that] "the destruction of form is the impermanence of form.
The destruction of imagined form, its non-existence, is the impermanence of form.
They will teach that the impermanence of form (*rūpānityatā*) is the non-abiding and destruction of conceptualized form after a single moment;

and that the impermanence of form is the destruction of form consisting of *dharmatā*, which is its being devoid of imagined form—this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore, these three meanings are to be understood according to the principle of repetition.
He says that they exalt themselves by being afflicted with false knowledge,
and thus they will instruct as follows:
"Whoever searches in this way, he shall course in the perfection of wisdom."

Intending to show that liberation does not occur as long as one remains attached to erroneously conceived entities—given that neither the properties (*dharma*) nor the substrata (*dharmin*) are negated by the aforementioned explanation—he said:
"Furthermore, Kauśika, the impermanence of form is not to be viewed as the destruction of form," and so forth.
Rather, the very nature of form and the other aggregates, which is like an illusion, is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

The intention is that this [perfection of wisdom] is to be practiced because it brings about the attainment of the state of a Tathāgata by serving as the cause for the complete abandonment of the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations, together with their habitual tendencies, which are rooted in the misconceptions regarding existence, non-existence, and so forth.

He states the ninth measure of praise, beginning with "Furthermore, Kauśika, as many as... and continuing until he demonstrates that the merit produced is far greater than that of one who establishes as many beings as there are in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the fruit of stream-entry.
Now, one might object: "Establishing [beings] in the fruit of stream-entry is their placement within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).

Yet, the gift of a manuscript of the *Prajñāpāramitā* preceded by faith and so forth, as well as the act of showing it to them and the like, are tainted (*sāsrava*). How then can the latter benefactor produce more merit than the former benefactor?
For what reason? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, Kauśika, the fruit of stream-entry," and so forth. This means:

because the Mother of the Victors (*jinajanani*) is the cause of all noble dharmas, such as the state of a Tathāgata—which is a mass of vast, stainless, and infinite qualities—the fruit of stream-entry arises from this Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) all the more so.

Therefore, because this [scripture] possesses the nature of being a complete cause through the gift of books and so forth, it generates much greater merit than the gift of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) or other distinct natures such as Buddhahood.
He states the first mere praise:

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in Jambudvīpa, as many as there are, in the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*); having raised the question "For what reason? as before, he provides the answer in the same manner, saying:
"Therefore, Kauśika, [the merit of] a once-returner," and so forth.
He states the second [case]:

"Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in Jambudvīpa, as many as they may be, in the fruit of a non-returner," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt, "For what reason is that? according to the previously mentioned intention, he speaks in order to resolve it in the same manner.
Therefore, O Kauśika, [the sūtra says] "one who is a non-returner," and so forth.
He states the third [case]:
"Furthermore, O Kauśika, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in Jambudvīpa, as many as there are, in the state of an arhat," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt as to why it is so in the manner prescribed, he says, as before:
"For this reason, Kauśika, [there is] arhatship," and so forth.
He states the fourth [verse].
Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in Jambudvīpa in the state of a pratyekabuddha;
having raised the question "For what reason? according to the method already stated, he says the same thing:
"For this reason, Kauśika, [the merit of] the state of a pratyekabuddha... and so forth.
He speaks of the fifth [case]: "Furthermore, Kauśika, as many beings as there are in Jambudvīpa, to all of them... and so forth.
"Should offer" (*upanāmayet*) means "should give."
With what intention [is this said]?
He says: "In this very *prajñāpāramitā*, etc.

Having cultivated the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), having attained growth by means of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), having attained increase by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and having attained vastness by means of the special path of the bodhisattva, he reaches [perfection] on the stage of a Tathāgata.
"He will fulfill the qualities of a Buddha"— this distinction in meaning must be stated.
Therefore, "than the former" refers to anyone who might generate the mind directed toward enlightenment.
"And whoever else, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), should give a book"—the meaning is [more meritorious] than those two persons.
Now, one might ask: "How can there be such greatness of merit for one who gives merely a book from someone who performs a superior deed by first generating the thought of awakening?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Niya-tam eṣa" and so forth.
"Niyatam" means necessarily; the meaning is that he is inevitably one who does not turn back.
This is what was said:

"Since an irreversible bodhisattva is certain to attain perfect awakening and is thus a distinguished field of merit by virtue of bringing an end to the suffering of sentient beings, the gift of a book to such a person alone yields far greater merit than the gift of a book to a person of indefinite lineage who has merely generated the thought of awakening."
He states the sixth [verse] with the words:
"Furthermore, Kausika, let alone those of Jambudvipa," and so forth,
up to the end of this section.

"one should generate the mind directed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Immediately following this, the passage beginning with "And furthermore, Kauśika, any other son of good family or daughter of good family... and so forth, which was previously mentioned, is to be repeated here;
thus he speaks of the seventh [case].
"But let it be, Kauśika, in a world-system of four great continents," and so on—in this same manner, the text continues until the end of the section.
It should be followed accordingly.
He speaks of the eighth [stage] with the words:
"Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone in a thousand-peaked world system," and so forth.
"By a greater measure" means by a superior manner.
Regarding the phrase "for what reason," the answer to the question should be stated as before.
He speaks the ninth measure of praise:
"Furthermore, Kauśika, as many beings as there are in Jambūdvīpa, all of them," and so forth.
It is not only because of his own perfect awakening, but also because of his acting for the benefit of others.

To demonstrate that there is even greater merit in instructing and admonishing a Bodhisattva who possesses swift superknowledge— even though that Bodhisattva has not yet attained full awakening— the text says:
"In whatever way, O Blessed One," and so forth.
In that context, "robes" refers to clothing;
"almsfood" refers to cakes and the like;
and "lodgings" refers to mattresses and the like.

A seat refers to the staff-seat (*daṇḍāsana*) and so forth. One approaches—that is, goes toward—the one who is afflicted by diseases, the sick person. Appropriate medicine refers to *harītakī* and the like.
"Requisites" refers to items such as small boxes; "those acts performed" means robes and so forth that have been given.
Because they possess the power to yield fruit visible in this very life, one makes them bear great fruit.
The connection with the preceding is that [the merit] produces great benefits by yielding fruit in another birth;
the sense is that this is because Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas are indistinguishable in their status as the supreme objects of veneration (*dakṣiṇīya*).
If one asks, "Why is this so? [the answer follows].
For it was said by the Blessed One himself in the Āgama at the time of his final nirvāṇa, after having partaken of the alms-food of Cunda the smith’s son:
“Let there be no remorse for Cunda the smith’s son on account of this.
Ānanda, you must dispel the remorse of Cunda the smith’s son.”
And he should be told this:

"The alms-food by partaking of which the Tathāgata fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and the alms-food by partaking of which he passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder— these two alms-foods yield equal and peerless fruit."
Regarding the phrase "of equal maturation with the peerless":
by demonstrating that their fruits are equal, it is made known that these two possess equal worthiness of offerings (*dakṣiṇīyatva*).

Now, one might ask: since proximity [to enlightenment] results from the repeated practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), why is proximity indicated here by means of instruction (*avavāda*) and admonition (*anuśāsanī*)?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason is that? he says:
"For it is thus, O Blessed One," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:

This is the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*), because through instruction and admonition (*avavādānuśāsanī*), there occurs the proximity [to the goal] due to the arising of distinguished moments;
indeed, this is even more so through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
He concludes for the purpose of praising, exalting, and commending those who grant encouragement to Bodhisattvas by giving the cry of "Excellent! Excellent! (*sādhu sādhu*).
Thus says the noble Vimuktisena:
"By speaking of the very rapid approach [to the goal], you inspire enthusiasm;
you favor us by means of instruction."
"You surround him by means of instruction.
[The opponent asks: "How can there be a favor toward one person by increasing the enthusiasm of another?
Anticipating this question, he says:
Therefore, it says, "For they have given birth," and so forth. This means:
"Because it is accomplished by increasing the enthusiasm for the mind of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, [it is] that which effects the welfare of the world for the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas."
"Because [it leads to] unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, there is benefit for sentient beings through increasing their enthusiasm for these [perfections].
Explaining this very point by way of its contrapositive, he says:
"If indeed," and so forth.
They would not attain perfect enlightenment;
therefore, the implication is that one should not act for the sake of sentient beings. And he states this by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
The phrase beginning with "Therefore... [indicates that] they awaken to perfect enlightenment; hence, the thought is that they act for the benefit of the world.

In this context, those qualities such as praise and so forth are described as being of the nature of that [enlightenment] because they demonstrate the increasing greatness of merit; they are characterized solely by the realization of the reality of things as they are (*yathābhūtārtha*), and do not consist of mere eulogies (*arthavāda*) or the like, according to the aforementioned classifications.
Thus should they be understood.
And so it has been said:
"Praise, exaltation, and commendation are directed toward the perfection of wisdom."

"Through three sets of nine degrees of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa), it is so intended. By establishing it thus, that which is stated in various other sūtras and introductory narratives— that the Blessed One dwells together with all the bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who have been praised, lauded, and extolled by all the Buddhas— becomes logically consistent.

In the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, the commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this is the fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Enumeration of Merit. Immediately following this, the mental application of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-manaskāra*) must be explained, because one should perform the dedication of the mental application of resolute belief— which has been praised, extolled, and lauded by all the Buddhas— toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

And since that [non-conceptualization] is of many kinds due to the differences in the objects of exclusion, he speaks—beginning with "Then indeed, Maitreya," etc.—to indicate the mental application (*manaskāra*) of specific transformation.

In that context, "Maitreya" is the name of a meditative absorption (*samādhi*); by attaining that, for someone, the state of being Maitreya is the fruit resulting from the realization of that absorption.

Because he has realized the fruit of the loving-kindness (*maitrī*) previously vowed, or because he has acquired such qualities through being manifested by the gateway of liberation that is loving-kindness (*maitrī-vimokṣamukha*), he has become Maitreya; thus he is called Maitreya.
He is a *bodhisattva* due to his union with right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*), and a *mahāsattva* due to his connection with all modes of skillful means (*upāya*).
This is because the *Amoghapāśa-sūtra* states that the terms *bodhisattva* and *mahāsattva* denote wisdom and skillful means, respectively.
"Accompanied by rejoicing and dedication" means:

dedication preceded by rejoicing; because it is a dedication performed through a mental attention (*manaskāra*) that takes as its object the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is a "mental attention of distinguished dedication," and [the term] is accompanied by that—this is the summary.

For instance, this mode is also possible: having rejoiced in the meritorious bases of action consisting of giving and so forth belonging to others by means of the mental attention of rejoicing (anumodanā-manaskāra) which will be explained below, one should dedicate it toward awakening.

And thus, immediately thereafter, he will say: "Having rejoiced in this way, one should utter the words: 'I dedicate this meritorious base of action associated with rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.
The word "from that" (tataḥ) means from the meritorious bases of action consisting of giving and so forth belonging to all sentient beings.
It is called "supreme" because it possesses a twofold supremacy.
He says that this twofold supremacy consists of supremacy as the most excellent due to its intense heat, and supremacy as the eldest due to its being without a second;
thus it is called "the most excellent" and "the eldest."

The state of being the most excellent is also twofold: by way of being superior through skillful means (*upāyakauśala*), and by way of being preeminent through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Thus it is said: "It is called 'excellent' (*vara*"); "it is called 'preeminent' (*pravara*)."
It is said that "it is declared to be sublime" in order to state that nothing more sublime than both [of these] exists.
Furthermore, preeminence is twofold:
by way of being supreme and by way of the absence of equals.
And it is stated thus to show that, because there is nothing superior, it is unsurpassed;
it is called "supreme" and it is called "unsurpassed."
He says that there is nothing superior to these two;
it is called "unsurpassed" (*niruttama*).
And according to the method described, it is called "unequaled" (*asama*) because it is not shared with the *śrāvakas* and others.
Because it is the cause for attaining equality with the peerless Buddhas, it is called "unequaled and equal" (*asamasama*).
Desiring to point out the mental attention of dedication in the form of non-apprehension (*anupalambhākāra*), he says:
"When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti... and so forth.

"Throughout the world in the ten directions, everywhere, all-pervadingly. This means that throughout the entire world-system in the ten directions, it pervades all directions, beginning with the east.

The world-systems situated in the directions—east, west, south, and north—which are respectively immeasurable (*aprameya*), incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), infinite (*aparimāṇa*), and inconceivable (*acintya*), are specified by the phrases "immeasurable among the immeasurable," and so forth, according to their respective order.
Likewise, the distinction in meaning should be stated as "situated in the upward and downward directions, in infinite and boundless [realms]," and so forth,
regarding "the immeasurable and immeasurable," etc.,
referring to those who are free from passion according to the world (*laukika-vītarāga*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*).

The terms "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) and so forth should be understood as referring, respectively, to the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas, because they have transcended the path of knowledge that is immeasurable, incalculable, infinite, inconceivable, and boundless.

Regarding the phrase "those whose paths are cut" (*chinnavartmanām*), and so on: they are "those whose paths are cut" because their enemies have been slain and their outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted.
By virtue of being free from afflictions and having attained mastery, they have cut off the path of the stream.
By virtue of being well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom, they have severed the conduit to the proliferation of existence.
By virtue of being noble and great elephants, they have exhausted their tears.
Because they have accomplished what was to be done and because they have performed their duty, they have crushed all thorns.
The phrase "for those who have laid down their burden," and so forth, has already been explained.

Alternatively, through the five clear realizations (*abhisamaya*)—namely, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), and the summit awakening (*mūrdhābhisambodha*)—one successively abandons the objects that are to be abandoned.
The five phrases beginning with "chinnavartmanām" refer to the five realizations (*abhisamaya*).

Corresponding to these five realizations, through the application of the realization of the dharmas to be attained, the five phrases beginning with "svapahṛtabhārāṇām" are to be explained in their respective order.
"Etasminnantare" means in the middle.
Untainted ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom constitute the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom.
The abandonment of all obscurations is the aggregate of liberation.
The direct realization of distinguished knowledge is the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Since all of this is common to the śrāvakas and others, he speaks for the sake of what is uncommon, beginning with the words "And those which... and so forth.
In that regard, substantially, there are six perfections (pāramitās).
In terms of name, however, there are ten,
because the four perfections are differentiated [by the addition of skillful means and so forth].
For instance, supramundane non-conceptual gnosis (*jñāna*) which gradually effects the abandonment of all obscurations is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Furthermore, those comprised by the knowledge obtained subsequent to the supramundane path would be the perfections of skillful means (*upāya*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*).
Having first indicated the six perfections according to their predominance, he speaks in order to include the remaining perfections:
"the perfection of skillful means for the attainment of the qualities of a Buddha" and "the perfection of power" are easy to understand.
The "perfection of superknowledge" (*abhijñā-pāramitā*) should be understood as either all the superknowledges of a Buddha or specifically the sixth one.
The "perfection of full comprehension" (*parijñā-pāramitā*) is the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
If it is asked how the perfection of knowledge, despite being preeminent, is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), the answer is given:

Because the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*) is the knowledge obtained subsequent to non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*), by which knowledge one discerns the realization and personally experiences the enjoyment of the Dharma for oneself, and causes others to do so—
and because both of these [experiences] do not exist within that non-conceptual knowledge itself— the perfection of wisdom is therefore not non-conceptual.
As for the "perfection of aspiration" (*praṇidhānapāramitā*), it is already well known.

"The perfection of the knowledge of the omniscient one" refers to the stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā). "And that which is the desire for welfare" refers to sympathetic joy (muditā) and equanimity (upekṣā).
"Buddha-qualities" refers to the eighteen unique attributes of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) and so forth.
"The bliss of perfect enlightenment" refers to *samyaksambodhisukha*.
The fruit of abandoning the latencies and their continuities of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations is the perfection of sovereignty over all phenomena; that is,
the capacity to accomplish the welfare of the world in all its aspects.
"Unconquered, the conqueror of all" means that he is not surpassed by Māra, the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*), and others, and has instead conquered them.

"The performance of supernatural power" (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) refers to the miracle of supernormal power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), which is the cause for planting the seed of enlightenment after first winning over [beings].
And as for the passage beginning with "that which is unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*), etc.:
because of the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is respectively unobstructed, unattached, and for that very reason unimpeded.
Because it lacks an equal, it is unequaled (*asama*).
It is equal to the unequaled because of its equality with both the conditioned and the unconditioned;
it is incomparable because it transcends all other comparisons;
it is immeasurable because it is incapable of being delimited by infinite knowledge.
To the question "What is that which is thus distinguished by these qualifiers?", he says:
"the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of things as they truly are.
Knowledge alone, which is capable of performing the miracles of instruction and so forth, is called "power" because it is unimpeded.
Regarding the phrase "that which is the power of the Buddha's knowledge among powers":
the very knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āśravakṣayajñāna*) is the most preeminent among all powers.
Regarding the phrase "that which is the vision of the Buddha's knowledge": [it refers to the direct realization of that same state].
Knowledge is the perfect awakening to the truths and so forth, the five superknowledges, vision,
and the perfection of the ten powers.
The "ten powers" refers to the ten beginning with the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible.
Regarding the "four grounds of self-confidence" (*caturvaiśāradya*):

when making the claim, "I am a perfectly awakened one," and so forth, there is fearlessness because no challenger exists to question it; these four forms of fearlessness constitute the state of being supremely and perfectly fulfilled through those four grounds of self-confidence.
He states that "the realization of which is conventional, while the other is ultimate," beginning with the words "And that which... and so forth.
"By way of the realization of the ultimate truth" means that the turning of the wheel of Dharma occurs through bringing the illusion-like nature of phenomena to mind.

"Turning" (pravartana) refers to the expansion within the mental continuum of those to be trained, by means of repeatedly bringing [the Dharma] to presence like a wheel, through the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* which illuminates the Dharma— that is, one's own realization.
Precisely that [is] the grasping of the torch of Dharma because it dispels darkness;
it is the sounding of the drum of Dharma because it brings about perfect awakening.
The blowing of the Dharma-conch is due to fulfilling the minds of those to be trained;
the sounding of the Dharma-conch is by way of its being public;
and the striking of the Dharma-conch is due to the firm destruction of all obscurations.
By way of its color, it is the raining down of the rain of Dharma;
by way of its clarity and intelligibility, it is the performance of the sacrifice of Dharma;
and by way of its pleasantness, it is the satisfaction of all sentient beings.
It is called "invitation" (*sampravāraṇa*) because it brings about happiness by means of being worth hearing.
Regarding the phrase "and those who there," and so forth:
they are "disciplined" (*vinīta*) because they have been trained in the qualities of a Buddha, and "instructed" (*śikṣita*) because they have been taught in the qualities of a Pratyekabuddha.

They are called "resolved" because of their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in the dharmas of the disciples (*śrāvaka*). They are "fixed" because they have attained a specific spiritual lineage (*gotra*) for the realization of their own enlightenment; for that very reason, they are "destined for perfect awakening.
[The term] "those in training" (*śaikṣa*) refers to...
These belong to those who have entered upon the first fruit and so forth;
"belonging to those beyond training" refers to the Arhats.
In that regard, one who has received full ordination through a ritual consisting of three proclamations and so forth is a *bhikṣu*; likewise is a *bhikṣuṇī*.

Through the undertaking of the three refuges and the undertaking of the five precepts (*pañca-śikṣāpada*), there is a twofold division: the lay follower (*upāsaka*) and likewise the lay follower female (*upāsikā*).
"May my teacher recognize me as a lay follower who has undertaken the three refuges."
Likewise, because there are two readings in the Vinaya— “May my teacher remember me as one who has gone for refuge to the Three and has undertaken the five precepts, an upāsaka”—
and [the phrase] “those to be cultivated by mind” refers to one, two, or three persons who inspire confidence in the mind.
"Without remainder, entirely without remainder":
this should be stated respectively because [the cause] is infinite and because it bestows immeasurable fruit.
"In a single mass," and so forth.

Because it has been taught in connection with the past Tathāgatas, having unified them as being of a single nature, having concentrated them in the mind, having synthesized them in the form of being immeasurable and so forth, having counted them, having weighed them in relation to everything from Bodhisattvas down to those in the animal realm, and having established them as a standard by means of the "supreme" [perfection] whose characteristics will be described below—
One should rejoice through rejoicing.

This means that one should personally cultivate an excellence of intention, characterized by extraordinary faith and great joy, as well as an excellence of intention toward accomplishing all of that, in accordance with the intention of the agent.
Speaking precisely for the sake of the foremost [goal], he says:
"O Best One," and so forth;
this has already been explained.
"He spoke these words."

The meaning is that one should utter the words: "By means of mental attention directed toward the non-apprehension of the aggregates of morality and so forth of all Tathāgatas, I dedicate the merit accompanied by rejoicing for the sake of all sentient beings toward unsurpassed enlightenment.
This is what is meant by "the bringer" (*āhāraka*);
the ellipsis is to be supplied as "the producer for me or for all sentient beings."

Having explained the mental attention of dedication through non-apprehension (*anupalambha-pariṇāmanā-manaskāra*), he now asks a question in order to resolve potential objections regarding that matter, saying:
"In this regard, one belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle," and so forth;
[namely,] "by means of which things does one dedicate?"
The meaning is that he brings forth [the result] by means of those causes, such as the lineage of Tathāgatahood and so forth.
In some places, the reading is "he rejoices" (*anumodeta*);
even there, since the mental application of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-manaskāra*) is the subject under discussion, the meaning should be understood as "he dedicates."
And so he will state immediately thereafter:
"By which things does one dedicate?
By which objects and by which aspects?"
The objects of focus (*ālambana*) are the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) and all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); the modes of grasping them are the aspects (*ākāra*).
"That mind" refers to the conceptual construction of a grasper (*grāhakavikalpa*). "Moreover" (*api tu*)... [indicates] that...
The word *api tu* is a particle used in the sense of the word *kim*.
[It implies: "They would be perceived in such a way that one makes them the objective cause (*nimitta*).
This is because it is impossible to perform a dedication (*pariṇāmana*) without making things such as the object (*vastu*) the objective cause; for those [objects] exist only as past.

The meaning is: having superimposed [attributes] that are already present, they are made objects of cognition through conventional manifestation (*udbhāvana-saṃvṛti*); do they then actually exist in reality (*tattvataḥ*) in that very same way? If the view is that they are so perceived, then in that case:
For the perception of a real entity as something subverted by valid cognition is determined to be an error,
just like the cognition of a mirage and the like.
Therefore, the process of transformation is considered to proceed by the power of that [ignorance],
being as if weak and driven by the misconception of self and what belongs to the self.

Such is the thought. Since the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is unreal because it is superimposed and because its occurrence is dependent upon cognition, they are not perceived in reality, like a dream, an illusion, or a mirage; thus he says:
"Those [elements], O Venerable One," and so forth.
Even so, there would be the consequence of a perverted transformation (*viparyasta-pariṇāma*); therefore, he says:
"If it [perceives] that which is non-existent," and so forth:
it would take as its objective support (*ālambana*) by making the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) its object;
it would take as its sign (*nimitta*) by determining the form of the universal (*sāmānyarūpa*).

Perverted perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) is the error consisting of grasping at signs within perception—which is by nature the apprehension of signs—due to the absence of its own object; it is a delusion because one grasps something as being what it is not.
Perverted mind (*citta-viparyāsa*) is likewise the perversion of the mind, which is the consciousness that grasps an objective support (*ālambana*).

The perversion of view (*dṛṣṭiviparyāsa*) is the perversion, as previously explained, of that wisdom (*prajñā*) which consists of the discernment of the aspects of vision itself and has the nature of investigation.

The phrase "it would not be" is connected with the preceding [text] as "but rather it would be," meaning that the mental application of dedication through non-apprehension (*anupalambha-pariṇāmanā-manaskāra*) is, in fact, of the nature of the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), and so forth— this is the remainder [of the sense].

Therefore, by establishing the erroneous nature of perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth in some other way, nothing would have been said that does not contradict the subject at hand. However, if perception and the rest are erroneous because their own objects do not exist,
how could something else— which possesses a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)— be of the nature of a "perceptual error" (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) and so forth?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For it is thus," and so forth.
By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even passion" (*rāgo 'pi*), hatred and the other [afflictions] are included.
"Having conceptualized" means having superimposed.
"Having intended" means... [the rest of the sentence follows].

Furthermore, because passion also arises from perverted perceptions (*saṃjñā*) and so forth when repeatedly taking them as objects, it should be understood that passion is likewise a perversion of perception.
This is what has been stated.

Because, having superimposed non-existent qualities such as permanence upon an entity that is actually endowed with qualities such as impermanence, and repeatedly taking that very [superimposition] as an object, there arises— caused by perverted notions such as attachment and so forth—
a state consisting of the perversion of perception and the like; therefore,
the mental attention of transformation through non-apprehension arises in exactly that same way.
He states another position,
beginning with "But even if," etc.:
"But even if [it were] according to the object, according to the objective support, and according to the form..."
The word "existing" (*saṃvidyamāna*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Likewise, one must supply the phrase "is it not existing? after "bodhi" and "citta. Having thus accepted [the opponent's position], he says:
"Thus," and so forth: the realization is that all phenomena— both the grasped and the grasper— as well as all their latencies and all the elements, are non-existent.
If it is argued, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", he says:
"And if," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:

If things such as objects do not exist in the way they appear, and likewise for the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and so forth, then by means of which objects and so forth would one transform which mind and so forth into awakening?
Since one does not transform anything at all, anywhere, by anyone, when transformation is thus impossible in every respect, it is a "perversion of transformation.
One who is thus perverted with respect to reality—

With the intention that "just as the conceptualizations of impermanence and so forth lead to the realization of the ultimate reality through a traditional lineage, the mental application of transformation (*pariṇāmanā-manaskāra*) is indeed accepted because things and so forth exist conventionally; therefore, you have said nothing additional," he says, "Not this, O noble Subhūti," and so forth.

Alternatively, with the intention that "because there is an absence of ultimate attachment toward that object of focus and so forth, the transformation is not a perverted transformation, since it is a transformation [performed] conventionally like that of an illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*)," he says:
"O Noble Subhūti, this is not [the case]," and so forth. One might ask: "Even though it is logically consistent, why should it not be taught to a beginner? Anticipating this question, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yadapi hi syāt" (even if it might be so) and so forth:

because of the lack of firmness due to the deficiency of realization and conviction, that very [faith] is described as being merely faith (*śraddhāmātraka*) through the distinction of weak, medium, and intense,
by means of the three terms beginning with "merely affection" (*premamātraka*).

Alternatively, faith (*śraddhā*) alone is described in three ways—as conviction, clarity, and aspiration—respectively regarding existence, possession of qualities, and capability; thus it is designated as mere love (*prema*) and so forth.
"It would vanish" means it would perish.
The meaning is that this is because of a lack of skill in distinguishing between the conventional and the ultimate.
To the objection that it would then follow that [the statement] should not be spoken at all, he says:
"Of one who is irreversible," and so forth.

The meaning is that one who is supported by a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)—even an ordinary person (pṛthagjana)—attains knowledge of the nature of both truths by virtue of being sustained by a spiritual friend.
For the sake of a conclusion, he says:
