It is undifferentiated because there is an absence of distinction characterized by multiplicity.
It is "uninterrupted" because there is no interruption due to differentiation, characteristics, or cessation;
or it is described as such respectively because it is devoid of the diversity of specific and general characteristics.
Thus begins the passage starting with "iti hi," and so forth.
That which is the suchness of the conventional is also considered the suchness of the ultimate;
for there is no difference between them, and that principle is established according to how things appear.

According to this principle, that very purity of the illusion-like nature—which arises from the disappearance of the attachment to self and what belongs to self regarding form and so forth—is itself the purity of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) of the fruits such as stream-entry, by virtue of being free from all opposing factors.

Thus, the purity of the fruit is the purity of form and so forth; because they are non-dual, undivided, inseparable, and uninterrupted, the purity of form and so forth is stated to be the purity of the fruit, and likewise, the purity of the fruit is stated to be the purity of form and so forth. This is the intended meaning.
And so it has been said: "The purity of the fruit is indeed the purity of form and the rest; because there is no distinction or separation between these two, purity is thus proclaimed. (28)
Having thus stated purity in general, he speaks of it specifically with the words "Furthermore," and so forth. "The purity of omniscience" means:
The meaning is the purification of the three types of omniscience.
Therefore, this has been stated:
it comes to be.

The purity of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) results from the Śrāvakas’ abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and from the Pratyekabuddhas’ abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions as well as a portion of the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) consisting of the conceptualization of the apprehended (*grāhyavikalpa*).
The purity of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) results from the Bodhisattvas’ abandonment of the obscurations to the paths of the three vehicles.

"The purification of the omniscience of the Tathāgatas is ultimate because it arises from the dharmadhātu through the abandonment of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations along with their latent predispositions.
And so it has been said:
"Of the three paths of the afflictions and the cognizable, belonging to the disciples, the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas], and the sons of the Victor..."
Purification through abandonment is, however, absolute for the Buddha in every respect. //29//

Thus, in the section on the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñatā*), in the context of explaining purification, the ultimate and the non-ultimate purification of the Tathāgatas and the Śrāvakas respectively have been stated. To explain how that [purification] occurs, he says:
"Then indeed, the Venerable... and so forth.
It is a light that produces profound illumination; it is without reconnection, without defilement,
without attainment, and without realization.
The nine categories of meaning spoken by the noble Śāriputra— beginning with "non-manifestation" (*anabhinirvṛti*) and "ultimate birth" (*atyantopapatti*)—

are to be understood as being, respectively, the nature of the ninefold path of cultivation, starting from the "mild-mild" (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) and so forth. Furthermore, the statement made by the Blessed One, "because of purity at every stage," is to be applied to the abandonment of the ninefold types of opposing factors (*vipakṣa*), beginning from the "intense-intense" (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) and so forth.

Because of the statement "in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm," the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) belonging to the nine stages beginning with the desire realm is to be understood. As for what was said— that "in the desire realm and at the peak of existence, [the factors] are devoid of the limbs of enlightenment and the path"—
some maintain that this refers to Śrāvakas who are unskilled in means, and thus there is no contradiction with the present [statement].
Others maintain that the path of cultivation consists of nine stages, beginning from the stage of "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*) up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*).

However, the mention of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth is intended solely to demonstrate that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no [actual] abiding therein for the Mother.
But it does not illuminate the nine stages.
Thus, this is the summarized meaning:

within the nine stages as previously described, for each stage respectively, there are nine types of paths—beginning with the "weak-weak" and so forth—which serve as the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to the nine types of opposing factors (*vipakṣa*), beginning with the "strong-strong" and so forth, in their respective order.
Furthermore, because it is the cause of purification, there is both ultimate and non-ultimate purification.
And so it has been said:
"The path beginning with the softest-of-the-soft [levels] is the purification in the nine stages."
"By way of being the antidote to the stains of the highest-of-the-high degree and so forth. [30] Thus it is said. He explains how there is non-figurative and ultimate purity:
"He does not know," and so forth:
he does not know the essential nature;
he does not fully cognize the distinctions.
"Because of its purity" means because it is the antidote to the three realms.
Why is it that [the mind] is directed toward the object?
This is a question and not a censure;
he states that very point in the passage beginning with "form" (rūpa).
Now, one might ask: "If form is eternally present, why is it not perceived? Anticipating this question, he says: "Because of its purity."
Because, in reality, they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).

Now, one might object: "Should it not be the case that the antidotes of the 'intense-intense' grade and so forth correspond to the opposing factors (*vipakṣa*) of the 'weak-weak' grade and so forth? Why, then, has it been taught otherwise? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom [is not a cause] for omniscience," and so forth.
Because there is no removal of the established reality of dharmas (*dharmatattva*), it does not cause harm;
because it does not produce what was previously non-existent, it does not cause benefit—this is the connection with the preceding [text].
This is the collective meaning of the section beginning with "he does not grasp the antidote, he does not abandon the discordant factor, he does not know," and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Should it not be the case that a superior (*adhimātra*) counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) and so forth opposes a weak-weak (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) adverse element (*vipakṣa*) and so forth? Why, then, is it explained otherwise? This objection is resolved by showing that, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no assistance or the like for anyone; yet, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), the resolution is provided through the example of a washerman’s great effort in removing subtle stains, and through the implicit force of the argument regarding the arising of counteragents in the sequence of weak-weak and so forth. Thus, for that final moment of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as previously described, there is the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) of both the cognition and the cognizable objects belonging to the three realms.
Equanimity is the realization that all phenomena are like an illusion; it is considered such because it constitutes the nature of all remedies.
Thus, the ultimate purity is accepted as the primary quality of the Blessed Buddha.
And so it has been said:

"The antidotal nature toward the three realms is the equality of the means of cognition and the object of cognition; this is intended for the Path as a resolution to that objection. (31) Thus, immediately following the completion of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and within that same context, [the author] speaks in order to point out what was previously stated: "That which is the purity of form, that which is the purity of the fruit, and that which is the purity of omniscience. [The verse continues: "The purity of the fruit is the purity of the object of cognition; the purity of the object of cognition is the purity of the means of cognition. The purity of the means of cognition is the purity of the Omniscient One; thus, the purity of the three is established as non-dual. (32) In this regard, the purity of the fruit is the purity of the object of cognition because it is the object of the means of cognition. The purity of the object of cognition is the purity of the means of cognition because the means of cognition is dependent upon the object of cognition. The purity of the means of cognition is the purity of the Omniscient One because the Omniscient One is the subject who possesses that means of cognition. Therefore, the purity of these three is established as non-dual. This is because the Omniscient One is the subject who possesses the means of cognition, the object of cognition is the object of that means of cognition, and the fruit is the attainment of that object of cognition. Since there is no distinction between the subject, the object, and the attainment, their purity is established as non-dual. Furthermore, since the Omniscient One is the subject who possesses the means of cognition, and the object of cognition is the object of that means of cognition, and the fruit is the attainment of that object of cognition, and since there is no distinction between the subject, the object, and the attainment, their purity is established as non-dual. Moreover, since the Omniscient One is the subject who possesses the means of cognition, and the object of cognition is the object of that means of cognition, and the fruit is the attainment of that object of cognition, and since there is no distinction between the subject, the object, and the attainment, their purity is established as non-dual. Furthermore, since the Omniscient One is the subject who possesses the means of cognition, and the object of cognition is the object of that means of cognition, and the fruit is the attainment of that object of cognition, and since there is no distinction between the subject, the object, and the attainment, their purity is established as non-dual. Moreover, since the Omniscient One is the subject who possesses the means of cognition, and the object of cognition is the object of that means of cognition, and the fruit is the attainment of that object of cognition, and since there is no distinction between the subject, the object, and the attainment, their purity is established as non-dual. Furthermore, since the Omniscient One is the subject who possesses the means of cognition, and the object of cognition is the object of that means of cognition, and the fruit is the attainment of that object of cognition, and since there is no distinction between the subject, the object, and the attainment, their purity is established as non-dual. "O Bhagavat, from the purity of the self comes the purity of form," and so forth.

Just as the self—which is conceptually constructed by others—is pure by virtue of its ultimate non-arising, so too should the purity of everything from form up to omniscience be understood; such is the meaning of the three necklaces (*hāraka*).

The Blessed One has stated everywhere that [the distinction] is due to extreme purity, with the intention that the distinction between the reality and unreality of form and so forth, and of the self, in their respective causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*)—by way of being fit or unfit—is only conventional (*saṃvṛti*), but not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). He states that there is no realization of reality in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as previously described: *na hi kasyacid dharmasya āgatir vā gatir vopalabhyate.* (It is not that the coming or going of any dharma is perceived. He says: "In the path of cultivation as previously described, there is no realization in terms of ultimate reality."
"O Blessed One, because of the purity of the self, there is neither attainment nor realization.
In this regard, there is no attainment by means of the "foremost attainment," which is characterized by fitness;
and there is no realization by means of the path of liberation.
He says "in this way by reality" (tattvenaivaṃ);
[he explains] "because of purity" (viśuddhatvāt),
which means "because of emptiness" (śūnyatvāt).
But from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), he says that everything exists.
Regarding the phrase "by way of being limitless with respect to the self" and so forth:

the meaning is that because the nature of the self—the preceding cause which is delightful only when not investigated—is limitless, the limitlessness of form and the other aggregates is thereby understood.
Because it is pure and because it is devoid of arising in accordance with [false] reasoning,
he says "ya evamasya" etc., while concluding the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).

Thus, this realization or attainment which occurs through the sequence just described, beginning with the process of darkening (*dhyāmīkaraṇatā*) and so forth, is to be understood as the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*) of the Bodhisattvas, by virtue of its being free from defects.

Since the thorough knowledge of the path cannot be correctly attained without the thorough knowledge of all things, he speaks of the non-abiding in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa in order to explain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
He begins with the words, "That indeed, moreover... and so forth.

Because it realizes the equality of phenomena belonging to the three times by way of their non-arising, and because it is not within the sphere of the Śrāvakas and others—being thus remote and of a distant nature—it is considered the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, she does not abide on the near shore of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) because she perceives its defects through wisdom;

nor does she abide on the far shore of *nirvāṇa* because she acts for the benefit of sentient beings out of compassion; nor does she abide anywhere between these two, cyclic existence and *nirvāṇa*, as a substantial entity.
They are established even among sentient beings because of their ultimate purity.
Because through the correct penetration of wisdom and compassion, one is free from the apprehension of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
And so it has been said:
"It does not abide on the near shore, nor on the far shore, nor in between the two."
"Because of the knowledge of the equality of the paths, it is considered the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

(1) Thus, by way of a negative indication (*vyatireka-nirdeśa*) within the section on omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it should be understood that because Śrāvakas and others lack the knowledge of the equality of the paths, they have become distant from the perfect perfection of wisdom.

However, the perfection of wisdom consisting merely of their own personal realization remains situated in both nirvāṇa and saṃsāra due to a deficiency in compassion and wisdom, by virtue of perceiving entities and non-entities.

In this way, it should be understood that in what follows as well, the teaching is sometimes given by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), sometimes by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and sometimes by both ways.
Now, [it is said]: "That which is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), that very thing you consider to be emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."

According to this principle, the knowledge of the equality of the time-periods (*adhvasamatājñāna*) is simply the comprehension of the meaning of the words (*padārthāvabodha*), and since that exists for everyone, how could the Śrāvakas and others be far removed from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?
To this, he says: "Even so," and so forth.
By the use of the word "also" (api), it is meant that not only [is it abandoned] by another form such as existence and so forth,
but rather, even in this way— that is, even through the application of the cause for dogmatic adherence that "it does not abide anywhere"— [one will abandon it].
"Riñciṣyati" means "he will cast far away."
It should be stated respectively as "in the present" and "in the future.
What is the reason here for the mother's distancing [from the child] through the realization of the cause? Anticipating this question, he says:
"Even by name," and so forth.

In this context, "name" refers merely to designations such as "Perfection of Wisdom," which serve as the signs (*nimitta*) for entities characterized as imagined (*parikalpita*) and so on. Attachment (*saṅga*) is the perversion that consists in taking that which is a locus of attachment as an object of clinging.
This has been stated:

"Just as when an object created by a magician appears, one who does not know its true nature perceives it as having intrinsic existence and thus fails to perceive its lack of self-nature; so too, due to a deficiency in spiritual friends and skillful means, there arises an attachment to objective perception characterized by error when one practices through engagement with signs."

"Because the thorough knowledge of that equality does not exist for Śrāvakas and others, whose nature is characterized by non-understanding, they remain far from the Mother of the Jinas. On the other hand, for Bodhisattvas and others, who have dispelled the delusive signs of adherence to the notion of intrinsic existence, the thorough knowledge of all phenomena such as form is itself the thorough knowledge of their equality; therefore, it is stated by implication that they are correctly near to this Mother. Thus he says:
"O Bhagavan, it is wonderful," and so forth.
By the use of the word "up to" (*yāvat*), the phrase beginning with "well-purified" (*supariśuddha*) is included.
It is called "well-expounded" (*svākhyāta*) because it is taught as the opposite of the realization of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
It is well-expounded because it brings about the full realization of the Mahāyāna;
it is perfectly consummated because it brings about the attainment of the ultimate limit of the excellence of all virtues.
These, beginning with "name" and so forth, are also called "attachments."
This very point should be understood through the distinction between Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas;
and so it has been said:
"By means of what is not a skillful method, that [perfection] is far removed because of the apprehension of signs."
"By means of skillful means (upāyakauśalya), her correct proximity has been declared. Thus,

he says [the following] in order to demonstrate that the practice of the Śrāvakas and others— which, although it serves as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*) by way of distancing them from the Mother— constitutes a discordant factor (*vipakṣa*) for Bodhisattvas because it proceeds from the error of apprehending real entities (*vastūpalambhaviparyāsa*).
"What are they? and so forth.
"Empty" means the absence of a self as imagined by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The connection is with what will be said [later], "he perceives.
"To such an extent" means delimited by numbers such as "immeasurable" and so forth.

"By the first production of the thought of awakening" (*cittotpāda*)—here, "production of the thought of awakening" is an indication for the factors conducive to awakening, such as generosity and so forth. To the question, "In what way is the production of the thought of awakening an attachment? he says:
"By what? and so forth.
He says "If he... and so forth, because [the mind] functions through perversion (*viparyāsa*).

"This is that first thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Thus, by means of the application of conceptual adherence (*abhiniveśa*), one perceives that thought of awakening as it is. Then, when one dedicates it through the application of conceptual adherence, thinking, "I dedicate this first thought of awakening," the meaning of the sentence is that there is a connection [of cause and effect] by way of this method.
He asks, "Why is there such a misconception?
and replies, "And the nature of the mind is not... and so forth. [The phrase] "to transform" means...

It should be understood that by means of the mental application of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-manaskāra*) distinguished by the twelve types of divisions as previously described, the non-arising nature (*anutpādatā*) of the mind’s intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) cannot be dedicated; for, because it is a mere designation (*upalakṣaṇa*), it cannot even be conceptualized (*sañjñātuṃ*) as having the form of a single or multiple entity.
This is because the two terms "one conceives" (*sañjānīte*) and "one dedicates" (*pariṇāmayati*) are the subject matter under discussion.
This is what is meant:

"Since the emptiness of the aggregates such as form, the fact that all phenomena belonging to the three times—whether they pertain to the contaminated, the uncontaminated, or both—possess natures such as the past and so forth, and the practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment such as generosity, proceed from a perversion consisting in the notion of perceiving them as having ultimate reality, they constitute the adverse side; therefore, their nature, which is suchness, cannot be apprehended."
And so it has been said:

"Regarding the emptiness of the aggregates such as form, regarding phenomena belonging to the three times, and regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment such as generosity—the notion that there is 'practice' therein is the adverse factor. (3)
He states the antidote for bodhisattvas by way of the reversal of the aforementioned faults,
beginning with the words "Therefore, then...

Since the adverse factors must be abandoned, the meaning is that one should perform the acts of demonstrating generosity and so forth to others through conformity with reality— that is, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension regarding the gift, the giver, the recipient, and so on.

"In this way, one does not destroy oneself" means that by abiding personally in giving and so forth through the application of following reality (*bhūtānugama*), one does not ruin oneself through the specific perversion of apprehension (*upalambha-viparyāsa*). "And these" refers to those previously mentioned which have form and so forth as their objects.

Having given the cry of approval, saying "Excellent! Excellent!", because he had spoken in a manner that was not contrary to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), yet was somewhat coarse and attached, [the Blessed One] spoke for the sake of a more subtle non-attachment:
"Therefore, Subhūti... He "attends to it by way of signs" (*nimittataḥ*) because he brings it to mind by taking the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and so forth as an object.
But how is attachment described in this way?
He says: "Furthermore, as many as... and so forth.
This, then, is the meaning of the context.

The application of oneself and others to generosity and the like through the purity of the three spheres— by virtue of not perceiving a self and so forth— and by virtue of being rightly engaged and because it is to be adopted as it precludes all bases for the accumulation of attachments,
is in every respect an antidote. Likewise,
paying homage and so forth to the Tathāgatas and others is an antidote, as it serves as the cause for the accumulation of merit.
Even though it exists, because it is of the nature of subtle attachment, it is not in every respect an antidote.
And so it has been said:
"Lack of egoism regarding giving and the like, and the enjoining of others to those [virtues]."
"This negation of attachment refers to subtle attachment toward the Victors and others. Thus,
how is it that even subtle attachment is an adverse factor?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason? he says:
"For attachment, Subhūti, arises from signs.
Explaining that very point, he says:
"Thus indeed he," and so forth.
There is a distinction between "grasping with certainty that this alone is reality" (*tattva*)— which does not take [the object] as a causal sign (*nimitta*)—
and "taking it as an objective support" (*ālambana*) through repeated mental engagement.
Nor is it "seen, heard, thought, or cognized": it is not "seen" because it is not perceived by visual consciousness; it is not "heard" because it is not perceived by auditory consciousness;
and it is not "thought" because it is not experienced by olfactory, gustatory, or tactile consciousnesses.
Because it is apprehended by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is a cognizer;
the word "not" (*na api*) should be connected to each [term].
He expresses this very point through the distinction between the profundity of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the profundity of the knowledge (*jñāna*).
By the words beginning with "profound" (*gambhīra*), etc.:
"nature" (*prakṛti*) means intrinsic being (*svabhāva*), that is to say, suchness (*tathatā*).
"Because of its solitude" (*viviktatvāt*) means because it is empty of all apprehension (*upalambha*).

"Profound by nature" means that it is profound because, by its very nature—that is, through the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of gnosis—it is not an object for śrāvakas and others; this is because its nature is utterly pure.
"Because it is secluded by nature" means...
The meaning is that they are perfected through perfection by way of being respectively without change and without error.
This has been stated:

"Because all lineages (*gotra*) of phenomena—which possess the nature of both knowledge and the object of knowledge—are by their very essence empty by nature, they possess profundity; therefore, apprehension in any form whatsoever is a subtle attachment, which is the adverse factor (*vipakṣa*)."
Thus it has been said:
"That profundity arises from the very nature of the discernment of the path of Dharma."
How, then, is it to be avoided? He says:
"naturally secluded" (*prakṛtiviviktā*).
Because it is naturally secluded by virtue of being free from the fault of accepting [the existence of] entities (*bhāva*), [it is to be avoided].
Therefore, I pay homage.
To address the doubt that "if it is said 'perfection of wisdom' (prajñāpāramitā), then all phenomena (sarvadharma) are not isolated," he says:
"all phenomena," and so forth.

[Objection: Since there is no comprehension [of it] by way of its being self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*), how can that isolation from all phenomena (*sarvadharmaviviktatā*) be the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) whose nature is self-cognition?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For thus, Subhūti," and so forth.
This has been stated:

"When consciousness arises—appearing as if external, manifesting a proliferation of various distinct forms just as in dreams and the like due to the absence of the perfection of external objects—then, because one understands that consciousness is, conventionally, like an illusion, all phenomena (dharmas), being non-different from it, are unproduced, empty, and like illusions; such is the Blessed One’s [teaching]."
"Because their isolation (viviktatā) is also understood from the perspective of perfect enlightenment,
entities arise conventionally, but not in the ultimate sense."
By that [emptiness], all this is both real and unreal from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Thus, immediately following this, in order to clarify the reality of the meaning in accordance with the *Ārya-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, he says:
"Therefore, then," and so forth.
The phrase "not fully awakened to in reality" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
He provides support for what has been well said by means of the passage beginning with "tathāhi" (for instance).
He asks, "What kind of primordial nature (prakṛti) is it? and then explains.
"And that which... and so forth.

That which is *prakṛti*—the intrinsic nature, suchness—is itself *aprakṛti* (non-nature) because it is devoid of its own essential form. And that which is *aprakṛti* is the *prakṛti* of all phenomena, because they possess a single characteristic, a single form; that is to say, because they are characterized by the absence of characteristics and lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
Concluding this very point, he says:
"Therefore, then," and so forth.
Now, one might object: "If entities possess distinct intrinsic natures (svabhāva) because they are produced by distinct causes, how can they have a single characteristic?
Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason? he says:
"Indeed, Subhūti," and so forth. He thinks as follows:

since these [dharmas] have a nature of arising that is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they lack a plurality of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) based on their being produced from distinct causes; therefore, because they do not possess a manifold form in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is only a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
"Thus these," and so forth.

According to the sequence described, the single nature (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena, such as form and the rest, is that which is the thorough knowledge of the equality of knowledge and the object of knowledge; therein, the previously mentioned millions of attachments become abandoned in the form of subtle attachment.
And so it has been said:
"Knowledge of the single nature of all phenomena is the relinquishing of attachment. (5)
But how was the profundity of the Dharma previously described as being by its very nature? To this he says:
"O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound.
The word "how" constitutes a question arising from doubt.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the profundity of space":

because the difficulty of comprehending that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has been described through its non-apprehension— which consists in the negation of all objects apprehended by consciousness and which indicates the equality of knowledge and the knowable— therefore, by that [profundity], [the nature of the Tathāgata is characterized].
The meaning is that its profundity is like that of the *kāśa* grass.
And so it has been said:
"By means of the negation of [the categories such as] being seen and so forth, its difficulty of comprehension is proclaimed."
"What, then, is the reason that this nature is so difficult to understand?
To this he says: "O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to comprehend.
Here too, as before, there is a question arising from doubt.

"No one fully awakens" means that because the nature [of phenomena] has the intrinsic essence of suchness (*tathatā*), there is no full awakening through forms such as form (*rūpa*) or the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*); since it is held to be beyond the reach of thought,
this is what is meant by its being difficult to understand.
And so it has been said:
"Because it is not cognized through form and the other [sensory objects], its inconceivability is asserted.
(6) To the question, "Why is it precisely inconceivable? he says:
"Unthinkable," and so forth.
The word "how" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

It is not to be known by the mind, nor is it to be traversed by the mind; because, due to its unconditioned nature, there is no resolute mental application (*adhimokṣamanaskāra*) and thus no resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*); and because the mental application of reality (*tattvamanaskāra*) is not fully cognized, it is not to be traversed by the mind.
Therefore, this refers to its inconceivability.
As for the question "How is it precisely uncreated? and so forth, [the text] says "uncreated," etc.
"How so? is the supplementary question. "Due to the non-perception of the causal agent" means because the causal factor (*kāraka-hetu*) is not apprehended.
For it has been described that the relationship between cause and effect is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).

In this regard, it is first of all not determined by a formless [cognition], because all cognitions are identical insofar as they are mere consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*); how then could there be a distinction such that "this is the cognition of this" and "this is not the cognition of that"?

For it is from the cognition of the seed that the cognition of the sprout arises, and from the non-cognition of that [seed] that the non-cognition of that [sprout] arises; thus the seed would be the cause and the sprout the effect.
Nor is the seed determined by that [cognition] because it is produced from the seed;
for otherwise, there would be no cognition of the eye simply because [the cognition] is produced from the eye.

If it is argued that even for a cognition devoid of form (nirākāra), there exists some unique excellence of its own nature (*ātma-atiśaya*), produced by the capacity of the causal factors, from which this systematic determination arises—
then even this "excellence of nature" is merely another name imposed upon the form itself.
Nor can a thing become something else merely by being given a different name. If it is argued that this is not an aspect (*ākāra*), then let it be pointed out what it is.
If it is claimed that because it is difficult to perceive, it cannot be designated as "this," [we reply:]...
Since this very distinction— that "this is the seed" and "this is the sprout"— is established on that basis, how could there be an inference in the absence of its perception?
For indeed, when a staff or a horn is not perceived, one does not conclude, "This person has a staff," or "This animal has horns."
Nor [is it known] by means of a mental aspect (ākāra); for the mental aspect is not pervaded by the real entity (vastu).
Even though that [cognition] exists, because this [cognition of two moons] occurs despite its absence, it is not non-erroneous due to being such a delusion.
Furthermore, the claim that "that which is non-erroneous does not occur when the object is absent, and there is no deviation of one thing based on the deviation of another" is also incorrect.
For at the time of establishing the causal relationship, a person of limited vision has no basis for the certainty that "this form is indeed an error, this one is not";
nor is this being said with reference to one who possesses supersensuous vision.
Furthermore, in the absence of certainty, the establishment of the relationship between cause and effect is not tenable;
nor is it logical for cognition to possess the form of an object.
For if cognition were to determine the form of the object of knowledge by means of a single part, then it would follow that everyone would be omniscient.

Because all cognitions are endowed with aspects such as "knowability" that are common to all things, even if a cognition were to possess the aspect of the object in its entirety, the distinction between cognition and the cognized would be impossible due to their identity, resulting in the cessation of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, if consciousness were to possess the aspect of the cognized in its entirety, that [distinction] would not exist. Enough of this excessive elaboration. Out of favor toward people of dull intellect and with the desire to dispel the misconceptions of those disciples present here, this division between the opposing side and its antidote is presented exactly as it has been described.
It should be understood in this way;
and so it has been said:
"Having done thus, one should indeed be known as such in the path to omniscience."
"This division of the discordant factors and their antidotes is exhaustive. [Thus it is said. To explain the application for the sake of cultivating those two, he says:
"For by that," and so forth.
Since the adverse factors and their remedies are, respectively, what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, the meaning is:
"Therefore, for that purpose, how should one conduct oneself? He states the application regarding form and so forth.
When one does not course in form through the mode of attachment, then one courses in the perfection of wisdom.
This should be understood in the same way for what follows.
He speaks [as follows] for the purpose of the application to the impermanence and other [qualities] of form and so forth.
"If form is impermanent," and so forth;
this states the application regarding the non-fulfillment of form and the other aggregates.
"If form is incomplete," and so forth, expresses this.
Because it is empty of characteristics, the imagined form (*parikalpita-rūpa*) is incomplete;
because it is endowed with a multitude of qualities, the nature-of-dharmas form (*dharmatā-rūpa*) is complete.
"That is not form," and so forth.

This is because of the distinction between the property and the possessor of the property as imagined by the intellect. Even if one does not practice in this way either, one should connect this with what is to be said later: "one practices in the perfection of wisdom."
Because a state of excellence has arisen through the teaching of the Dharma as previously described, he says,
"It is marvelous," and so forth.
It is "marvelous" because, by speaking of another purpose, he expresses it in a different manner.

Therefore, by this explanation of the application (*prayoga*), it has been stated that the nature of the apprehension of form and so forth is "with attachment" (*sasaṅga*), while the nature of the non-apprehension of the mother is "without attachment" (*asaṅga*).
He states the application regarding the attachment to form and so forth:
"Form is with attachment, [form] is without attachment," and so on.
"With attachment" and "without attachment" mean "with apprehension" and "without apprehension," respectively.
Now, one might object: since it is impossible to meditate without forming a conceptual adherence (*abhiniveśa*), how can this be said?
Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason?", he says:
"Unattached," and so forth. She is "unattached" due to the absence of clinging. The two terms "unbound" and "unreleased" have already been explained.
Because it has the nature of emptiness as dependent origination, it is not transcended [by conceptualization].
This is what is meant:

"Since omniscience is such that it cannot be made an object of conceptual construction—because it is not a reality as it is grasped through attachment, and because it is not attached to as it truly is—one does not produce attachment toward it."
The phrase beginning with "evam hi" (for thus) is the conclusion.
He states the application regarding the absence of modification with the words beginning with "āścaryam" (it is a marvel).
Through teaching and non-teaching, respectively, there is the decline or the increase of the Mother who consists of the scriptural texts:
through teaching, by way of forms contradicted by reasoning and scripture, there is increase due to their arising in another mental continuum;
through non-teaching, by means of uninterrupted meditative seclusion, [there is decline] within one's own continuum.
The increase [of the vowel] occurs because of the observation of the meaning of the particle *dhik*.
However, since the primary mother [the letter *a*] is by nature immutable, he says that none of this applies to her:
"Even when being pointed out," and so forth.
Prefaced by the words "it is excellent" because it is not contradictory, he clarifies this very point by means of an illustration, saying:
"It is just as if," and so forth.
He speaks for the purpose of showing that there is no agent in the application [of the example].
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, with a person created by illusion, and so forth.
Because its nature is that of a false appearance, it lacks agency; thus, it is neither led astray nor repelled by the afflictions of attachment and aversion.
For this very reason, it should be understood that it is not defiled by the afflictions arising from those [states].
Because the application of difficult practice is threefold, he speaks of the difficulty of the objective for the sake of the application toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),
beginning with "one who performs what is difficult" and so forth.
"Does not float up" means he does not waver, nor does he turn upward.
It means that it does not produce joy;
and "it does not turn back" means that it should not undergo any retreat at all.
"This is the armor" refers to the armor that will be described below.

Now, one might ask: since effort is exerted only after having understood that there is the possibility of attaining excellence in wisdom and so forth, what indeed is the extraordinary difficulty here?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason? he says:
"By space," and so forth. This is what is meant:

"Even though all phenomena are like space, by not apprehending them as real, and even in the absence of the excellence of wisdom and so forth that arises from that [non-apprehension], there is a supreme difficulty in undertaking the armor for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). This refers to those things which are equal to space and equal to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The two [types of practice] have been stated according to the distinction between worldly and supramundane renown.
To explain the application of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*)—which is difficult to practice in its preparatory stage—he said:
"O Blessed One, he who wishes to liberate space..."
Regarding the phrase "one who wishes to apply himself to the knowledge of the path," the word "one" is the understood subject.
He speaks of the difficulty of the task regarding the practice for the sake of omniscience, saying:
"O Blessed One, he wishes to lift up space."
"One who desires to achieve omniscience" is the supplementary phrase.

"Having attained the perfection of great vigor" means being endowed with a great resolve whose essence is emptiness and compassion, manifested through the activities of donning the armor and actual practice.
"He arms himself with armor" means that he exerts himself toward the three kinds of difficult tasks.
He speaks thus regarding the fruitless application [of effort] so that one may attain the fruit according to one's capacity.
Now, with the words "Then indeed," and so forth:
"a certain monk" means a person who is unremarkable, that is to say, an individual not distinguished by name, lineage, or other such attributes.
"I pay homage.

Indicating that other attendants as well have attained realization according to their respective capacities, he pays homage through the practice of emptiness, non-arising, and so forth, having developed an extraordinary degree of faith born from his own corresponding realization.
He states the very practice:
For it is said, "O Blessed One," and so forth:
"space" refers to the emptiness of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*);
"open space" refers to the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of cognition (*jñāna*).
In order to show that [the practice] does not depend on another, he says:
"Let the Blessed One command," and so forth;
[and then], "Indeed, it is not so."
He demonstrates independence from others;
for protection and so forth by another would entail dependence on others.
Asking this very point, he says:
"Thus, Kauśika, if [he should]... and so forth.
The meaning of the statement is that because he dwells in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), his protection and other benefits will come about spontaneously, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, it says that his protection and other benefits arise spontaneously due to his resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in phenomena that lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Furthermore, beginning with "Kauśika," he describes the application of the knowledge of the sevenfold manifestation,
starting with the words "What do you think, Kauśika? and so forth.
In that regard, they are like dreams because of the manifestation of transformation through the transformation of consciousness;
they are like illusions because of the manifestation of a composite whole through the gathering together of mantras and medicinal herbs;
they are like mirages because of the manifestation of contradiction through their non-existence.

Because they are cognitions of sound, phenomena are like echoes through the manifestation of cognition; because they do not transfer the form of the object of knowledge, they are like reflections through the manifestation of non-transference;

because their support has vanished, they are like a city of Gandharvas through the manifestation of supportlessness; and because they are devoid of a cause, they are like magical emanations through the manifestation of the absence of an agent. Thus it is stated in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*.

However, since brevity is intended here, it should be understood that by the statement "all phenomena are like an echo," which indicates the middle, the triads of the beginning and the end are also indicated.
Thus, the tenfold application of the bodhisattvas has been explained by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
The [attitude] of the śrāvakas and others should be understood as the opposite of what was stated for the [bodhisattvas].
And so it has been said:
"Regarding form and the rest, regarding their impermanence and so forth, and regarding their being unfilled and being filled..."
And the application of conduct lies in its non-attachment, by way of negation. ||8||
Unchanging and not an agent, its application is threefold;
it is unfailing and desired because it brings about the attainment of fruit according to one's capacity. (9)
"One who is not dependent on another and who realizes the sevenfold teaching"—
thus he speaks of equanimity (*samatā*) to indicate that the application (*prayoga*) should be cultivated by way of equanimity.
And with the words "he does not conceive of them," etc., [it is shown that] with a mind concentrated therein, he does not conceive of them because he does not perceive them.
And those phenomena do not exist,
because they are not perceived by the concentrated mind, and because one does not cognize them. Because one does not perceive them.
Furthermore, those phenomena accessible through that knowledge do not exist;
this is to be construed as "because they are not apprehended.
He speaks thus for the purpose of a conclusion:
"If he dwells thus," and so forth. This refers to the mental engagement with entities such as form, and the mental engagement with signs such as blue.
The conceptual elaboration that "form is twofold" or "twentyfold," and so forth,

as well as the conceptualization of the attainments such as the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), are to be understood as the fourfold non-apprehension of the dharmas of the knower and the known, established by the negation of those [conceptualizations].
And thus it has been said:
"The non-conceptualization of that [object] regarding form and so forth is considered fourfold; this is the equality of application.
Having thus realized the equality of application, the path of seeing (darśanamārga) must now be explained, and that consists of sixteen moments.

The noble Vimuktisena states: "The words beginning with 'Then, indeed, by the power of the Buddha' are for the purpose of making known the absence of any interval between moments (*kṣaṇāntarābhāva*), for the purpose of stating that [the Buddha] acts as a witness, and for the purpose of establishing that this was spoken by all the Buddhas.

Furthermore, because there is no [need for] injunctions or prohibitions for others due to the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśala*), it is said that there are "a thousand Buddhas," since in the Sahā world-system during the Fortunate Aeon (*bhadrakalpa*), a thousand bodhisattvas will certainly attain Buddhahood.
"By names" means by groups of words or sentences;
"by words" means by groups of syllables ending in nominal or verbal suffixes;
"by syllables" means by individual phonemes such as *e*, *vaṃ*, and so forth.
This very chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom is the meaning of the "Chapter on Purity.
In that context, the citation of past Tathāgatas is for the purpose of making known the utility of their teaching;
the mention of Maitreya is an illustration of a future Tathāgata.
For the purpose of revealing the aim and utility for the sake of future sentient beings.
The eighth chapter, titled "Purification," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Ninth Chapter. Now, he speaks regarding the meaning of the path of seeing: "Prajñāpāramitā."

For each truth, there are the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*), and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*); thus, it consists of sixteen moments.
This is the meaning of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the section concerning the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*).
And so it has been said:

"In the system of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), this path of seeing (*dṛṅmārga*) regarding the truths of suffering and so forth consists of the moments of the receptivities (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). Thus,
this is merely a name.

The meaning is that this is merely a reflection of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And that [reflection] is not apprehended as "this is that," because it is, in reality, devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

He asks, "What is meant by 'name'? and replies: "It is merely the object of speech. Then, in order to demonstrate the form of that which is true—the non-conceptual reflection—he asks, "For what reason? and so forth.
"Form is neither permanent nor impermanent.
By virtue of its lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), form is free from permanence and impermanence; thus, "it is neither permanent nor impermanent"—this is the first aspect.
"Form is neither bound nor liberated; it is utterly pure."

The second [point] is that it is pure, having departed from the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, because there is neither bondage nor liberation by virtue of the absence of suffering and the departure from suffering.
"For this reason, Subhūti," means:
because it is the cause for the perfect awakening to all dharmas without error.

He will teach this very *prajñāpāramitā*, which illuminates the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) exactly as it is; the meaning is that no other [teacher] possesses the capacity to reveal such a reality of phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "through the purity of form" (*rūpaviśuddhitaḥ*):
The third is "pure" because it is devoid of both emptiness and non-emptiness.
Regarding "purity through the purity of the non-arising, non-ceasing, non-defilement, and non-purification of form":
because there is an absence of the intrinsic nature of self and non-self, it is neither arisen nor ceased, neither defiled nor purified; thus it is pure—this is the fourth.
Regarding "through the purity of space":
because it is empty of cause, non-cause, and [intrinsic] essence, it is pure like space; this is the fifth.
Regarding "by way of the non-staining and non-appropriation of form":

The sixth is "unsullied by all afflictions and secondary afflictions" because of the dissociation from their arising and non-arising. The seventh is "liberated through the non-appropriation of the defilement of origination and non-origination."

The eighth [point] is that it is inexpressible by its very nature, like space or an echo, because it is free from conditions and non-conditions, and because it is unperceivable through verbal expression.

The ninth [point] is that because there is no connection between cessation and non-cessation, the meaning of the Truth of Cessation cannot be conveyed to another continuum by means of verbal expression.
The tenth is that because of the absence of both the peaceful and the unpeaceful, it is not an object of perception.

"By way of being unstained by the nature of all things that are stained or unstained": because it is devoid of the distinction between the sublime and the non-sublime, and because it is unstained by all things—whether they be the stained phenomena of the *sāsrava* (with-outflows) or the unstained phenomena of the *anāsrava* (without-outflows)—it is a purity that has transcended both extremes; this is the eleventh [point].
"Even before" means:
It is all the more so for those who perform the acts of memorizing and so forth that their gains are well-obtained;
the meaning is that because memorizing and so forth are distinguished by the experience of auditory consciousness,
they do not suffer from eye disease and the like.
The twelfth [point] is that there is no arising of any disease because of the state of being secluded from both emergence and non-emergence.
Regarding the phrase "in greater measure":

the meaning is that from the eighth [bhūmi] onwards, there is the presence of a greater number of listeners, such as Śakra and others, who have descended [to the world] out of their regard for living beings.
He speaks of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path with the words beginning "Many, Subhūti," and so forth.
Since the sons of the gods are not benefited by the perfection of wisdom, what is the reason for them to provide protection and so on for one who is teaching it?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason? he says:
"He [is the one] of gods, humans, and asuras," and so forth.
"The unsurpassed jewel."
Because it is the cause for the pacification of all evils and is devoid of both path and non-path, it extends unsurpassed delight.
Because it benefits the sons of gods and others, the unsurpassed jewel is the eradication of the miserable realms; this is the thirteenth [point].
Furthermore, "Subhūti," and so forth.

The meaning is that not only because there is a great multitude of listeners present, but also because it bestows unsurpassed joy, merit will be generated as the causal source for attaining Buddhahood through the reason of being a Dharma-preacher.
He speaks of the knowledge of the Dharma regarding the path.
However, by the words "api tu khalu" and so forth,
[the author asks]: even though there is great power, what is the cause for there being many obstacles?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For it is thus," and so forth.
Because of its great majesty and because it is desired by many, it has many adversaries.
"According as there is essence," and so forth.
The meaning is that in whatever manner there is a progressive increase in essence, in that same manner there is a multiplicity of adversaries.
Having thus indicated it in general, he now states it specifically:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, this is the unsurpassed great jewel.

Because it has arisen for the sake of the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, it is free from conceptualization regarding all phenomena; thus, by virtue of being a jewel of non-conceptual excellence, and because it is unattached to what is right or wrong, the direct realization of the fruit is the state of being free from conceptualization—this is the fourteenth [great jewel].
He speaks of the receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding the path with the words beginning "And not,
Subhūti," and so forth; for that which is imagined does not, at first, waver.
The dependent nature does not adhere, and the perfected nature is not grasped; such is the distinction in meaning.
This is what is said:
the fifteenth [topic] is the non-association with the signs of phenomena by virtue of being free from both correct practice and incorrect practice.
Even though phenomena exist, their description does not constitute grasping. Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Thus, indeed," and so forth. The meaning has already been explained.
He states the subsequent cognition regarding the path.
By the words "due to non-arising," and so forth:

the sixteenth aspect is the non-arising of knowledge regarding both—that which is to be known, characterized by the relationship between the signified and the signifier, and that which is devoid of the distinction between leading to liberation and not leading to liberation—concerning the word.
Stating the meaning of being unstained in another way, he says:
"Thus, for instance," and so forth.
He states that even in this way, adhering to the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) leads to a fault:
"If even thus," and so forth.
According to the principle stated above, the moments of omniscience consist of sixteen aspects.

Thus, the path of seeing for Bodhisattvas has been explained by way of its positive formulation; by implication, the path of seeing for Śrāvakas and others is to be understood through its opposite, namely by way of the aspects such as impermanence and so forth.

And so it has been said: Form is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is pure, having transcended the limits of the past; it is unarisen and unceasing from the beginning, resembling space and free from all defilement. (12)
It is free from grasping and by its very nature beyond verbal expression, because its meaning cannot be conveyed to others through speech. (13)

The non-apprehension [of objects] brings about ultimate purity and the impossibility of disease; when there is no conceptualization regarding the severance of the lower realms, there is the direct realization of the fruit. //14//
Non-association with signs regarding both the thing and its expression, and the non-arising of cognition—these are the moments of omniscience. (15)

Having thus explained in detail, he concludes with the section beginning "That, moreover... (*sā khalu punar...*) by way of summarizing all the meanings within the context of the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*), specifically the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
In that context, it is "introductory" (*āveśikā*) because it brings about [the realization] by means of the generation of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
The "establisher" (*niveśikā*) is so called because she establishes [others] through instruction (*avavāda*) and the like.

The "demonstrator" (*sandarśikā*) indicates [the goal] in a general form through the practice of armor (*sannāha-pratipatti*), and in a specific form through the practice of setting out (*prasthāna-pratipatti*).

The "bringer" (*āvāhikā*) brings [one] by means of the practice of equipment (*sambhāra-pratipatti*). The "conductor" (*nirvāhikā*) leads [one] forth by means of the practice of departure (*niryāṇa-pratipatti*). The "extractor" (*niṣkarṣikā*) draws [one] out.
In all instances, the phrase "of no phenomenon whatsoever" is to be connected [to the preceding].
He says, "Then indeed," and so forth, meaning that those who are satiated by the nectar-like flavor of the non-perverted Dharma pay homage.

Some say that *siṃhanāda* (lion’s roar), *kilakilā*, and *prakṣveḍita* arise from the swelling of joy (*prasādaudvilyasamuttha*). Others say that *aṭṭahāsa* (loud laughter) is produced by joy, while *kilakilā* is the dancing preceded by that [laughter], which is called *prakṣveḍita*.

In relation to the first turning of the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī, this is the second. He says "This is not," and so forth, for the purpose of refuting adherence to [the notion of] ultimate reality.
Explaining that very point, he says:
"Nor... and so forth.
Concluding the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), he says:
"This is the great perfection," and so forth.
"Unattached" means the state of non-attachment.
If one asks, "Even when there is perception, what is the cause for not seeing phenomena?"—anticipating this question with "For what reason?", he says:
"For that [is not... and so forth.
This is easily understood.
"He will set in motion" means he will produce.
Because a dharma arises through the operation of the totality of causes, one might ask:
"How can it be said thus?
Anticipating this question, he says: "For what reason? [and provides the following answer].
"Extremely," and so forth.
The meaning is that the cause itself does not exist. "Will cause to cease" means it will destroy.
[The opponent asks: "Since destruction is determined when an entity that is contrary to the ongoing continuum is produced by means of a hammer or the like, how can this be said?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason is that so?", he says:
"O Blessed One, for all phenomena are indeed unproduced from the very beginning."
They are unarisen because their cause for arising does not exist from the very beginning.
Explaining this very point, he says:
"Because all phenomena are by nature secluded."
The point is that since [all things] are empty by their very nature, how could there be any contradiction? Concluding the discussion on omniscience, he says:
"For indeed, Subhūti, emptiness," and so forth.
The thought is that [the Buddha] is unarisen because of being empty and so forth.
This is "that" [wisdom], beginning from "the omniscience that teaches all dharmas" up to "having made [himself] worthy of offerings.
Because it is spoken with reference to ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is easy to understand.
According to the principle stated above, one should not entertain any misconception regarding the summary of the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*).
Thus it has been said:
"This very [omniscience], again this very [omniscience], indeed this very [omniscience]—thus it is threefold."
This concludes the exposition of the threefold qualification. ||16||

Thus [it is asked]: for what reason, moreover, is there no separate path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) regarding the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñatā*) as was described in the case of the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*)? It is because it is taught that a bodhisattva, having observed the attainments of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas through both knowledge and vision, transcends them; therefore, it is not to be directly realized [by the bodhisattva]. For bodhisattvas, it is thus indicated. However, for the śrāvakas and others, the very object already perceived is repeatedly brought before the mind, which constitutes the path of cultivation; since this is easy to understand, it has not been explicitly stated.
Furthermore, the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) for bodhisattvas should be understood according to the sequence previously stated.

However, in the case of the śrāvakas and others, when the four truths are permeated by aspects such as impermanence alone, their contaminated (*sāsrava*) states consisting of cultivation—such as "Heat" (*ūṣma*) and so forth—are not explicitly mentioned because they are [already] clear; this is how it should be understood.

Now, one might ask: since the path of the śrāvakas and others is taught within the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñatā*), has the Knowledge of All (*sarvajñatā*) not already been explained? Why, then, is there a separate exposition of the Knowledge of All?
It is said: For therein,
in the system of the knowledge of paths (mārgajñatā), this path of the Śrāvakas is to be known as the non-apprehension of the aspects of the four noble truths.

Thus, it has been stated that the path of the Śrāvakas and others is to be meditated upon by the Bodhisattva through the sequence beginning with the cultivation of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Therefore, for the sake of thoroughly knowing all things without exception, "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*) is mentioned separately, as its distinctness is implied by way of the aspects such as impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth. Since there is much to be said on this matter, enough of this digression.

Having fully understood the three types of omniscience (*tri-sarvajñatā*), one cultivates them again by way of a synthesis of the knowledge of all aspects, paths, and bases for the sake of mastery; thus, the "clear realization of all aspects" (*sarvākārābhisambodha*) must be explained.

In this regard, the general definition should be understood as follows: the establishment of the modes of objects such as impermanence and so forth—which are the natures of the remedies against the opposing tendencies of grasping at permanence and so on—as "aspects" (*ākāra*).
Therefore, the fault of aspects being without a real basis (*nirvastuka*) does not manifest here.
And it should be understood that these aspects (ākāra) are considered to be of exactly three types, due to the distinction between the three forms of omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Thus it has been said:
"The definition of an aspect is the modes of the cognition of things."

"Because there are three types of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they are considered to be exactly threefold. (Verse 1) Thus, having taken the four Noble Truths as the basis, and proceeding according to the section on the three types of omniscience, he speaks first according to the section on *sarvajñatā*— while elucidating how many aspects (*ākāra*) exist within each truth— to the effect that "when this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One," and so forth.

"This is the perfection of non-existence" means that, taking as its cause and basis the non-existence and non-occurrence of things in their eternal form— just like space— it has the aspect of being non-existent and impermanent.
"The equality of the unequal" means:
Based on the non-apprehension of all phenomena, it is equality and non-arising;
the aspect of suffering is "unequal" because it is dissimilar to other aspects.
In reality, that is equal to non-arising and equality.
Regarding "secluded":
by means of the emptiness of the self in the highest and most absolute sense, it is "seclusion" (viveka) because its aspect of emptiness brings about an abundance of qualities.
Regarding "unassailable":

because all phenomena are not apprehended as having a self-nature, and because it is not shared by any non-Buddhist teachers, the aspect of selflessness is unassailable due to its being impervious to those non-Buddhists.

Thus, in this way, there are four aspects within the truth of suffering— namely, non-existence, non-arising, solitude, and being invincible— which correspond respectively to the characteristics of impermanence and so forth.
Regarding the term "trackless" (*apada*),
there are four [aspects] therein.

The form-possessing aggregates are called "name," and the body is the aggregate of form; since this [body] is the cause of those [aggregates], by way of logic, taking up their state of being nameless and bodiless, the lines are "footless" (*apada*) in the sense that they do not truly produce or support the aspects of causes.

"Without intrinsic nature" means that, based on the fact that it has no coming and no going, its nature is non-arising and non-ceasing; thus, the aspect of origination is, by way of reasoning, like space.
Regarding "inexpressible": because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) do not exist, even by way of conventional designation (*udbhāvana-saṃvṛti*), words [do not apply].
Based on the fact that it cannot be expressed in words, it is beyond conceptualization;
its mode of manifestation is ineffable.
"Nameless" (anāma):
Based on the non-apprehension of the five aggregates, the aspect of the condition is "nameless" because it is not associated with mental factors (*caitasika*).
Thus, these four aspects—trackless, space-like, ineffable, and nameless—are respectively characterized by the cause and so forth, and they exist within the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Regarding "non-coming":
because all phenomena have the nature of cessation, the aspect of cessation is non-coming, based on the fact that they do not go anywhere.
Regarding "unassailable":...
Because there is no withdrawal of objects due to their being primordially quiescent, by virtue of the non-apprehensibility of all phenomena,
the aspect of quiescence is unwithdrawable.
"Inexhaustible" means:
Based on its connection with inexhaustible qualities by way of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, the sublime aspect is inexhaustible.
Regarding "non-arising":
it is because of the absence of causes, whether single or manifold.
Based on the non-origination of all phenomena, the aspect of departure is non-arising.

Thus, these four aspects—non-going, being unassailable, inexhaustibility, and non-arising—correspond respectively to the intrinsic natures of cessation and so forth, and they exist within the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
[Regarding the term] "non-agent" (*akāraka*):
Because the path is the antidote to the grasping at a creator, the aspect of the path is "non-acting," based on the non-perception of an agent.
Because all phenomena lack selfhood and consist of non-apprehensibility due to being sublated by valid cognition, the aspect of the logical principle (*nyāya*) is "non-knowing" (*ajānaka*).
[It is] "non-transmigration."
Based on the non-arising of death and rebirth, or destruction and production, in the form of the *dharmadhātu*, the aspect of practice is "non-transmigration.
It is called "non-discipline" [in the sense of being beyond training].

Based on the non-apprehension of the past, future, and present time periods, and because the disciplining of afflictions is impossible [in that context], the aspect of "leading to liberation" (*nairyāṇika*) is itself "non-discipline" (*avinaya*).

Thus, these four aspects—being without action (*akāraka*), being without knowledge (*ajānaka*), being without transition (*asaṅkrānti*), and being without discipline (*avinaya*)—respectively constitute the nature of the Truth of the Path and so forth, serving as the antidotes to the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
For those who follow the right method (*nyāyānuyāyin*), regarding birth...

Based on the fact that beings do not perceive [phenomena] as arising, the five forms—dream, echo, reflection, mirage, and illusion—are respectively characterized by being without intrinsic nature, unarisen, unceasing, primordially peaceful, and naturally parinirvāṇized. Generally, these serve as the antidotes to the cognitive obscurations;
thus, through omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the Pratyekabuddhas are subsumed.
These [qualities] exist within their impure path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which consists of the antidote to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding "non-affliction" (*asaṃkleśa*): non-affliction is the absence of afflictions, based on the fact that they lack the intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*) of attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Regarding "non-purification":
non-purification is the absence of purification based on the non-apprehensibility of the basis, which is the afflicted sentient being.

"Untainted" (anupalepa) means that, by virtue of the intrinsic luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaratva*) of space, there is an absence of staining by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); this absence of staining is "untainted.
"Non-proliferated" (*aprapañca*)...

Non-proliferation (*aprapañca*) is the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), based on the transcendence of all forms of mental estimation (*mananā*) that consist in objective apprehension (*upalambha*).
Regarding "non-estimation": it is the absence of mental estimation, based on immovability and unshakeability resulting from the total eradication of all apprehension.
"Non-conceptualization is immovable.
This means that, based on the fact that the *dharmadhātu* remains as it is throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), its state of being without decline is "immovable.

Thus, these six aspects—non-affliction, non-purification, non-staining, non-proliferation, non-conceptualization, and immovability—are, respectively, the antidotes to the conceptualizations of: affliction, purification, the latencies of the afflictions, the proliferation of form and so forth, the apprehension of one's own realization, and the loss [of that realization].

They serve as the antidotes to the six specific cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the Pratyekabuddhas; thus, they exist within the untainted path of vision (*anāsrava-darśanamārga*), which consists of the antidote to the cognitive obscurations.
In total, there are twenty-seven aspects of omniscience (*sarvajñatākāra*).
And so it has been said:
"Beginning from the aspect of non-existence up to the form of immovability—these four for each truth are recorded as fifteen on the path. (2)
Immediately thereafter, the aspects (*ākāra*) of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) must be explained.

In this context, based on the distinction between the side of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and its opposite, the truths of origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*) constitute the cause, while the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and cessation (*nirodha*) constitute the result. Having thus indicated them by way of their meaning, one should understand that within the truths of origin, path, suffering, and cessation, there are respectively eight, seven, five, and sixteen aspects.
In that regard, the cause is threefold:
desire (*chanda*), passion (*rāga*), and the delight of craving for renewed existence (*nandī-paunarbhavikī-tṛṣṇā*). He speaks [the following] as the antidote to desire.
Regarding "detachment" (*virāga*):
it is based on the non-falsity and truthfulness of all phenomena by way of their emptiness.
Detachment is the absence of passion.
It is taught with the underlying intention that there is an absence of the desire to act; for, at the stage of *chanda* (aspiration), passion (*rāga*) is primary,
and thus aspiration is described as existing only in the absence of that [passion].
Or rather, due to the absence of passion— which is of the nature of an effect—
the absence of the desire whose cause is that [passion] has been stated.
Otherwise,
according to the principle that "if the cause is unimpaired, the effect cannot fail to arise," there would be no non-arising of the effect.
He speaks by way of the antidote to attachment.
Regarding "non-arising":
because all phenomena are like an illusion, based on their non-conceptual nature, the absence of arising— that is, the absence of volitional desire— is "non-arising."
This was stated with the underlying intention that there is non-attachment toward phenomena.

Since desire (*chanda*) is primary as the direct cause for engagement during the state of passion, it is taught that through the absence of that [desire], passion itself becomes absent. Furthermore, he speaks by way of the antidote to the craving for delight (*nandī-tṛṣṇā*), which is the cause for renewed existence.
Regarding "peaceful" (*śānta*):
based on the non-apprehension of signs such as blue, yellow, and so forth in all phenomena, there is an absence of the primary lack of tranquility within craving; thus, it is peaceful.
Regarding the threefold origin—namely attachment, aversion, and delusion—he speaks [of peace] as their antidote.

"Faultless" means that, by virtue of having reached the perfection of qualities such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, there is an absence of faults; thus it is "faultless," which is to say, free from passion (*arāga*).
"Hatred" means up to "delusion.
It is to be understood as the source because from it arise passion and the other afflictions; therefore, he speaks by way of its antidote.

"Free from afflictions" (niḥkleśa) means that, based on the non-existence of conceptual construction—the adherence to duality and so forth—there is an absence of the arising of the causes of affliction; thus it is "free from afflictions.
The condition [for this] is the lack of adherence to a [real] sentient being.
Because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the condition for all misfortune, he says, as its antidote:
"without a sentient being" (*niḥsattva*).
In the sense of being non-perverted, by taking recourse in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the absence of conditions is "without a sentient being."

Thus, beginning from the aspect of dispassion (*virāga*) up to the aspect of being devoid of a sentient being (*niḥsattva*), the causes are, respectively: desire (*chanda*), attachment (*rāga*), and delight (*nandī*);
and the origin (*samudaya*) consists of passion, hatred, and delusion (*rāga-dveṣa-moha*).
That which is the source is conceptual construction;
that which is the condition is the adherence to a self-entity.
As their respective antidotes, there are three, three, one, and one—thus eight aspects exist within the truth of origination.
Regarding "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*):

because it serves as the basis for the arising and manifestation of the origination of all phenomena, and because it brings about the cessation of opposing factors and the acquisition of their antidotes, the aspect of the path (*mārgākāra*) is immeasurable due to its providing space for immeasurable sentient beings.
As to how it provides space for immeasurable sentient beings, he says:
"Non-approaching the two extremes" means that,
by virtue of non-attachment to all phenomena, there is no apprehension of approaching the two extremes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa because they have been abandoned.

Regarding "undifferentiated": based on the fact that all phenomena are undifferentiated and non-dual in their nature as the *dharmadhātu*, the aspect of the method (*nyāyākāra*) is undifferentiated through the cessation of its opposites.
And as for how this is logical, he says:
"uncontaminated," which is based on the lack of longing for the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Not defiled by that conceptualization" means not grasped by it. "Non-conceptual" means...
Based on the equality of conceptual construction, the mode of practice is non-conceptual.
As to how that practice is, he says:
"immeasurable."

Based on the nature of immeasurable phenomena (*apramāṇa-dharmatā*), and prioritizing the absence of conceptual constructions regarding the inferior and the sublime— whether in the relinquishing of what has been attained or the acquisition of what has not yet been attained— it is immeasurable (*aprameya*) because it is devoid of any limit to the knowable.
It is "unattached" (*asaṅga*).
In each respective realization, based on the non-attachment to all phenomena like the sky, the aspect of deliverance is unattached.

Thus, there are aspects that are immeasurable, unattached, and free from conceptual construction—respectively: the path which provides space for all sentient beings and the manner in which it provides such space;
the principle and the manner in which it is a principle.
That which is practice, the manner in which one practices,
and that which is the departure—
these two, two, and two, making one, constitute the seven aspects within the truth of the path.
Regarding "impermanent":

because all phenomena are non-existent, they are unconditioned by causes and conditions; thus, the meaning of "impermanent" is the meaning of "non-existent," in the sense that it is eternally non-existent.
"It is suffering" is said because, taking into account the equality of space with respect to all phenomena, the suffering of conditioned formations pervades all things.
"It is empty" is said...
