It is "empty" because it is devoid of a self and so forth as imagined by others, based on the non-apprehension of all phenomena even through the slightest trace of a connection with a governing self.
It is "non-self" because, based on the non-adherence to all phenomena as being non-self in their own right, the person and so forth lack intrinsic nature; thus they are non-self.
Regarding "signless" (*alakṣaṇa*):
because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are unproduced, they are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and thus signless.

Therefore, the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, together with the fifth aspect of being signless as their essential nature—these five aspects exist within the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

Regarding "all-emptiness" (*sarvaśūnyatā*): because the extremes characterized by prior and posterior states, as well as the middle, are entirely joined with the two extremes and thus lack any final limit, the sixteen aspects of the truth of cessation are "all-emptinesses" by virtue of their being infinite and limitless.

In that regard, through the cessation of internal, external, and both types of entities, there are three aspects of emptiness— internal, external, and both— which have the nature of the aspect of cessation; these pertain to emptiness in relation to the receptacle world, the ultimate truth, the conditioned, the unconditioned, the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, and the beginningless and endless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Through the cessation of the eightfold adherence— which consists of conceptual designation and pertains to the non-existence of the dharmas already attained— there is, respectively, the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
great emptiness; emptiness of the ultimate truth; emptiness of the conditioned.
The emptiness of the unconditioned;
the absolute emptiness;
the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.
And non-dispersal emptiness—these eight modes of emptiness have the nature of the mode of peace.
The mode of excellence is the mode of natural emptiness through the cessation of an agent imagined by others.

Through the cessation of those things whose nature consists in the error regarding objects, there are three modes of emptiness consisting in the non-apprehension of the characteristics of all phenomena; these have the nature of the mode of emergence.

Since the aspect of emptiness whose intrinsic nature is non-existence— by virtue of the cessation of intrinsic nature— is itself characterized by the aspect of deliverance, it refers to the cessation, the peaceful aspect, the sublime aspect, and the aspect of deliverance regarding the cessation of internal and other entities,
and how that [cessation] is peaceful.
Because of the cessation of the eightfold adherence;
and because it is sublime by nature;
and because it is an escape through the cessation of the three kinds of delusion.

And that which is the departure [from suffering] is the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvatā*); thus, three, eight, one, three, and one—making sixteen aspects respectively—constitute the aspects within the truth of cessation.
In total, there are thirty-six, which are the aspects of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*).
And so it has been said: "With respect to the cause, the path, suffering, and cessation, they are proclaimed respectively as eight, seven, five, and sixteen. (3)

Immediately following that, the aspects of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) must be explained. In that context, there is a summary of the three types of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) by way of the category of all noble persons (*āryapudgala*). Therefore, he speaks of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), beginning with the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, according to the distinction of the paths of omniscience.

The meaning is that, based on the non-apprehensibility (*anupalabdhitā*) of those very factors conducive to enlightenment, the applications of mindfulness and the rest are themselves the perfections (*pāramitā*).
This is what is meant:

therein, for the sake of entering the four truths at the outset of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there are four modes of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)—namely, body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—which have been examined in terms of their specific and general characteristics; this constitutes the path of examining the objects, because by means of it one examines the fourfold objects beginning with the body.

Then, for one who has descended [into the path], there are the four aspects of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), which consist of the energy that serves as the cause for, respectively, abandoning unwholesome states already arisen and preventing those not yet arisen from arising, as well as for increasing wholesome states already arisen and producing those not yet arisen; these constitute the path of exertion,
because energy is initiated by way of the abandonment of hindrances and so forth.

The attainment of mental pliancy for one who possesses vigor consists of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)—endowed with the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) and the concentrations of desire, vigor, mind, and investigation—which constitute the path for the preparation of concentration;
for in this way, pliancy is brought about through the gateway of desire and the others.
For one who has thus prepared the mind...

Immediately following that, there is the application (*prayoga*) of Heat (*ūṣman*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*); their intrinsic nature consists of the five aspects of the faculties (*indriya*) of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This is the path of preparation for the correct clear realization (*samyag-abhisamaya-prāyogika-mārga*), because through the application of Heat and Summits, one becomes the dominant condition (*adhipati-bhūta*) for the attainment of the Noble Path by means of the faculty of faith and so forth. Following the attainment of Heat and the others, there is the application of Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*agradharma*); their intrinsic nature consists of the five aspects of the powers (*bala*) of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This is the path of integration with the clear realization (*sarvathā-abhisamaya-saṃśleṣa-mārga*).

Following the powers such as faith (*śraddhābala*), for the sake of penetrating the truths, there is the application of the stages of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), which are not overcome by their opposites such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*). For one who has realized the fourfold stage beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), the path of seeing the truths (*satyadarśanamārga*) consists of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*)— namely, mindfulness, investigation of dharmas, energy, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity— which constitute the path of clear realization (*abhisamayamārga*).
Therefore, because of the perfect awakening to the reality that is to be personally realized from the very beginning,

for one who has fully understood and seen the truths, there is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). This consists of the aspects of the Noble Eightfold Path— right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration— and is the pure path leading to liberation, since by means of it one proceeds toward liberation after the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) for the sake of purifying the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
For this very reason, this is the sequential order of these factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

Thus, with reference to the sevenfold path—beginning with the path of the examination of the objective basis (*vastu*)—there are thirty-seven aspects based upon the path to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Immediately following that, he states the divisions of the path to the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*).
Regarding the perfection of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness:
the first is the gate of liberation of emptiness, which has the intrinsic nature of the aspects of emptiness and selflessness, and serves as the antidote to views.

Because it is signless (*animitta*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*) by which one is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpāpoḍha*), the second gate of liberation, the signless, has as its intrinsic nature the aspects of the truths of cessation and the path; it is the antidote to the signs of views and conceptual construction.

As for what was stated—that "the signless [consists] of the aspects of tranquility"—that refers to the Śrāvaka path which is permeated by the signs of objective entities; therefore, there is no contradiction with this [present teaching].

The third gate of liberation, the wishless (*apraṇihita*), has as its intrinsic nature the aspects of the truths of impermanence, suffering, and origination; it is the antidote to aspiration for the three realms.
Thus, these three aspects of the three gates of liberation constitute the path of counteraction.
This is the perfection of the eight liberations.

Because of the non-cultivation and cultivation of the perception of form, respectively, one—being either possessed of form internally or formless internally—relying upon internal meditative absorption or the formless attainments, [perceives] external forms as beautiful or ugly.
The two liberations [beginning with] "one perceives" are the antidotes to the obscuration regarding emanation (*nirmāṇāvaraṇa*).

Regarding the emanation of beautiful and ugly forms, there is, respectively, mental application (*ābhoga*) and aversion (*prātikūlya*), which constitute affliction (*saṃkleśa*); as the antidote to that, one dwells having personally realized and attained the beautiful liberation-door with the body.

By relying upon the perception of mutual dependence and the perception of mutual conformity toward beautiful and ugly forms within oneself, through the attainment of the perception of their mutual single flavor, one obtains mastery over the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) regarding forms as desired; thus, this is one [liberation].

"Deliverance" (*vimokṣa*) refers to the five aspects: the three aspects of the path of emanation which are the deliverances; the four aspects of the formless attainments, which are by nature the path of dwelling in accordance with liberation; and the single aspect of the cessation of perception and feeling, which is by nature the path of peaceful dwelling. These five aspects constitute the path of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
This is the perfection of the nine successive dwellings.
The ninefold supramundane path consists of the aspects of the four dhyānas, the formless attainments, and the attainment of cessation.
This is the perfection of the four truths;
it is the path of abandonment, comprising the four aspects of the uninterrupted paths characterized by the dissociation from afflictions, which are subsumed within the four truths.
"This is the ten perfections" means that the path to Buddhahood consists of the ten aspects of the perfections, such as generosity and the rest.
Thus, with reference to these six kinds of paths— the path of antidotes and so forth— there are thirty-four aspects based upon the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
Immediately after that, the aspects (*ākāra*) of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) must be explained.

In that regard, since the path is without superior, it is one and only; however, the unique distinction of this special path (*viśeṣamārga*) must be stated according to the differences in its aspects, such as the powers (*bala*) and the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*).
Thus he says: "This is the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*)."
The power of knowing what is possible and impossible,
the power of knowing the ripening of karma,
and the power of knowing the various inclinations [of beings].
the power of knowledge regarding many world-systems,
the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties [of beings],
and the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere;
The power of knowledge regarding affliction and purification,
the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes,
and the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth.
Regarding the "power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows" (*āśravakṣayajñānabala*), because it is invincible due to having conquered its adversaries, there are ten aspects of power.
This is the perfection of fearlessness (*vaiśāradyapāramitā*).

When one makes the self-assertion, "I am a Buddha," when one declares that passion and so forth are obstacles, when one reveals that the path to omniscience and so forth is the definitive departure, and when [one proclaims] oneself as one whose outflows are exhausted—
And because there is no one to challenge him when he has accepted [the debate], he maintains an unshrinking mind; thus, there are four aspects of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
This is the perfection of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid-pāramitā*);

it is so called because, respectively, with respect to synonyms, the characteristics of phenomena, local dialects, and the distinctions among phenomena, he possesses unattached and unimpeded omniscience by virtue of the absence of any obstruction to the taste of realization or to the objects of knowledge.
The four aspects of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—of phenomena, meaning, etymology, and eloquence—are as follows:
"This is the perfection of the unique qualities of all Buddhas";
there is no faltering.

There are six aspects consisting of: a mind that is distracted, one whose mindfulness is lost, one that is not concentrated, the perception of various objects, equanimity without discernment, and so forth.

With respect to the purification of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there are six aspects consisting of the absence of decline from zeal, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and liberation.

The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) consist of the three aspects of bodily, vocal, and mental actions being preceded by and following after knowledge; and the three aspects of unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding the past, future, and present. Because they transcend all calculation due to their uniqueness when compared to Śrāvakas and others, these are the aspects of the Tathāgata’s suchness (*tathāgatatathatā*).

Because all the teachings spoken by the Blessed Buddhas do not deviate from their defining characteristics and their meaning, they are based on non-falsity; thus, the aspect of suchness spoken by all Buddhas is one.
This perfection is self-existent.
By means of omniscience, the Pratyekabuddhas are included.
These [qualities] exist within their contaminated path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which consists of the antidote to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Regarding "non-affliction" (*asaṃkleśa*): non-affliction is the absence of afflictions, based on the fact that they do not have the intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*) of attachment, aversion, or delusion.
Regarding "non-purification":
non-purification refers to the absence of purification, based on the non-apprehensibility of the basis, which is the afflicted sentient being.
"Untainted" (*anupalepa*): because space is luminous by nature, its lack of being stained by afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) constitutes "untaintedness.
"Non-proliferated" (*aprapañca*).

"Non-proliferation" (*aprapañca*) refers to the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), based on the transcendence of all forms of mental estimation of phenomena that consist in objective apprehension.
Regarding "non-estimation": it refers to the absence of mental estimation, based on immovability and unshakeability resulting from the total eradication of all apprehension.
"Non-conceptualization is immovable.
This means that, based on the fact that the *dharmadhātu* remains as it is throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), its state of being without decline is "immovable.

Thus, these six aspects—non-affliction, non-purification, non-staining, non-proliferation, non-conceptualization, and immovability—are, respectively, the antidotes to the conceptualizations of: affliction, purification, the latencies of the afflictions, the proliferation of form and so forth, the apprehension of one's own realization, and the loss [of that realization].

The antidotes to the six specific cognitive obscurations exist within the untainted path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the Pratyekabuddhas, which consists of the antidote to the cognitive obscuration.
In total, there are twenty-seven aspects of omniscience (*sarvajñatākāra*).
And so it has been said:
"Beginning from the aspect of non-existence up to the state of immovability—these four for each truth are recorded as fifteen on the path. (2)
Immediately following that, the aspects of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*) must be explained.

In this context, based on the distinction between the sides of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and its opposite, the truths of origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*) constitute the cause, while the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and cessation (*nirodha*) constitute the fruit. Having thus indicated them by way of their meaning, one should understand that within the truths of origin, the path, suffering, and cessation, there are respectively eight, seven, five, and sixteen aspects.
In this regard, the cause is threefold:
desire, attachment, and the delight that is craving for renewed existence. He speaks [the following] as the antidote to desire:
Regarding "detachment" (*virāga*): it is detachment because of the absence of passion, based upon the non-falsity and reality of all phenomena in the form of emptiness.
It is taught with the underlying intention that there is an absence of the desire to act; for it is held that in the stage of *chanda* (aspiration), passion (*rāga*) is predominant,
and thus aspiration is described as being present only through the absence of that [passion].
Or rather, it has been stated that due to the absence of passion— which is of the nature of an effect—
there is an absence of the desire whose cause is that [passion].
Otherwise,
according to the principle that "if the cause is unimpaired, the non-arising of the effect would not occur," he spoke by way of the antidote to attachment.
Regarding "non-arising":
because all phenomena are like an illusion, there is an absence of arising—that is, of volitional desire—based on the non-conceptuality of all phenomena; this is "non-arising."
This was stated with the underlying intention that there is non-attachment toward phenomena (*dharmas*).

Since desire (*chanda*) is primary as the direct cause for engagement during the state of passion (*rāga*), it is taught that through the absence of that [desire], passion itself becomes non-existent. Furthermore, he speaks by way of the antidote to the craving for delight (*nandī-tṛṣṇā*) which is the cause of renewed existence (*punarbhava*).

"Peaceful" (*śānta*): because the signs (*nimitta*) of all phenomena, such as blue, yellow, and so forth, are not perceived, there is an absence of the non-quiescence that is primarily characterized by craving; thus it is "peaceful.
Regarding the threefold origination (*samudaya*), namely attachment, aversion, and delusion, he speaks [of peace] as their antidote.
"Faultless" means that,
by virtue of having reached the perfection of qualities such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, there is an absence of faults; thus it is "faultless," which is to say, free from passion.
Aversion and delusion— that is to say, up to and including these—
are to be conceived as the source, because from them arise attachment and the other [afflictions]; therefore, he speaks by way of their antidote.
"Free from afflictions" (niḥkleśa):
because the conceptual construction—the adherence to duality and so forth—is non-existent, there is an absence of the arising of the causes of affliction; this is "free from afflictions.
The condition [for affliction] is the adherence to the existence of sentient beings.
Because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the condition for all misfortune, he says, as its antidote:
"devoid of a sentient being" (*niḥsattva*).
In the sense of being non-erroneous, with reference to the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), the absence of conditions is "devoid of a sentient being."

Thus, beginning from the aspect of dispassion (*virāga*) up to the aspect of being devoid of a sentient being (*niḥsattva*), the causes are, in their respective order: desire (*chanda*), attachment (*rāga*), and delight (*nandī*);
and the origin (*samudaya*) consists of passion, hatred, and delusion (*rāga-dveṣa-moha*).
That which is the source is conceptual construction;
that which is the condition is the adherence to a self-entity.
As their respective antidotes, there are three, three, one, and one—thus there are eight aspects within the truth of origination.
Regarding "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*):

because it serves as the basis for the arising of the manifestation of all phenomena, and because it brings about the cessation of opposing factors (*vipakṣa*) and the attainment of their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), the aspect of the path (*mārgākāra*) is immeasurable due to its providing space for immeasurable sentient beings.
As to how it provides space for immeasurable sentient beings, he says:
"Non-approaching the two extremes" means that,
by virtue of non-adherence to all phenomena, there is no apprehension of approaching the two extremes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa because they have been abandoned.
Regarding "unmixed":
by virtue of the non-distinction and non-diversity of all phenomena in the form of the *dharmadhātu*, the aspect of the method (*nyāyākāra*) is unmixed through the cessation of its opposites.
And as for how this is logical, he says:
"unconceived," because of the lack of longing for the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Untouched by that conceptualization" means not grasped by it. "Non-conceptual" [means...]
Based on the equality of conceptualization, the mode of practice is non-conceptual.
As to how that practice is, he says:
"immeasurable."

Based on the nature of immeasurability (*apramāṇa-dharmatā*), and placing before oneself the absence of conceptual constructions regarding the inferior and the sublime— whether in the relinquishing of what has been attained or the acquisition of what has not yet been attained— it is immeasurable (*aprameya*) by virtue of being devoid of any limit to the knowable.
It is "unattached" (*asaṅga*).
In each respective realization, based on the non-attachment to all phenomena like space, the aspect of deliverance (*nairyāṇika*) is unattached.

Thus, there are aspects that are immeasurable, unattached, and free from conceptual construction—respectively: the path that provides space for all sentient beings and the manner in which it provides such space;
the principle and the manner in which it is a principle.
That which is practice, the manner in which one practices,
and that which is the departure—
these constitute seven aspects within the truth of the path, being two, two, and two, plus one.
Regarding "impermanent":

because all phenomena are non-existent, they are unconditioned by causes and conditions; thus, the meaning of "impermanent" is the meaning of "non-existent," in the sense that what is eternally non-existent is impermanent.
"Regarding 'suffering' (duḥkha): based on the equality of space with respect to all phenomena, the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkha) pervades all things.
Regarding 'emptiness' (śūnya):..."
It is "empty" because it is devoid of a self and so forth as imagined by others, based on the non-apprehension of all phenomena even through the slightest trace of a connection with a governing self.
It is "non-self" because, based on the non-adherence to all phenomena as being non-self in their own right, the person and so forth lack intrinsic nature; thus they are non-self.
Regarding "signless" (*alakṣaṇa*): based on the non-origination of all phenomena, that which is without intrinsic nature is signless.
Thus, the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, together with the fifth aspect of being signless in nature, constitute the five aspects within the truth of suffering.
Regarding "the emptiness of all" (*sarvaśūnyatā*):

because the extremes characterized by prior and posterior states, as well as the middle, are entirely joined with the two extremes and thus lack any final limit, the sixteen aspects of the truth of cessation are the "emptinesses of all" (*sarvaśūnyatā*) by virtue of their being infinite and limitless.

Therein, through the cessation of internal, external, and both types of entities, there are three aspects of emptiness— internal, external, and internal-external— which have the nature of the aspect of cessation with respect to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, and the beginningless and endless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

By the cessation of the eightfold adherence— which consists of conceptual designation and occurs within the absence of a self-nature in phenomena— there is, respectively, the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
Great emptiness,
emptiness of the ultimate truth,
and emptiness of the conditioned.
The emptiness of the unconditioned;
the absolute emptiness;
the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.
The non-dispersal emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*)—these eight modes of emptiness have the nature of the aspect of peace (*śāntākāra*).
The aspect of excellence (*praṇītākāra*) consists of the aspect of natural emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) through the cessation of an agent imagined by others.

Through the cessation of those things whose nature is the error regarding objects, there are three modes of emptiness consisting of the non-perception of the characteristics of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-lakṣaṇānupalambha-śūnyatā*); these have the nature of the aspect of emergence (*niḥsaraṇākāra*).

Since the aspect of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence by way of the cessation of intrinsic nature is itself characterized by the aspect of emergence, it refers to the aspect of cessation, the aspect of peace, the aspect of excellence, and the aspect of emergence; that is, the cessation of internal and other entities,
and how it is peaceful.
Because of the cessation of the eightfold adherence;
and because it is sublime by nature;
and because it is an escape through the cessation of the three kinds of delusion.
And that which is the departure [from suffering], namely "the nature of non-existence"—these three, eight, one, and three, respectively, constitute the sixteen aspects within the truth of cessation.
In total, there are thirty-six; these are the aspects of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*).
And so it has been said: "With respect to the cause, the path, suffering, and cessation, they are proclaimed respectively as eight, seven, five, and sixteen. (3)

Immediately following that, the aspects (*ākāra*) of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) must be explained. In that context, there occurs a summary of the three types of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) by way of the category of all noble persons (*āryapudgala*). Therefore, he speaks of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*), beginning with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), according to the distinction of the paths of omniscience.

The meaning is that, based on the non-apprehensibility (*anupalabdhitā*) of those very factors conducive to awakening, the foundations of mindfulness and so forth themselves constitute the perfections (*pāramitā*).
This has been stated:

therein, for the sake of entering the four truths at the beginning of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there are four modes of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)—namely, body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—which have been examined in terms of their specific and general characteristics; these constitute the path of the examination of things, because by means of them one examines the fourfold things, beginning with the body.

Then, for one who has descended [into the path], the four aspects of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), which consist of the vigor that serves as the cause for— respectively— the abandoning of unwholesome states already arisen and the non-arising of those not yet arisen, and for the further increase and arising of wholesome states, constitute the path of exertion (*vyavasāyika-mārga*),
because vigor is initiated through the gateway of abandoning hindrances and so forth.

The attainment of mental flexibility (*citta-karmaṇyatā*) for one who possesses vigor constitutes the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), which are endowed with the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*) and the concentrations of desire, vigor, mind, and investigation. These are the path for the cultivation of concentration, because they bring about mental flexibility by means of the gateway of desire and the others. For one who has thus cultivated the mind...

Immediately following that is the application of *uṣman* (heat) and *mūrdhan* (summits); its intrinsic nature consists of the five aspects of the faculties (*indriya*) of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This is the path of application for the correct realization (*samyag-abhisamaya*), because through the application of *uṣman* and *mūrdhan*, one becomes the dominant condition (*adhipati-bhūta*) for the attainment of the Noble Path by means of the faculty of faith and so forth. Following the attainment of *uṣman* and the rest is the application of *kṣānti* (patience) and *agradharma* (supreme mundane dharmas); its intrinsic nature consists of the five aspects of the powers (*bala*) of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This is the path of complete integration with the realization in every respect.

Following the powers of faith and so forth, for the sake of penetrating the truths, there is the application of *kṣānti* (patience) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), which are not overcome by their opposites such as lack of faith; thus, for one who has realized the fourfold stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so on, the path of seeing the truths (*satyadarśanamārga*) consists of the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)— namely, mindfulness, investigation of dharmas, energy, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity— which constitute the path of clear realization (*abhisamayamārga*).
Therefore, because of the realization of the reality that is to be personally realized from the very beginning,

for one who has fully understood and seen the truths, there is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). This consists of the aspects of the Noble Eightfold Path— right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration— and is the pure path leading to liberation (*viśuddhanairyāṇikamārga*), since by means of it one proceeds toward liberation after the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) for the sake of purifying the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
For this very reason, this is the sequential order of these factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Thus, with reference to the sevenfold path beginning with the path of the examination of objects, there are thirty-seven aspects based upon the path to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Immediately following that, he states the divisions of the path to the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*).
Regarding the perfection of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness:
the first gate of liberation is emptiness, which has the intrinsic nature of the aspects of emptiness and selflessness, and serves as the antidote to views.

Since that which is signless (*animitta*) is cessation (*nirodha*), and by means of that path free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) one attains the signless, the second gate of liberation, the signless (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*), has as its intrinsic nature the aspects of the truths of cessation and the path; it is the antidote to the conceptualization of signs associated with [wrong] views.

As for what was stated—that "the signless [is characterized] by the aspects of tranquility" (*śamākāra*)—that refers to the Śrāvaka path which is permeated by signs of objective entities (*vastu-nimitta*); therefore, there is no contradiction between that statement and this [definition].

The third, the wishless (*apraṇihita*) gate of liberation, has as its intrinsic nature the aspects of the truths of impermanence, suffering, and origination; it is the antidote to aspiration toward the three realms (*traidhātuka*).
Thus, there are three counteractive paths consisting of the aspects of the three doors of liberation.
This is the perfection of the eight liberations.

Because of having either not yet cultivated or having already cultivated the perception of form, respectively, one—either possessing form internally or being formless internally—relying on internal meditative concentration or the formless attainments, [perceives] external forms as beautiful or ugly.
The two liberations beginning with "one sees" are the antidotes to the obscuration regarding emanation (*nirmāṇāvaraṇa*).

Regarding the emanation of beautiful and ugly forms, there is, respectively, mental application (*ābhoga*) and aversion (*prātikūlya*), which constitute affliction (*saṃkleśa*); as the antidote to that, one dwells having personally realized and attained the beautiful liberation-door with the body.

By relying on the perception of mutual dependence and the perception of mutual conformity toward beautiful and ugly forms within oneself, and through the attainment of the perception of their mutual single flavor, one attains mastery over the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) regarding forms as desired; thus, this is one [liberation].

Regarding "liberation" (*vimokṣa*): there are three aspects of liberation which constitute the path of emanation; four aspects consisting of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), which have the nature of the path of abiding in accordance with liberation; and one aspect consisting of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāveditanirodha*), which has the nature of the path of peaceful abiding. Thus, these five aspects constitute the path of abiding in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
This is the perfection of the nine successive abidings (*navānupūrvavihārapāramitā*).
The nine supramundane paths consist of the aspects of the four dhyānas, the formless attainments, and the attainment of cessation.
This is the perfection of the four truths;
thus, the path of abandonment consists of the four aspects of the uninterrupted paths characterized by the dissociation from afflictions, which are subsumed within the four truths.
"This is the ten perfections" means that the path to Buddhahood consists of the ten aspects of the perfections, beginning with generosity (*dāna*).
Thus, with reference to these six kinds of paths, such as the path of counteraction (*pratipakṣamārga*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) has thirty-four aspects based upon the paths.
Immediately following that, the aspects of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) must be explained.

Among these, since the path is unique due to its unsurpassed nature, one must explain the uncommon distinctions of this specific path according to the differences in the aspects of the powers (*bala*), the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth; thus he says:
"This is the perfection of power."
The power of knowing what is possible and impossible,
the power of knowing the ripening of karma,
and the power of knowing various inclinations.
the power of knowledge regarding the manifold world-systems,
the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties of beings,
and the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere;
The power of knowledge regarding affliction and purification;
the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes;
the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth.
Regarding the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āśravakṣayajñānabala*): because it is unassailable due to having conquered its adversaries, there are ten aspects of power.
This is the perfection of fearlessness (*vaiśāradyapāramitā*).

When one makes the self-assertion, "I am a Buddha," when one declares that passion and so forth are obstacles, when one reveals that the path to omniscience and so forth is the definitive departure, and [when one proclaims] oneself as one whose outflows are exhausted—
And because there is no one to challenge him when he has accepted [the debate], he maintains an unshaken mind; thus, there are four aspects of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
This is the perfection of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid-pāramitā*).

It is so called because, respectively, through the absence of obstruction by the taste for realization, the obscuration of the knowable, and resistance, he possesses unattached and unimpeded omniscience regarding synonyms, the characteristics of phenomena, regional dialects, and the distinctions between dharmas.
The four aspects of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—of phenomena (*dharma*), meaning (*artha*), etymology (*nirukti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*)—are as follows:
"This is the perfection of the unique qualities of all Buddhas";
there is no faltering.
There are six aspects consisting of a mind that is fabricated, characterized by loss of mindfulness, lack of concentration, perception of various objects, non-discernment, and equanimity.

With respect to the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there are six aspects consisting of the absence of decline from zeal, vigor, mindfulness, meditative absorption, wisdom, and liberation.

The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) consist of the three aspects of bodily, vocal, and mental actions being preceded by and following after knowledge; and the three aspects of unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding the past, future, and present. Because they transcend calculation due to their uniqueness compared to the Śrāvakas and others, these are the aspects of the Tathāgata’s suchness (*tathāgatatathatā*).
Because there is no deviation from the characteristics and meaning of every dharma spoken by the Blessed Buddhas, based on its non-falsity, the aspect of suchness spoken by all Buddhas is one;
this perfection is self-existent.
By means of omniscience, the Pratyekabuddhas are subsumed.
These [qualities] exist within their impure path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which consists of the antidote to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding "non-affliction" (*asaṃkleśa*): non-affliction is the absence of afflictions, based on the fact that they lack the intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*) of attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Regarding "non-purification": non-purification refers to the absence of purification, based on the non-apprehension of the basis, which is the afflicted sentient being.
"Unstained": because space is naturally luminous, its lack of being stained by afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) constitutes "unstainedness.
"Non-proliferated" (*aprapañca*): [refers to the absence of conceptual proliferation].

Non-proliferation (*aprapañca*) is the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), based on the transcendence of all forms of mental estimation (*mananā*) that consist in objective apprehension (*upalambha*).
Regarding "non-estimation": it is the absence of mental estimation, based on immovability and unshakeability resulting from the total eradication of all apprehension.
"Non-fluctuating thought" means that, by virtue of the abiding nature of the *dharmadhātu* throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there is no falling away; thus it is "non-fluctuating.

Therefore, these six aspects—non-affliction, non-purification, non-staining, non-proliferation, non-thought, and non-fluctuation—correspond respectively to the abandonment of the conceptual constructions of: affliction, purification, the latencies of the afflictions, the proliferation of form and so forth, the apprehension of one's own realization, and regression.

The antidotes to the six specific cognitive obscurations exist within the uncontaminated path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the Pratyekabuddhas, which consists of the antidote to the cognitive obscuration.
Taken together, these constitute twenty-seven aspects of omniscience (*sarvajñatākāra*).
And so it has been said:
"Beginning from the aspect of non-existence up to the form of immovability—these four for each truth are recorded as fifteen on the path. (2)
Immediately following that, the aspects of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*) must be explained.

In this context, based on the distinction between the side of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and its opposite, the truths of origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*) constitute the cause, while the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and cessation (*nirodha*) constitute the result. Having thus indicated them by way of their meaning, one should understand that within the truths of origin, the path, suffering, and cessation, there are respectively eight, seven, five, and sixteen aspects.
In this regard, the cause is threefold:
desire (*chanda*), passion (*rāga*), and the delight that is craving for renewed existence (*nandī ca paunarbhavikī tṛṣṇā*). He speaks [next] as the antidote to desire.
Regarding "detachment" (*virāga*): it is detachment because of the absence of passion, based upon the non-falsity and truthfulness of all phenomena in the form of emptiness.
It is taught with the underlying intention that there is an absence of the desire to act; for it is held that in the stage of *chanda* (zeal), passion (*rāga*) is predominant,
since zeal is described as existing only in the absence of that [passion].
Or rather, by the absence of passion— which is of the nature of an effect—
the absence of the desire that has that [passion] as its deficient cause is stated.
Otherwise,
according to the principle that "if the cause is unimpaired, the non-arising of the effect would not occur," he spoke by way of the antidote to attachment.
Regarding "non-arising":
because all phenomena are like an illusion, based on their non-conceptuality, there is an absence of arising— that is, of volitional desire— which is "non-arising."

This was stated with the underlying intention that there is non-attachment toward phenomena. Since desire (*chanda*) is primary as the direct cause for activity during the state of passion, it is taught that through its absence, passion itself becomes non-existent.
Furthermore, he speaks [the following] as an antidote to the craving for delight (*nandī-tṛṣṇā*), which is the cause of renewed existence (*punarbhava*).

"Peaceful" (*śānta*) means that, because the signs (*nimitta*) such as blue, yellow, and so forth of all phenomena are not perceived, there is an absence of the lack of pacification primarily characterized by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Regarding the threefold origins— namely, passion, hatred, and delusion— he speaks [of peace] as their antidote.
"Faultless" means that,
by virtue of having reached the perfection of qualities such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, there is an absence of faults; thus it is "faultless," which is non-attachment.
"Hatred" means up to "delusion.
It is to be understood as the source because from it arise attachment and the other [afflictions]; therefore, he speaks by way of its antidote.
"Free from afflictions" (niḥkleśa):
because the conceptual construction—the adherence to duality and so forth—is non-existent, there is an absence of the arising of the causes of affliction; this is "free from afflictions.
The condition [for affliction] is the adherence to the existence of sentient beings.
Because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the condition for all misfortune, he says, as its antidote:
"without a sentient being" (*niḥsattva*).
In the sense of being non-erroneous, with reference to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the absence of conditions is "without a sentient being."

Thus, beginning from the aspect of dispassion (*virāga*) up to the aspect of being devoid of a sentient being (*niḥsattva*), there is, respectively, that which is the cause: zeal (*chanda*), passion (*rāga*), and delight (*nandī*);
and that which is the origin (*samudaya*): passion, hatred, and delusion (*rāga-dveṣa-moha*).
That which is the source is conceptual construction;
that which is the condition is the adherence to a self-entity.
As their respective antidotes, there are eight aspects within the truth of origination: three, three, one, and one.

Regarding "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*): because it serves as the basis for the arising and manifestation of the origination of all phenomena, and because it brings about the cessation of opposing factors while inducing their antidotes, it provides space for immeasurable sentient beings; thus, the aspect of the path is "immeasurable.
Furthermore, as to how it provides space for immeasurable sentient beings, he says:
"Non-approaching the two extremes" means that,
by virtue of non-adherence to all phenomena, there is no apprehension of the approach to the two extremes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa because they have been abandoned.
"Undifferentiated" means that,

by virtue of the non-differentiation and non-diversity of all phenomena in the form of the *dharmadhātu*, the aspect of the correct principle (*nyāya*) is undifferentiated through the cessation of its opposites.
And as for how this is logical, he says:
"uncontaminated," which means by virtue of having no longing for the stages of any Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
"Untouched by that conceptualization" means not grasped by it. "Non-conceptual" [means...]
Based on the equality of conceptual construction, the mode of practice is non-conceptual.
And as to how that practice is, he says:
"immeasurable."

Based on the nature of immeasurability (*apramāṇadharmatā*), and placing foremost the absence of conceptualization regarding the inferior and the sublime— whether in the relinquishing of what has been attained or the acquiring of what has not yet been attained— it is immeasurable (*aprameya*) because it is devoid of any limit to the knowable.
It is "unattached" (*asaṅga*).

In each respective realization, based on the non-attachment to all phenomena like space, the aspect of deliverance (*nairyāṇika*) is unattached. Thus, there are aspects that are immeasurable, unattached, and free from conceptualization—respectively, those which do not follow the two extremes, which are undifferentiated and ungrasped, and which are immeasurable and unattached. These are: the path that provides space for all sentient beings, and how it provides space for all sentient beings;
the principle, and how it is a principle.
That which is practice, the manner in which one practices,
and that which is the departure—
these constitute the seven aspects within the truth of the path, categorized as two, two, and three respectively.
Regarding "impermanent":
because all phenomena are non-existent, they are unconditioned by causes and conditions; thus, being eternally non-existent is the meaning of "non-existence," which is the meaning of "impermanent."
"Regarding 'suffering' (duḥkha): based on the equality of space with respect to all phenomena, the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkha) pervades all things.
Regarding 'emptiness' (śūnya):..."

"Empty" refers to the absence of a self or anything else imagined by others, based on the non-apprehension of all phenomena even insofar as they are connected with the slightest trace of a relationship to a governing self.
"Non-self" refers to the lack of intrinsic nature in persons and so forth, based on the non-attachment to all phenomena as being non-self in their own right.
Regarding "signless" (*alakṣaṇa*):
because all phenomena are unproduced, they are without intrinsic nature and thus signless.
Therefore, the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, together with the fifth aspect of being signless in nature—these five aspects exist within the truth of suffering.
Regarding "the emptiness of all" (*sarvaśūnyatā*):

because the extremes characterized by prior and posterior states, as well as the middle, are entirely joined with the two extremes and thus lack any final limit, the sixteen aspects of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*)— which are the emptinesses— are called the "emptiness of all" by virtue of their being infinite and limitless.

In that regard, through the cessation of internal, external, and both types of entities, there are three aspects of emptiness— internal, external, and both— which have the nature of the aspect of cessation; [these apply] to emptiness, the receptacle world, the ultimate truth, the conditioned, the unconditioned, the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, and the beginningless and endless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

By the cessation of the eightfold adherence— which consists of conceptual designation and occurs within the absence of a self-nature in phenomena— there is, respectively, the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
Great emptiness,
emptiness of the ultimate truth,
and emptiness of the conditioned.
The emptiness of the unconditioned;
the absolute emptiness;
the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.
The non-dispersal emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*)—these eight aspects of emptiness have the nature of the aspect of peace (*śāntākāra*).
The aspect of excellence (*praṇītākāra*) consists of the aspect of natural emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) through the cessation of an agent imagined by others.

Through the cessation of those consisting of error regarding objects, there are three aspects of the non-apprehension of the characteristics of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-lakṣaṇānupalambha-śūnyatā*); these have the nature of the aspect of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇākāra*).

Since the aspect of emptiness whose intrinsic nature is non-existence— by way of the cessation of intrinsic nature— is itself characterized by the aspect of deliverance, it refers to the cessation of internal and other objects with respect to the aspect of cessation, the aspect of peace, the aspect of excellence,
and the aspect of deliverance; and how it is peaceful.
Because of the cessation of the eight kinds of adherence;
and because it is sublime by nature;
and because it is an escape through the cessation of the three types of delusion.

And that which is the departure [from suffering], namely the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvatā*)— these three, eight, one, and three respectively constitute the sixteen aspects within the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
In total, there are thirty-six aspects of the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñatā*).
And so it has been said: "In regard to the cause, the path, suffering, and cessation, they are proclaimed respectively as eight, seven, five, and sixteen. (3)

Immediately following that, the aspects (*ākāra*) of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) must be explained. In that context, within the section concerning all noble persons (*āryapudgala*), there is a summary of the three types of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Therefore, he speaks of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) beginning with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) by way of the distinction between the paths to omniscience.

The meaning is that, based on the non-apprehensibility (*anupalabdhitā*) of those very factors conducive to enlightenment, the foundations of mindfulness and so forth themselves constitute the perfections (*pāramitā*).
This is what is meant:

therein, for the sake of entering the four truths at the outset of omniscience, there are four modes of the foundations of mindfulness—body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—which have been examined in terms of their specific and general characteristics; this constitutes the path of examining the objects, because by means of it one examines the fourfold objects beginning with the body.

Then, for one who has descended [into the path], there are the four aspects of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), which consist of the energy that serves as the cause for, respectively, abandoning unwholesome states already arisen and preventing those not yet arisen from arising, and for increasing wholesome states already arisen and producing those not yet arisen; these constitute the "path of exertion" (*vyavasāyika-mārga*),
because energy is initiated through the gateway of abandoning hindrances and so forth.

The attainment of mental flexibility (*citta-karmaṇyatā*) for one who possesses vigor consists of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), which are endowed with the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*) and the concentrations of desire, vigor, mind, and investigation; these constitute the path for refining concentration, because flexibility is brought about through the gateway of desire and the others. For one who has thus refined the mind—

Immediately following that, there is the application of *uṣmagata* (heat) and *mūrdhan* (summit); its intrinsic nature consists of the five aspects of the faculties (*indriya*) of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This is the path of application for the correct realization (*samyag-abhisamaya-prāyogika-mārga*), because through the application of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, one becomes the dominant condition (*adhipati-bhūta*) for the attainment of the Noble Path by means of the faculty of faith and the others. Following the attainment of *uṣmagata* and the rest, there is the application of *kṣānti* (patience) and *agradharma* (supreme mundane dharmas); its intrinsic nature consists of the five aspects of the powers (*bala*) of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This is the path of complete integration with realization (*sarvathā-abhisamaya-saṃśleṣa-mārga*).

Following the powers such as faith, for the sake of penetrating the truths, there is the application of the stages of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), which are not overcome by their opposites such as lack of faith. For one who has realized the fourfold stage beginning with "heat" (*uṣmagata*), the path of seeing the truths (*satyadarśanamārga*) consists of the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)— namely, mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity— which constitute the path of clear realization (*abhisamayamārga*).
Therefore, because of the perfect awakening to the reality that is to be personally realized from the very beginning,

for one who has fully understood and seen the truths, there is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). This consists of the aspects of the Noble Eightfold Path— right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration— and is the pure path leading to liberation, since by means of it one proceeds beyond the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) for the sake of purifying the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
For this very reason, this is the sequential order of these factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

Thus, with reference to the sevenfold path beginning with the path of the examination of the objective basis (*vastu*), there are thirty-seven aspects based upon the path to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Immediately following that, he states the divisions of the path to the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*).
Regarding the perfection of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness:
the first gate of liberation, emptiness, has the intrinsic nature of the aspects of emptiness and selflessness; it is the antidote to views.

That which is signless (*animitta*) is cessation (*nirodha*), and that by which one reaches the signless—namely, the path free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—is the second gate of liberation, the signless (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*). Having this nature of the aspects (*ākāra*) of the truths of cessation and the path, it is the antidote to the signs of views and conceptual construction.

As for what was stated—that "the signless [consists] in the aspects of tranquility" (*śamākāra*)—that refers to the Śrāvaka path which is permeated by the signs of objective entities (*vastu-nimitta*); therefore, there is no contradiction between that and this [teaching].

The third gate of liberation, the wishless (*apraṇihita*), has the nature of the aspects of the truths of impermanence, suffering, and origination; it is the antidote to the aspiration for the three realms (*traidhātuka-praṇidhāna*).
Thus, there are three paths of counteraction consisting of the aspects of the three gates of liberation.
This is the perfection of the eight liberations.

Because of having either not cultivated or having cultivated the perception of form, respectively, one—either possessing form internally or being formless internally—relying on internal meditative absorption or the formless attainments, [perceives] external forms as beautiful or ugly.
The two liberations beginning with "one sees" are the antidotes to the obscuration regarding emanation (*nirmāṇāvaraṇa*).

Regarding the emanation of beautiful and ugly forms, there is, respectively, mental application (*ābhoga*) and aversion (*prātikūlya*), which constitute affliction (*saṃkleśa*); as the antidote to these, one dwells having personally realized and attained the beautiful liberation-door (*śubha-vimokṣamukha*) with the body.

By relying on the perception of mutual dependence and the perception of mutual conformity toward beautiful and ugly forms within oneself, and by attaining the perception of their mutual single flavor, one gains mastery over the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) regarding forms as desired; thus, this is the first [liberation].

"Emancipation" refers to the five aspects: the three aspects of emanation which constitute the path of transformation; the four aspects of the formless attainments which constitute the path of dwelling in accordance with liberation; and the single aspect of the cessation of perception and feeling, which constitutes the path of dwelling in peace. These five aspects constitute the path of dwelling in happiness in the present life;
this is the perfection of the nine successive dwellings.
The ninefold supramundane path consists of the aspects of the four dhyānas, the formless attainments, and the attainment of cessation.
This is the perfection of the four truths;
it is the path of abandonment, comprising the four aspects of the uninterrupted paths characterized by the dissociation from the afflictions, which are subsumed within the four truths.
"This is the ten perfections" means that the path to Buddhahood consists of the ten aspects of the perfections, beginning with generosity. Thus,
with reference to these sixfold paths— such as the path of counteragents— the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), which has the paths as its basis, comprises thirty-four aspects.
Immediately after that, the aspects (*ākāra*) of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) must be explained.

In that regard, since the path is without superior, it is one and only; however, the unique distinction of this specific path (*viśeṣamārga*) must be stated according to the differences in its aspects, such as the powers (*bala*) and the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*). Thus he says: "This is the perfection of power."
The power of knowing what is possible and impossible,
the power of knowing the ripening of karma,
and the power of knowing the various inclinations [of beings].
the power of knowledge regarding many world-systems,
the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties [of beings],
and the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere;
The power of knowledge regarding affliction and purification,
the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes,
and the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth.

The power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āśravakṣayajñānabala*) consists of ten aspects of power, based on the fact that it is unassailable because its opposing factors have been conquered.
This is the perfection of fearlessness (*vaiśāradyapāramitā*).

It is [the perfection] because, when one makes the self-assertion "I am a Buddha," when one declares that passion and so forth are obstacles, when one reveals that the path to omniscience and so forth is the definitive exit, and when one [declares] oneself to be one whose outflows are exhausted...
And because there is no one left to challenge him once he has accepted [the debate], the four forms of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) are based on a mind that is undaunted.
This is the perfection of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid-pāramitā*);

it is so called because, respectively, with respect to synonyms, the characteristics of phenomena, local dialects, and the distinctions between phenomena, it possesses unimpeded and unattached omniscience by virtue of the absence of any obstruction consisting in the relish for realization or the cognitive obstructions.
There are four aspects of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) regarding phenomena, meaning, etymology, and eloquence.
This is the perfection of the unique qualities of all Buddhas;
there is no faltering.

There are six aspects consisting of: a mind that is distracted, one whose mindfulness is lost, one that is not concentrated, the perception of various objects, equanimity without discernment, and so forth.

Regarding the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there are six aspects consisting of the absence of decline from zeal, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and liberation.

The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) consist of the three aspects of bodily, vocal, and mental actions being preceded by and following after knowledge; and the three aspects of unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding the past, future, and present. Because they transcend all calculation due to their uniqueness compared to the disciples (*śrāvaka*) and others, these are the aspects of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata.

Because all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not deviate from the characteristics and meanings [of reality], they are based on non-falsity; thus, the aspect of suchness spoken by all Buddhas is one.
This is the perfection of the Self-Existent One, because, based on the lack of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena, the realization thereof does not depend on another.
The first is the self-arisen form that exercises mastery over all phenomena;
this is the perfection of the wisdom of the Omniscient One.
Based on the thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature and all aspects of all phenomena, the second is the form of Buddhahood, which is the complete awakening to all aspects.

Having established this, there are thirty-nine aspects (ākāras) based upon the path of omniscience in all its modes (sarvākārajñatā), which are respectively ten, four, four, eighteen, one, one, and one; these consist of the distinctions of the aspects according to power and so forth, their intrinsic nature which is suchness (tathatā), those self-arisen ones (svayambhuvaḥ) who have mastery over all dharmas, and that purpose for which they exist, namely, the complete awakening to all dharmas in all their modes.

Furthermore, these very aspects (ākāra) should be understood according to the distinctions of the Śrāvakas and others within the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), due to the distinctions among the truths of the path (mārgasatya).
And so it has been said:
"Beginning with the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and ending with the aspect of Buddhahood."
Of the disciples, the bodhisattvas, and the Buddhas, respectively. ||4||
"They are considered to be thirty-seven, thirty-four, thirty, and nine,

according to the division into the three types of omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), in accordance with the Truth of the Path. (Verse 5) Thus, therein, the aspects of omniscience (*sarvajñatākāra*) are both untainted (*anāsrava*) and tainted (*sāsrava*), respectively, according to the distinction between Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
The aspects of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*), because Bodhisattvas do not abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) completely.

The aspects of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are exclusively without outflows (*anāsrava*), because a Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*), through the abandonment of the obscurations of affliction and the knowable along with their latencies (*savāsanakleśajñeyāvaraṇa*), possesses knowledge of all phenomena. When counted together, these constitute one hundred and seventy-three aspects.
As for what was stated regarding the sixteen [aspects] by name:

The phrase "in eight aspects" is intended to mean that these are the aspects which serve as the specific antidotes to that very obscuration of afflictions; therefore, there is no contradiction with that [previous statement].
The ninth chapter, titled "Praise," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Tenth Chapter.

Since the aspects (ākāras) are to be cultivated through distinguished applications (prayoga), and since it is impossible to describe them without one who applies them, [the author], indicating the practitioner who is a fit vessel for hearing and so forth, says:
"Then, indeed, Śakra... and so on.
Because they have constructed monasteries and other edifices dedicated to the Tathāgata, they have performed services for previous Victors;
because they have given alms-food and other offerings, they have planted roots of merit under many Buddhas;
and because they are sustained by spiritual friends, they are embraced by spiritual friends.
Only those endowed with the three aforementioned qualifications are, primarily, the vessels for hearing this Mother characterized by the letter A.
Thus it has been said:
"Those who have performed their service toward the Buddhas and have planted roots of merit under them..."
"Supported by auspicious friends, she is a vessel for hearing [the Dharma]. Thus,
"by a mere trifle" means by a small amount.

They have attended upon many Buddhas by means of propitiating [them] through the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding the body and so forth; they have questioned [the Buddhas] by inquiring about their own nature in order to resolve matters of doubt;
and they have been made to inquire further by questioning them regarding the causes [of phenomena].
It should be understood that those who have planted roots of merit under many Buddhas through the practice and fulfillment of the ten perfections, such as giving,
and who have performed services for the Tathāgatas, are alone the vessels for receiving [the teachings] and so forth.
And thus it has been said:

"Through the practice of honoring the Buddha, inquiring [about the Dharma], and [observing] the conduct of giving, morality, and so forth, one is considered by the virtuous to be a vessel for receiving, retaining, and [understanding] [the teachings]. Thus, this reflection of Śakra is indeed appropriate; for he who possesses the aforementioned cause is the very one who exercises resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*). So it is said.
"O Blessed One, [he who]... and so forth.

Furthermore, the three phrases beginning with "you will train in that way" should be understood as referring to the distinctions between the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the special path (*viśeṣamārga*), corresponding respectively to the stages of preparation (*prayoga*), the main practice (*maula*), and the conclusion (*pṛṣṭha*).
[Objection: But if there is no realization of a distinguished meaning, how can one be considered irreversible merely by means of receiving [the teaching], etc., and how should he be maintained?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Profound," and so forth.

This refers to three phrases: [one who possesses] meager roots of merit, one who is by nature uninquiring, and one who has not practiced in the past—[the latter] being the opposite of the three causes consisting of the aforementioned service to the Tathāgata, inquiry, and the practice of giving, morality, and so on.
This is to be applied.
This is what has been said:

"Because one applies oneself to the Perfection of Wisdom with a distinguished resolute intention by means of the causes such as the worship of the Buddha as previously specified—by way of negation (vyatireka)—therefore, he should be understood as irreversible."
And because of the deficiency of the causes as previously stated, they reject [the teaching]; thus he says:
"But those who have conviction," and so forth.
Now, how is it understood that there was a prior rejection with the intention of rejecting?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"As it were," and so forth.
Because the mother’s intention to reject [the teachings] now arises from the smallness of her roots of merit, therefore her rejection is understood to have existed even previously.
The meaning is that otherwise, it would be impossible for there to be limited roots of merit (*parīttakuśalamūla*).
He states this very point with the words,
"Indeed not, O Blessed One," and so forth.
"What was said by Śāriputra is indeed appropriate," he said,
beginning with the words "Profound," and so forth.
What is there to marvel at?
Nothing at all, because the effect conforms to its cause.
He spoke thus because an extraordinary degree of serene confidence had arisen within him.
"I pay homage," and so forth. [An objection is raised: "How can there be homage to another when, in the case of homage to one's mother, there is no connection to anyone else?"
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?
he says, "Because it has emerged from that," and so forth.
Since one attains Buddhahood through the repeated practice [of the perfections] toward the Mother during the stage of a bodhisattva, omniscience (sarvajñatā) has emerged from that.

In the state of Buddhahood, because the perfection of wisdom is revealed to those to be trained, the perfection of wisdom is characterized by the knowledge of the omniscient one; thus, through this relationship of cause and effect, homage to the perfection of wisdom is homage to the knowledge of the omniscient one. "In this way" means as follows.
The meaning is: as both the cause and the fruit of the knowledge of the omniscient one.
One should practice the perfection of wisdom through the knowledges consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, respectively;
thus the three phrases are to be applied.
Immediately after the instruction for the practitioner, he asks a question regarding the practice,
saying, "How, O Blessed One," and so forth.
Because the question is appropriate to the context, the Blessed One gives his approval, saying, "Excellent, excellent."
"Regarding this matter," and so forth:
beginning with the twenty applications that are about to be explained, one should inquire for the sake of one's own realization;
one should pose questions for the sake of the realization of others.
"You regard, practice toward, and know the Tathāgata"— this is the meaning.
In that regard, he states the application of non-abiding with respect to form and the other aggregates by means of the passage beginning with "here," etc.
The two words "rūpe" and "rūpam" should be stated according to the distinction between the substratum and its essential nature.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"Since," and so forth.
This has been stated:
"Because there is a negation of abiding in form and so forth by virtue of their lack of intrinsic nature, therefore there is the application [of the reason] of non-abiding therein.
He speaks for the purpose of the application of non-connection:
"Kauśika, one does not apply [the thought] 'this is form'"; the meaning is that one does not enter into conjunction with it. He then asks: what follows from that? And he says:
"From which," and so forth.
"Thus he attains yoga":
thus, by way of the conventional, he attains yoga through the absence of yoga in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*).
The meaning is that non-application toward those very things constitutes their application.
He describes the profound application with the words beginning "profound," and so forth.

Because the suchness (*tathatā*) of form and so forth is profound, it is understood as "profound" within the context of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) in the sense that no foundation can be apprehended; thus,
he speaks of the practice that is difficult to fathom with the words beginning "difficult to fathom."

Because form and so forth are difficult to fathom, and because they are by nature untroubled, there is the conviction that "it is difficult to fathom" within the context of the knowledge of the paths;
explaining this very point, he says:
"It is difficult to grasp."
Because it is difficult to grasp by means of auditory consciousness and the mental consciousness drawn forth by it,
he states the practice of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) with the words beginning "immeasurable," and so forth.

Because form and so forth are immeasurable, in the context of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is called "immeasurable" in the sense that no limit can be apprehended; this is due to its objective support (*ālambana*).
Alternatively, with respect to the profound realization, the uncommon realization, and the unsurpassed realization, there are three kinds [of immeasurability] respectively.
Regarding that which was described as the profound application and so forth,
he clarifies the profound application by stating "it is thus" and so on, in order to show that it has been well spoken.

Thus, this is the summarized meaning: when one does not abide in reality through the application of the conceptual adherence that "form and so forth are profound," then, because of being non-erroneous (*aviparyasta*), one enters into the yoga of profundity with respect to them.

And when one does not even enter into the yoga [thinking] "it is profound," then one does not abide even in the notion that "form and so forth are profound. In this way, by negating the abiding in yoga, the purpose is the practice of non-erroneous profundity.
Regarding the phrase "it has been explained":
following this, the meaning of both *duravagāha* (difficult to fathom) and *apramāṇa-prayoga* (immeasurable application) should also be stated.
"And these three applications, beginning with 'profound,' are each [divided into] weak, middling, and intense."
Thus says the noble Vimuktisena.
To explain the application for the sake of awakening after a long period of hardship, he says:
"O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound."
Regarding the phrase "of one who is subject to regression," and so forth:
because of belonging to a fixed lineage (*niyatagotra*), someone may be irreversible (*avaivartika*) yet still indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The term "determined" (*vyākṛta*) is included for the purpose of excluding that [uncertainty].
Since it is possible for doubt and so forth to arise because a mother lacks knowledge of all aspects, one might ask: what is the reason for speaking in her very presence?
Anticipating this question with "For what reason?", he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "He indeed," etc.:
because he possesses the excellence of the Dharma taught as the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the realized *dharmadhātu*, he will not have any longing due to the absence of false knowledge,
and he will not have any doubt due to the disappearance of uncertain cognition.
Because he is free from ignorance, he will not be bewildered; because he is endowed with perfect knowledge, he will not dispute;
therefore, it is my thought that one should speak only in his presence.
By implication, because others may experience further terror and so forth, the practice of attaining awakening with difficulty over a long period is shown.
He states the practice for obtaining the prophecy [of future buddhahood] with the words beginning "But if," up to "what fault?"
What fault, such as doubt, could there be?
He says that for one who possesses freedom from terror and so forth by virtue of the power of the lineage (*gotra*), there is none; thus he speaks the words beginning with "from afar" (*dūrāt*).
"From afar, from far away" means for as long as a very long time;
he says this very thing in the words "one who has set out on the long journey."
Alternatively, because he has resolute confidence in its profound meaning from afar, and because it is not within the domain of the śrāvakas and others,
[the text says] "he will obtain the perfection of wisdom" and so forth;
first of all, he sees it from a distance.
Then, his body gladdened by the sight [of the Buddha], he pays homage.
Then, with the force of his increasing faith, he attends upon him by performing circumambulations and other such acts.
Then, having performed the proper sequence of actions, he sits down and listens.
In this way, for the sake of vision and so forth, he will attain the perfection of wisdom;
"not now after a long time" means not at some distant future, but right now at the very time of vision and so forth.
He says this very thing with the words beginning "near" and so forth,
and "not a single Tathāgata" and so forth.
"He will not bypass one, two, or three Tathāgatas;
thereafter that bodhisattva will receive the prophecy"— it is not thus, but rather the meaning is "from them" (i.e., from all of them).
Explaining that very point,
he says: "But rather, he will please them"—
that is, those one, two, or three Tathāgatas— by correctly practicing the training as it has been prescribed for them.
He will cause [beings] to rejoice;
and he will make the vision of the Tathāgata not fruitless by means of a prophecy.
He will make the vision of one, two, or three Tathāgatas, and so forth, not empty by means of a prophecy.
Because of the attainment of grammatical analysis regarding the rule (*niyama*).
He states that very point with the words beginning "and from seeing the Tathāgata," and so forth.
The conclusion beginning with "And when the prophecy... is easy to understand.
To explain the meaning of the practice of the irreversible [bodhisattva], he says:
"Then, indeed, the venerable Śāriputra," and so forth.
How much more so, then,
for one who, having heard it, shall grasp it—
by means of correct grasping and so forth?
