Since he is endowed with the practice of turning back [from lower realms], what doubt can there be that his roots of merit are fully matured? The meaning is that there is no doubt whatsoever.
He expresses agreement because of the excellence of what was said.
With the words "It is so," and so forth, he speaks in order to further strengthen the previously stated application:
"It occurs to me, O Blessed One," and so forth.
This is an illustrative example by way of comparison.
An example of similarity:
"upavartsyate" means "upapatsyate."

One might ask: "How is a bodhisattva whose roots of virtue are fully matured to be identified by the grasping and so forth of the *prajñāpāramitā*, since such grasping and so forth can also occur for others? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because for the most part," and so forth.

This is because, for the majority who are not free from those karmas that lead to the ruin of the Dharma, their minds will be averse to the *prajñāpāramitā* due to being turned away from its correct apprehension and so on, and they will cause it to waver through their intent toward abandonment.
And because those who have not accumulated roots of merit do not enter into the Perfection of Wisdom due to their failure to understand its meaning,
nor do they become serene through the attainment of serene faith;
therefore, it is the sense of the statement that those who have accumulated roots of merit are the ones who perform such acts as correctly grasping [the teaching].
Regarding the phrase "in the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*): the limit of reality is the dharmadhātu; because it illuminates that, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is so designated.
He now states the application for departure (*niryāṇaprayoga*).
Just as, O Blessed One, it was said by the passage beginning with "a man [coming] from a hundred-yojana [distance]," and likewise by the passage beginning with "in this very way":

for one who possesses the practice of avoiding obstructive factors and so forth— like a man setting out from a wilderness forest hundreds of yojanas wide— for whom this Mother of the Jinas arises for the purpose of hearing her and so on, [it will certainly lead to the goal].
Because of this departure, it should be understood through practice that "I am [attaining] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment"— this is the meaning.
He says that very thing:
Nor by that [means], and so forth.
[The author] asks: "If there is no presence of dharmas contrary to that, how could there not be fear of falling onto the level of the Śrāvakas and others?
Suspecting this, he says: "For what reason? and so on.
For it is said:

"Because, by virtue of arising from the mere selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*), he obtains for the sake of vision and so forth the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which is contrary to the levels of the Śrāvakas and others, and which illuminates the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of all phenomena without exception."
"Therefore, because one perceives a mother who is contrary [to that state], there is no fear of falling to the level of the Śrāvakas and so forth.
Because he had spoken well, [the Buddha] said, "So it is, Śāriputra,
so it is," and placing his hand upon him, spoke again for the sake of bestowing further empowerment.
"May it be manifest," and so forth.
He speaks "Just as if, O Blessed One, here some person... and so on, for the sake of uninterrupted practice.
"Or a clump of grass, or the sign of a clump of grass," means "or a branch, or the sign of a branch.
[The opponent asks: "Since no such clumps of grass and so forth are perceived, how can it be said that the great ocean is nearby?"
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because it slopes gradually," and so forth.
This is what is meant:

Because the ocean possesses a nature that slopes gradually downward— which is contrary to pillars and the like produced by their own causes— therefore, from the very perception of its nature, there is the non-perception of pillars and such;
thus, one who hears the *Prajñāpāramitā* should understand that [the ocean] is near.
It must be ascertained through the power of uninterrupted application by means of practice such as constant cultivation.
How is it inferred that the proximity to the effect of prophecy is brought about by the cause of hearing from the Mother?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For it is thus," and so forth. This is what is meant:

"There is no fault because, by means of an inference based on a *svabhāvahetu*—namely, the capacity of the cause to produce an effect due to its independence from any other factor—one infers that [the Buddha] has drawn near to the state of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).
He states the practice for one who is close to full awakening with the words beginning, "Just as, O Blessed One, in spring... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "among the withered leaves and petals": this refers to those fallen, aged leaves.
As before, having raised the doubt as to why this is so, he says:
For it is said: "These are the preceding signs," and so forth.
That production of an effect which is inferred from a complete collection of causes is its own nature (*svabhāva*), because it does not depend on any other entity.
Thus it has been described.
This is understood by the aforementioned reasoning.

"This has been brought near" means that it has been presented through the power of the preparatory practice for imminent enlightenment, based on the realization that she is the locus of the qualities of the newly manifested weapons and so forth.
He speaks the passage beginning with "Just as, for example," for the purpose of explaining the practice for swift awakening.
She is called "pregnant" because she has conceived a fetus.
Because her time for delivery is near, she is heavy with child;
she writhes due to the stretching of her limbs.

Furthermore, through the prior improper mental attention associated with sexual conduct—which was practiced, cultivated, and developed during the stages of preparation, the main act, and the conclusion, respectively—she [experiences] this everywhere again.

Furthermore, by bringing it to mind and practicing it repeatedly, one thinks— this being the ellipsis— "I am experiencing this very kind of present, unbearable bodily sensation, which is suffering. And as he hears this, his mind takes delight in it.

Because one who possesses the practice of swiftly bringing about the fruit of the *dharmakāya*—the quality to be established—through the power of the aforementioned application, the mind delights in the *prajñāpāramitā*, preceded by hearing it; that is to say, it develops devotion.
[The author] now states the ultimate application:
"O Blessed One, it is wonderful," and so forth.
By the word "as far as" (*yāvat*), the inclusion of the phrase "having a protector" (*sanāthāḥ*) and others is intended.

Since the Bodhisattvas have been well-supported and well-guided by the Blessed One through their introduction to the stages (*bhūmi*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*) via prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*) and other means, and since they have been well-entrusted through their being handed over to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), it is therefore wonderful.

Even though compassion has all things as its object, it is marvelous that it favors specific individuals by the power of their fitness (*bhavyatā*) and the perfection of their distinguished intention (*viśiṣṭāśaya*).
He explains this very perfection of distinguished intention:
This is shown by the passage beginning with "tathā hi" (for thus).
They have set out for the benefit of many beings because they will perform their purposeful activity through a future connection;
they are for the happiness of many beings because they are performing that purposeful activity at this present time.

The connection with the preceding [phrase] is as follows: because they exert effort for the sake of increasing or diminishing, respectively, the latencies (*vāsanā*) of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas produced through connection with past time, they have "set out out of compassion for the world.
Furthermore, he speaks generally by way of connection with the past, future, and present times.
"For the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great body of people.
"Desiring to teach the Dharma" means desiring to speak the Dharma for the sake of others by practicing the turning of the wheel of Dharma and so forth within the Perfection of Wisdom.
He speaks for the sake of the practice of neither increasing nor decreasing:
"In this regard, O Blessed One, of a bodhisattva," and so forth.
By the instruction to practice the perfection of wisdom through the non-perception of the increase or decrease of form and the other aggregates, that practice is explained.
He speaks for the purpose of the practice of the non-perception of dharma, adharma, and so forth:
"He does not perceive dharma," and so on.
Because this practice consists precisely in the realization of the non-perception of dharma, adharma, and the rest, one thus reaches the fulfillment of cultivation.
He speaks for the purpose of the practice that brings about the cessation of the perception of inconceivable forms, saying:
"O Blessed One, this which is being taught is inconceivable," and so forth.

Since form and the other aggregates are inconceivable because they cannot be conceptualized as having the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, if one does not perceive them, then by the cessation of the perception of grasping them, one courses in the perfection of wisdom through the aforementioned practice; such is the meaning.
In order to inquire about the practice free from conceptual construction, he asks:
"O Blessed One, who here will have faith? and so forth.
To provide an answer, he says:

"Śāriputra, he who has practiced," and so forth. [The author] speaks in response to two questions: first, the question regarding the attainment of essential nature—"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become one who has practiced?"—and second, the question regarding the attainment of a designation according to its meaning—"How does he obtain the name 'one who has practiced'? He says this while resolving both inquiries.
"Here, Śāriputra," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "Since he possesses the power and fearlessnesses that are the objects of his thought, why does he not conceptualize?
Anticipating this question with the words "For what reason?", he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "For the powers, Śāriputra," etc.:

because they are in reality of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, and because one attains non-conceptual application through the capacity for practice that consists of not conceptualizing form and so forth, nor their signs, nor their intrinsic nature, the powers and so forth are "inconceivable" (*acintya*) by virtue of transcending thought;
thus, the meaning is that one does not conceptualize them.
He speaks for the purpose of explaining the practice of the gift of the jewel of the fruit:
"O Blessed One, the *prajñāpāramitā* is profound; O Blessed One, the *prajñāpāramitā* is a heap of jewels.

Being profound by virtue of being the antidote to the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*), it [bestows] the jewel of the fruits—beginning with the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*) up to the jewel of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—for those who possess the practice of bestowing the jewel of the fruit through the realization of the first fruit and so forth.
Because it is a giver, it is a heap of jewels.
To explain the meaning of its application toward purification, he says:
"a heap of purity," and so forth.
Based on the very purity of space itself,

for those who practice its application through the cultivation of the purity of form and so forth, it is a "pure heap" because it serves as the cause for the removal of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable.
He speaks next for the purpose of explaining the application of its limit:
"O Blessed One, it is wonderful," and so forth.
It is wonderful that even for one of such great majesty, obstacles can arise.
He said, "Well said," beginning with "It is so, Subhūti," and so forth. [The opponent objects:
"This is indeed without logical justification."
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For thus," and so forth.
Because Māra, the Evil One, will fall into eagerness and agitation.
The meaning is that because they create obstacles for that purpose, there are many such hindrances.
If this is so, then why is it written quickly? He says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "swiftly" (*śīghram*) and so forth:
Aryavimuktisena states that the mention of "in a year" is for the purpose of making it known that there is no external time [apart from] the totality of the conditions such as the seasons and so on.
"It must indeed be written in that manner.

This means that for those who possess the understanding that there is no abandonment of the legal pursuit (*abhiyoga*) for a year and so forth, it "must indeed be written" quickly and without obstacle, because they obtain the benefit of a fixed deadline; this is the remainder of the sense.
Now, one might ask: if it is written over the course of a year, how can it be called "quickly"?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason is that? he says:
"For it is thus," and so forth.
This is the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), because for great jewels there are many...

Obstacles may arise; therefore, the intended meaning is that although there may be many obstacles over the course of a year for this Mother, whose nature is the supreme jewel, the writing [of her] should nevertheless be done quickly.
The application should be understood exactly as stated.
And so it has been said:
"Because of not abiding in form and the other [aggregates], and because of the negation of yoga with respect to them."
Because suchness is profound, it is difficult for them to fathom. ||8||
Because of the lack of authority in that [view], awakening occurs only with great difficulty after a long time;
and regarding the prophecy, the state of non-retrogression, and the departure [from saṃsāra] along with its uninterruptedness. (9)
[The Buddha is distinguished] by the proximity to enlightenment, by the swiftness [in attaining it], by the absence of increase or decrease regarding the welfare of others,
by the non-perception of dharma and adharma and so forth, and by the non-perception of form, the inconceivable, and so forth. ||10||
"Non-conceptual with respect to form and so forth, which are its signs, as well as their non-existence;
it is the bestower of the jewel of the fruit, pure, and limited.
Thus, this sequence of these twenty applications is logically appropriate.

For, by abiding through the application of non-attachment toward form and so forth, and by engaging in the practice of yoga, he understands the profundity, the difficulty of penetration, and the immeasurability of those forms and so forth. Consequently, because his practice is not yet correctly established, the beginner attains the prophecy and the stage of non-retrogression with great difficulty, whereas the other attains them easily; thus he sets forth, remains unseparated from it, and draws near to it.
Then, while acting for the sake of others, he neither increases nor decreases.

Consequently, through the abandonment of all conceptualizations regarding generalities such as dharma and adharma, as well as particulars such as form and the inconceivable, he becomes free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*).
By bestowing the jewel of the fruit, he attains supreme purity and the ultimate consummation.
"Previously, for one year, the mental continuum has been refined through application"—this refers to the sequence of practice characterized by realization.
Following that practice, since the applications are practiced even more intensely preceded by the perception of their qualities, those qualities must be explained.
In this regard, he speaks first to explain the quality of obstructing the power of Māra.
"Here, O Blessed One, in this perfection of wisdom," and so forth.
"Will not prevail" means it will not have power.
"Of one whose undertaking is faultless," and so forth.
Regarding one who has undertaken the practice of reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā* and so forth without interruption,
and whose undertaking is flawless— because obstacles are incapable of affecting such a person to that extent—
it is said: "When, O Blessed One," and so forth.
"How is it so now? means: in what manner is it now, or by whose power, or by whose capability?
"By the power of the perfectly awakened ones.
Because the two questions were posed through conceptual construction, their resolution follows accordingly.
This is what was said.

"In the stage of the cultivation of application, because they have obtained the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgatas, they will perform [acts such as] receiving [the teachings] through the arising of the quality that obstructs the power of Māra.
To the question, "In what way is it the influence (*anubhāva*) of the Tathāgatas upon them?
and anticipating the inquiry, "For what reason is that?", he says:
For this, Śāriputra, is the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena; this is easy to understand.
To clarify this very point, he says:
"Those [beings] in the immeasurable [worlds]," and so forth.
To state the second quality, that of being known through the Buddha’s mindful attention (*samanvāhāra*), he says:
“And those who [will] this perfection of wisdom,” and so forth.
Because they look upon it with the capacity for its implantation, they will attend to it.
They will embrace [this teaching] by generating its capacity;
he explains that very point in detail with the words beginning,
"Those who, O Blessed One," and so forth.

He says, "By the power of the Buddhas," and so forth, because they will perform [the acts of] hearing and so on through the arising of the quality of being known by the Buddha’s attention— due to obtaining the Tathāgata’s attention during the stages of preparation, the main part, and the conclusion.
He says this to show that what has been said is well-spoken.
"Thus it is," and so forth.
Pointing out the third quality, that of directly perceiving the Buddha, he says:
"They are known," and so forth.
They were known by means of the divine eye with the intention of bestowing distinguished meanings;
they were presided over by the eye of wisdom.
They have been seen with the Dharma-eye;
they have been surveyed with the Buddha-eye—this is quite clear.
But who are they? He says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "ye ta," this is what is meant: "Those who perform [the practices of] hearing and so forth, possessing the quality of directly perceiving the Buddha through the attainment of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision— they are the 'knowers'."
Explaining the fourth quality, which is the state of being close to perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), he says:
"Having heard and having grasped," and so forth;
[the phrase] "they will become near" means:

By virtue of attaining proximity to the Tathāgatas, they will come to abide nearby due to the arising of the quality of drawing near to perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Demonstrating the fifth quality, that of great purpose (*mahārthatā*), he says: "Furthermore, Śāriputra, those who... and so forth.

"They will not abide in suchness" means that because they lack the practice for perfect enlightenment within suchness— by virtue of its meaning as being non-otherwise— they will not abide therein at that very moment.
"Of those too" refers to this.

Because of the attainment of great benefits through the arising of qualities such as great purposefulness, those who possess the retention and recitation of this [text] written in a book are never separated from the Buddhas; they are destined for the happy realms, and they attain perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, with regard to their engagement in the welfare of others even beyond [the attainment of] Nirvāṇa, four terms should be understood in their respective order: "of great purpose," "of great benefit," "of great fruit," and "of great maturation.
Moreover, in this context, "maturation" (vipāka) should be understood as the most excellent ripening.
"With effort" means:
the writing of that [text].
"Exertion" (pariṣpanda) refers to retention and recitation.
The mental engagement with the Mahāyāna Dharma according to its designation,
performed constantly by a bodhisattva through the three types of wisdom,
serves for the nourishment of the element, for entry [into reality], and for the accomplishment of the goal. Thus it is said.

If it is asked how there is a specific benefit for the *Jinajanani* (Mother of the Victors) alone when all Mahāyāna teachings possess benefits, one might wonder for what reason this is so; anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For it is thus, O Prajñāpāramitā," and so forth.

The meaning is that because she has appeared through the sequence of hearing and so forth for the sake of penetrating the reality of phenomena by way of the selflessness of all phenomena, therefore her benefit is primary.
To state the sixth quality, which is the excellence of defining the teaching, he says:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, these [disciples] associated with the six perfections," and so forth.

The mention of the six perfections is because the remaining perfections serve as companions to the perfections of giving and so forth. For instance, because beings who have been assisted by the three perfections beginning with giving are established in the wholesome through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)— which is comprised within the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgrahavastu*)—
the perfection of skillful means serves as a companion to those three perfections.

In this present life, due to the abundance of afflictions, one lacks the capacity for wholesome action; however, by making a mental aspiration for the state of having weak afflictions in the future, the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhipāramitā*) acts as an auxiliary to the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

Having relied upon service to holy beings and hearing the true Dharma, one turns away from the weakness of one's intention (*āśaya*) and attains the power of intention within the sublime realm (*pranīte dhātau*).
Thereby, through the attainment of the capacity to establish the mind internally, the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*) acts as an auxiliary to the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).

The perfection of knowledge (*jñānapāramitā*) is the companion of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) because of its capacity to produce supramundane wisdom preceded by the objective support of hearing the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
"On the road" (*vartanyām*) means in the eastern region.
"Having reached the ninth stage of ripening" (*navamaṇḍaprāpta*) means...
The connection with the preceding text is as follows: "When various Dharma-preachers have obtained meanings whose essence is like fresh cream (*navamaṇḍa*), the sūtras will circulate.

By this passage, it should be understood that the purpose is to eliminate the Dharma-preachers' longing for the Buddha's attention and so forth, through the attainment of qualities by way of performing the Tathāgata’s work and defining the [Buddha] land.
He says that very thing with the words beginning "having been attended to," and so forth.

Because the realm of sentient beings is utterly incapable due to the heightening of the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*), he speaks while considering the circulation of the jewel of the Dharma to be impossible.
"This too," and so forth;
he says this very thing regarding "in the final time.
By "final period" (*paścimasamaya*), he does not mean the eternal time postulated by Kaṇāda and others.
Because it lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) due to being either sequential or non-sequential, it is non-existent.
Rather, it is a certain arrangement of entities (*bhāvasanniveśa*), namely a later time, a convention, or a subsequent period.
It is not everywhere in the northern direction; rather, it is in the northern region, such as the land of China (*cīnaviṣaya*) and so forth.
He says, "Even at such a time as this, some will have planted roots of merit," beginning with the words,
"Those there, Śāriputra," and so forth.
Nevertheless, not seeing their great number, he says:
"Of how many," and so forth. He says "many," and so forth, to show that the arising of many occurs through the power of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and other such factors.
They are "many" because of the multiplicity of their individual natures;
they are "very many" because of the abundance of their lineages.
Speaking of the seventh [quality], which consists of the quality of the complete fulfillment of all dharmas free from outflows, he says:
"Moreover, Śāriputra, although there are many," and so forth;
"even among those many, few are [those who act]" refers to those who perform the acts of hearing [the Dharma] and so on.

The meaning is that those who perform the *anavala* and other [practices] are few, because they have attained the fulfillment of the qualities that counteract many [defilements], and because they have perfected the qualities of the fulfillment of the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
To explain the eighth quality, that of being the protagonist of the narrative, he says:
"The predecessors were bound by them," and so forth.
They were bound because they took refuge in [the Buddha] through the practice of the three refuges and other such means.

The three terms "paripṛṣṭāḥ," "paripṛcchitāḥ," and "paripraśnīkṛtāḥ" should be stated respectively for the purpose of fully understanding the three natures— the imagined and so forth— or for the purpose of realizing the supremacy of practice, objective support, and attainment. [They are] those who act with perfection because they perceive even the slightest thing that is not to be known.

"How can those who have forgotten hearing the Dharma that leads to the stage of Buddhahood be performers of what is beneficial with regard to unsurpassed enlightenment? Anticipating this question, he says: "For it is because of them," and so forth.
"They will come into practice.

Because the quality of being a "person of discourse" arises from the gain of expounding discourses on the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), conceptualizations associated with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) will proceed.
In order to point out the ninth quality, that of being "indivisible," he says:
"And well-established in them," and so forth; they are established in their modes of conduct. "They cannot be divided" means: [they cannot be led astray].
By virtue of attaining the Tathāgata’s assistance, they give rise to the quality of being indivisible; thus, they cannot be divided—that is, they cannot be turned back from awakening.
"According to their inclination" means according to their aspiration for the Mahāyāna as taught in the sūtras.
"According to the mantra" means...
"The deities protect them through mantras, and the mind abides in virtue;
diseases, untimely death, and misfortune are destroyed.
Thus, because of these many benefits and the practice of mantra-conduct, some say they cannot be divided.

Others maintain that it is impossible for Māra, the Evil One, to turn them back from the *prajñāpāramitā* by any means whatsoever, whether through the power of medicinal herbs or the power of mantras.
[An objection is raised: "But since they have not attained awakening in such a short time, how can it be said that they cannot be divided?
Anticipating this question, he says: "For what reason? [and provides the following answer:]
"Yathāpi nāma," and so forth.
The meaning is that because his vigor has been cultivated for no small number of incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), there is no turning back when enlightenment is not attained immediately.
Explaining the tenth quality, the arising of uncommon roots of virtue, he says:
"And those sons of good family," and so forth.
In that context, *prīti* is the pursuit of supramundane dharmas.
"Serene confidence (prasāda) is that which rests upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
joy (prāmodya) is the purity of the mind"—this is the teaching of the Sage.
Alternatively, the explanation is exactly as stated previously.
"They shall obtain" means they will attain [it] through the acquisition of uncommon roots of virtue.
Speaking of the eleventh quality, which is the accomplishment of the truth of one's vow, he says:
"Of the many people," and so forth. [The question is:
"How do they act for the benefit of sentient beings without prior impulsion?
Anticipating this doubt with the words "For what reason?", he says:
"Thus by them," and so forth.
"Speech uttered" means that the words of the vow were articulated.

"By engaging them in the generation of the mind of great awakening (mahābodhicitta), we shall cause them to set out and show them [the path]," and so forth, has already been explained. "We shall cause them to manifest [their potential]" by setting them in motion toward the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and so forth.
[This is] because of establishing them on the seven stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā).
"We shall establish them in perfect enlightenment.
[Objection: Even in the case of verbal expression, if that object is not actually accomplished, how can there be causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*)?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For it has been rejoiced in," and so forth.
Because, having known with my own mind the purity of their intention, I, the Tathāgata, have expressed verbal approval.

Therefore, the meaning is that by obtaining the assent to their vow and through the gradual practice of its application, they bring about the fulfillment of the vow’s true purpose; thus, by the arising of this quality, they act for the benefit of all sentient beings without exception.
To state the twelfth quality, which is the quality of embracing sublime fruits, he says:
"And so, those sons of good family," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "those with noble resolve" (*udārādhimuktika*): they are called "those with noble resolve" because, through their resolute conviction in the profound and vast meaning, they embrace the noble fruit. Having thus explained the twelfth quality, [the author] now states the thirteenth quality—the excellence of practicing for the benefit of sentient beings—by means of attaining the capacity to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings: [The verse says: Having attained the power to act for the sake of beings, They always bring about the welfare of all beings. They do not seek even a little for themselves, But are intent on the great benefit of others. This is because they have attained the power to act for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, they always bring about the welfare of all beings. They do not seek even a little for themselves, but are intent on the great benefit of others. This is because they have attained the power to act for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, they always bring about the welfare of all beings. They do not seek even a little for themselves, but are intent on the great benefit of others. This is because they have attained the power to act for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, they always bring about the welfare of all beings. They do not seek even a little for themselves, but are intent on the great benefit of others. They do not seek even a little for themselves, but are intent on the great benefit of others. "In those Buddha-fields as well," and so forth.
Because he has conceived great respect through the teaching that transcends the scope of his own knowledge, he says,
"It is marvelous," and so forth.

It is a marvel that even for the Blessed One—who has abandoned all latencies of cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*) regarding phenomena such as the past—conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) still functions in accordance with his vision.
The term "as far as" (*yāvat*) indicates a limit, thereby including non-dharma and so forth.
[This] was not seen by visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*).
That which has not been heard by the auditory consciousness;
that which has not been cognized by the olfactory consciousness;
that which has not been discerned by the mental consciousness.
The phrase "there is nothing" is to be applied here.

Because of the statement that the sense faculties have the nature of the latencies of *dauṣṭhulya*, when the sense faculty—which has ignorance as its nature—is abandoned in the state of Buddhahood, there occurs a discernment of objects through the cognition of the sense faculties, just like the cognition of the mind (*manobuddhi*).

Since all cognition of the Blessed One is held to have all things as its object, there is no fault in the fact that, due to its purity, there is nothing such as the "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*) in the cognitions of the eye and so forth.
Thus, it should be understood that sensory cognition is established in accordance with what preceded it.
Demonstrating the fourteenth quality, the certainty of attainment, by way of the contrast between the mother’s non-attainment and the incomplete attainment, he says:
"And those who, at that time," and so forth.

The three phrases beginning with "anveṣamāṇānām" (of those who are searching) are to be applied to the stages such as the initial application [of the path]. Regarding what was said starting with "it is a marvel," he states that it is well said by saying "evam etat" (it is so).
This is the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, perceive everything as being like an illusion.
To refute what was asked—"What is the reason for this?"—he says:
"In that [state], moreover," and so forth.
"This was stated by the Blessed One without any logical justification.
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?", he says:
"For it is by them," and so forth.
"Even though they do not seek it, they will obtain it.

This is because, through the cultivation of application based on the possession of previously accumulated roots of merit that lead to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in its entirety, there arises the quality of attaining certainty, whereby they will indeed obtain it.
"And those others besides that" means those other sūtras, such as the *Samādhirāja*, which are distinct from that *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Regarding the phrase "by oneself":
this is stated thus because of the attainment of favorability and by virtue of the intention to express the agent as the object (*karman*).

The three words beginning with "will approach" (*upagamiṣyanti*) should be applied respectively according to the distinctions in the arising of knowledge through hearing and so forth, or according to the realization of the three natures such as the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the rest.
As before, having raised the doubt "For what reason?", he says:
"It is thus," and so forth.
This is the nature of things (*dharmatā*): that one who has not abandoned diligence in the present life seeks out the text with great care.
And as he seeks the goal, by relinquishing his own nature,
even though he has transcended birth and, by being separated from his former body, has transcended another life, yet in yet another future life—
The meaning is that even one comprised within another caste will attain [the goal] through the acquisition of the qualities of destiny (*niyati*).
Because it is the supreme state, he says:
"Only these," and so forth; "not others" means those devoid of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
"Why? is a question expressing doubt.

He says, "And all others will be reborn," because [rebirth] depends upon common roots of merit (*sādhāraṇakuśalamūla*). "And others" refers to those who are not associated with the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
As before, having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says the same thing:
"For it is thus," and so forth.
"Associated with non-apprehension" means associated with the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
"Connected with emptiness" means they fully elucidate the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya). The qualities should be understood exactly as previously described.
And so it has been said:
"The qualities consist of fourteen kinds, beginning with the destruction of the power of the Māras.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of Qualities," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The Eleventh Chapter. Following the [discussion of] qualities, what are the faults that create obstacles to application, by the avoidance of which applications are to be cultivated? To speak of those obstructive faults, he says:
"These qualities, O Blessed One," and so forth.
"Furthermore, some" means "how many indeed. He provides the answer: "Many."

Nevertheless, he says "of how many forms" because it is not known exactly how much Māra-activity there is; that is, how many, meaning how many in terms of a limited number, are there? They are numerous.
Demonstrating that there are forty-six faults, he first describes the attainment of difficulty with the words beginning "of those," namely:
"inspiration [arising] after a long time."
The arising of knowledge regarding the mother takes a long time. To express the state of possessing extremely swift eloquence, he says:
"That too," and so forth.
Because it arises so rapidly that its sequence cannot be discerned, the knowledge that is produced will become unstable and will be distracted;
thus, one falls away from the perfection of wisdom.
Speaking of the physical corruption, he says:
"Stretching their limbs," and so forth.
In that context, they are "stretching" by means of turning their bodies;
they are "laughing" by means of performing great boisterous laughter and the like.
It should be stated that they mock others by means of their own limbs or those connected to them.
Demonstrating the corruption of the mind, he says:
"With distracted minds," and so forth.
"Possessing mutual consciousness" means having a consciousness that mutually takes as its object a pleasing thing.
Pointing out the state of recitation and so forth performed improperly, he says:
"Mocking one another," and so forth.
By the phrase "they will write," study (*svādhyāya*) and other such activities are implied as well.
Stating the reasons for their aversion, he says:
"We do not find a firm footing here," and so forth.

Because it is not the object of knowledge consisting of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintāmayajñāna*), one should connect [the text] as follows: "we do not find a firm footing nor a taste," respectively.
"Not here for us" (*na no'tra*):
"not for us" (*no'smākam*).
"For as many productions of thought as they proceed with while abounding in lack of faith, for that many eons they will undergo the bondage of saṃsāra.
What is the reason for this?
Anticipating the question "Why is that?", he says:
"For this [reason]," and so forth.
He speaks in order to state the failure of the cause.
"Furthermore," and so forth.
"Productive" (*āhārikā*) means that which brings about production (*utpādikā*).
It should be stated that [this is done] by means of both the application and the intention, namely "having abandoned" and "having relinquished.
Those of "limited intelligence" (*parīttabuddhi*) are those of small intellect.
It is the "root" of the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñā*), meaning it is the primary cause for the correct awakening to the Dharma.
"Branching out" refers to the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.
Teaching the loss of the taste of excellence, he says:
"It is just as if," and so on.
"This is indeed without logical justification.
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For those of small intelligence," and so forth.
"How is it that even in the Buddha’s word, practice in the Śrāvakayāna and so forth is censured? Anticipating this question, he says: "For what reason? and so on.
"Indeed, Subhūti," and so forth.
The meaning is that one is censured for engaging in what has been prohibited.

The three terms—"we shall subdue," "we shall pacify," and "we shall lead to final nirvāṇa"—are to be understood as corresponding respectively to the paths of preparation (prayoga), seeing (darśana), and cultivation (bhāvanā).
Having refuted the practice of the śrāvakas, he speaks for the sake of the practice of the bodhisattvas, beginning with the words, "But furthermore... and "And they should not think... etc.
For the sake of all sentient beings, one should not harbor pride through the performance of any roots of virtue.
Demonstrating how one does not fall away from the supreme vehicle, he says:
"It is just as if," and so forth.
"Having obtained an elephant" means having perceived it through touch and so forth. "The light" refers to illumination. "One should contemplate" means...
One should examine it.
"Not indeed this" means that because it is impossible to grasp the color and shape [of the elephant] from the elephant's footprint, it is certainly not so.
To explain the loss of the summary, he says:
"Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, one seeking jewels," and so forth.
Due to not understanding the measure [of the teaching], one would not plunge into it.
"Certainly not! [he replied].
"Because of the loss of the great ocean containing the enumeration of jewels, he is by no means a wise man.
This is the response.
This refers to the seclusion of body and so forth.
"In this very life," and so on: without creating a cause for future rebirth in the present life, I shall withdraw my own mind from the afflictions and bring about its extinction like a lamp.

Now, one might ask: "If birth, which is the locus of all calamities, is to be ceased, how can its occurrence be prevented? Anticipating this question with the words "For those who have set out in the Mahāyāna," and so forth, he says: "For those who have set out in the Mahāyāna... [and so on].

The meaning is that because they have set out in the Mahāyāna and have donned the armor for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world, there is an absence of calamities even at the time of birth due to the power of their skill in means (*upāyakauśala*).
Regarding the phrase "in [a state of] little zeal":

One might ask: "How can contentment with just that much be prohibited, given that gain and honor are themselves bonds? Anticipating this question, he says: "For they are the leaders of the world," and so forth.
This is what was said:
"When one grasps [at gain and honor] through attachment to a self, gain and honor increase because of the growth of afflictions (*kleśa*).
However, when one wins over others through giving and so forth, and—like a lotus—remains unattached therein, acting for the sake of the world as a charioteer, then there is no fault whatsoever."
First, explaining the failure of the relationship between cause and effect, he says:
"And furthermore, those who... and so forth.
To clarify this very point, he says:
"Namely, for example," and so forth.
*Palagaṇḍa* means a carpenter;
*palagaṇḍāntevāsī* means his pupil.
Regarding the Vaijayanta palace:
in the center of the surface of Sumeru is a golden city named Sudarśana;
each of its sides measures two thousand five hundred yojanas in length.
It is one and a half *yojanas* in height.
In the center of that city is Śakra’s palace named Vaijayanta; each of its sides measures two hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length, and it is as high as is beautiful.
Regarding the phrase "desiring to make" and "desiring to construct," these two terms refer to the distinction between acting slowly and acting quickly.
"Not so," he said.

This means that it is certainly not the case, because the vimānas of the sun and moon have dimensions of fifty and fifty-one yojanas respectively, which are greater than those of Vaijayanta; thus, it indicates a reversal of cause and effect.
He speaks in order to state the downfall of one who has no further reply:
Subhūti, it is just as if someone were to say this:
therein, "color" refers to whiteness and so forth;
"shape" refers to length and so forth.
The splendor consists in the perfection of the primary marks and so forth;
supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) consists in such things as traveling through space;
and a sign (*nimitta*) is the unique characteristic of a thing.
He is incapable because his intellect has been deceived by the mere perception of similarities in color and other such qualities.

Now, one might ask: since even in the Śrāvaka vehicle there are instructions on qualities such as compassion that lead to the attainment of *tathāgata*-hood, how is it that omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) must be sought through that [vehicle]?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For [he] is indeed a bow-maker," and so forth.
Because it is not taught in all its aspects, it is taught...
The meaning is that [the Buddha] is not distinct from them.

By the loss of the three bodies—the Dharma-body, the Enjoyment-body, and the Emanation-body—there are, respectively, the analogies of a universal monarch, a meal of a hundred flavors, and a priceless jewel.
Speaking of the arising of appearances consisting of various conceptualizations of objects, he says:
Furthermore, beginning with "Moreover," and so forth;
he says "It is possible," and so forth, for the purpose of demonstrating the fourfold fault.

"It is not so" means that, in reality, it is because [the nature of things] is knowledge resembling an illusion; such is the thought. "They will think it has been written" refers to the attachment to writing.
"Or 'it is non-existent'" refers to the adherence to non-existence. Or they will adhere to the perfection of wisdom in the syllables.
Attachment to syllables;
"without syllables" means attachment to the absence of syllables is described.
Explaining the mental attention directed toward the country and so forth, he says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding the perfection of wisdom," and so on.
In that context, "country" refers to Magadha and the like.
A village consists of a single house and so forth;
a city is an abode for eighteen types of people;
a market town is a specific location where merchants predominate.
A *janapada* is a region inhabited by the four social classes (*cāturvarṇya*).
A *rāṣṭra* is a district such as Campā and others.
A *rājadhānī* is the place where kings reside.
"Ākhyāna" refers to the *Jātakamālā* and similar works. A "gulma-sthāna" is a marketplace or a place for trade; it is a specific kind of commercial establishment. A "viśikhā" is a market street.
A palanquin is a vehicle for the infirm.
The reversal of the pleasant and unpleasant refers to the separation from what is dear and the encounter with what is not dear.
"What must be done" refers to that which is to be performed constantly.
Seeing shrubs and eyes at the place of the crossroads, and seeing nooses and so forth; the remainder is not analyzed because it is easy to understand.
Demonstrating the relishing of gain, honor, and fame, he says:
Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding the passage beginning with "of the bodhisattvas," and so forth:

"the relish of gain, honor, and praise. In this context, "gain" refers to the acquisition of jewels and the like; "honor" refers to the binding of the auspicious turban and similar marks of distinction.
"Verse" (*śloka*) refers to their fame; "experience" (*anubhavana*) is the tasting (*āsvāda*).
To explain the search for skillful means regarding what is not the path, he says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti," and so forth.
Regarding the question of how one does not feel attachment toward things associated with emptiness and so forth,
he raises the doubt, "For what reason? and says,
"Moreover," and so on.
The second decade.
Thus far, these obstacles to his engagement have been explained. Now, however, the discordances prior to engagement must be stated.
He speaks for the purpose of avoiding the deficiency of zeal (*chanda*):
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the listener of the Dharma," and so forth.
"Zeal" means being endowed with aspiration.
"Afflicted with *kilāsa*" means being possessed of indolence, that is to say, lacking in vigor.
In order to explain the deficiency caused by the difference in the objects of their respective desires (*chanda*), he says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the listener of the Dharma may have desire," and so forth.
In that regard, one who understands the meaning of the subject matter is "possessed of insight" (gatimān);
one who comprehends just that much of the meaning is "possessed of intelligence" (matimān);
and one who possesses the application of wisdom is "possessed of memory" (smṛtimān).
By the phrase "it will be cast into another region," it is indicated that the teacher’s sphere of interest differs from the sphere of interest of the listener.

When "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth are mentioned, one is not "one who understands through a brief indication" (*udghaṭitajña*), because of a lack of thorough knowledge regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form.

When it is stated that "form has the characteristic of transformation" (*rūpaṇā-lakṣaṇaṃ rūpam*) and so forth, one is not "one who understands through detailed exposition" (*vipañcitajña*), because of a failure to comprehend its meaning.
One who is unlearned does not understand the meaning because of the mere recitation of such statements as "form is twofold" or "it is twentyfold.
To clarify precisely this deficiency in what has been taught, he says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Dharma-preacher... and so forth.
Because the teacher of the Dharma and the listener have different objects of desire— one wishing to give and the other wishing to go to another land—
it is for the sake of ensuring freedom from the pride of gain and from having few desires that [the Buddha] says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Dharma-preacher is one who values material things," and so forth.
By this very verse, both the application and non-application [of the ascetic qualities] are explained.

For it is taught that the non-application of the ascetic qualities (*dhūtaguṇa*) occurs through the weightiness of gains and so forth, while the application of the ascetic qualities occurs through having few desires and so forth, respectively.
He speaks [the passage] beginning with "Furthermore" for the purpose of explaining the nature of wholesome and unwholesome qualities.
In that context, one who possesses wholesome qualities is "faithful," while by the opposite of that, one is "unfaithful."
By this very explanation of the "one who takes away," both renunciation and stinginess are explained;
for thus, "desiring to give up wealth" refers to the renunciation of a disciple,
while "not desiring to speak" [refers to stinginess].
Avarice on the part of the teacher is prescribed;
by this very point, the refusal of gifts is stated.
For it has been explained that, as before, the gift belongs to the student, whereas for the teacher, non-acceptance is indicated by having few desires.
He speaks for the sake of those who understand through concise statements and those who understand through detailed explanations,
beginning with the words "Furthermore," and so forth.
"Desirous of comprehending the meaning" means:
Desiring to understand the meaning through the state of being one who understands upon hearing once;
"by way of being an obstacle to the Dharma" means by way of leading to the rejection of all dharmas.
They will not come into existence;
they will not descend in the form of books and so forth. Due to their being "those who understand through detailed exposition," they will not enter the path of awakening to that [teaching].
"Of one who has not attained the status of a Dharma-preacher" means of a Dharma-preacher who has not attained [that status]. "A counter-argument" means...
"I shall not listen" is a contrary statement;
he speaks this for the purpose of [distinguishing between] those who are proficient and those who are not proficient in the Dharma of the Sūtras and so forth.
Furthermore, "and so forth" [means]:
"desiring to speak" means desiring to speak because of his mastery of the Dharma, such as the sūtras and other teachings.

"Without desire" means being devoid of the longing to hear those very dharmas, such as the sūtras and so forth, due to a lack of familiarity with them. [This refers to one who] is not endowed with the six perfections.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with": the deeds of Māra have been described by this very same section. For, by the expression "desiring to speak," there is the endowment with the six perfections due to the intention to benefit sentient beings.

By the term "lacking desire" (*acchandika*), the absence of generosity and so forth due to a disposition toward discord is described; thus ends the third decade. Skill in means and lack of skill in means, the attainment and non-attainment of *dhāraṇīs*, and the desire to write [the scriptures].
Desiring to write [this], and demonstrating the presence or absence of desire and so forth regarding the wish to listen, beginning with the listener (*śrāvaṇika*), he says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti," and so on.

Due to being weighed down by drowsiness and the like, the listener lacks the desire to hear; thus, for the listener, the possession (*samanvāgama*) and so forth are stated as objects of negation. For the teacher (*daiśika*), however, because of the desire to speak, the possession and so forth are stated as objects of non-negation.
It should be understood that,
beginning with the teacher, he explains the very same meaning as previously stated,
saying: "Furthermore, Subhūti, the Dharma-preacher," and so forth.
He speaks for the sake of turning away from rebirth in the miserable states (*apāyagati*):
"Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding the perfection of wisdom," and so forth;
"thus, suffering," and so forth.
The hell-beings experience the sufferings of the flames of the Avīci hell and so forth; the animal realm experiences the sufferings of devouring one another and so forth;
and the hungry ghosts experience the sufferings of hunger, thirst, and so forth.
All asuras are terrified by the discus of Viṣṇu and other such weapons;
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering by their very nature (*jāti*).

Having just heard that "the end of suffering must be achieved right here," [they will]—as the remainder of the sentence implies—become averse to rebirth in the miserable states (*apāyagati*) for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings. Therefore, [the author] speaks for the purpose of inspiring joy regarding the attainment of a happy rebirth (*sugatigamana*).
Furthermore, and so forth:
therein, it is "non-eternal" (*aśāśvata*) due to the interruption of the continuum;
it is "impermanent" (*anitya*) by virtue of momentary impermanence (*kṣaṇikānityatā*).
It is suffering because it is associated with the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*);
it is subject to change because the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) arises from it.
Thus, in this way, all things are impermanent, and so forth.
It should be understood that this is an explanation of such statements as "all conditioned things are impermanent.
"They will fall into a state of agitation" means they will turn away from the conduct of awakening due to their longing for the happy realms, such as the first fruit [of the path] and so forth.
Previously, having established the listener first and the teacher afterwards for the most part, the deficiency was explained.
Now, however, having established the teacher first and the listener afterwards, the deficiency is stated again in order to make known the fixed sequence of obstacles.
In that regard, he speaks for the purpose of practicing alone, away from assemblies:
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
even those monks who are Dharma-preachers will delight in solitude."
"Even those who listen to the Dharma will come to hold the assembly in high esteem.
This was said for the purpose of ensuring that they desire to follow along and do not provide an opportunity [for others to interrupt].
"Those Dharma-preachers will speak thus," and so forth;
"they will revile" means they will pursue [them with hostility].
"And they will not give me an opportunity" means that although it has been said, "I shall give the *prajñāpāramitā*," they will not provide the occasion for its gift;
this is said because of their desire for some material thing and their unwillingness to give that [Dharma].
"And that Dharma-preacher," and so forth; "and they are not willing to give" means that the listeners of the meaning are not willing to give.
He speaks for the purpose of going in a direction that would prevent obstacles to life,
saying, "he will go by this or that way," and so forth.
"Famine" means that because food is lacking, alms are difficult to obtain.
Regarding the term *ayogakṣema*: *yoga* is the attainment of what is desired, and *kṣema* is freedom from harm. Because both of these are absent, it is called *ayogakṣema*.
Due to the cessation of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), there is an obstacle to life;
and in that particular location, there may also be an obstacle to life.
"May you go to the direction free from obstacles"—this is the ellipsis.
Thus ends the fourth decade.
He speaks for the purpose of going to and returning from a direction afflicted by famine.
"And that Dharma-preacher, them," and so forth.
"Kaccit" means "at some time.
"Nānubhaṃtsyanti" means "they will not follow."
He speaks for the purpose of traveling to and from directions disturbed by thieves and the like, beginning with the words,
"Furthermore, Subhūti," and so forth.
In that context, "creature" (*jantu*) refers to scorpions and the like.
A malignant planet is a beast of prey;
non-humans such as pretas and the like are [the dangers];
and a wilderness is a place of fear.
Reptiles are snakes; flesh-eaters are yakṣas and others who consume raw meat; "they will turn back" means they will retreat.
He speaks for the purpose of showing the dejection caused by visiting families:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a Dharma-preaching monk [may visit] the family of a friend," and so forth. He speaks for the purpose of providing a summary:
Thus, Subhūti, "Māra," and so forth.
He explains the application of the divisions of Māra by means of a question regarding the cause, beginning with:
"In this regard, Blessed One," and so on.
"Exert yourselves! means that he will make an effort to cause [others] to turn away from the Mahāyāna,
and thus he will act through various stratagems.
By means other than the methods previously described, he will strive to create obstacles.
Indicating the cause for this, he says:
"For [the Buddha] was born from the Perfection of Wisdom," and so forth.
He speaks for the purpose of introducing a counterfeit [teaching], saying:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra," and so forth. Because it conforms to another sūtra, it has come down in the sūtras.
Because it is seen in its own sūtras such as the *Arthaviniścaya*, it is included within the sūtras (*sūtraparyāpanna*).
It will cast doubt by generating uncertainty through the inclusion of sūtras that resemble the Mother [the *Prajñāpāramitā*].

Regarding the terms "those of little intelligence," "those of dull intelligence," and "those of limited intelligence," they should be understood respectively as referring to those who do not fully understand the three natures, beginning with the imagined (*parikalpita*).
Explaining that very point, he says: "blinded.
To express the production of a craving for objects that are not [truly] such, he says:
Furthermore, Subhūti, and so forth:
"He realizes the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)" means he attains the departure (*niryāṇa*) of a Śrāvaka.
Because verbal expression is necessarily produced therein by him, there are six faults.
Having indicated a certain variety of Māra’s activities, he speaks of others by way of extension:
"In this way, Subhūti, Māra... and so forth. He speaks thus, supporting what was previously stated by means of the analogy of the great jewel with many adversaries.
"Thus it is, Blessed One," and so forth.
Regarding the question of what the cause for there being many adversaries is, having raised the doubt with the words "For what reason? he says:
Namely, "because of its rarity," and so forth.
He said, "Well said," beginning with, "It is so, Subhūti," and so forth.
He says, "Even though there are many obstacles,
it is obtained solely through the power of the Tathāgata," beginning with the words,
"Moreover, Subhūti," and so forth.
"What is the reason for imagining the power of the Tathāgata?"—anticipating this question with "For what reason?", he says:
"Even Māra... and so forth.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on Mara's Deeds," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Twelfth Chapter.
Clarifying the very exertion of the Tathāgatas by means of an illustration, he says:
"It is just as if," and so forth.
"An unpleasant dwelling" means a dwelling that is not pleasant;
"disagreeable" means [the same].
He is not desired by the mind. As before, having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:
"For by this, we... and so forth.
In that regard, others too should sustain her, well-supported by someone through provisions such as food;
and they should protect her, well-guarded by means of protection provided against thieves and other dangers.
By removing physical impurities and the like, they should cherish them with great care.
From "accident" (*āpatataḥ*), such as the falling of lightning and so forth; from "calamity" (*utpātataḥ*), such as all infectious diseases and epidemics.
The occurrence of the undesired and the arising of undesirable things;
he states this as the meaning of the illustrative example.
"In the same way, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas," and so forth.
Here, only those Tathāgatas residing in this world-system are to be understood,
because he will state [this] immediately thereafter.
"Those others in other world-systems," and so forth; "they shall not create obstacles" means that,
according to the principle previously stated, they shall not commit the forty-six faults.
The phrase "they will thus fall into longing" is to be connected with what precedes.
And so it has been said:
"Six defects are to be understood, along with four sets of ten. (12)

Thus, immediately after the faults, the applications (prayoga) should be cultivated— preceded by the knowledge of their characteristics— by means of adopting the virtues and abandoning the faults according to their respective order.

Regarding the applications, their characteristic should be stated as having the nature of specific cognition and activity when understood through the instrument (*karaṇa*) case-derivation, and as having the nature of intrinsic being (*svabhāva*) when understood through the object (*karman*) case-derivation.
And so it has been said:
"That by which something is characterized is to be known as the characteristic (lakṣaṇa), and that is threefold:
cognition (jñāna), the specific attribute (viśeṣa), the activity (kāritra), and the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) which is characterized. (13)

In that regard, first, explaining the knowledge characterized by wisdom—which is divided according to the three types of omniscience—by way of the door of omniscience, he says, "For thus, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas," and so forth. [An opponent objects: "This is indeed without logical justification."
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?", he says:
"For this [is]... and so forth.
In that regard, she is the mother because she gives birth.
She is the mother because she nurtures;
she is the revealer of omniscience because she brings it forth;
and she is the one who shows the way to the world by making known [reality] through forms such as emptiness.
In this regard, some of our own colleagues raise the following objection:

"If, conventionally, the entire circle of objects of knowledge is pervaded by a single momentary cognition occurring simultaneously, then the infinity of things— which is established through the determination of their finite measure— would be contradicted."
For in this way, when it is determined that there is no entity other than the one already mounted upon a single cognition, how could [all entities] not be finite?
This argument is without substance.
If this objection is raised on the basis of assuming a cognition devoid of mental images (*nirākāra-vijñāna*), [then the following applies].
Then everything becomes inconsistent.

For instance, whatever collection of things experiences existence, all of that is designated as being "pervaded" by the omniscient consciousness because it is delimited by that consciousness through its mere existence.
However, this is not because they are pervaded by others due to the lack of spatial limits;

nor does the mere fact that things are delimited by a single cognition entail a loss of their own intrinsic nature (*ātmasvabhāva*), such that they would abandon their infinite nature simply by virtue of being delimited by a single cognition.

For many entities, such as blue, yellow, and so forth, which exist simultaneously in a variegated carpet or the like, do not lose their nature even while their forms are determined in a single moment of cognition.
They do not abandon their individuality, nor do they mutually permeate one another;
rather, they are delimited by knowledge exactly as they exist.
Not in any other form;
likewise, the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world is apprehended by the mind of the Omniscient One exactly as it experiences its own existence.
Since the world of beings and so forth is situated without limit in the cardinal and intermediate directions, it is apprehended precisely as being limitless, and not as having a boundary;
how, then, could there be the consequence of its being finite?
It might be argued: "If the apprehension of the whole is admitted, how could there not be an apprehension of the limit?
This is not so.
For what is the necessary connection here that wherever there is a grasping of the totality, there must necessarily be a grasping of the limit?
To explain: among all those existing things, not even a single one exists whose nature is known by the cognition of an omniscient being.
Rather, all [dharmas] indeed arise and perish only as their true natures are known by the mind of the Omniscient One;
not even a single one is excluded—this is the meaning of the term "all.
And this alone constitutes their pervasion by a single cognition.

Otherwise, one would have to deny that they are even denotable by all words, lest there be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of their being finite; thus, this [objection] is trivial. As it has been said: "Since there is no entity other than that which is mounted upon a single cognition, how could they not be finite due to such a delimitation?"
That too is incorrect;

for in the position of those who maintain that cognition is formless (*nirākārajñānavāda*), there is no superimposition of objects upon the nature of cognition; rather, they are known by it through its mere existence.
Nor is infinity accepted on the grounds that things possess a nature incapable of being delimited by cognition,
such that their finitude would follow from the fact of their being known.

However, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is infinite because its spatial extension is limitless; the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), moreover, is infinite even in terms of its numerical extent.
Nor is there any contradiction with its being an object of cognition simply because it lacks spatial limits and so forth, such that it would follow that it is not an object of cognition.

If it is asked, "If he does not grasp it as having limits, how can he be omniscient?"—it is for this very reason that he is omniscient; precisely because he does not grasp it as having limits, he is omniscient. Otherwise, by grasping infinite reality as finite, he would be mistaken.
For instance, one who perceives what exists as existing and what does not exist as non-existing is called "all-knowing.
Now, there is no limit to the world of sentient beings and the receptacle-world;
therefore, one who perceives the absence of a limit produced by movement as being indeed non-existent is [all-knowing].
However, seeing that the limit established by the cognition of the Omniscient One actually exists as something existing, how could he not be called omniscient?

On the view that cognition is formless (*nirākāra-jñāna*), the apprehension of objects is untenable because such cognition is indistinguishable in all cases; therefore, the distinction between one object and another would be impossible through it.
Thus, the position of formless cognition—
"It should never even be proposed as an example because it is defective"—
this too is incorrect;
for a distinction according to specific objects (pratikarmavibhāga) is not admitted in the case of the knowledge of an omniscient being.
Because that [consciousness] has all things as its object;
for it is not accepted that it is the cognition of blue alone or yellow alone, but rather of everything.

For one of limited vision whose knowledge—according to the position of formless (nirākāra) cognition—grasps a restricted range of objects, the fault is stated to be the impossibility of a distinction between individual cognitions, since there is no difference [in the cognition] regarding all [objects].

For, because there would be no restriction such that "this is the cognition of blue" and not "the cognition of yellow," it would entail the absurd consequence that every ordinary person is omniscient.
But for the Omniscient One, that is precisely what is desired;
so what undesirable consequence could possibly accrue to him?
Therefore, its arising in a formless state through the power of yoga during the stage of omniscience is entirely uncontradicted.
If it is argued that there would be no thorough knowledge of things to be abandoned and things to be adopted through differentiation,

that too is not so; for if, when infinite objects appear simultaneously, there were a contradiction in the appearance of the things to be abandoned and the things to be adopted— or if there were no such contradiction— then [the objection would hold].
For that object of reality, which appears together with other things, there would either be a loss of its true nature, or even if its nature were not lost, it would not appear as differentiated; or,
even if it appeared as differentiated, if no subsequent determinative cognition— either pure worldly perception or reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— were produced, [it would remain unmanifest].
All this could indeed be said;
however, while the entire universe is manifesting, even that object which is to be rejected or accepted appears as something distinct,
with its own essential nature unimpaired and its manifestation uncontradicted.
Subsequently, it is indeed determined by a pure worldly reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśa-pratyaya*) produced through the power of the omniscient knowledge (*sarvajña-jñāna*).
How, then, can there be said to be a lack of full comprehension of that [object] through its distinctions?
Thus, it has been demonstrated that this objection does not apply to the position of formless cognition (*nirākāra-jñāna*).
Now, an objection is raised against the position of those who maintain that cognition possesses a form (sākārajñānavāda).
Even in that case, there is no contradiction;
for just as that infinite object, accompanied by infinite forms, experiences its own existence, [so too does cognition].
In the same way, that omniscient consciousness, being produced by apprehending the forms of infinite objects, is entirely uncontradicted;
for there is no contradiction in a single cognition being produced through the apprehension of the forms of multiple objects.
If it is argued that for a single entity to possess multiple forms is a contradiction, we say no;
because those forms are unreal. For if the forms of a single entity were ultimately real, then there would indeed be a contradiction in its being manifold.
Since it is accepted that the mental aspects (ākāra) are indeed unreal,
if it is argued that [the Omniscient One] would thus be deluded because he possesses deluded cognition, we say: no.
There is no fault here because of thorough knowledge according to reality (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*).
For if one were to grasp what is unreal as being real, then one would be deluded;
however, when one knows unreal aspects precisely as being unreal, [there is no error].
In that case, how could it be erroneous?

If it is argued: "When one grasps a form mounted upon a cognition distinct from the object, yet engages in worldly transactions such as 'seen' with respect to objects, how can this be non-erroneous? We reply: No, because of the thorough knowledge of the correct means.
For if one were to abandon the appropriate means of apprehension and grasp an object by means of another, non-primary method, then one would be mistaken.

However, in the position of those who maintain that cognition possesses a form (sākārajñānavāda), there is no operation for the apprehension of an object other than the experience of the cognition’s own internal form.
Therefore, how could one who perceives an object through a cognitive operation characterized by the appropriate distinction of its objective attributes be deluded?

Consequently, just as with the objects of knowledge, it is said that an infinite reality is pervaded by that single cognition, because the cognition arises by assuming the forms residing in infinite things.
And in whatever manner entities ascend into the nature of the cognition, [in that very manner they are known].
Alternatively, they are determined by that very subsequent reflective consciousness (*parāmarśacetas*) following it.
However, in the mind of an omniscient one, entities do not ascend as being followed by limited distinctions;
rather, whatever degree of existence there is, all of that indeed ascends [into his cognition].
Because the capacity [of the mind] to produce the knowledge of an omniscient one is unimpeded with respect to its status as an objective support for everything,
and because mental consciousness has all objects as its domain;
therefore, it is impossible for an omniscient mind to apprehend only a limited number of things and their forms.

Alternatively, by means of the subsequent attainment—the pure mundane cognition of reflective awareness—there can be no delimitation such as "how much is this? because it does not function as a circumscription limited to a specific spatial extent; for if there were such a delimitation, there would be finitude.
Even if a reflective awareness were to arise in the form, "there is nothing other than what appears," still, the consequence of finitude does not follow.
For instance, if that which appears [to cognition] were to appear as having an end within the non-conceptual mind of the Omniscient One,
then the finitude of entities would be determined by the subsequent reflective cognition (*parāmarśacetas*) obtained after that [non-conceptual perception].
Furthermore, by the exclusion of that [limit], infinity would be lost;
for whatever object appears in the mind of an omniscient being must appear as infinite,
since his power is entirely unimpeded.

Therefore, that which does not appear as something other than that [object] is indeed finite, and its exclusion is performed by the mind of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa-cetas*); thus, you have all the more established the finitude of entities—this argument is quite trivial.

Furthermore, for those who maintain that all yogic cognition is without an external object (*anālambana*) and is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory with reality like a true dream-vision, the objection regarding finitude has no room at all.

It might be argued: "In the treatise, the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of yogins is described as having only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, and not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, how can yogins perceive the very intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) of entities through a cognition that has only the universal as its object?"

For that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), when excluded from what is of a different class, is called a "universal characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) in the treatises because it serves as the cause for a cognition of a non-differentiated form.

Therefore, it is not contradictory that the yogic cognition apprehending it—which arises with a clear manifestation through the power of meditative cultivation—has only the particular characteristic as its object.
[Objection: How can that which has a universal as its object be an apprehender of the particular characteristic?
If it is asked how mutually contradictory things can be apprehended by a single cognition, it is replied:
although some entities are mutually contradictory, they are nonetheless not contradictory with respect to cognition;
for it is observed that even by a single cognition, multiple contradictory objects are apprehended simultaneously.
For instance, it is contradictory for those things whose defining characteristics exist through mutual exclusion to possess identity;
however, it is contradictory for those things that cannot coexist to occupy the same location.
Yet, because these [aspects] appear within a single cognition, neither their identity nor their occupation of the same location follows as a logical consequence.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in their appearing within a single cognition. Indeed, it is observed that even things that are contradictory appear in a single cognition;

for example, the simultaneous apprehension by visual consciousness of both the pure and the impure, which are characterized by mutual exclusion, as well as the simultaneous grasping of a snake and a peacock, which cannot coexist.
This might be so:
if even contradictory things can appear within a single cognition without contradiction,
then why does the experience of pleasure and pain, or of attachment and aversion, not arise together within a single cognition in the mental continuum of living beings?

That pleasure and the rest are not perceived simultaneously should be understood as being due to their non-arising because of the absence of their causes and thus their non-proximity, and not because of any mutual contradiction.
Furthermore, how past and future objects are apprehended has already been explained previously.

Alternatively, the apprehension of the past and the future occurs precisely through the apprehension of the present, which—either directly or indirectly—possesses the nature of being assisted by or assisting them.
Just as the non-existence of a jar or similar object is understood precisely through the perception of a bare ground, so too [is the Blessed One perceived].
Furthermore, it is not the case that the Blessed One is known through inference, because there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*);
for both [the Blessed One and his qualities] are objects of direct perception, since he exists in the present, endowed with all his specific attributes. Enough of this digression.
Clarifying her status as a progenitor, he says:
"For she has issued forth from this," and so forth.
