Thus, by being a progenitor herself, she is the one who demonstrates omniscience and is the very one who brings about the realization of omniscience.
Demonstrating knowledge of the world, he says:
"That which the Blessed One has spoken thus," and so forth;
[namely,] "they are not broken, they are not destroyed."
The meaning is that, by virtue of momentary impermanence (*kṣaṇika-anityatā*) and continuous impermanence (*prabandha-anityatā*), respectively, they do not perish and do not come to ruin.
Since these are the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the characteristics of things (*vastudharma*), one might ask: how is it that those two [destruction and ruin] do not occur?
To this he says: "Why is it that they are not broken and not utterly destroyed? [The reason is as follows:]...
"Because they have emptiness as their intrinsic nature," and so forth.
Since, in reality, they lack an intrinsic nature,
when the aggregates— by virtue of being empty and so on— lack the intrinsic nature of functional entities (*vastu-dharma*), momentariness and the impermanence of the continuum do not exist.
The intention is that they exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*).
In order to indicate the knowledge of the mental activities of all sentient beings, he says:
"Furthermore," and so forth.
In order to support the point he has asserted, he asks by saying, "And how, Subhūti," and so forth. To provide the answer, he says:
"By way of the lack of intrinsic nature of sentient beings," and so forth.
Because sentient beings have an illusory-like nature, there is a thorough knowledge [of them] in the form of being immeasurable and so on. Concluding, he says:
"Thus, Subhūti," and so forth.
By this very method, there is a thorough knowledge of their mental activities;
thus he says, "And those which... and so forth.
"By way of the non-existence of sentient beings" means that,
because sentient beings— meaning their actual existence— are not perceived in reality, they have the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
He understands the mental conducts of sentient beings by way of their forms as objects of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth.
Speaking of the knowledge of the contraction of the mind, he says: "contracted minds," and so on.
"He [knows] that contraction is from destruction, and destruction is from non-destruction.
By means of that object, the mind that has entered into the true nature (*dharmatā*) knows contraction as destruction—that is, as perishing—from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
He also knows destruction, which is perishing, as belonging to that which is perishable.
Because of its existence, he understands it as ultimately imperishable and undestructible, just as it truly is.
To explain the knowledge of mental distraction, he says:
"Scattered minds," and so forth.

"From the nature of phenomena" (dharmatā) means that because the dharmadhātu is non-arising, those minds which function outwardly due to a lack of mental attention toward it are scattered from the perspective of conventional truth.

Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he understands as it truly is that characteristics are without defining marks (*alakṣaṇa*) because they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they are not exhausted by way of the impermanence of characteristics because their continuity does not cease; and they are undistracted because there is no possibility of going outward. To explain the knowledge of the aspect of the non-exhaustion of the mind, he says:
"Immeasurable and inexhaustible minds," and so forth.

"Empowered" means that by means of great compassion, that mind is empowered throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Because it is, as appropriate, devoid of the three conditioned characteristics, it is unceasing, unarisen, and non-abiding; therefore, because it cannot be associated with the nature of a substratum (*dharmin*), it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because it is impossible to measure, it is immeasurable; because its destruction is untenable, like the *dharmadhātu*, it is inexhaustible.

By means of such a mind, the Tathāgata—through the immeasurability and inexhaustibility that are like space—perceives, as they truly are, the immeasurability and inexhaustibility of the minds of all sentient beings, as they appear upon the surface of the mirror of his own samādhi.
Speaking of the knowledge that cognizes minds possessed of passion and so forth, he says:
"Defiled minds," and so forth; "defiled by non-defilement," because they exist as mere delusion.
By means of the afflictions characterized by defilement, karma, and birth— which in reality are not afflictions—
they are defiled and impaired through the power of error;
thus they are "non-conventional."
Their functions are not fixed.
Explaining the knowledge of minds free from passion and so forth, he says:
"minds that are undefiled," and so on.

"By nature luminous" means that although minds are of such a nature even during the stage of an ordinary person— because they are produced from causes of impure error— they are nonetheless, due to their lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), destined for the realization of a self whose form consists of non-arising and so forth as established by valid cognition;
and because they are not subject to reversal even through the arising of antidotes, they possess the assistance of passion and other afflictions that are capable of being removed.
The luminous [states] consist solely of their own perfectly pure intrinsic nature.

Having generally indicated the mind with passion and so forth, as well as the mind free from passion and so forth, he speaks first of one section beginning with "sunk minds" (*līnāni cittāni*) in order to explain the means for those states in due order,
and secondly of the section beginning with "exerted minds" (*pragṛhītāni cittāni*).
"Hidden in the non-abode" means that they are hidden—
that is, adhered to— by way of being causes for passion and so forth within the non-abode, which is unfit to be a locus, such as the relishing of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
"Subhūti, those minds are ungraspable; they are not to be grasped.
In that regard, a mind that is excited or suspected of being excited should be calmed by means of the sign of tranquility through mental attention to an object that inspires spiritual urgency.
A mind that is sunken or suspected of being sunken should be uplifted by means of the sign of exertion through mental attention to an object that inspires joy.

The mind that has attained equanimity is grasped by means of effortless mental attention (*anābhoga-manaskāra*) and the sign of equanimity (*upekṣā-nimitta*); thus, the minds are firmly held as causes for dispassion and so forth.
Furthermore, because they no longer require further grasping, they are not to be grasped;
they are not to be further exerted.

Speaking generally of the synonyms for those very two—mind and knowledge—he further states another explanatory passage in their respective order, beginning with "the minds that are with outflows," etc., saying:
"Subhūti, those minds are without intrinsic nature; they are non-existent conceptualizations."
Defiled minds, because they are to be turned back through the arising of their antidotes, lack an inherent nature of their own;
therefore, they are equivalent to non-existence.
Subhūti, those minds have reached the state of non-being.
"Effortless" means that the untainted minds culminate in the absence of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
and because they proceed as a naturally pure continuum by their own inherent force, they are effortless.
To further explain the distinction between these two, he states the [six] "extracts" (hāraka) beginning with "six are with passion" (*sarāga*), and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "that which is the state of passion of the mind":

that state of passion of the mind, which consists of attachment to sense objects and the like, does not—according to the correct principle—constitute the mind’s suchness (*yathābhūtatā*), which is by nature self-luminous and like an illusion.
Because these two are, respectively, of a mobile and immobile nature by virtue of being removable or unremovable;

likewise, that state of the mind as it truly is—which is the uncontaminated state for the noble ones through the cultivation of the antidote—is not "with attachment," because it is the very nature of that antidote.
Therefore, in the impure state, minds are "with attachment" only conventionally.
"O Subhūti, that which is the departure of the mind," and so forth:

that which is the departure of the mind— the state of freedom from passion— is not the passionate state of the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), because those two states, characterized by passion and its absence, are of different natures.

Likewise, that state of being as-it-is (yathābhūtatā) of a mind whose passion has been abandoned through the abandonment [of defilements] by means of suppression and so forth, which is the self-cognition of that [mind] as isolated from [passion], is not a state of passion in the mind.
Therefore, in the state of isolation, minds are free from passion.
Following this principle, the text should be explained with respect to the remaining [categories] such as "with hatred" and so on.
To explain the knowledge of the vast mind, he speaks two strings of pearls by way of positive and negative concomitance:
"O Subhūti, those minds are without the yoga of origination; they are not included within the sphere of origination," and so forth.
Because they do not arise in reality, they are devoid of connection with causes and thus lack the nature of origination.

Because they are free from manifestation and are unimpeded within the realms of desire and so forth, they are included among those things that do not originate; thus, due to their non-apprehension, they are not extensive.
"They do not diminish," and so forth.
Because there is no destruction, they do not diminish;
because there is no arising, they do not increase.
For this very reason, because there is no departure due to the absence of going anywhere, they do not go at all; thus, by virtue of the intrinsic nature of the *dharmadhātu*, these minds are vast.
In order to explain the ignorance regarding the vast mind (*mahadgata-citta*), he states two "ornaments" (*hāra*) by way of negative and positive concomitance:
"Those minds, Subhūti, are not coming, they have no going, and they are not included [within categories]" (*anāgatikāni... agatikāni... aparyāpannāni*).
Because the existence of the effect [in the cause] has been refuted, and because there is an absence of its arrival from the past time-path, thoughts are "without coming.
Because they perish in their entirety, movement toward the future time is impossible; thus, they are "without going."

Even in the present, because they are devoid of a nature that is either one or many, these minds are indeed unconditioned and thus immeasurable. Subhūti, those minds are equal through their equality; they are equal by virtue of their own intrinsic nature.
Because they are, in reality, of the nature of non-arising, minds are equal through their equality with the lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) of the self and so forth;

yet, because they appear in the form of bringing about all virtuous qualities according to conventional truth (tathyasaṃvṛti), they are thus "great" in being equal to the nature of illusion (māyāsvabhāva).
Describing the knowledge of immeasurable minds, he says:
"Immeasurable minds," and so forth. "Because they lack a fixed basis": for there exists no specifically determined basis for them; thus, they are immeasurable.
Establishing the knowledge of the non-demonstrable mind, he speaks of the two types of holders as before:
"Subhūti, those minds are with demonstration," and so forth;
"those minds, Subhūti, are equal demonstrations, for they have the nature of mind."
All cognitions are equal in vision because they are self-cognized as being like an illusion; they have the nature of perceiving that which is equivalent [to the object].

Because they are accumulated by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the wholesome and unwholesome, they have the intrinsic nature of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*); thus, having the form of accumulated latencies, they are "with demonstration" (*sanidarśana*).
This is because they are without defining characteristics (*alakṣaṇatvāt*), and so forth.

In reality, because it lacks a present nature and is thus uncharacterized (*alakṣaṇa*), and because its causal relationship with the past and future forms is logically untenable in sequence, and because it is devoid of objective referents (*arthavivikta*)—being beyond the range of the three types of vision beginning with the "fleshly" eye, or indeed all five—it is invisible, having reached a state of non-manifestation. Thus, the mind is "unindicatable. Demonstrating that such knowledge, as previously described, is in some sense said to be "reversed" by virtue of being non-obstructive (*apratighātitva*), [the author] states eight verses beginning with "minds that are obstructive" (*sapratighāni cittāni*).
"Conceived of as non-existent," and so forth.

Minds that are conceived of— meaning superimposed— by means of what is non-existent (asat), namely by way of arising and so forth, are empty, devoid of intrinsic nature, and dependent upon objective referents (ālambana).
Conventionally, these are dependent upon objects; thus, because they are sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they possess resistance (*sapratigha*).
"Non-dual" and so forth:
they are non-dual by virtue of being devoid of both arising and non-arising.

In reality there is only non-existence, yet through conventional truth there is existence; thus, things that have arisen from what was unreal are non-obstructive because they are established by valid cognition.

"That which, Subhūti, belongs to one who has something superior," and so forth: for a mind that has fallen into an inferior state due to attachment to a self and so on, that which is its suchness—the realization of selflessness—therein exists no conceiving or apprehension of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, in this way, they are "surpassable" according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
For [it is said] "even the slightest," and so forth;
because, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), [they are not].
Not even an atom’s worth of mind is perceived as having the nature of a real entity;

therefore, just as in the state of Buddhahood, in the state of an ordinary person as well, because all signs such as form have departed by virtue of the naturally pure intrinsic nature, minds are thus in reality non-conceptual and unsurpassed.

Regarding the passage beginning with "asamasamāni hi" (for they are equal to the unequaled): because of the inequality caused by defects such as arising (*utpāda*), the minds that function as the apprehenders of an unequaled object are "unequilibrated" (*asama*) due to being distracted and lacking meditative composure (*asamāhita*). Thus, those which are unequilibrated are [described as] "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasamāni*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "samasamāni hi": since no inequality of defects is possible, the *dharmadhātu* is "equal" (*sama*); and because they are identical to it in terms of non-arising and so forth, they are "equal" (*samāni*).
They are composed by virtue of having provided an antidote to distraction;
they are composed as being equal to space because their intrinsic nature does not exist in reality;
thus, they are "liberated by nature," and so forth.

Because they are devoid of birth following from logic (*nyāya*), minds are liberated by their very nature; because their form as existing entities does not exist, they have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.
Consequently, since there is no liberation preceded by the removal of bondage, minds are unliberated.
"For the mind," and so forth.
Since the Tathāgata has not apprehended the mind of the three times because it is non-existent due to its lack of a nature that is either one or many,
it is therefore liberated by nature through the removal of the two kinds of obscurations.
Having thus explained the classification, he speaks in order to describe the knowledge of the mind:
"Mind-states are invisible," and so forth.
Subhūti, it is "invisible because of non-existence.
Because it is devoid of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatva*), the imagined mind (*kalpita-citta*) is invisible due to its non-existence.
The dependent nature (*paratantra*) is unknowable because it is non-existent due to the absence of a cause.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is ungraspable because it is not fully established due to its own-form being non-existent.
Each of these is to be connected individually with the three, beginning with the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
Or, because it does not fall within the range of illumination of the five [faculties], such as the Buddha-eye and so forth, it should be understood as being "invisible" and so on.
For in this way, Subhūti, the phrase "perfection of wisdom" serves as a concluding statement at the end of the section concerning the knowledge that brings about the concentrated mind and so forth.
Each [term] should be connected individually.
Speaking of the knowledge of the mind’s opening and so forth, he says:
"The openings and closings," and so on.
In this context, that extension of the mind toward its own object by way of affirmation is *unmiñja*;
the withdrawal of the mind from other objects by way of negation is *nimiñja*.
Because they arise from that [mind], they are called "opening" and "closing.
The two terms "of other beings" and "of other persons" are stated because of the distinction between worldly and supramundane renown.
[The passage begins with] "dependent upon form," and so forth.
The meaning is that all mental states indeed arise based on the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, by way of both affirmation and negation.
Explaining this very point, he says: "Does the Tathāgata exist," and so forth.
"Does the Tathāgata exist after death?"— this question is asked because of the doubt arising from the fact that he remains in an invisible form.
[This refers to] the view of the Sāṃkhyas and others regarding the nature of form and so forth.
The "opened" conceptualization (*unmiñjita-vikalpa*) belongs to the Lokāyatikas,
who hold that [the self] does not exist because it perishes entirely without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-vināśa*).

The "closed" conceptualization (*nimiñjita-vikalpa*) belongs to the Digambaras and others, who hold both views— that it exists and that it does not exist— because the substratum (*avasthātṛ*) is one while its states (*avasthā*) are distinct, thus [the self] both exists and does not exist as previously described.

Because it cannot be described as being either identical to or different from [the aggregates], the conceptual construction of the Pudgalavādins— which is based on the negation of both "it exists" and "it does not exist"— does not apply. Furthermore, since these conceptual constructions are ultimately unarisen, they do not find any foothold whatsoever in the Tathāgata, whose nature is the unreal conventional self.
Likewise, in the teaching on emptiness, certain points—
such as "the self is eternal" and so forth— are established in other sections as questions to be set aside (*avyākṛta*), with respect to those persons who are not yet ready for instruction.
They are to be spoken of.

Within that circle of the assembly, the adoption of these various distinctions is made solely in accordance with the dispositions of the disciples present, who are possessed of self-views of the types previously described.
He speaks in order to explain the knowledge of the aspect of suchness (*tathatākārajñāna*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding the passage beginning with "the Tathāgata":
Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows form in such a way that it is "thusness" (tathatā).
"That which is dependent origination, that very thing you consider to be emptiness.

This means that because the aggregates, such as form and so forth, are thoroughly understood through their aspect of suchness (*tathatā*), there is likewise a thorough understanding of suchness regarding [the states of] opening the eyes and so on.
And speaking of the Perfectly Enlightened One’s knowledge of awakening to suchness, his supreme explanation, and his designation, he says:
"For in this way, Subhūti, by means of the suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of the aggregates," and so forth.
"He designates suchness" means that he establishes the suchness which follows after all phenomena in a single form; by this, the knowledge of designating suchness is explained.
He states that very point with the words beginning "And that which is perceived," etc.
Now, one might ask: if it is distinct from the substratum (dharmin), how can there be non-difference of suchness (tathatā)?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For it has been said," and so forth;
because the five aggregates are the world, and so on.
"It is designated and reckoned" was stated by the Blessed One in the section on the teaching of all phenomena through the five aggregates.
Therefore, the world is not distinct from that which is characterized as impermanent and so forth.
It was stated as having distinct subjects merely with regard to the practice of those to be trained who were present;
in order to explain that very point, he says:
"Therefore, then," and so forth.
"Free from manifold existence and non-existence," and so forth.
Because it is, in reality, of the nature of non-arising, it transcends the characteristics of entities; thus, it is neither unity nor multiplicity.
In the form of emptiness, this single suchness pervades all phenomena, [arising] from the manifold existence of things such as pots and cloths.
It is free from non-existence characterized by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*);
likewise on the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), special advancement (*viśeṣamārga*), and final consummation (*niṣṭhāmārga*).
It should be applied thus: because it is inexhaustible, because it is unchanging, and because it is non-dual, this suchness (*tathatā*) is one alone, in due order.
By the phrase "having attained perfect enlightenment by relying on the perfection of wisdom," the knowledge that realizes suchness is indicated. [The sūtra says: "He shows the world to the world."
To the world that clings to the existence of phenomena, he declares the world to be like an illusion.
By perceiving the imagined, dependent, and perfected natures as being like an illusion, he knows suchness in its proper order;
he knows it as non-erroneous suchness.
One knows non-other suchness (*ananyatathatā*).
These three terms should be stated.
By the phrase "having fully awakened to suchness, one is called a Tathāgata," the thorough comprehension of suchness is indicated.
"Who else here, Blessed One, would have faith?
[The Buddha replied: "No one at all—neither those of indeterminate lineage nor others—would have faith."
What then? He says that the person (*pudgala*) is indeed distinguished, beginning with "irreversible" (*avinivartanīya*), and so forth. These are called "fully awakened."
By this, the knowledge that designates suchness (tathatā) has been indicated.
It is described as "indestructible" because of the statement:
"Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena remains constant"; thus, suchness is indestructible.
It is indicated as being characterized by exhaustion.
Thus, by unifying the four types of knowledge beginning with the realization of suchness, the characteristic of knowledge—subsumed under omniscience—is shown to be of sixteen kinds.
And so it has been said:

Likewise, regarding the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the world's nature of being subject to dissolution, the mental activities of sentient beings, their contraction, and their outward wandering; (14)

And in the state of inexhaustible aspects, in that which is pervasive regarding those with passion and so forth, in the great, in the immeasurable, and in consciousness that is non-demonstrable; ||15||
And regarding the knowledge of the invisible mind, there is that which is designated as "opening" (unmiñja) and so forth;
thereafter follows the knowledge of those [minds] by way of their suchness (tathatā). //16//
"This exposition of the Sage’s awakening regarding suchness is the summary of the characteristics of knowledge by way of the section on omniscience. (17) Thus,
immediately following that, he speaks in order to explain the characteristics of knowledge by way of the section on the knowledge of the path:
Then indeed, headed by Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and so forth:
"O Blessed One, how are the characteristics established here?"—
in what manner are the characteristics of knowledge being pointed out within the section on the Knowledge of the Path?
"Empty," and so forth.
The eight cognitions—of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, non-purification, and non-existence—are stated by their own respective names.
The cognition of intrinsic nature is *nirvāṇa*.
Non-reliant gnosis is the *dharmadhātu*;
gnosis characterized by space is *tathatā*.
Thus, these three types of gnosis are established; yet, this [establishment] is without logical justification.
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because these, characterized by knowledge, are indeed non-dependent," and so forth; because, in reality, these...
Because they have the nature of non-arising, they are not bound to anything; therefore, their intrinsic nature is as previously described—this is the meaning of the sentence.
He speaks thus for the purpose of not disturbing the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"These are not characteristics," and so forth.
"To shake" means to disturb.
Having raised the doubt, "Why is that exactly so?", he says:
"Even including the worlds of gods, humans, and asuras," and so forth.
"Precisely characterized by this" means that its intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-svabhāva*) is like an unshakable illusion.
He says this for the sake of understanding non-conditioned phenomena (*asaṃskāra*):
"Nor have these characteristics been established by any hand.
The meaning is that it is precisely because entities are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
In order to explain non-conceptual knowledge (*avikalpajñāna*), he says:
"O sons of the gods," and so forth.
[The question is: "How is it not established as being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?"
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because it is unconditioned.
This means because it does not arise from causes and conditions.
In order to explain the knowledge of their distinctions, he says:
"Then, O Blessed One, those [teachings], etc.
[The question arises: since they were revealed by the Tathāgata, how could they have existed previously?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Just as these [are] eternal," and so forth.
"They have been explained."
The phrase "by way of distinctions such as emptiness" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Speaking of the knowledge of the absence of characteristics, he says:
"O Blessed One, they are profound," and so forth.

"Unattached gnosis" (*asaṅgajñāna*) refers to that which is free from all clinging, the gnosis of the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇajñāna*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) in its perfected state— that is, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) of the Buddhas.
This very point is expressed by the words beginning with "for the sake of unattached gnosis."
Furthermore, when being cultivated for the sake of unimpeded knowledge during the stage of non-attainment, the perfection of wisdom becomes the object of the Tathāgatas’ knowledge in all its aspects;
thus it is said to be "the one who reveals this world.
It reveals the world because, through the sixteen types of knowledge of the knowledge of paths as previously described, it brings about the direct realization of the reality of the world.
And so it has been said:
"In emptiness and the signless, in that which is devoid of aspiration, in non-arising, non-ceasing, and so forth, and in the unshakeable nature of phenomena (dharmatā). (18)
"In the absence of formative activity and conceptualization, and in the states of differentiation and the lack of characteristics—
under the heading of the Knowledge of the Path, the characteristic of knowledge is intended.
Thus, immediately following that, he speaks for the sake of the characteristic of knowledge by way of the Knowledge of All Aspects:
"Just as, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas... and so forth.
In that context, speaking of the knowledge based upon one's own dharma of the Perfectly Enlightened One, he says:
"This dharma, the Perfection of Wisdom," and so forth.
"By way of non-abiding" means by way of non-attachment.
"They dwell" means they dwell having brought face-to-face the realized meaning for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
He speaks [the following] in order to explain honor (*satkāra*), respect (*gurukāra*), reverence (*mānanā*), worship (*pūjanā*), and obedience (*ājñā*):
"Venerating the Dharma," and so forth.
He explains the meaning of "worshipping" by distinguishing between the stages of preparation (*prayoga*) and completion (*pṛṣṭha*).
Having indicated it generally as "honoring" (*arcayanti*) and "revering" (*apacāyanti*), he speaks for the sake of specific detail:
"Only the perfection of wisdom," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt, "What is the basis for making this distinction?", he says: "For what reason? (tatkasya hetoḥ).
"Therefore, Subhūti," and so forth. In that context, they are "grateful" (*kṛtajña*) because of performing a return favor; they are "thankful" (*kṛtavedin*).
Because even a small benefit is remembered due to its great significance;
"vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to the Mahāyāna, which is the path consisting of the stages of realization, vision, and so forth.
It "graciously assists."
"He protects [them] continuously" means that he praises those two respectively.
To express the knowledge of the unconditioned (*akṛtaka*), he says:
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is said by the Tathāgata, and so forth:
therein, they are uncreated because of the non-existence of a cause of production;
they are unmodified because of the absence of a cause of destruction.
Because they are devoid of the nature of the conditioned, they are unconditioned.
Speaking of the all-pervading gnosis, he says:
"For the perfection of wisdom," and so forth.
Thus, knowledge has proceeded with respect to all phenomena.
Knowledge has arisen through the realization of their being uncreated and so forth.
To the question, "If things are in reality unarisen, how can there be the seen, the seer, and the act of seeing? he says:
"O Blessed One, when... and so forth.
In that regard, they are "without knowledge" because there is no discernment by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
they are "without seeing" because there is an absence of apprehension by means of the visual and other sensory consciousnesses (*cakṣurādivijñāna*).
He states that this is merely a statement lacking logical justification, beginning with the words "And how? and so forth.

Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty because they lack production in reality, and since they are non-dependent because the relationship between apprehended object and apprehending subject is untenable, the meaning is that they are neither knowers nor seers.
And by relying on the perfection of wisdom, through the awakening to dharmas of such a nature, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), non-seeing itself is seeing for the world;
however, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtyā*), it is exactly as it is commonly perceived—this is the intended meaning.
Pointing out the knowledge that reveals objects not previously seen, he says:
"Because form is not seen," and so forth.
The meaning is that for the world, the very non-perception of form and the rest is, in reality, true perception.
He states this very point:
"By the words 'How, Blessed One,' and so forth:
'It does not have form as its object' means that it does not appear as form and so on; because that very [consciousness] is what the world perceives, one does not know it as 'all'."
One knows the real as "real" and the unreal as "unreal. Because of this statement, the non-perception of the unreal world is itself perception.
He speaks next for the purpose of explaining the remaining types of knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "How so? and so forth:

"The world is empty" refers to the knowledge of the aspect of the emptiness of the world (*lokaśūnyatākārajñāna*). "It indicates the world" refers to the knowledge that indicates the emptiness of the world (*lokaśūnyatāsūcakajñāna*).
Thus it makes known; that is, the knowledge that makes known the emptiness of the world. Thus it reveals the world.

The knowledge that perceives the emptiness of the world—these three knowledges should be understood as being for the sake of those disciples who have been gathered, matured, and liberated, respectively.

Regarding this, Ārya Vimuktisena states: "With reference to the three types of omniscience and the context of the three kinds of noble persons, they are to be understood as functioning partially, functioning by way of indication, or functioning through direct perception, respectively."
"Thus the world is inconceivable" means the knowledge of its inconceivability.
"Thus the world is peaceful."
"Knowledge of peace" means that the world is secluded;
this is the knowledge of the cessation of the world.
By the passage beginning with "Thus the world is purified," it should be understood that the knowledge of the cessation of conceptualization (*saṃjñānirodhajñāna*) has also been declared.
One should ascertain that the sixteen knowledges, as previously described, are subsumed within the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
And so it has been said:
Relying upon one's own duty (svadharma), [there is] the honoring of him in his dwelling, in his status as a teacher,
in the respect shown to him, and in the sincerity of that worship. ||20||
Knowledge, which possesses a pervasive function, reveals that which was previously unseen;
it is the eye that indicates and makes known the aspect of emptiness to the world. (21)
"The vision of inconceivable peace and the cessation of worldly perception—
this is declared to be the characteristic of gnosis in the system of the knowledge of all aspects.
(22) Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the World," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāraloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Since the "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is that which is to be known as distinguished from those things delimited by the forms of cognition in their general aspect,
[the author], following the definition of cognition, introduces the definition of the particular in a general way, saying:
Then indeed, the Venerable [Subhūti], and so forth.
"By means of a great task" refers to those [tasks] characterized by distinctions such as being inconceivable and incomparable, which have the truths of suffering and so on as their objects.

The meaning is that [the path] is established for the sake of the state of a Tathāgata and so forth by means of the sixteen moments of the receptivities and knowledges of the dharma- and subsequent-knowledges (*dharmānvaya-jñānakṣāntijñāna*), which have the nature of specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇasvabhāva*).
And thus it has been said:
"By means of those objects of the truths distinguished by inconceivable and other specific qualities..."
"The specific characteristic is indicated by six and ten moments.
(23) Here, the word *vata* is used for emphasis.
Furthermore, as to what these specific qualities such as "inconceivable" and so forth are, he says:
"By means of inconceivable activity," and so forth.

The characteristic of excellence is explained by way of the distinctions of being inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and incalculable, which respectively comprise the four moments of the Truth of Suffering.
"By means of the activity of the Unequaled Equal."

This is a qualification for all [of these]. And their explanation will follow from the text itself. He says this in order to explain that this is a mere restatement (anuvāda) devoid of any logical justification.
Regarding the phrase "How so? and so forth:

the four preceding teachers maintain that the four terms beginning with "the state of a Tathāgata" should be applied according to the distinction of the four types of gnosis, such as the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*).
Because it accomplishes the state of a Tathāgata and so forth, its activity is inconceivable; likewise, in what follows, its activity should be understood as incomparable, and so on.
Regarding the question of how it is impossible to conceive of the activity of the mind, mental factors, and so forth, one might ask:
"For what reason? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the mind is not," and so on.
Mind (*citta*) is the knowledge of the mental; volition (*cetanā*) is mental action (*mānasa-karman*);

or, in the case of one who knows that, verbal and bodily actions are [mental]. Alternatively, mental factors such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth do not function here with respect to Buddhahood and the like by way of being an objective support (*ālambaka-bhāva*).
The meaning is: "because of the departure of all errors.
Or, "to weigh" means to determine its essential nature through the intellect.
"Indeed, it is immeasurable," and so forth; because it is impossible to measure.
"Indeed, it is incalculable."

Because it cannot be counted by means of oneness and so forth, how much less could there be a subsequent [term]? Since there is no equal, because of the absence of an equal, how could there be a subsequent term that is more distinguished? Therefore—
Because he is equal to himself and equal to all, the Blessed One, the Omniscient One, is "unequally equal.
This is what is meant: "The state of being a Tathāgata and so forth is expressed by all such terms as 'inconceivable' through various exclusions (vyāvṛtti)."

Having understood that the state of being a Tathāgata and so forth—distinguished by qualities such as inconceivability—is itself the ultimate nature of the word, the noble Subhūti, out of doubt regarding form and the other aggregates, asks:
"But what, then," and so on.
He speaks with the intention that the underlying principle is the same.
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is; form also," and so forth.
As before, having raised the doubt, "For what reason? he speaks, explaining first that [form] is inconceivable and incomparable according to the previously stated intention:
"For, Subhūti, that which is the *dharmatā* of form," and so forth.
By the passage beginning with "Form also, Subhūti, is immeasurable," he explains its immeasurability.
"How can they be non-objects of cognition (aprameya) when valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) exist?
Anticipating this question, he says: "For what reason? and so forth.
"For form, Subhūti, no measure is known," and so forth.
"Because of its being immeasurable" means that because all phenomena are ultimately unarisen, they are immeasurable; therefore, no measure exists.
Therefore, it is not discerned; this is the meaning.
By the words "form also," and so forth, he explains its incalculability.
"Because it transcends calculation.
This means that, by virtue of being like an illusion, it is not encompassed by calculations such as oneness and so forth.
In order to clarify the inconceivability and other qualities, and for the sake of demonstrating incomparable equality, he says: "Subhūti, even form..."
"Equal and equal," and so forth.
"Because of being equal to space":
because there is nothing equal to or superior [to them], they are equal to space; therefore, they are "equal to the unequaled."
Explaining once more in general terms, he says:
"What do you think? and so forth, [to which the answer is] "Certainly not."
The intended meaning is that [they are empty] because they lack intrinsic nature in reality.
To state the point illustrated by the example, he says:
"In just this way, Subhūti," and so forth.
"In this manner" means by way of the instruction using the analogy of space. "The qualities of a Tathāgata" refers to [the following].

In order to conclude by means of these very [qualities] such as inconceivability and so forth, he speaks for the sake of summarizing the realization of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas in all its aspects,
beginning with the words "By this also," and so on.
To clarify that very point, he says:
And these, Subhūti, are the dharmas of the Tathāgata, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "pertaining to consciousness":
this is a designation for the inconceivability and other qualities of an object that has attained an appearance similar to an illusion.
[This is] from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). For the purpose of summarizing, he says:
"Therefore, Subhūti," and so forth.
He says that for those who possess the causes, the teaching of the untainted dharma is never fruitless;
thus he speaks the passage beginning with "In this [teaching], moreover," and so forth.
And regarding the phrase "without grasping at the outflows":
Without having deposited the seeds of the latencies of the afflictions, the minds are liberated from the afflictions;
"dustless and stainless, the Dharma-eye regarding phenomena has become purified.
By means of the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) concerning the Truth of Suffering and so forth, it becomes dustless.
The Dharma-eye regarding the objects of knowledge has arisen, free from stains and devoid of faults as previously described through the knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).

Having attained "receptivity" (*kṣānti*), one has either attained the receptivity for the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*) or the receptivity for the knowledge of the phenomenon of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*), [realizing] that all phenomena are unarisen.
And those bodhisattvas numbered twenty.

Although the lineage of the Buddhas is beginningless, and although innumerable beings attain final nirvana upon the appearance of each enlightened one, there is nonetheless no exhaustion of those wandering in saṃsāra;
they are infinite like space.
For even when many obstructions such as mountains and the like are present, [space is not diminished].
Some maintain that there is no exhaustion of space.

Others, however, argue that because those things observed to possess the property of diminution in the presence of their respective counteragents (pratipakṣa) are capable of ultimate diminution when those counteragents reach complete perfection— just as in the case of impurities in gold and the like— and because transmigrating beings possess the property of diminution through the manifestation of counteragents characterized by selflessness (nairātmya) and so forth, it follows by the force of the reason of essential nature (svabhāvahetu) that there is an annihilation of transmigrating beings.
In order to explain the distinction of including all noble persons (*āryapudgala*) within the first moment of the [Truth of] Origination, he says:
"O Blessed One, it is profound," and so forth.
[An objection is raised: Since there is no obstruction to Buddhahood and the like within the Mother (the Perfection of Wisdom), how can she possess the nature of a great task?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason? he says:
"For here," and so forth.
"Endowed with omniscience" refers to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is dependent upon the perfection of wisdom.
He explains that the Mother herself is dependent upon all activities by means of the analogy,
beginning with "Just as, for example," and so forth.
"Anointed on the head" means consecrated by the eighteen great clans;
or else, one who has been consecrated with water from the trunk of a royal elephant.
Regarding the phrase "one who has attained power and vigor over the realm":
because he is free from the fear of losing his own kingdom, he has attained power (*sthāma*) over the territory of the realm;
and because he possesses the capacity for both restraint and favor, he has attained vigor (*vīrya*).
"Tasks" refers to activities;
"conjoined with ministers" means they are dependent upon them.
In that regard, because there is an absence of activity of body and speech, one should apply the terms "having little concern" and "having laid down the burden" respectively.
Anticipating the objection that realization is impossible without attachment to possessions, he says:
"How so, Blessed One? and so forth.
He states the counter-argument for the sake of refutation with the words, "What do you think? and so on.
"Either grasping or attachment"—
the meaning is that these are apprehended respectively by the conceptual constructions of the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka).
"Certainly not so, Blessed One."
This is the summarized meaning here:

because for a noble person (*āryapudgala*) established on the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and so forth by means of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*), a conceptualization of the form "this is the fruit to be grasped" and "I am the grasper" does not manifest,
since such knowledge is the antidote to all conceptualizations.

Otherwise, because experience of an object as it truly exists would be impossible through conceptual cognitions, there would be no possibility of the Path due to being devoid of authentic knowledge; consequently, in the absence of the abandonment of afflictions, the fruit of Arhatship would not arise, just as it does not during the stages of hearing and reflection. Therefore, [this occurs] only for the yogi who has arisen from the Path and so forth.

Just like the conceptualization of speech and so forth that involves the attachment to a perceived unity, a cognition free from superimposition—one devoid of the imagination of grasped object and grasping subject—arises.
And thus, because there is no apprehension of the reality of things, one says, "I do not perceive that phenomenon.
Stating this very point, he says:
"Thus it is," and so forth.
He speaks thus in accordance with the conceptualizations of people who rely on apprehension:
"Even omniscience, O Blessed One," and so forth.
Therefore, the sense is that one should not speak to them.
Explaining the specific quality of being experienced by a particular kind of person, which is comprised within the second moment, he says:
"Moreover, however," and so forth.

In this regard, they are endowed with the causes respectively by virtue of their lineage (*gotra*) consisting of conviction in the profound Dharma through both natural and acquired dispositions; they have planted roots of merit over a long period of time;
and for the sake of increasing these two lineages through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata, it is said that "between the two states, they have performed services for previous Victors."

In this regard, the three terms "profound," "difficult to see," and "difficult to realize" are to be understood through the non-apprehension of the three natures, such as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the others.
Pointing out the specific quality of uncommonness subsumed within the third moment, he says:
"If, O Blessed One," and so forth.

"On the stage of those who follow through faith" means that prior to the state of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), they would perform the practice of giving and so forth on the stage of equipment (*sambhārabhūmi*) by way of apprehension (*upalambha*).

"Patience" refers to the patience of reflecting on the Dharma (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*). In the stage of hearing, one should take delight in it and seek it out through the distinction between the preparatory and the fundamental [paths]. In the stage of reflection, one should likewise reflect upon and weigh it in that same manner.
In the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāvasthā*), it should be stated that one should examine and contemplate as before.
In order to demonstrate the distinction of swift direct knowledge (*kṣiprābhijñatā*) comprised within the fourth moment, he said:
"When this was said, the Blessed One... and so forth.
By the use of the word "up to" (*yāvat*), the inclusion of bodhisattvas and others is intended.
"Nirvāṇa" refers to the state of a Tathāgata.
To express the distinction of being neither deficient nor redundant, which is comprised within the first moment of cessation, he says:
Then indeed, those belonging to the realm of desire, and so forth.
"This is the Great Perfection" (mahāpāramitā) means that because there is no deficiency or incompleteness, it is endowed with great majesty.

Having gone not far, they disappeared; this means that after traveling on foot as far as the range of the Blessed One’s ordinary vision, they departed by means of their own supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Inconceivable," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Fourteenth Chapter. Speaking of the excellence of intense practice comprised within the second moment, he says: "O Blessed One, that bodhisattva who... and so forth.
"Simultaneously with hearing" means immediately after merely hearing.
In that regard, by virtue of the contradiction between hearing, reflection, and meditative cultivation, it does not shrink back, does not sink down, and does not remain fixed, respectively.
Since he is devoid of ignorance, doubt, and false knowledge, the meaning of the words "he does not waver," "he does not hesitate," and "he does not desire" must be explained.
Because of his connection with longing, he rejoices;
thus, he will not turn his mind away [from the goal].
He will not give rise to a mind of regret; thinking "I shall follow after him," because he does not abandon the Dharma-preacher, it is said:
"He will follow the Dharma-preacher and will not let him go."
He says "Just as, Subhūti," and so forth, in order to explain this very point by means of an illustration;
and "situated in the body" (*kāyagatā*) refers to its being placed upon the chest.
"Or [it is] contained in books," because it is held in books.
In order to state the specific excellence of attainment (*samudāgama-viśeṣa*) comprised within the third moment, he says:
"It may be, Blessed One, by these... and so forth.
It might be; it could be.
The question is posed with an interrogative intonation: "By what?
[The answer is: "By these very qualities," namely, by the power of conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the armor, and so forth.
He says, beginning with "Subhūti, there might be a bodhisattva," while refuting [the objection] by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
He also speaks while indicating [the same point] by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, by which... and so forth: [the opponent] suspects that this is indeed without logical justification, and thus asks, "For what reason? to which [the author] replies:
For it is said: "Thus, in this [state], etc. This means:
because, due to the deficiency in the mother's infusion of impressions (*vāsanā*), there occurs longing, trembling, and so forth.
"Therefore, he is by nature one who does not ask questions beforehand.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"Furthermore," and so forth.
"Lasting for that duration" means persisting for several days;
"and it is withdrawn" [is the meaning].
It is removed by the force of the cognition of contradiction.
And as for the statement "it is unremovable," this means it is impossible to provide an answer due to the abundance of counter-questions.
Having raised the doubt, "Why is that so?", he says:
"For it is thus, Subhūti," and so forth.
This means that such is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that an effect conforms to its cause.
However, in the passage beginning with "by whom [this] was not previously fully inquired about," the sense is that this occurs at all times.
For it was stated immediately thereafter: "one [or another] disputant," and so forth;
that for some time he conforms to the meter.
Through the power of practice for just a few days, one’s desire becomes limited to that extent;
this is the thought, based on the principle that the effect conforms to its cause. Thus it is said, "it is lifted up."
One falls away from faith;
one desponds even while engaged in faith.
It is "wavering and unstable" because it does not take specific dharmas as its object.
He says that very thing:
"and like a tuft of cotton.
A tuft of cotton (*tūlapicu*) is cotton-wool that has been processed for making cotton wicks (*tūlavarti*).

Therefore, because it does not share the property of being non-abiding, it must be stated that what is similar to it— that is, its likeness— will not assist, will not follow after, and will not attend upon [the mind] during the stages of hearing and so forth, or during the stages of application and so forth, respectively.
Pointing out the specific object of focus (*ālambana-viśeṣa*) as comprised within the fourth moment, he says:
"Namely, for example," and so forth.
Because of the absence of external and internal calamities,
both "well-being" (*svasti*) and "without obstacle" (*anantarāyeṇa*) are employed.
He says that very thing:
"unbroken and unimpaired.
"On the way" means that it will meet its destruction right there in the middle of the path.
"Faith exists," and so forth. In that context, faith is conviction regarding existence;
patience is the acceptance of dharmas such as non-arising.
Ruci is the absence of attachment.
Chanda is the desire to act.
Vīrya is enthusiasm for the wholesome.
Heedfulness (*apramāda*) is the cultivation and non-cultivation, respectively, of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is the determination and ascertainment [of the truth].
High resolve (*adhyāśaya*) is a mind inclined toward benefiting others and so forth.
Renunciation is the relinquishing of all one's possessions along with their fruits;
dignity is humility in all circumstances;
and affection is a state of mental well-being.
Joy (*prāmodya*) is a particular kind of gladness.
Serenity (*prasāda*) is a particular kind of devotion arising from seeing the possession of virtuous qualities.
Affection (*prema*) is the desire for that which is capable of being practiced.
"Unflagging perseverance" (*anikṣiptadhūratā*) is the non-abandonment of the burden of one's vow.

The example of "taking as an object that which has no object" is for the purpose of illustrating the state of the adverse factors and their antidotes regarding the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) for those who practice with intervals and without intervals.
He speaks in order to explain the specific basis (*ādhāraviśeṣa*) comprised within the first moment of the path.
"Just as, Subhūti, it is like a woman," and so forth. [The opponent] objects: "This is entirely without logical justification. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For what reason? and so on.
Warding off [the objection] by means of the nature of things, he says:
"Just as if," and so forth.
"Should carry away" means one should lead the water away.
In the same way, having raised the doubt as to "for what reason," he says as before:
"Just as it is called," and so forth.
"By means of the perfection of wisdom and skill in means" means by means of emptiness and compassion.
The two pots, one mature and one raw, are intended to demonstrate the relationship between the receptacle and the non-receptacle for the dharma of practice.
Explaining the specific quality of completeness as comprised within the second moment, he says:
"one of a nature characterized by poor wisdom," and so forth.
"Unpolished" means that bark garments were taken up at the place where [the Buddha] entered the water. "Unadorned" means...
Because of not removing rotten wood. "Having mounted one afflicted by a burden" means having climbed onto one heavily laden with a weight.
"He will perish like one whose goods have not been ferried across;
he will come to ruin like one who has not yet secured the equipment for his destination;
and being 'deprived' means deprived of what he had not yet attained."
"In the interim, he will become despondent and fall into dejection;
he will undergo internal dissension,
and he will fall into despair regarding the stage of a Buddha."
Since there is no certainty regarding future objects, how can it be said that "this will remain"?

Anticipating this question with the inquiry "For what reason?", [the author] says "For it is thus, Subhūti," and so forth, based on an inference of capacity that follows from the mere presence of unimpaired causes.
The inclusion of both "refined" (*ākoṭita*) and "unrefined" (*anākoṭita*) vessels is for the purpose of making known the deficiency and completeness of practice.
Demonstrating the distinction of perfect acceptance (*samparigraha-viśeṣa*) as comprised within the third moment, he says:
"A certain man who is aged," and so forth.
In this context, he is "worn out" because his limbs are decayed by old age;
he is "aged" due to having reached advanced years;
and he is "senile" because of his inability to distinguish between well-spoken and ill-spoken words.
"Exhausted" means impaired.
Having raised the doubt as to why this is so, he says:
"Just as indeed," and so forth.

The illustration of the old man’s being taken up or not taken up is intended to elucidate, as appropriate, how through the grasping or non-grasping of the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, one either falls into or does not fall into the extremes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
This concludes the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Similes," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāraloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The fifteenth chapter.
Explaining the distinction of non-savoring (*anāsvāda*) as comprised within the fourth moment, he says:
"By the beginner," and so forth.

In this context, it should be applied as follows: they are to be served (*sevitavya*), honored (*bhaktavya*), and attended upon (*paryupāsitavya*) respectively by means of body, speech, or by providing attendants and so forth, through propitiation;
thus, "you should apply yourself to yoga."
Be intent on practice through the yoga of the non-apprehension of the donor, the recipient, and so forth.
"Do not grasp at form" means do not seize upon it through the yoga of attachment to form and the rest.
Having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:
"For it is not grasped," and so forth.
Because its nature is non-arising in reality, omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is not to be apprehended in any manner whatsoever.
"Pe-yā-la-mi-ti" (and so forth).
"All that in the Unsurpassed" means,
O son of good family, this passage [extends] up to the four perfections beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*).
It is to be taught in successive order; that is,
first by means of the refutation of the self (*ātman*) and so forth, [one establishes] the external.

Having established [the student] in the [Mahāyāna] vehicle, one should subsequently lead them to the realization that the three realms are mind-only by means of explaining the imagined, dependent, and perfected natures.

Following that, one should point out the two types of conventional truth—the real and the unreal—distinguishing between what is fit and unfit for authentic purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), and how they depend on their respective preceding causes, being delightful only so long as they are not analyzed. Then, abiding in the real conventional truth, one should practice generosity and the other perfections according to how things appear, just like a magical person (*māyāpuruṣa*).
In the ultimate sense, non-arising is that which must be cultivated; in this manner, one should be introduced to the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Thus, the sixteenfold specific characteristic has been explained, by which the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*) for Bodhisattvas and others in the two [knowledges]—namely, the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*) and so forth—is distinguished from the paths of the Śrāvakas and others.

Therefore, for them, that which is devoid of the aforementioned distinctions has not been mentioned, because it is easy to understand due to its characteristic of being the production of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth.
And thus it has been said:
It is the inconceivable and the incomparable, the transcendence of measurement and number; it is the inclusion of all noble ones, and the uncommon knowledge to be realized by the wise. (24)
The swiftness of wisdom, deficiency and fulfillment, the practice, the realization, the common object of focus, completeness, and total inclusion. ||25||

And the "absence of relish" (anāsvāda) should be understood as the sixteenfold distinction; it is the path of distinction by which it is distinguished from other paths. (26) Thus, since [the path] has been defined by the characteristic of distinction, the characteristic of its activity must now be stated: what is its function?
In that regard, while explaining the activity of bringing about welfare and happiness, he says:
"O Blessed One, you are the performers of what is difficult to do," and so forth.
"Of such a form" means:
The meaning is that it is the complete cause for the accomplishment of Buddhahood.
In that regard, with the intention of providing happiness for the future and for the present, the two terms "for the benefit" (*hitāya*) and "for happiness" (*sukhāya*) are stated.
And he says that these two would arise through compassion.
"Having set out for the sake of compassion for the world. This statement of purpose (*uddeśa*) is made in order to demonstrate the activity of providing protection and so forth,
beginning with the words, "We shall become the protection of the world," and so on.
In that context, explaining the activity of providing protection, he says:
"And how, Subhūti," and so forth.
Therein, "they strive" means they exert vigor (*vīrya*).
They should be applied respectively through application, lack of contentment, and vigor.
They are called "protections" because they establish one in the state of being subject to non-retribution.
In order to explain the activity of "taking refuge," he says:
"How so? and so forth.
In that context, "birth" (jāti) is existence after having not existed.
Old age is the state of becoming decrepit; illness is a lack of physical well-being; death is the relinquishing of the group-homogeneity projected by prior karma;
and sorrow is mental distress.
Lamentation is weeping accompanied by the recollection of the qualities of those who are dear;
suffering is an unpeaceful physical sensation; and mental distress is a mental state, as described previously.
"Distress" refers to the bearing of burdens and so forth.
"Refuge" is used in the sense of providing ultimate benefit.
Explaining the function of the dwelling, he says:
"In what way? and so forth;
[the phrase] "for the sake of non-attachment."
"It is a refuge for the non-arising of form and so forth" means for the purpose of turning back the causes of suffering. Clarifying precisely the sense of "non-attachment," he says:
"How is there non-attachment, O Blessed One? and so forth.
Regarding "from knowledge and vision":
in this context, knowledge and vision consist in the direct realization of the meaning as it has been explained.
Explaining the function of being the ultimate resort (*parāyaṇakāritra*), he says:
"And how, Subhūti," and so forth;
"That which, Subhūti, is the further shore (*pāra*) of form, that is not form."
In the sense of reaching the ultimate limit, that which is the "far shore" of form—its non-arising and lack of intrinsic nature—is not form from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), just as the far shore is emptiness, so too is form.
For it has been said: "Since no phenomenon exists apart from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)."
"Just as the far shore, Subhūti, so too is form"—
this means they have already been fully awakened.
Since all phenomena are realized even now as being of the nature of emptiness, just as they were in the state of Buddhahood, the implication is that application to this sūtra would be useless.
One might ask: "Since conceptual construction consisting of error exists, how can they be said to have attained perfect awakening? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For it is not here," and so forth.
The meaning is that because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has the nature of non-arising, there is no conceptual construction whatsoever beyond form and so forth.
"All phenomena are fully awakened" is the sense; the remainder is that this is "in reality" (*tattvata eva*).

The sense is that, on the level of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), application to the sūtras becomes fruitful for the purpose of removing superimpositions (*samāropa*) that have existed since beginningless time. Explaining precisely this realization of conventional reality, he says:
"This too," and so forth.
They cultivate and contemplate various means in many ways, yet they do not realize [the goal], for this is supremely difficult and impossible to perform all at once.
Nevertheless, they do not become discouraged, nor do they fall into indolence in fulfilling the perfections such as generosity;
[they think], "These are the dharmas."
Because they possess characteristics such as being naturally extinguished (*prakṛtiparinirvṛta*),
they become the ultimate refuge.
Through their teaching of the Dharma, for the purpose of bringing about the realization of the equality of *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*, they become saviors.
In order to explain the function of being an island (*dvīpa*), he says:
"And how, Subhūti," and so forth.
"Separated by water" means...
The portions of land situated in the midst of water;
"form delimited by the prior limit and the posterior limit" means it is delimited by the prior limit,
which is the cause, and the posterior limit, which is the effect.
That which exists in the midst of it has an illusory nature.
By this "delimitation," Subhūti,
[it is meant] by way of non-arising in reality.

"‘This is peaceful,’ and so forth: by means of these five phrases, the Truth of the Path is communicated respectively in the paths of preparation, seeing, cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning."
They become islands for the world.

By virtue of their similarity to well-situated dry land surrounded by water, they are to be resorted to because they teach the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation, and nirvana through the realization of all phenomena delimited by the past and future limits;
and because they provide the basis for the attainment of one's own and others' welfare.

As for the phrase "How so? and so forth: furthermore, the activity of producing light is, by way of its similarity to an island of jewels accompanied by light, itself the activity of being an island for the destruction of the darkness of ignorance—since that destruction is included within the destruction of craving and the other [afflictions].
However, it should be understood that the separate treatment [of this activity] is due to the predominance of the light of knowledge in the destruction of ignorance.
Regarding the phrase "the eggshell of ignorance" and so forth...

Ignorance (*avidyā*) itself is the membrane of the eggshell, appearing in the forms of the grasped and the grasper. For those beings who are completely enveloped by it— meaning those whose external knowledge is obstructed— and who are overwhelmed by darkness, meaning those overcome internally by the seed of the latencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā-bīja*), [there exists] the darkness of all ignorance.
The connection is that they "shake off" or remove the darkness of ignorance, both external and internal.
To the question "What are they doing?", he says:
"illuminating through wisdom," which means producing the light of knowledge.
Speaking of the activity of a leader, he says:
"And how, Subhūti," and so forth,
[ending with] "they become leaders."

They are "leaders" because, by means of their role as charioteers, they reveal the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena—such as form and so forth—by virtue of their intrinsic nature, and because they bring about the practice of the welfare of others.
Asking for the sake of the three types of effortless activity and so forth, he says: "In what way? and so on.
"They become the refuge of the world" means that they become the support through the withdrawal of the activity of the three kinds of functional action.

In this regard, because they withdraw the welfare of sentient beings by functioning effortlessly as teachers of the Dharma within the scope of omniscience, they become the support; thus, explaining first the effortless functional action, he says:
"Here, Subhūti," and so forth.
"Having the nature of space" means having space as its ultimate limit.
Explaining this very point, he says:
"Just as space," and so forth.
In that context, space is the mere absence of substance.
It is "not come" because there is no coming from past time, and it is "not gone" because there is no going in future time.
It is "uncreated" due to the absence of a causal agent, and "unchanged" due to the lack of a cause for destruction.
It is "unconditioned" because the formative forces that would establish it are untenable.
Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature throughout the three times, it is, respectively, non-abiding, non-staying, and non-established.
Therefore, it is unarisen and unceasing. He speaks thus for the purpose of summary:
"In the same way, Subhūti," and so forth.
"Because they are like space, they are non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). Because they are equal to the sky, they are free from discursive thought (*nirvikalpa*).
Regarding the phrase "the future," etc., [it is] without logical justification.
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?", he says:
"That which, Subhūti, of form," and so forth.
Emptiness is the nature of non-arising.
Even if there is indeed no coming or going for it, how could this not also apply to form and the other aggregates?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because they have emptiness as their destination," and so forth;
because their intrinsic nature is non-arising.
All phenomena have emptiness and so forth as their intrinsic nature. Among these, they are "empty" because they are like an illusion;
they are "signless" because of the departure from all signs.
Because it transcends the sphere of aspiration, it is wishless (*apraṇihita*);
because it is naturally luminous like space, it is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
They do not deviate from that state.
They do not transcend that intrinsic nature.
Immediately after this, Subhūti, it is thus that bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas,
have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The connection is with the concluding verse of the *Hāraka* section, which will be stated as "the noble ones become the refuge of the world.

Furthermore, the section on the Knowledge of All Aspects (*sarvajñatā*) should be understood as illuminating *nirvāṇa* in relation to all-encompassing activity, from [the benefit of others] up to the effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*).

The section on the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñatā*) [is so called] because, by way of teaching the Dharma, they become the "refuge" through the presentation of the respective *nirvāṇas* of the vehicles and the non-realization thereof.
Explaining the activity of not directly realizing the departure via the three vehicles and their respective fruits, he says:
"They have non-arising as their destination," and so forth.
In that regard, they have non-arising as their destination because they are free from imagined suffering.
Because they are free from the suffering of conceptual construction, they have the state of non-arising as their destination;
because they are separated from the suffering of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they have the state of non-existence as their destination;
and because there is an absence of a conceptually constructed origin, they have the state of dream as their destination, since only that which appears like a dream exists.
Just as the self does not exist because it is sublated by valid cognition, so too do those who follow the course of the self [not exist], because the imagined collection is non-existent.
Since the collection of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is like an illusion and thus lacks any discernible delimitation, they have no finite destination.

The three terms "having a peaceful destination," "having a destination that is nirvāṇa," and "having a destination from which there is no returning" should be understood as referring, respectively, to the cessation of the three kinds of existents beginning with the imagined.
Likewise, because they have the nature of the threefold path beginning with the imagined (parikalpita), they are "without coming," "without going," and "of immovable course."
Immediately following this as well, the connection should be made with the word "dhāraka" (sustainer) as before. Speaking of the activity of motion (*gati-kāritra*), he says:
"For those whose motion consists of form," and so forth.
The nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which has form and so forth as its objective domain and whose intrinsic nature consists of form and so forth,
becomes the destination of the world. Thus,
because they teach all phenomena in accordance with the section on the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), Bodhisattvas become the refuge of the world.
One should understand that the characteristic of activity is indeed of eleven kinds,
as it has been said:
"It is the beneficial, the blissful, the protection, the refuge, and the shelter for humanity."
And he is the ultimate refuge, the island, and known as the leader. ||27||

"Effortless, consisting in the non-realization of the fruits through the three vehicles—this is the final activity; this is the characteristic of activity. Thus, having distinguished [the Buddha-nature] by means of the characteristic of activity, he speaks of its essential characteristic for the sake of understanding: [The verse continues: "Unconditioned, it is not produced by causes and conditions; it is eternal, because it is free from arising and ceasing; it is pure, because it is free from the adventitious stains; and it is supreme, because it is the ultimate limit of all phenomena. (29) This is the essential characteristic of those [beings] who are defined by the characteristic of activity. To explain the meaning of "practice," he says: "The practice of the Bodhisattvas consists in the non-abandonment of sentient beings, the non-attachment to dharmas, and the non-perception of a self. (30) This is the essential characteristic of the practice of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "attainment," he says: "The attainment of the Bodhisattvas consists in the non-abandonment of the welfare of sentient beings, the non-abandonment of the maturation of sentient beings, and the non-abandonment of the purification of the buddha-field. (31) This is the essential characteristic of the attainment of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "power," he says: "The power of the Bodhisattvas consists in the power of the superknowledges, the power of the analytical knowledges, and the power of the unhindered eloquence. (32) This is the essential characteristic of the power of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "manifestation," he says: "The manifestation of the Bodhisattvas consists in the manifestation of birth, the manifestation of renunciation, the manifestation of asceticism, the manifestation of going to the seat of awakening, the manifestation of overcoming the hosts of Māra, the manifestation of attaining perfect awakening, the manifestation of turning the wheel of Dharma, and the manifestation of passing into parinirvāṇa. (33) This is the essential characteristic of the manifestation of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "activity," he says: "The activity of the Bodhisattvas consists in the activity of the ten powers, the activity of the four fearlessnesses, the activity of the eighteen unique qualities, and the activity of great compassion. (34) This is the essential characteristic of the activity of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "characteristic," he says: "The characteristic of the Bodhisattvas consists in the characteristic of the nature of reality, the characteristic of the absence of characteristics, and the characteristic of the unconditioned. (35) This is the essential characteristic of the characteristic of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "merit," he says: "The merit of the Bodhisattvas consists in the merit of giving, the merit of morality, and the merit of meditation. (36) This is the essential characteristic of the merit of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "wisdom," he says: "The wisdom of the Bodhisattvas consists in the wisdom of the knowledge of all aspects, the wisdom of the knowledge of paths, and the wisdom of the knowledge of all things. (37) This is the essential characteristic of the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "means," he says: "The means of the Bodhisattvas consists in the means of skillful means, the means of the vows, and the means of the powers. (38) This is the essential characteristic of the means of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "result," he says: "The result of the Bodhisattvas consists in the result of the stage of the śrāvaka, the result of the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the result of the stage of the Buddha. (39) This is the essential characteristic of the result of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "purity," he says: "The purity of the Bodhisattvas consists in the purity of the body, the purity of speech, and the purity of mind. (40) This is the essential characteristic of the purity of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "perfection," he says: "The perfection of the Bodhisattvas consists in the perfection of generosity, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. (41) This is the essential characteristic of the perfection of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "non-duality," he says: "The non-duality of the Bodhisattvas consists in the non-duality of subject and object, the non-duality of existence and non-existence, and the non-duality of samsara and nirvana. (42) This is the essential characteristic of the non-duality of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "ultimate truth," he says: "The ultimate truth of the Bodhisattvas consists in the emptiness of all phenomena, the signlessness of all phenomena, and the wishlessness of all phenomena. (43) This is the essential characteristic of the ultimate truth of the Bodhisattvas.
