To explain the meaning of "inconceivability," he says: "The inconceivability of the Bodhisattvas consists in the inconceivability of their body, the inconceivability of their speech, and the inconceivability of their mind. (44) This is the essential characteristic of the inconceivability of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "immeasurability," he says: "The immeasurability of the Bodhisattvas consists in the immeasurability of their lifespan, the immeasurability of their light, and the immeasurability of their sphere of activity. (45) This is the essential characteristic of the immeasurability of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "unfathomability," he says: "The unfathomability of the Bodhisattvas consists in the unfathomability of their wisdom, the unfathomability of their power, and the unfathomability of their skillful means. (46) This is the essential characteristic of the unfathomability of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "inexpressibility," he says: "The inexpressibility of the Bodhisattvas consists in the inexpressibility of their name, the inexpressibility of their form, and the inexpressibility of their qualities. (47) This is the essential characteristic of the inexpressibility of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "equality," he says: "The equality of the Bodhisattvas consists in the equality of all phenomena, the equality of all beings, and the equality of all buddha-fields. (48) This is the essential characteristic of the equality of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "non-differentiation," he says: "The non-differentiation of the Bodhisattvas consists in the non-differentiation of the dharma-realm, the non-differentiation of the suchness, and the non-differentiation of the ultimate reality. (49) This is the essential characteristic of the non-differentiation of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "non-arising," he says: "The non-arising of the Bodhisattvas consists in the non-arising of birth, the non-arising of death, and the non-arising of rebirth. (50) This is the essential characteristic of the non-arising of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "non-ceasing," he says: "The non-ceasing of the Bodhisattvas consists in the non-ceasing of the continuity of the lineage, the non-ceasing of the continuity of the dharma, and the non-ceasing of the continuity of the community. (51) This is the essential characteristic of the non-ceasing of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "non-dwelling," he says: "The non-dwelling of the Bodhisattvas consists in the non-dwelling in samsara, the non-dwelling in nirvana, and the non-dwelling in the middle way. (52) This is the essential characteristic of the non-dwelling of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "non-grasping," he says: "The non-grasping of the Bodhisattvas consists in the non-grasping of the self, the non-grasping of phenomena, and the non-grasping of the person. (53) This is the essential characteristic of the non-grasping of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "non-attachment," he says: "The non-attachment of the Bodhisattvas consists in the non-attachment to gain, the non-attachment to honor, and the non-attachment to fame. (54) This is the essential characteristic of the non-attachment of the Bodhisattvas. To explain the meaning of "non-conceptualization," he says: "The non-conceptualization of the Bodhisattvas
"Who, O Blessed One, [will practice] this? and so forth.
To make known their essential nature, he says:
"Those, Subhūti, who have practiced," and so forth.
In order to explain the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), he asks by saying, "What is their intrinsic nature? and so forth. To provide the answer, he says:

"Having a nature secluded by discipline (*vainayika-vivikta-svabhāva*). Discipline (*vinaya*) is that by which one is disciplined; it is the *dharmadhātu*. That which arises from it is "secluded" (*vivikta*) because of its separation from opposing factors (*vipakṣa*). Those whose nature is such are so described. By this very term, [it is shown that] their nature is secluded from afflictions (*kleśa*), by virtue of having a nature secluded from passion and so forth;

and their nature is secluded from the signs of afflictions (*kleśaliṅga*), by virtue of possessing a nature secluded from the physical and mental dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*) that are the signs of passion and so forth.

The fourfold nature is taught for the purpose of introducing the path of cultivation to those who have resolute faith in the state of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*): its nature as being secluded from the afflictions (*kleśa*), by virtue of being secluded from improper mental attention toward the signs of passion and so forth; and its nature as being secluded from the discordant factors and their antidotes, by virtue of being secluded from passion and non-passion, hatred and non-hatred, and delusion and non-delusion.
In order to explain that very destination, he says:
"O Blessed One, is it thus? and so forth. "Thus, those who have gone" means those whose destination is such.
They are those who have reached the state of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
To confirm that this has been well said, he says:
"It is so, Subhūti," and so forth.
In order to explain the nature of what is difficult to perform, he says:
"One who performs what is difficult," and so forth.
"It is thus."

Because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are absolutely non-existent and thus lack any connection [to a self], he is a "performer of what is difficult" by virtue of his armor-like resolve (*sannāha*) to bring about the parinirvāṇa of all sentient beings— a task that is otherwise impossible.
Clarifying the nature of this armor, he says:
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "This indeed," etc.:
therein, because of the absence of attachment to present form and so forth, there is no connection with form and so forth;
because of being turned away from longing for them in the future, there is no connection for the sake of form and so forth.
"This is indeed without logical justification.
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?", he says:
"Because it is unconnected with all phenomena."
The thought is that, in reality, it is delightful solely when not investigated.
Demonstrating its absolute nature, he says:
"O Blessed One, of this bodhisattva," and so forth.

"Thus for one clad in the great armor" means for one endowed with a resolute nature. In that regard, because they have been correctly entered upon, the stage of the Śrāvaka and the stage of the Pratyekabuddha are not to be desired by a Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the Buddha-ground is not to be desired by way of longing.
To explain how this point is established, he says:
"Subhūti, whom do you [desire]?"
"By the power of the purpose," and so forth.
Intending to resolve [the objection] with the thought that the Mother is the antidote to all apprehension (*upalambha*), he says:
"For it is impossible," and so forth.
In that regard, due to the deficiency of causes, there is no possibility and it is impossible;
because the fruit is impossible, there is no occasion and no opportunity.
And by virtue of the impossibility and lack of occasion for falling to the levels of the Śrāvakas and so forth, there is exclusive cultivation.
It should be elucidated by way of non-attachment.
Pointing out the nature of the summary, he says:
"But rather, it is the Buddha-stage itself," and so forth.
"It is to be expected" means that this is because of the firm conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that all phenomena are like an illusion; by this,
the cultivation of the summary (*uddeśabhāvanā*) is indicated.
It would be illuminated as being subject to deviation.
Stating that its nature is non-perception, he says:
"O Blessed One, it is profound," and so forth.
It is not to be cultivated by anyone,
because of the non-apprehension of the object of cultivation, the cultivator, and the act of cultivation.
He says this very thing:
By the words "tām hi" and so forth;
having raised the doubt as before— "for what reason?"—
he says "na hi" and so forth.
For indeed, no dharma whatsoever is established as real,
characterized by agent, object, action, and so forth.
How then can there be cultivation (bhāvanā) and so on?
"The cultivation of space" means,
in reality, the cultivation of that which is like an illusion.
He explains that very cultivation through its divisions, such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
By the passage beginning with "the cultivation of all dharmas" and so forth:

therein, through the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is the cultivation of all dharmas because it encompasses the non-arising of all realizations (*abhisamaya*); through the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*)...
Through training in all paths without attachment, there is the cultivation of non-attachment;
through omniscience, because it encompasses all things without exception, there is ultimate cultivation.
Because it consists of the path of distinction through the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), there is no possibility [of its being otherwise].
Because it is characterized by the path of culmination (*niṣṭhāmārga*) through the peak realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*), there is the cultivation of non-appropriation.
In order to state that its intrinsic nature is non-attachment, [the Buddha said]: "It is so, Subhūti; it is so."
He speaks with the preliminary act of giving from his own hand:
"Therefore, Subhūti, because of the profound [perfection of wisdom]," and so forth.
"Therefore" means for the reason that is about to be stated.
He states the reason itself with the words beginning "kaccit" (I hope). The word *kaccit* functions in the sense of "because."
"He does not form an attachment" means he does not grasp at things as real entities;
he does not become attached to the words or the counsel of others.

He does not listen to the open declaration, the covert speech, or the secret counsel of others who say, "This is not the word of the Buddha for the monks of our own school," nor does he follow another out of mere faith.
Through the attainment of clarity that is personally realized within oneself, one does not become led by others.
One penetrates through the understanding of the texts and so forth;
one gains resolute conviction through the focal point of the meaning.
Having raised the doubt as to why that is so,
he says "For it is thus," and so forth.
The meaning is that without the implantation of latencies (*vāsanā*) from previous births, there can be no absence of terror and the like.
And by means of fearlessness and so forth, the cultivation of the aspects of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) would have been explained.
Now, pointing out the nature of the objective support (*ālambana*), he says: "O Blessed One, that bodhisattva who... and so forth.
"By way of aspect" means by way of the mode of apprehension. "Discriminated" means determined.
"Inclined toward omniscience" means by a continuum of mind that culminates in the three types of omniscience.

By this, the cultivation of the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*) would have been explained. [The author] says, "O Blessed One, how... and so forth, because a mental continuum whose own nature has been fully known is capable of discerning another.

In response, he says—refuting [the objection] by means of the mental continuum consisting of the cultivation of all phenomena as being like an illusion during the stages of preparation (*prayoga*), the main part (*maula*), and the conclusion (*pṛṣṭha*)—that "the continuum has been investigated as inclining toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
He states the three phrases beginning with "and inclining toward space" (*ākāśanimnā ca*), etc., meaning: "this is that investigation."

The meaning is that this investigation is "correct" by means of a continuous stream of certainty as previously described. Anticipating the objection that "this is merely without logical justification," he says: "For what reason? [and so forth].
"Immeasurable," and so forth.

Because, in reality, omniscience is immeasurable and without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to its transcendence of the relationship between the means of cognition and the object of cognition (*prameya*), as is appropriate; therefore, there is investigation by means of a mental continuum determined through the cultivation of the illusion-like nature.
The meaning of the sentence is that otherwise, there would be the apprehension of an entity due to the existence of such properties as "knowability" (*prameyatva*).
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"O Subhūti," and so forth.
In this context, "attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to the path of equipment (*sambhāramārga*), which consists of the ethical discipline and other qualities of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
"Realization" (*abhisamaya*) refers to the path of application (*prayogamārga*), which consists of the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) for one who has completed the equipment.
"Adhigama" refers to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), characterized by the penetration of the all-pervading realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The path that takes mundane dhyānas and formless attainments as its object is the mundane path of cultivation (*laukika-bhāvanāmārga*).

The fruit of the path, consisting of the knowledge of the truth of suffering and so forth, is the supramundane path of cultivation (*lokottara-bhāvanāmārga*). The mild path (*mṛdu-mārga*) is that which has the nature of the mild-mild (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) and other grades, acting to abandon the intense-intense (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) and other grades of afflictions.
Consciousness that destroys afflictions of medium and superior degrees and so forth, characterized by medium and weak [degrees] and so forth, is the middle path.
Its arising uproots afflictions of weak and superior degrees and so forth, having the form of superior and weak [degrees] and so forth.
The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the stage of mere resolve (*dhimātra*).
Destruction (*vināśa*) is the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), which is the means for abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*) on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Arising (*utpāda*) is the correct path of uninterrupted transition (*samyagānantaryamārga*), which brings about liberation through the abandonment of the afflictions. Cessation (*vyaya*) is the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), which realizes the gnosis that is distinct from the afflictions.

Some maintain that cessation (*nirodha*) is the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*), consisting of the paths of preparation, uninterrupted transition, and liberation, which pertains to the remaining types of afflictions.
Others hold that the path of distinction is cessation, which brings about the production of extraordinary qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*).
Cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), which shatters all obstructions that are otherwise impenetrable.
Elimination (*vibhāvanā*) is the path of culmination (*niṣṭhāmārga*).
The knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*) is both specific and general. A "place" (*pradeśa*) is a particular location (*deśaviśeṣa*).
"It cannot be fully awakened to by anyone" means that it cannot be realized through forms such as material form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
He says this very thing:
"Not by means of form," and so forth.
If that is so, then how is it that this was stated: "The objective support consists of all phenomena, mundane, wholesome, and so on"?
How can this be?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For form itself," and so forth.
The meaning is that, according to the conventional perspective of yogins, form and the other aggregates themselves, when realized as being like an illusion, are Buddhahood.

As it has been said: "For the result of the teaching is the awakening to the true meaning of that which is merely well-known as being unreal. [This refers to] the perfection of generosity alone, and so forth.

In this regard, the three perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, as well as portions of the perfections of vigor and meditative concentration, constitute the equipment of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*). The equipment of wisdom (*jñāna-sambhāra*), however, consists of the perfection of wisdom along with portions of the perfections of vigor and meditative concentration. Because all of these are indistinguishable in their being like an illusion, they constitute the state of a Tathāgata.

Having gained an extraordinary degree of serene confidence through the correct awakening to the Dharma, Śakra and the others manifest the majesty of the Mother, preceded by prostrations at the feet of the Blessed One; thus he says:
Then, indeed, Śakra and so forth:
therein, [the Dharma] is profound because its intrinsic nature is the suchness (*tathatā*) of form and the other aggregates;
it is difficult to fathom, difficult to see, and difficult to realize, respectively, because it is like an illusion during the stages of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
"This too is for the sake of the purpose" means that by the word "also," it is not only the non-grasping of those to be trained, but rather this profoundity of the Dharma is also seen.
"In [the state of] little zeal" means that the mind is inclined toward inactivity.
The sense is that although there was no request for a teaching of the Dharma, the wheel of Dharma was nonetheless set in motion out of great compassion due to the entreaty of Brahmā.
Repeating this as something well said, he says:
"It is so," and so forth.
He speaks for the purpose of concluding [the discourse]:
"Profound indeed is this," and so forth.
[The opponent asks: "What is this profundity? and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "where there is nothing whatsoever," etc.,
he speaks thus while describing the nature that is contrary to all the world:
"by virtue of its profundity like space," and so forth.
It is profound because its cause is delightful only when not subjected to analytical investigation, being as deep as space;
it is profound because, in reality, its nature as an effect is like an illusion, being as deep as the self;
it is profound because, due to the absence of arising, all phenomena do not arrive [from anywhere].
It is profound because all phenomena do not arrive due to their destruction and separation.
This is what was said:
"I have realized the Dharma, which is preceded by the realization of the nature of cause and effect as being like a dream, and whose intrinsic nature is the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising."
"...is taught as having been perfectly awakened.
Clarifying the very nature as it has been described, he says:
"It is marvelous," and so forth.
It is marvelous due to the excellence of its cause; it is wonderful due to the preeminence of its fruit;
and it is contrary to the entire world because it is opposed to all worldly views.
To explain that very point, he says:
"For the sake of non-apprehension," and so forth.
"This" refers to...
Consisting of the Perfection of Wisdom.
This is the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Gods," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The sixteenth chapter. Explaining the nature of non-obstruction, he says:
"Then, indeed, the Venerable... and so forth.
"‘This is not’ [means]:

because it is the perfect realization (*abhisamaya*) that completely fulfills the aspects of the three kinds of omniscience, the quality of knowledge regarding all things such as form and so forth is unimpeded; thus, this Dharma of teaching is not obstructed anywhere.
To express its nature as being without a basis (*apada*), he says:"
"Unobstructed," and so forth.
"Because of the non-apprehension of all bases" means that,
through the equality of knowledge and the object of knowledge, it has the characteristic of being unobstructed in the sense that no foundation whatsoever is apprehended.
He is not overcome;
because he is without a second, that is, because he is alone, he possesses a peerless characteristic.
It is characterized by similarity.
It is "without an adversary" because it has completely transcended all opposing factors; thus, it is characterized by being beyond opposition.
It has the characteristic of being an antidote;
because it is not produced,
it is unborn and trackless.
Its intrinsic nature is that of a firm foundation.
Because it is the non-arising of all forms of rebirth, it is non-production; for its form exists as that which abides in all states of existence, such as those of the gods and so forth.
"Because all paths are unapprehendable": since it is not apprehended as being any path whatsoever, it is "no-path" (apatha), meaning it is not a path.

Regarding the term "without station" (apada), five terms beginning with "of unimpeded character" are employed for the purpose of distinguishing [it] from the application, vision, cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning.
Speaking of the nature of non-origination, he says:
"Truly, this one is born after [the Buddha]," and so forth.
This refers to a disciple related to the Blessed One.
Because he was born later, he is like the Tathāgata; thus he is "born after" (anujāta).
How is it that even a disciple is "born after" like the Tathāgata?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason? he says:
"For thus, O Blessed One," and so forth.
Because he teaches every single dharma—even those whose objects are not yet realized—by means of perfect emptiness.

Therefore, the meaning is that he is born after [the Tathāgata], just like the Tathāgata himself. To dismantle the notion that this "being born after" refers to the nature of things (*vastudharmatva*), he says:
"O sons of the gods," and so forth.
"Because of being unborn":

because he is unarisen in reality, Subhūti, the disciple of the Tathāgata, is "unborn"; he has followed after that very suchness (tathatā) and has attained it, having conformed to it through identity.
"Because it is designated as 'suchness' (*tathatā*) precisely because it exists in that way (*tathābhāva*), its [the suffix -tā] is short," says Master Vasubandhu.
He asks, "How so? and replies with the words beginning, "Just as the Tathāgata," and so forth.
"Thus indeed Subhūti":

because he has followed the suchness of the Tathāgata by way of the suchness just described, he is therefore "born after" (anujāta) due to being unborn; this is how the connection with the preceding [text] should be made.
The same should be understood for what follows.
To the question, "If through the practice of yoga one attains that suchness (*tattathatā*), how could it not be born as the very nature of things (*vastudharmatva*)?", he says:
"From the very beginning," and so forth.
"From the beginning" means precisely from the very first.
"This is indeed without logical justification."
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because that which is... and so forth, concluding with "...is the suchness of all phenomena."
This means that there is no production of the common characteristics of form and so forth, which are regarded as substantial entities.
Thus, through the mutual non-differentiation between the Tathāgata and the suchness of all phenomena, it is made known that the suchness of the Tathāgata has all things as its object.
And for this reason, he says that it belongs to Subhūti as well:
"And which... and so forth.
Therefore, he is said to be "born after" because of his connection with the attainment of suchness (*tathatā*).
He says, "In that case, suchness (*tathatā*) would be substantially existent," and so forth, beginning with "And that too...
and "Not suchness."

Since a negation of that which lacks an object is untenable, even suchness is conventional and like an illusion; this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "born after the Tathāgata," the accusative case is used due to its connection with the prefix *anu*.
In the reading "of the Tathāgata," a connection with him is intended.
To the question, "If [the Buddha] is in reality of the nature of *dharmatā*, how is he 'born after'? he says:
"Of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
Regarding "stability":
it is the nature of continuity according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
If that were so, the Elder Subhūti would be subject to transformation and so forth; thus he says:
"Like the Tathāgata," and so forth.
In that regard, because there is an absence of increase, decrease, or transformation, they are respectively "unchanging" (*avikāra*) and "immutable" (*nirvikāra*).
Because of the separation from the conceptual constructions of self and other, they are "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*) and "beyond conceptualization" (*nirvikalpa*).
Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of Subhūti, why is it that its intrinsic nature is unchanging and so forth?
He asks: "Why is this so?"
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"And that which is the suchness of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
Because this is one alone—undifferentiated—there is no distinction between the object of division, the agent, and the action.
Because of non-apprehension, it is non-dual, without division, and the suchness of non-duality; thus the distinction in meaning must be stated.
In no way [is it established], because it lacks a substratum anywhere;
nor from anything, because of the absence of a cause; nor from a related entity...
It belongs to no sentient being whatsoever.
However, because it would entail being a functional entity (*vastu*) through its relation to things such as kinship, it would not be *tathatā* (suchness) itself; thus he says:
"Since that... and so forth.
"Thus indeed is Subhūti.

Because the suchness of all phenomena and the suchness of the Tathāgata possess this same single nature, and because they are subsumed within the suchness of the Tathāgata, the suchness of Subhūti has a nature that is unchanging and so forth;
therefore, it is by means of unconditioned suchness—
The meaning is "not born after.
If it is asked: "If all [beings] are not born after in the form of suchness (*tathatā*), what is the distinction of Subhūti?"
True;
however, it is precisely that which has become the subject of dispute which is being pointed out.
Otherwise, how could one who composes a sentence that fails to refine the understanding of the listener not be considered insane?
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"That which is unconditioned suchness," and so forth;
"it is never not suchness."
The meaning is that it is always suchness (*tathatā*). Concluding, he says: "Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is everywhere," and so forth.
"In all cases" means at all times.
"Manifested" means brought forth or accomplished.
Regarding the term "aluptam" (unlost): that which is lost is unperceived and unseen; "unlost" means not lost, that is to say, seen and perceived.
Regarding the phrase "due to the non-perception of a differentiator": [it refers to the fact that no distinction is observed].

Because suchness possesses a single nature established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because no valid cognition is found that differentiates it, both [the two] just mentioned are non-different; thus, this is not lost.
However, while the suchness of the Tathāgata consists of the suchness of all phenomena, the suchness of Subhūti is not of that same kind.
Therefore, he asks: "How could the two be non-different through suchness? and says:
"Such as the suchness of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
The particle *nānyatra* is used here in the sense of the nominative case.
As it has been said:
It may be so.
Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is not other than the suchness of all phenomena, but rather is of that very nature, so too is the suchness of Subhūti.
It is not the suchness of nothing; the meaning is that it is the suchness of everything.
He says that very thing with the words "That very same [is it]," and so forth; that which is the suchness (tathatā) of Subhūti.
That very [nature] is to be understood as the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "by following non-other suchness":
by conforming to the suchness that is the intrinsic nature of the self, he has approached that suchness which abides in all phenomena.
If it is asked, "How is there a conformity [to reality] by virtue of having suchness as its intrinsic nature? he says:
"And not here," and so forth.
This designation has been made merely from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, in this state of being like an illusion, no entity whatsoever has attained any correspondence or similarity anywhere.

The suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena belonging to the three times is constant throughout the three periods; the suchness of the Tathāgata, however, because it is free from arising due to its natural luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaratva*), is not of that same nature.
If it is asked how there can be identity between these two, he says:
"Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
In that regard, because there is no destruction preceded by arising, it is not past.
It is not future because it is dissociated from arising that is yet to be; it is not present because it is impossible for it to have attained existence.
Thus is the suchness of all phenomena.

The meaning is that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) establishing the nature of being like an illusion is equal in all cases. Or, even if there is a designation of that suchness (tattathatā) as pertaining to the three times by way of the distinctions of the adventitious attributes of conventional entities, nevertheless, there is indeed no difference between the Tathāgata and the suchness of all phenomena; thus he says:
"By the suchness of the Tathāgata as well," and so forth.
It is not only by means of the suchness of the self, but also by means of the suchness of the Tathāgata;
for having attained suchness, Subhūti [is identical] with that very suchness of the Tathāgata.
He has followed the suchness of the past and so forth,
and through the suchness of the past and so forth, he has followed the suchness of the Tathāgata; therefore, the sense is that there is no differentiation within liberation.

Furthermore, the four modes of extraction (*hāraka*) should be understood through the distinctions of the individual and collective [categories] such as the past and so forth. Concluding [the section], he says:
"For thus, Subhūti, suchness... and so on.

In response to the doubt of someone who might think, "Since the states of a bodhisattva and a Tathāgata are indeed different in form, how can suchness have the nature of being non-different from all phenomena? he says:
"And that which is... and so forth, concluding with "this is that suchness."

Because it possesses a single nature at all times, that suchness (tathatā) is logically established by which one attains perfect awakening through the removal of all types of adventitious defilements.
Those things which do not possess a nature of being either one or many have no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha).

Just as entities asserted by ourselves and others do not possess a nature of being either one or many—due to the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*)—so too is the Tathāgata like an illusion; this is the meaning.

The reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because the activity of discerning persons is pervaded by having a purpose, and thus investigation concerns only those things capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*).

For men who seek effective action (*arthakriyā*), what purpose is served by investigations into objects that are non-existent? Therefore, an entity that performs effective action must be admitted. Furthermore, since it consists of mutual exclusion (*anyonyavyavaccheda*), there is the following alternative: it must be either of the nature of the knowable (*jñeya*) or of the nature of cognition (*jñāna*).

In that regard, if the first position is held, then there would be either a nature of mutual conjunction, or else [the atom] would be surrounded by many atoms of the same kind—either separated from one another, their own forms not yet fused, and held apart by their mutual capacities, or else without intervals; thus there are three positions. Among these, regarding the first position: if there were a conjunction with one [atom] by means of a single part...
At that time, there would follow the consequence of the other [atom] having parts, resulting in the loss of its unity because of its contact with other atoms through various distinct natures;
even in the case of conjunction by way of its entire self, when the former...

When one atom is conjoined with another atom in its entirety, then the latter is also conjoined with the former; thus, because conjunction depends upon both entities, there is an interpenetration of their mutual natures, and consequently, no atom possesses a single, unitary nature.
For instance, the preceding atom is conjoined with the succeeding atom in its entirety.
Since it would have to abandon its own nature entirely to assume the nature of the other, that which is being conjoined would be non-existent;

likewise, since the other also conjoins with the former, it would have to abandon its own nature entirely to become the nature of the former, and thus that which serves as the locus of conjunction would be non-existent.

Furthermore, since affirmation and negation characterized by mutual exclusion cannot coexist in a single entity at one time, how could there be a single nature? Even in the second alternative, the position of being surrounded,

although contact with those of the same class is not desired, nevertheless, since an aperture consists of light and darkness, contact with heterogeneous atoms of light and darkness is indeed admitted.
For it is not logical that something which has not been pervaded by light should be devoid of darkness, nor that something which has not been made a locus for darkness should be devoid of light;
because the manifestation of those two is restricted solely to locations and so forth where they are mutually absent, the fault described immediately above consequently follows.

Now, if contact even with heterogeneous atoms is not admitted, then there are two alternatives regarding that central atom: does it face another atom with the very same nature by which it is situated facing one atom, or does it face it with a different nature?
In this regard, if the first position is held, then that which has a nature facing a single-form atom is a single part.
For example, the atom situated in the eastern direction relative to that very same atom.
And all surrounding atoms have a nature facing a single atom; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Because it is accepted that [the atoms] exist with that very same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is no lack of proof (*asiddhatā*). Because they exist in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there is no contradiction (*viruddhatā*). However, if they were situated in different locations, they could not possess an intrinsic nature directed toward a single intended atom, because that atom lacks other successive intrinsic natures, and because it is impossible for something to be "facing" [another] by means of an intrinsic nature that does not exist. Therefore, the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*). Consequently, since there would be no surrounding arrangement, it follows that the surrounding atoms would occupy the same location in reality.

In the absence of aggregation, it is not logical to admit that the atom possesses a single nature, precisely because it would lack the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) to be accomplished by it. However, in the second case, since the atom would be joined with various other natures facing various other atoms, there clearly follows the consequence of its having parts, which entails the loss of its unity.
This is because the distinction between entities is characterized by a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).

As for the third position—that of immediate contiguity—it follows the very same position as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), since it is a synonym for it; for there is no way other than mutual contact for things that lack any intervening space.
Furthermore, that very same object does not become something else when expressed by a different word, for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Now, suppose it is held that the atom remains unconnected [to a spatial direction], yet it is surrounded on all sides by many other atoms situated in proximate and remote locations which are denoted by the term "direction."
That is incorrect;
for in the absence of both prior and subsequent parts, this statement does not establish itself as meaningful in relation to anything else.

If it is argued that the form which is perceived when something is superimposed is non-existent there in its true nature—just as in the case of the distinction between "this side" (*pāra*) and "the other side" (*apāra*) according to the logical principle—and thus there is no real state of having parts (*sāvayavatva*) in the ultimate sense, we say: no.

Even in the case of "this side" and "the other side," for those who maintain the existence of external objects, their forms must be accepted as truly real because they do not intermingle due to the difference in relative perspective, just like the case of father and son.
For that which is "this side" in relation to one thing can never be "the other side" in relation to that same thing.
Otherwise, if both "this side" (pāra) and "the other side" (apāra) were not ultimately real, how could those situated on the banks designated as "this side" and "that side" exist without confusion?
For indeed, the "other-sideness" of the intended "this side" is said to consist precisely in its being other than what is considered "that side.
And if that [otherness] were merely imagined, it would follow that the two are identical.
And in that case, there would be no unmixed existence for those things dependent upon it;
for a distinction constructed by conceptualization is not a factor in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Now, because the existence of an object cannot be experienced through the power of cognition, the object is absolutely beyond perception; and because a specific effect arises by the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it is impossible to conceive of anything other than that [condition]. Therefore, non-dual knowledge—which is established in its own right, possesses a single nature, and is ultimately devoid of the relationship between apprehended and apprehender—is [the reality]. For if it were causeless, there would be the undesirable consequence of its being either eternally existent or non-existent; and if it were eternal, [there would be no production of effects].

Furthermore, because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth would otherwise be untenable, the Yogācāras maintain that cognition itself is the entity (*bhāva*). This [cognition] arises dependent upon its own causes and perishes immediately after arising; yet, due to the power of the maturation of the latencies (*vāsanā*) for the attachment to entities (*bhāvābhiniveśa*) occurring throughout beginningless existence, various forms (*ākāra*) appear therein.
Regarding this, there is a dilemma: are these forms ultimately real (*tāttvika*), or are they merely delightful when unexamined, like a reflection and the like?

If the first case is true, then because [the cognition] is not distinct from the multiple forms existing as real entities, multiplicity would accrue to the cognition just like the nature of those forms; so how could there be unity?

If, on the other hand, the unity of the cognition is determined by the fact that it is experienced all at once, then because the forms are not distinct from that single cognition, their unity—just like the nature of the cognition itself—would be unavoidable.
If it is argued that "let it be so," it is not so.

For if one form appears as qualified by movement and so forth, then the remaining forms also would necessarily be of that same nature, because their essential being is not distinct from the preceding form.

The experience of diverse forms is contradicted; therefore, the multiplicity of forms is absolute. Since the superimposition of mutually contradictory properties—unity and multiplicity—is thus established, the multiplicity of forms and consciousness remains ultimately real. Consequently, there is a loss of the accepted non-dual system. Alternatively, if one thinks that forms such as blue and so forth are of the nature of experience themselves—just like pleasure and the rest—and thus does not accept the variegated nature of a single [consciousness], then the aforementioned fault would not follow. Thinking this, [the opponent asserts] that even cognitions of the same kind...
It is described that many [cognitions] arise simultaneously, like cognitions of heterogeneous types.
In that case, there is this further fault:
for that cognition which is considered to be in the middle is held to resemble an atom surrounded [by others].
Now, there is a dilemma: does that by which one [atom] faces another do so by that very same nature, or by another?

If it is the former case—that it faces others by that very same nature—then, because there would be no surrounding arrangement [of atoms], the remaining atoms could not exist in other directions; consequently, since they would not arise in the divisions of directions such as east and west, the appearance of the spatial configuration of a blue circle or the like would not occur.

However, in the alternative view that [the difference between cognitions] is due to another [cognition], since the difference between entities is characterized by a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), how could there be unity? Thus, the same fault encountered in the analysis of atoms falls upon this position as well.
[Objection: But since cognitions are formless (*amūrta*), there can be no priority or posteriority based on spatial location; so how could cognitions occupy a central position like atoms?
[Reply: This is true.
Furthermore, let this other defect of his be noted:

by one who desires the reality of the forms appearing as spatially extended, it must be postulated that many cognitions—which, though themselves devoid of spatial location, exist—arise in such a way as to occupy a spatial extension.
For otherwise, if even when postulating the arising of multiple cognitions, the appearance of their arising as spatially extended were false, then...
The postulation of the arising of multiple cognitions would be entirely futile.
Furthermore, apart from the manifestation of blue and other objects as occupying spatial extension, no other experience of blue and so forth is perceived that could be real.
If that [manifestation] is unreal, what else could possibly be real? Thus, this [objection] is trivial.
If it is objected: "Even so, atoms are material (mūrta), whereas consciousness is immaterial (amūrta); how then can that same fault apply here?"—this is not a fault.
For it is precisely that blue and so forth, appearing in uninterrupted succession, that is accepted by some as being of the nature of a single atom.
In another case, the name alone— specifically "the nature of consciousness"— differs,
but there is no difference in the actual meaning characterized by the state of being situated in spatial contiguity.
Nor is it appropriate to attribute an equal fault by means of the mere application of a different name.
Rather, it is produced by the uninterrupted continuity of the teaching;
and since that [continuity] exists even when there is a difference in name alone, how could the fault not be equal?
Now, even if it is argued that because of the dissimilarity between cognition and the object of cognition, the defect residing in the object is accepted by the cognition,

we reply as follows: if multiple cognitions were to arise simultaneously, then the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) perceived as having objects such as a jar or a word would not be successive in its occurrence.
Nor can it be asserted that non-conceptual cognitions themselves arise simultaneously, because conceptual constructions arise by way of the ascertainment of their experience.

Consequently, since these conceptual constructions do not arise with an unperceived nature, there would follow the consequence of simultaneous ascertainment of experience; thus, the conceptual construction experienced as occurring sequentially would not exist, which contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Now, if it is thought that consciousness itself, though single, assumes a variegated form like the appearance of a multi-colored gem (*mecakamaṇi*), that is incorrect;
for that which is variegated cannot be one.
Just like the conditions existing within various [distinct] continuums;
and since this consciousness is variegated, there is the perception of a contradiction.
Because it is perceived as variegated, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
It is not contradictory because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
If it is asked, "How then is there a contradiction between variegation and unity, such that variegation would exclude unity? it is said in reply:
Indeed, there exists nothing else denoted by the term "variegated" (*citra*) apart from multiple intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).

Since multiplicity and unity are necessarily characterized by the mutual exclusion of their respective essential natures, they possess a contradiction defined by their existence as mutually exclusive states; thus, contradiction is established.

Furthermore, if two contradictory things were to share a single intrinsic nature, the entire universe would become a single substance, and consequently, the undesirable consequence of simultaneous arising and destruction would be unavoidable.
Otherwise, it would be merely a name, namely "one";
and since there is no dispute regarding a mere name, the reason is not inconclusive.
Furthermore, one should not say that the example—the appearance of a variegated gem—is unestablished.

For even in that case, since it would be of a single form, it would not be pervaded by manifold forms; thus, the appearance as manifold forms and so forth would be untenable, as the same objection applies equally.
Now, it might be argued:

The difference between a manifesting object such as blue and an entity situated in another place or time is not apprehended by perception; for since both are not manifesting [simultaneously], there is no grasping of the thought, "This is different from that.
Nor is there a cognition that "this is different from this manifesting [object]" when it is situated in the same place and time, because perception, being non-conceptual, does not grasp it.

Therefore, because the distinction between the grasper and the grasped, as well as among the objects of cognition themselves, is not apprehended, it is held that only a non-dual manifold appears in perception as a single form.
This too is refuted by the very same [argument]:
because it is contradictory for a single entity to possess manifoldness.
Furthermore, it is argued that even a variegated [object] is one because its acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are non-different.
That is incorrect, because its unity is contradicted by the fact that its forms are mutually excluded.

Nor is its state of having a distinct *yogakṣema* (acquisition and preservation) from this [other object] apprehended by perception; for if simultaneous appearance were of the nature of non-distinct *yogakṣema*, then even the difference in essential nature (*svarūpānyatva*) would appear.
How, then, could there not be an appearance of difference?

If non-duality is postulated because difference is not perceived, then why is duality not likewise postulated because identity— in the form "this is non-different from that"— is not perceived? Or, if it is argued that only the bare object, devoid of both difference and identity, is perceived,
then how is there the manifestation of blue and other such variegated appearances?

If a variegated appearance is admitted, that very thing is called the "appearance of difference" in the world; so how can there be a denial of difference? Now, if it is thought: "If these forms were indeed real in nature, then all this contradiction would arise."
To the extent that this consciousness is indeed like a pure crystal stone, not yet having attained the distinctions of forms such as blue and so forth— even in such a state,

due to the power of the maturation of the latencies of beginningless misconception (*viparyāsa-vāsanā*), there occurs the appearance of forms, just as an elephant, a horse, or the like appears to a person whose eyes are affected by spells and other factors when looking at a lump of clay and so on.
Thus, it is [the case] even when one accepts that, in ultimate reality, cognition is of a single form and a single entity.
"There is no contradiction because of their falsity, since by your pointing out the defects you are establishing the very falsity and oneness of the forms;
and that is already accepted by us.
This is incorrect.

For instance, that which is experienced as a form with an extremely clear aspect such as blue, well-known even to children, is unreal; whereas that non-dual cognition which is not so experienced and is distinct from the clearly manifest aspect is real.
What more eloquent statement than this could there be here? Why is it that such extremely clear awareness is impossible if [the object] were non-existent?
If it is argued that [it exists] in reality, it is said in reply:
if a form does not exist in a particular place, it cannot be cognized there.

Just as in the case of suffering, forms such as pleasure do not exist, and yet blue and other [colors] appear as consciousness—this is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Since the falsity of the forms has been established, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*); and since they exist in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is no contradiction (*viruddha*).

In that regard, if it is being proven that there would follow the consequence of non-cognition from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in a general sense.

Furthermore, one should not say: "In that case, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to express the presence of the probans (*sādhana-dharma*) when the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) is reversed, how could the reason (*hetu*) not have a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)?
For it is not the case that [the nature of] consciousness is being proved here in a general sense, nor is there any inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) here.
To explain: consciousness is of two kinds—primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*).
In this context, that which is primary is the non-inert form. And since that is the unique, self-constituted attribute of cognition itself, how could it belong to an unreal mental image?
For instance, that which is of the nature of non-cognition does not possess primary awareness.
It is like a lotus in the sky.

Furthermore, since forms such as blue and so forth—which are of the nature of ignorance—are apprehended as non-existent, this is a "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Even figuratively, [their existence] is not possible.
For it is precisely the production of a cognition appearing in its own form that is called "secondary apprehension.
And this is untenable for that which is non-existent and devoid of all causal capacity, such as a horse's horn,
because non-existence is defined by the absence of all capacity.
For instance, that which is incapable does not possess secondary cognition, just like a horse’s horn.
And forms such as blue and so forth, which are intended to be non-existent, are incapable; thus, there is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Since forms are unreal, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is not contradictory (*viruddha*).

Thus, since consciousness (*saṃvedana*) is pervaded by these two—primary and secondary—which are defined by their mutual exclusion, and because that pervader has ceased, there is necessarily the cessation of consciousness as well, which is pervaded by it; therefore, [the reason] "because of non-existence" does not apply to consciousness.
"There is no room [for this objection], so there is no lack of certainty.
If it is argued: "But surely, because even non-existent forms such as water are perceived in mirages and the like, there is indeed a lack of certainty," we say: No.

For even in that case, if the form of water and so forth exists neither internally nor externally, then how could there be a cognition of that which is absolutely non-existent? Thus, the objection is exactly the same.
Nor should it be said that they are experienced by the force of a causal connection (*pratibandha*);
for [if that were so], they would not possess the nature of cognition (*jñāna-svabhāva*).

Because it would follow that the mental aspects (ākāra) must exist in the same way as cognition (jñāna). Alternatively, if the nature of cognition is admitted to consist in the mental aspects, then it follows that cognition itself is non-existent, just like those aspects.
Furthermore, mental aspects cannot arise from cognition, because that which is formless cannot possess a produced form.
Nor [can it be known] from the forms themselves, because the forms of cognition are unreal and thus lack the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*).
Furthermore, there exists no relation other than identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
Consequently, that which has no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with something else is not necessarily perceived when the latter is perceived.

Just as when the nature of cognition is being experienced, the son of a barren woman does not exist; likewise, there is no twofold connection—characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*)—between cognition and the intended forms (*ākāra*). This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Since the absence of a relationship has already been established, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhatā*).
Because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is no contradiction (*viruddhatā*).
And because it would entail the consequence of all cognitions being perceived, the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*).
Therefore, since this form (*ākāra*) which you have postulated as existing simultaneously with the cognition is without a cause, how could there be any dependence?
In this case, the reason must be stated as being "occasional" due to its existence;
even for one who considers [the object] to be unreal (*alīka*)...

Just as for you there is the appearance of both cognition and the object of cognition by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), so too for us, even though it is unreal due to ignorance and unconnected to that [object], it appears as something other by way of conventional reality within a truly non-representational (*nirākāra*) cognition.
As for the claim that [the object] appears [as such],
this too has been refuted by the very same [argument].

For us, however, since we accept the relationship that cognition itself takes on the form of the cognizable (*jñeya*) from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), the appearance of those two is not contradictory.

Now, if it is accepted that [the object] possesses a cause so that this fault may not arise, then, because the aspects of the apprehended and the apprehender are dependently originated, they lack the status of being merely imagined; consequently, the nature of the dependent (paratantra-svabhāva) follows, since there is no dependence other than dependent origination.
Even if this is so, one might ask: how is ultimate existence obtained?

If this is argued, it is replied: For even in the case of consciousness, since its existence is not other than its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) arising from conditions, an ultimate existence that is inseparable from dependent origination is unavoidable.
Furthermore, if there were no cognition [of objects] either sequentially or simultaneously, it would result in the loss of the admitted falsity of the forms [of cognition].
Now, as for what has been stated...

If no form (*ākāra*) is admitted, then it follows that cognition, being always devoid of form, would be experienced by all living beings simply because it does not fail to meet the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāptatva*).
This might be the case;

indeed, it is experienced. However, due to the power of the delusion produced by the form that appears in experience, it does not meet the conditions for perception for those of limited vision (*arvāgdṛś*); therefore—
It is incorrect to say that because it lacks the certainty of being perceived as experienced, there is no perception of it, just as there is none of a single moment;

for if internal or external forms were possible, then— due to the power of the delusion produced by the cognition of those forms— it might be the case that they do not ascertain the knowledge even though it exists.
But when neither internal nor external things exist, then by whose experience could they be deceived, such that— even though experiencing non-duality— they would not ascertain it?
Now, if this view is held:
"It is the very nature of error that it displays unreal forms; therefore, even though the form is non-existent, its perception will occur by virtue of error. This too is incorrect.
For, by the word "error" (bhrānti), one must mean either a state of cognition that serves as the cause for the latent impression (vāsanā) arising from a delusion, or—
Alternatively, it might be said that the effect is merely an erroneous cognition produced by such latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Regarding these two positions, in the first case, since the forms are not necessarily connected to that cause, their perception through its power would be illogical, as it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle.

Nor is it correct to say that there exists a causal relation (pratibandha) characterized by origination from that [the object], because— as in the previous case— it would entail a state of dependence on another.

Furthermore, regarding the second alternative, even if a relation were to exist there, it would be characterized by identity (tādātmya) among the mental aspects, not by origination from that [object], since they are experienced simultaneously with it.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for two things existing at the same time to stand in the relation of cause and effect, the consequence that [the imagined nature] is dependent—because it is not distinct from that [dependent nature], just like an illusion—is unavoidable; therefore, this argument is trivial.
It might be argued as follows:
[It might be argued: "Because the forms of the delusory grasped and grasper are absent, self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) in states such as deep sleep will be real, being of a single nature.
That is incorrect; for if mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as its object...
Furthermore, because it does not apprehend mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) exclusively, it possesses a variegated nature through the discernment of the [mental] aggregate. Now,

even if the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), together with its associated states, is determined to be devoid of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper,
it nevertheless rushes toward variegation itself.
For you accept that the latent predispositions of error exist;
or else, [you might say] they do not— thus there are two alternatives.
If the first [alternative] is held, then ignorance (*avidyā*) is simply the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the adherence to false forms; and that impression is said to be a causal potency (*śakti*).

Since this potency is essentially identical with the cognition that serves as its cause, the subsequent effect—which consists of an adherence to false forms—arises from each preceding cognition that functions as its cause. Thus, by virtue of ignorance, it appears in such a manner, and by this very force, its manifold nature (*citratva*) is established.
Nor should it be said that there is no restriction [regarding the object] based on the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*);
for the claim that consciousness as previously described is itself the immediately preceding condition is trivial.
If it is argued that in that case the potencies consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are distinct, we say: no.
Because the multiple real capacities are not distinct from [consciousness], multiplicity would simultaneously accrue to consciousness just as it does to the nature of its capacities;
and in that case, the aforementioned fault applies.

Likewise, because the capacities are not distinct from a single cognition, the oneness of the capacities—just like the nature of cognition itself—is unavoidable; thus, how could there be a distinction between the immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?

Now, if the second position—that [consciousness] is not [of that nature]—is held, then the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that all embodied beings would be liberated without effort and so forth would be unavoidable.

Alternatively, if it is argued that all cognition of an ordinary person proceeds without having undergone the coloring (uparāga) of forms such as blue and so on, then the consequence of losing its unity will not arise;

because it is of a non-variegated nature, it is established as having the nature of the cognition of blue and so on, yet this is due to its being the nature of that cognition and not due to its assuming the form of blue and so on.
For indeed, the mode of apprehending the object is itself the aspect (*ākāra*), and not a resemblance to that [object].
As for the fact that blue and so forth appear as if external, it is not because they are aspects of cognition;
rather, while experiencing the cognition that perceives blue and so forth, the cognizer, through delusion, determines that blue and so forth to have an external form.
This too is false.
For instance, if there were no connection whatsoever with the blue object and so forth, how could there be a cognition of the blue and so forth?
Indeed, apart from assuming that likeness (*tādrūpya*), there is no other way for inactive cognition to grasp an object.
An aspect is not established by means of a resemblance that exists apart from the production of that likeness,
for that would lead to an over-extension;
rather, it is precisely through the production of that likeness that the cognition is perceived as possessing an operation, and that alone is called its mode of apprehending the object.
And the fault in that case has already been stated.
If it is argued that "blue and so forth do not exist at all in any way," this is not so.

For instance, it must be explained: if blue and so forth exist neither internally nor externally, how is it that this is experienced so vividly in a non-conceptual consciousness? Nor can it be said that it does not appear at all, because its appearance is established by the experience of everyone.
Nor is it logical that what appears with vivid clarity should be the object of conceptual construction, such that it could be said by a deluded person, "It is apprehended in that way. Furthermore,
if it is still maintained that it is apprehended by conceptual construction even in this manner, that is incorrect.

Because if all cognition were experienced as being entirely devoid of form, then even a subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would be unable to determine a specific form such as blue, due to the absence of any necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
If it is argued that this is simply the nature of error (*bhrānti*), [we reply:]...

It has been stated here that, given the consequence of [the object] being dependent on another (*paratantra*), how could there be a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for this [cognition] with respect to an error?

Therefore, because such a connection is absent, it is untenable that there can be a cognition of non-existent things like blue even by way of being an object of conceptual construction (*vikalpaviṣayatayā*).
If this is so, then let it be that in the impure state, cognition is indeed false, appearing in a variegated form.
"In the state of complete purity, because error has vanished, it will possess a single nature consisting solely of non-duality. To this it is replied:
"If, in the impure state, all cognition were indeed false,"
Then, it must be explained how that form of truth arises in the pure state;
for it is not logical for a form of truth to arise from what is false,
because the latter lacks the capacity [to produce it].
Or, if it possesses causal efficacy, how could it be false? If even such a thing were false, how could anything else be true?
Therefore, that [arising] would be entirely without cause;
and that is untenable, because it would entail the consequence of its being eternally existent and so forth.
Nor should it be said that [it ceases] due to the disappearance of delusion.
For if the cessation of all mental aspects were possible in the state of purification, then this [conclusion] would indeed be conceivable;
however, even when error ceases, the cessation of the aspects is not possible,
because there is no necessary connection between them according to the reasoning already stated.

Furthermore, in the absence of a necessary connection (*apratibandha*), the cessation of one thing does not entail the certain cessation of another, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), like the case of a cow and a horse.
Moreover, it might be argued that for someone, non-dual knowledge—devoid of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and singular—will exist by its very nature (*nisargasiddha*); but that is incorrect.
For if it were established by nature, then because it would not depend on the assumption of a specific substratum, such an existence would never cease for anyone.
And consequently, there would be a contradiction with [the principles of] dependent origination and so forth.
It might be argued:

"That nature of the cause is such that, because it arises through the power of each preceding moment of its counteragent, it will belong to some [effect] alone by virtue of having a nature dependent upon specific causes."
This does not shine at all;

for, by establishing the formlessness (*nīrūpatā*) of everything through the aforementioned rules, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is ultimately untenable— thus, this is merely something trivial.

Therefore, when it is investigated, not even a single part-like intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities is established as being unitary because it lacks parts; in that case, how could a plurality be established, since plurality consists of a collection of those [parts]?
Thus, the reason is not unestablished.

Now, it might be argued that the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*)— due to the absence of both a single and a manifold nature— in everything that appears does not manifest through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),

because this [perception] has only existent things as its object; nor does it manifest through inference (*anumāna*), because there is no perception to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) required for inference,
and if it were grasped by inference, [there would be an infinite regress].
If it is asked, "How is the reason established, given that there is no proof because [the pervasion] does not reside in nine ways? We say:

No. For it has been demonstrated that, by means of the combined methods of inference, the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) is pervaded by the state of being devoid of both a single and a manifold intrinsic nature.
And among those [methods], the pervasion of at least one inference is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For someone, it is apprehended through an inference whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been grasped by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, since the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is ascertained by its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could there be an infinite regress?
Because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), it is not contradictory (*viruddha*).

For instance, if the aforementioned reason were to reside in an ultimate intrinsic nature (*pāramārthikasvabhāva*) by proving the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*), [then it would be contradictory].

In that case, how could a reason that is restricted to its object by way of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) possibly apply elsewhere—to a form such as *māyā* which lacks a real nature because it cannot withstand the scrutiny of investigation?
For this would entail the loss of its status as a property of a real entity (*bhāvadharma*). Thus, how can the reason be considered contradictory (*viruddha*) with respect to the well-known example?

Now, it might be thought: "For me, the very example adduced does not possess both properties; for while illusion and the like are admitted to exist as real entities (*vastu-sattva*) in the form of consciousness, [the property of being non-existent] is not established. Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)."

That is incorrect; for thus, the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) has been established through the methods of inference as previously described for all cognitions that are considered to be real entities.
Therefore, the existence of things is not perceived by the power of one's own whim.

Therefore, this objection— that because even things like illusions, though sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), are established as having the nature of consciousness, the example would be unestablished (*asiddha*)—
is of no consequence. This might be so,
provided that their existence in both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) were established.
But how is the exclusion of the reason from the counter-example (vipakṣa) ascertained, such that it does not become vitiated by the fault of a doubtful negative concomitance (sandigdhavyatireka)?
It is said:
For when the determination of one thing is inseparable from the exclusion of another form, that [latter] is defined by its standing in the avoidance of the former.
For example, existence is a determination that is inseparable from the exclusion of non-existence;
and likewise, unity and plurality are determinations that are inseparable from the mutual exclusion of each other's nature. Therefore, they are characterized by existing through mutual exclusion.

Furthermore, those two things which are defined by their existence through mutual exclusion—since the affirmation of one is inseparable from the negation of the other—lead to the understanding that there is no third category.
This is just like the case of existence and non-existence.

And since oneness and manyness are likewise defined by their existence through mutual exclusion, then, because there is no third category, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is encompassed by oneness and manyness; thus, the reason indeed exists in the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaye*).
How, then, can there be room for the aforementioned fault regarding "exclusion" (*vyatireka*)?

But surely, in this case, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it is a part of the very meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatva*); for since the nature of "one" and "many" consists in the differentiation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is indeed no difference between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), which are respectively their opposites.

And therefore, if the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), then the reason (*hetu*) is also unestablished because it is of a nature non-different from that [probandum]. If, on the other hand, the reason is established, then the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of entities is also established. For no one accepts that things such as a rabbit's horn—which lack both unity and plurality—possess the nature of an existent entity (*bhāvasvabhāvarūpatā*). Thus, if you argue this.
That is incorrect;
for it has been demonstrated in detail how the reason (*hetu*) is established,
and once that is established—

Even if non-substantiality (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) is established by way of a positive formulation (*vidhirūpatayā*), nevertheless, because the adherence to things as real is difficult to abandon, one who is deluded fails to produce certainty regarding the non-substantiality that truly pervades all things. Therefore, for the sake of such a person, the proof establishes the fitness for conventional usage (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*) of the lack of intrinsic nature in all entities; thus, there is no fault of the reason being a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*), just as in the case of non-existence [established] through the non-perception of what has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta-anupalambha*). This is not to be challenged.

Now, if it is insisted that, for the sake of conventional practice, the very absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) must first be established with respect to the deluded person, we reply as follows: when the actual cessation of intrinsic nature is established through the exclusion of unity and plurality— which are the pervaders of intrinsic nature— just as the exclusion of a *śiṃśapā* tree follows from the exclusion of "tree."
In that case, how could the reason (hetu) be a part of the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā)?
For there is no synonymy between two statements regarding the exclusion of the pervaded (vyāpya) and the pervader (vyāpaka), which consist in distinct forms of exclusion;
nor can that which is not synonymous be a part of the meaning of the proposition. Thus, this [objection] is trivial.
Is it not the case that the qualification "from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthataḥ*) is redundant?
For, since a non-contradictory reasoning (*nyāya*) is the ultimate reality, the term "ultimate reality" denotes the cognition produced by a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*).
In that case, since even that [cognition] has the nature of a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), how can it possess the status of ultimate reality?
And if the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of entities is established on the basis of that [cognition], then from what source is the status of that cognition itself to be established?
It is not logical for it to be established by that very [means] itself,
because of the contradiction of something acting upon itself;
nor can it be established by another means of valid cognition.

Because it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress. If, on the other hand, that single cognition is set aside and established as the basis, then the selflessness of all objects has not been demonstrated.

This is well said; however, because it is concordant with the ultimate reality (paramārtha) which is devoid of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), the aforementioned cognition possesses the nature of ultimate reality, and its lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) follows from that very fact.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction regarding its occurrence within itself, since the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena is established by way of their universal form (sāmānyarūpeṇa).

And since that nature of the cognition itself is included within that universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), just as the cognition of perishability regarding all phenomena— arising from causes such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth— does not exclude itself, so too the very nature of things (*bhāvasvabhāva*),
which is delightful only when unexamined because it is devoid of superimposed forms such as real production and so on, is expressed by the term "lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

And since that intrinsic nature of an entity is perceptible, its lack of intrinsic nature—which is of the same nature as it—is also directly perceived; just as when a floor is perceived as distinct from a jar, the absence of the jar, which constitutes its very essence, is perceived.
Otherwise, because their conditions for existence and cessation would be separate, their non-difference would be lost.
Consequently, an entity would not be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), because there is no connection with the state of being devoid of intrinsic nature;
nor can that connection be characterized by origination from it, since, being a non-entity, that state cannot be an effect.
Therefore, since that [natureless state] is not apprehended through direct perception by the foolish, there is sublation by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*).

Likewise, because it is fit for the conventional usage of non-existence—just like a jar—due to its non-apprehension despite meeting the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptānupalabdhi*), it simply does not exist; thus, there is sublation by inference (*anumānabādha*).

If it is argued that, just as the moon’s lack of being the moon is evident even to commoners down to cowherds, the refutation by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) is likewise unavoidable because of the failure to perceive the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) [in phenomena],
that is incorrect.
For, the absence of intrinsic nature in entities is said to be their being devoid of any superimposed form.
And although that [nature] is indeed grasped by the apprehension of the intrinsic nature of things,
it is not ascertained by the foolish because its true form is obscured by an appearance of arising and so forth that has been superimposed through delusion— just like momentariness.
Therefore, since ascertainment is impossible and thus there is an absence of perceptibility, there is no sublation by perception.
Even though it is thus apprehended, because it is unfit for conventional usage, it is as good as unapprehended; therefore, it does not meet the criteria for perception,
and consequently, there is no sublation by inference.

Furthermore, because of the qualification "from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no sublation by cognition (*pratītibādha*) through the non-denial of the perception of existence; thus, this [objection] is trivial. Nor should it be asked, "How can a form be superimposed by that [cognition] since an objectless error (*nirbījabhrānti*) is impossible?
For what connection could there be between a false error and that which is real?
It cannot be of the same nature as that [the object], because the real and the false are contradictory;
nor can it arise from it, because the false is not an effect.
