Therefore, it is not contradictory for its prior cause to be merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) material.
For that cause as well, there is another preceding cause that is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).
Since such a succession of causes is beginningless, delusion is never without a substratum (*anupādāna*).
If it is asked how there is such a specific determination (*pratiniyama*):
It is said: Just like the nature of an ultimately real entity (*tāttvika-bhāva*), this very same intrinsic nature belongs to the conventional (*sāṃvrta*) as well—
namely, that which is dependent upon other conventional causes and is designated as a specific conventional cause-and-effect relationship.
If it is asked, "In what sense, then, is it conventional (*sāṃvṛtta*)?"—
it is because a thing that is indeed capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*) is called "conventional" due to its inability to withstand analytical scrutiny.
For instance, the entire aggregate of things is pervaded by both the real (*tathya*) and the unreal (*atathya*), since these two are characterized by mutual exclusion.
And since the state of having a real nature has been refuted, it follows by implication that these [entities] must abide in the other [state, namely, being devoid of intrinsic nature].
Therefore, there is no fault, as this very form [of being devoid of intrinsic nature] has been accepted by all things themselves.

Now, one might object: "Since a desired object cannot be established without a reason, you who undertake the adoption of a reason in order to prove the lack of intrinsic nature in all phenomena have thereby admitted the existence of that [reason], which contradicts your thesis of the lack of intrinsic nature in all phenomena."
Furthermore, [to claim] "non-existence" involves a contradiction with one's own words, like the proposition that "one's own mother is barren," because these are mutually contradictory.
For it is not from that very same reason that the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established,
since there is a contradiction in something acting upon itself.
Nor [can it arise] from another, because that would entail the fallacy of infinite regress; if you say this, we reply: no, for there is an absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā).
Furthermore, because the answer has already been stated in the passage beginning with "And for that very reason," there is no contradiction with scripture,

since— even though things lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*)— the relationship between action and its fruit is established by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Thus, there is no contradiction with that [scripture].
Nor should it be raised as an objection.

Now, if it is thought: "For one who maintains the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvavādin*), since all objects are non-existent, defects such as the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*) are difficult to avoid."
That is incorrect.

For indeed, the entire conventional practice of inference and the object of inference proceeds by relying upon a subject (*dharmin*) as it is perceived even by ordinary people, while abandoning the distinctions of properties (*dharmabheda*) imposed by mutually contradictory tenets.
The reason (*hetu*) is established as being invariably concomitant with that [subject], and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is likewise.

Otherwise, if the reason (*hetu*), the property (*dharma*), or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) were based on a particular tenet (*siddhānta*), then a subject (*dharmī*) qualified by a qualification established only in one tenet would be unestablished for the other party because it is the locus of dispute; thus, due to the non-establishment of the qualified subject, the reason would be "unestablished in its substratum" (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Likewise, if the essential nature [of the reason] is unestablished, the subject of the example is also unestablished; thus, because there would be a total absence of cognition of fire, impermanence, and so forth from the existence of smoke and the like, the entire practice of establishing the probandum by means of the probans would be annihilated.
This objection is trivial, since some form of mere consciousness—excluded from such forms as non-cognition and so forth—is indeed established.
It might be argued as follows:
for one who employs a proof (sādhana) to negate a superimposed aspect by relying upon a subject (dharmin) that is actually appearing,
defects such as the unestablished nature of the basis (āśrayāsiddhatā) do not apply.
But you [the opponent] negate the subject (*dharmin*) precisely as it appears;
how then can those [fallacies], such as the unestablished basis (*āśrayāsiddha*), not apply?
It is not so, for there is the qualification "from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthataḥ*).

It is the same [in both cases]: when a subject (*dharmin*) appears, what is being proven is the negation of an imputed real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and not the negation of the essential nature of the subject itself.
Now, if it is thought: "If the ultimate intrinsic nature is negated, what else remains?"
The claim that "the form of that subject (dharmin) must appear" is also incorrect;
for appearance is not pervaded by ultimate intrinsic nature (pāramārthika-svabhāva), such that it would cease upon the cessation of that [ultimate nature].
Even though [objects] such as a double moon or a mass of hair are unreal, they nonetheless appear;
nor can it be argued that although the double moon and so forth are unreal in their external form,
they are nevertheless ultimately real in their nature as cognition, and thus their appearance is logical— because they appear with a variegated form and as being situated in space.

A single cognition cannot be variegated, because that would entail the loss of its unity; nor can it be multiple, since the arising of multiple cognitions has already been refuted. Furthermore, it cannot reside in space, because [cognition] is formless.

Therefore, the double moon and such are not ultimately real. Thus, if the ultimate nature [of the object] is negated, the fact that they nevertheless appear is contradictory; hence, the acceptance of an entity as being ultimately real [is required].
It is not to be performed;
nor can there be an admission of non-existence, because that [non-existence] is characterized by the cessation of existence,
and when existence is unestablished, the negative particle (*nañ*) would be without an object.

Since a negation cannot function when there is no object to be negated by means of its application, and since that [negation] which is preceded by such an object is likewise unestablished, the defects that arise from the positions of absolute existence or non-existence do not attach to us.
Consequently, the claim that— because they consist in mutual exclusion— the affirmation of one thing necessarily follows by force of logic upon the negation of the other, is inconsistent.
Because, in reality, there is no entity to be excluded that has the nature of a positive existence (*bhāva*).

And thus, since there is an absence of both the nature of existence and non-existence, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which functions either directly or indirectly with respect to cognition and its object—is in no way real; this is established.
Nor should it be thought that [conceptual construction] arises from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) even in the absence of the nature of existence and non-existence.
Even so, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) having that as its object arises like the conceptual construction of a hare’s horn and the like.
For even if it is not directly dependent upon an external object,

there is nonetheless a dependence characterized by its arising, because it is produced through the awakening of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) that is non-distinct from that [external object] within a preceding cognition.

It may indeed be so; for when a cognition arises at the same time [as its object], there is a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) because [the object] is not distinct from it. Thus, the conceptual image (*vikalpārūḍhapratibimba*) is engaged with through affirmation and negation in some manner.

For, according to the method described above, since there is no cognition produced by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is an absence of that conceptual image; consequently, because no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises, how could there be a conceptualization regarding the nature of existence or non-existence? This is what must be stated.

By this, that which some describe is refuted: namely, that for a discerning person, it is appropriate to adhere to an object established by valid cognition as being true, and to regard anything else as false.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of losing one's status as a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*). Therefore, since the adherence to the reality or unreality [of things] is difficult to abandon, how can all errors be eliminated?
That too has been answered:
because adherence is not distinct in form from cognition, in the absence of that [cognition], how could adherence be logically tenable?

Thus, since all conceptualization is pervaded by the conceptualizations of existence and non-existence, and because that which is pervaded cannot exist in the absence of its pervader, one who examines with the eye of wisdom all phenomena—according to the sequence of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—as being devoid of any ultimate reflection on existence or non-existence, delightful only when unexamined, lacking any external core like the trunk of a plantain tree, and resembling a plantain stalk; for such a person, upon the perfection of the power of cultivation, all causes of delusion are dispelled, just as in the case of the cognition of the true nature of a gem.

Thus, by virtue of grasping the object as it truly is, that which is inherently authoritative arises as the conventional light of knowledge— self-cognized as the nature of non-dual wisdom resembling an illusion, produced from pure conventional causes, and having great compassion and wisdom as its essence through the abandonment of all perversions; by the very nature of dependent origination, the seed of conceptual construction does not arise again.

And thus, as for what is said by some— that ignorance is destroyed by knowledge, and that knowledge is the cognition of reality as it is— even if the Tathāgata’s knowledge were, according to you, conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), then since that knowledge would be of the nature of ignorance, how could there be the cessation of ignorance in the absence of the arising of [true] knowledge, as long as ignorance persists?
"How can there be liberation as long as [ignorance] has not been abandoned?"— this is inconsistent. For ignorance is the cognition of superimposed properties such as permanence and so forth.
However, the cognition of a property that is not sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) contrary to that [ignorance] is "knowledge" (*vidyā*).

The distinction between these two—based on error (*viparyāsa*) and non-error—is extremely well-established. Therefore, even if they are conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), since the cessation of error occurs through the comprehension of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*) via the arising of contradictory properties, how could there be "ignorance" (*avidyātva*) based upon that? Thus, the claim that liberation is impossible because that [ignorance] has not been abandoned is merely a triviality.

Thus, it is precisely the non-perception of any ultimately real entity by the eye of wisdom that is intended as the supreme vision of reality; it is not a vision resulting from a deficiency of conditions or from a lack of mental attention—like those with closed eyes or those blind from birth.

Consequently, because there would be no abandonment of the latencies of the misconceptions regarding existence and so forth, the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable—which arise from the latencies of such misconceptions regarding existence and so forth—would emerge, just as they do for one who has emerged from the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Therefore, one would remain truly unliberated.
One should become a yogi.

Since it is precisely the aforementioned knowledge of reality that brings about liberation and not otherwise—lest there be an over-extension of the principle—one must therefore adopt the previously described vision of the supreme reality.

When the vision of selflessness, which is the antidote to all defects, has been directly realized, the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are abandoned, because they are diametrically opposed to it.

Therefore, due to the absence of any obstruction, just like the rays of the sun when the veils of clouds and the like have vanished from the sky, the light of the yogin’s direct perception proceeds unhindered toward all dependently originated things— which are devoid of conceptual constructions such as their "real" production and so forth.
For indeed, consciousness is of the nature of illuminating the intrinsic character (*svabhāva*) of things.
Moreover, even though that object is present, it would not manifest [to cognition] due to the existence of an obstruction.
If there were no obstruction, then by obtaining a particular inconceivable power, why would it not manifest every single object?
Therefore, through the thorough knowledge of all things exactly as they are, in both their conventional and ultimate forms, the state of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatva*) is attained.
Therefore, this alone is the supreme path for the abandonment of all obscurations and the attainment of omniscience;
however, this is the distinction of yogins from ordinary beings:
for they, like magicians, [perceive] illusion as merely that which is established according to its true nature.
Because they fully understand reality, they do not adhere to phenomena as being real;
therefore, they are called yogins.

However, those who—like children watching a magical illusion—cling to that illusion as being real, and likewise cling to its existence, are called "fools" because of their erroneous attachment; thus, everything is consistent. Consequently, those whose minds are intent upon awakening to reality and non-reality, having established through the knowledge derived from hearing and reflection that the non-dual mind—which is thoroughly understood through both reasoning and scripture as being like an illusion—is indeed the nature of true conventional reality, [proceed] by way of the dharma-nature of dependent origination through the sequence of the eight clear realizations, beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

By cultivating through special meditation that is respectful, uninterrupted, and long-lasting, the lords of yogis attain a continuous stream of non-dual cognition alone—resembling an illusion—which has been connected since beginningless existence and in which all conceptual constructions have been withdrawn.
This alone is the primary antidote.

However, the initial cognition, which is accompanied by verbal expression and established as "resembling an illusion," is merely concordant with that [antidote] and is not itself the primary antidote.

For instance, even in the system that maintains external objects (*bāhyārthanaya*), the cultivation of the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and so forth is not performed by establishing the form of a real entity within the mind.
This is because a real entity is to be realized through non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is impossible at the outset [of such cultivation].

If it were present [already], cultivation would be rendered useless. Therefore, in that case as well, the practitioner is satisfied with this ultimate [result]: a conceptual reflection permeated by mere names, which conforms to the realization of reality, wherein there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a real entity.
In this regard, how is it that discursive speech (*jalpa*) is not increased by the repeated practice of names and forms?

If you argue that for one whose inner self is stilled, there is a gradual withdrawal of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then this is the same in the other case as well; so, enough of this over-elaboration.

Thus, in order to demonstrate the majesty of this teaching on suchness, which is delightful in every aspect, he says, "In this [assembly], moreover," and so forth, to show that no sign has arisen by the power of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Regarding the phrase "the sixfold transformation with eighteen great signs," it is expressed in the singular because it functions as an adverbial modifier of the action.

And therein, regarding the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), there are two transformations: with respect to the earth, both conditioned (*abhisaṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), they are, respectively, shaking and rising.

Regarding the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), with respect to the fourfold classes of sentient beings—the unwholesome, those with various inclinations toward deities, the proud, and those possessing knowledge—they are, in order: sinking, going upward, and going downward.
And there is the "Roaring Sound.

Furthermore, the eighteen great signs arise from the distinction between weak, medium, and intense degrees of activity regarding these very six transformations; they range from "trembling" up to "utterly roaring," according to the explanation of their meanings.
Alternatively, it may mean that the center rises while the ends sink.
One [perceives] that the forest is rising;
this same [perception], when reversed, is the second.
Likewise, the third is when one perceives that the eastern direction is rising while the western direction is sinking.

The fourth is the reverse of this very one. Likewise, the fifth is when the southern direction rises and the northern direction sinks; the sixth is the reverse of this very one. Thus, there are six transformations.
Furthermore, the eighteen great signs are to be understood in the same manner. Concluding [the section], he says:
"For thus," and so forth.
"Born after the Tathāgata":
thus he is born after [the Buddha] by virtue of being born after the modes of omniscience.
Speaking of the nature of non-arising, he says:
Furthermore, the Elder Subhūti says, "Not form," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt as to why that is so,
he says, "For thus," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
"In this way" means:
because he is like an illusion and because he has followed after the aspects of the knowledge of the paths, he has followed after the Tathāgata.
Explaining that suchness has the nature of non-apprehension, he says:
"This practice is profound," and so forth.
Because the nature of the aspects of the knowledge of all modes is non-apprehensible, suchness is the profound practice.
Repeating [the statement] as something well-spoken, he says:
"It is thus," and so forth.
He states that the teaching of the Dharma by the Blessed Ones is not fruitless.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In this," and the phrase "by those performed through prior preparation":

some teachers maintain that by means of those [preparations]— namely, the accumulations of merit and wisdom acquired during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-bhūmi*) and so forth, which constitute the prior preparations— and by those [preparations] thus performed and accomplished, one attains *kṣānti*, that is, resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), in the cultivation of phenomena as being like an illusion.

Others say that the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is attained through the penetration of the all-pervading realm of phenomena (*sarvatraga-dharmadhātu*).
For what reason is there room for the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) for those who have set out in the Great Vehicle?
To this he says: "O Blessed One, what is the cause? and so forth.
In this context, he states that the cause consists of the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) which is the condition (*pratyaya*), and the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*);
specifically, the cause is the deficiency in wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya-kauśalya-vaikalya*).
He says, "By these, Śāriputra," and so forth.
He says "kiñcāpi" and so forth for the sake of figurative explanation; and he provides a clear illustration with the words "tadyathāpi" and so forth.

Regarding the term *pakṣiṇaḥ* (birds): one who has two wings (*pakṣau*) is a *pakṣī*; since a human (*nara*) may also be a *pakṣī* due to the existence of the factions of friends and enemies, the word *śakuni* (bird) is used [to specify].
Furthermore, since even a jackal (*śivā*) and the like might be considered a *śakuni*, the word *pakṣī* is stated [to exclude them].
The statement beginning with "No, indeed this is not so" is entirely without logical justification.
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?", he says:
because it is a fixed law of the nature of things that a heavy substance falls from an elevated place.
He states [the properties] such as being wounded and so forth with the words "For it is thus," and so on.
He states the meaning of the illustrative example (dārṣṭāntika) [with the following].
"Thus it is," and so forth.
Regarding "falls":

even for one engaged in giving and the other perfections, a fall occurs into the level of the Śrāvakas and others if they lack the application of skillful means (upāyakauśala) regarding the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
And by this, it is indicated that the application of both [the means and the wisdom] is primary for the final departure (*niryāṇa*).
The characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvalakṣaṇa*) should be understood exactly as it was described in its sixteen modes.
And so it has been said:
The signs of the afflictions and their causes, the discordant factors and their remedies, seclusion, the difficult-to-perform, the solitary,
and the objective that is non-apprehension. (29)
That which is called the perception of an object, as well as the adherence to what is prohibited and the misconception that is non-obstructive— this is [the view of self].
He is devoid of coming, going, and birth. ||30||
"The non-apprehension of suchness and its sixteenfold nature, as well as that which is characterized like a characteristic— this is considered the fourth characteristic. (31) Thus,
the thorough knowledge of the aforementioned applications is indeed like the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
In order to explain that which is conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), he says:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva," and so forth.
In this context, he "attends to" [the object] by way of bringing it directly before him.
One determines it through the power of certainty.
"By means of the application of signs" means by means of the application of exclusive adherence.
Because it is not understood through both mundane and supramundane knowledge, one does not know and does not see; this is to be applied to the phrase "desiring to dedicate.
Emptiness itself is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Having raised the question, "For what reason is it as before [due to] dedication?
he says, "For thus," and so forth.
This should be understood as stated by way of a negative formulation (*vyatireka*), since the context concerns the exposition of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

The skill characterized by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), which brings about the manifestation and full realization of all the qualities of a Buddha—such as generosity and the rest—within one’s own continuum by way of the aspect of knowledge that takes the signless (*animitta*) as its object, is intended here as the "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*) within this "complete awakening in all aspects" (*sarvākārābhisambodha*).

Here, "liberation" (*mokṣa*) refers to a specific state of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*); because it is conducive to that state, it is called "conducive to liberation. This occurs first within the teaching whose nature is complete awakening in all aspects.
Therefore, because it is the cause for descending [to lower realms] and consists of wisdom derived from hearing and reflection, one falls into two stages due to the lack of skill in means and wisdom.
And so it has been said:
"Skill in the full realization of signless giving and so forth..."
"In this realization of all aspects, that which is conducive to liberation is intended.
Thus, he speaks in order to clarify skillfulness in this manner.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Just as I... and so forth:

concerning what was said—that "this one will remain on the stage of a Śrāvaka and so forth"—just as I understand its meaning, there arises a doubt regarding the attainment of great enlightenment through the accumulation of vast merit and other means.
How, then, is it attained? He says:
"Therefore, then," and so forth.
The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to be cultivated.
And one must possess skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).
In this context, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the thorough knowledge of all phenomena in all their aspects;
skillful means (*upāya*) is faith (*śraddhā*) toward the Buddha and other [objects of refuge].
Vigor in giving and so forth;
mindfulness of the desire for what is wholesome and so forth;
and [the analysis of] action, agent, and activity.
And [the last] is the concentration of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-samādhi*).

Thus, because of the absence of sense-faculties and their objects, it has been stated that one should cultivate the fivefold roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), which have as their nature faith, vigor, concentration, and wisdom, and whose intrinsic nature is non-sensory.
And so it has been said:
Faith has the intellect and so forth as its object; vigor has giving and so forth as its sphere; mindfulness is the perfection of intention; and meditative concentration is non-conceptuality. (33)
"Knowledge of all phenomena in all their aspects is wisdom (prajñā)";
thus, reiterating this as well-said, he says:
"It is so," and so forth.
Even so, he says "profound," and so forth, to show that unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not attained by all through faith and the other [faculties];
it is difficult to realize because it is not attained by those of middling [capacity] with respect to faith and the rest.
Because it cannot be realized even by those very [beings] who are gentle, it is supremely difficult to realize;
speaking in accordance with that, he said:
"It is so, O sons of gods," and so forth.
"By those of poor wisdom," and so forth.

They are of poor wisdom because they lack the thorough knowledge of phenomena in all their aspects. They are of inferior vigor because they lack the vigor directed toward the objects of generosity and the other perfections.
Due to their separation from the samādhi that is free from all conceptual construction, they are liberated only in a limited way;
because they lack faith directed toward the Buddhas and others as objects, they are unskilled in means.
For one who associates with evil friends due to a lack of mindfulness regarding beneficial things and so forth,
this would be said:
"This is the nature of things (dharmatā), because..."

By those of sharp faculties, such as faith and the rest, perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) is easily understood; by those of dull faculties, through those same qualities, it is difficult to understand—this is the implied meaning.
By those of middling faculties, the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabodhi*) is attained; by those of dull faculties, the enlightenment of a disciple (*śrāvakabodhi*).
And so it has been said:
"Perfect enlightenment is easily understood by those of sharp faculties, but is considered difficult to understand by those of dull faculties.
(34) Thus, in order to refute the notion that [enlightenment] is difficult to attain based on the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), he says:
"That which the Blessed One has thus... and so forth.
"How so?
means "by way of refutation alone.
"How is it that nothing at all is fully awakened to? [is the question].
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because of emptiness.
The meaning is that because it is unarisen, there is no dharma to be fully awakened to.
Clarifying that very point, he says:
"For thus, O Blessed One," and so forth.
"For the sake of abandonment" means for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions by means of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).

"One should fully awaken to that which is to be fully awakened"— this refers to the stage of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). "One should understand that which is to be understood"— this refers to the same.
By means of the special path (*viśeṣamārga*).
"By this too" means even by means of the non-apprehension of agent, object, and action.
He says that even in emptiness there is no self-arising.
"Because of impossibility," and so forth. In that context, "impossibility" refers to the non-existence of the cause, and "non-occurrence" refers to the absence of the effect.

Then, because it is not an object of mundane or supramundane knowledge, the two terms "non-conceptualized" (*avikalpita*) and "unfalsified" (*avitathya*) should be applied in their respective order; this is what is meant:

since phenomena are unarisen and thus not objects of knowledge, how could there be a self-attained, unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? Rather, it is thus through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in phenomena.

Furthermore, because the equipment of merit and wisdom must be accumulated and realized by a yogin through conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)—just like a person created by illusion—it is "difficult to realize.
Strengthening this very point, he says:
"By the word 'empty' also," and so forth.
In the same way, having raised the doubt as to "for what reason?", he says:
"For indeed, O Long-lived One," and so forth.
[He says] "I shall fully awaken."
The meaning is that because a bodhisattva, whose nature is space by virtue of emptiness, lacks any such application as "I shall fully awaken," awakening is difficult to achieve.
And so forth:
those very things which are without intrinsic nature are what must be fully awakened to.
As before, having raised the doubt "For what reason?", he says: "Because [all] phenomena (dharmas) are equal to space," and so forth.
The meaning is that because phenomena are like space, and likewise because they are devoid of arising, enlightenment (bodhi) is difficult to realize.
Refuting even their existence conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), he says:
"And if, O Venerable One," and so forth. [The things] would not cease in this way because of the presence of a desire for permanence;
having thus indicated by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), [he continues].
He states it by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*):
"Therefore, since... and so forth.
A reversal (*vivṛtti*) is simply not possible.
In that regard, as to how it is difficult to realize through that [wisdom], he says:
"But what [is it]? and so forth.

Do the subjects (*dharmi*), such as form and the rest, or the reality (*tathatā*) distinct from them—the phenomenon (*dharma*) characterized as the reality of form and so forth, or something separate from that—cease when [the wisdom] ceases?
The word *kimiti* (why/how) is used everywhere as an interrogative particle with the intention of referring to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
thus, the meaning of the sentence is "Certainly not" (*no hīdam*).

Having indicated generally the impossibility of manifestation across the seven stages beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*), he speaks again regarding the three stages beginning with the Immovable (*acalā*) by means of the distinction between the qualities of the awakener and the qualities to be awakened.
"Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, does form fully awaken? and so forth.
This is said with reference to the Buddha-stage, the All-Illuminating (Samantaprabhā).
"What do you think? and so forth.

As for the question "Which one?"—for that very reason, because a turning back is impossible, which dharma could possibly turn back from that very *dharmatā*, that is, from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), by way of being established through the yoga of non-attachment to all things?
The meaning is: none at all.
"What is it?"— it is nothing at all. "Kaccid" is an indeclinable particle.
The particle *nu* functions here in the sense of "now.
Concluding, he says:
"In this way, O Long-lived One," and so forth.
"By way of reality" means by way of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

"By way of stability," some say, means by way of the conventional establishment of designations (*prajñaptivyavasthāna*). Others say that "by way of reality" and "by way of stability" refer respectively to the absence of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of both the knower and the known.

If it is argued that the state of being self-arisen, which is being refuted on the basis of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), is instead established from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), then it would be irrelevant to the present subject; thus he says,
"By which," and so forth.
By whatever kind of method of the Dharma and by whatever manner of the non-arising of phenomena it is taught, no one actually undergoes transformation; rather,
the view is that one transforms only conventionally.

If it is argued that conventional reality itself does not exist, [the author] states that in that case there is not only sublation by perception and so forth, but also sublation by what has been accepted [by oneself], beginning with the words:
"Furthermore, those who... and so on.

Because, through the teaching on the non-arising nature of all phenomena, there is no formal distinction [between vehicles], since there is only one single being whose essence is awakening—the mind—that itself is the vehicle (yāna) because it is that which is to be traversed; namely, the Bodhisattvayāna, the Buddhayāna, which is comprised within the stage of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, due to the non-arising of the three vehicles of the Śrāvakas and others during the causal stages, there would be no formal distinction among the three types of Bodhisattvas belonging to those respective vehicles.
The meaning is that there is a contradiction with what has been accepted.

Even though all phenomena are unarisen, since one accepts the existence of at least one bodhisattva by virtue of the presence of "bodhi," how could the threefold classification of bodhisattvas be established? To this he says:
"But why, venerable sir," and so forth.
Does the elder, the venerable Subhūti, not accept even a single bodhisattva?
For the meaning is that he is being questioned regarding the non-existence of the three types of persons.
Although he already knew [the answer], he spoke in order to cause a resolution to be granted through those words:
"First, this venerable Elder Subhūti must be questioned.
Questioning him, he said:
"What then are you? and so forth.
Avoiding [the question] by means of a counter-question, he says:
"What then, venerable sir," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the suchness of suchness":
even non-arising is, in reality, non-existent.
Explaining that this is not so, he says:
"Nevertheless," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by three modes," this refers to the methods such as the Śrāvaka-yāna; since these result in the exclusion [of external objects], he asks, "What then? and so on, implying that [the external object] is perceived by only one [of those modes].
"Even by one" means that because the principle (nyāya) is the same even in the form of the Mahāyāna, he says:
"For this is not..."
In order to refute that which is to be established as well, he says:
"But is it not the case," and so forth.
"For this is not [so]" has already been explained.
Concluding the subject at hand, he says:
"In this way, O Venerable One," and so forth.
[The question is: "How does it occur to you in this manner?"
Since supreme enlightenment exists according to the conventional truth of the yogis, the existence of a bodhisattva does not [follow] from that [convention] in the ultimate sense.
Therefore, as for [the thought] "this one belongs to the vehicle of the śrāvakas" and so forth—why do you think this? Rather, you should not even give rise to such a thought. This is the meaning.
Applying the very point reached through a succession of objections (*codyaparaṃparā*) to the state of being a sign conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīyaliṅgatva*), he says:
"In this way, of these," and so forth.
"Being clearly distinguished" (*pravibhāvyamānānām*) means being examined (*nirūpyamāṇānām*).
In that regard, "non-distinctness" (*aviśeṣatā*) is due to the non-perception of differences among the three kinds of bodhisattvas;
"absence of distinction" (*nirviśeṣatā*) is due to the realization of suchness as a single unity;
and "absence of manifoldness" (*nirnānākārāṇatā*) is because it is impossible to differentiate [them] apart from the modes already described.

The three phrases beginning with "the mind does not sink" should be applied respectively to the possession of the *mokṣabhāgīya* aids to liberation that are weak, middling, and superior. Speaking in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), he says: "Excellent, excellent," and so forth.
Because there are many different types of enlightenment, he says:
"Which one? and so forth;
this is easy to understand.
For one who has generated the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and is striving for the sake of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), he says:
"O Blessed One, in the unsurpassed [vehicle]," and so forth.
Pointing out the summary statement that "one should abide in equanimity," he says:
"Among all sentient beings," and so forth.
"Even-mindedness" is due to the absence of attachment; "not uneven-mindedness" is due to the lack of aversion.
"With a mind of loving-kindness" means:

"By means of a mind directed toward present objects" and "by means of a mind of benefit" mean that he speaks specifically of the purpose of both the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the mind of benefit (*hita*). Regarding "by means of a mind directed toward future objects," it is the same.
"With a virtuous mind" means with a mind that has subdued pride;
"with an unobstructed mind" means one that is free from aversion.
He says that very thing:
"with a mind of non-violence" means "with a mind of non-harming."
The passage beginning with "by that which is devoid of arising, one should conceive of them as a mother" and so forth is easy to understand.
However, the designations of "brother," "sister," "friend," "minister," "kinsman," and "blood relative" should be understood as being illustrative (upalakṣaṇa).
In that regard, by taking the mother, father, and so on, two at a time and making each a single unit, five aspects are to be described.

This would mean: "I am the protector of all sentient beings. This is said because, by means of the five mental aspects of equanimity, loving-kindness, benefit, non-aversion, and non-harming, as well as the mental aspects of mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, friend, minister, kinsman, and blood relative, one correctly attains the wholesome state of *ūṣmagata* (heat) while taking all sentient beings as the object; thus, one is a protector of all sentient beings.
And so it has been said:
"In this context, all sentient beings are taught to be the object of the 'Heat' [stage]; the ten aspects, beginning with equanimity toward them, are proclaimed. (35)
With reference to the head, he says:
"And himself," and so forth.
This is what is meant:
For one who has personally desisted from all evils and is established in practice through giving and so forth,

as well as for others, by means of inciting them toward the cessation of evil and toward engagement in the wholesome— through the modes of incitement, praising, and approval— the state of being "on the summit" (*mūrdhan*) arises with respect to that object.
And thus it has been said:

For one who has personally desisted from evil and is established in giving and other virtues, there is the enjoining of these same practices upon others and the speaking in praise of them in accordance with their suitability. (36)
"Reaching the summit" refers to the stage of patience (*kṣānti*); thus it is said,
"in this manner, regarding the truths, up until the entry into the bodhisattva’s fixed course."

Just as the distinction between objects and aspects was explained in relation to the summits (*mūrdhan*) through the distinction between one's own and others' bases, so too, by means of such modes as personally and causing others to undertake [the practice] regarding the four truths beginning with suffering, the first fruit, and the stages (*bhūmi*) beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*), patience (*kṣānti*) arises toward that very object; this is the meaning.
And so it has been said:
"Knowledge of reality supported by oneself and others, as well as patience"—
referring to the supreme dharmas, he says "maturing sentient beings," and so forth.
In that context, unobstructed form refers to the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth of a bodhisattva,
while the abiding of all phenomena is buddhahood.
This is what is meant.

For one who is themselves established in the ripening of sentient beings and so forth, the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) arise with respect to that objective support through such modes as encouraging others to undertake those same practices.
And so it has been said:
Likewise, the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) are to be understood through [the qualities of] maturing sentient beings and so forth.
(37) Thus, these aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are each of three kinds, distinguished as weak, medium, and intense.
Among them, the weak stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) consists of a mind of equanimity and loving-kindness, based on the absence of malice toward others at that time.
The middling [level] is taught by means of the three thoughts beginning with "beneficial," based on the intention for the welfare of others in the future.

The superior [level] is taught by means of the arising of the thoughts beginning with "measureless," based on the desire to bring about what is desirable for others both in the present and in the future. The soft [level] that has reached the summit is taught by means of the application of self and others to the cessation of evil, based on the desire for others to cease from the causes of suffering.

The middling [degree] regarding generosity and so forth consists in establishing others in them by means of establishing oneself and others therein, based on the desire to connect them with the causes of happiness.
The superior [degree] is twofold: regarding the cultivation of dependent origination, it consists in setting oneself and others in motion toward it by means of setting others in motion.
This was stated with the intention of abandoning the misconceptions regarding pleasure and pain.

Furthermore, the statement that "mild, medium, and intense receptivity (*kṣānti*) occurs respectively toward the truths until the entry into the bodhisattva’s determination" was made with the intention of establishing others on the noble path, beginning with the first fruit, and even up to Buddhahood; however, it should be understood that intense receptivity consists of a single moment.

The weak, medium, and intense levels of the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*agradharma*) are described by the expression "the ripening of sentient beings" and "the abiding of the true Dharma without obstruction. These are stated, respectively, for the sake of maturing others in the three vehicles without distinction, and specifically for the sake of establishing them on the path of the Bodhisattva; they are based upon the desire to provide a foundation for the ultimate excellence of all perfections.
As it is said in the *Abhidharmakośa*:
"Just as the highest degree of patience (*kṣānti*) itself is momentary, so too are the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
This is because [the former] pertains to one's own welfare.
However, here, the distinction between weak, medium, and intense degrees is explained with reference to the basis of the welfare of others.
Because the gradations of states for the sake of others are possible, this [text] is not contradicted by that.
If it is asked, "Why is there an instruction on the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so forth at each clear realization (*pratyabhisamaya*"?
It is said in reply:

Through the differentiation of the cultivation of the objects of all aspects of the path, there occurs— in due order across the three types of clear realization beginning with the knowledge of all aspects—
the attainment of the supramundane paths of seeing and meditation, preceded by the attainment of the mundane aids to penetration (*laukikanirvedhabhāgīya*).
This applies to the three types [of clear realization] beginning with the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*).

Some maintain that this was stated in order to refute the notion of simultaneous arising, because in the course of practice (*bhāvanā*), through the successive distinctions of higher and higher stages, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) knowledge— comprised within the path of all aspects (*sarvākāraviśeṣamārga*)— arises according to the sequence of weak, medium, and intense.
In the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, the commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this is the sixteenth chapter, titled "Suchness."

The community of irreversible bodhisattvas should be described as consisting of those who possess the aforementioned aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), as well as others such as those on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth.

This classification is established as follows: first, those situated on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) consisting of the aids to penetration; second, those situated on the path of seeing comprised of receptivities (*kṣānti*) and cognitions (*jñāna*); and third, others situated on the continuous path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
And thus it has been said:
"Those bodhisattvas who, having taken up the factors of penetration, abide in the paths of seeing and cultivation— "
"The group is irreversible" (38).

Thus, in this context, the characteristic of irreversibility for those established in the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) should be understood through twenty modes, such as the cessation of [clinging to] form and so forth, and freedom from doubt.
And so it has been said:
This is the characteristic of irreversibility for one established in the factors of penetration, as determined by twenty signs beginning with the turning away from form and so forth. Thus,
because its intrinsic nature is suchness, there is a turning away from form and so forth.
In order to demonstrate this, he says:
"Of the one who is irreversible," and so forth.
In that context, the aspects are comprised within the counteragents (*pratipakṣa*).
The *liṅgas* are the signs belonging to their own substratum;
the *nimittas* are those pertaining to the implements used for its enjoyment.
Alternatively, the *ākāra* is a specific physical manifestation of joy, such as the bristling of hair, the shedding of tears, and so forth.
The *liṅga* is a specific verbal expression, such as joy, supplication, and so forth.
The *nimitta* is a specific performance,
such as hearing, retaining, reciting, worshipping, and so forth.
Or these words may serve as successive explanations for one another.
By asking, "How, O Blessed One, should we understand this? he poses a question regarding the cause for an unconfused comprehension; [the Blessed One], providing the answer, says:
"And that which, Subhūti," and so forth.
"The stage of suchness" is because all stages are like an illusion.
He says that very thing:
By the words "all" and so forth,

because they are ascertained through both reasoning and scripture, one does not conceive of them otherwise— due to the impossibility of any other cause— and thus one does not conceptualize them according to their respective order.
"From there as well" means from the circle of the assembly (*parṣanmaṇḍala*). "In this way" means as follows.
Because it is characterized by the cessation [of attachment] toward form and so forth;
thus, at the time of reflection and hearing, one should consider that "only suchness is the truth, while everything else is delusion."
He releases [his mind] and plunges [into reality].
Because he does not illuminate the grasping at phenomena, he does not engage in idle chatter.
By way of revealing that all things are like an illusion, he speaks only words endowed with meaning, never words devoid of meaning.
Due to his application to the cultivation of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he does not scrutinize what others have done or left undone, nor what they should or should not do.
As for the statement "it must be maintained": that which is inferred as the arising of an effect from a complete collection of causes is [the object of inference].

Because it does not depend on any other factor, that [nature] is described as its own-being (*svabhāva*); thus, according to this principle, it is to be ascertained through the inference of capability.
Having understood this, he says the following to indicate the exhaustion of doubt through the attainment of serene confidence (*prasāda*).
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "Moreover," etc.:
"He gazes at the face" means that he does not look at the face out of a desire for propitiation based on the expectation of attaining a thorough knowledge of the reality that is to be known.
"Relies upon" means that,
by virtue of being a refuge and so forth, one does not appropriate [them] for oneself through the fulfillment of one's vow.
He speaks for the purpose of eliminating the eight inopportune moments,
beginning with the words "Furthermore, he... and so forth,
up to "he is not reborn in the states of woe."
The absence of rebirth in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals has been stated explicitly.
By way of illustration, one should also understand the absence of holding wrong views, not hearing the Buddha’s word, and being born in a border region.
Furthermore, one does not assume the state of a woman.
From the statement regarding the prohibition of female existence, it is understood that one does not take on the state of being sense-deficient, dull-witted, or mute.
By the word "and" (ca), the meaning is that one does not take rebirth as a long-lived deity.
Out of compassion, for the purpose of establishing oneself and others in the qualities of wholesome dharmas, he says:
Furthermore, and so forth. In that context, "taking life" (*prāṇātipāta*) is the destruction of the lives of others.
"Taking what is not given" (*adattādāna*) is the unauthorized appropriation of another's property from its place by means of theft.

Sexual misconduct consists of approaching those who are not one's partners, such as women under protection and so forth. Wine is to be known by the wise as being of three kinds: some is made from tree-barks along with fermenting agents (*guṇa*), another from honey, and another from flour and fermenting agents (*kiṇva*) mixed with water.
They know *maireya* to be prepared from molasses, *dhātrī*, water, and *dhātakī*.
That which, when eaten or drunk, causes intoxication is traditionally known as *madya* (intoxicant).
All this [intoxicant] is of three kinds, and it is the adversary of pure virtue (*śukladharma*).
He says that "negligence" is what has come up again by way of incidental discussion; speaking of what is non-existent is false speech;
and speech that causes division among others is slanderous speech.
Harsh speech is the utterance of unpleasant words.
Idle chatter is speech produced by all the afflictions.
Covetousness is the longing for the possessions of others.
Malice is hatred toward sentient beings.
Wrong view is the perception that [anything] does not exist.
"By all means" refers to the employment of mantras and so forth.
"Entirely" means having all sentient beings as its object; "in every way" means even by such modes as being weak and so forth.
He should neither commit nor perform any such thought.

To explain the purpose of giving and other virtues dedicated toward the sphere of all sentient beings by means of the exchange of self and others, he says, "Furthermore," and so forth; "whatever dharma" refers to the Sūtras and so on, which he "masters" means he takes them up.
He gives;
he bestows it together with its fruit,
through the perfect awakening to the Dharma.
In order to express the longing for the profound Dharma, he says,
"Furthermore," and so forth.
In that context, the desire for another path—
Doubt (*kāṅkṣā*) arises from a lack of sufficiency;
indecision (*vimati*) is the deviation from the straight path;
and skepticism (*vicikitsā*) results from hesitation due to the absence of various increases in wholesome qualities within the lineage-dharma (*gotradharma*).
Bondage exists in every respect due to a deficiency in awakening.
He speaks of the purpose of friendly actions of body, speech, and mind by way of being committed to the welfare of others,
beginning with the phrase "speaking what is beneficial," and so forth.

In that regard, through engagement in bodily action characterized by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he speaks beneficially because he utters what is wholesome for the future. Likewise, through the excellence of vocal action, he speaks measuredly because his speech is limited.
He speaks affectionately because, being originated from a mind permeated by loving-kindness, it brings pleasure to the ear and so forth.
By the perfection of application,
he speaks by way of illustration for the sake of not dwelling with the five hindrances— sensual desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt—
as well as [the state of] having little sloth-and-torpor.
He says, "And he becomes free from latent tendencies," for the purpose of abandoning all latent tendencies such as ignorance by means of having cultivated their antidotes.
In that regard, he is free from latent tendencies because of the absence of those latent tendencies comprised within the outflows of ignorance and views.
However, this does not apply to those [actions] comprised within the outflows of desire and existence, because the bodhisattva intentionally takes up existence.
With the aim of establishing mindfulness and clear comprehension through constant meditative concentration, he says:
"As he goes forth," and so on.
In this context, approaching is "going forward" (abhikrama), and departing is "returning" (pratikrama). Because of the application of clear comprehension (saṃprajñāna), his mind is not distracted;
because of the presence of mindfulness (smṛti), he is one whose mindfulness is established (upasthitasmṛti).
It is not too slow nor too hurried, for the purpose of avoiding the interruption of the modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*);
it is pleasant because it manifests a tranquil appearance;
[this is so] when one foot is not improperly placed.
He does not lift his foot from the ground hastily;
he does not place his foot on the ground hastily for the sake of avoiding places containing living beings. He speaks thus for the sake of clean robes and so forth, due to his pure conduct.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, for him," and so forth:
therein, "little affliction" means having few diseases.
It has few disadvantages and little affliction from others.
Thus, these are its eleven aspects in the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata).

Because he is virtuous as acknowledged by the entire world, he says "yāni khalu... and so forth, in order to show that there is no possibility of the existence of eighty thousand families of worms within his body.
Every single member of the entire swarm of worms, in every form even the most minute, and in every manner such as color and so forth—
all eighty thousand of them— [are present].
Having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:
"For it is thus of that," and so forth.
He speaks for the sake of the mind's lack of crookedness through the purification of the roots of virtue.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Just as... and so forth:

therein, purification of the body is the state of having limbs adorned with the primary marks and so on; purification of speech is the state of possessing the Brahma-voice and so on. These two are stated to be the effects of the purification of the mind.
Therefore, for the purpose of distinguishing the purification of the mind, he speaks of its preeminence,
beginning with the words "What, moreover," and so forth. In that context,
"the state of having few duties" regarding the mind refers to being indifferent toward gain and other such things.
The absence of deceit in the mind arises from not grasping at the faults of others; the absence of guile in the mind arises from the lack of falsely displaying non-existent virtues;
and the absence of crookedness in the mind arises from speaking in accordance with reality.
Because it is free from stinginess and other such faults, there is no crookedness of mind;

and by means of this [mind] which is inclined toward the Mahāyāna, being indifferent to gain, honor, and so forth, he speaks for the sake of undertaking the twelve ascetic qualities (*dhūtaguṇa*), beginning with the words "Furthermore... and so on.
In this context, gain (*lābha*) is the acquisition of material things;
honor (*satkāra*) is the state of being highly esteemed;
and fame (*śloka*) is renown.
He does not become burdened by that, nor does he incline toward it.
In this regard, these are the twelve dhūta-qualities,
namely:
Wearing robes made of dust-heap rags, possessing only three robes,
and subsisting on whatever food is received.
The practice of eating only almsfood, the practice of eating at a single sitting,
and the practice of not eating after the proper time.
dwelling in the forest, dwelling at the foot of a tree, and dwelling in the open air;
These are: dwelling in cemeteries and remaining in the sitting posture.
He speaks thus for the purpose of preventing the arising of mental states such as stinginess, which are the opposites of the perfections, by means of the practice of specific virtues such as giving.
"He becomes full of envy and avarice.
Because this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), the opposites of all the perfections (*pāramitā*) are to be understood.
Since all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are subsumed within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), it is the true nature of things (*dharmatā*).
He says "and not deep," and so forth, for the purpose of proceeding toward the yoga of the Perfection of Wisdom that is free from contradiction.
Because it cannot be shaken, it is "firm-minded."
Possessing profound intelligence, which is a limb for perceiving subtle meanings,
he brings about a thorough integration through conjunction.
Because he has made the realm of sentient beings his own, he speaks for the sake of aspiring to the hells for the benefit of others.
Furthermore, and so forth:
confess the abandonment of the bodhicitta you have taken up;
relinquish it by not generating it again.
Because it is free from oscillation, it is not agitated;
because it neither grasps nor abandons, it does not waver.
Thus, for one who has reached the stage of the "Summits," there are six aspects.
In order to show that he is not led by others because he has attained conviction in the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), he says,
"Furthermore," and so forth.
The fourfold set of terms beginning with "the nature of reality" is employed because of his realization that the four truths, such as suffering, are like an illusion (*māyopama*).

"He does not proceed by faith in another" means that, because he acts through direct perception of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he does not rely on another's conviction. To clarify this very point, he speaks by means of an illustration:
"Subhūti, it is just as if," and so forth.
Because it cannot be taken away, it is "unseizable" (*asaṃhārya*). Because its cessation is impossible, it is "of a nature not subject to turning back" (*apratyudāvartanīya-dharma*).
Because he stands in solitude, he becomes certain regarding omniscience.
Elaborating upon this very point, [the text] says:
"one who is intent upon perfect enlightenment."
In order to bring about the realization of Māra’s true nature as Māra—who teaches a counterfeit path by virtue of his knowledge of the skillful means of Buddhahood—it is said:
"Furthermore," and so forth.
"This" refers to the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"In this very life" (*iha*) means: "bring an end to suffering in this very birth," with the understanding that this is to be accomplished through the cultivation of the Four Noble Truths.
"Ah, alas! (*aho vatā*) and so forth:

"Alas, what a pity! For in this very life, first of all, this personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) of yours—due to the lack of realization of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—is not yet fully perfected for the sake of future lives."

If he will not be reborn, then for what reason do you think that another personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) should be taken up for the sake of sentient beings through the power of vows and so forth? This is the meaning.
[This refers to] those who teach other paths, saying, "This is Māra."
Because it is impossible for him to turn back due to his awakening, he is "irreversible.
Those same two aspects would belong to one who is in the stage of the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*).
In order to show that his practice is approved by all Buddhas everywhere through the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-viśuddhi*), he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "If that [is] for the bodhisattva," etc.:

"Having heard thus from another" means that having heard from another—from Māra himself—such words of separation as "This was not spoken by the Buddha," and so forth, the mind does not fall away from the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). This is the meaning.
In the stages of preparation, the fundamental, and the subsequent, one does not fall away, nor does one regress;
nor is there any alteration of the mind—these points are to be applied respectively.
"Practicing in such a manner" refers to this.
The meaning is: practicing by means of the conduct authorized by the Buddhas.
Concluding [the section], he says:
"If that bodhisattva mahāsattva," and so forth.
Thus, for one who has reached the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*agradharma*), there would be a single aspect (*ākāra*).

It should be characterized that a Bodhisattva established in the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) does not turn back from unsurpassed enlightenment by means of these very aspects as they have been described.
And so it has been said:
"The turning away from form and the other [sensory objects], as well as doubt, momentariness, and decay."
Establishing oneself in what is wholesome and then enjoining others to do the same. ||40||
Generosity and the like are dependent on others, as is the lack of aspiration even for profound meanings.
There is loving-kindness, non-dwelling with the body and so forth, and fivefold [non-dwelling] due to hindrance. ||41||
There is the abandonment of all latent tendencies, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and purity; the robes and other requisites [are pure], and worms do not arise in the body. ||42||

Absence of crookedness in thought, undertaking of ascetic practices, freedom from envy and so forth, proceeding in accordance with the nature of reality, and seeking even the hells for the sake of the world. ||43||
Not being led astray by others, including Māra who teaches other paths, and the realization that "this is Māra" itself—this is the conduct approved by the Buddhas. (44)

"Established in the 'Heat' [stage], in the 'Summits,' in the 'Patience' stages, and established in the 'Supreme Mundane Dharmas,' by these twenty signs one does not turn back from perfect enlightenment. (45) Thus,

immediately after the characteristics of the non-retrogressive state for those established in the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), the characteristics of the non-retrogressive state for those established in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) must be explained by means of the sixteen moments beginning with the "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
And so it has been said:
"The six moments of patience and knowledge, as well as five and five [moments] on the path of seeing—these should be known as the characteristics of the irreversible Bodhisattva. (46)

In that regard, explaining the "receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) by way of turning away from the realization of phenomena such as form and so forth, he says:
"Furthermore," and so on.
Because there is no arising of established distinctions, one does not perform volitional construction (*nābhisaṃskaroti*).
Because it is not a new undertaking (*apūrvākaraṇa*), one does not produce [it].
Anticipating the question, "Why is that as before? he says:
"For thus," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "empty of specific characteristics":

because of the non-apprehension of the realization of phenomena such as form through the nature of phenomena that is empty of intrinsic being, he has attained and entered the bodhisattva’s certainty— the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering— and thus does not apprehend even that phenomenon.
Because he does not construct that [conceptualization];
the meaning is that he does not produce it.
"One who possesses the receptivity to the knowledge of non-arising" means one who has attained the receptivity as previously described.
He says that "knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering" arises from the firmness of the unsurpassed bodhicitta.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover," etc., employs the three phrases starting with "equal to space" for the purpose of demonstrating the beings who abide on the paths of seeing, meditation, and the special path; or alternatively, it should be understood as referring to those engaged in the preparatory stages, or indeed in hearing, reflection, and cultivation, and so forth.
It should be applied there: the mind is firm because it possesses the essence of being free from obstacles;
it is unshakable because it brings about the direct perception of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

It is "unassailable" by others because it is not within their domain; or it may be construed as meaning that one does not fall away from the [designated] place due to the application of formal undertaking. It is so called because of the turning back of the mind toward the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
He says, "the receptivity to the subsequent cognition regarding suffering," and so forth,
beginning with "furthermore.
[This refers to one] who has turned away from the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"One becomes engaged in omniscience.
In that regard, there is cessation when there is engagement,
and there is engagement when there is cessation.
However, in this context, cessation and engagement are specified not merely as cessation and engagement in general, because those two do not constitute the correct meaning;
likewise, in the third moment—
In connection with subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), a fall to the level of the Śrāvakas and so forth is not possible;
because that [subsequent knowledge] has the nature of being an antidote to the three realms, it is described as having the aspect of their cessation.
Through the power of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), by means of the complete exhaustion of the factors of dhyāna and so forth, regarding suffering—
He says, "subsequent knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*),
and so forth, beginning with "he, desiring...
This is an illustration of the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvasamāpatti*) and so on.

In this context, he dwells in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) by bringing them face-to-face for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life; he masters the meditative absorptions by realizing their fruits.

Furthermore, he enters into the meditative absorptions as objects of focus in order to demonstrate that the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) attained through the abandonment of each respective factor serves as the antidote to the realms of form and formlessness.
Because he has taken up a favorable personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), he does not take rebirth through the power of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

This should be understood as follows: since the Bodhisattva has not attained detachment (*vairāgya*) at the stage of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*), he once again takes up objects belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Because his body and mind have become light due to the removal of unwholesome states, it is said that there is the "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the origin" (*samudaye dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "Moreover," etc.:
because lightness of body and mind arises through the non-removal of conceptual constructions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya-vikalpa*), one does not become heavy with names and so forth.
Fame and renown are stated as a dyad due to the distinction between external and internal glory.
Because he has realized that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), his mind is undisturbed by the absence of name and so forth due to the lack of dejection;

and because he enjoys sensual pleasures without attachment through the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśala*) consisting in the cultivation of the illusion-like (*māyopama*), it is said that there is "dharma-knowledge regarding the origin" (*samudaye dharmajñāna*).

"If he [returns] to the household," and so forth. "Household" means the home; "attachment to desires" (*kāmābhiṣvaṅga*) refers to the intense clinging (*abhiniveśa*) toward the objects of desire encountered therein.
Aspiration is the intent toward things not yet attained.
The notion of nirvana arises from the realization that the phenomena of nirvana are like an illusion.
To clarify this very point by means of an analogy, he says:
"Namely, for example," and so forth.
Because they perceive the cessation of the life-faculty and other faculties, they have a perception of fear; because this is the nature of the occasion (*samaya*), they are not at ease.
Some say that they do not desire things in the future, are not greedy for those in the present, and are unattached to those that have perished.
And others say that [the term] "and so forth" refers to the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) and the rest.
Because they are pleasing and grant ease, they are called "of lovely form" (*priyarūpa*) and "of agreeable form" (*sātarūpa*). While dwelling in the midst of a house...
"And they indeed become devoid of desire"—this is the connection with what precedes.

Because one always practices celibacy through the vision of the defects in sense objects, there is the "receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the origin" (*samudaye 'nvayajñānakṣānti*); thus he says.
"Neither by even nor uneven," and so forth.
Not by even or uneven means not according to the principle of *uddhāra-vṛddhi* (interest on capital).
Because it is acquired through righteous means, it is "by dharma"; because he is always a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), it is not "by adharma."
Because their mental continuums are moistened by calm abiding (*śamatha*), they do not inflict crushing or injury upon others.
Anticipating the question "Why is that so?", he says:
"For it is by them... and so forth.
Some say that "by noble beings" (*satpuruṣaiḥ*) and so forth is a praise [of the path].
Others say that because of the attainment of the sixteen-moment path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the sixteen phrases beginning with "by noble beings" correspond to them respectively.

[Regarding the origin of suffering (*samudaya*): because it is the nature of a noble being (*satpuruṣadharmanya*) and because of the complete purity of requisites and livelihood (*upakaraṇājīvaviśuddhi*).
He says, "subsequent knowledge," and so forth,
beginning with "furthermore.
This refers to the one known by the name Vajrapāṇi.
There is another certain distinguished great yakṣa;
because his body, speech, and mind are respectively unconquerable,
the terms "unassailable," "inviolable," and "unapproachable" are to be applied accordingly.
Because his private organ is concealed within a sheath, he is endowed with the male organ of a bull-like leader.

The class of mantras consists of the types of mantras such as those of Noble Tārā and others. The medicinal herbs consist of *bhṛṅgarāja* and others produced during lunar eclipses, solar eclipses, and other such portents.
"Mantras, classes [of beings], and medicinal herbs" refers to spells, medicines, and so forth.

Some maintain that the word "and so forth" includes such things as yantras. Others hold that "mantra-class" refers to supramundane [spells], while "medicinal herb" is characterized by the collection of many substances.
Others say that worldly knowledge is a single-limbed medicine;
it is a class of mantras due to its connection with a deity,
and it is an herb for the purpose of countering arisen diseases.
Others say that knowledge arises from a connection with female deities, and medicine is for the purpose of preventing future calamities;
because there is an absence of quarrels involving body or speech, he is not one whose nature is to engage in strife or dispute.

Because one abides in emptiness, there is the forbearance regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) with respect to cessation, due to the negation of dwelling in the practice and application of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
thus he says, "Furthermore," and so forth.

By the mention of "practice and application" (*yogānuyoga*), it is indicated that the sequence of practice and application for the truths of suffering and origin, as well as for the truths of cessation and the path, has been made known respectively.
Thus says Ārya Vimuktisena:
"Attachment to the aggregates and so forth is the first [type of] yoga."
Others say that "pursuit" (*anuyoga*) refers to extreme attachment (*atyantābhiniveśa*) occurring subsequently.

He states that there is "knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation" (*nirodhe dharmajñāna*) because, having eliminated opposing factors, one prohibits dwelling in discourses on obstructive phenomena or in pursuit and application.
"Not socializing," and so forth.

By the mention of "discourse" (*kathā*), it is indicated that because the conceptualization of objects (*vastu-vikalpa*) has already been eradicated at the very time of the knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) serves as the specific antidote to the conceptualization of mere discourse.
And it is with reference to this state that it is said:
"All this is mere name, established in mere conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).

Apart from the designator (*abhidhāna*), the designated (*abhidheya*) does not exist. Thus, because one has fully understood the faults of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is the cessation [of conceptualization] due to the negation of dwelling in the application and practice of the discourse on the diverse and manifold army of dharmas—such as giving and the rest—which constitute the equipment for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*). In cessation...
He says, "the receptivity to subsequent knowledge," and so forth, including "not an army.
In this context, "army" refers to the collection of dharmas that constitute the equipment for enlightenment.
By this, the suitability of the extensive realization at the stage of the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) is indicated.

For some say that this is because of the statement in the *Āryapañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*: "One who abides in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*) does not perceive the smallness or the greatness of any phenomenon.

This is so because, regarding cessation, there is a negation of dwelling in the discourse concerning the battle between the adversary and the antidote—the objects of grasping and the subject of grasping—which are to be abandoned as the opposing side and its counteragent, and which involve engagement and application.
He says, "subsequent knowledge," and so forth, including "not talk of battle.
For one who has reached such a state, the fourfold cessation of maturation occurs by its own inherent nature.
Namely: first, the cessation of the collection of sense faculties;
second, the cessation of the city of the primary and derived elements that serve as the basis for the sense faculties;
and third, the cessation of the withdrawal from the objects of the sense faculties.
As it says, "not [dwelling in] a village," and so forth.
"Districts" (*janapada*) and so on are specific types of towns (*nigama*).
The cessation of attachment to a self (*ātmābhiniveśa*) is the fourth.
As it is said:
"Not a discourse on the self," and so forth.
The inclusion of the words "name" and so on is for the purpose of distinguishing the self itself through its relationship with what belongs to the self.
Furthermore, this fourfold cessation of maturation (vipāka-nirodha) should be understood as belonging to each of the three realms respectively.
Among these, the cessation of the sense faculties, their bases, and their objects in the desire realm and the form realm is well known.

In the formless realm (*ārūpya*), however, there is the cessation of the faculties because of the continued existence of the faculties of equanimity (*upekṣā*), life (*jīvita*), mind (*manas*), and perception (*saṃjñā*).
Since the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantati*) here relies upon both the [homogeneous] group (*nikāya*) and life,
there is thus the cessation of the support for the faculties.
Because the cessation of mental objects (dharmas) is possible, the cessation of the objects of the sense faculties is possible;
furthermore, since the adherence to a self exists everywhere, its cessation is also logically established.

By means of the realization of the specific qualities of generosity and so forth, and by the prohibition of dwelling in the application and addiction to stinginess, immorality, and the like, he speaks of "receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path" (*mārge dharmajñānakṣānti*).

With the phrase "no discourse contrary to the Dharma," and so on, by the negation of discourse contrary to the Dharma, it is made known that receptivity constitutes the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), as it is the cause for the dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśavisaṃyoga*).
The undertaking of physical or verbal action is quarreling (*kalaha*).
