Deformity produced by speech or mind is wrangling (*bhaṇḍana*). Hostility (*vigraha*) and dispute (*vivāda*) have already been explained.

They are "desirous of the Dharma" because they follow after wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*). They are "proponents of non-differentiation" because they speak, respectively, of the relinquishing and the acquisition of the conditioned and unconditioned natures of the dharma of practice and its fruit. They are "desirous of friends" because they long for the attainment of a more distinguished state.
They are "proponents of the Dharma" because they proclaim the dharmas that are not shared with the Śrāvakas and others.
Because they have attained mastery over rebirth, they are born there.
Clarifying that very patience as it was described, he says:
"Furthermore," and so forth.
"Kovidāḥ" means the wise.
"Yadbhūyastvena" means for the most part.
Because not even a particle of a phenomenon is perceived due to the fact that all phenomena have the nature of the three gates of liberation, he says: "knowledge of phenomena regarding the path."
Furthermore, beginning with the words "Moreover," etc.:

because of the realization that all phenomena are like an illusion, and due to the absence of even the slightest perception of a phenomenon, it does not occur to him: "Am I irreversible, or am I not irreversible?
The states of application and so forth should be joined with the occasions of doubt, uncertainty, and despondency.
He explains that knowledge is the cause for the attainment of dissociation because it constitutes the path of liberation through the absence of doubt and other such hindrances.
Clarifying this very point by means of an illustration, he says:
"Just as, for example," and so forth.
By means of the obstruction of Māra’s activities and so forth, he makes known the very function of attaining dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
Again, expanding upon this by means of an analogy, he says: "Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a man... and so forth.

The meaning is that it is to be removed in every way— that is, to dispel it, to prevent its manifestation for a time, to suppress it, to move it, or to shake it, which is to say, to displace it from its own place and to render it unstable right there. By this, it is indicated that because it can be turned back by the world including the gods, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) on the path— which transcends the world including the gods and enters into the state of certainty (*nyāma*)— serves as the antidote to the three realms.

The phrase "even for one who has passed beyond birth" indicates that even for one who has gone to another life, because there is no arising of the minds of śrāvakas and so forth, and because there is no departure via another vehicle, the practice is characterized by its exclusivity (*aikāntikatva*).

He states that it is the "receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the path" (*mārge 'nvayajñānakṣānti*) because, through the attainment of firm conviction, one remains decisively established in the three stages of one's own level, which consist of the three types of omniscience.
Even for one who has passed beyond birth, it occurs thus: "I am not," and so forth.
"In one's own stage" means in the three types of omniscience.
Having raised the doubt as to why that is so,
he says "for thus," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by the mind":
By the attainment of the five superknowledges;
by knowledge means by the perfect awakening to the truths.
"It is thus and not otherwise" means that the state of arhatship is not to be realized by Bodhisattvas;
the meaning is that it is exactly as the Blessed One has said, and not otherwise.
He contemplates in this way;
he attends to it in this way; that is, he ascertains it through direct perception and inference.
"The empowerment of the Buddha" means:
The form of the Buddha.
Truly, this one is unbound;
truly, this one is inevitable.
Anticipating the question "Why is that so?", he says:
"For thus, of this one," and so forth.
Because of being resolutely committed [to the goal], he abandons his life for the sake of the dharmas such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) on the path.
He says, "subsequent knowledge," and so forth,
beginning with "furthermore.
In that context, the relinquishing of the self follows from the relinquishing of the body.
From the relinquishing of the mind comes the relinquishing of life.
Others say that the mention of both is for the purpose of making known the relinquishing of the self, whether individually or collectively.
*Prema* is affection (*sneha*).
"Veneration" means great respect.
By the phrase "this is mine as well," it is indicated that there is a commonality in the inclusion of all phenomena through the attainment of dissociation from them.
Expanding upon this very knowledge as it has been described, he says:
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "Moreover," and likewise raising the question "For what reason? he says:
"For in that way by him," and so forth.

The characteristic of an irreversible Bodhisattva situated on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is to be understood as the sixteen moments directly realized through the aforementioned aspects, which illuminate the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) for those Bodhisattvas possessing inconceivable skillful means (*upāya*).
Thus it has been said:
The turning away from the perception of form and so forth, firmness of mind, the cessation of the two inferior vehicles, and the complete exhaustion of the factors of dhyāna and the rest; ||47||
Lightness of body and mind, the skillful means for engaging in sensual pleasures, constant practice of celibacy, and purity of livelihood; ||48||

The word "not" (na) applies to the aggregates and so forth, to obstacles, to the provisions, to that which possesses the sense faculties and so forth, to battle, and to stinginess and so forth; it does not apply to application and devoted practice. ||49||
The cessation of dwelling, the non-apprehension of even the subtlest dharma, certainty regarding one's own stage, and abiding in the three stages. ||50||
"The sacrifice of life for the sake of the Dharma—these sixteen moments are the signs of non-retrogression for the wise one established on the path of seeing.
(51) If it is asked: "How can these moments, which are to be personally realized within the mental continuum of a yogin, serve as signs for the understanding of others?"
It is said:

because the moments of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), having been correctly realized, produce an effect corresponding to themselves—which is the object of another's understanding, such as the turning away from the notions of form (*rūpa*) and so forth—comprised within the pure mundane subsequent mind (*laukikapṛṣṭhacitta*) that is free from the aspects of grasped and grasper (*grāhyagrāhakākāra*). This occurs in accordance with the realization.

Thus, the conduct of yogins is everywhere [of this nature], except when it is for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings; therefore, these are their characteristics. This concludes the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Aspects, Signs, and Indications of Irreversibility," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Eighteenth Chapter.

In order to demonstrate the characteristics of one who is irreversible while abiding on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), [the author] introduces the topic by connecting it with the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), saying:
"Then indeed," and so forth.
It is called "marvelous" because of its possession of uncommon qualities (*asādhāraṇadharma*).

By attaining the patience (*kṣānti*) as described, he is endowed with a great accumulation of qualities through the dissociation from the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*). By attaining the knowledge (*jñāna*) as specified, he is endowed with immeasurable qualities because the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing do not arise again.
Subsequently, by attaining the knowledge that accomplishes the omniscience of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is endowed with boundless qualities.
Thinking that the restatement, "It is well said; it is thus, Subhūti, it is just so," would be without logical justification, he asks, "For what reason?
and then says, "By one who is irreversible," and so forth.
Because the aspects are infinite, [the merit] is infinite in every respect.
It is boundless because it is the object [of cognition] and indestructible because it is unmoving for all the world.
Having thus established the connection, he states the subject at hand:
"The Blessed One is powerful," and so forth.

Since the Blessed One is capable of explaining [the letters] beginning with "A," it follows that the Blessed One must explain profound points for the purpose of defining the characteristics of one who is irreversible while established on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The repetition of the term "profound, profound" is an emphatic expression intended to indicate the repeated practice of the path.

"Stations" (*sthānāni*) is a designation for "abiding. This is intended to demonstrate their continuity by making known that they are the cause for the complete fulfillment of realization— that station on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) wherein Bodhisattvas, having abided, fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).

Based on the principle that "cognition of the qualified does not arise without the qualifier having been apprehended," he speaks— "Excellent, excellent! and so forth— in order to qualify the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
"Profound" means that the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is profound.
"Desiring to conclude" means...
Desiring to explain this, he asks: "What, then, is its profundity? and says:
"Profound," and so forth.
This designation is one in which the state (bhāva) is the primary factor; the meaning is "profundity.
In that regard, emptiness consists in the discernment of the grasper.

It is signless (*animitta*) because of the absence of an object to be grasped. It is wishless (*apraṇihita*) because even non-dual cognition— which is devoid of subject and object— is not a real entity to be attained.
It is "without formative activity" (anabhisaṃskāra) because it is dissociated from the three characteristics such as birth, or because it proceeds without effortful exertion;
it is "non-arising" (anutpāda) because its cause does not exist.
Due to the departure from rebirth-linking, there is non-arising;
due to the absence of the factors adverse to the path of seeing, there is non-existence;
and due to the dissociation from the factors adverse to the path of cultivation, there is dispassion.

Some maintain that the distinction in meaning among these—emptiness and the others—should be stated as follows: it is "cessation" because it is the nature of not producing suffering in the future; it is "nirvāṇa" because it is the state of abiding in the signless, peaceful, and blissful dwelling; and it is "disappearance" because it is the fruit of the non-occurrence of suffering in the present life.
It should be understood that by all these terms, it is the *dharmadhātu* itself that is indicated through its various exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).

And in order to demonstrate that the profundity of emptiness and so forth consists in being free from the two extremes of superimposition and denial, he asks a question with an interrogative intonation, saying:
"Of these very [terms]," and so on.
Immediately after "O Blessed One," the word "what" (*kim*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
He states [the response] for the sake of refutation:
"Of all phenomena," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:
"For form," and so forth.
Asking how this is so, he says:
"And how, Subhūti," and so forth. He says this by way of refutation:
"Just as, Subhūti, suchness is, so too is form profound," and so on.
The meaning is that just as emptiness is profound, so too are form and the other aggregates profound by virtue of their being ultimately unproduced.
By this, the extreme of superimposition— the notion that "form and the rest exist within suchness"— is refuted.
Just as the suchness of form is, so too is form profound; for according to the statement,

"That which is dependent origination is itself emptiness," it follows that the very suchness of form and the other aggregates is, from the perspective of conventional reality, form and so forth— delightful only when not subjected to analytical investigation.
And by this, the extreme of negation—that suchness is not other than form and so forth—is refuted.
Concluding, he says:
"In that, Subhūti, there is no form," and so on.
"Marvelous" means:
wonder arises from the simultaneous statement of two meanings regarding one and the same thing.
By the phrase "as far as," there is the inclusion of the prohibition of dogmatic adherence (*abhiniveśa*) and the prescription of non-adherence, and so forth.
"By means of a subtle method" means that he was dissuaded from [clinging to] form through a sequence that avoids alarm, and *nirvāṇa* was indicated.
He was dissuaded in order to eliminate engagement with form and so forth, because form and so forth are negated within suchness (*tathatā*).
In that very context, nirvāṇa would also be described through the practice of emptiness.
Thus, this is the summarized meaning:
form and so forth do not exist within emptiness and the rest.
"Nothing other than that is emptiness and so forth.

That which is, respectively, the state of being free from the extremes of superimposition and denial is the profundity of emptiness and so forth; thus, "emptiness and so forth" refers to the profundity.
Because it is endowed with profundity, it is "profound."
Regarding the "path of cultivation," it has been said: "The path of cultivation is profound; profundity consists of emptiness and so forth."
"Being free from the extremes of superimposition and denial—that is its profundity.
(52) Having thus indicated the qualification, he speaks as follows regarding the cultivation of the path of the qualified [object]:
"These, Subhūti," and so forth.
"He will reflect" means he will weigh it with wisdom consisting of hearing; "he will contemplate" means with wisdom consisting of reflection;
"he will closely examine."
[This refers] to that consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).

Or, it should be applied respectively as "by means of the wisdom (*prajñā*) arising from the preparation (*prayoga*), the fundamental [attainment] (*maula*), and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*) within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
To what object-domain (*viṣaya*), then, does the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertain? He says:
"Thus have I [heard]," and so forth.
In that regard, "I must abide thus," as it was instructed in the *Prajñāpāramitā* concerning the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
In this way I must train;
just as it has been explained in the Prajñāpāramitā with reference to the path of seeing, so must I practice.
It should be stated that this was taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā* with reference to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
And so it has been said:
"Reflection, deliberation, and profound contemplation constitute the frequent path of cultivation."

"In the factors of penetration (*nirvedhāṅga*), in the path of seeing (*dṛṅmārga*), and indeed in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) [these are found]. (53) For this very reason, with reference to the four aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
the path of seeing, and the path of cultivation, [it is said:]

Thus, there are six phrases: "accomplishing in such a way," "attending closely in such a way," "examining in such a way," "applying oneself in such a way," "striving in such a way," and "exerting oneself in such a way.
How can that very same [object] be the object of the path of cultivation? There is no fault, because it is continuous; each preceding moment serves as the object for each succeeding one.
In order to explain the benefits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), he asks,
beginning with "This one," and so forth:
"That bodhisattva who, engaged in reflection and so on, correctly applies himself to yoga even for a single day in this path of cultivation..."
How much merit does he produce in a single day?
To provide an answer, he says:
"For example," and so forth.
One is of a passionate temperament (*rāgacarita*) because of excessive attachment even toward a minor object.
One is of a discursive temperament (*vitarkacarita*) due to an abundance of conceptual variations of passion.
Because she is beautiful both in her overall form and in her individual parts, she is, respectively, "well-formed" (*abhirūpā*) and "graceful" (*prāsādikā*).
She is "pleasing to behold" (*darśanīyā*) because she is favorable to one's vision.
A "sign" (*saṅketa*) is the communication that "you must go to this place."
"One should not bring it under control"—
some say this means "one should not obtain it," while others say it means "one should not see it."
"In the beginning, middle, and end, I shall act in such a way as to accomplish activities conducive to the amorous pleasures desired by her— doing this, playing thus,
and sporting in this manner."
The phrase "I shall investigate in this manner" should be applied because of the ability to proceed as one desires in all respects.
"To this extent" means the number of discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) of a person whose conduct is dominated by passion (*rāga*). One abandons them through the exhaustion of karma.
By means of suppression, one turns one's back on [the defilements];
by not producing what has not yet arisen, one casts off and brings to an end the continuity of births within *saṃsāra*.
Thus, through the acquisition of immeasurable wholesome qualities, there are three kinds of moments for casting off, turning one's back on, and bringing to an end incalculable eons.
This would have been stated for the purpose of making known the activity of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
"He who here," and so forth;
he abides as instructed according to the section on the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
With reference to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), he trains as it has been described;
with reference to the weak, medium, and intense paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), he practices, contemplates, and meditates upon it exactly as it was taught and as it was indicated.
The connection is: "he enters into yoga. Concluding [the section], he says:
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva," and so forth.
Having stated that one performs such an amount of karma in a single day, the remainder of the sentence is that one abandons it through the continuity of births for as long as immeasurable eons.
Now, the classification of the types of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) should be examined.
For there are three basic types—weak, medium, and strong—and when each of these is further divided into weak, medium, and strong, they become nine types.
Just as it is for the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), so too should the nine types of the opposing factor (*vipakṣa*) be understood.

In this regard, it should be understood that by means of the weakest-weak path, the strongest-strong conceptualization is abandoned, up to the point where by means of the strongest-strong path, the weakest-weak conceptualization is abandoned.
Because a superior path is impossible from the very beginning, and because there is an absence of superior afflictions once a superior path has arisen.
Just as coarse dirt is shaken off from a garment first, and the subtle [dirt] afterwards;
and just as coarse darkness is destroyed by subtle light.
The subtle is overcome by the intense; the white dharmas are powerful while the black ones are weak,
because even a momentary, mild Noble Path uproots the intense afflictions that have been nourished through the succession of beginningless saṃsāra.
Master Vasubandhu maintains that it is like the extraction of long-accumulated humors by means of *trivṛt* medicine, or like the destruction of a great mass of darkness by a momentary, small lamp;
for therein, by means of indirect designation (*anyāpadeśa*), there is the demonstration of an ever-increasing abundance of merit.

By mentioning the "conquered merit" (*abhibhūyamānapuṇya*) as a distinction of the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), he indicates the distinction of the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*). Considering that Bodhisattvas are those whose afflictions consist of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-kleśa*), he says,
"And whoever is devoid of the perfection of wisdom," and so forth, in order to explain the most intense type of conceptual construction.
He speaks for the sake of the soft-soft path,
beginning with "This very [gift] is superior to that," and so forth.
"Than that" means it is superior to the donor's gift.
It is more distinguished because it involves the acquisition of incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite merit. Speaking of the superior-middle conceptualization, he says:
"Furthermore," and so forth.
"One should give and establish" means that one should bestow [the gift] and ensure its long endurance. He speaks for the sake of those on the weak and middling paths.
"And whichever bodhisattva," and so forth.
"To a much greater extent" means having the nature of the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) and so on.
He speaks thus in order to demonstrate the superior-mild conceptualization (*adhimātra-mṛdu-vikalpa*).
Furthermore, and so forth;
by the use of the word "up to," there is the inclusion of those beginning with the non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
And, by perceiving even the slightest fear [of transgression], he practices the precepts in their entirety.
He speaks for the sake of the weak and superior paths, beginning with the words "And the bodhisattva who... and so forth,
followed by "from that mental attention."
From the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
he says "Furthermore," and so forth, in order to reveal the intermediate and superior conceptualizations.
"And endowed with patience" means being possessed of patience such as the endurance of harm from others. He speaks this for the sake of the middling and weak paths.
"Whatever," and so forth.
"The gift of Dharma" means correct bestowal;
for this very reason, this [instruction] is distinguished from the previous one by the phrase "one should teach the Dharma."
Communicating the middling-of-the-middling conceptualization, he says:
"Furthermore," and so forth.
Because his vigor is intense, he is one who has initiated vigor (*ārabdhavīrya*).
He speaks for the sake of the middling-middling path,
beginning with the words "And furthermore, whoever... and so forth,
up to "should dedicate."
One should dedicate [the merit] with the view of apprehension (*upalambha-dṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, immediately following this, a distinction will be stated regarding dedication as taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
This very dedication of apprehension preceded by the gift of Dharma would constitute a "middling-mild" conceptualization (*vikalpa*) in comparison to the dedications that are about to be described.
He speaks for the sake of the middling-superior path,
beginning with "Furthermore," etc.,
[referring to] that which is taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
"From that" means from the perspective of the one who dedicates by way of the non-apprehension of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanupalambha-yoga*).
In order to explain the subtle and intense conceptualization (*mṛdv-adhimātra-vikalpa*), he says:
"Furthermore," and so forth.
"Furthermore, he applies himself to yoga in seclusion.
This means that after the transformation, one should effect the concentration of the mind while dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
He speaks thus for the sake of the path that is superior-in-intensity and weak-in-faculty (*adhimātra-mṛdu*).

And furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "yaśca khalu punar" and so forth: "he should again apply himself to yoga in seclusion" means that he should once more direct his attention [to the object].
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"And again, while entering into meditative absorption (*pratisaṃlāna*)," and so forth.
He speaks in order to describe the weak and medium degrees of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
"O Blessed One, when there is volitional construction (*abhisaṃskāra*)... and so forth.

Volitional construction is mental engagement (*cittābhoga*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and error (*viparyāsa*). When [this occurs], how is it that at the time of dedication one produces much greater merit? It is said that because one follows after the seeds of conceptualization, and because one follows after even that conceptualization as being like an illusion—thus proceeding without error—one produces much greater merit from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). In order to explain the meaning of the superior-middle path, he says this while providing the rebuttal.
"So too now," and so forth.
"He" refers to the mass of merit produced by formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*). "Now" means:
This occurs during the stage of the eighth type of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
but not previously, because [previously] it arises from cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*).
It is empty by means of the emptinesses of the internal, the external, and both.
It is empty by virtue of the power of the emptiness of the great ultimate truth;
it is void through the emptinesses of the conditioned, the unconditioned, the absolute, the beginningless and endless, and the non-dispersal;
and it is insubstantial through the nine kinds [of emptiness], such as the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Others maintain that the four terms beginning with "empty" (*śūnyaka*) correspond respectively to the practices of equipment (*sambhāra*), setting out (*prasthāna*), armor (*sannāha*), and departure (*niryāṇa*).
Speaking of the subtle-subtle conceptualization (*mṛdu-mṛdu-vikalpa*), he says:
"Furthermore, in whatever way... and so forth.
"Yathā yathā" means:

by whichever mode—such as the internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and so forth—a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices], the remainder being that he is "subsequently comprised within the realization of the incalculable, the immeasurable, and so on.
"Thus the dharmas" refers to this.
[He says] "like an illusion" regarding the meaning of the path of the highest-of-the-high degree: "And just as, Subhūti, a bodhisattva... and so forth.
Because of the departure from all seeds of conceptual construction, one generates immeasurable and incalculable merit.
By the term "immeasurable," the "unlimited" is also implied.
Asking what the distinction in meaning is, he says:
"Of the immeasurable," and so forth.
"What is the distinction?
means: what is the specific characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), and what is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)? Such is the sense.
"What is the distinction? means: what is the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), and what is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)?
He states [the following] for the sake of explaining the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
"Immeasurable," and so forth.

"Wherein the means of valid cognition cease" means that because it is impossible to apprehend through direct perception or to measure through inference regarding this sphere of merit, the means of valid cognition— namely, direct perception and inference— do not operate therein.
That is immeasurable and without measure.
Some maintain that by this, the unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛtatva*) and the sovereignty (*vibhutva*) of realization are indicated;
for it cannot be exhausted by means of calculation.
That merit which, by virtue of its being beyond number—that is, impossible to establish through calculation—is "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*).
Some say that by this, his attainment of equality is indicated.
He speaks next for the purpose of defining its essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*):
"O Blessed One, it might be so," and so forth.
"Paryāya" means a classification or distinction. Since "yat" is an indeclinable, it has the sense of "yena" (by which).
"Immeasurable" (*aprameya*) is an elliptical expression for "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) and so forth.
Repeating those words because they were well spoken, he says: "That Subhūti here... and so on.
Having thus restated [the objection], he says, in order to establish [the response]: "It might be so, Subhūti," and so forth.
Regarding the word "by which" (*yena*):
"Consisting of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*":

although in the ultimate sense it has the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), due to the distinction between conceptualization and its antidote, it manifests in nine modes as described— corresponding respectively to the nine stages beginning with the *anāgamya* and the *dhyānāntara*, or by the power of great skill in means (*mahopāyakauśala*) to the nine stages beginning with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) should be understood as proceeding in a continuous series (prabandhena).
And so it has been said:

Because it is continuous, this [path] is intended to be ninefold in its modes; furthermore, it is divided into nine by the distinctions of weak, medium, and intense, each of which is again subdivided into weak and so forth. (54)

Now, one might ask: since the statement regarding the production of distinct, innumerable, and immeasurable merit is made with reference to each individual type [of practice], and since the causes themselves are manifoldly diverse, how can the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) consist of only nine types? With this intention, he says: "But for whom? and so forth.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of emptiness," and so forth.
This means: of the various types of the path of cultivation whose intrinsic nature consists of the three doors of liberation.
Because it is understood that this is a designation specifically for the ninth category, as it exists at the ultimate limit of excellence, he says:
"Of what [is it the emptiness]? and so forth.
"[It is not] of others."
Therefore, what is the designation for all other phenomena, beginning with the first type?
To provide an answer by means of that [question], he says:
"What do you think? and so forth.
Since the principle that "all phenomena" refers to the first and subsequent categories as being exclusively empty is uniform everywhere, they possess the nature of the three gates of liberation.
The Tathāgata has taught all these categories;
having established that the statement regarding emptiness and so forth applies to every category, he now explains the meaning of the synonyms.
"And those, Subhūti," and so forth.
Regarding "immeasurability" (*aprameyatā*):
by the word "also" (*api*), "incalculability" (*asaṃkhyeyatā*) and the others are included.

Since designations such as "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) and "immeasurable" (*aprameya*), which are by nature verbal expressions, are applied to a single reality in a form produced through various exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), they are therefore incapable of establishing a differentiation of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) characterized as previously described from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Thus he says: "Therefore, then," and so forth.
"Of these" refers to the incalculable [qualities] and so forth.

Conventionally, however, those teachings—the nature of which is the Dharma-realm flowing forth from great compassion that is without an object, and whose nature consists of the Dharma of instruction as described—are intended by the Tathāgata to manifest the arising of great fruit for foolish beings; thus he says "desires," and so forth.
"Etad" refers to [the categories] beginning with the incalculable.
"The exposition of the accomplishment of the teaching" means that the teaching is accomplished.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: that by which something is produced is the "accomplishment of the teaching" (*deśanābhinirhāra*), which is the *dharmakāya*; its "manifestation" (*udbhāvanā*) is the exposition according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
And so it has been said:
"Expositions such as 'incalculable' and so forth are not tenable from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)."
"They are considered by the Sage to be the outflow of compassion from the perspective of conventional truth" (55).
Because these are taught as the outflow of the Tathāgata’s compassion, he states "It is marvelous," and so forth, implying that they must encompass all objects of experience.
By the phrase "up to" (*yāvat*), there is the inclusion of "immeasurability" and so forth.
Regarding "of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmāṇām*):
it is the *dharmatā*—the nature of reality—of the nine types of phenomena beginning with the first, which is the form of nirvāṇa.
Because no distinction is perceived between the expression and its meaning, it is inexpressible;
this refers to that which was just mentioned,
namely "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*).
"Form and so forth.
Having restated [the objection] as "This is so because it has been well said," and so on, as before;
then, raising the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Subhūti, that which... and so forth. "The emptiness of all phenomena" is stated as emptiness by way of excluding other distinctions such as being an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and so on.

Therefore, the meaning is that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are empty and cannot even be expressed in words. Now, one might object: since the reality of the path—the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—is intended as being ultimately inexpressible in terms of identity or difference due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), then the disappearance of the adverse factors and the arising of their antidotes would not be tenable, respectively.
He says, "Because there is no imparting of any excellence whatsoever," beginning with "But what, Blessed One? and so forth,
and "Certainly not, Subhūti," and so forth.

If this were so, then by the path designated as "cultivation" (bhāvanāmārga), neither would any of the ninefold class of conceptualizations— such as the "excessive" (adhimātra) and so forth— be abandoned, nor would any of the ninefold class of paths— such as the "soft-soft" (mṛdu-mṛdu) and so forth— be attained. Therefore, with the intention that [the opponent's position] is simply untenable, he states the following, bringing forward an undesirable consequence:
"If, Blessed One," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the inexpressible":

because the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is precisely that [inexpressible] differentiation, there is likewise an absence of decrease or increase even for the perfections such as generosity (*dāna*), and so on.
"Even of the perfection of generosity," and so forth.
If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?
he says, "If, O Blessed One," and so forth.
"How so? means "as if by way of reproach.
To provide further elaboration, he says:
"And yet, O Blessed One," and so forth.
And so it has been said:
"Decrease and increase are not applicable to an entity that is beyond verbal expression.
What has been diminished by the path called 'cultivation,' and what has emerged? (56)
He says, "In this way, etc.," to show that even the production of an undesirable consequence does not occur from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha).

But from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), explaining how the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) performs purposeful action (*arthakriyākārin*) just as unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyaksaṃbodhi*) does, he says:
"Moreover, however... and so forth.
"It is not thus.
By way of apprehending a real entity, the thought arises: "Does the perfection of generosity increase or does it decrease?
"Just as in the case of the unsurpassed," and so forth.

The meaning is that, by means of mere sovereignty, through the production of a mind in those to be trained (*vineya*) that reflects upon a distinguished object according to their respective merit and knowledge, and by increasing the merit dedicated [to awakening], unexcelled perfect enlightenment— which does not confer any further excellence— is conventionally the accomplisher of the desired goal; thus one dedicates [the merit].

In the same way, this path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which has been realized through meditation by the removal of adventitious stains, bestows nothing superior because it is like an illusion; yet, according to conventional truth, it performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) through the sequence of the disappearance of the discordant factors and the arising of their antidotes—it is with this intention that it is thus presented.
And so it has been said:
"Just as awakening is, so too is this [path] the accomplisher of the desired goal.
To explain this very point in detail, the five "carriers" (hārakas) beginning with "Furthermore" (*punaraparam*) are introduced.
He asks: what is the characteristic of awakening? He says:
"What, then, is this? and so forth.

"This is suchness" means that it is the nature of the Tathāgata, consisting of the Dharmakāya and so on, which has suchness as its own essence, is like an illusion, and is of the nature of non-conceptual knowledge.
The intention is that the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) also has suchness (*tathatā*) as its very nature.
And so it has been said:
"Enlightenment has the characteristic of suchness, and that [bodhisattva] is also considered to have that same characteristic.
(47) Furthermore, Subhūti, suchness neither increases nor decreases; by virtue of its essential nature, it is the same for the path to enlightenment—this is the remainder of the sense.

For in this way, by the mutual conformity of the nature of cause and effect with their respective meanings as effect and cause, the non-reversal of the relationship between cause and effect would be manifested.
Furthermore, indicating the efficacy of the path from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), he says:
"If a bodhisattva," and so forth.
"Connected with that" means bound to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
"Frequently and abundantly" means repeatedly and in great measure.
The two are mentioned because of the distinction between the stages of preparation (*prayoga*) and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*);
for it is impossible to dwell in a state of identity with [the practice] during the fundamental stage (*maulāvasthā*).
"In this way" refers to this.
Introducing [the topic] in such a manner, he says:
"In this way indeed, Subhūti," and so forth.
"Of the object" means of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
The eighteenth chapter, titled "Emptiness," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The nineteenth chapter:
Anticipating the objection that [the object] is not possible even conventionally by way of generating a cognition in which a distinct object appears as performing a causal function, he says:
"But how so, Blessed One? and so forth.

The meaning is that a bodhisattva does not awaken to enlightenment through either the first or the final single moment of mind, because in each individual preceding and succeeding moment of mind, there is no manifestation of the entire range of objects— such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)— which bring about the realization of a Buddha's enlightenment. Since it is stated that "sentient beings possess a single stream of consciousness," and because [a single mind] is incapable [of such realization], does he then awaken to enlightenment through multiple moments of mind that manifest the dharmas capable of accomplishing the desired goal simultaneously produced?
Thus, that position was not suspected.

He says that this position— that one awakens to enlightenment through a succession of many preceding and succeeding mental moments, which arise in sequence and whose nature consists of the dharmas that accomplish the unsurpassed awakening of a Buddha— is also not tenable.
"O Blessed One, as for the phrase 'the preceding,' etc.:

'not brought together' means that because the subsequent and the initial [moments] arise and perish respectively without any continuity (*niranvaya*), they are unconnected and not joined with one another."
How so?
Because there is no connection, a mind that perceives a qualified object does not arise; consequently, there is no accumulation of the roots of virtue.
Therefore, the implication is that there is no unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Since the previously mentioned position is not accepted, he speaks—beginning with "What do you think? and so forth—in order to provide a resolution for the latter position by means of the well-known example of a lamp: "of an oil lamp," etc.
Of a lamp:
"by the first impact" means by its being closed for the first moment.
"No, indeed not," was said because each [of the elements] individually lacks the capacity [to produce consciousness].
Clarifying that very point, he says:
"No, Blessed One," and so forth.

At the first moment of the merging of the flame and the wick, because it is indistinguishable from the simultaneous production resulting from the sequence of its own causal series—occurring without a second moment—the relationship of burner and burned, characterized as that of cause and effect, is untenable; thus, the wick is not burned by the flame upon its initial impact. If it is argued that "then it must be burned by the final moment of the lamp," he replies:
Nor is it the case that the wick is burned by the flame without depending on the initial impact;
rather, it is in dependence upon the first moment of the lamp that the wick is burned by the subsequent flame,
because the final moment is impossible without the initial moment.
He states that the principle [applies] to the final moment just as it does to the first moment:
"And not, O Blessed One," and so forth.

For in the second case as well—at the moment of the arising of the specific flame and the wick—since there would be the consequence of eternal existence and so on in the absence of the first moment, there is no conventional arising; consequently, the relationship of the burned and the burner, characterized as cause and effect, is absent.
If it is argued that the wick was not burned by the flame at the final moment,
but rather by the very first moment of the lamp, [the author] replies:
"And not by the final," and so forth.
Rather, it is in dependence upon the final moment of the flame that the wick is burned by the preceding flame;
for without the final moment, the first moment lacks the capacity to burn it.
Since each [of the two] is individually incapable, he asks again, posing a question in order to directly demonstrate that the capacity which is accepted for both together does indeed exist:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Has that wick been burnt?
Because it is impossible to alter a matter once accepted, he says:
"It has been burnt, Blessed One," and so forth.

Even if the preceding and succeeding moments are indeed mutually unconnected due to their simultaneous, traceless destruction and arising respectively, nevertheless, when the first moment of the lamp-wick has arisen as a specific aggregate, it is— by way of the nature of dependent origination consisting of causal conditions— and by virtue of the power of the relationship between cause and effect, which is delightful only when not analyzed— invested with a particular excellence of capacity; thus,
the second moment of the lamp-wick would indeed be distinct [from the first].

In that case, even if destruction were causeless, because the relationship of the burned and the burner— characterized as cause and effect— exists, the meaning is that the wick is burned by both the initial and the final moments. Immediately thereafter, he says the following, connecting the subsequent point with the subject at hand:
"Even so, Subhūti," and so forth. This is easily understood.

If it is asked: "If there is no complete awakening (abhisambodhi) through each [moment] occurring in a temporal sequence of before and after, then is one awakened by means of those that have arisen simultaneously? he says:

"And not by those productions of thought" means that one does not attain perfect awakening even by many mental moments arising simultaneously; the sense is that this is impossible, because of the statement that "sentient beings possess a single stream of consciousness."
If it is argued that he awakens in another way, he says:
"And he does not awaken apart from those productions of thought."

If one does not attain perfect awakening through another mind distinct from the mind as previously described, then because [such a mind] is impossible, it would follow that awakening is altogether impossible; to this he says:
"And yet, one attains perfect awakening," and so forth.

By means of the logic of the lamp-example, which demonstrates the application of a single object across preceding and succeeding moments, the Bodhisattva attains perfect awakening through these two productions of consciousness: first, having perceived the initial cognition—which manifests a few factors that bring about enlightenment—subsequently, there arises a final cognition manifesting a distinguished object that exceeds what was manifested in that [initial] one; it is through these two productions of mind that he fully awakens.
"Unsurpassed enlightenment" is the meaning.
Furthermore, by means of the very same analogy of the lamp as previously described, the eightfold profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is to be understood.
And so it has been said:
"Enlightenment is not joined with a preceding mind, nor with a succeeding one;
through the application of the lamp analogy, the profound nature of reality is eightfold.

(58) Having thus explained what arose incidentally, [the author] now, for the purpose of describing the characteristics of irreversibility for Bodhisattvas abiding on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), [states] regarding that object:
The eightfold profundity is what must be explained; thus, first speaking of the profundity of arising, he says:
"O Blessed One, this is profound," and so forth.
By the words "and it is perfectly awakened," etc., [it is shown that] through conventional reality, the realization of awakening occurs in two moments.
That too is not tenable; thus he says:
"What do you think? and so forth.
Is that mind which exists in the first moment, even though it has ceased, going to arise again in the second moment conventionally,
such that awakening (bodhi) would be connected with two moments?
He says this because it is impossible for that which has perished without parts to arise again.
"Not so," [it is said].

Since an effect is impossible without a cause, even though the operation belongs to the final moment, the operation of the first moment is metaphorically attributed [to it] through a causal succession;
thus, enlightenment is logically possible over two moments. However, the meaning is that even conventionally, the operation of the first moment is not primary.
Then this would have been said:
"This profundity of production is not [a matter of] the preceding and succeeding moments, nor is it the production of a distinguished object attainable through cultivation.
For the sake of explaining the profundity of cessation, he says:
What do you think, Subhūti? Is that mind which has arisen subject to cessation?
In this context, "arisen" means past, having its existence already perished;
he says this because, in reality, it is of the nature of cessation.
Regarding "possessing the nature of cessation" (*nirodhadharmin*): cessation is emptiness; because that very dharma exists in this [phenomenon], it is called "possessing the nature of cessation."
The meaning is that its nature is suchness (*tathatā*).
To the question, "Does that cease in the second moment?", he says:
"What do you think? Will that which has the nature of cessation itself cease?"
"Because it is of that very nature, it has passed into the state of being swallowed by cessation the very moment it arises; with the intention of asking, 'How much more so will it cease?
he said: 'Certainly not, Blessed One.
[The questioner] asks: 'Is that which is yet to come endowed with the property of cessation?'"
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that mind which is unarisen subject to cessation? "No indeed," he replied.
"Because destruction has the nature of the cessation of existence, that which is unarisen is certainly not subject to cessation."
Is there a cessation of that [nature] in another moment? To this he says:
"What do you think, Subhūti, will that which is subject to cessation cease?"
"Certainly not.
Because there is an absence of a first moment, there is a lack of cessation in the second moment; therefore, it will certainly not cease in another moment.
If it is asked, "In that case, does cessation belong to the present? he says:
What do you think, Subhūti? Will that mind which has the nature of being neither produced nor ceased ever cease?
It has the nature of non-production because the production of what is already present would be purposeless;
it has the nature of non-cessation because there is no destruction at the time of its existence.
"Certainly not," he said.
"The thought is that [the self] is devoid of the nature of being either one or many.
If this is so, then it follows that non-existence is what ceases; to this he replies:
What do you think, Subhūti? Will that dharma which is by its very nature already ceased in its own-being ever cease?
That dharma which is ceased in its own-being by its very nature is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form and so forth.
Is that very phenomenon designated as "existence" (bhāva) to be ceased?
No, indeed.
Immediately following this, because the cessation of entities belonging to the three times has been refuted, non-existence (abhāva), being non-existent, is not ceased at all.
"In that case, would the likeness to an illusion be ceased?
He said: "What do you think, Subhūti, will that which is the *dharmatā* of phenomena be ceased?
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is by its very essence a state of non-cessation— being delightful solely when not analyzed— it does not cease at all in reality.
However, because every arisen thing, which is by nature like an illusion, ceases conventionally, it is called the "profundity of cessation."
He speaks regarding the profundity of suchness:
"What do you think, Subhūti, will he remain just as suchness remains? The word "bodhisattva" is to be supplied as the subject.
Because it possesses the object of non-conceptual knowledge, he says:
"O Blessed One, it will remain just as suchness remains.
This refers to the Bodhisattvas of the three times remaining just like suchness.
If it is argued that suchness would then be eternal, he says:
"What do you think, Subhūti? If it were to remain exactly as suchness is, then would it not be immutable?
By the elision of the vowel *a*, [the word] becomes *akūṭasthā* ("not immutable").
Do you think that it might be eternal, rather than being eternally immutable? That which is dependent origination is itself considered by you to be emptiness.
Because of this statement, since [the world] has as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) conventionally real, momentary entities, he says: "Not so.
If it is argued that, because it has the form of an entity, it is therefore not profound at all, he says:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is suchness profound?
"It is profound, Blessed One.
[This is said] regarding the comprehension of the categories of phenomena such as form and so forth.
Furthermore, because it is impossible to directly realize that [mind] as something distinct from suchness (tathatā), suchness is profound and difficult to understand; this is what is meant.
To explain the profundity of the object of knowledge (jñeya-gāmbhīrya), he asks:
"What do you think, Subhūti—is the mind in suchness?"
Because the state of being a substratum does not exist within suchness, he says:
"Certainly not. Then, [anticipating the objection] that the mind would therefore be non-different from suchness, he says:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the mind suchness? "No indeed," he replied.
"Because conventional reality and ultimate reality are mutually exclusive, the mind is certainly not suchness."
If it is argued that, by implication, the mind is other than suchness, he says:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the mind other than suchness?"
Since no phenomenon exists apart from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),
with this intention he said:
"Certainly not."
This has been stated:
this entire reality is "mind-only," which is neither distinct from suchness nor non-distinct from it; this is the profundity of the object of knowledge.
To explain the profundity of knowledge, he says:
“Subhūti, do you perceive suchness?
“No indeed,” he replied.
“Because its intrinsic nature is suchness, I do not perceive suchness in reality.”
Therefore, the view that non-seeing itself is seeing is the depth of knowledge.
To explain the depth of conduct, he says:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does one who conducts himself in this way conduct himself in the profound?"
"Thus" means in the form of suchness (*tathatā*). He says that in reality, it does not move at all anywhere.
"O Blessed One, he who practices in this way does not practice anywhere.
Clarifying this very point, and anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Because," and so forth.
This is what is meant:
because for one who abides in suchness,
those specific practices and mental activities do not proceed in their respective order, due to the absence of any ultimate cause and effect.
They do not engage [in them];
therefore, by the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*), non-engagement everywhere is itself engagement—this is the profundity of practice (*caryā-gāmbhīrya*).
To explain the meaning of the profundity of non-duality (*advaya-gāmbhīrya*), he says:
"O Subhūti, that bodhisattva," and so forth.
"Where does he course? means in what object does he abide?

"Ultimate reality" (paramārtha) means that because of the absence of the dualistic activity of signs and signlessness, one courses in the dharmadhātu; such is the sense in which there would be the profundity of non-duality.
Clarifying this very point, he says:

What do you think, Subhūti? Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the ultimate reality course in signs? “Not so,” he replied. Because of the negation of the perceptions of sign and signlessness, he does not at all course in signs characterized by attachment to existence and non-existence.
To explain the profundity of skill in means, he said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that sign not unmanifested?"
"Unmanifested," "unabandoned," and "not relinquished"—this is what is meant.
[The Bodhisattva replies: "Certainly not. By the power of the non-apprehension of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanupalambha*), there is indeed no sign (*nimitta*) that remains undestroyed.
If that is so, then [one might ask] whether the sign has been abandoned.
To this he says: "What do you think, Subhūti?
Does a sign become eliminated for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom?"
He says that because there is no effort toward abandonment, the sign is not abandoned at all:
"No, Blessed One," and so forth.

This means that while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, a bodhisattva does not strive or exert himself with the thought, "In this very present life, how may I attain the abandonment of signs?"—that is to say, he does not apply himself in such a manner.
And as to what fault there would be in its abandonment, he says:
"If, however," and so forth. To the question of how there can be both the abandonment and non-abandonment of one and the same thing, he says:

"O Blessed One, this [passage] beginning with 'this' means that one understands form and so forth—which, by way of conventional reality, is like an illusion—as having such characteristics, such an intrinsic nature, such a cause, and such a condition.

Because it is ultimately unarisen, one cultivates mastery within the signless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, there is abandonment from the perspective of ultimate truth, yet non-abandonment from the perspective of conventional reality; this is the profundity of skill in means."

Thus, by virtue of attaining the gateway to the inconceivable liberation, and by engaging in conventional discourse that accords with the realization of the eightfold profundity— such as arising and so forth— through the practice of mutually contradictory meanings,
the characteristics of one who is irreversible while abiding on the path of cultivation should be understood as being like those of the sixteen moments.
And so it has been said: "There is profundity in arising and in cessation, in suchness, in the object of knowledge, in knowledge, in conduct, and in non-dual skillful means. (59)
By the description of the characteristics of non-retrogression, the Saikṣa Bodhisattva-saṅgha has been declared.

Subsequently, through the abandonment of conceptualizations regarding affliction and purification, one attains the equality of both; thus, one becomes an Aśaikṣa, because there is nothing further to be learned. Therefore—
In order to elucidate the characteristics of the Saṅgha of those in training (śaikṣa), it must be stated that there is equality between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; thus he says:
"O Venerable Subhūti, as for the one who is a bodhisattva," and so forth.
The word *apinu* functions in the sense of the interrogative particle *kim*, used here as a question.
Does the perfection of wisdom increase?
The meaning is that it undergoes growth.
He says: it does not increase at all.
"Should it be so," and so forth.

Here, the non-conceptual knowledge regarding cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) is stated with the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) that they are respectively like a dream and so on.
The intended meaning (*abhiprāya*), however, is characterized as follows:

If, with reference to the abandonment of the conceptualization of the adverse side and its antidote, the increase of cultivation for one who has gone during the day occurs due to the realization of the equality of those two, then it would likewise increase for one who has gone into the midst of a dream; however, since it does not increase in the dream just as it does not increase during the day, [the author] asks "For what reason? and states the following in order to clarify this very point:
"Indeed, it is non-conceptual," and so forth.
If the perfection of wisdom were to increase while one is practicing during the day, then by the power of that practice, there would be expansion even in dreams; however, this is simply not the case.

Because worldly and transcendental phenomena are understood to have the nature of mere appearance, similar to a dream, it is impossible to conceptualize saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—which possess the nature of a dream and a day respectively—through the dualistic discrimination of adverse factors and their remedies as being distinct.
This is because the Blessed One has stated that both the dream and the day are non-conceptual and identical in essence.
Thus it has been said:
"Because all phenomena are like a dream, there is no conceptualization of existence or peace.

To this, [the opponent] objects: "If all phenomena are indeed similar to a dream, then just as in the state of dreaming, there would be an absence of the ten wholesome actions and so forth even in the waking state.
To this, [the Buddha] says: "Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, whether it be a woman... and so on.
"What? implies a sense of reproach, meaning "not at all.
Accumulation (*ācaya*) arises from the increase of its own nature;
it is an accumulation by virtue of the capacity to produce an effect.

The point is that, in the same way, because [actions] such as ritual applications (*prayoga*) would be non-existent due to their being equivalent to a dream, there would be an absence of auspicious and inauspicious karma even during the day.
He states that from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is neither accumulation nor increase, beginning with the words "just as [things] are like a dream," and so forth.

However, since the connection between action and its fruit is accepted conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), he says that the example would be unestablished because the mind in a dream is impaired by sleep (*middha*); therefore, the fruit [in a dream] is not equal [to that of waking experience].
Now, as for the passage beginning with "Furthermore, O Venerable One," etc.:
"of that karma" refers to [the karma] existing in the state of dream. Explaining this very point, he says:
Regarding the phrase "How so? and so forth:
therein, because of the accomplishment of the ritual application (*prayoga*) and so on, or due to the injury of body, speech, and mind, there is a distinction in meaning to be expressed as follows:

"He has been killed" (*hataḥ*), "well killed" (*sādhu hataḥ*), or "thoroughly killed" (*suṣṭhu hataḥ*); and because one's own activity is perceived in every instance, the meaning is "he has been killed by me."
This has been stated as follows:

Just as in the system of external objects (*bāhyārthanaya*), where destruction is causeless due to momentariness and the diversity of the world is established as being born of karma, so too—according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)—no one is killed by anyone, nor is the substance of anything seized by anyone. Nevertheless, for one who possesses improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) and the like, through the gateway of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) that consists in killing and so forth—which brings about the production of a thing whose continuum has been interrupted—the following occurs:

Just as wholesome and unwholesome actions such as killing are established as occurring during the day, so too in the case of a dream, for one who has accumulated wholesome or unwholesome karma, there is a nourishment of that accumulation upon waking through conceptualizations such as "Oh, I have killed!"— due to the intensification of attachment to the state of the preliminary application (prayoga-avasthā) and so forth; this is so even according to the system of external objects (bahir-artha-naya).
The example "as in the state of dream" is unestablished;

therefore, according to the Madhyamaka method, even in the waking state, with respect to objects that are like dreams and their corresponding referents, wholesome states and so forth are established for those whose connection to all delusions remains unbroken through their attachment to existence and so on.

However, because it is an unclarity resulting from unwholesome practice due to causes of error such as drowsiness (*middha*), the fruit in a dream is inferior; whereas in the waking state, because the causes of error such as drowsiness have vanished, there is a superior fruit due to the appearance of things being clear and undisturbed.
Since the existence of the fruit of karma is accepted even in the state of dreaming, the fault of not being a monk (*abhikṣutva*) and so forth should not be raised [as an objection].

This is because the status of being under restraint (*saṃvara*) or not under restraint (*asaṃvara*) is established solely by virtue of the Blessed One’s designation, just as in the case of one to whom the training has been given (*śikṣādattaka*).

If the nourishment of karma were to occur through the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then even for a Tathāgata, it would occur due to the persistence of conceptual construction despite the presence of its antidote; thus he says:
"If, venerable Subhūti," and so forth.
While conceptualizing, one produces the perception of exhaustion, forming the perception of exhaustion such as, "The aggregates of my cyclic existence are exhausted," and so forth.
For that action as well—that is, for the action of mental attention (*manaskāra*) which effects the abandonment of afflictions—there is accumulation (*ācaya*) due to the increase of its own nature;
there would be accumulation by virtue of its capacity to produce an effect.

The implication is that, because there exists a specific fruit to be obtained from accumulated karma, the Tathāgata would remain unperfected. [To address this,] he says, "Certainly not so," meaning that the conceptual construction of the Tathāgata— such as "birth is exhausted for me"— is established in accordance with those to be trained (*vineya*), but not in reality.
In order to substantiate this very point, having raised the doubt "for what reason?", he says:
"all conceptual constructions and mental constructions," and so forth.

"All conceptual constructions" (*sarvakalpa*) refers to forms and other objects, which consist of both specific and general characteristics and serve as the objective supports for non-conceptual and conceptual cognitions. "Mental construction" (*vikalpa*) regarding them is the apprehension thereof; it is "abandoned" or "devoid" of that because of the realization of the non-conceptual nature of phenomena (*nirvikalpadharmatā*). This is the meaning.
If it is asked why mental action and the mind do not arise for others in the absence of an object of perception (*ālambana*), he says:
"In this very way," and so forth.
This is the nature of things (*dharmatā*); by virtue of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*), action and the mind do not arise without an object of perception.
Therefore, it arises only with an object.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"Seen, heard," and so forth. In that regard:
"Entities possessing such-and-such a nature arise from causes possessing such-and-such a nature"—
according to this principle, a certain cognition that takes defilement as its object grasps defilement,
while a certain cognition that takes purification as its object grasps purification.
Some say that "volition" (cetanā) means "intellect" (buddhi).
Others say that because of the statement "volition is mental action," it is simply action (karman) that has been stated by way of a synonym. Concluding, he says:
Therefore, then, O Venerable One, and so forth.

Since the past and the future lack existence, they cannot logically function as objects of cognition; and since a present object cannot be grasped by means of knowledge possessing an image (*sākāra-jñāna*) and the like, [the author] asks: if all objects of cognition are empty, how can volition (*cetanā*), which itself possesses an object, arise? To this he says:
"O Venerable Subhūti," and so forth.
"Secluded" means they are empty by virtue of being devoid of the nature of an objective referent (*ālambana*).
He says that [it] arises from the object of unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
Regarding the phrase "having made it a sign" (*nimittīkṛtya*) and so forth:

the meaning is that one takes as a sign—that is, superimposes—upon form and so forth their specific, uncommon characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-cihna*), even though in reality it is signless (*animitta*), according to how it appears.
By the word "as far as" (*yāvat*), there is the inclusion of [the formula] beginning with "name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
Regarding the phrase "having recourse to worldly convention," the ellipsis is that "it is stated immediately after [the statement] 'it arises,' with reference to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
Having established that the connection between action and its fruit exists even in a dream, he speaks again, raising a doubt in accordance with those people who rely on perception (*upalambhika*).
"Venerable Subhūti," and so forth.
Even though the matter has already been resolved, he speaks with the intention that "who, being sensible, would resolve it again and again through endless doubt?
Thus he says: "This, venerable Śāriputra, is Maitreya," and so forth.
Regarding the term "body-witness" (kāyasākṣī): a non-returner who has attained cessation while practicing for arhatship is a body-witness.
In the same way, the noble Maitreya is a bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*) because he has set out toward the state of Buddhahood.
"This matter" refers to what was transformed in the dream.
"What is that gift? is the question.
Addressing the noble Maitreya by means of Subhūti’s very words, he said:
"Then indeed, O Venerable One," and so forth. [This was said] once it had been established.

Even if, for the sake of others, one were to repeatedly state refutations in response to repeated doubts arising from the differences among individual disciples to be trained, it would still not be possible to effect the removal of misconceptions for all of them at the very time of a single Buddha’s appearance, because he acts only for the benefit of those who are capable [of being saved]. With this in mind—intending to show that the succession of future Buddhas arises precisely through the context of answering these questions—the author, wishing to provide a refutation, says: "This question is taught as incomplete; for if it were completed, there would be nothing further to be done, which would entail the consequence of the appearance of future Buddhas being useless."

When the Venerable Subhūti spoke thus, and so forth; referring to the possibility [of such a name], he speaks while conceptualizing: "But, Venerable Subhūti, what is this that is called a 'name'? and so forth.
In that regard, it is said that emptiness does not provide an answer:
"Furthermore, that which... and so forth.
It is not capable of such a response.
Because it does not exist, it is not capable;
nor are form and the other [sensory objects] capable,
as he says in the passage beginning with "I [perceive] that too."

The grasping consists in [the conceptualization of] the dharma that would relinquish through the distinctions of the non-apprehension of agent, object, and action; the dharma that is to be relinquished; and the dharma by which one would relinquish.
This was stated with reference to the self as an object:
"whatever dharma is designated. He says that the non-apprehension of all dharmas would otherwise be untenable.
"Is it indeed," and so forth.
"Kaccid" means "if. This is what is being said:

If these phenomena such as form and so forth were realized by you exactly as you describe them in words, then, since there would exist the apprehension of a realized object just as there is the apprehension of an object of conceptual construction, how could there be the non-apprehension of all phenomena through the state of relinquishment?
[The Bodhisattva] says: "It is not realized in that way."
"By me, O Venerable One," and so forth.
In the stages of preparation and so on, one should apply [the phrase] "I do not know," and so forth. To the question "How then?
he says: "But furthermore," and so forth.
This is what is meant:

by means of non-conceptual knowledge characterized by the non-apprehension of all phenomena, all phenomena are realized as having such a nature because they have illusion-like nature; yet, because conceptualization does not arise during the state of realization, one would not touch them with the body.
It should not be expressed by speech,
nor should it be attended to by the mind.

Because realization would not occur if one follows after conceptual constructions due to the arising of cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*), and because, subsequent to that realization, there is conventional discourse through the conventionality of manifestation.
He says that the sphere of the śrāvakas is the realization of non-conceptual knowledge;
thus he speaks of "profound wisdom" and so forth.
He states that such is indeed the realization of the śrāvakas.
"From where [could this come], Śāriputra," and so forth.
Since the realization is equal by virtue of mere non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*), [the meaning is: "He is one of profound wisdom";
thus, one should not give rise to such a thought.
Explaining their very equality, he says:
"Do you perceive," and so forth.
This means: at the time of realization, do you perceive or apprehend with conceptual cognition that state of arhatship characterized by the knowledge of the exhaustion and non-arising of phenomena?
He says "No, indeed" because [perception] is contrary to realization due to its being erroneous.
He states that such is precisely the principle for Bodhisattvas at the time of realization.
"Even so, Śāriputra," and so forth.
Thus, in this way, the very same refutations as previously stated should be understood as the responses to the objections concerning the non-existence of karma and so on.
And so it has been said:
"The refutations of the objections concerning the non-existence of karma and so forth have been stated as above. Thus,
in order to conclude the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, he speaks with reference to the immediate purpose of that teaching, beginning with "he, while practicing,
is not terrified," and so on.

Because he has gained power through the practice of non-apprehension, he does not think, "I shall not attain perfect awakening," but rather he applies himself to yoga with the thought, "I shall certainly attain perfect awakening.
Having cultivated the equality of both, he becomes a Buddha.

Immediately following the phrase "in his own buddha-field," [the author], explaining the twofold purification of the buddha-field through the distinction between the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), says:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra," and so forth.
In that context, the impurity of the world of sentient beings consists of hunger and the like; as its antidote, there is the introduction of purity such as divine enjoyments and so on.

Likewise, regarding the impurity of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*)—such as stumps, thorns, and so forth—it is the purification of the two kinds of Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra*) in their respective order, through the application of purity such as being level like the palm of a hand, which serves as the antidote to that [impurity]. Thus it has been stated in brief: "Regarding the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), whatever..."
Its purification comes from the offering of purification;
likewise is the purity of the vessel-world, that is, the Buddha-field. (61) Thus, the detailed explanation is easy to understand according to the sūtra.
Regarding this, something is said:
having raised the doubt as to why that is so,
he says, "For in that way, by him, everything," and so forth.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"In that way, the mind... and so forth.
Therein, "by everything" means by way of all colors, shapes, objects, and forms.
Every object is differentiated by its various classes;
in every respect, it is so through the distinctions of each of those individual classes, in all possible modes.
Because they will lack their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), they will not come into being; because the marks produced by them will be absent, they will not be cognized.
Having raised the doubt as to why this is so, he says:
"Delighting in the skillful relinquishment of all possessions," and so forth.
Elaborating upon this very point, he says:
"Therefore, with such a mind," and so forth.
Regarding "ill-will, anger, and resentment":
ill-will (*vyāpāda*) is hatred toward sentient beings;
anger (*krodha*) is malice toward both sentient and non-sentient objects; and resentment (*roṣa*) is the persistence of enmity.
By generating a specific state of mind, I shall act accordingly; by accomplishing through practice, I shall proceed accordingly;
and by exerting extraordinary vigor, I shall persevere.
Because of the absence of water, there is a waterless wilderness; that is the fear.
Anticipating the question "Why is that so?", he says:
"Unafraid," and so forth.
Water endowed with the eight qualities— fragrant, sweet, cool, light, clear, and pure— does not afflict the belly or throat of the drinker.
Thus, through the acquisition of water, they obtain water endowed with the eight qualities;
distinguished as mild, moderate, and intense, they are happy, possessed of happiness, and bestowed with every form of bliss.
Upon coming within the range of vision, this [water] will manifest.
It will arise as something fit for enjoyment.
Food and so forth are the requisites for life because they serve as the cause of its maintenance.
"After a long time" means after an exceedingly long period.
Anticipating the question "For what reason is that? as before, he says:
"For whatever moment of mind," and so forth;
because whatever moment of mind [arises], in reality...

That which is unproduced by way of conventional reality—this very state characterized by long duration—is beginningless because it is devoid of a first cause; it is a "limit" (*akoṭi*) that is unprecedented.

Its "end," the portion consisting of the state of Buddhahood, has emptiness as its intrinsic nature, and is thus called a "non-limit. Therefore, one should not experience terror or the like due to the realization of awakening after a long time;
the meaning is that one should not conceive of it as being difficult to accomplish.
Regarding the phrase "from fears and terrors":
external fear consists of [threats from] predatory beasts and the like; internal terror consists of fevers and the like.
If it is argued that no one would engage in the purification of the Buddha-field as described because it is impossible to carry out, he says:
"Then, in that assembly... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in this place":
because it is possible through the yoga of repeated practice to purify the designated buddha-field,
he says that the sign of receiving a prophecy has arisen by the power of the perfection of that intention.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, and so forth.
"He vanished into the crown of his head" means that this is the nature of things (*dharmatā*): when a prophecy is to be made regarding one's status as a Tathāgata, [the light] enters there.
Then, the rays were absorbed within the seam of the uṣṇīṣa.
Because of the arising of excellence through the vision of the signs, there was worship performed by Āryagaṅgadeva, and so forth.
And immediately upon its manifestation, and so forth.
Having grasped the relationship in many ways, he asks about the purpose of the smile, saying:
"Then indeed, the Venerable Ānanda... and so forth.
He speaks while making known its essential nature.
"O Ānanda," and so forth.

Some maintain that by means of this prophecy—"he will fully awaken to perfect enlightenment"—the role of witness is indicated for the members of the assembly regarding their conviction in the attainment of such purity of a buddha-field.
He speaks thus even before the state of full awakening, while still bestowing the prophecy.
"This very bliss," and so forth. He states,
"Then indeed, O Venerable One," and so forth, because there is wonder at the arising of only those things that have been manifested therein.
Because it was well said, he says:
"It is so," and so forth.
In that regard, they have crossed over the mire because of their abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
