Because they abide in the realization of the summit (*mūrdhābhisamaya*), they have approached the perfection of enlightenment.
Speaking also of the community of disciples (*śrāvakasaṃgha*), he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, for him... and so forth:
having raised the doubt, "Why is that?", he says, "As many as those... and so forth.
He speaks thus because those who have performed meritorious deeds have fulfilled their vows:
"Then again," and so forth. Concluding, he says:
"Of Suvarṇapuṣpa," and so forth.
Having heard this most wonderful account, he asks about the previous connection (pūrvayoga), saying:
"By her, O Blessed One," and so forth.
Revealing his own nature, he says:
"O Ananda," and so forth.
He states that this prophecy in all its aspects is precisely in accordance with his previous vow.
"Having performed the preparatory purification," and so forth.
In this context, she is "one who has performed the preparatory purification" because she has attained the path of vision (*darśanamārga*);
she is "one who has reached the culmination" because she has understood the intrinsic nature of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
In the same way, he confirms it with his own hand, saying:
"It is thus," and so forth.
In the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, the commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this is the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Sister Gaṅgadevā."
The twentieth chapter.

Having fulfilled the accumulations through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) by means of the purification of the Buddha-field already accomplished, one must subsequently explain skill in means as that which performs the Buddha-activity in one's own Buddha-field according to the suitability of beings.
In that regard, in order to establish its subject matter, he asks by saying, "In the Prajñāpāramitā," and so forth. He speaks for the sake of providing an answer:
"Here, Subhūti," and so forth.

"Form"—that is, observing that *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena) as *dharmatā*, meaning observing form as a real entity through the *dharmatā* of emptiness; he should observe it in such a way that he does not perceive it, namely, that emptiness does not exist by way of an intrinsic nature of emptiness.
The point is that it should be observed in such a manner that it is not apprehended.
This has been stated:
that the sphere of skillful means consists of [realities] such as emptiness, which are like an illusion. But how, then, in practice...
He says, "Even so, one does not attain it," beginning with the words,
"O Blessed One," and so forth.
In order to provide a resolution for this, he speaks while demonstrating the application of skillful means (*upāyakauśala*).
"Since, Subhūti," and so forth.
"Endowed with the excellence of all aspects" means complete in [the perfections of] giving and the rest.
"Precisely while not in meditative equipoise" means:
And the perfection of wisdom, which consists of great skill in means, will be embraced by me;
yet, with the intention that emptiness has not been directly realized, he fixes his mind precisely upon this very concentration on emptiness.
And herein, in the interim, through the power of the Mother of the Victors, he does not fall away from the factors conducive to enlightenment.

And he does not effect the destruction of the outflows—the abandonment of the outflows of desire and existence—by intentionally taking rebirth for the sake of sentient beings; yet, through the objective support of the concentration on emptiness, he achieves mastery over the destruction of the outflows.
To clarify this very point, he says:
"At which time," and so forth.
"How is it that even through practice, it is not to be directly realized?
Having raised this doubt, he says: "For what reason?"
"Thus, one who has ascended to the wholesome," and so forth;
"he does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)"—
this is what is meant.

Due to the power of the application of knowing the proper and improper time for the realization of the contemplation that brings mastery through the cultivation of all aspects, even while established in that samādhi,
one would not realize emptiness.
Furthermore, skillful means (upāya) is of ten kinds.
In that regard, first, for the purpose of explaining the means for transcending obstructive factors by way of transcending obstacles, he says:
"Just as, for example," and so forth.
Therein, because he is endowed with qualities of valor and form that are weak, middling, and superior respectively, the nine phrases beginning with "he would be supremely heroic" are to be explained.
He is wise because of his capacity to grasp the meaning of the texts;
he is capable of speech due to his proficiency in the instruments [of articulation];
and he is capable of responding because of his ability to answer questions.
He is endowed with eloquence because he is free from paralysis;
he is endowed with comprehension because he accomplishes the objectives he has undertaken;
and he knows the proper time and place because he thoroughly understands time and other factors in terms of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.
He knows the proper positions; having been well-trained primarily in archery, he has attained the highest mastery in all weapons.
Because he can ward off many firm weapons, he is one who possesses a shield against many weapons and is armored against firm weapons.
The *kalās* are transformations of the body and so forth that cause others to be won over.
The *śilpasthānas* are fields of craft such as painting and the like.
"Possessing mindfulness," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
He is capable of crossing over because of his capacity for accomplishment;
that is, by means of a certain conjunction of causal factors, such as the encounter with enemies and so forth.

By inducing transformations of mind, speech, and body, I shall respectively cause [them] to depart in a manner that is most terrifying, formidable, and hair-raising; yet, through peace and security, being free from all calamities, I shall cause them to go forth;
and through well-being, nourishment, and physical health, I shall liberate them.
Those who, out of a desire for the same object, persist in enmity are adversaries (*pratyarthika*).
Those who have fallen on the side of the enemy are enemies (*pratyamitra*).
One who is exceedingly affectionate due to compassion is a friend (*snigdha*).
He is compassionate due to his possession of courtesy.
Anticipating the question "For what reason is that so?", he says:
"For thus, O Blessed One," and so forth.
Because he is free from affliction of body and mind, he is unscarred and uninjured.
Having thus pointed out the illustration, he states the illustrated meaning:
"In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva," and so forth.

In that regard, the concentrations (*samādhi*) together with their attendants—namely loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are the fulfillment of the intention to bring beings into contact with happiness, to separate them from suffering, to prevent them from being parted from happiness, and to perform what is beneficial, respectively.
Having raised the doubt as to why this is so, he says:
"For thus, of this... and so forth.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"At which time," and so forth.
By the phrase "and having transcended the faction of Māra," the means for transcending obstructive factors (*antarāyika-dharma*) would be indicated.
Summarizing, he says:
"In which," and so forth.
He speaks of the means for dwelling in non-abiding by virtue of having cultivated the equality of all things.
Subhūti, it is just as with the bird, and so forth;
even there, he is neither supported nor established.
Because space is non-existent, he is not supported there by the intellect, nor is he stationed there with the body.
And by saying "he dwells in that very [state]," the means for dwelling without a fixed basis (*apratiṣṭhitavihāra*) would have been indicated. He states the meaning of the simile:
"In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva," and so forth.
Demonstrating the means of following one's previous vows through the fulfillment of those vows, he says:
"Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a strong man... and so forth.
By the phrase "...as long as he does not wish [to stop]," it is made known that there is a continuation based on the impetus of the vow.
Applying the subject matter at hand to the Bodhisattva, he says:
"In this very way, Subhūti," and so forth.
By means of the paths of cultivation and the path of distinction, [the roots of goodness] are respectively matured and well-matured.
Concluding [the discussion], he says:
"Therefore, Subhūti," and so forth.
He speaks thus while demonstrating the uncommon means by virtue of having thoroughly practiced all difficult tasks.
"O Blessed One, he is a doer of what is difficult," and so forth.
This should be applied as follows: "He courses in emptiness through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, respectively.
Repeating these words because they have been well spoken, he says:
"Thus it is," and so forth. Having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:
"For thus," and so forth.
Establishing this very point, he says:
"When a bodhisattva," and so forth.
Anticipating the question, "For what reason is that? as before, he says:
For it is said, "Thus for him," and so forth.

By the statement "he does not realize [it directly]," it is indicated that there exists an uncommon means, because he does not attain the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) due to the power of his intention not to abandon any sentient being.
Because all phenomena are non-apprehendable, [the Blessed One] spoke in order to explain the method of non-attachment, beginning with:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva... and so forth. [The phrase] "by means of the notion of a sentient being" [is used].
"By means of attachment to entities.
And as for the phrase "nor does one fall away":

since falling away is possible through the perception of relish (*āsvādana*), the statement that there is no falling away from all wholesome qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) must be intended to indicate the method of non-relishing.
Having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:
"For it is embraced by skill in means," and so forth.
He speaks thus for the sake of the meaning of non-apprehension as the door of liberation that is emptiness.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva:
"For a long time these beings have wandered in the pursuit of objective apprehension," and so forth;
[he] enters into the bliss of the liberation of the concentration on emptiness, and so forth.

The method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-upāya*) is elucidated through the attainment of the perfection of the cultivation of the gate of liberation that is the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi-vimokṣamukha*).
Regarding the purpose of the signless method (*animitta-upāya*) due to the non-apprehension of signs, he says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva as follows:"
"For a long time these beings have [perceived] by means of the perception of signs," and so forth.
"He enters the signless concentration, the door of liberation"— by this,
the statement that he reaches the fulfillment of the cultivation of the signless concentration, the door of liberation, the signless means (*animittopāya*) is expressed.
He speaks for the sake of the skillful means of non-aspiration through the non-apprehension of aspiration:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva:
'For a long time these beings have [perceived] with the notion of permanence,' and so forth."
"Regarding 'the wishless concentration and liberation':
by means of reaching the perfection of the cultivation of the gateways of the wishless concentration and liberation, the skillful means of non-aspiration is indicated.
Although emptiness and the other [gateways] are common to the Śrāvakas and others,"
To specify that particular means, he says:
"Whosoever, Subhūti, is a bodhisattva," and so forth.

In that context, three ways of practicing through the apprehension of objects—in contrast to the three gates of liberation, such as emptiness—have been stated; and their explanation has been provided in sequence by the passage beginning with "the notion of a composite whole," and so on.
In the phrase "from emptiness" (*śūnyatātaḥ*) and so forth, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of "starting from" (*ādi-āditvena*) with a word ending in the locative case.
This is what has been stated:

that it is impossible for a bodhisattva, being thus endowed with the qualities of knowledge through the very application of compassion and the rest, not to strive toward emptiness and the other [perfections].
In order to teach how to pose a question for the sake of the means and signs of irreversibility by means of explaining the dharmas of irreversibility preceded by a question, he says:
"For thus, a bodhisattva," and so forth.
He explains by way of negative indication (*vyatireka*).
"If it is so," and so forth. Having raised the doubt, "Why is that so?", he says, "For whoever this... and so forth.

In that regard, the unique quality (*āveṇika-dharma*) is the non-abandonment of all sentient beings; for the sake of generating the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, it does not indicate, does not manifest, and does not demonstrate that [non-abandonment] respectively.
Because he does not understand, he does not answer when questioned, nor does he provide a resolution; these [consequences] should be applied respectively.
"That stage" refers to skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).
In order to explain it by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he asks rhetorically:
"Could it be so, Blessed One? and so forth. Refuting that very point, he says:
"It could be so, Subhūti," and so forth.
"One should practice in this way," and so forth;
one should understand that skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) and the non-abandonment of all sentient beings are to be cultivated.
"One should dismiss [the visualization] in this way."

By means of answering or not answering those questioned by others in accordance with their irreversible realization, the method for maintaining the state of being irreversible or non-irreversible is indicated through the signs of irreversibility.
Furthermore, he speaks of the method for the object that is immeasurable by virtue of possessing knowledge of all objects, beginning with the words:
"Therefore, O Blessed One," and so forth.
"Unassailable" means that by virtue of those bodhisattvas being unassailable, the immeasurability of the domain of skillful means is made known.
Thus, one should grasp the tenfold skillful means exactly as described, endowed with both its domain and its application.
And so it has been said:
"Its object, its application, the overcoming of enemies, its lack of fixed location, its accordance with the piercing [of the target], and its unique characteristic. (62)
"Non-attachment, non-apprehension, being free from signs and aspirations,
its characteristic, and its immeasurability— these are the ten forms of skill in means.
(63) Thus, what then is the distinction between the omniscience of the three [knowledges] and the complete awakening to all aspects?

Some maintain that the three types of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) have as their objects specific aspects (*ākāra*) according to the aforementioned determination of aspects, whereas the realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*) has as its object all aspects collectively.

Others hold that the establishment of the three types of omniscience is based on their defining characteristics (*lākṣaṇika*), while the realization of all aspects is based on practical application (*prāyogika*).

Others maintain that the realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*) is characterized by the establishment of the discordant factors and their antidotes within the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*), yet it is not so [in the ultimate sense] because its nature is quiescent (*prakṛtiśānta*).
The realization of all aspects is hereby concluded.

Now, for one who has attained the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), the culmination of that attainment—the "Summit Awakening" (*mūrdhābhisamaya*)—must be explained. First, its defining characteristic (*liṅga*) must be stated, by which it is characterized. Therefore, because of extreme familiarity [with reality], even in the state of dreaming, there is the first characteristic: the momentary perception of all phenomena as being like a dream. To explain this, he says:

Furthermore, Subhūti, "if even when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has entered into a dream," and so forth— this means that when a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the yoga-dharma, embraced by wisdom and skillful means, has reached its culmination, [even] within a dream...
For him, the mental applications of yoga-vision proceed precisely with regard for the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) through the direct realization of such dharmas.
To explain the meaning of the sign, which is the non-arising of a mind that longs for the second level of the Śrāvakas and so forth, he says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti," and so on.
In this context, *spṛhā* (longing) is the desire for the attainment of what has not been attained before;
*anuśaṃsācitta* (the mind of appreciation) is the wish for non-separation from what has been attained.
He speaks for the purpose of indicating the signs of seeing a third Tathāgata and so forth.
"Of the assembly of many hundreds," and so forth.
He speaks "having risen into the air," and so forth, for the purpose of indicating the sign of perceiving the fourth miraculous power of a Buddha.
He speaks for the sake of the meaning of the sign of generating the mind [of awakening] through the teaching of the Dharma, which is like the fifth dream:
"The bodhisattva mahāsattva does not tremble," and so forth.

"Sentient beings in the hells," and so forth.
Asking, "What is this so-called characteristic of the purification of the states of woe?
he says: "In that regard, Subhūti, how [is it]? and so forth.

He speaks by way of positive concomitance (*anvayamukhena*) for the purpose of indicating the sign of the accomplishment of the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna-samṛddhi*) that extinguishes the burning of seven cities and so on.
"In the burning of a city," and so forth.
This should be applied as follows: according to the distinction of weak, medium, and intense, [the fire] should respectively "be extinguished," "become cool," or "go out.
He speaks also by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*):
"If it does not subside," and so forth.
Indicating both cases, he says: "If, however," and so forth.
"Karma ripens" refers to the rejection of the true Dharma.
Karma that is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*) is not experienced as mental distress and so forth until the accomplishment of the basis of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).
"From that very [source]" means from what was accumulated in previous lives.

He states the meaning of the inferential mark (liṅga)— the accomplishment of truthful speech through the departure of non-human beings such as yakṣas and the like— by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka).
Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding the passage beginning with "by which aspects," and so forth:
therein, [the mind] is "grasped" because it enters by itself; it is "impelled" because, through the bestowal of capacity, it brings about transformations of the body and so on.

The five terms beginning with "unknown"—to be applied respectively with the preceding word "not"—refer to the comprehension of all categories of phenomena through the fivefold clear realization (*abhisamaya*), such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Explaining also by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti," and so forth.
This concludes the twentieth chapter, titled "The Examination of Skill in Means" (*Upāyakauśalyamīmāṃsāparivarta*), in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Now, for one who has entered into the realization of the summit (*mūrdhābhisamaya*), [this practice] is more powerful due to the greatness of its own nature,

Because he does not show respect, he will despise him;
because he is a source of laughter, he will mock him;
and because of his excessive speech, he will deride him.
By engaging in criticism, he will revile; by proclaiming deformity, he will despise;
and by instilling a particular kind of pride, he will generate arrogance.
He will give rise to conceit;
likewise, through the distinctions of overweening pride (*atimāna*), pride of pride (*mānātimāna*), and arrogance (*abhimāna*), he will increase conceit by means of these six steps;
he will cause conceit to grow.
He will stiffen pride;
he will support pride;
he will increase pride.
"It will increase pride" should be applied in due order:
"Because it causes false pride, it will produce pride.
"By means of that pride," and so forth.

Pride (*māna*) is the inflation of the mind thinking, "I am superior to one who is inferior," or "I am equal to one who is my equal. Excessive pride (*atimāna*) is [the inflation of the mind] thinking, "I am superior to one who is my equal," or "I am equal to one who is superior.
Pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*) is [the inflation of the mind] thinking, "I am superior to one who is superior."
*Abhimāna* (conceit) is the intention of having attained what has not been attained.
*Mithyāmāna* (false pride) is the thought "I am virtuous" even when one lacks virtue.
[The phrase] "he will distance himself from omniscience," and so forth, refers to this.
This is what is meant: through conceit (*māna*), one will distance oneself from omniscience, which consists of the three types of omniscience;

and through excessive conceit (*atimāna*), conceit-beyond-conceit (*mānātimāna*), and overweening conceit (*abhimāna*), one will respectively distance oneself from the unsurpassed Buddha-knowledge, the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*).
Self-arisen gnosis is the realization of the summit (*mūrdhābhisamaya*).
The gnosis of omniscience is the gradual realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*).

And through false pride, one will distance oneself from unexcelled perfect enlightenment—the realization of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) preceded by the realization in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*).
"Will not be cultivated," and so forth.
These three phrases are for the purpose of generating knowledge through hearing and the other [stages].
Alternatively, they should be applied respectively for the sake of thoroughly understanding the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected natures.

In the course of this discussion, while pointing out the various classifications of the deeds of Māra, he speaks regarding the meaning of the "mild deeds of Māra," beginning with the words "Furthermore...
The phrase "by means of a name-designation" refers to the utterance of that [specific] name.
"By means of the empowerment of the name" refers to the designation by such names as "Mātra" and so forth. Having raised the doubt, "Why is that?", he says:
"For this is your name," and so on.
In that context, because he has abandoned the village and resides at a distance of one *krośa*, he is called an "Āraṇyaka" (forest-dweller).
He is a *paiṇḍapātika* because he has undertaken the practice of accepting alms-food;
he is a *pāṃśukūlika* because his robe consists of rags gathered from streets;
he is a *khalubhaktika* because he eats only after taking all the food and other provisions at once.

One who eats only a single meal because they consume food only as much as desired is an *ekāśanika*. One who sleeps on whatever is spread out, such as a piece of cloth and so forth, is a *yāthāsaṃstarika*. One who possesses no more than the three robes, such as the outer cloak (*saṃghāṭī*) and the others, is a *traicīvaraka*.
One who dwells in a charnel ground is a *śmāśānika*.
Likewise, one who dwells at the foot of a tree is a *vṛkṣamūlika*. One who remains seated throughout the night is a *naiṣadyika*.
He is one who dwells in the open air because he lacks an upper covering; he is one who wears only a felt robe and so forth because he does not possess [extra] robes;
he is one of few desires because he lacks any longing for more.
He is content because he is satisfied with just that much;
he is secluded because he is free from transgressions;
and he is one who has abandoned the washing of feet because of his fewness of desires.
As before, having raised the doubt "For what reason?", he says "For thus" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
He speaks of the "middle" for the purpose of explaining the deeds of Māra;
and [he says] "And that Māra," and so forth.

having raised the doubt as to why that is so by means of the phrase "tat kasya hetoḥ," he says "tathā hi" and so forth.
Anticipating the objection, "If it is truly existent, how can this be the work of Māra?", he says:
"Those who indeed... and so forth.

"Those who," and so forth.
He speaks regarding the work of Māra by way of the non-prediction of the states of the primary Buddhas.
"Furthermore," and so forth.
In that regard, it has been followed, reflected upon, and examined in due order during the stages of preparation and so forth;
or, according to some, by means of knowledge consisting of hearing and the rest. Having weighed both of these together—
The connection is as follows: having examined how that which was reflected upon by him and the name designated by Māra coincide and accord with one another, he will think [it is the Buddha].
Having raised the doubt as to how this could be the work of Māra if it were indeed true, he says:
"And those which by me," and so forth;
"by means of such a designation, for those who disparage bodhisattvas, awakening is difficult to attain," and so forth;
"but if," and so forth.
"Having wandered through and transmigrated"—the meaning is:
having purified oneself by means of the confession of misdeeds and having attained freedom from conceit.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
And as for the passage beginning with "If that," and so forth:
therein, by means of the antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā*), he will censure it;
or by means of the antidote of non-occurrence (*samudācāra-pratipakṣa*), he will vomit it out.
Out of shame regarding oneself and others, one will feel disgust for it;
by the power of the basis, one will relinquish it;
and by the power of restoration, one will confess it.

Because it is difficult to obtain due to being accessible only after a long period of time, one might ask: "For what reason is that? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For that [insult] is indeed more serious," and so forth.
Since it arises from the contempt of others, the occasion for such mental affliction (*mananāpatti*) is indeed more serious.
The meaning is that by this [means], awakening becomes difficult to attain, yet not impossible.
For instance, those things which are subject to diminution in the presence of their opposites possess opposites capable of completely uprooting them, such as gold-stains and the like.

Furthermore, according to the principle that all such factors as the obscuration of the true Dharma possess the aforementioned qualities, the grounds for conceit and transgression indeed go to complete exhaustion.
As for the statement beginning with "they perish," it should be understood as referring to a situation where there is no cultivation of the antidote;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with reason and a contradiction with many sūtras.
The expression "certainly" is also explained by this very [point].
Furthermore, the expression "not certain" is to be understood as referring to the fact that even in the absence of the cultivation of the antidote, there is an occasional result.
Demonstrating through an analogy that the state of being a place for reflection and rebirth is indeed heavy, he says:
"Namely, for example," and so forth. "The four root downfalls" refers to the primary downfalls known as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying.
Due to the loss of the monk's restraint, he is no longer a monk; due to the absence of the state of a novice, he is no longer a śramaṇa;
and due to the separation from the status of a lay follower, he is no longer a son of the Śākyas, even in another birth.
Because one is incapable of attaining [the goal] through pride, this downfall of conceit is a most grave offense. To demonstrate its extreme gravity, he says:
"Let alone," and so forth.
"From the five" refers to [the five heinous crimes], such as drawing blood from a Tathāgata with a malicious mind and so forth.
"More grave" means that one experiences dwelling in hell for a duration determined by the number of times the thought associated with the mind (mānasa) arises.

Having thus pointed out the work of Māra by means of the mere mention of names, he speaks again— starting with "Furthermore," and so forth— in order to explain the subtle work of Māra even through the quality of seclusion (*viveka*).
In that context, a "forest retreat" (*vanaprastha*) is a specific type of forest.
Because of subsequent regret, as long as meditative concentration has not been attained, one's bodily, vocal, and mental actions are impure; by the opposite of that, they are pure.
Having raised the question, "Why is that so?", he says, "For it is thus," and so forth.
He speaks for the sake of the activity of the middle wheel:
"And moreover," and so forth;
[he refers to] "this solitude."
"Relying on that which consists of the perfection of wisdom and skill in means," and so forth.

Due to the distinctions in the apprehension of the weak, medium, and superior [levels], one is respectively "relying" (*niḥśrita*) and "clinging" (*ālīna*) therein, in solitude such as dwelling in the forest and so on.
"Resolved by that very [thought]" means having fallen into a state of resolve due to self-exaltation.

"Subhūti, whoever... and so forth.

while dwelling in that seclusion consisting of forest-dwelling and so forth, he is not seen in this seclusion of a bodhisattva, such as [the practice of] great skill in means and the like.
He speaks thus for the purpose of demonstrating the excessive activity of Māra.
"Nevertheless, him... and so forth.
"By means of a confused dwelling" refers to being possessed of mental attention directed toward the disciples (*śrāvaka*) and others.
"By dwelling in a crowded place" means because he dwells outside the Mahāyāna.
Because he is untouchable by other bodhisattvas, he is a "caṇḍāla among bodhisattvas."

One who reviles other bodhisattvas or oneself is a "reviler of bodhisattvas" (*bodhisattvadūṣī*). One who merely by words professes to have undertaken the conduct of a bodhisattva is a "counterfeit bodhisattva" (*bodhisattvapratirūpaka*). One who is devoid of the qualities of a bodhisattva is a "semblance bodhisattva" (*bodhisattvaprativarṇika*).
Because he harms the community of bodhisattvas, he is a *kāraṇḍavaka* among bodhisattvas;
because he uses things improperly, he is a thief.
For what reason is this so? Having raised this doubt, he says:
"Fallen into conceit," and so forth.
Because they are joined with evil qualities (*pāpadharma*), they possess impure qualities (*aviśuddhadharma*). Because they lack spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they have no teacher (*anācārya*).
Because they speak otherwise, they possess the qualities of non-noble ones.
To explain the meaning of the ninth sign—namely, self-realization through direct knowledge, heroic exertion, and service to spiritual friends—he says:
"Furthermore, for whomsoever... and so forth.
The twenty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Deeds of Māra," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*. 60.
Explaining the ninth sign itself, he says:
"Then indeed, O Blessed One," and so forth.
In that context, the six perfections in their state of fruition are the Teacher.
The stage of having attained illumination (*labdhālokāvasthā*) is the path (*mārga*), because it demonstrates the path of initial realization;
the stage of increased illumination (*vṛddhālokāvasthā*) is "light" (*āloka*), because its nature is superior illumination;

and the stage of having advanced toward one portion of the reality-meaning (*tattvārthaikadeśaprasṛtāvasthā*) is a "torch" (*ulkā*), because it has entered into one part of the reality that is the absence of subject and object.
Immediately following this, due to the arising of the knowledge of reality, there is the manifestation of the stage of immediate meditative concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*).

On the first ground, it is "protection" because it wards off all calamities; on the second ground, it is "refuge" by virtue of abiding in the state where the application of that intention is never fruitless.
Because it is an object of faultless delight, it is a "refuge" in the third stage;

because it is the station for reaching the state of supreme nobility, it is a "final resort" in the fourth stage; and because it is distinct from the three realms, it is an "island" in the fifth stage.

Because her nature is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), she is the Mother on the sixth stage; because her form is skillful means (upāya), she is the Father on the seventh stage; and because her essence is aspiration (praṇidhāna), she exists for the sake of gnosis (jñāna) on the eighth stage.

Because they have the characteristic of the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*), they conduce to awakening on the ninth stage; because they possess the excellence of the perfection of gnosis (*jñānapāramitā*), they conduce to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment on the tenth stage—this is the distinction in meaning.
As remedies for attachment to enjoyments and dwellings, which are causes for not advancing, there are, respectively, the perfections of generosity (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).

The perfection of patience and the perfection of vigor are established respectively as the antidotes to the causes of desistance—namely, the suffering born from the misconduct of worldly beings and the exhaustion resulting from long-term application to the side of purity. Likewise, the perfections of meditative concentration and wisdom are established as the antidotes to distraction and faulty insight, which are the causes of loss. Thus, the number is established as six by way of the arrangement of these opposing factors and their antidotes;
furthermore, by means of the four perfections that serve as causes for non-distraction, there is one [resultant] perfection.

Distraction is that which, by relying on non-distraction, gives rise to the qualities of a Buddha through the realization of the reality of phenomena (dharmatattva) exactly as it is; thus, its numerical determination is established by way of being the basis and locus for the complete attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha. Likewise, [the same applies] to the perfection of generosity through the favoring of sentient beings, and to the perfection of ethical discipline...
Because of non-affliction;
because of enduring affliction through the perfection of patience;
and because of engaging in the performance of duties through the perfection of vigor.

Having made sentient beings fit for ripening, one brings those with distracted minds to concentration through the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and those with concentrated minds to liberation through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Thus, ripening occurs through instruction; in this way, [the bodhisattva acts] in accordance with the ripening of sentient beings.
The establishment of the number [of categories] should also be understood in this way. Having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:

She is the "mother" because she gives birth at the beginning,

As before, anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Perfection of Wisdom," and so forth.

It is stated thus because it is the ultimate state.

Thus, he speaks for the purpose of indicating the signs of drawing near to the awakening of the twelve Buddhas.
And thus, O Blessed One, when a bodhisattva practices in this way, and so forth.

"In this manner," and so forth.

this is considered the twelvefold sign of yoga that has reached the summit. Thus,
for one characterized by such signs, how many types of progress are there?
In order to explain the first increase—the merit consisting of the honoring of the Tathāgata and so forth by sentient beings of Jambudvīpa and other realms—he says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if those beings who are in Jambudvīpa," and so on.
Since Jambudvīpa is used as an illustration, this includes the beings of the trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu) as well, because it is stated thus in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*.
Anticipating the question "Why is that so?", he says:
"For in whatever way," and so forth.
[He] "becomes worthy of offerings."
He attains the status of a field of merit. Why is this so?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Thus, indeed," and so forth.
"Having set aside" means having abandoned.
As before, having raised the question "For what reason?", he says: "Because they are persons without a counterpart," and so forth.

Others maintain that the three terms beginning with "persons without a counterpart" are used because [the Buddha] is a teacher who has attained the objects of direct perception, inference, and scripture.
He speaks with the words beginning "In what way? and so forth, in order to state that merit can also be overwhelmed by another means;
[the phrase] "those residing in the victim" refers to this.

"As if they were worthy of death" means that by the performance of evil deeds, they destroy their human and other states, thereby depriving them of their very moments of existence. "Of the givers" refers to those who provide [sustenance].
Of those who cause others to undertake [the practice];
of the donors;
that is, of the direct givers.
"Purifying the sacrificial fee" means making it truly fruitful.
"By this mental attention" refers to its nature as the instruction in the path for sentient beings and so forth.
Having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:
"For he who [perceives] these," and so forth.
"He himself" means:
Upon the objective support of the Mother, who possesses great skill in means, that very mental attention which intends to benefit sentient beings arises;
it is a mental attention whose nature consists of loving-kindness and so forth, characterized by the thought, "May she [the Mother] protect this [being].
To "exhaust" means to transcend.
In order to clarify the increase in the nature of the mental attention (*manaskāra*) regarding the second distinguished perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he says:
"Subhūti, it is as if, for example, by someone... and so forth.
"By one who is engaged in the knowledge of the jewel-treasure (*maṇiratna*)."
This is due to a thorough understanding of the treatises on their examination;
"by one who knows the varieties of precious gems" means through mastery of their defining characteristics.
"Until she or another has obtained [it]" means that either this Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) or another dharma-nature (dharmatā) from sūtras such as the *Samādhirāja* has been attained;
with respect to the book, it is "either she or..."
Some say "or not. He states that being non-separate from emptiness is possible with the words beginning "That which,
however," and so forth.
Anticipating this, he says: "If [it were so]," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says: "In that very same way," and so forth.
"Wisdom," and so forth.
This is what is meant: because the perfection of wisdom is empty, it is in reality devoid of increase or decrease.

Therefore, because all phenomena are empty, when there is the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that even the mental engagement (*manaskāra*) which takes them as its object is empty, one is not devoid of the mental engagement of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) due to being non-perverted; such is the meaning of the passage beginning with "devoid of the mental engagement of the perfection of wisdom.

In order to explain the nature of the increase [of merit] through the attainment of the third excellence—the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—he asks, "If, O Blessed One," and so forth.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "But indeed, not... and so forth.
[He explains that one] "attains awakening."
This is what is meant:

since the negation of decrease and increase for a bodhisattva is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, identical to the negation of decrease and increase for the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he therefore accumulates the equipment of merit and knowledge through the conventional cultivation of the illusion-like nature,
and fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Otherwise, if decrease and increase were possible in reality, then error would be non-existent;
therefore, he says that this alone is the truth.

“If, Subhūti, a bodhisattva,” and so forth. With the intention that by the phrase “this bodhisattva practices” some kind of real entity (*tāttvika-dharma*) might be implied, he asks: “But, Blessed One, does the perfection of wisdom practice? and so on.
"But how," and so forth.
If [it were argued that] by means of the negation of the aforementioned modes [of existence], [the object] exists everywhere, [we reply]: "Certainly not" (no hīdam). This is what is being said.

The meaning is: how, moreover, does the Blessed One practice in another manner—that by which this bodhisattva practices—as was previously stated? He says that it was stated [previously] from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
"What then, Subhūti, do you perceive? and so forth.
The sense is "in reality. Concluding, he says:
"Thus indeed," and so forth.

Precisely because all phenomena are non-apprehendable, when there is no logical possibility [of their arising] from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), one practices according to conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) through the cultivation of the illusion-like; thus, there arises a distinguished resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding non-arisen phenomena.
Because of the absence of fear regarding all apprehension through the practice of the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) and so forth, this practice is rendered fearless.
The three phrases beginning with "practicing in this way for the sake of generating the knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*) and so forth" are to be applied.
Furthermore, the four phrases beginning with "the unsurpassed Buddha-knowledge through the distinctions of the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and so forth" are to be applied.

He speaks [as follows] for the purpose of increasing [the practice] characterized by the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) of the fourth dharma—the object to be realized and the subject that realizes it.
"O Blessed One, that which [is the suchness] of all dharmas," and so forth.
He speaks by means of a counter-question, stating that the prophecy is according to conventional truth:

"In all dharmas," and so forth,
ending with "it does not occur to me thus."

By this, having established that the perfection of wisdom consists in the absence of conceptualization during the realization of the summit (*mūrdhābhisamaya*), he expresses the Bodhisattva’s lack of such conceptualization under his own guise.
The twenty-second chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Spiritual Friend," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
He says "Then again, by that... and so forth, for the sake of increasing the possession of the fifth distinguished root of virtue.
It is profound because it is as deep as space, being free from all that causes terror in foolish people.
Because they are, respectively, secluded due to being devoid of the nature of cause and fruit, and because they are difficult to see and difficult to realize due to their emptiness,

It should be stated that they will attain yoga.

Some maintain that the three phrases beginning with "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍena*) refer to the three aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*)—namely, the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara*), the discipline of acting for the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyā*), and the discipline of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka*)—because they are free from opposing factors (*vipakṣadharma*). Furthermore, the other three phrases beginning with "complete" (*paripūrṇena*) refer to the presence of those very same favorable factors (*anukūladharma*).

Others maintain that the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) is unbroken, flawless, and untarnished due to the absence of bodily, vocal, and mental ignorance; and it is complete, pure, and unadulterated because of its perfection in the knowledge arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The three phrases beginning with "endowed with patience" (*kṣāntisampannā*) refer to the three types of patience, such as patience toward suffering (*duḥkhavāsanā*).

The four phrases beginning with "having attained vigor" (*ālabdhavīryā*) refer to the distinctions of vigor consisting of application (*ālambha*), preparation (*parikarma*), investigation (*pratyavekṣā*), and practice (*pratipatti*).
The six phrases beginning with "delighting in meditation" (*dhyānārāmā*) [refer to the six perfections].
Because of its connection with the names of the *anāgamya*, the *dhyānāntara*, and the first, second, third, and fourth *dhyānas*.
Having raised the doubt as before—"For what reason is that?"—he says:
"For whichever bodhisattva," and so forth.
In order to explain the increase in the nature of approaching the sixth class of all devas, he says:
"And training thus in the perfection of wisdom," and so forth.
"I too" refers to Śakra.
"They will not arise"—
the meaning is that this is due to the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgatas and others.
The twenty-third chapter, titled "Śakra," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The twenty-fourth chapter.
In order to increase his own form by means of the seventh [perfection], the overcoming of all Māras, it says:
"Then, indeed, the Blessed One," and so forth.
The three phrases beginning with "they train" are stated according to the distinctions of the paths of preparation, immediate succession, and liberation.
"Pierced by the arrow of grief" means that they have attained dejection by overstepping their own proper domain. "He moves with an unconcentrated mind."
He enters into yoga with a concentrated mind;
for it is not practiced here in the same manner as it is taught in other sūtras.

The meaning is as follows: since no comprehensible entity is indicated here, it is impossible to understand this teaching through knowledge consisting of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-mayajñāna*); therefore, one would not attain, respectively, its unfathomable depth and its flavor.

Furthermore, being satisfied, uplifted, and joyful—due to the arising of soft, medium, and intense pleasure—and likewise gladdened and filled with joy and gladness due to the production of the three types of mental well-being (*saumanasya*).
Because he is incapable of creating obstacles during the preparatory stages and so forth, he becomes filled with exultation, his mind gladdened, and joy and rapture arise within him.
Anticipating the question "Why is that?", he says:
"He keeps [them] at a distance," and so on.
"Udgata" means "protruding.
"Adhyākrānta" means "overwhelmed.

Regarding the four terms beginning with "for the sake of non-designation," some say they refer to the fact that [these beings] are subject to rebirth in the destinies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras.
In that regard, it quarrels by initiating external actions in its own place;
it disputes through litigation in royal courts and similar venues;
and it is embroiled in conflict through the taking up of weapons and the like.
Because he fully recognizes suffering, he reviles; because he restrains [the offender] from striking, he rebukes; because of the onset of hatred, he becomes resentful;
and because anger arises, he produces malice.
"Having donned the armor"—
this means that if that omniscience were to be abandoned, then for the sake of removing the evil arising from quarrels and the like,
one must exert vigor for a duration equal to as many eons as there are moments of the initial resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*). This is the meaning.
Because the sin is so grave, he asks whether there is a possibility of escape, saying, "Venerable One, is it so? and so forth.
By taking the position that such a possibility exists, he declares the pervasion—that for all [such acts], the Dharma is indeed capable of providing a remedy—saying:
"Regarding 'the means of deliverance' and so forth:

this means that for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the teacher of the Dharma is one who possesses the present dharma through the confession and remediation of offenses such as the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* within the Saṃgha; likewise, for those of the Mahāyāna, he is one who has taught [this] in the Bodhisattvapiṭaka and other such texts."
Beginning with the Bodhisattvas because of their preeminence, he speaks clearly, saying: "In that regard, Ānanda, whoever... and so forth.
Because he has already confessed his misdeeds, he does not confess them again.
Because one does not undertake the restraint of non-action, one does not practice for the sake of restraint in the future.
The three phrases beginning with "they must be removed" refer to the removal of coarse, medium, and intense forms of physical obstruction and so forth.
[The phrase] "ill-obtained" means:

The meaning is that one generates such a thought as: "When another speaks, I shall speak in return," whereby quarrels and the like become difficult to avoid despite being [erroneously] regarded as praiseworthy.
"Harsh" (*paruṣa*) or "rough" (*karkaśa*):
it is "harsh" because it causes discomfort to the ear, and "rough" because it produces mental distress.
The passage beginning with "duruktāni" (ill-spoken words) is stated because of the divisions of malicious speech (*paiśunya*), harsh speech (*pāruṣya*), and frivolous chatter (*sambhinnapralāpa*).
Likewise, having raised the doubt as to why this is so, he says:

Agitation is fury;
a frown is the contraction of the forehead.
One should abide in the presence of all sentient beings.

To explain the increase characterized by attaining a state equal to that of people who resemble those in the eighth stage of the treatise, he says: "And how, Ānanda," and so forth.
In that regard, they are mounted upon the single vehicle by virtue of their equal practice of the armor;
they are mounted upon the single path by virtue of their similar practice of the setting-forth;
they have identical intentions because of the unity of their practice of the accumulations; and they have set out together on the same vehicle because of the equality of their practice of departure.
"In which" refers to giving and so forth;

The twenty-fifth chapter.
In order to clarify the increase in the nature of the training that is purified by the ninth skillful means, he asks,
beginning with "But where," and so forth.
To demonstrate that one who trains in [the cessation of] destruction and so forth is training in Buddhahood, he says "If... and so on.
Just as suchness itself is designated by various exclusions—such as "destruction," "non-arising," and so forth—it has been explained accordingly.

Asking how it is that training is prescribed in one place while training is [actually] established elsewhere, he says: "For what reason? and so forth, beginning with "Subhūti, that which... and so on.
Having restated those words, he replies by means of a counter-question, saying:
"What do you think? and so forth.
"Suchness" (tathatā) means, in short, omniscience, which is to say, Buddhahood.
Likewise, having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:

Because all conceptual constructions are destroyed within it, Buddhahood is "destruction"; yet because the dharmadhātu is devoid of annihilation, it is "indestructible."
The meaning is that omniscience has the nature of exhaustion and so forth through the relationship of identity (*tādātmya*).
The phrase "it arises" and so on is to be understood as the opposite of non-arising and so forth.
He speaks for the sake of praise by way of its being perfectly pure training.
"Therefore, then," and so forth.
Anticipating the question, "For what reason is this as before? he says, "Because they are the essence of all sentient beings," and so forth.
In that regard, "bird-killers" refers to fowlers; "meat-sellers" refers to hunters (*niṣādas*); "fishermen" refers to those who catch fish with nets;
and "shepherds" refers to those who kill deer and other such animals.
Due to the absence of visual and auditory consciousness, one is blind or deaf; due to the deficiency of an eye, one is one-eyed;
due to the amputation of hands and so forth, one is maimed;
and due to a crooked back, one is hunchbacked.
One is called *kuṇi* because of having a short mountain-like protuberance above the elbow;
one is called *laṅga* because of having dissimilar calves and thighs;
and one is called *khañja* because of a stumbling gait.
He is "jaḍa" (dull-witted) because of his inability to speak suddenly;
some maintain that where the reading is "jaḍḍa," the meaning is the same.
He is "lola" (fickle) because he speaks while uttering the word "lāla."
Lalla is so called because he utters the syllable *la* with a heavy accent (*guru*). Kalla is so called because of his high-pitched hearing (*uccaiḥ-śravaṇa*).
He is deficient in limbs (*hīnāṅga*) due to the small size of his hands, feet, and other members.
He is called "one with deficient limbs" because his limbs are either too few or too many;
he is called "one with deformed limbs" because of their misshapenness.
Having raised the question, "And why is that so?", he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "For he has," and so forth:
[the author] says that the realization of the purification of the powers and so on is not tenable if it were merely by way of the natural purity [of the mind].
Then, starting with "When, O Blessed One," and so forth, [he speaks] because of the realization of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
"Thus it is," and so forth.
As before, having raised the doubt "for what reason is that?", he says:
"Because all dharmas," and so forth.

This has been said: although all phenomena are pure by nature, for the sake of generating such true knowledge in sentient beings who do not fully understand the purity of the intrinsic nature of phenomena, one attains the purification of the powers and so forth through conventional reality by means of the practice of the illusion-like nature of phenomena, which prevents despondency.
In order to explain the increase characterized by the attainment of the lineage of the tenth stage,
he says: "For example, Subhūti,
those who are on this great earth are few," and so forth.
Because of an abundance of alkaline matter they are saline;
because of their dryness they are arid.

By the statement "those Bodhisattvas are few," it would be indicated that those belonging to the Buddha-lineage who are capable of attaining further increase at the time of ascending to higher stages are very few in number.

For the sake of increasing that which consists in the cause for attaining the fruit of the eleventh stage, Buddhahood, he speaks of three necklaces (*hāraka*) through the distinction of mild, medium, and intense analogies, beginning with:
"Furthermore, it is as if... and so forth.
[He refers to] "the path of the perfection of wisdom."
The meaning is that it is the increase of the eleventh [stage], which has the attainment of the Tathāgata as its cause.
He speaks of the increase of the nature of the non-arising of thoughts that are the opposites of the twelve perfections, saying:
"For in this way, Subhūti, in the perfection of wisdom," and so forth.
In that regard, by means of the adherence to the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected entities, they are respectively comprised, grasped, and taken up.
They are followed through because of their realization as being free from error.
For the sake of increasing the characteristic of the knowledge that encompasses all fourteen perfections, he says:
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and so forth. The sixty-two views are to be found in such works as the *Brahmajāla-paripṛcchā*;
they are not written here because of the excessive length of the text.
Clarifying precisely this aforementioned increase, he says:
"Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a person... and so forth.
He speaks thus for the sake of the increase that has the purpose of attaining all fifteen kinds of excellence.
Therefore, Subhūti, [the text says] "bodhisattva," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt as to why that is so with the words "for what reason?", he says:
"because it is the foremost of merits."
In order to elaborate upon this very point, he asks a question, saying, "What do you think? and so forth.
Anticipating the objection as to why that is so, he says [the following], as before.
"Thus, [it is] of great benefit," and so forth.
In that regard, the four phrases beginning with "by one desiring to go to the state of unsurpassedness through the realization of the four paths, such as the path of seeing" are to be understood.
Furthermore, the three phrases beginning with "the Buddha’s playful manifestation for the sake of attaining the three bodies—the Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Emanation-body"—are to be explained.
He says, "What more need be said? and so forth, meaning that even a *śrāvaka* could attain all perfections.
He says that one is not merely a *śrāvaka* because of practicing for the sake of another [goal],
stating "even the perfection of a *śrāvaka*" and so forth.
He speaks in order to explain the increase in the nature of being drawn near to the sixteen aspects of perfect enlightenment.
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way," and so forth.
Regarding that, he says, "Even attachment there is a bond," beginning with the words,
"If, however," and so on.
The meaning is that "he does not practice" because of the error of perceiving entities as real.
He states that non-attachment is the reality, beginning with the words "Now, even that... and so forth.
The increases should be understood exactly as stated.
And so it has been said:
"The merit and so forth derived from the worship of Buddhas by as many people as there are in Jambudvīpa..."
Having made many comparisons, the increase is sixteenfold.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Training," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Having thus explained the increase of the *mūrdhābhisamaya* (culminating clear realization) that has been developed, he speaks in praise to describe its *nirūḍhi* (firm establishment), which is characterized by reaching the limit of becoming fully integrated into one's being: "While practicing...
and so forth, ending with "...they are to be envied."
By this, he speaks of the rarity of those who have attained the realization of the summit (*mūrdhābhisamaya*).
Because of the excellence of the faith that has arisen, he now expresses his aspiration for what is desired and, making known its firm establishment, says:
"By those belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle," and so forth.
"Being carried away" (*uhyamānān*) means being impelled.
"On the same, ultimate shore," meaning in *nirvāṇa*, which is to say, in Buddhahood; this is because of the absence of all defects and imbalances.
Some [commentators] maintain that these are "desired, contemplated, and embraced" respectively by virtue of accomplishing the welfare of oneself, others, and both.
Others say it is by way of accomplishing the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*).

Regarding the phrase "of the Buddha-qualities" (*buddhadharmāṇām*), this refers to the qualities associated with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the self-arisen qualities (*svayambhūdharmāṇām*), and the unassailable qualities (*asaṃhāryadharmāṇām*).
These are taught through the distinction of the three types of omniscience, beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Thus, in this way, the unsurpassed fulfillment of the dharmas of the three types of omniscience has been explained;
and its meaning is that it is firmly established in the welfare of sentient beings without abandoning them.
"O Blessed One, not for me," and so forth.

"Endowed with great compassion" means that even in such a state of realization, they are possessed of great compassion because they manifest great compassion in order to avoid falling into [the extreme of] nirvāṇa, and because they generate the thought of awakening for the sake of leading sentient beings [to maturity] and so forth. Having raised the doubt, "Why is that?", he says:
"By that great compassion," and so forth.

The four phrases beginning with "we have crossed over" correspond respectively to the distinctions of the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), special qualities (*viśeṣamārga*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
This is what is stated.

By the power of correct skillful means alone, in this state of non-conceptual realization, because there is no absence of the manifestation of great compassion and so forth, there is the supreme, firm establishment of the complete fulfillment of the dharmas of the three types of omniscience— such as the aforementioned knowledge of all aspects— characterized by not abandoning the welfare of sentient beings. And thus it has been said:
"The supreme fulfillment of the qualities of the three types of omniscience, which does not abandon the welfare of sentient beings, is called 'establishment' (nirūḍhi). Thus,
in order to demonstrate the stabilization of the mind— characterized by the firm state of one who has been thus established through this very establishment— the author asks a question and says:
"O Bhagavan, whoever among them," and so forth.
The connection is: "Whoever rejoices, how much merit does he produce?

By the terms "those who have set out in the first vehicle," "those who have entered into the practice," "those who are irreversible," and "those bound by one more birth," there is a fourfold classification based on the designation of the four types of attainers of the two paths—vision and cultivation—which serve as the antidotes to the four previously mentioned conceptual constructions, as appropriate.
Some say it is "proclaimed.
Others say it is distinguished by the increase of the signs (*liṅga*), the firm establishment [of the signs], the stabilization of the mind, and the realization of its own nature.
On the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one has first set out in the vehicle (*yāna*).
Those who have entered the practice on the seven stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā) are those practicing the course;
those on the triad of stages beginning with the Immovable (acalā) are irreversible.
Others say that on the tenth stage, they are bound by only one more birth.
To provide an answer to the question while making known the stabilization of the mind, he says:

"By the tip of a leaf" means by the measure of a leaf.
This is what is said.

According to the principle that "the measure of a real entity whose magnitude is possible can be grasped by yogis through a measurement of its extent," the measure of the three-thousandfold world system beginning with the four continents is taken, but not the measure of the merit of rejoicing; thus, under the guise of a different subject, the state of mental composure characterized by meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which is the nature of merit transcending all measure, has been described.
And so it has been said:

"By means of the great abundance of merit produced through comparisons involving a thousand, two thousand, and three thousand world-systems of four continents, this samādhi is proclaimed. (4) Thus, these characteristics and so forth should be understood as being, in their respective order, the nature of the four aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)— namely, Heat (*ūṣman*) and the others— within the context of the Culminating Clear Realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*).
Immediately following the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

In that regard, the fourfold adverse factor—the conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper—must be explained along with its antidotes. To begin with, indicating the first conceptualization of the grasped, which has as its basis the entire side of active involvement, [the text] says:
"O Blessed One, they are possessed by Māra," and so forth.
"Those possessed by Māra, those belonging to the faction of Māra, and those fallen from the abode of Māra"—
these three phrases are stated to express censure of mild, medium, and intense degrees. Likewise, having raised the doubt as to "for what reason" that is so, he says:
"Those who destroy the abode of Māra," and so forth.
Having indicated this by way of negation (*vyatireka*), he speaks of that same conceptualization by way of affirmation (*anvaya*, positive concomitance), saying:
"They should be rejoiced in, O Blessed One," and so forth.

The meaning is that for Bodhisattvas who have become free from the notions of duality and non-duality through the cultivation of the illusion-like nature, their engagement in acts such as rejoicing in the arising of such mental states should be performed.
Repeating what has been well said, he says:
"It is so, Kauśika," and so forth.
Explaining the second type of conceptualization of the apprehended object, which is based on the side of cessation (*nivṛtti*), he says:
"By those sons of good family, Kauśika," and so forth;
[the phrase] "they will not become dispassionate" means:
The meaning is: "by the power of the conceptualization that apprehends the cessation regarding the object to be abandoned.
Likewise, praising [the teaching] as being non-erroneous, he says:
"It is so, Blessed One," and so forth.
This is what is meant:

the two sides of engagement and withdrawal, which have respectively the natures of non-perception and perception, are to be grasped in the form of taking up and abandoning. Thus, the conceptualizations of the object (*grāhya-vikalpa*) based on the sides of engagement and withdrawal—because their activity is not tied to a real entity and they appear falsely—are, in their own nature, not in accordance with their objects. Each of these consists of nine types according to the distinctions of the objects to be explained hereafter; because they act as obstacles, they are adversaries (*vipakṣa*), like the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"These two are the objects of knowledge.
And so it has been said:
"In both engagement and withdrawal, each of those two consists of nine aspects."
"The two types of conceptualizations regarding the apprehended should be understood as having the nature of non-corresponding objects.
(5) Having thus pointed out the two types of conceptualization regarding the apprehended, it must now be stated that there are two types of conceptualization regarding the apprehender.
First, speaking of the conceptualization regarding the apprehender which has as its basis the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who exists as a substantial entity (*dravyasat*), he says:
Thus, [the text says] "by those accompanied by rejoicing," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt, "And why is that?",
he says, "For it is thus by those," and so forth.

The meaning is that because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)—through their conceptual attachment to the notion that the self is a real entity (*dravyasat*) and the grasper—rejoice in roots of virtue, it is said that they receive fruits such as honor and so forth, but not others such as Buddhahood.
[Objection: But do ordinary beings not also realize that "all phenomena are selfless"? Therefore, the definition of the first conceptualization of the grasper is not all-pervasive.

[Response: That is worthless, for what is intended here is that while for them it is a mental engagement based on resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manaskāra*), here it is intended as a mental engagement with reality (*tattva-manaskāra*).
To explain the second type of conceptualization of the grasper (*grāhakavikalpa*), which exists as a designation (*prajñaptisat*) and has noble persons (*āryapudgala*) as its basis, he says:
"O Blessed One, those who, having generated the aspiration... and so forth, ending with "...will become bringers of perfect enlightenment."

The meaning is that, through their conceptual adherence to the idea that the self is a real entity existing as a mere designation (*prajñaptisat*) and acting as a grasper, and by generating a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Noble Ones, they will primarily become the producers of unexcelled enlightenment as this [mind] increases.
Because it is not in contradiction with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he speaks in accordance [with their view], saying:
"It is so, Kauśika," and so forth.

The three phrases beginning with "rejoiced" (*anumoditāni*) and so forth should be explained according to the distinctions of weak, medium, and intense rejoicing. Now, it might be argued that even for a noble one (*ārya*), this occurs; as it is said: "O monks, at the time of dawn during the night, I heard the howling sound of a jackal, and likewise at that time, I was the king of beasts named Aninda."
The statement "the earth exists" is a non-pervasive determination based on a second conceptualizing subject;
such speech by the noble ones (*ārya*) is merely conventional and not ultimate, and thus it is insubstantial.
This has been stated.

The two types of conceptualization regarding the grasper (*grāhakavikalpa*) are those based on the person as a substantial reality (*dravyasat*) and as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*), corresponding respectively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble persons (*āryapudgala*). When these two have become the objects (*grāhya*) of that [conceptualization], they do not exist in the form of a grasper; at that time, they are not graspers for anyone. Thus, their nature is devoid of the form of a grasper. Because they appear falsely, they do not possess their own essential nature according to their objects. Due to the distinctions of the objects to be explained, each of these two has nine varieties. Because they act as obstacles, they are the adversaries (*vipakṣa*).
And so it has been said:
"The conceptualizations of a substantially existent being and of a nominally existent being are considered to be the two types of subjects;
distinguished by the categories of ordinary person and noble one, each of these two consists of nine aspects. (6)
If it is argued that they are the objects of apprehension, then if those two objects do not exist in that way, for whom could they be considered the subjects of apprehension?
Thus, their characteristic is emptiness by virtue of the state of being a subject of apprehension. (7) Thus.

In that regard, as for how the first conceptualization is to be grasped according to the distinction of its objects—namely, "is it not the case that [the mind] is not a conceptualization"?—he states the meaning of this first conceptualization with the words beginning, "How, O Blessed One? and so forth.
"How" means in what manner the illusion-like mind is not illusion, nor is it any other phenomenon, insofar as it is not realized in any way whatsoever as having true reality (*tattva*).
Explaining by means of a counter-question, he says:
"What do you think? and so forth.
That phenomenon which is absolutely isolated is that phenomenon which is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).
Because it has not arisen, it does not attain existence;

nor is there a valid application of the negative particle (*nañ*) that is devoid of an object. Or, if it were based on conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it would be conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) and not ultimate (*tāttvika*). Thus, by this logic, it does not attain non-existence either. This is the meaning, as before. Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"Not so, Blessed One," and so forth.
He says that because all phenomena (*dharma*) are indeed secluded (*vivikta*), there is no relationship of cause and effect; and as for that phenomenon...
"Extremely secluded," and so forth;
"either bringing in or carrying out" means either producing or destroying.
Expanding upon this very point,
he says, "And how, O Blessed One," and so forth.
Concluding that, in reality, there is neither an object of awakening nor an awakener, he says:
"O Blessed One, when... and so forth. Because it was well-spoken, he [the Buddha] confirmed it with his own hand, saying, "Excellent, excellent," and so forth.
However, he says that from a perfectly pure cause, a perfectly pure result arises by way of conventional reality,
beginning with the words "Subhūti, for this reason," and so forth.
The intended meaning is that because of their being like an illusion, there is no subversion regarding cause and effect.
"One should not even form an attachment to 'seclusion,' and so forth.
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva... and so on.
"Emptiness was taught by the Victors as the relinquishing of all views."
But those for whom emptiness itself has become a view, they have declared to be incurable.

According to this principle, since even the attachment to solitude is of the nature of a misconception (*viparyāsa*), there would be no perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) at all. If one asks, "How then does one, having relied upon it, attain perfect awakening? the text replies:
"In this way indeed, Subhūti," and so forth.
Thus, because it is delightful only when not investigated— that is to say, because it is of the nature of conventional reality—
for this very reason, with reference to the ultimate truth, he says: "Nor, Subhūti, [is there any attainment] of the perfection of wisdom," and so forth.
Summarizing from the perspective of conventional truth, he says:
"And he fully awakens," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of what has been spoken":
Regarding the statement "he does not fully awaken,
yet he fully awakens," he speaks thus in accordance with that very point.
"Thus it is," and so forth.
The intention is that [the Buddha] is called a "performer of what is difficult" by relying on conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
For this very reason, he speaks with reference to ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
“As I have said, O Blessed One,” and so forth.
Regarding the statement “one who performs what is difficult to do,” having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:
“For thus, O Blessed One,” and so forth.

He says, "If, O Blessed One," and so forth, because he courses in the Mother of the Jinas by means of correct engagement— due to the absence of conceptualization regarding intrinsic nature through non-depression and so on during the teaching on the non-apprehension of agent, object, and action. He speaks thus for the sake of the second conceptualization.
"O Bhagavan, it is just as if," and so forth.
By the phrase "because of being non-conceptual, O Bhagavan," the elimination of conceptualization regarding the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is indicated.
He speaks for the sake of the third conceptualization:
"Of the illusory person," and so forth.

By the phrase "it does not occur thus as supreme," the negation of conceptualization regarding the full attainment (*samudāgama*) in practice is established. He speaks for the sake of the fourth conceptualization:
"Of the appearance," and so forth.
By the example of the appearance, the exclusion of the conceptualization of an objective support (*ālambana*) has been shown.
He states the meaning of the fifth conceptualization:
"Whether there is anyone dear to the Tathāgata," and so forth.

By the phrase "because of being non-conceptual, O Blessed One," it is shown that even for a bodhisattva, through the illustration of the non-existence of what is dear or not dear to the Tathāgata, there is the removal of conceptual constructions regarding the counter-agent and its opposite.
He speaks next for the sake of the sixth conceptual construction:
"Indeed, O Blessed One, just as... and so forth.
By the phrase "having abandoned all conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts," the non-apprehension of conceptualizations regarding one's own realization is demonstrated.
He speaks [next] for the sake of the seventh conceptual construction:
"By the Tathāgata, the Arhat," and so forth.
By means of the illustration of the emanation of a Tathāgata, the removal of the conceptualization of an agent who follows from that emanation is shown.
He states the meaning of the eighth conceptualization:
"Of which that emanation is [the effect]," and so forth.
By this example, the distinction from causal activity and conceptualization is demonstrated. He states the meaning of the ninth conceptualization:
"By the skillful mason," and so forth.
By the phrase "and that wooden structure is free from conceptual construction" (avikalpa), the absence of conceptualization regarding the efficacy of the action is expressed.

This is what has been said: by means of the isolated [nature], through the entry into the stages (bhūmi) such as the Immovable (*acalā*) which have the nature of not perceiving the isolated, and through the practice of the lineage of the Buddhas which is like an illusion, when there is the full attainment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth, one takes as an object non-erroneous knowledge as a mere appearance, characterized by the qualities and defects of that which is to be adopted and that which is to be abandoned.

The first conceptualization of the object of apprehension (*grāhyavikalpa*) is based on the side of active engagement (*pravṛttipakṣa*), which should be undertaken as follows: through the power of correct skillful means (*samyag-upāyakauśala-bala*), one engages with the antidotes and their opposites by way of being universal (*sarvatraga*) and so forth; with respect to one’s own realization by way of its being neither inferior nor superior; in the distancing from the stages of the Śrāvakas and others; in the activity for the benefit of sentient beings through emanations corresponding to their inclinations; and in the fruit, which is the act of establishing all beings in nirvāṇa, by way of being faultless and thus entirely worthy of adoption. This is the first conceptualization of the object of apprehension.

The ninefold [obstructions] to be abandoned by Bodhisattvas during the stage of application for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the context of the clear realization of the summits (*mūrdhābhisamaya*) have been explained by way of negation through the presentation of their respective antidotes.
And so it has been said:
This [treatise] concerns: intrinsic nature and lineage; the practice and its full realization;
the object of knowledge and the absence of error therein; and the antidotes and their opposites.
"Regarding one's own attainment, the agent, his activity, and the fruit of that activity—
