conceptualization based on the side of engagement is considered to be ninefold.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Illusion-like," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The twenty-seventh chapter:
Regarding how the second type of conceptualization of the apprehended object, which is based on the side of cessation, is ninefold, he states the meaning of the first conceptualization as follows:
"This is indeed substantial," and so forth.

Because wisdom and compassion act as the causes for not falling into cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) or nirvana (*nirvāṇa*), they possess sovereignty over all that is to be realized; thus, by stating that "he who practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) practices in the essence, the primary," the conceptualization of a deficient realization is refuted.
However, he says that even there, one should not form an attachment to its being the "essence."
"Alas, this is indeed essence-less," and so forth.
It is "essence-less" because there is no apprehension of an essence. He speaks thus for the sake of the second alternative.
"They are to be saluted," and so forth.

By stating that those who practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) while endowed with the support of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and the like are worthy of salutation, the conceptualization regarding the absence of such support is refuted.
He states the meaning of the third conceptualization:
"And those who here [practice] this profound *prajñāpāramitā*," and so forth.

By the phrase "and they do not directly realize that *dharmatā*," because it makes known the excellence of their practice (*pratipatti*), the absence of the conceptualization regarding the deficiency of practice is shown.
He states the meaning of the fourth alternative, beginning with:
"Then indeed, the Venerable... and so forth.
"They do not realize [it directly]" means:

The point is that it is not difficult for Bodhisattvas not to realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because they have attained mastery over its realization. Therefore, the conceptualization of "being dependent on others" is refuted.
He states the meaning of the fifth conceptualization:
"But this, O sons of gods," and so forth;
"we shall discipline sentient beings" [is said] because of their being like an illusion.

Furthermore, by means of the yoga of non-retrogression for the sake of training sentient beings in all dharmas, and by the absence of proceeding toward other vehicles, there is an indication of the freedom from conceptualization regarding the cessation of the objective; this is because one has set out upon the path to the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment without falling away from the aim of the knowledge of all aspects.
He speaks next regarding the meaning of the sixth conceptualization:
"O sons of the gods, space," and so forth. Having raised the doubt, "Why is that?", he says:
"Because of the seclusion of space," and so forth.

"They don the armor for the sake of sentient beings" means that by donning the armor for the purpose of disciplining the entire realm of sentient beings, which is comparable to space, it is implicitly stated that the activity of the path is non-localized, thereby distinguishing it from the conceptualization of localized activity.
He states the meaning of the seventh alternative:
"By space, he... and so forth.
By making known that sentient beings attain the nature of space, he demonstrates the absence of conceptual differentiation regarding the diversity of realizations.
He states the meaning of the eighth conceptualization:
"And this is the armor," and so forth.

By means of donning the armor for the sake of sentient beings, because he acts with prior reflection, the non-attachment to the conceptualization regarding the knowledge of staying and going is demonstrated.
He states the meaning of the ninth conceptualization:
"And that [emptiness] is absolutely," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt, "Why is that so?", he says:
"By way of the isolation of sentient beings," and so forth:
because no ultimate substance is perceived, one should understand that form and the other aggregates are like an illusion.
By the word "up to" (*yāvat*), the inclusion of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and so forth is intended.
Since even the dharmas realized by the Tathāgatas and others are empty, there is the seclusion of all dharmas. Concluding [the section], he says:
"Thus, O sons of gods, the solitude of all phenomena is to be seen.
"Thus, by not becoming despondent during the teaching on non-apprehension, there is practice," and so forth.
"Thus, O sons of gods, regarding the solitude of all phenomena," and so forth.
He asks, "What is the reason for fearlessness?
and replies with the words beginning, "For what reason," and so forth;
he provides the answer by means of the non-apprehension of agent, object, and action.
"Because of its solitude. Concluding, he says: "By this, O Blessed One," and so forth.
This is what has been said:

because it transcends [all things] precisely due to their emptiness, one does not despond since there is an absence of anything to be feared; therefore, one primarily courses in the perfection of wisdom whose very nature is transcendence (*niryāṇa*). And in this way, the removal of conceptual constructions regarding transcendence (*niryāṇa-vikalpa-apoha*) would be demonstrated as following from that.

This is what has been stated: [the faults consist in] falling into either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; lacking the support of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and skill in means (*upāyakauśala*) when realizing emptiness, thereby lacking full comprehension; being deficient in the path because it is not an antidote to all cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);

being dependent on others for realization because of reliance on the instructions of the Tathāgatas and others; the cessation of the objective through failing to engage in the greatness of being foremost among all sentient beings; and the operation of a limited path because it is merely an antidote to the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Because there is the attainment of the first fruit and so forth by means of that which involves apprehension; because there is the non-abandonment of all latent tendencies of ignorance; because there is lack of knowledge regarding staying and going; because there is the failure to encompass the entirety of the Mahāyāna; and because there is the subsequent following after all forms of omniscience and all nirvāṇas while being possessed of faults—it must be ceased as an object of apprehension (*grāhya*). Thus, the second conceptualization of the apprehended (*grāhya-vikalpa*) among Bodhisattvas, which arises from the state of being produced within the mental continua of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas based on the side of cessation (*nivṛtti-pakṣa*), [is to be abandoned] during the stage of the activity of mind and mental factors on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
That which is to be abandoned has been demonstrated by way of its exclusion (*vyatireka*) through the presentation of the respective states of its antidote.
And so it has been said:
"Because it causes one to fall into existence and peace, there is deficiency..."
And for one who has attained [the path], when there is an absence of grasping and when [the factors] have reached a state of non-deficiency in their practice. ||10||
In being dependent on others for understanding, in the cessation of the initial teaching, in partiality, in diversity, and in the delusions regarding the place and the departure. ||11||
"And [the thought] 'in going behind'— this ninefold conceptualization is based on the side of cessation and arises from the minds of the Śrāvakas and others. (12) Thus.
How is it that the first conceptualization of a grasper, which has as its basis a person who is a real entity (*dravyasat*)—an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*)—is of nine kinds?
To explain the meaning of the first conceptualization, he says:
"Nor is there anyone at all, O Blessed One," and so forth.
The meaning is that there is an absence of the conceptualization of grasping and releasing.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"For what reason? and so forth.
He states the meaning of the second alternative,
beginning with "Furthermore, indeed," and so forth:
"One who courses thus courses in the perfection of wisdom."

The meaning is that one who practices in this way—through the teaching on the non-apprehension of all phenomena (*sarvadharmānupalambha*) and by means of being free from despondency and so forth—practices correctly in the Mother of the Victors (*jinajananī*) because of the absence of conceptualization regarding mental attention (*manasikāra-vikalpa*).
He states the meaning of the third conceptualization as follows:
"A bodhisattva practicing in this manner," and so forth.
"They pay homage to him who courses thus" means that they prostrate because he has attained the experience of being free from the conceptual constructions that adhere to the three realms.
He speaks regarding the meaning of the fourth conceptual construction:
"Those who, Subhūti, by means of the immeasurable... and so forth.
They "behold with the Buddha-eye" means that they examine [the object] with the intention of producing a distinguished meaning, through the discernment of the conceptualization of locations.

They favor [beings] by accomplishing their tasks, and they attend to them by determining their capacity for spiritual development. It is precisely because of the Tathāgatas' favor that he asks the question.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "And those who," etc.:
having raised the doubt as before, "For what reason?",
he says, "Those, Subhūti," and so forth.
Expanding upon this very point, he says:
"Let them remain," and so forth.
He states the meaning of the fifth alternative:
"By means of two," and so forth.
By the phrase "they do not become abandoned," the conceptual construction of adherence to non-existence (*abhāvābhiniveśavikalpa*) is prohibited.
And by the phrase "all phenomena are thereby perceived as empty," the conceptual construction of adherence to existence (*bhāvābhiniveśavikalpa*) is likewise rejected.
He speaks for the sake of the sixth conceptualization:
"Furthermore, Subhūti," and so forth.

This means that because he has accomplished the stated purpose—"The conceptualization of the designation of the entities of phenomena (dharmavastu-prajñapti-vikalpa) must be abandoned by me"—he acts exactly as he speaks and speaks exactly as he acts.
And for this very reason, he is called to mind.
To explain the meaning of the seventh alternative, [the text] says:
"Subhūti, for one who courses thus," and so forth.
That is to say, "by means of dwelling in the perfection of wisdom.
The meaning is that this dwelling effects the abandonment of attachment and conceptual construction.
To clarify this very point, he says:
"For what reason? and so forth.
It should be understood that he "dwells" by means of the distinction between the concentrated (*samāhita*) and the non-concentrated (*asamāhita*) states.

Beginning from the *pramuditā* (Joyful) stage up to the attainment of the realization of the *samantaprabhā* (All-Radiant) Buddha-stage, the eleven phrases beginning with "you will become a Protector" (*nātha*) should be recited in their respective order.
Summing up, he says:
"In this way, those sons of the gods," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt, "Why is that so?", he says: "In that very same way."

Regarding the passage beginning with "By this, Subhūti," the meaning is as follows: because the Buddha Bhagavats, when a Bodhisattva dwells in the aforementioned dwelling, utter an inspired exclamation (*udāna*) preceded by the proclamation of his name and so forth and the teaching of the Dharma, they therefore increase his enthusiasm.
Clarifying this very point by means of an illustration, he says:
"Just as, for example," and so forth.
Because all bodhisattvas are infinite and it is impossible to mention them by name, he speaks by way of extension.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of others," etc.:
if it is argued that there are no bodhisattvas worthy of praising the buddhafield of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, he says,
"In this very way, Subhūti," and so forth.
This has been said:

just as I teach the Dharma, intent upon proclaiming the names and so forth of the bodhisattvas residing in the buddha-fields of other Tathāgatas in order to encourage the bodhisattvas residing in my own buddha-field, in the very same way do those [Buddhas] such as Akṣobhya and the others.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgatas are intent upon proclaiming the names and so forth of the bodhisattvas residing in my buddha-field while teaching the Dharma.
Regarding the meaning of the eighth conceptualization, he says:
"Is it for all of them? and so forth.
"Not so," he said.
Explaining the words of the rebuttal, he says, "No, Subhūti," and so forth.
Rather, those who...
"Those who are irreversible" means that because they have abandoned the conceptualizations of their opposites, they have attained irreversibility on the eighth stage and those beyond it.
And he speaks regarding the meaning of the ninth conceptualization:
"O Blessed One, there exist those who are irreversible," and so forth;
he says that they "do exist."
"Subhūti, they do exist," and so forth.
Having raised the doubt, "What then are those? he speaks again in order to demonstrate [the answer], beginning with "Those who at present... and so on.

The mention of Akṣobhya is because, for the most part, beings of purified mental continuums arise in that buddha-field; intending to extend this [description] to others as well, he says, "Those also, Subhūti," and so forth.
The mention of the bodhisattva Ratnaketu should be understood as being intended to indicate all bodhisattvas of a similar class.

The meaning is that, by the power of being sustained by exceptionally distinguished spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and others, those Bodhisattvas who dwell in Buddha-fields such as Akṣobhya’s— having attained mastery over supernatural powers (*ṛddhivaśitā*) because they are free from the conceptualization of obstruction regarding their movement at will even prior to the immovable stage (*acalā bhūmi*)— exist as objects for the proclamation of their names and so forth, with the exception of those who are irreversible (*avinivartanīya*).
This has been said:

[it refers to] grasping and releasing according to conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*); in reality (*tattvataḥ*), it is the mental engagement through non-mental-engagement; and by way of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is the non-adherence to the three realms within emptiness.

In the non-abiding state of abiding, through non-attachment to all attachments, through the substantial existence of all dharmic designations, through attachment preceded by non-attachment due to lack of devotion to the knowledge of reality, through the cultivation of equanimity as a counteragent to its opposite, and through the failure to correctly understand the perfection of wisdom regarding the counteragent, there occurs an obstruction to proceeding according to one’s will; and through attachment to ultimate entities, the self is grasped as if it were substantially real.

"Proceeds"—thus, this first type of subject-object conceptualization associated with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), which has nine aspects, is to be abandoned by Bodhisattvas during the stage of application (*prayoga*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It has been explained by way of negation through the presentation of its antidotal state.
And so it has been said:
The first should be known as the grasper (grāhaka) in the grasping and releasing [of objects], in the mental attention (manaskriyā), and in the conjunction of the three elements (dhātu). ||13||

"In the case of [the notions of] place, adherence, and the designation of the entity of phenomena; in attachment and its antidote; and according to one's desire and the destruction of the [six] destinies"—thus, how is it that the second conceptualization of grasping, which has as its basis a person existing as a designation (*prajñaptisat*), is of nine kinds?
He states the meaning of the first alternative, beginning with:
"Furthermore, Subhūti," and so forth.
"They have conviction" means:

With the intention of attaining the state of being foremost among all beings and so forth, they attend to all phenomena as "unproduced" or "quiescent. Yet, they have not yet attained the excellence of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) nor the irreversible mastery; thus, the absence of conceptualization regarding the departure from the objective is demonstrated.
He states the meaning of the second alternative with the words, "But for those indeed... and so forth.
By the phrase, "the stage of the Śrāvaka and the stage of the Pratyekabuddha have been abandoned by them," he expresses the absence of conceptualization regarding the determination of the path.

"Only the stage of Buddhahood is to be expected for them"— by this also, the absence of the conceptualization that restricts oneself to one's own path is shown, because otherwise, due to the presence of error, the stage of Buddhahood would be impossible.
He speaks regarding the meaning of the third conceptualization:
"They too shall be prophesied for unexcelled [enlightenment]," and so forth.
As before, having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:
"For those, Subhūti," and so forth.
"Thus practicing in the perfection of wisdom" means not rising up through the separation from the conceptual constructions of arising and ceasing.
He states the meaning of the fourth alternative,
beginning with: "Furthermore, Subhūti," and so forth,
[ending with] "they will abide in the state of non-retrogression."

The meaning is that those Bodhisattvas who, without harboring doubt and so forth, will extensively engage in hearing [the Dharma] and the like, and who will practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and other observances in their presence, they too— being free from the conceptualization of union and separation— will abide in the state of non-retrogression.
He speaks next regarding the meaning of the fifth conceptualization.
"What need is there to mention those who... and so forth.

The connection with the preceding is as follows: by means of the non-apprehension of conceptual constructions regarding the bases such as form and so on, those who, having gained resolute faith in the *prajñāpāramitā* and abiding in suchness, shall teach the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of the mark of Buddhahood—they will, moreover, stand firmly in the state of being irreversible.
He states the meaning of the sixth alternative:
"When, O Blessed One, suchness... and so forth.
Having reiterated those words with "That which, Subhūti... and so forth, he speaks in order to provide a rebuttal.
"Subhūti, there is nothing other than suchness," and so forth.

Since all phenomena have the *dharmadhātu* as their intrinsic nature, and since no phenomenon other than suchness is perceived, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) no one at all will abide in suchness;
however, from the conventional perspective (*saṃvṛti*), the intention is that they will abide because they are free from the conceptualization of the loss of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Clarifying by taking the ultimate truth (paramārtha) alone as the subject, he says:
"First, suchness itself," and so forth.
He states the meaning of the seventh conceptual alternative:
"Subhūti, it is not that suchness attains unsurpassed [enlightenment], and so forth.
In reality, neither suchness nor any other dharma awakens to enlightenment; rather, it is through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) that there is aspiration.
The thought is that one awakens through the non-apprehension of an object to be sought, due to the absence of conceptualization regarding existence.
He states the meaning of the eighth conceptualization:
"Subhūti, it is not suchness that teaches the Dharma."

In reality, suchness does not teach the Dharma; rather, it is taught through conventional truth by means of the existence of causes, because of the absence of the conceptualization of the non-existence of causes—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the ninth conceptualization, he says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, that dharma which might be taught is also not apprehended."
The meaning is that there is no apprehension of the dharmas being taught due to the absence of conceptualization regarding the apprehension of opposing dharmas.
This is what has been stated:

[there is no apprehension] in the non-departure from the aforementioned objective through the departure of Śrāvakas and others; in the determination of path and non-path through the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful; and in arising and cessation through the conventional relationship of cause and effect, by virtue of their appearing as either uninterrupted or otherwise.
In the state where all things are joined and separated, like a bird remaining in the sky;

in the destruction of the lineages of the Śrāvakas and others through the gateway of the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and so forth; in the absence of longing due to the non-existence of phenomena distinct from suchness (*tathatā*); in the absence of a cause by relying on ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); and in the perception of objects such as adversaries and Māras as having the nature of extreme stinginess—through the adherence to real entities, the self, which exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*), functions as the grasper. Thus [it is for] the Noble Ones...

The second type of conceptualization regarding the grasper (*grāhakavikalpa*), which consists of nine varieties, is to be abandoned by Bodhisattvas during the stage of the functioning of the mind and mental factors on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); it is explained by way of negation (*vyatirekamukhena*) through the presentation of its antidotal state.
And so it has been said:
Regarding the lack of departure as taught, the determination of what is and is not the path, cessation along with origination, and the union with and separation from entities; ||15||
"When there is [the perception of] place, lineage, destruction, prayer, absence of cause,
and the apprehension of an adversary, there is another conceptualization which is the grasper. Thus,
it would follow that this is a conceptualization of the graspable, not a conceptualization of the grasper.

There is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika). Among these, the first alternative is that representation which has the appearance of an object and consists of the aspect of the apprehended (grāhyākāra).
The second, however, is that which lasts for only a single moment and consists of the aspect of the apprehender (grāhakākāra).
The third is that very same [wisdom] at another moment;
the fourth is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) when it is free from those mental aspects.
Thus, there may be the lineage itself without the conceptualization of a lineage; this is the "concluding quarter" (paścātpādaka).
First, there may be a conceptualization of the lineage (*gotra*) that is itself the lineage, such as the lineage at the time of the full realization of the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*).
There may be that which is the lineage alone but not a conceptualization of the lineage, such as the lineage currently being realized.
There may be a conceptualization of the realization but not a conceptualization of the object (*ālambana*); this is the first alternative.

That which is the conceptualization of attainment (*samudāgama-vikalpa*) is also the conceptualization of the object (*ālambana-vikalpa*), such as the application toward a correct object for one who is attaining it.
There may be a conceptualization of the object alone that is not a conceptualization of attainment, such as: [text fragment].

"The perfectly established object" (pariniṣpanna-ālambana)— the remainder should be inferred by this method. Having thus explained the adverse factors together with their remedies on the path of seeing (darśanamārga), it is maintained that the path of seeing is accompanied by three kinds of causes for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of great enlightenment (mahābodhi).
Now, that must be explained.
Stating the first cause, which is the establishment of others by demonstrating the path of vision and so forth regarding great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), he says:
"O Bhagavan, it is profound," and so on.
As before, having raised the question "For what reason?", he says:
"And indeed, O Blessed One," and so forth. [This refers to] the non-arising of all dharmas.

By declaring that those who wish to awaken to unsurpassed enlightenment through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) without performing such acts as prostration are "doers of what is difficult," the path of seeing and so forth is established for them by way of inspiring them toward enlightenment.
He then says that, from the standpoint of relying on ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), nothing is difficult.
"Kauśika, it is so," and so forth.
Praising [Subhūti] for his eloquent speech, he says: "Whatever the noble Subhūti... and so forth.
"It does not cling anywhere" means it does not adhere to anything. Strengthening the point he himself has stated, he says:
"Am I [correct]? and so forth.
"And the conformity to the Dharma" means the practice of the dharma of emptiness as it was intended.
He said, "Well said."
Regarding the passage beginning with "Indeed, you," and so forth:
having raised the doubt as to why that is so,
he says, "For whatever [it may be]," and so forth.
"Why is this so?"— anticipating this question with the words "For what reason?",
he says: "Subhūti, O Kauśika," and so forth.

Since the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which effects the abandonment of the weak, medium, and intense afflictions (*kleśa*) within each of the three realms beginning with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), has been shown in the form of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one should state nine phrases starting from "even the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is not apprehended" up to "even phenomena (*dharma*) themselves are not apprehended.
Because there is a general non-apprehension of the cause and effect of all phenomena, there is, respectively, an abiding in the seclusion of all phenomena.
And the dwelling in the non-apprehension of all phenomena is to be grasped.
If it is argued that, in this way, the dwelling of Bodhisattvas is exactly the same as that of the Śrāvakas, he says: "But as for that which... and so forth.
"For them" means that those others who are distinct from the dwellings of the Tathāgatas should dwell by means of this dwelling.
By the very statement of the benefits of the bodhisattva dwellings, the demonstration of the path of seeing and so forth toward great enlightenment for others would have been declared.
The twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Essence," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The twenty-eighth chapter.

It is said that the monks performed an offering because they had attained the vision of the path through the realization of the path—beginning with the vision of awakening as previously described—which was brought about by perfected causes.
This is expressed in the passage beginning with "Then, indeed," and so forth.
It should be understood that the gathering of sons of gods who had taken up māndārava flowers was due to the power of the monks' previous vows for the sake of obtaining flowers.
Furthermore, he says "and they made a vow" and so forth, meaning that because they had attained conviction through realization, they made a vow for the sake of further and further increase,
and thus spoke these words.
Then indeed, O Blessed One, and so forth—
this has been explained.
"Twenty thousand kalpas" means:

Starting from humans with immeasurable lifespans down to those with a lifespan of ten years— this first intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) is characterized by decline through the emergence of weapons, disease, and famine. From those with a ten-year lifespan, they gradually undergo an increase.

The lifespan becomes eighty thousand years. Then, once again, as the lifespan decreases in the same manner until it reaches ten years, there are eighteen intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa) distinguished by these increases and decreases.
After that, from those with a ten-year lifespan, they undergo an increase once more.
The twentieth intermediate kalpa is the period of increase when the lifespan reaches eighty thousand years;
likewise, the period of decrease for the first intermediate kalpa is exactly as long as the total time of both increase and decrease for all the others.

The period of increase for the western [continent] is thus; all [periods] are equal in duration. In this way, through one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) of the destruction of the receptacle worlds (*bhājana*), and through nineteen intermediate kalpas of their becoming empty, the world undergoes dissolution (*saṃvartate*) for twenty intermediate kalpas;
it remains dissolved for twenty intermediate kalpas.
Thus, with one intermediate kalpa for the formation of the receptacle world, and nineteen for its subsequent abiding, the world undergoes evolution for twenty intermediate kalpas;
it remains evolved for twenty intermediate kalpas. In this way, a great kalpa is delimited by eighty intermediate kalpas.
This [great kalpa] beginning with the Bhadrakalpa is like a star in duration, yet it is not so for those whose roots of merit consist of their vows, because of the extreme length of time involved.

Therefore, it is precisely in the context of the decrease (*apakarṣa*) that the duration of time is delimited by the aforementioned measure of an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*), and thus it is said to be "twenty thousand eons.

To introduce the second cause for explaining how the Perfection of Wisdom is handed over to others through the gateway of the correct text, meaning, and so forth, solely for the sake of the conditions for awakening (*bodhinimitta*), he says:
"For those who, Ānanda... and so on.
Anticipating the question "Why is that so?", he says:
"For it is thus among humans," and so forth.

The seven phrases beginning with "they do not revile" should be understood, respectively, as referring to the contradiction of the seven clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), starting with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"He will not fail his vow" means the vow set forth regarding the domain of unsurpassed enlightenment.
If he does not fail it by making a different vow, then that root of virtue will not yield its maturation toward the state of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha; this is the meaning.

Having provided this introduction, he now speaks the words beginning with "Therefore, then," etc., for the purpose of a gentle entrustment in connection with the Tathāgata. "I entrust" means I hand over.

"I entrust [this] further and hand it back" means for the purpose of its reception and so forth; because of this handing back, some say that the noble Ānanda is the compiler (*saṅgītikāra*) of this Mother [Prajñāpāramitā].
Others say that because of the handing back specifically for the purpose of its retention and so forth, Mahāvajradhara himself is the compiler.
In this context, "loss" (vipraṇāśana) means alteration; "abandonment" (utsarjana) means rejection in every respect; "forgetting" (vismaraṇa) means non-attention (amanasikaraṇa).
A "neighboring word" (padasāmantaka) is a part of a word.
Because she brings about the three bodies (*kāya*), she is respectively the mother, the progenitress, and the giver of birth.

Therefore, because it brings about the arising of omniscience itself, he says "this should be taken up," and so forth, for the sake of the middling entrustment. For the sake of the superior entrustment, he says:
"Yathā tad" and so forth;
the connection is with "tattat kartavyam ca" and so on.
[The phrase] "tayā hītaiṣitayā" means by that which is devoid of desire.

Out of a desire for the welfare of the Tathāgatas, and even by way of the Bodhisattva connection, he speaks for the sake of a mild entrustment, beginning with the words, "Those who... and so forth. He speaks for the sake of a middling entrustment.
"Whosoever," and so forth.
He speaks "This, Ānanda," and so forth, for the purpose of an extensive entrustment.

And in order to explain the third cause—the characteristic of merit consisting in the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and so forth, which is itself immediate for the attainment of enlightenment—he says:
"If you, Ānanda, [were to teach] those belonging to the vehicle of the disciples," and so on.
The mention of "a single moment, a fraction of a moment, or a muhūrta" is for the purpose of indicating, respectively, persons of sharp, medium, and dull faculties.
In this context, the ultimate limit of time is a *kṣaṇa*. One hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute a *tatkṣaṇa*; sixty of those make a *lava*;
thirty *lavas* make a *muhūrta*. For even the final constituent of a syllable has a duration equal to a *nimeṣa*.
If it is asked how, according to this principle, he teaches the Dharma in a single moment, it is replied:
through the sovereign power of the teaching Bodhisattva, there arises in the listener, in a single moment, a cognition characterized by the manifestation of the taught Dharma;
therefore, it is designated that "the Dharma has been taught to him."
The three causes for attaining perfect enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) should be understood exactly as they have been stated.
And so it has been said:
"The manifestation of enlightenment to others, and the entrustment of its cause."
"The cause immediately preceding its attainment is characterized by an abundance of merit" (17). Thus,

in order to demonstrate that the power of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)— only when accompanied by the aforementioned causes— is capable of ensuring that conceptual constructions do not appear, he speaks, providing the illustration of the non-appearance [of the Buddha] despite the manifestation of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
Then indeed, the Blessed One [spoke] beginning with "eternal," and so forth.
In that context, it is like the ocean because it is a mine of all the jewels of qualities;
it is profound because of the realization of the profound Dharma.
Because it has transcended the entire domain of Māra, it is unshakeable (*akṣobhyā*).
To state the illustrative meaning, he says:
"In this way, Ānanda, all dharmas..."

The fourfold set of phrases beginning with "all phenomena do not even come into the range of vision" is for the purpose of demonstrating the non-appearance of the four kinds of conceptual constructions regarding the grasped and the grasper on the path of seeing.
In order to substantiate this very point, he says:
"For what reason? and so forth. Why is it thus?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?
he says, "For they are devoid of activity," and so forth.
This is what is meant:

The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-cognizant because it is inactive like space; likewise, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is non-seeing because, being comparable to a magically created man, it is inconceivable.
Even the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is incapable of causal efficiency, because it does not make anything known due to its non-occurrence. Concluding [the argument], he says:
"Practicing in this way," and so forth.
But what is this "great enlightenment" (mahābodhi) for the sake of which the path of seeing— accompanied by the three aforementioned causes— is intended?
Introducing the subject of great enlightenment (mahābodhi), he says:
"Great enlightenment is the supreme perfection of all training," and so forth.
Likewise, having raised the doubt as to why that is so, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "eṣā hi" and so forth:
"having lifted them up, they would set them down again" means that having raised them upward, they would cause them to fall back down once more.
And the passage beginning with "na ca teṣām" and so forth is stated with reference to the perceptions of those to be trained (vineyajana).
However, conceptual construction does not manifest for the Blessed Ones.
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says "immeasurable," and so forth; the intended meaning is that it is because they are free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatvāt*).
Now, one might ask: "Since other trainings such as generosity and so forth exist, why is the training in the perfection of wisdom specifically prescribed?
To this he says: "As many as there are, Ānanda," and so forth.
Having thus provided a general introduction, he now speaks of the nature of great enlightenment (mahābodhi).
"Indeed, it is inexhaustible," and so forth.
Because there is no exhaustion, Great Enlightenment—whose intrinsic nature is inexhaustible gnosis—is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Anticipating the question, "For what reason is this so?", he says:
"Because of non-existence" means because of the absence of destruction.
Elaborating upon this very point, he says:
"For of space," and so forth.

In this regard, the determination of its own nature through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The realization of its distinctness through inference (*anumāna*) is the exhaustion (*kṣaya*).
The ascertainment of its limit—either through scripture (*āgama*) or through both—is the culmination (*paryanta*).

This is the intended meaning: just as space cannot be apprehended through means of valid cognition and the like because its intrinsic nature consists merely in the absence of substance, so it is with the mother.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"For what reason? and so forth.
If it is argued that the measure and other characteristics have been explained by stating the extent of the text, he says:
"Not by me, O Ānanda," and so forth.
The meaning is: "of the Prajñāpāramitā, which is of the nature of reality."
To the question, "Then by what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth would [these] exist? he says:
"The collection of names (nāmakāya)," and so forth.

Among these, the designations for the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena are the collection of names; the designations for their specific qualities (viśeṣa) are the collection of phrases (padakāya); and the syllables (akṣara) which serve as the basis for both of those are the collection of phonemes (vyañjanakāya).
The meaning is that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) which consists of names and so forth, being bound by [conceptual] measures, is not the perfection of wisdom in the primary sense.
To clarify this very point, he says:
"For what reason? and so on.

This is what was stated: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the wisdom of the Tathāgata is *prajñāpāramitā*; because it is taught by that [wisdom], the *prajñāpāramitā* consisting of the text is designated as such through figurative usage (*upacāra-vṛtti*).
For this very reason, with reference to reality (*tattva*), he says:
"For this is not possessed of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)," and so forth.
Asking for the reason why the nature of reality (*tattvarūpa*) is not stated as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "But by what [means]? and so forth. To provide the answer, he says:
"Because of its inexhaustibility," and so forth.
"Because of its solitude" means that, due to the absence of arising, its intrinsic nature is the knowledge of non-arising.
Regarding the phrase "of that which is isolated":
the meaning is that the emptiness of an unarisen entity is not perceived, because the substratum (dharmin) does not exist.
"Because it is immeasurable" means that it cannot be measured due to the absence of cessation and arising.
He states that the Tathāgatas of the three times are characterized by the knowledge of non-arising and non-cessation.
"Those [Buddhas], Ānanda," and so forth.
They have perished through momentary impermanence and have completely vanished through the impermanence of the continuum. Concluding, he says:
"Therefore, then," and so forth. This means:
regarding the stains of the afflictive and cognitive obstructions, which are conceptualized as being either arisen or unarisen—

Since no phenomenon exists apart from the *dharmadhātu*, and because phenomena whose nature is the *dharmadhātu*— like space— are devoid of cessation and arising, and are excluded from existence as established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that analyzes whether they possess a singular or multiple nature, or the relationship of cause and effect, they are like a sky-lotus. Consequently,

because there is respectively neither the destruction nor the arising of defilements, Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*)— which consists of the knowledge of non-destruction and non-arising, is characterized by the non-erroneous realization of all phenomena, and is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as it truly is— is the *dharmakāya*.
It is thus described. And so it has been said:
"The knowledge of the destruction and non-arising of defilements is called awakening."
Because of the absence of destruction and because of non-arising, they [are so called] with respect to the objects of knowledge respectively. ||28||

And when reality has been thus indicated, some—due to their intense attachment to perception and their intention to describe the destruction of existing things—describe "knowledge of destruction" (*kṣayajñāna*) as the cognition that "it is destroyed" when [a defilement] is exhausted, and "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*) as the intention toward the non-arising of future things. Therefore, in order to directly establish the true nature of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) by removing this point of misconception, he says:
"This is profound," and so forth.
Explaining it in that very way, he says:
"Because of imperishability," and so forth;
[this means] because space is imperishable and because all phenomena are non-arisen.

The meaning is that great enlightenment, which consists of the knowledge of non-destruction and non-arising, is inexhaustible because there is no destruction of phenomena—just as there is no exhaustion of space—and because there is no arising of phenomena.

To the question, "Why is such a perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) realized through cultivation while one is still in the stage of a beginner, characterized by attachment to objective apprehension? he says:
"How so, Blessed One? and so forth.

This is not a fault, because [the text] says that from the very moment of the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one meditates on all phenomena as being like an illusion, devoid of arising and ceasing;
thus it says, "by way of the inexhaustibility of form," and so forth.
Explaining it further by another method, he says:
"In this way indeed, Subhūti," and so forth.

In that context, ignorance (*avidyā*) here refers to the state of the afflictions (*kleśa*) in a previous birth; likewise, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) refer to the state of meritorious and other types of karma; and similarly, consciousness (*vijñāna*) here refers to the five aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) in this present birth.
After the moment of rebirth-linking consciousness and prior to the arising of the six sense bases, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
From that point until the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness has not yet come together, there is the sixfold base (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
As long as one is not yet capable of discerning the causes of the three types of sensation, there is contact (*sparśa*) resulting from the coming together of the triad.
The state of experiencing pleasure and so forth prior to sexual passion is sensation (*vedanā*).

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the state prior to the search for objects, characterized by the active manifestation of passion for the qualities of sensual pleasure and sexual intercourse. Grasping (*upādāna*) is the state of searching for those objects. Existence (*bhava*) is the karma leading to rebirth, acquired through the frantic pursuit of the causes for obtaining those objects.

By that karma, there is a new linking of existence in the future, which is birth (*jāti*). That which follows thereafter, up to the stage of feeling (*vedanā*), is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Thus, with two factors each at the beginning and the end, and three in the middle, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) consists of twelve links divided into three sections.
Because there is no exhaustion of this [dependent origination], it is "indestructible," as previously stated.
The contemplation of dependent origination is free from the two extremes because it is devoid of permanence and annihilation.
It is that which is without beginning, end, or middle.
One contemplates dependent origination as being like an illusion, devoid of arising, ceasing, and abiding.
It is said that dependent origination should be grasped precisely in this manner:
"For one who contemplates in this way," and so forth.
In that regard, mental attention is the accomplishment of the inexhaustible;
skill in means is the investigation of dependent origination.
Explaining that very point, he says:
"How [is it] in the *Prajñāpāramitā*? and so forth.
If it is argued that there would then be a cessation of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), he says:
"Furthermore, it is indeed thus," and so forth.
"Without cause" means that, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), causes do exist. "Permanent," and so forth.
In that regard, it is eternal (*nitya*) because there is no cause for its arising;
it is stable (*dhruva*) because there is no destruction of what has arisen;
and it is everlasting (*śāśvata*) because it undergoes transformation in the form of manifestation and disappearance.
Because it is devoid of the attainment of another state, it has the nature of being non-transformable.
But how, then, should one bring to mind the presently perceived forms and so forth in the aspect of their inexhaustibility?
To this he says: "At whatever time, Subhūti," and so forth.

By means of the non-apprehension of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, the activity of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) would be illuminated through the abandonment of all grasping at a self and at phenomena.

Since it is thus the non-perception of all phenomena, those who describe the knowledge that "it is exhausted" regarding what has been exhausted with the intention of the destruction of existing things as the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge that "it is unarisen" regarding what has not arisen with the intention of the non-arising of existing things as the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*), [are in error].

Due to the deficiency of [the notions of] destruction and non-arising, this knowledge is not tenable for them. For, since the ultimate nature— which is *tathatā*— is in fact unceasing, being characterized by the cessation of the arising and destruction of what has arisen and what has not arisen respectively, then according to the power of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), what form of conceptual construction and so forth could have arisen and been destroyed, or what unarisen thing of a nature not to arise could have come into being, for those proponents who are attached to false entities?
Insofar as there is nothing at all,
therefore, the knowledge of destruction and non-arising should be understood exactly as it has been described.
And so it has been said:

"When primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has not been suppressed by the path called 'vision' (*darśana*), how could the collection of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) be exhausted, and how could it have reached the state of non-arising? (19).

Otherwise, if one were to admit the existence of real dharmas, it would be impossible to establish the Blessed One’s complete abandonment of the obscurations of conceptual construction, afflictions, and the knowable.

For, by contemplating that there is no self because it is empty of arising and passing away, one abandons the attachment to a self. Having perceived the aggregates and so forth—which are dependently originated, characterized by the nature of arising and passing away, and devoid of a self—one reflects that "this is mind-only and no external object exists," based on the rule of the simultaneous perception of blue and the cognition thereof. While not yet having abandoned the attachment to the aspect of the grasper (*grāhaka*), one sets aside the attachment to external objects; then, reflecting that "in the absence of the grasped (*grāhya*), there is the absence of the grasper," one [examines] even that which is characterized by the aspect of the grasper.

Having set aside the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) and determined that non-dual gnosis alone is, in reality, an existent entity, one should contemplate that even this [gnosis], because it is dependently originated, is without intrinsic nature like an illusion, and that in truth it is free from the conceptualization of absolute existence, non-existence, and so forth. When the power of such contemplation is perfected, for some, there arises—much like the cognition of a jewel or silver [when mistaken for something else]—a non-conceptual awareness in which all causes of error have been dispelled, which appears as an illusion-like self-reflection, and which is in some way personally realized within oneself; upon its arising, one abandons the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) through correct yoga.

Otherwise, if— just as space always maintains a nature consisting merely of the absence of substance, a nature that cannot be added to or removed— the momentary phenomena, which consist of mere cognition and are characterized as objects of cognition, were to exist in an ultimate sense, then nothing would be effected for them by the cultivation of their antidotes, just as nothing is effected for space itself. Therefore, since the Blessed One’s total abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the existence of phenomena are accepted [by you], this would involve the acceptance of mutually contradictory meanings due to the failure to eliminate the misconception of real existence.
It would be a cause for wonder.
And so it has been said:
"The existence of phenomena consists in the destruction of obscurations regarding that which is to be known."
"That which is stated by others regarding the Teacher is what causes me wonder here.

(20) Since liberation is thus untenable through such adherence to intrinsic existence (*bhāvābhiniveśa*), one must not perform the subtraction or addition—namely, the denial (*apavāda*) or superimposition (*samāropa*)—of any dharma whatsoever. Rather, this very dependently originated [reality], which is true in its conventional form, must be examined as being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) with respect to form and so forth, and in this manner...
It should be understood that one who perceives reality is liberated through the cessation of error, just as one illusory elephant defeats another illusory elephant.
And so it has been said:
"Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added."
"The real must be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated.
(21) Thus, by means of the cultivation of the reality of things according to the aforementioned absence of error, there is a transcending of all discordant factors.
This is stated by demonstrating the despondency of the Māras.
"At the time when, Subhūti," and so forth.
As before, having raised the doubt "for what reason?", he says:
"Because of dwelling in the perfection of wisdom," and so forth.
Concluding [the discussion], he says:
"Therefore, then," and so forth.

Now, one might object: since the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is primarily the cause of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), why is it said that "one should practice in the perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*)?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason?
he speaks as follows— beginning with "For in the Prajñāpāramitā"— in order to explain in detail the very path of vision (*darśanamārga*) under discussion.
Having thus explained each [perfection] individually, he speaks again in order to describe them as a collective whole,
beginning with the words "In the perfection of wisdom" (prajñāpāramitāyām).
This term "perfection of wisdom" is a designation for the fulfillment of the six perfections.
The meaning is that, prior to this statement, the six perfections reach the fulfillment of their cultivation through the practice of the perfection of wisdom alone.

However, since brevity of text is intended here, it should be understood that by way of illustration, each of the six perfections also attains the completion of their cultivation through the practice of the individual perfections of giving and so forth.
Thus it is said in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*:
"Subhūti, here, when a bodhisattva gives a gift, friendly physical, vocal, and mental actions are present toward sentient beings; such is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

By enduring the abuse and insults of those very recipients, there is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*). By not abandoning the enthusiasm for giving even through the abuse and insults of beggars, there is the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*)."

And for that very person, as they dedicate that gift toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) because of the absence of any distracted thought toward the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

And for that very person, while giving that gift, there is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) because, through the presence of the realization of illusion (*māyābuddhi*), they perceive neither benefit nor harm in anything.

In this way, for one who guards ethical discipline (*śīla*) up to the point of cultivating wisdom (*prajñā*), the inclusion of the fulfillment of each of the six perfections should be explained according to the Sūtra.

Therefore, this is what is meant: when each of the six perfections, such as generosity and the rest, exists individually within each [perfection], that mutual inclusion of all the perfections within generosity and the others—

occurring here in a single moment during the "summit" realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*), subsumed under the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*), manifested through the purity of the three spheres (*trimandalaviśuddhi*), and produced from thirty-six aspects— is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It should be understood thus.
And so it has been said:
"The mutual inclusion of each one of those [perfections], such as generosity and the rest,"

If it is asked: "Since such conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have already been abandoned previously, how can their abandonment be specified here in this state of reaching the ultimate limit of excellence (*prakarṣaparyantādhigama*), which consists of a single moment and is comprised of receptivity (*kṣānti*)? [The answer follows: ||22|| [Note: The provided text contains the verse fragment "sa ekakṣaṇikaḥ kṣāntisaṅgṛhīto' tra dṛkpatha" (This is the path of seeing here, consisting of a single moment and comprised of receptivity), followed by the objection regarding the timing of the abandonment of conceptual constructions.]

This is not a fault, because it is stated in such sūtras as the *Ārya-saṃdhinirmocana* that on the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the delusions that obstruct the great superknowledges (*mahābhijñā*) for entering the subtle secrets, as well as their seeds, are abandoned.

Therefore, through the total eradication of the causes—namely, those delusions along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanā*)—there is necessarily the abandonment of these fourfold conceptual constructions of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*) which constitute the culmination of realization; this occurs upon penetrating the tenth stage during the "summit" clear realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*).
The former masters maintain that, otherwise, abandonment is merely occasional.

For the sake of instructing those of dull intellect and with the intention of showing favor, each of the aforementioned types of conceptualization has been divided into nine varieties according to the distinction of their objects.
It should be understood, however, that for the sake of removing the contempt of those with sharp intellects, the antidotes have not been subdivided to such an extent.
Furthermore, this is the summarized meaning here:
all the aforementioned conceptual constructions of the grasped and the grasper arise from error (*viparyāsa*), and that error—

The [affliction] characterized by the persistent attachment to entities and so forth from beginningless time is indeed abandoned through the knowledge of their intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), which is its opposite because it takes a contrary object and aspect.
When that [affliction] is abandoned, how could the conceptualizations of the apprehended (*grāhya-vikalpa*) and so forth, which are rooted in it, continue to persist?

And when this path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has arisen, [it is abandoned] according to the nine types of each of the four conceptualizations, distinguished by the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.

By abandoning the one hundred and eight conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the grasped and the grasper, one perceives—through the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*)—the abandonment of the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*) of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) that produce those conceptual constructions.
Then, for the sake of attaining mastery (*vaśitva*) therein, one repeatedly cultivates that very [nature].
Thus he says: "And all skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)," and so forth.

Having attained the path of seeing, the yogin—being free from the fear of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable—enters the meditative absorption named *siṃhavijṛmbhita*. Subsequently, he examines dependent origination in its forward order, beginning with "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces," and in its reverse order, beginning with "the cessation of birth leads to the cessation of aging and death.
This is the skillful means to be understood in this context.
And so it has been said:
"Having entered that samādhi, he then contemplates dependent origination in the lion’s yawn, both in direct and reverse order. (23)

Having thus explained the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), [the author] states that since the abandonment of opposing factors (*vipakṣa*) and so forth are easily understood once the foundational practice (*ādhārapratipatti*) has been established, he speaks of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as the foundation.
He says: "O Subhūti, all skillful means," and so forth.
Here, "all skillful means" refers to the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these are comprised within the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), while those [other attainments] are comprised within the leap-attainments (*avaskanda-samāpatti*).
Therefore, this is what is meant:

starting from the first dhyāna up to cessation (*nirodha*), and then starting from cessation back down to the first dhyāna—in this way, by means of the two sequences of forward and reverse order, one characterized by the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and cessation.

Having gone through the nine attainments and returned, he enters the first dhyāna; then, having emerged from that, he enters cessation itself, and so on up to the cessation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Then, having emerged from that, he takes the immediately preceding attainment as his object, stabilizes the consciousness belonging to the desire realm in the form of a boundary, and emerging by the power of skillful means, he brings that very same non-concentrated consciousness into manifestation. From there, he enters cessation, and from there...

From that, having abandoned one state of meditative equipoise, namely the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; from that, the non-equipoised state; from that, having abandoned two states, the sphere of nothingness; from that, the non-equipoised state; and so on, until having abandoned eight states, one enters the first dhyāna, and from that—

One who wishes to embrace the *avaskandasamāpatti*—characterized by mastery, whose nature is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and which consists of skill in all means (*sarvopāyakauśalya*)—should practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). This is because, by abandoning [the meditative states] one by one starting from the first up to the state of non-cessation (*anirodha*), one proceeds through dissimilar gateways; thus it is called "going unequally" (*atulyagāmin*).
As it has been said:
Taking the consciousness belonging to the desire realm as its limit,
one goes to and returns from the nine meditative attainments— including cessation— in two ways. (24)

"By skipping one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight [stages], there is the leap-over attainment (avaskandha-samāpatti), which is the cessationless and incomparable state. Thus, with reference to this very meaning, it is stated at length in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*: "Furthermore, Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome dharmas..."

One should not entertain doubt because of such statements as: "Having attained and abiding in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*) and born of seclusion (*vivekaja*), characterized by joy and bliss (*prītisukha*). As for the one who says:
"The eight stages [of dhyāna and formless attainments] are entered in two ways—either in close succession (*śliṣṭa*) or by skipping one (*ekalaṅghita*).
The leap-over attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*) proceeds to a third stage of a different nature."

How is it that there is such a "leaping" meditative attainment (*avaskandasamāpatti*) based on this statement? Indeed, what similarity could there be between a crow and milk-rice? This is an entirely different kind of undertaking. For, through the greatness of the cause—consisting of the attendance upon immeasurable Buddhas over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons by Bodhisattvas endowed with such skillful means (*upāyakauśala*)—there is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
There would be a state of distinct superiority; thus, there is no fault.
He says, "At whatever time, Subhūti," and so forth, to indicate that one should practice the observation of the path of cultivation preceded by the recollection of the Tathāgata.
"With the passing of the day" means even with the conclusion of the day, at the very least for the duration of a mere flash of lightning.

In order to illuminate the abundant and diverse benefits of practicing the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), he says: "And whoever, Subhūti, is one who perceives [objects] as real," and so forth. "Should bring forth the perfection of wisdom" means that one should generate the path of cultivation.
Furthermore, explaining the benefits by means of the distinction between the question regarding the destination and its answer, he says:
"For one who is attended by the Tathāgata," and so forth.
[The question is: "What is the destination?"
"What kind of commonality (sabhāgatā) is this, such that there is no other destination? It is, rather, the destination of perfect enlightenment (samyaksambodhi).
Subhūti, these too are qualities; these too are benefits.
By "qualities" are meant virtues such as the production of much merit, and by "benefits" are meant things such as being taken into the mindful care of the Tathāgata.
The twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Scattered Flowers," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Twenty-Ninth Chapter.

Having thus explained the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), [the author], introducing the subject by stating that the fourfold conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakavikalpa*)—which is to be abandoned therein—must now be discussed with a focus on establishing the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*) and their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), says:
"Furthermore," and so forth.
And therein, the first conceptualization of the apprehended object is ninefold due to the distinction of its objects.
To explain the meaning of this first conceptualization, it is said:
"The perfection of wisdom is to be followed in accordance with all dharmas."
For the sake of abandoning the conceptualization that summarizes all phenomena, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) should be practiced through non-attachment to all phenomena.
Thus, in the subsequent sections concerning conceptualization, it should be understood that the meaning of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the meaning of the path of cultivation.
He speaks next regarding the second conceptualization:
"Because all phenomena are undifferentiated" means that,
for the sake of abandoning the conceptualization of the manifoldness of phenomena, all phenomena are of a single nature because they are undifferentiated in the form of the *dharmadhātu*.
He speaks thus for the sake of the third conceptualization.
"Because all phenomena are non-arising" is said for the purpose of abandoning the conceptualization that lacks the support of the Tathāgata, since all phenomena are, in reality, unproduced.
Regarding the fourth conceptualization, he says:
"All phenomena are equal in being changeless."

For the sake of abandoning the conceptualization regarding the absence of qualities on the path of preparation, [it is said] because all phenomena are equal to the dharmadhātu in their lack of transformation.
Regarding the fifth conceptualization, he says:
"Because of the non-apprehension of selflessness in all phenomena, through the realization of wisdom."

For the sake of abandoning the conceptualization regarding the absence of qualities on the path of seeing, one realizes through wisdom that all phenomena are not of the nature of consciousness because they are of the nature of non-self.
Regarding the sixth conceptualization, he says:
"And all phenomena are expressed merely by name and merely as conventional designations."

In order to abandon the conceptualization that there is an absence of qualities on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), [the author] says "and conventional usage," and so forth, because all phenomena are conventionally expressed merely through internal and external discourse; however,
in the case of external discourse, there might be attachment to something.
He states the meaning of the seventh conceptualization:
"All phenomena are beyond conventional expression," and so forth.

For the purpose of abandoning the conceptualization regarding the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), [it is said that] because all phenomena are like an illusion, they cannot be expressed by means of the knowledge derived from hearing and reflection, nor by mundane or supramundane knowledge, respectively; therefore, they are "beyond conventional expression."
By way of being expressed, not expressed, and unexpressed.
He states the meaning of the eighth alternative:
"by the non-measurability of all phenomena."
For the sake of abandoning conceptualizations regarding the path of seeing, [it is taught] because all phenomena are immeasurable by way of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"Because form is immeasurable," and so forth.
He states the meaning of the ninth conceptualization as follows: "the signlessness of all phenomena.
This is for the purpose of abandoning conceptualizations regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because all phenomena are signless due to their emptiness.

This is what is meant: [the absence of qualities] in the summary of the Dharma for the sake of favoring beings who delight in brevity; in the expansion of the Dharma out of compassion for beings who delight in detail; in the lack of the qualities of the path of preparation due to the non-performance of the prescribed meanings and the lack of being embraced by the Buddha's assistance;

in the lack of the qualities of the path of seeing due to the deficiency of their correct arising; in the lack of the qualities of the path of cultivation due to the non-existence of future [moments]; and in the path of preparation for Nirvana due to its peacefulness and so forth, and due to the realization of emptiness.

The first type of conceptualization regarding the object of apprehension (*grāhyavikalpa*), which has as its basis the side of engagement (*pravṛttipakṣa*), consists of nine varieties that must be abandoned by Bodhisattvas during the stage of application (*prayogāvasthā*) on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). These are explained by way of negation (*vyatirekamukha*) through the presentation of their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*). They are as follows: [the thought] "I must act such that, on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is the realization of the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), and on the path of cultivation, there is activity characterized by being like an illusion (*māyopama*).
Thus it is said:

Regarding the concise and the detailed, regarding being assisted by the Buddhas or not being so assisted, and regarding the absence of qualities in the three times— on these three paths to the supreme good.
"This first conceptualization of the apprehended object has the aspect of the preparatory application as its sphere of activity.
Having thus indicated the first [conceptualization], it must now be stated that the second conceptualization of the apprehended object is of nine types.
He states the meaning of the first conceptual alternative:
"by means of the penetration of all phenomena.
This is for the purpose of dispelling the conceptualization regarding the non-arising of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), because one realizes all phenomena in the form of the *dharmadhātu*.
He states the meaning of the second alternative:
"Because of the natural purity of all phenomena.

This is for the purpose of dispelling the conceptualization that does not attend to the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), since one has thoroughly understood the intrinsic purity of the nature of all phenomena.
He states the meaning of the third alternative:
"because all phenomena are inexpressible.
This is for the purpose of dispelling the conceptualization of mental engagement with the Śrāvaka vehicle, because all phenomena transcend the path of speech.
He states the meaning of the fourth alternative:
"by the equality of abandonment, due to the non-ceasing of all phenomena.

This is for the purpose of dispelling the conceptualization of mental engagement with the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas; because all phenomena do not cease due to the absence of their arising, there is an equality of abandonment.
He states the meaning of the fifth alternative:
"Because all phenomena have attained nirvāṇa.
This is for the purpose of removing the conceptualization that consists in non-attention toward perfect enlightenment, because through the equality of suchness, all phenomena have realized nirvāṇa.
He states the meaning of the sixth alternative,
beginning with "all phenomena" (*sarvadharmāḥ*), etc.

For the purpose of removing conceptualization regarding meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāvikalpa*), [it is said that] because of the non-existence [of things] in the past and future time-periods, they respectively do not come and do not go.
Therefore, being ignorant [of this], phenomena do not arise in the present, because they are absolutely non-arisen like the *dharmadhātu*.
He states the meaning of the seventh conceptualization:
"due to the non-perception of self and other."
For the purpose of removing the conceptualization of non-existence, because neither self nor other is perceived,
he speaks for the sake of the eighth conceptualization,
beginning with "all phenomena," and so forth.

The noble ones are Arhats because they are worthy of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), since they have eliminated the conceptual constructions of both cultivation and non-cultivation, and because defects such as arising do not exist for them; this is because their intrinsic nature is pure by virtue of being like an illusion.
To explain the meaning of the ninth [verse], he says:
"those who have laid down the burden."

This is for the purpose of removing conceptual constructions that do not correspond to reality, because one is "one who has laid down the burden" due to the absence of the weight of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations.
This is what is meant:

when the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) does not arise due to a deficiency in spiritual friends and so forth; when there is no mental attention toward the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) due to a lack of merit from having the sublime Buddhas as one's object; when there is mental attention toward the vehicle of the Śrāvakas due to belonging to the Śrāvaka lineage; and when the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas is brought to face [the mind] due to belonging to the Pratyekabuddha lineage.

Due to the lack of practice in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), when one does not attend to perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) because it involves apprehension (*sopalambha*), or when one practices non-apprehension (*nirupalambha*) because it involves non-apprehension; and due to the state of neither-apprehension-nor-non-apprehension, where there is no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) nor non-cultivation (*abhāvanā*) because of the absence of apprehension, and where there is falsity due to inverted adherence through the attachment to existence and so forth—[the thought] "I must effect a cessation [of this]" constitutes the second type of conceptualization of the object (*grāhyavikalpa*), which has nine aspects based on the side of cessation (*nivṛttipakṣa*).

On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), during the state in which the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) function, that which is to be abandoned by Bodhisattvas has been explained by way of negation (*vyatirekamukha*) through the presentation of the states of their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
Thus it has been said:
"The second is considered the sphere of activity for the functioning of the mind and mental factors. (27)
The non-arising of the mind is the lack of mental engagement with the seat of enlightenment;
it is the mental engagement with the Lesser Vehicle and the lack of mental engagement with perfect awakening. ||28||
"In cultivation and non-cultivation, and indeed in their opposites,
as well as that which is unreal— such is the conceptualization to be known on the path of cultivation.

(29) Having thus indicated the second type of conceptualization regarding the object (*grāhya-vikalpa*), it must now be stated that the first type of conceptualization regarding the subject (*grāhaka-vikalpa*) is of nine kinds.
He states the meaning of the first alternative:
"Because all phenomena are neither localized nor non-localized.

This is for the purpose of dispelling the conceptualization that designates sentient beings; for, because all phenomena by their very nature have the *dharmadhātu* as their intrinsic essence, they are devoid of any distinction between general or specific locations.
Clarifying that very point, he raises the question "For what reason?
and says: "For form," and so forth;
[the phrase] "by way of its natural essence" means...
Because its intrinsic nature is emptiness, it has a self-nature that is distinct from both the general and the particular, as well as from location.
To explain the meaning of the second conceptualization, he says:
"because it gladdens through the cessation of all phenomena."

This is for the purpose of dispelling the conceptualization of the designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*); because one experiences joy through the cessation of all phenomena, which is the womb of immeasurable qualities such as emptiness, compassion, and so forth.
Regarding the third conceptualization, he says:
"by means of non-disgust and non-cessation."
In order to eliminate the conceptualization of non-emptiness, because one is free from both attachment and non-attachment toward all phenomena by virtue of their being like an illusion;
he speaks regarding the fourth conceptualization as follows:
"by way of being neither attached nor detached."
In order to eliminate the conceptualization of attachment, [it is taught that] because all phenomena are by nature the *dharmadhātu*, they are secluded from both passion and the absence of passion.
To explain this very point, anticipating the question "For what reason?", it says:
"Form, indeed," and so forth.
Regarding the term "by way of reality" (*satattvena*): the word *satattva* should be understood as a synonym for *tattva* (reality).
He states the meaning of the fifth alternative:

"Because of being pure by nature" means that all phenomena are pure because they are unarisen by their very essence (*svabhāva*); this is for the purpose of eliminating the conceptualization that discriminates among all phenomena. He speaks thus for the sake of the sixth conceptualization.
"All phenomena," and so forth.

In order to eliminate conceptualization regarding the designation of entities, [it is said that] all phenomena are like an illusion; because they are free from attachment and non-attachment, they are characterized by non-attachment.
He speaks thus for the sake of the seven types of conceptualization.
"Enlightenment," and so forth.
This is for the purpose of eliminating the conceptualization of departure via the three vehicles. Since no phenomenon exists that is separate from the dharmadhātu.
Thus, because all phenomena have awakening as their intrinsic nature through the realization of the Buddha’s gnosis,
he states the meaning of the eighth conceptualization:
"All phenomena are empty and signless," and so forth.
This is for the purpose of dispelling the conceptualization regarding the impurity of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Since all phenomena have the nature of the three doors of liberation,
he speaks [the following] for the sake of the ninth conceptualization.
"All phenomena are medicine," and so forth.
This is for the purpose of eliminating the conceptualization that disturbs [proper] conduct.
Because all phenomena possess the nature of medicine through the pacification of faults such as hatred by means of the essential nature of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
