This has been stated as follows: because the designation of existence is untenable due to the impossibility of a substantial entity; because all designations of phenomena are mere appearances; because of the universal nature of the emptiness of all phenomena such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); because of the abandonment of attachment in every respect regarding the clinging to phenomena through the realization of their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); because of the failure to provide a formal instruction on the investigation of phenomena; because of the failure to provide a formal instruction on the subject matter itself; because of the perception of form and so forth in the departure via the three vehicles; and because of the incorrect practice regarding the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*).

Regarding purity, through the practice of apprehending [the reality of] giving and so forth, and regarding the disruption of the conduct, the self is indeed a substantially existent grasper; thus, the first type of conceptualization of a grasper, which has a substantially existent person as its basis, consists of nine varieties.

This is to be abandoned by Bodhisattvas during the stage of application on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and it is stated by way of negation (*vyatireka*) through the presentation of its antidote.
And so it has been said:
The first type of grasper should be known as that which has the conceptual designation of a sentient being as its object;
it consists of the investigation of attachment to the non-emptiness of the conceptual designation of phenomena. ||30||

And it is proclaimed [as an offense] regarding the performance of material things, regarding the three vehicles, regarding the impurity of ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), or regarding the violation of the conduct (*caryā*).

(31) Having thus indicated the first conceptualization of the subject (*grāhakavikalpa*), the second conceptualization of the subject must be stated in its nine forms; therefore, he speaks for the sake of the first conceptualization:
"All phenomena abide in loving-kindness," and so forth.

This is for the purpose of removing the deluded conceptualizations that constitute an obscuration to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), because all phenomena have the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) as their intrinsic nature.
He speaks next for the sake of the second conceptualization.
"All phenomena have become Brahman," and so forth.

For the purpose of removing the conceptualization of delusion regarding the obscurations to the knowledge of the path, he speaks for the sake of the third conceptualization— namely, that all phenomena are of the nature of nirvāṇa because they do not produce [anything], since no faults serve as their cause—
beginning with "of all phenomena," and so forth.
For the purpose of removing the conceptual constructions of delusion regarding the obscuration to omniscience— by virtue of all phenomena being free from longing and aversion—
he speaks of the fourth conceptual construction as "being boundless like the ocean."

In order to remove the conceptualizations that cause confusion regarding the path of universal peace, [the Buddha] speaks of the fifth conceptualization— due to the ocean-like nature of all phenomena as the cause for the jewels of qualities such as the ten powers— and because of its being limitless like the ocean, he says:
"by way of being limitless like space."

In order to remove the deluded conceptualization regarding the union and separation of the Tathāgatas and so forth, [it is said that] because all phenomena are empty and equal to space, they are as limitless as space.
Regarding the meaning of the sixth conceptualization, he says:
"by the variegated nature of Mount Meru."

In order to remove the conceptual construction of delusion regarding inequality— because it is equal to Mount Meru by virtue of being unshakable by the occurrence of all undesirable events, and because it is the variegated foundation of all phenomena— he speaks for the sake of the seventh conceptual construction:
"By way of the boundlessness of form":

this is for the purpose of removing the conceptualizations of delusion regarding suffering and so forth, because wisdom and the other [perfections] are themselves the nature of the *dharmadhātu* due to their boundlessness.
He speaks next for the sake of the eighth conceptualization:
"Like the rays of the sun," and so forth.

For the purpose of removing the conceptual constructions of delusion regarding the nature of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said that "by the infinity of all sounds," referring to the meaning of the ninth conceptual construction; this is because all phenomena are equal to the emergence of the rays from the solar disc due to their intrinsic luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaratva*), and thus they possess an infinite radiance like the solar disc.

For the purpose of removing the conceptualization of non-dual delusion, one should follow the perfection of wisdom through the infinity of all sounds, because all phenomena are equal in their nature as mere names and thus possess the infinity of all sounds.
This is what has been said.

Through the lack of thorough knowledge of all aspects, there is the delusion regarding the obscuration to the knowledge of all aspects; through the lack of thorough knowledge of all paths, there is the delusion regarding the obscuration to the knowledge of paths; through the lack of thorough knowledge of all things, there is the delusion regarding the obscuration to omniscience; through the lack of thorough knowledge [of the nature of] thorough knowledge, there is the delusion regarding all peaceful paths; through the lack of thorough knowledge of suchness and the objects of knowledge such as form and so forth, there is the delusion regarding the conjunction and disjunction of suchness and so forth; through the lack of thorough knowledge of the true nature of Māra and others, there is the delusion regarding inequality; and through grasping at the meaning according to the literal expression...

Regarding the delusion concerning the truths such as suffering, the delusion concerning the activity of the afflictions through the lack of thorough knowledge of their nature—such as attachment—and the delusion concerning non-duality through the lack of thorough knowledge of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper: the second type of conceptualization of a grasper, which has as its object the cause appearing as the designation of a sentient being and its establishment, is the grasper of a self that exists only as a designation (*prajñaptisat*). This conceptualization, which is based on a person existing as a designation, consists of nine types that must be abandoned by Bodhisattvas during the stage of the activity of the mind and mental factors on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). It is explained here by way of negation (*vyatirekamukha*) through the presentation of their respective antidotes.
And so it has been said:
"Furthermore, there are nine other objects concerning the designation of sentient beings and their causes;
these are connected to the path of cultivation, as they constitute the adverse factors to be overcome by that [path]. (32)

Regarding the three types of omniscience, there is [the obstruction] corresponding to each of their respective threefold obscurations, as well as [the obstruction] regarding the association with and dissociation from the path to peace, suchness, and so forth. ||33||
"In inequality, in suffering and so forth, in the nature of the afflictions,
and in the delusion regarding the absence of duality— the last conceptualization is considered [the final one].

(34) Having thus explained the adverse factors along with their antidotes within the path of cultivation as described, he says that through the very realization of that, all perfections of qualities arise due to the abandonment of the four conceptualizations.

"By the boundlessness of the attainment of all Buddha-qualities. This means that through the practice of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), when these four types of conceptualizations—which act as afflictions—have been exhausted and obstructed, one attains a state of joy and relief. Consequently, all the perfections of qualities (*guṇasampad*) comprised within the three vehicles become capable of producing every form of happiness for the world, due to their dependence upon compassion. Thus, by way of proceeding toward the goal in every respect, they attain a splendor through the fruits of the ultimate realization.

Just as rivers flow into the great ocean, all beings take refuge in the Bodhisattva who stands upon the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Thus, because the realization of all Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) is limitless and because its intrinsic nature consists of great benefits (*mahānuśamsā*), the path of cultivation is to be understood in this way.
And so it has been said:

When these [three] afflictions have been exhausted, the perfections of virtue—which bring about the happiness of the world in all its aspects—will, as if having sighed deeply for a long time, finally emerge. (35)
"All [virtues] resort, with a total mobilization, to that Great Being who possesses the fruit of his desire, just as rivers flow toward the great ocean.

Thus, immediately after the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*); therefore, he speaks for the sake of the "uninterrupted concentration" (*ānantaryasamādhi*).
"Of all the realms of sentient beings," and so forth.

This means that having established all the sentient beings within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system upon the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and upon the Bodhisattva's entry into the fixed course (*nyāma*), whatever merit (*puṇya*) flows forth—taking that as the point of comparison—the state of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is Buddhahood, is defined by a vastness of merit even more distinguished than that. That concentration (*samādhi*) which is the immediate predecessor, occurring directly before the attainment of Buddhahood, is [the "Cloud of Dharma"].

The "uninterrupted samādhi" (trānantarya-samādhi) is that by which the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to be cultivated as something infinite, being superior to the accumulations of merit and knowledge of all the realms of sentient beings.
And so it has been said:
[It is superior] to the three-thousandfold world-system of people [attaining] the perfection of the realization of the Disciples and the Pratyekabuddhas.
And having established them in the Bodhisattva's stage of certainty, they are like the impure. ||37||
"By means of the abundance of merit, immediately after the attainment of Buddhahood, there is the 'uninterrupted samādhi' (ānantarya-samādhi), and that is omniscience (sarvākārajñatā).

Thus, for this uninterrupted samādhi, the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is the non-existence of all phenomena; the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is mindfulness (smaraṇa); and the aspect (ākāra) is primordial peace (prakṛti-śāntatā).
It should be understood as being implied by the sense,
for otherwise it would be impossible to attain the concentration of immediate succession (*ānantarya-samādhi*).
And so it has been said:
Its object is non-existence, and mindfulness is considered its dominant influence;
here, the aspect is peacefulness.

And in this matter, because it is difficult to fathom, the succession of various challenges and divergent views of proponents who do not understand skillful means (*upāyakauśala*) spreads forth; therefore, these must now be refuted.
To address the first divergence of opinion, he says:
"By way of the boundlessness of the earth element."

The meaning is that, in order to dispel misconceptions regarding the possibility of an object of focus (*ālambana*) due to the non-existence of both the conditioned and unconditioned realms, one should realize the "uninterrupted samādhi" (*ānantarya-samādhi*) by way of its being like an illusion; for, because all qualities are established therein, it is equal to the earth, and since all phenomena possess the nature of an object of focus by way of conventional reality, it is as boundless as the earth element.

In the same way, even further on, the "uninterrupted meditative concentration" (*ānantarya-samādhi*)— the meaning of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)— is to be understood in this context. Because it is in every respect devoid of form (*nirūpa*), in order to refute the second misconception regarding the grasping of the intrinsic nature of the object of focus (*ālambana-svabhāva*), [the Buddha] establishes the intrinsic nature of the object of focus exactly as it is through the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-asamatva*) due to their primordial purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhatva*), and by virtue of the limitlessness of the element of water (*abdhatu-aparyantatā*).

Through the non-apprehension of existence and non-existence, with the desire to dispel the third misconception regarding the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), [the text explains that] because all phenomena are naturally luminous, they are equal to fire; because they consist of the nature of the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects as before, they extend to the limit of the meaning of the fire element; and because they have suchness as their intrinsic nature, the fourth misconception regarding the two truths—conventional and ultimate—is refuted by showing that, conventionally, all phenomena are equal to wind due to their lack of fixed abiding.

In order to refute the fifth misconception regarding the practice through the non-apprehension of giving and so forth, and because all phenomena are equal to space due to their being merely nominal designations, one determines the nature of the practice as before; and because there is no [separate] awakening to be attained due to the boundlessness of the element of space,

with the desire to eliminate the sixth misconception regarding the Jewel of the Buddha, he says that because all phenomena are of the nature of representation-only and thus equal to consciousness, they are likewise of the nature of the Tathāgata, and therefore the Perfection of Wisdom is to be followed by way of the boundlessness of the element of consciousness.
Thus [it is said] regarding the water element, the fire element, and so forth.
For the sake of addressing the seventh misconception, he says:
"wholesome, unwholesome," and so forth.

Because it is a mere name, in order to refute misconceptions regarding the Jewel of the Dharma, [it is shown that] since all phenomena are in reality unproduced and free from any accumulation of wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, they possess the nature of dharma as established conventionally; thus, by virtue of the immeasurability of the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas,
he speaks for the sake of refuting the eighth misconception.
"Of all phenomena," and so forth.

In order to refute misconceptions regarding the Jewel of the Saṅgha—by negating [the perception of] objects such as form and so on—it is because all phenomena, being like an illusion, are devoid of any accumulation of phenomena; thus, as before, they possess the nature of the Saṅgha by virtue of the immeasurability of the accumulation of all phenomena.
He speaks for the sake of removing the ninth misconception, beginning with "the samādhi of all phenomena" and so forth.

This is intended to eliminate the misconception regarding skill in means (*upāyakauśala*) that arises from perceiving generosity and the other perfections as objective entities; for, since all phenomena have the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, there exists skill in means in exactly that same way through the equality of the boundlessness of the samādhi of all phenomena.
Because of the attainment of the boundlessness of the samādhis of all dharmas,
he speaks [the following] for the sake of dispelling the tenth misconception,
beginning with "all Buddhas," and so forth.

In order to eliminate misconceptions regarding the realization of the Tathāgata by negating the apprehension of existence, non-existence, or both, [the author] states that because all phenomena have the nature of the Buddha-dharmas in the form of suchness (*tathatā*), they abide as the realization of the Tathāgata through the conventional reality of yogins;
thus, because all Buddha-dharmas are limitless,
he speaks for the sake of [correcting] the eleven types of misconception.

Regarding the phrase "by way of the boundlessness of all phenomena": because all phenomena, in their nature as *dharmatā*, consist of a boundless *dharmatā*—and thus cannot be established as being permanent and so forth through the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) that posits permanence and its opposites—it has been established, as before, for the sake of refuting misconceptions regarding the inversion of permanence and so forth. Since such inversions exist, he speaks of the "boundlessness of all phenomena" in order to address the twelve types of misconception.

Regarding "by way of the limitlessness of emptiness": in order to refute misconceptions regarding the path—arising from not realizing the fruit of the path already cultivated—it is said that because all phenomena have emptiness as their ultimate nature by virtue of being like an illusion, there is no realization [of them] as existing entities; thus, he speaks for the sake of the two misconceptions, the thirteenth and fourteenth.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the infinity of mind and mental factors":

in order to eliminate misconceptions concerning both the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*), because there is neither abandonment nor acquisition [of them], he speaks for the sake of the fifteen misconceptions by way of the infinity of mind and mental factors; this is because, conventionally, all phenomena are established as having the nature of adverse factors and remedies through the infinity of mind and mental factors, which are appearances arisen from ignorance.

"By way of the infinity of mental conduct (*cittacaritāparyantatā*). This is because, since there is no [independent] entity (*dharmī*), one wishes to eliminate misconceptions regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmanimitta*); because entities exist merely as dependent upon appearance; because all phenomena have the arising of mental conduct as their characteristic; and because they likewise exist with suchness as their characteristic. Thus, it is "by way of the infinity of mental conduct."
He speaks for the sake of refuting the sixteenth misconception:
"by way of the immeasurability of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.

This is for the purpose of removing misconceptions regarding cultivation—both in terms of the impossibility of specific and general characteristics and regarding the process of cultivation itself—because all dharmas have the nature of the non-apprehension of the wholesome and unwholesome by way of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and because, as before, cultivation exists through the immeasurability of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.

The limit [of the number] is to be understood through the distinction of their objects; for although the disagreements (*vipratipatti*) are infinite in their variety, they are stated as exactly sixteen because of the desire to dispel the disagreements of the disciples present [to the author]. These sixteen disagreements, which are mutually contradictory and take the form of doubt due to the inconsistency of the application of the meanings of the teachings, have as their basis the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), by virtue of having the aforementioned objects.

It should be understood that by bodhisattvas who desire what is wholesome, the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*) is attained after they have, as far as possible, refuted all those who propound views based on the discourse of people regarding the skillful means (*upāyakauśala*) of bodhisattvas— by means of skillful means relying on both truths— and have thereby produced a correct and complete certainty. And so it has been said:
Of those who propound endless chatter and idle talk. ||39||

In the occurrence of the objective support, in the determination of its intrinsic nature, in the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects, and in the ultimate truth together with the conventional; ||40||
In the application [of practice], in the three Jewels, in the means together with the occasion of the Sage, in error and the true path, and in the antidote and the discordant factor. ||41||
Regarding the characteristics and the cultivation [of the path], there are sixteen and ten disagreements among the proponents concerning the basis of the knowledge of all aspects. (42)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on the Samādhi of the Summit Realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*).

Having attained the summit realization, one brings the objects realized—both individually and collectively—in sequential order and contemplates them for the sake of stabilization; thus, for the purpose of the sequential realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*), it says:
"by way of roaring the lion’s roar."

This has been stated as follows: by means of the complete fulfillment of all aspects of the six perfections, such as giving, which are manifested through the purity of the three spheres; because the four [remaining] perfections are included within the perfection of wisdom;

and by means of the recollection of the Buddha in its three forms—which, characterized ultimately by non-recollection, sequentially illuminates the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—through the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) that bring about the perfect accomplishment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); likewise, by means of the recollection of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral phenomena.

As before, through the recollection of the noble community of irreversible bodhisattvas, and likewise through the recollection of the deities of ethical discipline and renunciation, and by awakening to the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena such as form, that realization is the gradual practice. Because it teaches the non-perverted meaning in this way, it is equal to the lion’s roar; thus, by roaring the lion’s roar regarding all phenomena, there is the gradual clear realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*).
It should be understood in this way;
and so it has been said:
"By means of generosity, wisdom, and so forth, up to the recollections of the Buddha and the rest, that [perfection] is attained."
The sequential practice is considered to be by way of the intrinsic nature of the non-existence of phenomena. ||1||
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the successive order.

For one who has cultivated the clear realization of the successive order, in order to make that very [realization] thoroughly familiar, there is the attainment of those same [stages] in a single moment; thus, for the sake of the "clear realization in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), he says:
"by way of the immovability of all phenomena."

The meaning of the individual components is as follows: because it is impossible to alter the realization of enlightenment in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), it is unshakable; and since form and all other phenomena are unshakable, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is to be understood through that unshakability.
The collective meaning is indicated by the statement:
"By way of its characteristics, the realization of enlightenment in a single moment is fourfold."
First of all, one entity is the intrinsic nature of all entities, and all entities have the intrinsic nature of one.
According to the principle that "one who has seen one entity in its true reality has seen all entities in their true reality," it is not only that many [entities] are subsumed within one;

rather, by means of the knowledge of giving and so forth in a single moment—which takes as its object [the truth] and is free from the error of grasping at specific, determinate things—there is a subsumption of the dharmas characterized by the eighty minor marks and the [thirty-two] major marks, such as the untainted giving and so forth.

Due to the awakening of the Bodhisattva, there occurs the first momentary perfect enlightenment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), characterized by all phenomena being non-maturation and untainted (*anāsrava*) in a single moment.
And so it has been said:
"Because of the inclusion of all untainted phenomena within even each single one [of them]."
"This awakening in a single moment by the Sage through giving and so forth is to be known.
If it is asked: "How is it that, when taking a single uncontaminated cognition as its object, there is a comprehension of all uncontaminated phenomena?"
It is said: Just as even a single step taken by a person, when propelled by that person, moves an entire waterwheel all at once due to the power of the prior craftsmanship of a skilled artisan,

so too, through the power of the *dharmadhātu* impelled by previous vows, a single moment of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), when being focused upon, brings forth all things of its own kind toward itself by the force of the relationship between cause and effect.
And so it has been said:
"Just as even a single bucket of a water-wheel, when pulled by a man, causes the whole wheel to move at once, so too does knowledge [cause all things to be known] in a single moment. (2)

Thereafter, when— through the cultivation of the antidotes and the removal of all adverse factors— the state of the ripening of the entire class of purifying phenomena arises for the Bodhisattva, possessing a white nature like the autumn moonlight due to the departure of all stains, then, because of the awakening to all uncontaminated phenomena that have reached the state of ripening in a single moment,
knowledge is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); such is the nature of the ripening of phenomena.

The second [type of] awakening in a single moment (ekakṣaṇābhisambodha) is characterized by all uncontaminated phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) in a single moment within the state of the path of cultivation;
and so it has been said:
"When the state of the nature of maturation consists entirely of purity, then the Perfection of Wisdom is known as knowledge in a single moment. (3) Thus,

having experienced the two accumulations through the practice of all phenomena as being like a dream in their proper sequence, one abides in the state of realization within all phenomena— such as the aggregates of appropriation— which have the nature of a dream, by means of the practice of the six perfections beginning with generosity.
"All phenomena are without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*) by way of being defined as having the nature of generosity and so forth.

Thus, one knows that phenomena consisting of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) are without characteristics in a single moment; in this way, there is the third "awakening in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), characterized by the single-moment realization that all phenomena are without characteristics.
And so it has been said:
"Abiding in phenomena that are like a dream through the practice of giving and so forth,
one realizes the signlessness of all phenomena in a single instant.

(4) Thus, subsequently, when a bodhisattva— having uprooted the latent tendencies for the appearance of duality through the internalization of the practice of abandoning the appearance of duality over a continuous and long period of time— is [awakened] from sleep by means of the subject-object relationship...

At that time, one does not perceive the object of apprehension nor the subject who perceives it, as in the case of one seeing a dream. Thus, one perceives in a single moment the non-dual reality of all phenomena—that all phenomena are indeed phenomena. In this way, the fourth type of awakening in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*) consists of the characteristic of all phenomena as non-dual and characterized by a single moment.
And so it has been said:
One does not perceive the dream and the seer of that dream through the conjunction of duality;
rather, one perceives the non-dual reality of all phenomena in a single moment.

Thus, with respect to the awakening in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), there is a sequence according to the distinction between cause and fruit, consisting of the states of the non-maturation and the maturation of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Having thus explained the two types of momentary realization of all phenomena as being without outflows (*anāsrava*), and having established the third—momentary realization of all phenomena as being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*)—on the grounds that there is no differentiation because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is of a single flavor in this state of distinguished attainment, and for the purpose of understanding that all phenomena have the nature of a dream; furthermore, since subject and object are not perceived in reality even in the state of dreaming, the realization of all phenomena as being non-dual in a single moment was taught for the purpose of realizing non-duality. Thus, by way of these characteristics, momentary realization is of four kinds.
Some maintain that [the ultimate] is to be realized by yogis in all four ways.

Others, however, think that although it is presented in four ways due to differences in exclusion (vyāvṛtti) according to the needs of the disciples present, nevertheless, a yogi must directly realize only one or another single way.
The seventh chapter: The Culmination in a Single Instant.
Why is it said that the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of the ocean?
Anticipating the question "For what reason?", he says:
"For form, Subhūti, is like the ocean," and so forth.

The specific similarity by which form and the other aggregates are equal to the ocean and the rest has already been explained in the commentary on the phrases "as limitless as the ocean" and so on, and thus it is not stated again here.
Summing this up, he says: "For thus, Subhūti," and so forth.
For one who has realized the single-moment perfect awakening (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), there is the realization of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāyābhisambodha*) in the second moment.
To that end, he says: "When, Subhūti, this bodhisattva," and so forth.

When, by means of mental attentions free from all illusion, according to the sequence already described, [he realizes] this perfection of wisdom as the illusory nature of all phenomena through the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

He will follow through with the knowledge of the path; he will investigate through the knowledge of all things; he will enter through the complete awakening to all aspects; he will reflect upon it through the summit realization; he will weigh it through the gradual realization; he will examine it through the momentary realization;
and he will cultivate it through the complete awakening to the Dharma-body.

Then, for this Bodhisattva, it is not difficult to attain the fulfillment of all qualities whose nature is the *dharmakāya*, the characteristics of the *sāmbhogikakāya* of the Buddha-field, and the unsurpassed Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) which consist in the nature of the *nirmāṇakāya* together with its activities; such is the meaning of the individual parts.
The collective meaning is now indicated.
And that realization of the *dharmakāya* is fourfold, distinguished as the *svābhāvikakāya* and so forth. Among these,

the first is the nature (*prakṛti*) or essence (*svabhāva*) of those factors— such as the applications of mindfulness— which consist of gnosis, are supramundane, and, by virtue of being the *dharmadhātu*, have attained a purity in every respect characterized by natural isolation, because they are untainted and stainless due to the adventitious nature [of defilements].

This body of the Sage, the Blessed Buddha, which is of the nature of non-arising, is attained through the supramundane path and is not produced; thus, in the sense of being uncontrived, it is the *svābhāvikakāya* (essential body), realized through the practice of all phenomena as illusion-like consciousness. The remaining three bodies, appearing through conventional truth (*tathyasaṃvṛti*), are in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the nature of *dharmatā*, manifested according to the various inclinations (*adhimukti*) of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and others.
This is stated for the purpose of establishing [the point];
for according to the principle that "since discernment is held to be non-different from that which is discerned," it follows that [discernment] is not distinct from that.
It should be understood that even these are established as distinct.
And so it has been said:
"Those untainted phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects..."
"The body of the Sage is the intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika*), characterized by their primordial nature.

Following this, there are the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) up to the noble eightfold path, as before; the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*);
and the two [formless attainments]: "possessing form internally, one perceives forms externally" and "being formless internally, one perceives forms externally."
Having personally realized with the body the beautiful liberation and attained it, one dwells therein—this is the first.

The four [formless attainments]—the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception—and the cessation of perception and feeling—this is the eighth. Thus, there are eight liberations.

The nine attainments (*samāpatti*) consist of the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
The tenfold totality (*kṛtsna*) consists of earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, white, consciousness, and space.

There are four [masteries] (*abhibhvāyatana*): one who possesses internal perception of form or no perception of form looks upon external forms, perceiving them as small or large, and knowing them by mastering them.

The fourfold [base] consisting of perceiving internal form while not being overcome by blue, yellow, red, or white—this constitutes the eightfold *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery). Because it uproots the continuity of the conflict of afflictions existing within the mental streams of others, it is called *araṇā* (the absence of conflict). *Praṇidhijñāna* (knowledge resulting from resolve) proceeds uninterruptedly throughout *saṃsāra*, even during states of non-concentration, because it successfully fulfills its vow to remove doubt and because all attachment to signs and obstacles has been correctly eliminated. Furthermore, there are the six *abhijñās* (superknowledges), the four previously mentioned *pratisaṃvids* (analytical knowledges), and the purities of basis, object, mind, and knowledge.
There are four purities.

There are ten masteries (*vaśitā*): mastery over life, mastery over the equipment of the mind, mastery over karma, mastery over rebirth, mastery over resolve, mastery over aspiration, mastery over consciousness, and mastery over dharmas.
There are ten powers (*bala*) and four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), which were explained previously.

The Tathāgata’s conduct of body, speech, and mind is completely pure; he possesses no perverse conduct that he would feel compelled to conceal out of fear of being discovered by others. Thus, his non-protection is threefold. Regarding those who wish to hear the Dharma, those who do not wish to hear it, and those who are both, he remains respectively free from attachment, aversion, and both, maintaining equanimity. He dwells mindful; this "application of mindfulness" is threefold, characterized by the non-transgression of the proper time for acting for the benefit of sentient beings. This is his nature of non-forgetfulness.

Through the abandonment of the seeds of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*), as well as the removal of their habitual impressions (*vāsanā*), there arises a great compassion characterized by the intention to benefit all beings toward all people;
furthermore, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),
as well as the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and so forth.

Some maintain that all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and so forth, which were previously mentioned, undergo a transformation through the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); being of the nature of non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañcajñāna*), they are designated as the second body, the *dharmakāya*.
And so it has been said:
The factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the liberations in their proper sequence, the ninefold meditative attainment, and the tenfold totality. (2)
The bases of mastery are of eight kinds according to their divisions;
[then there are] absence of strife, knowledge resulting from prayer, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges. ||3||
The omniformity [of knowledge], the four purities, the ten masteries, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the state of having nothing to guard; ||4||
The threefold application of mindfulness, the threefold nature of non-forgetfulness, the total eradication of latent predispositions, and great compassion for living beings. (5)
The eighteen unique qualities belonging exclusively to the Sage,
as well as omniscience— this is the Dharma-body.
...is thus designated.
||6|| Others, however, [say]:
"Those untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects..."

"The essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) of the Sage has their intrinsic nature as its characteristic. Having thus explained that by accepting the supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena according to the literal sense, the essential body is that which has the intrinsic nature of those [phenomena]— namely, non-arising— and that this very [body] is designated as the "dharma-nature body" (*dharmatā-kāya*) or "dharma-body" (*dharma-kāya*) through the elision of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

Anticipating the question, "What then are those untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena for which the Dharma-body is the natural characteristic (*prakṛtilakṣaṇa*)?", they introduce the verse beginning with "the factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*).

How are those non-dual mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) to be accepted as necessarily performing purposeful activity— such as teaching the Dharma— once they have been transformed through the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) by way of generating the appearance of distinguished objects for yogins according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*)?

Another [teacher] says they are "comprised" [within it]. If it is argued that, by the principle— "That which is dependent origination, that itself is emptiness"— the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), consisting of non-dual gnosis, is established precisely through the demonstration of the body whose nature is *dharmatā*, then, since the logic is the same, the two bodies— the Enjoyment-body (sāmbhogika) and the Emanation-body (nairmāṇika)— would also [be established].
If it has already been established [as being included], then a separate mention should not be made. Now,

if it is thought that the mention of it is due to its being recited in the scriptures and is thus a conventional designation for yogins, then by this same logic, it follows that the Dharmakāya— which consists of non-dual gnosis— should likewise be mentioned separately.
Some [explain] the four bodies:
the essential, that which is with enjoyment, the emanation,
and likewise another.
The Dharmakāya, together with its activity, is proclaimed to be fourfold.

Thus, because the term *dharmakāya* does not appear immediately after the term *svābhāvika* in this verse, [some maintain] that there are only three bodies (*kāyatraya*). Others, however, argue that—given the force of the purpose already demonstrated and for the sake of conforming to the structure of the verse while connecting it with the activity (*kāritra*) of gnosis itself—it was stated in this way; therefore, all four bodies mentioned in other passages remain entirely consistent.
One might ask: what is the distinction between the *araṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of non-conflict) of the Śrāvakas and others, and that of the Tathāgata?
The *araṇā-samādhi* of the Śrāvakas and others consists in the avoidance of causing the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*) in people through one's own sight.

For the Tathāgatas, however, there is the uprooting of the entire continuity of afflictions of all beings; thus, there is a specific meditative absorption (*araṇā-samādhi*) regarding villages and so forth.
And so it has been said:
"By the vision of the *araṇā* of a Śrāvaka, there is the avoidance of the afflictions of others."
Having cut off that stream of afflictions, the Jinas dwell in villages and other places without conflict. (7)

If it is asked, "What is the distinction between the knowledge resulting from the vows of the Śrāvakas and others and the knowledge resulting from the vows of the Tathāgata? it is said in reply: The knowledge resulting from the vows of the Tathāgata is held to be superior to the knowledge resulting from the vows of the Śrāvakas and others because it proceeds spontaneously by virtue of being signless (*nirnimitta*); because it is free from attachment to form and so forth due to non-adherence to objective entities; because it is unimpeded regarding all objects of knowledge through the abandonment of the afflictive obscurations and the obscurations to the knowable along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanakleśajñeyāvaraṇa*); because it remains as long as saṃsāra lasts; and because it always correctly possesses the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), thereby answering questions. Thus, the Tathāgata’s vow-knowledge is considered distinguished from that of the Śrāvakas and others.
And so it has been said:
"Effortless, unattached, unimpeded, and ever-present;
The Buddha's knowledge resulting from his vow is held to dispel all questions. (8)

Thus, because all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and so forth existing within the continuum of a Tathāgata possess a supreme distinction by virtue of having abandoned the two types of delusion—the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) together with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—these two aforementioned distinctions should be understood as being illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).
One might ask: "If the Dharmakāya, which consists of great compassion, remains eternally present, how is it that it does not always perform beneficial activity for all living beings?"

When the cause— consisting in the meeting with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and others— has reached full maturity by taking the Buddha and so forth as its object, and when the seed of previously planted roots of merit exists, then,

at whatever time for whichever sentient being the teaching of the Dharma and so forth is performed such that it becomes beneficial for their future, the Blessed One acts for their benefit through the fulfillment of his previous vows, performing purposeful activity in accordance with the appearance of that [being].
Although it is always present like a wish-fulfilling gem by virtue of its abiding as the Dharma-body whose nature is great compassion,
it does not appear to grant its fruit due to a deficiency in causes produced by the transgressions of one's own karma.
Therefore, just as even when the king of gods sends down rain, [the seeds do not sprout] because of putrefaction and so forth—
Just as a seed that has become a mere potentiality, such as sesame, does not manifest [as a sprout],

so too it should be understood that even upon the appearance of Buddhas— who are capable of fulfilling all desires— an unfortunate person does not obtain what is auspicious, such as hearing the true Dharma.
And so it has been said:
"When the cause has reached maturity, whenever and for whomever that which is beneficial ought to be done, he manifests himself before each such person. (9)
"For even when the rain-cloud pours down, a seed does not sprout;
likewise, even upon the appearance of Buddhas, one who lacks the fortune does not enjoy the auspicious.

Thus, according to the reasoning stated above, because there is an abundance of performing purposeful action through the gateway of manifestation in all cases, [the Blessed One is established as a valid means of knowledge].
Because the Blessed One lacks exhaustion both in terms of his continuity and his abiding throughout saṃsāra, he is respectively designated as "the Buddha" and "the imperishable, the eternal."

Therefore, one should not think: "How can the *dharmakāya*, which consists of gnosis, be said to be all-pervasive and eternal, when it resides within the continuum of specific yogis and arises at every moment?
For it has been said:
"Because of the vastness of its activity, the Buddha is described as all-pervasive."
And because of its inexhaustibility, that very [body] is also called "eternal.

Thus, following that, this third body of the Blessed Buddha— the Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*)— should be understood as having the nature of the Form Body (*rūpakāya*), its limbs adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, arising from the enjoyment of the joy and bliss of the supreme, irreproachable Mahāyāna Dharma in the company of great Bodhisattvas who have entered the ten stages.
And so it has been said:
"This body of the Sage, consisting of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, is considered the Enjoyment Body (sāmbhogika-kāya), because it enjoys the Mahāyāna. (12)
Furthermore, those thirty-two marks are as follows:
by means of following and rising to greet one's teachers and so forth, there arises the mark of having hands and feet marked with wheels. (1)
Because he has firmly undertaken the vows, his feet are well-placed like those of a tortoise.
From practicing the four means of attraction, like a royal swan, [he obtains] the quality of having fingers and toes joined by a web. (3)
Through excellent food, both hard and soft, and other such sustenance, there arises the quality of having soft and youthful hands and feet. (4)
Because his hands, feet, shoulders, and neck regions are elevated due to the giving of superior foods such as delicacies to be licked, he possesses the quality of having seven protuberances. || 5 ||
Because of his liberation of those condemned to death, he has long fingers.
Because he provides sustenance for living beings, his heels are long.
From abstaining from taking life comes the quality of having large and straight limbs. (8)
From the undertaking of wholesome dharmas comes the quality of having high-raised ankles.
Because he increases the wholesome practices he has undertaken, his body hairs grow upward. || 10 ||
From the gift of knowledge, arts, and so forth, performed with reverence, comes the quality of having shanks like those of the eneya antelope. (11)
Because he does not reject supplicants who come seeking wealth that is actually available, he possesses the mark of broad and shapely arms. (12)
Because he causes all people to undertake the holy life and protects the secret mantras, he possesses the characteristic of having the private organ concealed within a sheath. 13.
From the gift of excellent bedding, one obtains a golden complexion.
From the gift of a palace and its furnishings, one obtains smooth skin.
Because of his avoidance of social crowds and the like, he possesses body hairs that grow individually and curl to the right. || 16 ||
From seating all his elders in their proper places, he has a face marked by the *ūrṇā* (the circle of hair between the eyebrows). || 17 ||
Because he is in every way free from harsh speech and from discouragement, he has the upper body of a lion. 18.
Because of his pleasant speech, well-spoken words, and agreeable manner, he possesses well-restrained shoulders. (19)
Through the giving of medicine and so forth, there arises the state of having another mind as one's inner self.
From attending to the sick comes the quality of having a sense of taste that perceives the finest flavors. || 21 ||
The quality of having a body as well-proportioned as a banyan tree (*nyagrodha-parimaṇḍalatā*) results from encouraging others to establish groves, parks, and so forth.
Because of giving superior gifts such as monasteries and the like, he has a protuberance on his head (uṣṇīṣa). || 23 ||
From his speech being smooth and so forth, he possesses a broad tongue. (24)
The quality of possessing the voice of Brahmā arises from making the true Dharma known to all sentient beings in all world-systems.
(25) The quality of having a jaw like that of a lion arises from abstaining from frivolous speech. (26)
The whiteness of the teeth results from honoring all people and similar virtuous acts. || 27 ||
Because of his pure livelihood, he has even teeth. (28)
From the practice of truthful speech comes the quality of having teeth that are closely set. || 29 ||
From the non-habituation to slanderous speech comes the possession of forty even teeth.
From regarding all sentient beings as an only son, he possesses deep blue eyes. || 31 ||
And because of seeing the absence of hostility and so forth, there is the quality of having eyelashes like those of a cow. || 32 ||
And so it has been said:
"He whose hands bear the marks of wheels, whose feet are like those of a tortoise,
and whose fingers and toes are joined by a web."
His hands and feet are youthful and soft, and his body is supported by seven prominent protuberances. (13)
He has long fingers, broad heels, a full body, straight ankles, hair growing upward on his feet,
shanks like those of an antelope, and arms that reach his knees.
His secret organ is concealed within a sheath, like that of a supreme elephant. ||14||
He is golden-colored with delicate skin;
his body hairs grow singly, curling to the right;
his face is marked by a *ūrṇā*; and his torso is like that of a lion.
His shoulders were rounded, and the space between his shoulder blades was filled out. ||15||
His taste is inferior to the renowned supreme tastes;
his body is like a *nyagrodha* tree, equal to a circular mandala;
his head is crowned with a protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), and his tongue is broad and beautiful.
His voice was like that of Brahmā, his jaw was like a lion's, and his teeth were very white. ||16||
The teeth are equal in size, closely set, and complete in number, numbering four sets of ten.
With blue eyes and eyelashes like those of a bull—these indeed are the thirty-two marks. (17)

Whichever cause there may be here that establishes each respective characteristic, this [characteristic] is fulfilled by the complete attainment of that very cause; such is the characteristic of its full realization. (18)
Following after one's gurus and so forth, firmness regarding the vow of restraint, gathering [disciples], serving them, and the giving of excellent things. (19)

The undertaking of releasing those condemned to death, the increase of the wholesome, and so forth—such is the cause, as set forth in the sūtras, which establishes the [thirty-two] marks. (20) Thus, there are eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). Furthermore, they are as follows: because of being secluded from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), he has copper-colored nails (1).
Because of the resolute intention for the welfare of all sentient beings, his nails are glossy.
The high-arched nails result from being born into a noble lineage. (3)
The roundness of the fingers is due to their being faultless in their conduct.
The fingers are well-rounded due to having accumulated roots of merit. (5)
The fingers are tapered because they proceed in a perfectly regular sequence.
The state of having hidden veins results from the well-concealed nature of his physical actions, livelihood, and means of subsistence.
By virtue of severing the knots of the afflictions, there is the state of being free from knots. (8)
Because his mind regarding the Dharma is well-concealed, he has concealed ankles. || 9 ||
He has level feet because he delivers people dwelling in all places of difficulty.
Because he is skilled in overcoming men, he has the gait of a lion’s stride. || 11 ||
Because of his skill in overcoming the *nāgas*, he possesses the gait of one who strides like a *nāga*. || 12 ||
Because of his skill in moving through the air, he possesses a gait that strides with a leaping motion. (13)
14. Because of his skill as a bull among men, he has the gait of one who strides like a bull.
The quality of walking with the right side forward arises from following the path of circumambulation. || 15 ||
And through the skillfulness of being pleasing, there is graceful movement. || 16 ||
Constant straightness of course through the state of a mind that is not crooked. || 17 ||
The quality of having well-rounded limbs is due to his proclaiming pure virtues. || 18 ||
Because his nature is cleansed of evil, his body is polished smooth. || 19 ||
The quality of having limbs that taper gradually [from top to bottom] arises from teaching the Dharma in accordance with those to be trained. || 20 ||
Because of his pure conduct regarding the body and so forth, he possesses a pure physical form. || 21 ||
Because of his compassionate mind, he possesses softness of body. || 22 ||
Because of the purity of the mind, there is purity of the body. || 23 ||
Because the Dharma and Vinaya are complete, there is the perfection of the physical marks. || 24 ||
From proclaiming his vast and beautiful qualities comes the possession of a vast and beautiful bodily frame. (25)
Because of having an even mind toward all things, there is evenness of pace. || 26 ||
Through the teaching of the perfectly pure Dharma, there is the purity of the eyes. || 27 ||
From teaching the Dharma in an easily understood manner comes the quality of having delicate limbs. || 28 ||
Because his mind is always undepressed, his body is free from dejection. || 29 ||
Because of the excellence of his accumulated roots of merit, his limbs are well-developed. || 30 ||
Because of the exhaustion of further rebirth, his body is perfectly compact.
He possesses well-proportioned major and minor limbs by virtue of being a teacher who has clearly explained dependent origination. 32.
From the vision of objects as they truly are, there arises the state of pure illumination free from darkness.
He has a well-proportioned belly because he is one who brings disciples endowed with virtuous conduct to spiritual maturity. (34)
Because he has wiped away the defects of saṃsāra, his belly is smooth. || 35 ||
Because the horn of pride has been broken, there is the state of having an unbroken belly.
Because he prevents the exhaustion of the Dharma, he has a non-sunken belly. || 37 ||
Because he has penetrated the profundity of the Dharma, his navel is deep. || 38 ||
He possesses a clockwise-turning mark because he causes his disciples to adopt the practice of circumambulation from the right. 39.
Universally pleasing appearance arises from the cause of bringing about a retinue that is universally pleasing. (40)
Through purity of mind, there is purity of conduct. || 41 ||
Because he has removed unseasonable phenomena and discipline, his body is free from moles and dark spots. || 42 ||
The quality of having hands as soft and delicate as cotton arises from teaching the Dharma that brings about lightness of body and so forth. // 43 //
Because he has attained the state of a great śramaṇa who is gentle, his lines on the palms are gentle. 44.
Because he abides in the profound Dharma, his lines on the palms are deep. || 45 ||
Because he teaches the Dharma that is pure with respect to its future consequences, his lines on the palms of his hands are long.
Because he teaches the training extensively, his speech is not overly prolix. 47.
Because he has known all worlds as being like reflections, he possesses the state of being both the original object and its reflection. 48.
Through the quality of gentle speech and discipline, he possesses a soft tongue.
The thinness of the tongue results from being endowed with abundant virtues.
He has a red tongue because the Dharma and Vinaya are difficult for people who are like children and are impassioned to fathom. 51.
Because it is free from all longing, there is the quality of having a voice like the thundering of clouds.
Through the quality of speech that is sweet and so forth, there is the possession of a voice that is sweet, beautiful, and charming.
The state of having well-formed tusks results from having severed the fetters of existence.
His sharp fangs are due to his being a subduer of those who are difficult to tame. || 55 ||
He has white teeth because his Dharma and Vinaya are supremely pure. (56)
Because he stands evenly on the ground, his canine teeth are even. || 57 ||
His canine teeth are well-proportioned because they manifest the correct sequential realization [of the truths]. 58.
By virtue of establishing the excellence of wisdom, he possesses a prominent nose.
By being endowed with pure people, one is pure in conduct. || 60 ||
The quality of having wide eyes arises from the state of possessing the most sublime Dharma. || 61 ||
Because he has gathered a multitude of sentient beings, his eyelashes are thick.
Because he is beloved by all young women, his eyes are like the petals of white and blue lotuses.
He has long eyebrows because he always perceives the future. || 64 ||
He has smooth eyebrows due to his skill in the gentle Dharma and Vinaya. 65.
The quality of having very glossy eyebrows arises from having a continuum that is wholesome and supple.
Because he perceives faults everywhere, his eyebrows have hairs of equal length.
The quality of having full and long arms consists in being able to avert even the most extreme suffering.

69. Symmetry of the ears due to having conquered the battle against passion and the other [afflictions]. 70. Unimpaired faculty of hearing due to having an unimpaired mental continuum toward all sentient beings.
The forehead is unwrinkled because it does not undergo alteration through any views or actions. 71.
The broadness of the forehead [is due to] his being the crusher of all disputants. || 72 ||
By virtue of having fulfilled his supreme vows, he possesses the perfection of the most excellent limbs. || 73 ||
The hair-like quality [of her eyebrows] is like that of bees, insofar as they turn one away from attachment to sense objects. 74.
The state of having hair like a peacock’s crest is due to having abandoned the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that are to be eliminated through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Because he has fully understood the teaching with a subtle intellect, he possesses smooth hair. || 76 ||
Because his consciousness is not overwhelmed by passion and the like, his hair is not disheveled. || 77 ||
Because he always speaks words that are not harsh, his hair is not coarse. || 78 ||
Because he is strewn with the flowers of the factors of enlightenment, his hair is fragrant. || 79 ||
And because they conduce to beauty in every respect, his palms and soles are adorned with the śrīvatsa, the svastika, and the nandyāvarta. || 80 ||
And so it has been said:
"The nails and fingers of the Sage are copper-colored, glossy, and elevated; his veins are rounded, well-defined, tapering, hidden, and without knots. (21)
The ankles are hidden, the feet are even like those of a lion, an elephant, a twice-born, or a lord of cattle;
his stride is powerful, his gait is beautiful and to the right, and his limbs are straight and well-rounded.
Smoothness and regularity, purity and softness, cleanliness of the limbs, the presence of the primary marks, and the beauty of broad, well-rounded limbs. ||23||
Evenness of gait, purity of the eyes, delicacy, lack of dejection, excellence of the limbs, and well-knit body; ||24||
Well-proportioned limbs, purity of light undimmed by darkness, rounded, polished, uninjured eyes, a slender abdomen, and depth. ||25||
The navel is spiraling to the right and beautiful to behold from all sides;
his conduct is pure, and his body is free from moles and freckles. ||26||
The hands are soft as cotton; the lines on the palms are glossy, deep, and long;
the mouth is not overly large; and the lips resemble the bimba fruit in color and reflection.
The tongue is soft, slender, and red; his voice has the resonance of a thundercloud;
his tone is lovely and melodious; and his fangs are rounded, sharp, white, and even. ||28||
Her prominent nose was perfectly straight and exceedingly pure;
her eyes were wide, adorned with thick lashes, and possessed the beauty of lotus petals. (29)
His eyebrows and arms are long, smooth, very glossy, and possessed of even hair; his ears are plump, long, symmetrical, and free from any defects.
The forehead is unwrinkled; the head is broad and full;
the hair is dark like a bee, curly, smooth, and not matted in its form. (31)
"The hair of men is not coarse, but captivates [the senses] through its fragrance;
the *śrīvatsa* and the *svastika*—these are considered the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) of a Buddha. (32) Thus it is said.

Subsequently, that body which, in the form of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and others, continuously accomplishes the desired welfare of sentient beings throughout all world-systems until the end of *saṃsāra*, is [the *nirmāṇakāya*]. By way of its continuity...
The fourth [body] of the Buddha, the Blessed One, which is unceasing and emanational, should be understood as being common to all ordinary beings.
And so it has been said:
"By means of which he performs diverse benefits for the world equally;
that body of the Sage, uninterrupted until the end of existence, is the Nirmāṇakāya. (33) Thus.
Therein, first, having performed the activity of pacifying rebirth, characterized by non-attachment to and non-abiding in auspicious or inauspicious states of existence,

Having established [beings] in the four means of attraction, such as generosity, and having awakened them through the knowledge consisting of hearing and so forth regarding the discordant factors and their remedies by way of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, he— like a magician— being free from attachment and the like,

establishes them in the welfare of others characterized by loving-kindness and so forth, which is the true nature of the benefit of sentient beings; and subsequently, in his own welfare, in the practice of the six perfections manifested by the purity of the three spheres.
Immediately thereafter, [there is] the Buddha-path characterized by the ten paths of wholesome action, which consist of the welfare of oneself and others;

then, the practice of the intrinsic emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-prakṛti-śūnyatā*); and following that, on the first stage (*bhūmi*), characterized by the penetration of the all-pervading realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) through the empowerment of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Regarding the two dharmas,

he then establishes [the practitioner] in the conventional knowledge of all dharmas— such as the perfections of ethical discipline and so forth— which serve as the causes for fulfilling the accumulations on the second and subsequent stages;
in this manner, [he establishes them] in the perfection of wisdom.

By means of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), on the sixth stage, there is the non-apprehension of all phenomena characterized by the lack of attachment to the cultivation of the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge;
immediately thereafter, on the seventh stage, through the power of the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), there is the ripening of sentient beings;

then, on the eighth stage, through the power of the perfection of strength (*bala-pāramitā*), there is the bodhisattva path not shared with the śrāvakas and others, wherein there is once again the abandonment of attachment to all entities in that very same [non-apprehension].
Thereafter, upon the attainment of enlightenment through the power of the ninth perfection, the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*);

immediately following that, through the force of the perfection of gnosis (*jñāna-pāramitā*), having established [the bodhisattva] in the twofold purification of the Buddha-field on the tenth stage, he further settles him—within that very same nature bound to birth and determined for perfect complete enlightenment—in the welfare of sentient beings through the vigor of the world-systems of the ten directions, and in the qualities such as the transition resembling a Buddha in all world-systems. In this sequence, he again settles him within that very same nature of the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*), characterized by the dharmas that bring about the entirety of enlightenment.

In the factors of enlightenment; in the non-loss of the connection between action and its fruit; in the realization of things as they truly are; in the abandonment of all perversions; in the knowledge that abandons perversions lacking a real basis; in the purification of a bodhisattva characterized by natural purity;
and in the accumulations which are the cause of purification free from all stains.

Having established [beings] in the thorough knowledge that the conditioned and the unconditioned are non-distinct by virtue of their nature being emptiness, he settles them in the Tathāgata-stage and in nirvāṇa. Thus, like the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), his activity—which persists as long as saṃsāra lasts and consists of twenty-seven modes appearing to those to be trained—is understood to be the very cognition (*jñāna*) itself arising through the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). This cognition, brought about by relying on the sovereign basis [of the Dharma-body], performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) by way of generating appearances such as the Enjoyment-body (*sāmbhogikakāya*). This is what is intended regarding the Dharma-body; thus its activity is to be discerned.
And so it has been said:
"Likewise, his karma is held to be uninterrupted as long as saṃsāra lasts;
[it consists of] the pacification of the realms of existence and the fourfold gathering. (34)

[The application of wisdom] is directed toward the dwelling [in the world], toward the awakening to affliction and purification, toward the true nature of the welfare of sentient beings, and toward the six perfections. (35)
In the Buddha-path, in emptiness by its very nature, in the cessation of duality, in conventional designation, in non-apprehension, and in the maturation of embodied beings; ||36||
Regarding the prevention of attachment to the path of a bodhisattva,
the attainment of awakening, the purification of the Buddha-field, and with respect to certainty; ||37||

In the immeasurable benefit of sentient beings, in qualities such as serving the Buddhas, in the non-destruction of the factors of enlightenment, and in the seeing of truth through the ripening of karmic actions. ||38||
And regarding the abandonment of error, the method of its lack of substantial reality, purification along with its equipment, and in relation to the conditioned and the unconditioned; //39//
"The non-perception of differentiation and the establishment in nirvāṇa—

this is considered the twenty-sevenfold activity of the Dharmakāya. (40) Thus, in accordance with the authority of this verse from the *Śāstra*, the meaning of the text should be explained by supplying the missing words and so forth, in conformity with the sequence of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*).

Furthermore, since someone has largely [mis]read the verses of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* and not otherwise, beginning with the passage "May it occur to you, Subhūti," and so forth, whatever irrelevant portion of this Mother [the *Prajñāpāramitā*] was explained by him—due to his failure to state the meaning of the complete whole or its parts—that should be understood by the wise alone; thus, it is neither introduced nor refuted here.
In the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, the commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this is the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Following."
The thirtieth chapter.

Beginning from the stage of the beginner, by means of an introductory discourse on prior practice, he explains the sequence of seeking the realization of the perfection of wisdom whose intrinsic nature is the eightfold clear realization as previously described, saying:
"Furthermore," and so forth.
Sadāprarudita, however, being possessed of a collection of merit such as the undertaking of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), generosity, and so forth,

and because he follows the sound [of the Dharma] and seeks the abandonment of objective apprehension (*upalambha*), is observed to have been previously intent on seeking instruction regarding the factors of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so on while established on the stage of equipment (*sambhārabhūmi*).
But now, he is indeed a sovereign of the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*).
"By one who is indifferent to the body" means by virtue of the intention to give away even the bones, marrow, and so forth. "By one who is regardless of life" means...
Because he was encouraged to give even his heart.
Regarding "gain, honor, and fame":
therein, gain (*lābha*) refers to the abundance of material wealth.
"Honor" is the state of being highly esteemed;
"renown" is fame that pervades the ends of the quarters.
This occurs first on the stage of equipment (*saṃbhārabhūmi*).
Because of the statement: "In the stream of dharma, one receives instruction from the Buddhas."
Because he had not yet attained the stream of the Dharma, a voice was heard from the sky due to his state of meditative concentration:
"Do not [go] by the left," meaning do not look toward the left side;
"do not [go] by the right," meaning do not come looking toward the right side.
"Do not [go] by the east," and so forth; that is, do not move by way of the eastern or other directions, nor by way of a self, nor by way of the view of a real body (*satkāya*), and so on.
This is because things such as a self, which do not appear, are not apprehended as being existent.

The meaning is: proceed in such a way that you do not waver from those forms and so forth—which have not ascended to the path of vision (darśanapatha)—by realizing their non-existence as being without self (nirātmaka).
"Vitiṣṭhata" means "turn back.
This is what is being said:

By this negation of the arising of physical fatigue and other factors that obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*), all forms of concentration are indicated by way of illustration. [The obstacles are:
laziness, loss of the object of focus, lethargy and excitement, lack of application, and excessive application.

The instruction would have been given thus: "Go toward the eastern direction while attending to the perfection of wisdom with a concentration endowed with the eight formative forces of abandonment, which serve as the antidotes to the six faults; in this way you will hear it.
For, through the faith of the yogi—characterized by firm conviction in the qualities of concentration—zeal is produced.
Then, by the power of aspiration, one initiates vigor;
then, by the power of vigor, one attains pliancy of body and mind;
then, for one whose body and mind are pliant, laziness is turned away.
Therefore, the four beginning with faith serve for the abandonment of laziness.
Mindfulness is the antidote to the loss of the object of focus, because by means of it, the object is correctly established.
Clear comprehension (*samprajanya*) is the antidote to lethargy (*laya*) and excitement (*auddhatya*).
Through it, by attending to objects of joy such as the qualities of the Buddha and so forth, lethargy is abandoned;

and by attending to objects of spiritual urgency such as impermanence and so forth, excitement is abandoned. However, at the time when lethargy and excitement have not yet been pacified, there is the fault of non-application (*anābhoga*).
As an antidote to that, volition should be practiced.
When laxity and excitement have been stilled, the mind proceeds toward the object of focus, unwavering and flowing without deliberate effort.
Furthermore, there is the fault of renewed application because of that mental distraction; therefore, as its antidote, equanimity (*upekṣā*) should be cultivated.
To express his commitment upon receiving the correct instruction, he says:
"I shall indeed act in this way."
Anticipating the objection that "this assertion is indeed without logical justification," he asks, "For what reason?
and says: "For I desire to bring light to all sentient beings," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.

Having instructed by way of the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*), he speaks— beginning with "Again he heard a sound," and so forth— in order to instruct by means of the door of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*),
for the sake of full comprehension, for abandonment, and furthermore for direct realization.
The meaning of the meditative concentrations on emptiness and so forth is proclaimed to be threefold.

According to this statement, the form in which [an object] appears—such as the form of a jar—is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). For the sake of fully understanding that, the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) is taught.
Indeed, the imagined nature is to be fully understood because it exists merely as an error.

The signless concentration (*ānimitta-samādhi*) is for the sake of directly realizing the knowledge that is free from attachment to all phenomena and is like an illusion; for, according to the conventional truth of the yogi, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*), which has the form of reality, is the nature to be realized, whereas there is [the need to abandon] attachment to the person and to phenomena.
The wishless (*apraṇihita*) concentration is for the sake of abandoning the dependent nature (*paratantra*),
because the attachment to the grasped and the grasper must be abandoned as it arises from cognitive error (*viparyāsa*).

Some maintain that the three phrases beginning with "free from signs" (*nimittaparivarjitena*) are intended to demonstrate that one should act like an illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*) at the times of generating the wisdoms consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Others say that [this refers to] the stages of preparation, the fundamental, and the subsequent [stages] regarding meditative absorptions such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
To explain the characteristics of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), he says:
"Those which are emptiness," and so forth.

In that regard, on the stage of equipment (*sambhārabhūmi*), for the sake of accumulating the equipment of merit (*puṇyasambhāra*); and on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*)—which consists of the equipment of knowledge (*jñānasambhāra*)—for the sake of generating the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);
the meaning is that they teach all phenomena as being, respectively, unproduced, unborn, unceased, and non-existent.
"By one who thoroughly weighs" means by one who enumerates [them].
"By one who seeks the Dharma" means because of seeing the purpose of future dharmas. "By reverence for the Dharma" means...
Because of perceiving the present advantages:

having seen the noble Bodhisattva Dharmodgata accompanied by sixty-eight thousand [beings] and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, one must not allow the mind to undergo any change; furthermore, you must recognize such things as the deeds of Māra, and so forth.
"And having overcome them" means having overcome them by virtue of not being dependent upon them. He speaks thus while explaining skill in means itself.
"This is for the sake of disciplining sentient beings," and so forth.
Having taught the means by relying on conventional truth, he speaks by relying on ultimate truth:
"And at that very moment, by you," and so forth.
"At that moment" means immediately after witnessing the play of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Having raised the doubt as to why this is so, he says: "For what reason? and so forth.
"All phenomena," and so forth; "empty by way of intrinsic nature" means they are unarisen in reality.
The employment of the five terms beginning with "without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, are devoid of self.
Regarding the statement "like an illusion" (*māyopama*) and so on,

he speaks [thus] to show that one should not become lax in diligence after having encountered the noble Bodhisattva Dharmodgata— who remained absorbed in a single meditative concentration for seven years— following the previously mentioned purpose of the repeated teaching.
Furthermore, "you" and so forth;
"resistance" means opposition. "How far must I go? refers to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-bhūmi*).
He travels through the world-systems by means of the accomplishment of meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
For the purpose of worshipping immeasurable Buddhas and for the sake of hearing [the Dharma].
Having attended upon immeasurable Buddhas for immeasurable eons,
he attains supreme pliancy of mind through that service.

The meaning is that, although he possessed supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), because he lacked the power to perceive the liberation (*vimokṣa*) of the noble Dharmodgata, and due solely to the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the noble Dharmodgata himself and his superior skill in means for maturing him, he did not see [the city]; thus, he did not ask the voice, "How far must I go from here to the city of Gandhavatī, which is manifested by the liberation of the noble Dharmodgata?"
Regarding these, some say that "weeping" (*rudita*) is crying out with a loud voice, while "wailing" (*krandita*) is the opposite of that;
others say that "weeping" is the shedding of tears, and "wailing" is that same act accompanied by sound.
"Sorrow" (*śoka*) is a state of mental distaste, while "lamentation" (*parideva*) is speech such as "Alas! Woe! I am deceived! and so forth.
