Because of the instruction on the selflessness of phenomena and persons mentioned previously, and because of the application of mental attention to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that has been undertaken, when there is flexibility of mind even on the stage of equipment (*sambhārabhūmi*), one attains that which is called the "stream of dharma" (*dharmasrotas*).
Upon attaining this, one becomes capable of grasping both the words and the meaning [of the teachings].
And when that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has been attained, from the Buddhas...
He says that he attains a state of fervent longing for the sake of increasing concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*):
"Then indeed, Subhūti, of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita," and so forth;
likewise, "of him who was thus yearning."

For one who has thus developed aspiration, there are three phrases beginning with "by this very vigor," which distinguish the vigor for armor, for the welfare of sentient beings, and for [the practice of] skillful means.
Furthermore, "desirousness" (chandikatā) is the continuous longing for attainment.
Because there is no abandonment in the interim, it forms a continuous succession; because it exists there in concealment, it is twofold; by the opposite of that, it is flourishing (*sphītā*).
Because it is free from the calamities of foreign armies and the like, it is secure (*kṣemā*).
Because of the abundance of food and other necessities, it is well-supplied with provisions (*subhikṣā*).

It is "crowded with many people" because of the abundance of humans, elephants, horses, and so forth. A "market street" (*āpaṇakavīthī*) is a street of shops. It is "pierced through" because it extends from one end to the other.
Regarding the phrase "equal and equal" (*samasamaiḥ*): some say it means "of equal measure"; others say the repetition is for the sake of distributive emphasis (*vīpsā*).
"By means of those established for the passage of people, draft animals, and vehicles, without causing oppression.
In this context, "the place for people and vehicles" refers to the place for vehicles such as elephants, horses, and so forth;
"the place for draft-vehicle transport" refers to [the same].
The places for standing while on vehicles such as palanquins; the places for walking on foot; and the places for crossing.
These are established in hundreds of market streets and lanes where there is no crowding, being situated at points for the passage of people, draft animals, and vehicles.
Thus it is said; by them, [the work] was "well-completed," meaning it was brought to fruition.
Because the word *sthāpita* ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix, it does not undergo prior placement (as a compound), due to the irregularity (*vyabhicāra*) of that rule.
The term *khaḍakaśīrṣāṇi* refers to the heads of the *krama*.
"By a network of small bells" means by a multitude of tinkling bells.
Therein, it is "beautiful" because of its excellence; it is "delightful" because it reaches the heart through its color;
and it is "enchanting" because it produces joy.
"Of the five-membered orchestra" refers to a specific type of musical instrument equipped with lutes, flutes, and so forth.
"Carrying water that follows [the contours]" means...
The waters flow in a clockwise direction.
The word "vāriṇaḥ" (of the water) takes the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) to express a relationship, while the suffix is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
A *puṇḍarīka* is a lotus.
"By others" means by [flowers such as] the *saugandhika*, *daṇḍotpalā*, and so forth.
"With a circumference equal to the size of a cartwheel" means...
Circumference means roundness.
Regarding "blue" and so forth:
therein, "blue" is the designation; because they are blue by nature (*sahaja*), they possess the color blue.
The examples are due to the blueness resulting from conjunction.
Because both possess luminosity through the emission of light, they appear blue; in the same way, it should be understood for yellow and so forth.
"Buddha-guidance," and so forth.
"Buddha-guidance" is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Those whose minds are "endowed with"—that is, accompanied by—clarity (*prasāda*) consisting of a vivid regard for it; who have "well-gone," meaning they have understood and heard it; and who possess the knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*): these are those as described. [This occurs] "by means of the maturation of their prior karma."
The connection is with what precedes.
Regarding "in the middle of Gandhavatī": the connection is that it is in the middle of the crossroads (*śṛṅgāṭaka*), which serves as the landmark location within the city of Gandhavatī.
The three terms beginning with "enjoyment of the house" (*gṛhaparibhoga*) refer to the distinctions of mild, medium, and intense enjoyment;
[the phrase] "made of *karketana*" means made of sapphire (*indranīla*).
"Offered" means having produced physical ease (*kāyasukha*).
"Fully integrated" means having produced mental gladness (*cittasaumanasya*).
When there is a notion of self, there arises the notion of another; from the division of self and other, there follow grasping and aversion.
All afflictions arise bound up with these two;
thus, by this principle, all afflictions such as attachment and the rest, being preceded by the grasping and adherence to "self" and "mine," become the causes for the ripening of suffering.

However, through the cultivation of the illusion-like nature of all phenomena, and by means of the attainment of mastery over the afflictions for the sake of training sentient beings, the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by the Sons of the Conquerors—due to their specific intention—is not a source of fault, just like that of an illusory person.
For Bodhisattvas, constantly becoming universal monarchs,
indeed accomplish the welfare of sentient beings as householders throughout all their births.
Affliction becomes a factor of enlightenment, and cyclic existence takes on the nature of peace for those possessing great skillful means; therefore, the sons of the Victors are indeed inconceivable.
According to this statement, the enjoyment of sensual pleasures does not constitute a fault for Bodhisattvas,
because it is only the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by those who have undertaken specific vows that is considered defective.
[The phrase] "spread with cotton mattresses" [is used].
*Tūlikā* is well known. *Goṇikā*, however, is a specific variety of woolen blanket.
*Garbholika* is a cushion (*masūraka*).
"Cailavitānam" means a canopy of cloth.

The three phrases beginning with "by way of being the basis for phenomena" are employed in order to demonstrate faith—which consists of conviction, clarity, and aspiration—regarding existence, qualities, and capability.
"Adhiṣṭhitam" (presided over).

By hearing the means for attaining that which had been sought for a long time without interruption, he obtained mild, moderate, and intense happiness and mental well-being; thus, in due order, there are the six phrases beginning with "satisfied" (*tuṣṭa*).
He states that through the instruction of the Tathāgata, having attained purity of intention, the hearing of the *Prajñāpāramitā* arose:
"Then indeed, Sadāprarudita... and so forth.
He says that for those who possess the complete causes, hearing the Dharma is not without fruit:
"While listening," and so forth.
"The perception of non-reliance" means:
He says that the perception [of all things] is like an illusion,
and that every realization is characterized by the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya).
"Of that, 'many kinds,' and so forth:

the meditative stabilization in which, being established, one observes the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as being like an illusion and so on— that is the meditative stabilization named 'Observation of the Intrinsic Nature of All Phenomena.'"
In this manner, the samādhis such as "the non-apprehension of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena" (sarvadharmasvabhāvānupalabdhi) are to be explained.

Therein, based on the distinctions in the attainment of the weak, medium, and intense levels of the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), one should understand that the twelve samādhis beginning with "the contemplation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena" arise from those; furthermore, the fifty samādhis beginning with "devoid of illusion" (māyāvarjita) are to be understood as belonging specifically to the stage of practice through resolute conviction (adhimukticaryābhūmi).

And in the *Ārya-ratnamegha-sūtra*, it is stated that even while remaining on this very stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), a bodhisattva, though still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), has transcended all the misfortunes of the foolish and is endowed with qualities such as incalculable samādhis, dhāraṇīs, liberations (*vimokṣa*), and superknowledges (*abhijñā*).

It is said that by the power of the purification of one’s intention (*āśaya*) alone, for the sake of attaining the first stage (*bhūmi*), there arises in the state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*) detailed instruction preceded by the appearance of the Tathāgata;
thus he says, "He dwells in these concentrations," and so forth.

As for the statement in another section that on the stages such as the Joyous (*pramuditā*) one sees a hundred Buddhas and so on, that should be understood as referring to what is necessarily manifested.
Because there is no restriction regarding injunctions and prohibitions elsewhere.
Therefore, "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*) is that which consists in the perception of incalculable Tathāgatas within a single world-system.
If it is asked: "But how can this be so, given the contradiction in the simultaneous existence of two Tathāgatas in one world-system?"
Some say that he saw immeasurable Buddhas, Blessed Ones, residing in other world-systems.

As for the prohibition regarding birth—that two Tathāgatas who are neither prior nor subsequent shall not arise in the world—that was stated with reference to the commencement of their teaching; therefore, the meaning established therein is simply that the teaching of two Tathāgatas does not proceed simultaneously in the world.

Others maintain that because their arising consists in being dependent on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-paratantra-utpatti*), their very arising is simply the manifestation of the teaching; and this being so, he saw many Tathāgatas arisen simultaneously in this world-system, for they were established in a single sequence of teaching through a common intention and possessed the complete causes.
Since it is stated that there is "no before or after," their arising in succession is indeed permitted.
Although they have arisen, because there is no final nirvāṇa,
they truly exist by way of the Dharma-body and the Enjoyment-body;
they simply do not appear to those who lack merit.
Others, however, maintain that those possessing merit perceive [the Tathāgatas] according to their merit, whether they be few or many.

At that time, through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of a single Tathāgata residing there, or by the power of the noble Dharmodgata, during the performance of the miracle, there is a vision of immeasurable emanated (*nirmita*) Tathāgatas, as is the case for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Still others hold that, through the power of cultivating the bliss of the inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣa*), there is a vision of immeasurable Tathāgatas because the beginner’s own mind arises as being permeated by the manifestations of immeasurable Tathāgatas.
"Like a ball of rags" means that you should carry it, drawing it along with your head as if it were a bundle of cloth.
Having raised the question, "Why is that so?", he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "tasya hi" (for him), "distress" (*paritāpana*) refers to dejection (*vaimanasya*). "By that price" means that because one's person is sold for life, it is impossible to go there due to being dependent on another; consequently, there is an extreme deficiency in worship.

Some say that although divine worship could have been performed through the power of the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) even on the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-bhūmi*), the acceptance of that price was for the sake of honoring the Dharma, since his person had been sold for a price corresponding to that specific period of time.
Others say it was because he lacked the memory of the enjoyment of the supernormal knowledge of psychic power (*ṛddhy-abhijñā*), as he was intent upon hearing the Dharma.
Others say it is for the purpose of demonstrating enthusiasm toward the search for the Dharma among those of weak vigor.
Some maintain that it was by this sequence that the welfare of the merchant’s daughter and others was accomplished.
The three phrases beginning with "shattered" are intended, respectively, to destroy the afflictions of oneself, others, and both.
"Due to desire, with desire as the cause" means for the sake of desires already experienced or not yet experienced.
The three phrases beginning with "with a contented mind due to obtaining mild, moderate, or intense joy" [are to be understood accordingly].

Some maintain that because he perceived no obstacle to hearing the Dharma even when giving his heart and other organs through the power of his supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), he consented, saying, "I shall give.
This was due to his desire for the worship of the Dharma.
Not even an obstacle was taken into account by anyone;
thus it was abandoned.

With the intention that worship is great solely due to the greatness of the disposition (*āśaya*) and not due to the greatness of the material substance (*dravya*), he said, "Give whatever has been chosen.
*Kāraṇam* means suffering (*pīḍā*).
*Guṇajātiḥ* means the universal of quality (*guṇasāmānya*).
"Specific quality" refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a quality.
In that regard, they are pleasing because they are agreeable to the mind;
they are endurable because they do not give rise to faults.
"Subject" (*viṣayin*) refers to mastery (*vaśitā*), that is, sovereignty, which is to say, capacity.
The three terms beginning with "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) are used in consideration of the appearances for persons of sharp, medium, and dull faculties.
"Free from disease" (*aroga*) means being devoid of arisen illness.
Because he is unfit for future disease, he is free from affliction.
"In this way," and so forth.
"Niveśana" means a house.
"Utsṛjata" means "abandon.
Having raised the doubt as before—"For what reason?"—he says:
"I have no other wealth whatsoever," and so forth.
"Abundant" and "vast":
they are abundant because of the distinction of many kinds of substances;
they are vast because each individual kind is infinite.
"Grant permission," he said;
"give me leave.

"He saw it from afar" means that, by virtue of having attained a distinguished realization and through the power of seeing the liberation of the Noble Dharmodgata, he beheld the city of Gandhavatī from a great distance.
"Where is he, O Kauśika?"—
he asked this because, although he sought the Dharma, he lacked the enjoyment of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
"With seven seals"— so it is said.

Some say that it was placed there after being bound with seven very firm bonds for the sake of generating reverence by way of its rarity and great significance, and having been sealed at the seven locations of the knots with seven seals bearing his own name.
Others say that a miraculous feat (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) was performed because he knew their spiritual potential (*bhavyatā*) and desired to win them over completely.
Then, indeed, those flowers, and so forth.
This is for the purpose of asking a question regarding the thorough knowledge of the coming and going of the Tathāgatas.
Announcing the previous account, he said:
"Here, O son of good family," and so forth.
This is the thirtieth chapter, titled "Sadāprarudita," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The thirty-first chapter:
In order to generate the path of seeing by means of negating the coming and going of the Tathāgatas, [the author], proclaiming the selflessness of all phenomena, says:
"When this had been said, Dharmodgata... and so forth.

Some maintain that by demonstrating, respectively, that [the Buddhas] have as their nature suchness (*tathatā*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), suchness (*yathāvattā*), dispassion (*virāga*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), it is made known that the Blessed Buddhas are characterized by the eight clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) beginning with the illusion-like omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*);
for this very reason, he says:
"For indeed, O son of good family," and so forth.

"From these dharmas" means that the Tathāgata is not other than the dharmas such as the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) and so forth; rather, the meaning is that the suchness (tathatā) of these very dharmas is the Tathāgata.

Others, however, maintain that "excess" (*ādhikya*)—the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) consisting in the superfluity of reasons and examples—is a position asserted even by petty logicians (*kṣudranaiyāyika*).
Having raised the objection, "How then could the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord of Nyāya, have stated the superfluity of examples?", [the author replies:
where there is indeed only one person to be instructed, it is proper to state only one thing well-known to that person.
In that assembly, however, many people of differing views were seated; therefore,
it is appropriate to provide numerous examples for their sake,
or else to speak by way of alternative options.
They explain the resolution for every such additional statement as follows: these examples are not intended as a cumulative collection;
rather, because the reason—such as "being dependently originated"—is already implied by the mere mention of the example, it is not explicitly stated by the wise.
Having thus described the true nature of the Tathāgatas, he speaks in order to negate adherence to conceptual constructions.
For example, noble son, "a man," and so forth;
"a mirage" means the particular rays of the sun.
One who does not understand the true nature of things belongs to the class of the childish;
one who has a perverted understanding belongs to the class of the foolish.
However, water does not exist there by way of its own intrinsic nature.

In the cognition of a mirage, the heated saline soil is not the objective support (*ālambana*); for if a cognition of one form could have another as its support, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Since all entities possess mutually exclusive forms, water does not exist in reality within the mirage.
Therefore, the meaning is that the cognition which takes that as its object is erroneous because it lacks a real referent (*nirviṣayatva*).
Anticipating the question "For what reason? as before, he says:

"Indeed, a Tathāgata is not to be seen by way of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). This is because that which is imagined is absolutely empty; thus, a Tathāgata does not consist of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
He says, "For example, noble son, it is like an illusion," and so forth, in order to negate adherence to the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
The meaning is that because the forms of the grasped and the grasper are unreal, that which is conjured has no coming and so forth.
In the same way, noble son, it is said that there is no such thing as "Tathāgatas" for those whose nature is dependent (paratantra).
This was stated for the purpose of dispelling attachment to the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna).

For example, noble son, as in the passage beginning "a man who has fallen asleep," it is said that a dream is indeed false speech. In every case, the object of perception is external, characterized by a difference in place and time.
Whether in this birth, in another, at that very time, or at some other time.

Neither that place nor another place can be the object of dream-cognition, because if a cognition of one form were to have another thing as its objective support, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Furthermore, no other external form is logically tenable.
Because even in a very small dwelling, mountains, trees, essences, and so forth—measuring many yojanas and possessing resistance—are perceived;
therefore, such a cognition arises as nothing but an error, and thus the dream is false.
In this very same way, O son of good family, are all phenomena.
All phenomena, being devoid of arising as established by valid cognition, possess the perfected nature and are like dreams.
"Not understanding the true nature of phenomena" means not comprehending their state of non-arising.
"The six realms of existence" [is what follows].
Because the realm of asuras is established separately from the five destinies beginning with the gods,
and because they are disciples of the Blessed One.
It is better to fall away from moral conduct than ever from right view;
by moral conduct one goes to heaven, but by right view one attains the supreme state.

According to this principle, those very disciples of the Blessed One who are resolved upon the illusory nature of phenomena (*māyopama-dharmatā*)—in order to dispel the doubt of those of dull intellect who, upon the negation of the reality of the three categories of entities such as the imagined (*parikalpita*), might think that "the Tathāgata does not exist at all"—state that the Tathāgata exists as dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
It is as follows, O son of good family: "Just as, for example, the great ocean," and so forth.
"Taking up the roots of virtue of sentient beings":

because of the statement, "The variety of the world is born of karma," it is based upon the common virtuous karma of sentient beings; since they have the roots of virtue as their cause from the perspective of conventional truth, they are not without cause.
The phrase "of which conditions being present" implies by the force of the context that [the body arises] through their power.

Furthermore, the bodies of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are not causeless; for they attain completion through the power of the roots of merit (kuśalamūla) of those very beings who are to be disciplined by the Buddha, and thus the body is not without a cause.
Having now explained that [the body] is produced by common karma, he speaks in order to demonstrate that it is also produced by the uncommon karma of the Blessed Ones.
"Perfected through previous conduct," and so forth.

In that regard, because it is manifested through the stage of conduct characterized by resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), it is "perfected through previous conduct. Because it is produced from the causes consisting in the appropriation of the seven preparatory stages beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*) stage, it is "dependent on causes. Because it has arisen from the cooperative conditions of the three types of resultant stages beginning with the Immovable (*acalā*), it is "dependent on conditions."

Some maintain that the distinction in meaning is this: [the Tathāgata] has arisen from the maturation of past karma because he is comprised within the stage of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-bhūmi*).
Therefore, he says that the Tathāgata is not intrinsic, beginning with the words "not anywhere in the ten directions," and so forth.

Because of the statement, "That which is capable of causal efficiency is here ultimately real," [the author] says this in order to refute the dogmatic adherence of those who perceive [things) [dualistically], [showing that] the Tathāgata is indeed dependently originated— real in the ultimate sense— by virtue of the power of the relationship between cause and effect established by valid cognition.

It is just as, for example, in the case of a lute, noble son, and so forth. In that context, the *upadhānī* is the curved piece of wood or similar material placed at the top of the neck (*daṇḍa*) upon which the strings are wound; the *upavāṇī* are the specific types of strings situated along the side.
And by the statement, "That sound does not issue forth from the hollow," and so on,

he does not say that a single [cause] is the producer. Furthermore, by this designation of sound as being merely conceptual— namely, "sound is designated through the conjunction of all [factors]"— he rejects the notion that the assembly [of causes] possesses a real, productive intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is what is being said:
there are four possible alternatives—namely, that multiple causes produce a single effect or multiple effects, and likewise, that a single cause may also produce multiple effects or a single effect.

In this regard, if one holds the position that multiple causes produce a single effect, then when it is admitted that a single visual consciousness arises from the eye, visible form, light, mental attention (*manaskāra*), and so forth, despite the diversity of its causes...
Furthermore, because there is no difference in the effect, the difference in the cause could not be the differentiator of the effect.
Likewise, even in the absence of a difference in the cause, since there is no difference in the effect, the non-difference of the cause would not be the non-differentiator of the effect.

Consequently, if the difference and non-difference of the effect were independent of the difference and non-difference of the cause—judging by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—then they would be without a cause.

This being the case, because difference and non-difference would not be distinct from [the nature of] the universe, the world would be either eternally existent or eternally non-existent, since that which lacks a cause is independent of anything else.

[Objection: But surely the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer of the effect; and since this difference and non-difference of the effect follow the difference and non-difference of that complex, these two are capable of following positive and negative concomitance. Therefore, how could they possibly be without a cause?
If it is argued that they will exist [in the future], this is not substantial.

For there is no such thing as a "totality" (sāmagrī) other than the individual factors; rather, the very factors themselves, when complete, are what is denoted by the term "totality. And these, such as the eye and so forth, possess mutually distinct intrinsic natures (svabhāva).

If distinct entities, being together, are capable of producing a single, non-distinct effect such as visual consciousness, then why would other complete entities included within a different causal complex not also produce that same visual consciousness?
If it is argued that earth and the other elements do not produce it because they are distinct from the eye and so forth, [the response follows].
It must also be explained how the eye and the other [faculties], which possess mutually distinct intrinsic natures (svabhāva), produce [a cognition].
If it is argued that this is due to their having the nature of being producers (janaka-svābhāvya), [we reply:]...
It is not so, because non-productivity has been established as nothing other than being different from the producer.
Therefore, those things which differ from the nature that is the producer of one thing cannot be producers [of that same thing].
Because it is other than Janaka, like any other distinct entity.
This might be argued:
we do not say that another thing lacks the nature of being its producer.

However, that form which is the producer of one thing does not belong to another; furthermore, a producer acts only by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*) and not by the nature of another, because it does not possess that other's nature.

Therefore, since an exclusion from a producer by way of its own nature is unestablished, how could there be [entities] that are both distinct according to their respective natures and yet producers by virtue of their own nature? What [contradiction is there]?

There is a contradiction here. For instance, if something were excluded from a single producer, it would not possess that nature; yet, while it is not the case that it does not produce that effect, there is no logical principle (nyāya) by which that specific effect must be produced by that [one cause] alone and not by another.
If this were so—that the effect is produced by one alone—then what purpose would there be for others in producing that same effect?
This might be so;
indeed, entities possess no such thing as acting with foresight, by virtue of which this one [could act].
Others might desist, thinking, "What can we do here? [He] is capable.

For they, whose activities are devoid of intention and whose nature consists of the conditions (*upadhi*) resulting from the transformation of their own causes, simply become so due to that very nature; thus, they do not deserve censure.
If this is the case, then it follows that the very same nature of the effect which is produced by one cause is produced by another as well.
And this being the case, since a difference in the effect is not observed despite a difference in the cause,
the distinction between causes would not serve to differentiate an effect that is dissimilar [to them] yet non-different [from itself].
Now, if you think that [the causes] possess mutually distinct forms—

Furthermore, it is only the eye and so forth that, by virtue of a certain excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*), are determined to produce visual consciousness, and not others such as earth and so forth.
For it is precisely those [factors] like the eye that possess that excellence of intrinsic nature, and not others.
This much, however, may be granted.
From where does this excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*) in them arise?

If it were causeless, then because there would be no restriction for that which is independent, there would be the fear of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, that excellence of their intrinsic nature is said to come from its own cause.
The fact that this [effect] also has the nature of being produced by that [cause] arises from its own cause, which is distinct from it; thus, the succession of causes is beginningless.
Therefore, since such a succession of causes is accepted, even an infinite regress does not bring about any harm.

In this way, a distinct effect is produced from a collection of distinct causes, and a non-distinct effect from a non-distinct one; it is solely on this basis that the distinction and non-distinction of the result are stated to follow from the distinction and non-distinction of the cause.
This is not essential;

for according to the principle that "whatever reason expresses both [the proof and the refutation] with certainty is itself both the means of proof and the means of refutation," although there is no distinction in terms of their non-difference,
just as it is not the case that everything proves everything due to the specific capacity of the properties of the reason, so too is it in the case of non-distinction.
Nor does it bring credit to state this against the Sāṃkhyas and others— who accept the relationship between cause and effect— by saying that "not everything is the producer of everything.

For the Mādhyamika, who in reality denies the existence of the causal relation, how can he employ as if it were established for the sake of proving his own position a reason characterized by the capacity of causal properties, namely, "their excellence of intrinsic nature arises from their own causes," when such a reason is unestablished?
Now, if it is thought that the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge is unavoidable if one does not accept the capacity of the properties of the cause,
that is incorrect.
Because of the qualification "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*), there is no negation of things as they are perceived.
If you then argue that the negation applies to what is not perceived as it is, this is clearly like pulling out the hair of a tortoise.
If you say, "This is because we do not admit a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for what is not perceived as it is," [we reply:]...

Since, in reality, you accept that the causal relationship is accompanied by invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*) rather than being accompanied by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how is it not an acceptance based on a non-accurate observation?
For in perception, there appears only this much:
namely, that "when this exists, that comes to be."
And that [relation] has certainly not been refuted by us.

As for the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) whose nature is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because direct perception—being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*)—lacks the capacity to determine a nature established by valid cognition.

Nor is it reasonable to say that simply because an object appears, its nature—which is of such a kind and non-different from that [object]—must also appear; for even things like the [illusory] cluster of hairs (*keśoṇḍuka*) appear despite having no such nature.
The claim that "this appearance is erroneous" is also false,
because even for an appearance considered to be true, there is no basis for its truth.
If it is argued that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is the basis for truth:

This is not so; for the capacity to perform a causal function (*arthakriyākāritva*) is nothing other than the capacity to produce an effect, and according to the method already stated, its nature is found to be logically untenable from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Since it is accepted [only] conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), this [argument] is not a proof.
If it is argued that if everything were indeed false, there would be no fixed determination of place, time, and so forth—
This fault would arise if causelessness were admitted;

however, since [the effect] is delightful only so long as it is not subjected to analytical scrutiny due to its inability to withstand such investigation, each subsequent such effect—characterized by specific place, time, and so forth—proceeds by relying upon its own respective preceding causes.
For this very reason, even from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), things such as a hare's horn do not arise due to the deficiency of their causes.
If it is argued that since the logic is equal, why should there not be a negation even according to what is observed,
[we reply] because of the occurrence of contradictions with perception and other means of knowledge.
If it is then argued that this logic does not apply because of the impossibility of sublation (*bādhā*), [we reply as follows]:

This is not so; for in reality, it is according to logic that there is no sublation, because sublation is not admitted. And just as there is sublation according to what is observed, so too there is an absence of logic [in that claim].
Now, if the second position is accepted— that a single cause alone may produce multiple effects—
it is because the specific nature of the cause operates upon the specific nature of the effect; thus, the specific natures produced by the causal operation within the effect remain unmixed.
For instance, from the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), which is consciousness, the nature of apprehension arises for visual consciousness;
from that very same nature of apprehension, through the visual faculty, there is the specific determination of the capacity to grasp form;
and from the object, there is the conformity to its [the object's] form. Thus, even though they are not distinct...

Furthermore, it is argued that since the effect is in reality of an undivided nature, distinct particularities indeed arise from the distinct intrinsic natures of the causes; thus, even when there is a difference among the causes, there is no non-difference in their effect.
This is incorrect.

Because, if a mutual difference between the nature of apprehension and so forth were admitted, then that consciousness would be manifold, since it is non-different from the nature of apprehension and so forth, just like the individual natures of apprehension itself.
If it is argued that its difference from them is not established, and thus consciousness will not possess multiplicity; [we reply:

if a difference from them were admitted, that consciousness would be entirely causeless, because the operation of the causes would be employed only for [the production of] the self-nature and so forth perceived elsewhere than in consciousness; and in this way, it would follow that it must be either eternally existent or eternally non-existent.
This is a fault. Now, if difference is not accepted for fear of the aforementioned faults,

then, that being the case, there would be no mutual difference between the nature of perception and the rest, because they would have the same nature as a single cognition, just like the essence of cognition itself.

Therefore, because the postulation of a distinction between the objects of the causal operations would be futile, the previously mentioned objection—starting with "from the eye and other [senses] which possess distinct natures"—becomes applicable. Now, if it is thought: "Since we observe that the nature of an effect arises from multiple [causes] that possess exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from such things as non-perception, one may resort to the postulation of a distinction of properties (*dharma-bheda*), [asserting] that 'the nature of cognition arises from mental attention (*manaskāra*) whose essence is cognition,' and so forth."

The differentiation of properties, such as the nature of being perceived in accordance with their causes, is superimposed by conceptual construction through the distinction of the objects of causal operation;

since that [differentiation] does not exist, cognition is not manifold because it is non-different from them, and those [properties] are not different because they are not other than the single cognition— thus it is in both syllogisms.

"The reason is established. If this is so, then since those particularities, being constructed by conceptual thought (*kalpanā*), do not depend on the operation of causes— just like sky-lotuses and the like— it is not logical to assert that distinct particularities arise from the distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of their causes.

If you insist that [the causes] "depend" [on one another], then, since the nature of apprehension and so forth is established as being fashioned by the artisan of conceptual construction, the operation of the cause would be merely conceptual and could not be a real entity.
And in this way, the effect would be without a cause, because the operation of the cause is employed upon things whose natures are conceptually constructed.

Alternatively, if—out of fear of the aforementioned fault—you hold the view that the effect is a single, undivided whole, while the particularities are distinct and yet not separate from the essence of the effect; [then...]

In that case, since the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) are occupied by both distinct and non-distinct natures, they are in fact different— like the moon and the stars— and thus it follows by force of logic that the universal (*sāmānya*) is not merely distinct [from the particular];
furthermore, there is no fault characterized by the mutual contradiction of multiplicity and unity, but rather [the fault lies] in its being non-different from the nature of consciousness (*bodha*).

If it is admitted [that consciousness arises from form], the effect that is consciousness cannot arise from form because it is other than the nature of cognition, just like the self-nature of the nature of cognition. Alternatively, because it is not other than the aspect of the object, its arising from form would also be possible, just like the self-nature of the aspect of the object. Thus, within a single cause, both the possibility and impossibility of a single effect, as well as being both productive and non-productive simultaneously, are logically contradictory.
It might be argued:
"For indeed, an effect is seen as being produced.
That is incorrect.
Not every cognition, even if it is sublated by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is itself invalid;
otherwise, the perception of a double moon and the like would also have to be considered valid.
Now, as for the third position: that a single cause might produce multiple effects.
This is accepted [by you].

That is incorrect; for if multiple effects arise from a single cause, the non-difference of the cause does not entail the non-difference of the effect, and thus there would be a distinction [between them].
If [it is argued that] even difference is not the cause, then both difference and non-difference would be causeless for the universe.
If it is argued that even for that which is non-different, there exists such an excellence of its own nature (*ātmātiśaya*) by which a single cause produces multiple effects;
That cause produces one effect by means of a certain specific excellence; does it produce another by that very same excellence?
If it does so by that very same [excellence], how can there be a difference in the result?
Now, if it is by means of something else, then the non-difference of the cause is not logical; for there is no entity other than the excellence of its own nature (*ātma-atiśaya*).

This might be argued: if the cause produces the effect by attaining the very nature of the effect—as the Sāṃkhya maintains—then, because it would be contradictory for a single thing to attain multiple forms, the production of a plurality [of effects] would be illogical.

To the extent that the production of distinct and non-distinct effects occurs merely through the presence of a cause whose nature is restricted to producing distinction and non-distinction, this objection does not apply.
For this alone is the distinction or non-distinction of the effect based on the distinction or non-distinction of the cause:
namely, that from a cause whose nature is restricted to producing distinction and non-distinction, there arises an effect that is either distinct or non-distinct.
This too is false,
because this very investigation is being conducted here:
by what nature the eye produces the moment of the eye, does it produce the visual consciousness by that same [nature]?

If that [consciousness] were produced by that very same [nature], then that consciousness too would be the eye itself, because it is produced from a cause whose nature is to produce the eye, just like the eye.
Likewise, by whichever nature the eye produces visual consciousness, by that very same [nature] the eye [itself would be produced].
Thus, because it is produced from a cause whose nature is to produce visual consciousness, the eye too would be visual consciousness, just like visual consciousness.

Alternatively, if the eye were to possess the nature of both "eye" and "non-eye" because it is produced by causes that individually have the nature of producing both the eye and the non-eye, then likewise, consciousness would possess the nature of both "consciousness" and "non-consciousness" because it is produced by causes that individually have the nature of producing both consciousness and non-consciousness.
And if one accepts this [absurdity], then the refutation by direct perception and other means will all the more firmly embrace you.
Now, suppose it is held that the eye produces the momentary visual organ by one intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and produces visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) by another.
Are those two intrinsic natures distinct from the eye or non-distinct?

If they are distinct, then since a real entity is characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), those two alone would be the entities that produce [the effects], and the eye itself would be a non-entity because it would be performing no function.

Furthermore, if they were non-different [from the object], then even the eye— which is intended to be one— would have to possess differentiation, because it would be non-different from natures that are mutually distinct,
just like the two natures themselves.
And in that case, oneness would be lost.

Alternatively, there would be identity between the two intrinsic natures (svabhāva), because they are non-different from the single eye; thus, the fault already stated—namely, that "the eye [would possess] whatever intrinsic nature [belongs to the other]" and so forth—would apply here as well.

Now, if it is thought that a cause, having arisen from its own causes with the nature of producing a single [effect], produces a single effect just as it does, so too, having arisen from its own causes, it produces many;
those who speak thus have forgotten the very context of the discussion.

For, just as the production of many by a single [cause] was intended to be refuted, so too is the production of a single [effect] by a single [cause]. Why, then, is this said specifically against the Mādhyamika?
Even for one who is not a Mādhyamika, [the argument] is fruitless because he accepts that a single [cause] produces multiple [effects].

It might be argued: "If non-difference arises from a nature determined to produce difference, then the effect would not conform to the nature of the cause, which would entail the consequence of it being causeless. However, since from the eye—which possesses a nature determined to produce difference—there arises either the visual consciousness or the nature of the eye itself, how could difference not arise?

For it is not the case that an effect produces a distinct effect because it is accompanied by mutually distinct potencies with respect to its cause; rather, it does so by virtue of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
We shall now inquire into that very nature: what is this so-called "nature," which, being universal in form, [accounts for] the aforementioned manifold contradictions?
Thus, by disregarding that [objection], you were able to dwell in comfort, having set aside the burden of considering how to provide a rebuttal for others while protecting your own position.
If it is argued that this is due to the power of the reason (*hetu*) and its property (*dharma*), it is not so, because this has already been refuted previously.
Nor should it be said that "it has a visible form," because the nature of reality— which is devoid of the appearance of form and so forth—

is established by negating the forms such as arising and so on that are imagined based on the scriptures and other sources, even though they do not appear in a cognition that possesses the manifestation of form and the like; it is by means of such a cognition that reality is comprehended.

Or rather, that conventional consensus (lokapratīti) which exists within such a cognition is accepted as *saṃvṛti*; by it, this entire universe, whose nature is being perceived, is real, whereas otherwise it would be false.
Therefore, just as the relationship of cause and effect is unavoidable according to how things appear, so it being thus, when some people offer the following objection:

Existence (*bhāva*), concealment (*saṃvṛti*), and arising (*utpāda*)—by the term "existence," one accepts a thing that is simultaneously capable and incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Now, if arising is concealment, then regarding the statement "arising through concealment," since this would be accepted as "arising through arising," nothing undesirable follows.
Likewise, if non-arising is the ultimate (*paramārtha*), then the phrase "not arising ultimately" means "not arising through non-arising."
And thus, [the objection] that "it would be proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhyatā*) and so forth is stated;
however, due to ignorance of the definition of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), it is said incoherently out of mere pride, as it serves no purpose for the present context.
Now, the fourth position is that a single cause should produce a single effect.
That which is thus accepted does not shine at all;
for instance, if the eyes and other [senses] produce only their own homogeneous moments, they would lack the capacity to produce their own cognition.

The consequence of [the world] becoming blind, deaf, and so forth is clearly entailed. Furthermore, if it is admitted that [the sense organs] produce their own cognitions, then by the destruction of the very nature (*jāti*) of the eyes and other organs, after a single moment of cognition, neither the eyes and so forth nor cognition would exist; thus, blindness and the rest would effortlessly befall the entire world.

Therefore, those things which are dependently originated are, from the perspective of ultimate reality, delightful only when not subjected to analytical investigation, just like the camels and other creatures conjured by a magician.
And since all these entities, such as form and the rest, are likewise [dependently originated], this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Since the arising [of things] is seen in accordance with their appearance, the reason is not unestablished; since it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is not contradictory; and since the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) has been demonstrated for the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) by means of the preceding argument, it is not inconclusive.
By this logic, because its occurrence is dependent upon conditions, just as the word "as" (*yathā*) is merely conventional (*prājñaptika*), so too has the body of the Blessed Ones been established.

In that regard, it is "dependent on causes" because it is contingent upon its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*); it is "dependent on conditions" because it is produced by auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*); and it is "perfected through the application of manifold roots of merit" because it appears to those to be trained (*vineya*) by the power of their own roots of merit.
For the purpose of explaining the function of the aforementioned discernment of phenomena (*dharma-pratyavekṣā*), he says:
"Therefore, O son of good family," and so forth.

The meaning is this: since you will thus correctly understand all phenomena as unarisen and unceasing through the realization of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) according to the sequence just described, you will abandon the cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*) characterized by the adherence to existence and so forth by means of the knowledge of selflessness (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) which is its opposite; and by gradually removing the entire veil of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the veil of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) rooted therein, you will become fixed in unsurpassed enlightenment on the first stage and the subsequent ones.
Demonstrating that realization has arisen through the power of his unerring teaching of the Dharma to those to be trained, he says:
"In this, moreover," and so forth,
ending with "and no further doubt arises in me."

Because among those things that share a single security and well-being there is no abandonment of one while the other remains, when doubt is abandoned, the entire host of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing is also abandoned; and through the power of the teaching on the selflessness of phenomena and the efficacy of the path of seeing thus attained,
doubt does not arise again with respect to unsurpassed enlightenment.
"Based on the fulfillment of the roots of merit" means, with reference to the first stage, based on the preeminence of the perfection of generosity;
"for seven years" [is the meaning].
It is not that my compassion is deficient now, nor do I have any stinginess regarding the Dharma;
there is no "teacher's fist" on my part, nor is there any incapacity, nor am I of a nature inclined toward suffering.
My treatise is not yet finalized; I do not deliberate upon it, nor have I reached its conclusion. My disciples are neither capable of understanding it, nor are they respectful toward it.
Making it known that he would not teach by which [path], and causing [them] to feel deep yearning,
the Blessed One remained in seclusion for two months and half a month.
According to this principle, some maintain that [the Buddha] remained for exactly seven years in order to test the purity of the noble Sadāprarudita’s resolute intention (*āśaya*).
Others hold that it was for the purpose of purifying in every aspect the seven factors of enlightenment (*sambodhyaṅga*) attained through the power of realizing the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
He states that through the purification of the intention and by the power of cultivation, an appearance of signs arises that is free from error.
Then indeed, Sadāprarudita, and so forth.
"Having reflected" means having thought in this way.
Even though the supernormal power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhyabhijñā*) was possible, no worship was performed by means of it;
this is to be understood as being like taking payment for the sale of one's body.
"What kind of perfection of wisdom did he teach? and so forth.
Regarding that, [the passage begins] "This is the [teaching] of Dharmodgata," and so on.

Although all these modes of teaching, such as the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*), are equal insofar as they illuminate the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), nevertheless, because they are of human origin, these [passages] would indicate the intention of the speaker through their specific effects.

Therefore, some maintain that because they belong to an uninterrupted lineage of oral tradition (*sampradāya*), the distinction in their meaning should be understood through the indication of their intended purpose (*abhiprāya*).
Now, that very opinion is set forth.

In this regard, first, for the purpose of demonstrating the nature of each of the sixfold stages of realization— beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and culminating in the serial realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*)—
there are eighteen phrases beginning with "by the equality of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmasamatayā*).

Following that, for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the fourfold single-moment realization (*ekakṣaṇābhisamaya*), there are four phrases beginning with "by the boundlessness of the earth element" (*pṛthivīdhātvaparyantatayā*).

Immediately following that, there is the single phrase "by way of the boundlessness of the space element" (*ākāśadhātvaparyantatayā*), for the purpose of making known that the three bodies (*kāya*) have the single flavor of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Thereafter, there are the three phrases beginning with "by way of the boundlessness of the consciousness element" (*vijñānadhātvaparyantatayā*), for the purpose of revealing the essential nature of the three bodies—the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation bodies.

And immediately after that, there is the passage beginning with "by way of the non-apprehension of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmānupalabdhitayā*), for the purpose of illustrating the activity of establishing the Dharma body (*dharmakāya*) upon the stages of the Bodhisattva—consisting of the eight accumulations and the levels of resolute belief—as well as upon the stage of the Tathāgata, according to the capacity of those to be trained.
The collective meaning is that these four phrases are to be understood. As for the meaning of the individual words, it has already been largely analyzed and thus is not analyzed further.

Through the empowerment of the noble Dharmodgata and by the power of his own vows, merit, and gnosis, there arise—by way of the sequence of the production of gnosis consisting of hearing and reflection—the modes of teaching the Perfection of Wisdom, which has as its intrinsic nature the eightfold clear realization as previously described.
Regarding the concentrations (*samādhi*):

he says that they arose for the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita as mere appearances lasting only for that duration, like those in the state of dreaming—beginning with the words, "Then, indeed, of Sadāprarudita... and so forth.

The meditative concentration (*samādhi*) established in which one realizes the equality of all phenomena is called the "Samādhi of the Equality of All Phenomena"; likewise, the "Samādhi of the Isolation from All Phenomena," and so forth, should be described.

However, in every respect, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtras if these meditative concentrations, which have the Perfection of Wisdom as their object as previously specified, were to appear with a fixed or solid manifestation in the form of realization.

For it would contradict the literal meaning of the Sūtra, which states that Buddhahood is attained through three incalculable aeons (*kalpāsaṃkhyeya*) as follows: by the first incalculable aeon, starting from the stage of equipment (*sambhārabhūmi*) up to the first bhūmi is accomplished; by the second, beginning with the Vimalā bhūmi up to the seventh bhūmi; and by the third incalculable aeon, starting from the Acālā bhūmi up to the Buddha-bhūmi. Thus, [the literal reading] would be contradicted.

Because of the commonality of the three [categories], it is said that [the path is traversed] "in three incalculable eons," but not in an ultimate sense; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in explaining such sūtras as being of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
For instance, while fulfilling the stage of equipment (*sambhārabhūmi*), one passes through one incalculable eon;
immediately thereafter, while perfecting the stage of conduct through aspiration (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), one brings two incalculable eons to completion.

Thereafter, beginning from the *pramuditā* (Joyful) stage up to the *dharmameghā* (Cloud of Dharma) Bodhisattva stage, a Bodhisattva completes each stage over three incalculable eons (*kalpāsaṃkhyeya*) and attains the Buddha-stage of *samantaprabhā* (Universal Radiance). Thus, Buddhahood is attained through thirty-three incalculable eons; this is the view of the venerable Master Vasubandhu.

Furthermore, by the power of the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) based on the teaching of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which consists of the eight realizations (*aṣṭābhisamaya*) as previously described, many gateways of concentration (*samādhimukha*) are realized even on the very first stage, and so forth.
"Thus, these are the principal ones," and so forth.
Here, it is the means for accomplishing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that are the "gateways to concentration" (*samādhimukha*), and not the concentrations themselves; [as it is said]:
"On the first stage (*bhūmi*), the Joyful (*pramuditā*), one attains a hundred concentrations."
Because it is stated thus in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:
"Or rather, the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhimukha*) are precisely the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of meditative concentration."
In this regard, it should be understood that the mention of "one hundred" is intended as an illustration.
The thirty-first chapter, titled "Dharmodgata," in the *Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka*, a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The thirty-second chapter.
In order to explain the function of those very meditative concentrations that have been correctly attained, he says:
"And as soon as they are acquired, Subhūti," and so forth.
Furthermore, in order to generate reverence and for the sake of entrustment, he provides an introductory statement, saying:
"Thereupon, the Blessed One... and so forth.
By this also...
Since this [perfection] was so effective for the noble Sadāprarudita,
the meaning is that it is not only by the method previously mentioned; rather,
through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata— due to its great benefits and because of the many obstacles— it could not be written down even hastily.
Therefore, having introduced the subject through the power of the Tathāgata, he spoke as follows to announce this entrustment:
"Therefore then, Ānanda," and so forth.
What is the basis for this detailed entrustment?
Anticipating the question, "For what reason? he says:
"For herein, in this Perfection of Wisdom," and so forth.
Clarifying that very point, he says:
"What do you think? and so forth.

Thus, by way of favoring sentient beings who delight in either concise or detailed expositions, all eight topics—beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and ending with the *dharmakāya* together with its activities—are fully established.
Alternatively, first, the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) consists of the three types of omniscience, beginning with the knowledge of all aspects, which serve as the objective points to be aimed at.

Then, for the sake of mastery, one applies oneself to the cultivation of the three types of omniscience; thus, the "application to the three types of omniscience" (*trisarvajñatā-prayoga*) is the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*).

Following that, through intense practice, there is the attainment of excellence; thus, the "culminating clear realization" (*mūrdhābhisamaya*) is the stage of the excellence of the three types of omniscience.

Then, for one who has attained reliance upon the realized object, there is the refinement of the meaning through its analysis both individually and collectively; this is the sequential realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*) consisting of the stages of the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*).

Following that, because of the state of proceeding toward excellence, there is the perfect awakening in a single moment (*samyagekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), which is the stage of culmination regarding the three types of omniscience.

Then, "its fruit" refers to the Dharma-body together with its activity, which is the maturation of the three types of omniscience. Thus, out of compassion for sentient beings who prefer a medium-length treatment, this Mother of the Victors should be explained according to the sixfold summary of topics as previously described.
And so it has been said:
"The definition, its application, its excellence, its sequence,

its culmination, and its maturation— this is another summary of the six subjects. (1) Alternatively, first, the object (*viṣaya*) consists of the three types of omniscience, such as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), because it is the domain of engagement.
How does he apply himself?
Immediately following that, the fourfold clear realization beginning with the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*) is the application, which has the nature of the cause.
What is the fruit of that very object for one who thus engages in practice?

Following that, the Dharmakāya is the fruit of karma; thus, this Blessed Lady should be explained in exactly this way through a threefold summary of meaning, in accordance with sentient beings who take pleasure in concise and extremely concise expositions.
And so it has been said:
"The object is threefold, the cause is fourfold, the application is fourfold in nature;
the dharma-body is the fruit, and activity is another—thus is the summary of the meaning in three ways.
(2) Thus spoke the Blessed One, and so forth.

By the mere presence of that Person, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), teachings emerge at will from the mouths of the wicked and others; according to this principle, because he is determined to be the teacher for those disciples who are capable of liberation, the Blessed One—having attained joy and being delighted in heart—spoke, that is, uttered, the entire reality of the jewel of the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtras as just described.
